items: The Act of Union (1800) abolished the Irish Parliament; from 1 January 1801 Ireland was part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, governed by Westminster and a separate executive in Dublin.
Ireland sent 100 MPs to the House of Commons, a small minority of its roughly 650 members, so Irish measures depended on British votes.
Ireland was represented in the House of Lords by 28 Irish representative peers elected for life by the Irish peerage, and by four Church of Ireland bishops sitting in rotation.
The Union also united the Church of England and the Church of Ireland, so the Protestant Church of Ireland remained the established church of a mainly Catholic country.
William Pitt had hoped to follow the Union with Catholic Emancipation, but George III refused, and Pitt resigned in 1801; this broken expectation was the root of the Catholic question.
The Lord Lieutenant (viceroy), usually a British peer, headed the Irish executive and lived in Dublin Castle and the Viceregal Lodge in the Phoenix Park.
The Chief Secretary, a politician who sat in the Commons, ran Irish business in Parliament and became the most powerful figure in Irish government; Robert Peel held the post from 1812 to 1818.
The Under-Secretary was the senior permanent official in Dublin Castle, the name used for the whole Irish administration, which stayed separate from Whitehall.
Grand juries, chosen by the county sheriff from the leading Protestant landowners, levied the county cess (a local tax on land) and paid for roads, bridges, jails and courthouses.
Unpaid magistrates (justices of the peace), nearly all Protestant landowners, tried minor cases at petty sessions and quarter sessions, so most Catholics met the law through their landlords.
Town corporations such as Dublin Corporation were closed, self-electing Protestant bodies, which kept Catholics out of municipal office until the reforms of 1840.
Rural unrest by agrarian secret societies such as the Whiteboys and Ribbonmen led Peel to create the Peace Preservation Force in 1814, a paid force sent into disturbed districts at local expense.
The Irish Constabulary Act of 1822 set up a county constabulary under four provincial inspectors-general, Ireland's first regular rural police.

The Constabulary Act of 1836 merged these forces into the Irish Constabulary, an armed, centrally controlled national police under an inspector-general in Dublin; it became the Royal Irish Constabulary in 1867.
Ireland was policed more heavily and more centrally than Britain, which showed that the Union rested on coercion as well as consent.
The Relief Act of 1793 had already given Catholics the vote on the same terms as Protestants, entry to the bar and to junior army commissions, and the right to sit on juries.

The county franchise belonged to forty-shilling freeholders, men who held land on a lease for life worth at least 40 shillings a year; landlords created many such tenancies so their tenants would vote as they directed.
Voting was open (spoken aloud at the poll), so a tenant who defied his landlord could be identified and evicted.
Catholics still could not sit in Parliament, because MPs had to take the oath of supremacy and declare against transubstantiation, which no Catholic could do.
They were also barred from the senior judiciary, the rank of King's Counsel, high government office and the senior ranks of the army and navy.
The veto controversy: from 1808 some supporters of relief proposed that the Crown should have a veto over the appointment of Catholic bishops as a security for Emancipation.

The Irish bishops rejected the veto, and in 1814 the Quarantotti rescript from Rome, which accepted it, was repudiated in Ireland; O'Connell led lay opposition, and the issue split the Catholic leadership and stalled the cause after 1815.
The Catholic Association turned a gentry petitioning campaign into the first mass political movement in Irish or British history.
Daniel O'Connell and Richard Lalor Sheil founded the Catholic Association in Dublin in May 1823; at first it was a small body of lawyers and gentry paying a full membership fee of one guinea a year.
In 1824 O'Connell introduced associate membership at a penny a month, the Catholic Rent, which brought in tenant farmers, labourers and townspeople in their hundreds of thousands.
The Rent was collected through the parishes by collectors under the supervision of the local priest, so the Church's parish network became the Association's organisation.
Its funds paid for lawyers to defend Catholics in the courts, petitions to Parliament, newspaper publicity and, later, election campaigns.
Priests read the Association's addresses from the altar and chaired meetings; Bishop James Doyle of Kildare and Leighlin (who signed himself JKL) was its most influential clerical supporter.
The Association widened its demands beyond Emancipation to tithes, the grand jury system and the treatment of Catholics in the courts, which made it attractive to the rural poor.
O'Connell insisted on strictly legal, non-violent methods while warning that the government could not ignore millions of organised Catholics, a tactic of moral force backed by implied threat.
Alarmed by its growth, the government passed the Unlawful Societies (Ireland) Act in 1825 to suppress the Association.
O'Connell evaded the Act by re-forming the body as the New Catholic Association in July 1825, limiting it to activities the law still allowed.
In 1825 Sir Francis Burdett's Catholic relief bill passed the Commons but was defeated in the Lords, showing that petitioning alone would not succeed.
At the general election of June 1826 the Association used the Rent organisation as election committees in County Waterford, with Thomas Wyse a leading organiser.

The forty-shilling freeholders, led to the poll by their priests, elected the pro-Emancipation Protestant Henry Villiers-Stuart and unseated Lord George Beresford, whose family had dominated the county.
Pro-Emancipation candidates also won in Louth, Monaghan and Westmeath, breaking the landlords' hold over tenant votes.

Landlords punished some freeholders who had voted against them, and the Association used part of the Rent to support those evicted; the lesson was that the Catholic vote could defeat the ascendancy at the polls.
In 1828 the Wellington government appointed William Vesey-FitzGerald, MP for County Clare, as President of the Board of Trade; taking office meant he had to stand for re-election.
Vesey-FitzGerald was a popular landlord who supported Emancipation, but the Association decided to oppose any member of a government that resisted it.
O'Connell himself stood, although as a Catholic he could not take the oath needed to sit if elected.
Priests marched their parishioners in orderly columns to the poll at Ennis, and the campaign passed off without violence.
O'Connell won on 5 July 1828 by 2,057 votes to 982, defeating a sitting minister.
The result faced the government with the prospect of Catholic candidates winning most Irish county seats at the next general election and being unable to take them.
O'Connell was not allowed to take his seat in 1828; he was returned unopposed for Clare again in July 1829, after the Relief Act, and entered the Commons in 1830.
The Duke of Wellington (Arthur Wellesley), prime minister from 1828, and Robert Peel, Home Secretary, had both opposed Emancipation.
They feared that refusing it after Clare risked a rising or civil war in Ireland, where many soldiers of the army were themselves Irish Catholics.
The Lord Lieutenant, the Marquess of Anglesey, warned that Ireland was close to rebellion and openly favoured concession; he was recalled in early 1829.
The Commons had already voted for Catholic relief several times, so resistance depended on the Lords and the king.
The repeal of the Test and Corporation Acts in 1828, which had removed the disabilities of Protestant dissenters, weakened the argument that the constitution must remain exclusively Anglican.
Peel concluded that civil strife was a greater danger than Emancipation, and Wellington overcame George IV's resistance by threatening resignation in March 1829.
To make concession acceptable, Parliament first passed an act in February 1829 suppressing the Catholic Association, which O'Connell then dissolved.
The Roman Catholic Relief Act received royal assent on 13 April 1829.
Granted: Catholics could sit in both Houses of Parliament under a new oath of allegiance, and could hold almost all civil and military offices, including judgeships.
Withheld: Catholics could not be Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, Lord Chancellor or regent, or advise the Crown on appointments in the established church.
Restrictions: Catholic bishops could not take the titles of existing Church of Ireland sees, and the Act placed limits on religious orders, especially the Jesuits, and on public processions.
Its companion, the Parliamentary Elections (Ireland) Act 1829, raised the county franchise from forty shillings to £10, cutting the Irish electorate from about 216,000 to about 37,000.
The Act was not retrospective, so O'Connell had to seek re-election rather than take the Clare seat he had already won.
Protestant reaction: Brunswick Clubs had been formed in 1828 to defend the Protestant constitution, Orange opinion felt betrayed, and O'Connell called the Home Secretary Orange Peel.
Peel resigned his Oxford University seat in 1829 because he had reversed his position and wished to seek his constituents' approval; he lost the by-election and returned to Parliament for Westbury.

Wellington fought a duel with the Earl of Winchilsea in March 1829 after Winchilsea accused him of plotting against Protestantism; ultra-Tory anger split the Tory party and helped bring down Wellington's government in 1830.
Born on 6 August 1775 at Carhen near Cahersiveen, Co. Kerry, into a Catholic gentry family, he was raised by his uncle Maurice O'Connell of Derrynane and later inherited Derrynane.
He was educated at St Omer and Douai in France, which he left in 1793; the violence of the French Revolution left him with a lifelong hatred of political bloodshed, reinforced by the 1798 rebellion.
He was called to the Irish bar in 1798 and became the most successful barrister in Ireland, known for defending poor Catholics in the courts.
His first public speech, in January 1800, was against the Union, and he led the anti-veto party in the Catholic Committee and Catholic Board in the 1810s.
In 1815 he killed John D'Esterre in a duel arising from his attack on Dublin Corporation; he regretted it for the rest of his life.
Participant: he founded and led the Catholic Association, invented the Catholic Rent, decided to stand in Clare and was the campaign's chief speaker and strategist.
His methods were mass organisation, alliance with the clergy, legal agitation, monster petitions, public meetings, newspapers and the threat that the movement might slip out of control.
Contemporaries: Catholics hailed him as the Liberator; Protestants and the British press saw him as a dangerous demagogue and agitator.

Historians such as Oliver MacDonagh present him as the founder of modern mass democratic politics, while noting that Emancipation was conceded by Wellington and Peel to avoid a crisis, at the cost of the forty-shilling vote.
For O'Connell: the Rent, the Association and the Clare candidacy were his ideas, and without the crisis he created, Wellington and Peel would not have moved in 1829.
Against: the clergy supplied the organisation, Wyse and local leaders won Waterford, British Whigs and liberal Tories had long backed relief, and the final decision was the ministers' own.
Political dimension: Catholics could now enter Parliament and office, and a disciplined, peaceful mass movement had forced a reluctant government to change the constitution.
Political limits: the £10 franchise disfranchised most of the voters who had won the victory, and Protestants still dominated the magistracy, grand juries, corporations and Dublin Castle.
Religious dimension: the campaign fused Catholic and national identity and gave the Church a central place in Irish politics, which strengthened sectarian division.
Religious limits: the Church of Ireland stayed established and Catholics still paid tithes to it, the grievance behind the Tithe War of the 1830s.
Contemporary British view: a dangerous surrender to agitation; Irish Catholic view: a triumph that proved organised peaceful pressure worked.
Later view: the Emancipation campaign was O'Connell's greatest success because its aim was limited and could be granted within the Union, unlike Repeal later.
In the 1830s O'Connell led a group of Irish Repeal MPs at Westminster and, when Repeal got nowhere, worked with the Whigs to win practical reforms.
Returned unopposed for Clare in July 1829, O'Connell entered the Commons in 1830 and gave up his legal practice; supporters funded him through an annual collection, the O'Connell Tribute.
He supported Earl Grey's Whig government over parliamentary reform; the Irish Reform Act of 1832 raised Ireland's MPs from 100 to 105 but left the Irish electorate small.
At the 1832 election about 39 MPs pledged to Repeal were returned, but his Repeal motion of April 1834 was defeated by 523 votes to 38.
The Lichfield House Compact (1835) was an informal agreement under which O'Connell and his MPs kept the Whigs under Lord Melbourne in office in return for Irish reforms and fair appointments.

Under the Lord Lieutenant Lord Mulgrave, Chief Secretary Lord Morpeth and Under-Secretary Thomas Drummond (1835–1840), Catholics and liberals were appointed to office, stipendiary (paid) magistrates were used and the police were centralised in the 1836 Irish Constabulary.
Drummond told Tipperary magistrates in 1838 that property has its duties as well as its rights, and the Orange Order dissolved itself in 1836 after a Commons inquiry.
The Municipal Corporations (Ireland) Act 1840 abolished most of the closed Protestant corporations and gave the rest an elected council on a £10 householder franchise.
O'Connell became Lord Mayor of Dublin in November 1841, the first Catholic to hold the office since the reign of James II.
The Whig alliance won no Repeal and only a limited tithe reform, and when Peel's Conservatives took office in 1841 O'Connell returned to agitation.
Tithe was a tax of about a tenth of agricultural produce, paid in money by the occupiers of land to support the clergy of the Church of Ireland, the church of a small minority.

Catholics resented paying for a church they did not attend; the Tithe Composition Act of 1823 converted tithe into fixed money payments and extended it to pasture, bringing graziers and strong farmers into the protest.
The campaign of non-payment began at Graiguenamanagh, Co. Kilkenny, in 1830–31, where farmers organised by the Catholic clergy refused payment and protected each other's livestock from seizure.
Collectors (tithe proctors) and process servers seized cattle and goods for arrears, escorted by police and soldiers; crowds gathered at the sound of horns and chapel bells to block them.
At Newtownbarry (Bunclody), Co. Wexford, in June 1831 yeomanry fired on a crowd resisting a seizure and killed more than a dozen people.
At Carrickshock, Co. Kilkenny, on 14 December 1831 a crowd attacked a process server and his police escort, killing the process server and more than ten policemen.
At Gortroe near Rathcormac, Co. Cork, on 18 December 1834 soldiers fired on a crowd trying to stop a seizure from a widow, killing about twelve people.
The protest made tithe uncollectable in much of the south: arrears mounted, and the government had to advance money to clergy left without income.
The Whigs split over the appropriation of surplus Church revenues to non-religious purposes, which O'Connell supported, so a settlement was delayed.

The Tithe Rentcharge Act (August 1838) cut the charge by about a quarter and made landlords responsible for paying it as part of the rent, which ended the open conflict; tithe was only abolished with disestablishment in 1869.
Ireland had no statutory system of poor relief before 1838; relief depended on charity, a few houses of industry and county infirmaries.

A royal commission chaired by the Church of Ireland Archbishop of Dublin, Richard Whately (1833–1836), argued that Irish poverty was too widespread for workhouses and recommended assisted emigration, public works and agricultural improvement.
The Whig government rejected the Whately report as too costly and sent George Nicholls, an English poor law commissioner, who toured Ireland in 1836 and recommended the English workhouse system.
The Irish Poor Law Act (July 1838) divided Ireland into 130 unions, each with a workhouse run by a board of guardians elected by ratepayers, with local magistrates sitting ex officio.

Relief was given only inside the workhouse (indoor relief), and conditions were made deliberately harsher than the life of the poorest labourer so that only the truly destitute would apply (the workhouse test).
Families were separated by sex and age on entry, inmates wore a uniform and worked, and admission carried a stigma that the poor deeply resented.
The cost was met by a poor rate on property, shared between landlord and occupier, and from 1843 landlords paid the whole rate on holdings valued at under £4.
The workhouses had room for about 100,000 people and were designed for normal destitution, not mass famine; most had only recently opened when the potato failed in 1845.
O'Connell founded the Repeal Association in April 1840 (first called the National Association for Full and Prompt Justice or Repeal), with a penny-a-month Repeal Rent modelled on the Catholic Rent.
Repeal meant restoring a separate Irish Parliament under the Crown, not separation from Britain; O'Connell often hinted he would accept a federal compromise or substantial reform instead.
Support grew slowly until Dublin Corporation, led by O'Connell, debated Repeal in early 1843, and he declared 1843 Repeal Year.
The Catholic clergy again acted as local organisers, and Father Theobald Mathew's temperance movement, though separate, supplied disciplined crowds and bands.
About forty monster meetings were held in 1843, mostly on sites with historic associations such as Tara, Mullaghmast and Clontarf.
The largest was at the Hill of Tara on 15 August 1843; supporters claimed up to a million attended, and even hostile estimates ran to hundreds of thousands.
The Nation newspaper publicised the meetings and gave the campaign a younger, more militant tone.

In May 1843 Peel told the Commons that he would accept any alternative, even war, rather than the dismemberment of the empire, and the government dismissed Repeal magistrates and reinforced the army in Ireland.
The government banned the monster meeting called for Clontarf on 8 October 1843 the evening before it was due, and troops and artillery occupied the site.
O'Connell cancelled the meeting and sent people home, fearing a massacre; this preserved his policy of moral force but exposed the fact that he would not go beyond the law.
He and other leaders, including Charles Gavan Duffy, were arrested in October 1843 and convicted of conspiracy in 1844 by a jury from which Catholics had been excluded.
Sentenced to a year in prison and a £2,000 fine, he spent about three months in comfortable confinement in the Richmond Bridewell before the House of Lords quashed the verdict in September 1844.

Peel combined coercion with conciliation: the Devon Commission on land (1843), the Charitable Bequests Act (1844), a permanent and larger grant to Maynooth College (1845) and the Queen's Colleges (1845).
O'Connell was 68 in 1843, and after prison his energy and health declined; he talked of a federal alternative, which confused supporters.
From 1845 the Famine destroyed the Repeal Rent and the mass following, and O'Connell renewed his alliance with the Whigs when Lord John Russell took office in 1846.

Why Repeal failed: both British parties, Parliament and Protestant Ulster opposed it; Peel called O'Connell's bluff at Clontarf; the movement was overwhelmingly Catholic; and Famine and the Young Ireland split followed.
Young Ireland was a group of mostly young, middle-class writers within the Repeal movement who developed a cultural idea of the Irish nation.

Charles Gavan Duffy, a Catholic journalist from Monaghan, Thomas Davis, a Protestant barrister from Mallow, and John Blake Dillon, a Catholic barrister from Mayo, founded The Nation, first published on 15 October 1842.
The Nation became the most widely read paper in Ireland, passed from hand to hand and read aloud in reading rooms; it published history, ballads and essays.
Its idea of nationality was cultural and non-sectarian: a nation shared history, culture and, ideally, the Irish language, and included Protestants as well as Catholics.
The Library of Ireland, a series of cheap books on Irish history and literature launched by Duffy, extended the paper's educational work.

Young Ireland disagreed with O'Connell over federalism (1844), over his alliance with the Whigs, and over the Queen's Colleges (1845), which Davis welcomed as mixed education and O'Connell condemned as godless.
The final break came over the peace resolutions of July 1846, which O'Connell proposed so that the Association would declare the use of force never justified, clearing the way for his Whig alliance.
Thomas Francis Meagher's Sword Speech in reply, refusing to condemn force in all circumstances, led Young Ireland to walk out of the Repeal Association.
The Young Irelanders founded the Irish Confederation in January 1847, led by William Smith O'Brien, a Protestant landowner and MP for Limerick, with Duffy and Meagher.
James Fintan Lalor argued in The Nation that the land question should be linked to national independence, an idea that influenced John Mitchel.
Mitchel broke with the Confederation's moderates, founded the United Irishman in February 1848 to preach open revolution, and urged tenants to refuse rent and resist food exports.
The February 1848 revolution in France, which overthrew Louis Philippe, encouraged the Confederates to plan a rising, and Smith O'Brien and Meagher took an address of support to Paris.

Mitchel was convicted under the new Treason Felony Act in May 1848 and transported for fourteen years, and in July 1848 the government suspended habeas corpus, forcing the leaders into a hasty rising.
On 29 July 1848 Smith O'Brien's small band besieged police in the Widow McCormack's farmhouse at Ballingarry, Co. Tipperary; two rebels were killed and the rest dispersed.

Reasons for failure: no preparation or weapons, a starving and demoralised population, strong opposition from the Catholic clergy, government foreknowledge, and leaders who would not risk lives or property.

Smith O'Brien, Meagher, Terence MacManus and Patrick O'Donohoe were sentenced to death for high treason at Clonmel; the sentences were commuted to transportation to Van Diemen's Land, while Dillon escaped to America.

James Stephens, wounded at Ballingarry, and John O'Mahony, who also took part in the rising, escaped to France and later founded the Fenian movement, so 1848 became a link in the physical force tradition.
Aims after 1829: Repeal of the Union, the end of tithes, fair government and a share of office for Catholics, all by constitutional means.
Participant: he led the Irish party at Westminster, made the Lichfield House Compact, founded the Repeal Association, called Repeal Year and decided to cancel Clontarf.
He was shaped by events as much as he shaped them: Peel's firmness in 1843, the Famine from 1845 and Young Ireland's challenge set the limits of what he could achieve.

Strengths: an unrivalled orator and organiser, master of peaceful mass agitation, skilled parliamentarian and lawyer, and committed to religious liberty for all, including Jews and dissenters, and to the abolition of slavery.

Weaknesses: his reliance on bluff, his willingness to drop Repeal for Whig favours, rigid control of the movement, the patronage given to his family, and a Catholic-centred movement that alienated Protestants.
He died at Genoa on 15 May 1847 on his way to Rome; his heart was buried in Rome and his body in Glasnevin Cemetery, Dublin.
Contemporaries: to Catholic Ireland he was the Liberator; to the Times and British Tories he was a dangerous agitator; to Young Ireland in 1846 he was a tired leader who had sold Repeal to the Whigs.

Historians: Oliver MacDonagh and others see him as the founder of constitutional nationalism and mass democratic politics in Europe; critics note that Repeal failed and that his movement deepened the link between Catholicism and nationalism.
Born on 14 October 1814 in Mallow, Co. Cork, the son of an army surgeon, Davis was a Protestant who studied at Trinity College Dublin and was called to the bar in 1838.
He joined the Repeal Association in 1841 and co-founded The Nation in 1842, becoming its leading writer.
His essays argued for a nationality above religion, for the Irish language (he wrote that a people without a language of its own is only half a nation), for Irish history and for self-reliance.
His ballads, including A Nation Once Again and The West's Asleep, made romantic nationalism popular among the young.
He backed mixed, non-denominational education and welcomed the Queen's Colleges in 1845, which led to a bitter public clash with O'Connell.
He died of scarlet fever on 16 September 1845, aged 30, before the Famine took hold and before the peace resolutions split the movement.
Participant in the Repeal movement and Young Ireland, he was a witness rather than a leader in politics; his influence came through ideas and writing.
Contemporaries such as Duffy revered him as the soul of Young Ireland, while O'Connell's Catholic supporters distrusted his secular, mixed-education views.
Historians see him as the founder of cultural nationalism, an inspiration to Pearse and the Gaelic revival, and note that his ideal of a nation uniting Protestant and Catholic was never realised.
O'Connell's achievement: he created mass constitutional politics, won practical reforms with the Whigs and gave Irish Catholics political confidence.
O'Connell's limit: Repeal, his central aim after 1829, failed completely, and the movement collapsed after Clontarf, his ill health and the Famine.
Tithe War achievement: popular resistance forced the 1838 settlement; limit: tithe was only shifted into rent, and the established Church survived until 1869.
Poor Law achievement: Ireland gained a national relief system and local elected boards; limit: the workhouse model failed when the Famine created mass rather than individual destitution.
Young Ireland's achievement: The Nation created a cultural, non-sectarian idea of the nation and a body of history and ballads that shaped later nationalism.
Young Ireland's limit: it split the national movement in 1846, its rising of 1848 was a fiasco, and its non-sectarian ideal won few Protestants.

Contribution to nationalism: O'Connell left the constitutional tradition later taken up by Butt and Parnell; Young Ireland left the cultural and physical force traditions taken up by the Fenians and the Gaelic revival.
Land was the basis of wealth and power, and rural society was a ladder running from a small, mainly Protestant landlord class down to millions of landless labourers.
About 10,000 landlords, mostly Protestant, owned nearly all the land; many held estates in more than one county.
Absentee landlords lived in England or Dublin and ran their estates through agents, so rents left the locality and improvements were rare.
Middlemen leased large farms from landlords on long leases and sublet them in smaller lots at higher rents; landlords increasingly ended such leases after 1815.
Strong farmers held 30 acres or more, employed labour and often grazed cattle; they were the most secure and prosperous tenants.
Smallholders held between about 5 and 30 acres, mostly as tenants-at-will with no lease, who could be evicted at short notice.
Cottiers rented a cabin and a potato patch, paying their rent mainly in labour for the farmer or landlord.
Landless labourers hired conacre, a patch of manured ground taken for one season to grow potatoes, often at very high rents.
Most tenants had no legal security of tenure, and any improvement they made to their holding belonged to the landlord, which discouraged investment.
Ireland's population rose from about 5 million around 1800 to about 8.2 million at the 1841 census.
Early marriage and large families were common among the poor, because a couple needed only a potato patch and a cabin to set up home.
Holdings were subdivided among sons, so that by 1841 nearly half of all holdings were under 5 acres.
The potato yielded more food per acre than any grain, grew on poor soil and, with buttermilk, gave a nutritious diet.
By the 1840s about 3 million people depended on the potato almost entirely; an adult labourer ate up to about 12–14 lb a day.
The heavy-cropping but poor-quality lumper variety had spread widely among the poor, and potatoes could not be stored from one season to the next.
The 1841 census classed about 40% of all houses as fourth-class: one-roomed mud cabins, the lowest category of housing.
Wartime demand had pushed up grain prices and rents during the French Wars; after Waterloo in 1815 prices fell steeply, but rents fell slowly.
Tenants fell into arrears and many landlords, themselves heavily in debt from wartime spending and family settlements, could not afford to invest.
Landlords began clearing smallholders and middlemen to consolidate farms, especially for more profitable pasture.

Rural industry declined: hand spinning and weaving of linen outside north-east Ulster collapsed against factory competition, and the Irish cotton industry declined after protective duties ended in 1824.
Partial famines and fever followed harvest failures in 1816–1817, 1822 and the early 1830s, as well as several local failures in the late 1830s.
Agrarian secret societies such as the Whiteboys, Rockites and Ribbonmen attacked landlords, agents and new tenants who took farms after evictions.

The Devon Commission (1843–1845), a royal commission of landlords chaired by the Earl of Devon, found insecurity of tenure, lack of compensation for improvements and extreme poverty, but no reform followed.
Seasonal migration to Britain for the harvest, and emigration of about a million people between 1815 and 1845, were the poor's main escape routes.
Phytophthora infestans, a fungus-like organism probably brought from North America, rotted potatoes in the ground and in storage; it was first reported in Ireland in September 1845.
1845: between a third and a half of the crop was lost, causing severe hardship but few deaths in the first winter.
1846: the blight destroyed almost the entire crop, and the worst winter in memory followed.
1847 (Black '47): deaths peaked in the first half of the year; the small crop that year was healthy, but so few seed potatoes had been planted that hunger continued.
1848: the blight returned and the crop failed again, and 1849 brought further failure in parts of the west and a cholera epidemic.
Most victims died of disease rather than starvation: typhus and relapsing fever (both spread by lice), dysentery, scurvy and, in 1849, cholera.
Doctors, clergy, relief workers and workhouse staff died in large numbers from fever caught from the people they treated.

Regional variation: Connacht and west Munster suffered most, with Mayo, Sligo, Roscommon, Galway, Clare and west Cork worst hit; the east and north-east suffered least, though parts of Ulster also lost heavily.
About one million people died between 1846 and 1851, and over a million emigrated; the population fell from about 8.2 million in 1841 to about 6.6 million in 1851.
Peel's Conservative government secretly bought about £100,000 of Indian corn (maize) in the United States through Baring Brothers in late 1845.
The maize was sold at cost through government depots to keep prices down; it was hard to grind, caused stomach pain if badly cooked, and was nicknamed Peel's brimstone for its yellow colour.

A Relief Commission, set up in November 1845 and later chaired by Sir Randolph Routh of the army commissariat, coordinated hundreds of local relief committees, which raised subscriptions and bought food.
The Board of Works ran public works such as road building to give the poor wages to buy food, with costs shared between the Treasury and the local county cess.
Peel used the crisis to repeal the Corn Laws in June 1846, which lowered grain prices in the long run but did little for Ireland immediately; his party split and he resigned.
Mortality in the first season was low, so Peel's measures were later judged the most effective of the Famine, although the failure of 1845 was only partial.
Lord John Russell's Whig government took office at the end of June 1846, committed to laissez-faire: the belief that government should not interfere with trade or the food market.
It refused to import food or control prices in most of Ireland, leaving supply to private merchants; government depots opened only in the west and sold at market prices.
The Labouchere Act (August 1846) relaunched the public works with the whole cost to be repaid from local taxes, and wages were set below local rates so as not to compete with private employers.
Numbers on the works rose to about 700,000 by March 1847; payment was by task work, often late, and weakened, poorly clad people worked in the hard winter of 1846–1847.
Wages could not keep up with food prices, which more than doubled, and the works produced many roads that led nowhere.
Faced with rising deaths and costs, the government closed the works from March 1847 and switched to direct feeding.
The Temporary Relief Act (the Soup Kitchen Act, February 1847) set up government soup kitchens run by local committees, giving free rations to the destitute.
By July 1847 about three million people a day received rations, the most effective and cheapest relief of the Famine, but the kitchens were closed by September 1847.
The Poor Law Extension Act (June 1847) made the poor law responsible for all further relief, so that Irish property would pay for Irish poverty, and allowed outdoor relief for the able-bodied.
Its Gregory clause, proposed by William Gregory, MP for Dublin, refused relief to anyone holding more than a quarter of an acre of land, forcing smallholders to surrender their land to qualify.
Landlords used the clause and the rising poor rates to clear estates, since they paid the rates on smaller holdings; evictions rose sharply from 1847.
Many western unions went bankrupt because their ratepayers were ruined, and workhouses, holding far more people than they were built for, became centres of fever.

The Rate-in-Aid Act (1849) imposed a national rate of 6d in the pound on every union to support about twenty-two bankrupt unions in the west; Ulster guardians protested that the north was paying for the south and west.
The government treated the Famine as over by 1850, although local distress and high mortality continued in the west.
Born in Taunton, Somerset, in 1807, Trevelyan served in the East India Company in Bengal before becoming Assistant Secretary to the Treasury, its senior permanent official, in 1840.
He ran the Treasury's Famine relief from 1845, controlling the purchase of Peel's maize, the public works, the food depots and the soup kitchens.

Participant: he was the civil servant most responsible for carrying out the Whig policy of 1846–1847, though ministers such as Russell and Charles Wood, Chancellor of the Exchequer, set its principles.
He was an evangelical Protestant and a firm believer in laissez-faire and political economy; he feared that generous relief would make the Irish dependent.
He saw the Famine as an act of Providence that would force changes in the Irish land system and population, and blamed Irish landlords and the moral character of the people.
He insisted that relief costs fall on Irish property, closed the soup kitchens in 1847 and declared the Famine over, and his article and book The Irish Crisis (1848) defended the policy.
Contemporaries: the government knighted him in 1848 for his work; Irish nationalists, many relief workers and some officials in Ireland condemned his rigidity.
Later career: co-author of the Northcote–Trevelyan Report (1854) that created a merit-based civil service, and Governor of Madras from 1859.

Historians: Cecil Woodham-Smith's The Great Hunger (1962) made him the villain of the Famine; Robin Haines (2004) argued he was a scapegoat for ministers and worked hard within his orders; most see his ideology as typical of the Whig government.
Strength: Peel's maize, relief committees and public works kept deaths low in 1845–1846.
Strength: the 1847 soup kitchens showed that direct feeding could reach three million people a day cheaply.
Weakness: the Whigs' faith in laissez-faire meant no control of food prices or exports, and the public works paid too little, too late, to people too weak to work.
Weakness: the decision that Irish property must pay, through the Poor Law from 1847, put the burden on the poorest unions just when they were bankrupt.
Weakness: the Gregory clause turned relief into a tool for clearance, and relief was cut back in 1847 while hunger continued.
Food exports: grain, cattle, pigs and butter continued to leave Irish ports, though from 1847 imports, mainly of maize, were several times greater than grain exports.
John Mitchel, writing in 1861, said that the Almighty sent the potato blight but the English created the Famine; this nationalist view made the Famine a central grievance against the Union.

Historians such as Cormac Ó Gráda and Christine Kinealy agree the scale of death was not inevitable and that a richer UK could have spent far more; most reject the charge of deliberate genocide but blame ideology, parsimony and indifference.
Government relief was limited by laissez-faire and by the rule that Irish property should pay, so charity filled gaps in food, clothing, seed and medical care.
Private relief came from Irish local committees, landlords, the churches, the Society of Friends, British charities, emigrants and donors across the world.
Under Peel in 1845–1846 local relief committees of landlords, clergy and merchants raised subscriptions, and the government added grants to the sums they collected.
The worst-hit western districts had the fewest resident gentry and merchants, so the areas that most needed local charity could raise the least.

Newspaper reports and drawings from places such as Skibbereen, Co. Cork, in the winter of 1846–1847, especially in the Illustrated London News, made the Famine known in Britain and America and set off the great appeals of 1847.
Irish Quakers, a small community of prosperous merchants, set up the Central Relief Committee in Dublin on 13 November 1846, with Joseph Bewley and Jonathan Pim among its secretaries.
English Quakers formed a London committee, and William Forster and others, including the young James Hack Tuke, toured the west in the winter of 1846–1847 and reported on what they saw.
Their published letters and reports described cabins full of the dying and gave British readers the most trusted eyewitness accounts of the Famine.
The Friends opened soup kitchens in Cork and elsewhere in the winter of 1846–1847, and gave boilers, food and money to local committees regardless of religion.
American Quakers and other donors sent food shipments to the Committee, which distributed them through its network of local correspondents.
The Friends refused to proselytise and kept careful accounts, which earned them trust among Catholics and lasting gratitude.
From mid-1847 they withdrew from mass feeding, concluding that only the government had the resources, and turned to longer-term projects: seed distribution, fisheries and spinning schemes.
Their Transactions of the Central Relief Committee (1852) became a key source on conditions and relief.
The British Relief Association was founded in London on 1 January 1847 by bankers and merchants including Lionel de Rothschild to raise funds for Ireland and the Scottish Highlands.
A royal letter from Queen Victoria was read in churches in January 1847, the Queen gave £2,000, and the national day of fast and humiliation in March 1847 brought in large collections.
The Association raised about £470,000, the largest single private fund, and worked closely with the government, distributing food through Routh's commissariat.
Its agent, the Polish explorer Count Paul Strzelecki, worked in Westport and the west and used the funds to feed schoolchildren in the poorest unions in 1847–1848.
American relief included two warships lent by Congress, the Jamestown, which reached Cork in April 1847, and the Macedonian, both loaded with food raised by public subscription.
Donations also came from Irish emigrants in America and Britain, from India, Australia and Canada, from the Choctaw Nation in the United States and from the Ottoman Sultan.
Pope Pius IX issued the encyclical Praedecessores Nostros in March 1847, calling for prayers and collections for Ireland, and Catholic communities in Europe and America sent money.
Catholic priests sat on relief committees, wrote public letters describing conditions, ran collections and buried the dead; many died of fever.
Church of Ireland clergy, often the only resident educated men in poor parishes, were the backbone of many local committees and also died in large numbers.
Religious orders such as the Sisters of Charity and the Sisters of Mercy nursed fever victims and fed the poor in towns.
Souperism was the charge that some evangelical Protestants offered food, clothing or schooling only to those who attended Protestant services or sent children to Protestant schools.

Proselytising missions had begun before the Famine, as at Edward Nangle's Achill colony from the 1830s, and the Irish Church Missions founded by Rev. Alexander Dallas in 1849 expanded them in Connemara during and after the Famine.
Most Protestant relief, including the Quakers' and most Church of Ireland committees', was given without religious conditions, but the actions of a few tainted Protestant charity as a whole.
The legacy was lasting bitterness: taking the soup became a mark of shame in Catholic memory, converts were often ostracised, and the issue sharpened sectarian division.
Some landlords reduced or cancelled rents, imported food, set up soup kitchens and employed tenants, and a number of them were ruined by the cost or died of fever.
Others, burdened by debt, rent arrears and poor rates, cleared their estates, using the Gregory clause and the rule that landlords paid the rates on holdings under £4.
Mass evictions were recorded especially in Clare, Mayo and Galway; in the Kilrush union, Co. Clare, the poor law inspector Captain Arthur Kennedy reported the destruction of whole townlands.
Police returns, which began in 1849, recorded tens of thousands of families evicted between 1849 and 1854.

Assisted emigration: Major Denis Mahon of Strokestown, Co. Roscommon, paid passage to Canada for about 1,500 tenants in 1847; many died on the voyage or in quarantine, and Mahon was shot dead in November 1847.

Larger schemes followed, such as Lord Lansdowne's assisted emigration from his Kenmare estate, Co. Kerry, in the early 1850s, and many landlords found shipping tenants cheaper than supporting them in the workhouse.
Born Asenath Hatch on 24 February 1792 in Chelsea, Vermont, she was a teacher who, as a widow in New York, worked among the Irish poor and promoted temperance and a vegetarian diet.
She first came to Ireland in May 1844 and walked through almost every county, staying in cabins and reading the Bible to the people she met.
Her account of that tour, Ireland's Welcome to the Stranger (1847), described the poverty and the dependence on the potato before the Famine.

She returned in 1846 to give relief, set up a soup kitchen in Dublin's Liberties, then travelled to Ulster, Mayo, Erris and Arranmore, distributing food and clothing paid for by appeals in New York papers.
Participant and witness: she gave relief directly and independently rather than through a committee, and recorded what she saw at first hand.
Her Lights and Shades of Ireland (1850), whose Famine section was published as Annals of the Famine in Ireland (1851), condemned landlords, officials and proselytisers alike.
Contemporaries found her eccentric: some officials and clergy suspected her as a Protestant Bible reader, while the poor welcomed her; she left Ireland in 1848 and died in Jersey City in 1855.
Historians now value her as one of the most vivid and sympathetic eyewitnesses of the Famine, a woman relief worker who blamed the system rather than its victims.
Private relief saved many thousands of lives in 1846–1847, especially through Quaker soup kitchens and the British Relief Association's feeding of children.
It fed people faster than government schemes and reached remote places, and its reports exposed the scale of suffering to the public.
It could not match the scale of the crisis: total private giving was a small fraction of the roughly £7 million spent by the government, about half of it as loans.

Giving fell sharply after 1847 because of donor fatigue, the British commercial crisis of 1847, the belief that the Famine was over, and anger at the Young Ireland rising and at Irish ingratitude in 1848.
The Quakers concluded that private charity could not replace the state and withdrew from mass feeding, so by 1848 relief depended on the Poor Law.
Population fell from about 8.2 million in 1841 to about 6.6 million in 1851 and about 5.4 million in 1871.
The cottier and labourer classes were the hardest hit by death and emigration, and the potato-dependent class largely disappeared.
Holdings of 1 to 5 acres fell sharply in number, while farms over 15 and 30 acres increased, as landlords and surviving farmers consolidated land.
The Encumbered Estates Act (1849) set up a court to sell estates whose owners were bankrupt; by the late 1850s several thousand estates, perhaps a quarter of the land of Ireland, had been sold.

Most buyers were Irish land speculators and businessmen rather than the British capitalists the government hoped for, and many new landlords raised rents and cleared tenants more readily than the old.
Agriculture shifted from tillage to pasture: cattle and sheep needed less labour and rising British demand made them more profitable.
Subdivision ended: farmers now passed the whole farm to one son, while the other children emigrated, entered the Church or married into other farms.
Marriage came later and fewer people married, because a son had to wait to inherit the farm; the arranged match between farming families became the norm.
The dowry became central to the match: the bride's family paid money or stock to the groom's family, often used to give a dowry to his sister.
Emigration became a habit: remittances and prepaid tickets from relatives abroad paid the passage of later emigrants (see the notes on post-Famine Ireland).

The Irish language declined fastest, because its heartlands in the west and south lost most people; the 1851 census recorded about 1.5 million speakers, and English became the language of advancement.
The Famine left lasting hatred of landlordism and of British government among Irish Americans and at home, which fed Fenianism and, later, the Land War.
The Catholic Church gained from the changed society: the surviving farming class was more devout and better able to support priests, nuns and church building.
Achievement of private relief: speed, compassion and practical aid, above all by the Quakers, whose non-sectarian work is still remembered with respect.
Limit of private relief: it was too small, short-lived and unevenly spread, weakest where it was most needed, and shrank after 1847.
Damage: souperism and landlord clearances meant that some private responses deepened suffering and division rather than relieving them.
Impact during the Famine: about a million deaths, mass eviction and flight; impact after: a smaller, older, more commercial and more Catholic-devout rural society.
Contemporary British opinion often saw the Famine as an opportunity to modernise Irish agriculture; Irish nationalists, led by Mitchel, saw it as a crime of British government.
Historians stress continuity as well as change: consolidation, pasture and emigration had begun before 1845, but the Famine greatly speeded them up.
The Famine left fewer, larger and more commercial farms, with livestock replacing tillage and a more prosperous stronger-farmer class.
Population fell from about 8.2 million in 1841 to about 6.5 million in 1851, about 5.8 million in 1861 and about 5.4 million in 1871.
Tillage declined and pasture expanded, because cattle, sheep and dairy produce rose in price relative to grain and needed less labour.
Cattle were exported live to Britain, a trade carried by the new railways and steamships, and the growing British towns were the market.
Small holdings disappeared as cottiers died or emigrated and landlords consolidated plots; farms above fifteen acres became far more common.
The stronger farmers, holding large farms on long tenure, were the main gainers; they dominated parish life and later supplied much of the support for land and nationalist movements.
Agricultural labourers fell in number and remained poor, and the small farmers of the west stayed close to subsistence.
The Encumbered Estates Act (1849) and the Landed Estates Court (1858) sold bankrupt estates; some new owners were commercial investors who raised rents and cleared tenants.
Landlordism survived: the landlord class still owned almost all the land, and tenants had no legal security of tenure until the Land Act of 1870 gave limited protection.
Evictions fell from their Famine peak but remained a threat, so tenant right stayed a central grievance of the 1850s and 1860s.
The Famine hardened a pattern of late marriage, celibacy and single-heir inheritance that kept farms intact and pushed other children abroad.
A dowry was money or land that a bride's family gave on her marriage; farmers used it to portion a sister, to buy out siblings or to pay debts.
Farms usually passed intact to one son, so a farmer could marry only when his father handed over the holding and a bride with a dowry was found.
Matchmaking was widespread, and the match depended on land and money more than on affection.
Marriage was late, often in the thirties, and a large share of men and women never married, especially in the west.
Younger sons and daughters without a dowry had to choose between emigration, farm labour, the priesthood or religious life, and domestic service.
Late marriage and celibacy kept the birth rate down, so the population did not recover after the Famine.
Large-scale emigration continued long after the Famine and became part of normal life; the diaspora is covered in detail in the notes on emigration and the Irish abroad.
About a million people left Ireland in the 1850s, and emigration stayed high through the 1860s.
The United States was the main destination, followed by Britain, Canada and Australia; Liverpool and Cork (Queenstown) were major ports of departure.
Emigrants were young and unmarried, and women left in numbers roughly equal to men.
Chain migration meant that relatives and neighbours already abroad sent news and prepaid passages, so people followed established routes to particular towns.
Remittances sent home helped families pay rent and passage costs for further relatives.
Emigration relieved pressure on land, but it drained the countryside of young people and fed the idea of exile in nationalist politics.
The national school system, set up in 1831, became the main provider of primary education and a major influence on literacy and language.
The system was set up in 1831 through a letter from the Chief Secretary, Edward Stanley, and run by a board of Commissioners of National Education.
Its aim was combined literary and moral education for children of all denominations, with religious instruction given separately by each church.
The state paid grants, supplied textbooks and inspected schools, and a training college for teachers opened in Dublin.

The churches contested the plan: the Church of Ireland set up its own Church Education Society (1839), Presbyterians objected at first, and the Catholic bishops were divided between Archbishop Daniel Murray, who co-operated, and Archbishop John MacHale of Tuam, who opposed.
In practice most schools became denominational in character, because local clergy managed them and most pupils in each district were of one faith.
After 1850 Cardinal Cullen pressed for greater Catholic control of education.
The Christian Brothers, founded in Waterford in 1802 by Edmund Rice, ran their own free schools for poor Catholic boys and spread in the towns.
Lessons were in English, and the system reinforced the decline of the Irish language by teaching through English and treating Irish as no help to a career.
School attendance and literacy rose steadily, and by 1870 roughly a million children were on the rolls.
Higher education divided on religious lines, and the dispute fed into the Synod of Thurles.
Peel's government founded the Queen's Colleges at Belfast, Cork and Galway by an Act of 1845; they opened in 1849 and formed the Queen's University of Ireland in 1850.
They were non-denominational and had no chapel or chair of theology, so critics called them godless colleges.
The Catholic hierarchy was divided, but Rome condemned the colleges in 1847 and the Synod of Thurles in 1850 forbade Catholics to attend, and Cullen backed a Catholic alternative.
The Catholic University opened in Dublin in 1854 with John Henry Newman as first rector; it gave no state-recognised degrees and had few students, and Newman resigned in 1858.
Trinity College Dublin, an Anglican institution, remained the main university for Protestants, and Catholics were admitted to degrees but not to fellowships.
The Queen's College in Belfast served the Presbyterian middle class of Ulster and was the most successful of the three.
The railway network was built from 1834 and was largely complete by about 1860, changing trade, towns and communications.
The Dublin and Kingstown Railway opened in December 1834 and ran about six miles from Westland Row in Dublin to Kingstown (now Dún Laoghaire); it was the first railway in Ireland.
Growth began slowly: only about 65 miles were open in 1845, but the network grew to nearly 1,000 miles by 1855 and the core was largely in place by 1860.
The Great Southern and Western reached Cork in 1849, the Midland Great Western reached Galway in 1851, and Belfast was linked to Dublin in the 1850s.
Ireland adopted a broad gauge of 5 feet 3 inches, a decision of the 1840s that set a different gauge from Britain.
Railways cut the cost and time of moving cattle, butter, grain and fish, and tied farmers to British markets through the ports.
Fairs and markets shifted to railway towns, and junctions such as Mallow, Limerick Junction and Athlone grew in importance.
Newspapers, mail and ideas travelled faster, so national newspapers reached the provinces and political movements could organise nationally.
Tourism grew, with the line to Killarney opening in 1853, and the rail and steamer link to Britain eased travel and emigration.
Some small ports lost trade as goods moved inland by rail.
Dargan was the most successful Irish railway contractor of his day and a public figure who promoted Irish industry.
Born in 1799 near Carlow town, he trained as a surveyor and engineer in England and worked under Thomas Telford on the Holyhead road.

He won the contract for the Dublin and Kingstown Railway, which opened in 1834, and went on to build lines including the Dublin and Drogheda and the Ulster Railway, becoming the leading contractor in Ireland.
He also built the Ulster Canal and dredged the Victoria Channel at Belfast, which created Queen's Island, later the Harland and Wolff site.
In 1853 he financed the Dublin Industrial Exhibition on Leinster Lawn, which drew over a million visitors, and Queen Victoria visited it.
He lost heavily on the Exhibition, and his reputation as an Irish industrial pioneer was the main reward; he reportedly refused the offer of a baronetcy.
A fall from a horse in 1866 and the failure of some of his ventures ended his career; he died in Dublin on 7 February 1867.
Contemporaries praised him as a self-made Catholic businessman who employed thousands and acted from public spirit, and the National Gallery of Ireland (1864) was founded partly as his memorial.
Historians see him as a symbol of Irish enterprise within the British economy, but his work depended on railway investment more than on a wider Irish industrial base.
Belfast became an industrial city of linen, engineering and shipbuilding, unlike the largely agricultural south.
Mechanised flax spinning arrived in the 1820s and 1830s, and linen became the dominant industry of Belfast and the Lagan valley.
The American Civil War (1861–65) cut off cotton supplies, and the cotton famine raised demand and prices for linen.
Belfast's population grew from about 100,000 in 1851 to over 170,000 by 1871, with migrants from the Ulster countryside and Famine-hit areas.
Harbour works, including Dargan's Victoria Channel, allowed larger ships to reach the port, and engineering firms grew up to serve the mills.
Edward Harland took over Robert Hickson's shipyard on Queen's Island in 1858, and in 1861 he and Gustav Wolff formed Harland and Wolff.
Ulster had skilled Protestant labour, capital from the linen trade, local business networks and strong trade links with Britain.
Belfast had no local coal or iron, but cheap imports by sea and rail made industry viable.
Industry in the south declined under competition from British factory goods once tariffs were gone, and Dublin and Cork kept only brewing, distilling and food processing.
Catholics, mostly migrants from the countryside, made up about a third of Belfast's population, and they were concentrated in unskilled jobs and certain districts such as the Pound.
Sectarian riots broke out in Belfast in 1857 and 1864, tied to Orange marches and Catholic rivalry for housing and work.
Judgements differ on whether post-Famine Ireland was a story of recovery or of continuing weakness.
Achievement: farm incomes and living standards of the stronger farmers rose, and railways opened national markets.
Limit: the population kept falling, emigration continued and the rural poor of the west gained little.
Achievement: the national school system spread literacy to most of the population.
Limit: schooling in English weakened the Irish language.
Achievement: Belfast industrialised and grew faster than any other Irish town.
Limit: industrialisation was confined to the north-east, and the rest of Ireland depended on agriculture and on exporting people.
Contemporary view: many saw the stronger farmers' prosperity and the railways as evidence of improvement under the Union.
Later view: historians argue that the Famine made Ireland a more commercial but more unequal and emigrant society, with a prosperous farmer class above a shrinking labouring poor.
The Irish electorate was cut sharply in 1829, widened a little in 1832 and widened again in the counties in 1850, but voting remained open and influenced by landlords and clergy.
Alongside the Emancipation Act of 1829, a second Act abolished the forty-shilling freeholders and raised the county franchise to £10, cutting the Irish county electorate to about 37,000.
The Irish Reform Act of 1832 raised Irish seats from 100 to 105 and gave the vote in the boroughs to £10 householders, but the electorate stayed small beside Britain's.
Voting was open, not secret, until the Ballot Act of 1872, so landlords, agents and priests could pressure tenants and parishioners.
The Irish Franchise Act of 1850 gave the county vote to occupiers rated at £12 or more and the borough vote to those rated at £8 or more.
The 1850 Act greatly enlarged the county electorate, which was several times larger than before, while the borough electorate stayed small and even fell.
A larger county electorate of tenant farmers helped the Tenant League win seats in 1852, but the Famine, emigration and eviction had already cut the number of small tenants.
Religious rivalry shaped Irish politics at the end of the 1840s and in the early 1850s, with Orange marches and the Ecclesiastical Titles Act as flashpoints.
The Orange Order was founded in County Armagh in 1795, after the Battle of the Diamond, to defend the Protestant ascendancy and the link with Britain.
The Order was dissolved in 1836 after a parliamentary inquiry into its spread in the army, and was revived in Ulster in the 1840s.
On 12 July 1849 an Orange procession returning from Lord Roden's estate at Tollymore passed through Dolly's Brae near Castlewellan, County Down, where armed Catholic Ribbonmen had gathered.
Fighting followed and Catholics were killed, though the number is disputed (estimates range from a handful to dozens); Catholic homes nearby were burned.
An inquiry criticised the conduct of the Orangemen and the magistrate Lord Roden, and he was removed from the commission of the peace.
The Party Processions Act (1850) banned party marches, and it was repealed in 1872.
In September 1850 Pope Pius IX restored a Catholic hierarchy with territorial titles in England, and Lord John Russell, the Whig prime minister, denounced the move as papal aggression.
The Ecclesiastical Titles Act (1851) banned Catholic bishops from taking territorial titles in the United Kingdom; it was never enforced and was repealed in 1871.
Irish Catholic MPs and the Catholic Defence Association opposed the Act, which pushed Catholic and tenant-right politics together.
A new alliance of tenant-right campaigners and Catholic MPs promised independent opposition in the 1850s and then collapsed.
The Irish Tenant League was founded in Dublin in 1850 by Charles Gavan Duffy, Frederick Lucas, a Catholic convert and editor of the Tablet, and others, including Presbyterian ministers from Ulster.
It demanded the three Fs: fair rent, fixity of tenure and free sale of the tenant's interest.
Catholic clergy, notably Archbishop MacHale and Fr Lavelle, supported it, but Cardinal Cullen distrusted its priests-in-politics.
At the 1852 election more than 40 MPs were returned pledged to independent opposition, forming the Independent Irish Party.

In December 1852 William Keogh and John Sadleir accepted posts in Lord Aberdeen's government, Keogh as solicitor-general for Ireland and Sadleir as a Lord of the Treasury, breaking the pledge of independence.
Duffy, Lucas and others denounced them as betrayers, and the party fractured as members drifted to the Liberals.
Lucas died in 1855 and Duffy emigrated to Australia in 1855, ending the movement; Sadleir died by suicide in 1856 after the collapse of his Tipperary Bank, and Keogh became a judge.
Many nationalists lost faith in parliamentary action, which helped turn young men towards Fenianism.
Fenianism was a transatlantic revolutionary movement that aimed to end British rule by force and set up an Irish republic.
The Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB) was founded in Dublin on 17 March 1858 by James Stephens, with Thomas Clarke Luby and others, as an oath-bound secret society.
In New York in the same year John O'Mahony founded the Fenian Brotherhood, which raised money and men in the United States and took its name from the legendary Fianna.
Roots lay in the failed 1848 rising, the Famine bitterness, the disillusion with parliamentary politics after the Independent Irish Party and the exile experience of emigrants.
The IRB was organised in circles under local leaders and reported to Stephens, who took the title of Chief Organiser of the Irish Republic.
Its members were mainly artisans, clerks, shopkeepers and farmers' sons, together with soldiers in the British army whom the IRB tried to recruit.
The funeral of Terence Bellew MacManus, a 1848 rebel, in Dublin in 1861 showed Fenian strength, and Cullen refused to allow his body to lie in the Pro-Cathedral.
The movement's newspaper, the Irish People, began in Dublin in 1863 with Luby, John O'Leary and Charles Kickham as editors and Jeremiah O'Donovan Rossa as manager.
American Fenians included veterans of the Civil War, whose military experience raised hopes of a rising in Ireland.
The government crushed the Irish organisation before it could rise, and the 1867 rising failed, but Fenian actions in England and Canada kept the movement in the public eye.
In September 1865 the police raided the Irish People offices and arrested Luby, O'Leary, Rossa and Kickham, and in November Stephens himself was arrested.
Stephens escaped from Richmond Prison in Dublin in November 1865 with the help of warders, and went abroad.
Habeas corpus was suspended in Ireland in February 1866, allowing arrest without trial.
In 1866 Stephens postponed a rising he had promised, and in December American Fenian leaders removed him.
The rising took place in early March 1867 in bad weather: small risings in Dublin (Tallaght), Cork, Limerick and Tipperary were quickly crushed.
Informers had compromised the plans, and the Fenians lacked arms and trained leaders.
In September 1867 Fenians in Manchester freed two prisoners, Thomas Kelly and Timothy Deasy, from a prison van and killed a police sergeant, Charles Brett.
Three men, William Allen, Michael Larkin and Michael O'Brien, were hanged in November 1867 as the Manchester Martyrs and were mourned across Ireland.
In December 1867 a Fenian attempt to free a prisoner by blowing up a wall at Clerkenwell prison in London killed about a dozen people and turned British opinion against the Fenians.
Michael Barrett was hanged for Clerkenwell in 1868, the last public execution in England.
American Fenians launched raids into Canada, at Ridgeway in June 1866 and again in 1870, which failed to win Canadian territory.
Cardinal Cullen and most bishops condemned Fenianism as a secret society, and many priests denounced it.
Stephens founded and led the IRB, but his leadership failed at the decisive moment.
Born in Kilkenny in 1825, he took part in the 1848 rising at Ballingarry under William Smith O'Brien and escaped to Paris.
He returned to Ireland in 1856 and travelled the country, then founded the IRB in 1858 as its Chief Organiser.
He worked with O'Mahony's Fenian Brotherhood in America, which sent money and supporters to Ireland.
He organised the Irish People in 1863 and built a network by recruiting through secret circles, including in the British army.
He was arrested in November 1865, escaped within a fortnight and spent 1866 in the United States, failing to hold a rising on promised dates.
He was deposed by Fenian leaders in December 1866 and spent most of the rest of his life abroad in Paris; he returned to Ireland in 1891 and died in Dublin in 1901.
Contemporaries saw him as a gifted organiser and a charismatic figure but as autocratic, secretive and over-promising.
Historians credit him with building the first lasting revolutionary organisation, while criticising his indecision and his failure to launch the rising he had promised.
Kickham combined Fenian leadership with literature; he was a writer more than a conspirator.
Born in Mullinahone, County Tipperary, in 1828, he was left almost deaf and with poor sight by an accident with gunpowder as a boy.
He wrote for The Nation and joined the Fenians, becoming one of the editors of the Irish People.
Arrested in 1865, he was sentenced in 1866 to fourteen years' penal servitude and released in 1869 because of ill health, after a campaign for the release of Fenian prisoners.
He wrote the novel Sally Cavanagh (1869) about the eviction of a tenant family, and Knocknagow, or The Homes of Tipperary, which was very popular.
He became a leading member of the IRB's Supreme Council in the 1870s and died at Blackrock, near Dublin, in 1882.
A practising Catholic, he was caught between his faith and the bishops' condemnation of the movement.
Contemporaries admired his courage, honesty and endurance in prison.
Historians see him as the Fenian movement's voice for rural Ireland and its link between nationalism and literature.
After the Fenian scare, William Gladstone's first government (1868–74) tried to remove two Irish grievances.
Gladstone became prime minister in December 1868 and said that his mission was to pacify Ireland.
The Manchester executions and Clerkenwell showed that Irish discontent could threaten Britain and made reform politically urgent.
The Irish Church Act (1869) disestablished the Church of Ireland from 1 January 1871 and ended its status as the state church.
The Church lost most of its endowments, which passed to a commission, while serving clergy received compensation.
The Irish Land Act (1870) gave legal force to the Ulster custom of tenant right, which allowed outgoing tenants to sell their interest.
It gave tenants compensation for disturbance when evicted for reasons other than non-payment of rent, and for improvements.
Its Bright clauses offered loans to help tenants buy their holdings, but few did.
The Act did not stop evictions for non-payment, since landlords could raise rents, and so it failed to give security of tenure.
Fenian prisoners were released between 1869 and 1871 as the amnesty movement grew, and Isaac Butt founded the Home Government Association in 1870.
Judgements turn on whether Fenianism or constitutional reform did more to change Irish politics by 1870.
Fenian achievement: it revived physical force republicanism, built a disciplined oath-bound organisation across Ireland, Britain and America, and kept the republican idea alive.
Fenian limit: it failed militarily in 1867, was heavily infiltrated by informers, split between Stephens and the American leaders, and was condemned by the Church.
Contemporary views: the British government saw a conspiracy; many Irish nationalists admired the martyrs, while bishops and moderate nationalists feared it.
Later views: historians argue that Fenianism, through the Manchester executions and Clerkenwell, prompted Gladstone's reforms, and that its legacy lasted into 1916.
Liberal achievement: disestablishment ended the Protestant church's privileged position, and the Land Act recognised tenants' claims for the first time.
Liberal limit: the Land Act failed to prevent eviction, and neither measure answered demands for tenant ownership or self-government.
Fenianism or Liberal reform: the first showed that violence could force reform; the second showed that reform could not fully remove the grievances behind violence.
From the 1840s the Catholic Church became more disciplined and its practice more uniform, a change the historian Emmet Larkin called the devotional revolution.
Church building expanded sharply after Emancipation, with new parish churches and cathedrals raised on money collected from the faithful.
St Patrick's College, Maynooth (1795) trained most of the clergy, and by mid-century the clergy were better educated and under closer episcopal discipline.

Religious orders and congregations grew, among them the Christian Brothers (Waterford, 1802), the Presentation Sisters, the Sisters of Mercy founded by Catherine McAuley in Dublin in 1831 and the Sisters of Charity; they ran schools, hospitals and orphanages.

Parish missions given by Redemptorists, Vincentians and Jesuits, together with the rosary, novenas, confraternities, benediction and devotion to the Sacred Heart and the Virgin Mary, spread new forms of piety.
Larkin argued that weekly Mass attendance rose from perhaps a third of Catholics before the Famine to the large majority by the 1870s.
Historians link the change to the Famine, which killed and removed the poor who had been least regular in practice, left a more prosperous farmer class and strengthened clerical authority.
Catholic identity became tied to nationality, as the Church's building programme and schools made it the main institution of the Catholic majority.
Protestant identity was shaped by evangelical revival and by the defence of Protestant privilege.
Evangelicalism was a Protestant revival stressing personal conversion, Bible reading and missionary work; it grew in the Church of Ireland and among Presbyterians and Methodists from the 1820s.
The Second Reformation was the evangelical drive of the 1820s to 1850s to convert Catholics, using Bible societies, schools and missions.
Edward Nangle's mission colony at Achill (1834) and the Irish Church Missions of the 1840s were well-known examples.
In the Famine years, Protestant soup kitchens that required conversion led Catholics to coin the term souperism, and the bitterness lasted for generations.
The Orange Order, founded in 1795, was dissolved in 1836 and revived in the 1840s, and it expressed Protestant loyalty to the Crown, the Union and Protestant ascendancy.
Presbyterian leader Henry Cooke, an Ulster evangelical, promoted an alliance of Presbyterians and Anglicans against O'Connell and Catholic nationalism.
A great evangelical revival swept Ulster in 1859.
The Church of Ireland remained the established church until disestablishment took effect in 1871, though it served a small minority.
Young Ireland defined the nation through culture and history while the Irish language declined.
Young Ireland's idea of the nation was a community of shared history, culture and territory that could include Protestants as well as Catholics.
The Nation, founded in 1842, used poems, ballads and history to teach this idea.
O'Connell, though a native speaker, saw English as the language of progress, and had little interest in saving Irish.
The 1851 census, the first to ask about the Irish language, found roughly a quarter of the population reporting that they spoke it.
Irish was strongest in the west and south-west, where the Famine killed or scattered the poorest and the most Irish-speaking.
The national schools taught in English, and parents saw English as the key to a job or to emigration.
Cultural nationalism in the 1840s encouraged the study of Irish history, manuscripts and antiquities, but it did not stop the language declining.
Cullen was the architect of the Romanisation of the Irish Church and the leading Catholic figure of the period.
Born in County Kildare in 1803, he studied in Rome, was ordained there and became rector of the Irish College in Rome in 1832.
He was appointed Archbishop of Armagh and Apostolic Delegate in 1850, the pope's representative with special powers, and presided at the Synod of Thurles in 1850.
He became Archbishop of Dublin in 1852 and was made the first Irish cardinal in 1866; he died in 1878.
He championed ultramontane devotion, strict clerical discipline, church building, religious orders, parish missions and Catholic schools.
He opposed the Queen's Colleges and backed the Catholic University founded under Newman in 1854.
He distrusted Young Ireland, the Tenant League and priests in politics, and opposed the Fenians; he refused to let the body of Terence Bellew MacManus lie in the Pro-Cathedral in 1861.
He favoured co-operation with the Liberals and supported Gladstone's disestablishment of the Church of Ireland.
Contemporaries admired his devotion to Rome and his organisation but nationalists and some bishops, notably MacHale, resented his authority.
Historians see him as the central figure of the devotional revolution but debate whether he shaped Catholic political conservatism or reflected what the Church wanted.
The Synod met to unify the Irish Church after decades of diocesan independence and to settle the education question.
It was the first national synod of the Irish Catholic Church for about two centuries, the last having been held at Kilkenny in 1642.
Before 1850 each bishop ran his own diocese with little central direction, and clerical discipline and practice varied widely.
Rome wanted uniform practice and a clear Irish policy, and Pope Pius IX wanted the Church to resist the secular and mixed education of the Queen's Colleges.
The bishops were divided: MacHale of Tuam opposed the colleges outright, while Daniel Murray of Dublin was more willing to accept them.
A papal rescript of 1847 had condemned the Queen's Colleges, and the Famine had weakened the old order and made Church leaders open to reform.
Rome made Paul Cullen Archbishop of Armagh in 1849 and Apostolic Delegate in 1850, to organise the Synod and carry out Roman policy.
The Synod met in Thurles, County Tipperary, from 22 August to 9 September 1850.
Cullen presided as Apostolic Delegate, and the bishops of the four provinces attended.
The decrees condemned the Queen's Colleges as dangerous to faith and morals and forbade clergy to take posts in them.
It ordered the setting up of a Catholic University, which opened in 1854 with Newman as rector.
It laid down uniform liturgical practice and church discipline, with the Roman rite followed.
It regulated clerical dress, behaviour and the conduct of the sacraments, and increased the bishops' authority over priests.
It discouraged priests from political agitation, notably at the altar and election meetings.
Opposition came from MacHale and from lay Catholics and liberal clergy, who supported the Queen's Colleges and resented Roman control.
Rome supported Cullen, and the Synod's decrees were later confirmed there.
The Synod began the Romanisation of the Irish Church and shaped Catholic life and politics for the rest of the century.
Ultramontanism was the belief in strong papal authority over national churches and bishops, and the Synod made it the guiding principle of Irish Catholicism.
Romanisation meant closer links with Rome, uniform liturgy and devotions in the Roman style, and a centralised Church under the bishops.
The Catholic University failed to attract many students and had no state-recognised degrees, so the Synod's education policy had limited success.
Most Catholics who wished to attend university still entered Trinity or the Queen's Colleges, and the bishops later campaigned for a Catholic university with state support.
Cullen's authority over the bishops made him the dominant Catholic voice in public affairs for the next quarter-century.
Contemporaries disagreed: Protestants and some liberal Catholics saw an alien and authoritarian power, while supporters saw order and renewal.
Historians such as Emmet Larkin treat the Synod as the start of the devotional revolution, while others argue that the changes were already under way.
Aikenhead founded the first Irish Catholic religious order devoted to caring for the poor outside a convent.
Born in Cork in 1787 to a Protestant father and a Catholic mother, she became a Catholic.
Guided by Archbishop Daniel Murray of Dublin, she trained at the Bar Convent in York and founded the Religious Sisters of Charity in 1815.
The Sisters visited the poor in their homes, ran schools and nursed the sick.
In 1834 she opened St Vincent's Hospital in St Stephen's Green, Dublin, the first hospital in Ireland run by nuns, which treated the sick poor of all creeds.
She directed the order from Stanhope Street in Dublin, much of the time as an invalid, until her death in 1858.
She was a participant, as the founder, in the growth of Catholic social services.
Contemporaries admired her charity and her courage in running an institution while an invalid.
