Historians see her as a pioneer of active women's religious life and Catholic nursing and as a founder of institutions that shaped Irish health care.
Carleton was the leading chronicler of the Irish peasantry before the Famine.
Born in 1794 at Prillisk, County Tyrone, the son of a Catholic Irish-speaking tenant farmer, he went to Dublin in about 1817 and began writing.
He first wrote for the Christian Examiner, an evangelical Protestant paper, and his early stories had an anti-Catholic edge.
Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry appeared in 1830 and a second series in 1833, describing wakes, pilgrimages, faction fights and hedge schools.
Fardorougha the Miser (1839) and The Black Prophet (1847), a novel of famine, explored the life of the rural poor.
He was a witness to the world he described, rather than a political actor, and received a government pension in 1848.
Contemporaries admired his realism, but some Catholic nationalists resented his early anti-Catholic writing.
Historians value him as a source on pre-Famine rural life and as a realist who showed the violence and poverty as well as the humour.
Davis shaped the cultural idea of the Irish nation; his political role is covered in the notes on O'Connell and Young Ireland.
Born in Mallow in 1814 into a Protestant family and educated at Trinity College Dublin, he co-founded The Nation in 1842 with Charles Gavan Duffy and John Blake Dillon.
His songs and ballads, including A Nation Once Again and The West's Asleep, put history and patriotism into popular verse.
He urged the study and teaching of Irish history and the Irish language, and edited the Library of Ireland series.
He argued that the nation should unite Catholic, Protestant and Dissenter on a shared Irish identity.
He died of scarlet fever in September 1845, aged 30.
Contemporaries saw him as a model of principled youth; critics thought his ideas were idealistic.
Historians credit him with laying the cultural foundations of Irish nationalism, though his appeal to Protestants was limited.
Writers, musicians and antiquarians drew on Irish history and folklore.
Thomas Moore's Irish Melodies, published in numbers from 1808 to 1834, set Irish airs to words and were popular in Britain, Ireland and America.
James Clarence Mangan wrote poems for The Nation, including Dark Rosaleen (1846), adapted from the Irish, and died in 1849 in the cholera of the Famine years.
George Petrie, painter and antiquarian, showed in an essay published in 1845 that the round towers were Christian in origin and collected traditional music in The Ancient Music of Ireland (1855).
The Ordnance Survey of the 1830s, directed by Thomas Larcom, employed scholars such as John O'Donovan and Eugene O'Curry to record Irish place names and to study manuscripts.
O'Donovan edited the Annals of the Four Masters (1848-51), and O'Curry became professor of Irish history and archaeology at the Catholic University.
The Royal Irish Academy and the Royal Dublin Society supported scholarship, and the Famine drew writers to themes of hunger, eviction and emigration.
Irish scientists made international contributions in mathematics, physics and astronomy.
William Rowan Hamilton, Royal Astronomer of Ireland at Dunsink, discovered quaternions on 16 October 1843 while walking by the Royal Canal at Broom Bridge.
William Parsons, 3rd Earl of Rosse, built the six-foot reflecting telescope called the Leviathan of Parsonstown at Birr Castle, completed in 1845, then the largest in the world.
With it he observed the spiral structure of the galaxy later known as M51, the Whirlpool Galaxy.
Nicholas Callan, a priest and professor at Maynooth, built an early induction coil in the 1830s, and developed powerful batteries.
George Boole was the first professor of mathematics at Queen's College Cork from 1849, and published The Laws of Thought (1854), the basis of Boolean algebra.
Robert Kane, first president of Queen's College Cork, wrote The Industrial Resources of Ireland (1844), urging the use of science for economic development.
The Queen's Colleges, the Royal Dublin Society and the Royal Irish Academy supported such work.
Judgements turn on whether the changes were imposed from above or grew from below.
Achievement of the devotional revolution: a more disciplined clergy, more churches and schools, and a strong Catholic identity.
Limit: the Church's authoritarian leadership split bishops, alienated liberal Catholics and Protestants, and left the Catholic University weak.
Contemporary view: Protestants saw papal domination, while Catholic supporters saw renewal after the Famine.
Later view: historians broadly agree that the Church's changes gave Catholics a shared religious identity that later nationalism drew on.
Achievement of the arts and sciences: Moore, Carleton, Petrie, O'Donovan, Hamilton, Rosse and Boole won international recognition.
Limit: the Famine and emigration weakened the rural culture and the Irish language that cultural nationalists wished to save.

By 1870 Irish nationalism had tried repeal, rebellion and Fenian conspiracy without success. Home Rule offered a constitutional, moderate alternative that could attract Protestants as well as Catholics.
The Act of Union (1801) abolished the Irish parliament; Daniel O’Connell’s Repeal campaign failed in the 1840s and the Young Ireland rising of 1848 collapsed.
The Fenian (IRB) rising of 1867 was crushed, but the arrest and trial of Fenians produced a public movement for an amnesty for political prisoners in 1869, and Isaac Butt was among its leaders.
Gladstone became Prime Minister in December 1868 declaring that his mission was to pacify Ireland; he disestablished the Church of Ireland (1869) and passed a first Land Act (1870).
Those reforms failed to satisfy nationalists: the 1870 Act left tenants without real security, and many Irish MPs were Liberals who did not press for self-government.
Political agitation (organised public pressure through meetings, newspapers and electoral campaigns) was the method by which Home Rulers hoped to build a mass base, as O’Connell had done.
The electorate was small and unevenly spread: most Catholic tenant farmers had no vote, so early Home Rulers depended on small towns and a wealthy, often Protestant, professional class.
Butt, a Protestant barrister and former Conservative MP, founded the movement in Dublin in 1870 and made federal Home Rule a parliamentary question.
Isaac Butt (1813–1879) was born in Co. Donegal, the son of a Church of Ireland rector, and became a Dublin barrister and professor of political economy at Trinity College.
He began as a Conservative and unionist opponent of O’Connell, but his defence of the Young Irelanders in 1848 and of Fenian prisoners in the 1860s turned him towards nationalism.
The Home Government Association was founded in Dublin in May 1870, bringing together Protestant Conservatives, Liberals, Repealers and Catholic moderates.
Butt’s programme was federal: an Irish parliament in Dublin dealing with domestic affairs, with the imperial parliament at Westminster keeping control of the empire, defence and foreign policy.
Butt won the Limerick City by-election in 1871 as a Home Ruler, which showed that the new demand could win Catholic votes.
The Ballot Act (1872) introduced the secret ballot, so landlords and agents could no longer watch how tenants voted; the Galway election petition of 1872 had exposed clerical pressure on voters.
A national conference in Dublin in November 1873 replaced the Association with the Home Rule League and committed Home Rule MPs to sit as an independent party.
Butt’s method was constitutional: persuasion, parliamentary motions and public meetings, with a rejection of physical force.
The 1874 election produced the first sizeable Home Rule party, but Butt could not make it effective.
In the 1874 general election about 60 of the 103 Irish seats were won by Home Rulers (sources give 59 or 60), making them a significant bloc at Westminster.
Many of those MPs were Liberals who had added the label for local reasons and did not vote consistently with the party; the League had no pledge or whip to bind them.
Butt’s Home Rule motions in the 1870s were rejected by overwhelming majorities, and neither Disraeli’s Conservatives nor the Liberals took them seriously.
Butt’s approach depended on winning English sympathy through argument, and the Commons treated Irish business as a nuisance rather than a priority.
The party had little money or local organisation, so the movement remained a body of MPs and lawyers with few roots among the tenant farmers.
Younger members, including Joseph Biggar and John O’Connor Power, believed that politeness had failed and demanded more aggressive tactics.
Butt’s health and finances (he was chronically in debt) weakened his authority; he died on 5 May 1879, by which time his control had already slipped to the obstructionists.
Obstruction was the first tactic that forced the House of Commons to pay attention to Irish MPs.
Obstruction meant prolonged speeches, endless amendments and procedural objections designed to jam Commons business until the government gave way.
Joseph Biggar, a Belfast-born Presbyterian provision merchant and member of the IRB, was MP for Cavan from 1874 and began the practice.
Charles Stewart Parnell was elected MP for Meath in a by-election in April 1875 and joined Biggar’s obstruction from 1877, a famous South Africa Bill debate being an early example.

In 1877 Parnell, speaking of the Manchester Martyrs executed in 1867, said he did not believe any murder had been committed at Manchester, a deliberate break with Butt’s caution that won Fenian respect.
In August 1877 Parnell replaced Butt as president of the Home Rule Confederation of Great Britain, the body that organised Irish voters in English cities.

In January–February 1881 Irish MPs obstructed the coercion bill in a sitting of about 41 hours; the Speaker, Henry Brand, ended the debate on his own authority and the Commons later adopted the closure rule (1882).

The Liberal and Conservative leaderships both condemned obstruction as an abuse of parliament, and Butt himself deplored it, but it showed that a small, disciplined group could make the House of Commons unworkable.
The New Departure linked three forces that had previously worked apart: Fenian-minded nationalists, constitutional Home Rulers and the land-reform movement.
The agricultural depression from 1877 (bad weather, falling prices and cheap American grain) brought a threat of evictions and a crisis in the countryside.

Michael Davitt, released from Dartmoor Prison in December 1877 after serving seven years of a fifteen-year sentence for Fenian arms-dealing, travelled to the USA in 1878 and met John Devoy of the Clan na Gael.

In October 1878 Devoy sent Parnell a telegram offering Clan na Gael support if he adopted a more active programme: a general demand for self-government, a drive for peasant ownership of land, and independent action by Irish MPs.
Parnell never formally accepted the offer, but he moved towards it, and his public alliance with Davitt created the working partnership known as the New Departure.
The New Departure committed Fenians to co-operate with a parliamentary party, which was a break with the IRB’s refusal to accept constitutional politics.
It also tied Home Rule to the land question, so that a tenant-farmer movement could supply the votes and funds for national politics.
Many in the IRB, including the Supreme Council, opposed co-operation, and the alliance was always uneasy, with Davitt favouring land nationalisation and Parnell peasant proprietorship.
Between 1879 and 1885 Parnell fused a land movement, a parliamentary party and a national organisation into a disciplined machine.
The Land League of Mayo (Irishtown meeting, April 1879) was extended into the Irish National Land League, founded in Dublin in October 1879 with Parnell as president.
Parnell and John Dillon toured the United States from January to March 1880, raising funds and addressing the US House of Representatives, which gave the movement American money and publicity.
At the general election of April 1880 about 60 Home Rulers were returned; Parnell was elected for three constituencies and chose Cork City, which he held until his death.
In May 1880 Parnell was elected chairman of the Irish Parliamentary Party, defeating William Shaw (23 votes to 18), and pledge-bound unity became the aim.
United Ireland, founded in 1881 and edited by William O’Brien, became the party’s weekly newspaper.
The Irish National League, founded in October 1882, replaced the suppressed Land League; it put Home Rule, land reform and local self-government first, and Parnell kept personal control of it.

In 1884 the party required its candidates to sign a pledge to sit, act and vote with the party, and constituency conventions (usually with clergy in attendance) chose candidates, ending the independence of the old Home Rule MPs.
Funding came from the Irish diaspora and local collections, and the 1883 Parnell Tribute raised about £37,000 for Parnell’s personal use despite the disapproval of the Vatican.
Parish branches of the National League gave the party an organisation in nearly every county, with priests often serving as chairs or treasurers.
Between October 1881 and May 1882 Parnell went from prison to a deal with the government, and the murders in Phoenix Park nearly wrecked it.
Gladstone’s Chief Secretary, W.E. Forster, introduced coercion in 1881, allowing detention without trial; the Land Act of August 1881 followed (see the notes on land agitation).
Parnell was arrested on 13 October 1881 and imprisoned in Kilmainham Gaol; from there he and other leaders issued the No Rent Manifesto, and the Land League was suppressed a week later.

Captain William O’Shea acted as go-between, and in April–May 1882 a settlement (nicknamed the Kilmainham Treaty by its critics) was reached: Parnell was released on 2 May and the government promised to deal with rent arrears.
In return Parnell indicated that he would use his influence to discourage outrages and co-operate with the Liberals; it was an unwritten understanding, not a treaty.
Forster resigned in protest at the release, and Lord Frederick Cavendish was appointed Chief Secretary.
On 6 May 1882, the day Cavendish arrived in Dublin, he and the Under-Secretary Thomas Henry Burke were stabbed to death in Phoenix Park by the Invincibles, a small IRB splinter group.
Parnell denounced the murders and offered to resign his seat, and Gladstone refused the offer; the government nevertheless introduced the Prevention of Crimes Act (1882).
Five Invincibles were hanged in 1883 after the informer James Carey gave evidence.
The Arrears Act (August 1882) wrote off arrears for poorer tenants, and the National League’s foundation in October 1882 refocused the movement on Home Rule.
Parnell’s career is covered in two parts; this part runs from his background to the eve of the 1885 election.
Parnell was born at Avondale, Co. Wicklow, in 1846 into a Protestant landowning family; his mother, Delia Stewart, was American.
He studied at Magdalene College, Cambridge, and was High Sheriff of Wicklow in 1874, hardly an obvious future rebel.
He was elected for Meath in 1875, joined Biggar’s obstruction, became president of the Land League in 1879 and chairman of the Irish Parliamentary Party in 1880.
He was a direct participant: he organised the party, led the Land League, and negotiated with Gladstone and the Conservatives.

His speeches urged tenants to keep a firm grip on their homesteads (Westport, June 1879) and to isolate those who took evicted farms (Ennis, September 1880), phrases that Unionists later quoted against him.

Contemporary supporters admired his aloof, disciplined manner and his ability to hold together constitutionalists and Fenians; critics, including The Times, described him as a revolutionary in disguise.

Historians such as F.S.L. Lyons stress his political skill and his reliance on a loose alliance that was bound to be tested; others emphasise that he was a pragmatic parliamentarian, not a radical, who steered the Land War into a political settlement.
Judgement turns on whether the movement’s success owed more to Butt’s foundation or to Parnell’s machine.

Butt’s achievement was to found a national, respectable and constitutional movement and win about 60 seats in 1874; his limits were the absence of discipline, money and mass support, and the failure to win any concession.

Parnell’s achievement was to give the party discipline (the pledge, conventions), a press, American funding and a mass base through the Land League; his limit was his dependence on the agrarian movement and the Fenians, whom he could not fully control.
Butt thought the land question a distraction and accepted the 1870 Act, whereas Parnell made land the engine of the national movement.
Butt appealed to English opinion by argument; Parnell appealed to the threat of disruption, and by 1885 his party held the balance of power in the Commons.
Butt was a Protestant gentleman who lacked contact with tenant farmers; Parnell was also a Protestant landowner, but built networks that reached every parish.
Contemporaries saw Butt as an honourable failure and Parnell as a dangerous but effective leader; later historians generally accept that Butt prepared the ground and Parnell harvested it.
Kilmainham is read by some as a sensible deal that brought land reform and steered Parnell towards parliamentary politics, and by critics as an opportunistic retreat from the Land League’s aims.
Most Irish farmers were tenants at will or on short leases, and the law gave them little protection against eviction or rent increases.
Land was owned by a small landlord class, often Protestant and often absentee; most farmers rented their holdings, usually without a lease.
The tenants’ three demands became known as the Three Fs: fair rent, fixity of tenure and free sale of the tenant’s interest in the holding.
Ulster had the Ulster Custom, a tradition of tenant right that let outgoing tenants sell their interest; the 1870 Act gave it legal force there, though tenants elsewhere had no such protection.
Gladstone’s Land Act of 1870 offered compensation for improvements and for disturbance (eviction other than for non-payment of rent), but it did not fix rents.
Landlords could still raise rents beyond what tenants could pay and then evict for non-payment, which the Act did not forbid.
The purchase clauses (the Bright clauses) offered loans to tenants who wished to buy, but little land was sold under them.
The Act therefore left tenants without security of tenure, the main reason for the later land agitation (see also the earlier land legislation in the notes on Ireland before 1870).
A farming crisis turned long-standing grievances into a mass movement led by Davitt and Parnell.
From 1877 bad weather, poor harvests and cheap American grain brought falling prices; the wet summer of 1879 produced a partial potato failure.
Rent arrears mounted and evictions rose sharply: about 460 families were evicted in 1877 and more than 2,000 in 1880.
Michael Davitt, released from prison in 1877 and linked to Devoy through the New Departure, organised a meeting at Irishtown, Co. Mayo, on 20 April 1879 against a landlord’s high rents.
At Westport in June 1879 Parnell told tenants to keep a firm grip of their homesteads, his first major public identification with the agitation.
The Land League of Mayo was founded in August 1879, and the Irish National Land League was founded in Dublin in October 1879 with Parnell as president and Davitt as a leading organiser.
The League’s programme was to reduce rents and then to make tenants owners of their land (peasant proprietorship); Davitt personally favoured land nationalisation.
Funds came from Irish America, and Land League branches multiplied across the south and west in 1880.
The League fought evictions with collective action, and the government answered with coercion.
At Ennis in September 1880 Parnell urged that anyone who took a farm from which a tenant had been evicted should be shunned by the whole community.
The first victim was Captain Charles Boycott, agent for Lord Erne at Lough Mask, Co. Mayo, whose workers and tradesmen left him in 1880.
In November 1880 about fifty Ulster Orange labourers were brought in to save Boycott’s harvest, protected by around 1,000 soldiers and police; the cost of the operation became a national joke.
Moonlighting, the night-time maiming of cattle and attacks on property, accompanied the campaign, and Parnell’s opponents blamed the League.
The Ladies’ Land League, led in Dublin by Anna Parnell and formed in 1881, kept the campaign going when the men were jailed and helped evicted families with huts and relief.
Gladstone’s Chief Secretary, W.E. Forster, secured the Protection of Person and Property Act in March 1881, allowing the imprisonment of suspects without trial; hundreds of local leaders were jailed.
Parnell’s obstruction of the coercion bill in the Commons in early 1881 led to the introduction of closure.
The 1881 Act met most of the League’s demands, but Parnell would not let the League accept it without testing it.
The Land Law (Ireland) Act (August 1881) granted the Three Fs: fair rents set by land courts (Land Commission), fixity of tenure while the tenant paid the rent, and free sale.
Fair rents were fixed by the courts for fifteen years, and the first rounds of judicial rents reduced rents by about one fifth on average.
The landlord kept ownership but shared control of the holding with the tenant, a system known as dual ownership.
Leaseholders and tenants in arrears were excluded at first, which left about a third of tenants outside its benefits until the Arrears Act of 1882.
Parnell adopted a policy of testing the Act by sending selected test cases to the land courts, in effect telling tenants to wait.
Gladstone denounced Parnell at Leeds on 7 October 1881; Parnell was arrested on 13 October and the League issued the No Rent Manifesto five days later.
The manifesto flopped (the Catholic hierarchy and many tenants rejected it) and the League was suppressed on 20 October 1881.
The Arrears Act (August 1882) cleared arrears of rent for tenants rated under £30, with the state paying part, as part of the Kilmainham settlement.
When prices fell again in 1885–86, a new campaign sought rent reductions estate by estate.
The Plan of Campaign was launched in October 1886 in United Ireland by William O’Brien, John Dillon and Timothy Harrington.
Tenants on an estate demanded a reduction of rent; if the landlord refused, they paid the reduced amount into a fund controlled by trustees, which paid for the defence of evicted tenants.
It was applied on about 100 estates, including those of Lord Clanricarde in Co. Galway and Lord Massereene in Co. Louth.

Arthur Balfour, Chief Secretary from 1887, answered with the Criminal Law and Procedure (Ireland) Act (1887), allowing trial by magistrates without a jury for certain offences and the banning of organisations.
On 9 September 1887 police fired on a crowd at Mitchelstown, Co. Cork, killing three; nationalists called it a massacre and Balfour was nicknamed Bloody Balfour.
The Holy Office in Rome condemned the Plan of Campaign and boycotting in a decree of April 1888, an unwelcome intervention for nationalists.
Parnell was never close to the Plan: the Liberal alliance mattered more to him, and the movement was weakened by the Parnell split in 1890–91.
Conservative governments tried to defuse the land question by funding tenants’ purchase of their farms, a policy called constructive unionism or killing Home Rule with kindness.
The Ashbourne Act (1885), passed by Salisbury’s government, advanced loans of the full purchase price to tenants who bought from willing landlords, repayable by annuities.
Balfour’s Land Purchase Act (1891) extended the funds for purchase and aimed to make sales faster.
The Congested Districts Board (1891) targeted poor areas of the west, buying and dividing estates, improving fisheries and promoting crafts and agriculture.
Constructive unionism assumed that economic reform would reduce nationalist feeling; critics have argued it made landlords richer while the problem of poor western farms remained.
Gerald Balfour’s Land Act (1896) made small changes to the purchase terms, though little changed in practice.
A negotiated settlement between landlords and tenant leaders brought mass tenant purchase.
The Land Conference met in Dublin in December 1902, with Lord Dunraven (chair), Captain John Shawe-Taylor, William O’Brien and John Redmond, among others, and agreed a purchase scheme.
The Wyndham Land Act (1903), introduced by the Chief Secretary George Wyndham, offered tenants loans of the full price repayable over about 68 years at low interest.
Landlords were given a bonus of 12 per cent of the price as an inducement to sell.
More than 200,000 tenants bought farms under the Act within a few years, and the Treasury found the bonus costly; the terms were then revised.
The Evicted Tenants Act (1907) enabled reinstatement of tenants evicted in the Land War.
The Labourers (Ireland) Act (1906), a Liberal measure, provided for new cottages for farm labourers, with tens of thousands built by 1914.
The Birrell Land Act (1909), named for the Chief Secretary Augustine Birrell, allowed compulsory purchase where landlords would not sell and increased the powers of the Estates Commissioners.
By 1914 most tenants had bought, or were buying, their holdings, and landlordism had effectively ended as a political and social force.
Davitt was the son of an evicted Mayo tenant who became a Fenian, then the organiser of the Land League and later a Labour voice.
Born in 1846 at Straide, Co. Mayo, he was evicted with his family in 1850 and grew up in Haslingden, Lancashire.
He lost his right arm in a cotton-mill accident at the age of eleven, and educated himself while working.
He joined the IRB, was arrested for arms trafficking in 1870 and sentenced to fifteen years; he was released on licence in December 1877 after about seven years, mostly at Dartmoor.
He founded the Land League in Mayo in 1879, travelled to the USA, and was the main organiser behind Parnell’s public leadership.
He was re-arrested in February 1881 and held at Portland until May 1882; his prison experience produced Leaves from a Prison Diary (1885).
He argued for land nationalisation and was dismayed that the League accepted peasant proprietorship; he rejected the use of violence against individuals.
In 1890 he opposed Parnell’s continued leadership after the O’Shea divorce, and he founded the newspaper Labour World the same year.
He resigned his seat in 1899 in protest against the Boer War and published The Fall of Feudalism in Ireland in 1904; he died in 1906.
Contemporaries saw him as a dangerous agitator (unionists) or a hero of the tenants (nationalists); historians now stress his social radicalism and his role in joining Fenians and constitutionalists.
The land campaign changed who owned Irish land, but it was less successful in solving rural poverty and in delivering Home Rule.
Achievement: agitation forced the state to concede the Three Fs in 1881 and then to finance the transfer of land from landlords to tenants by 1914.
Limit: the settlement was reached by state funding and compromise, not by land nationalisation; labourers and small western farmers gained least.
Achievement: the Land League mobilised a mass base and made Parnell’s party a national force.
Limit: the agitation depended on Parnell’s control, and violence, divisions over the Plan of Campaign and the papal condemnation weakened it.
Contemporary unionists claimed concessions were extracted by intimidation, while nationalists said that only pressure had moved Westminster.
Historians differ on whether constructive unionism worked: it removed a major grievance, but did not stop the growth of nationalism.
Davitt’s social vision (land nationalisation, labour rights) was more radical than Parnell’s, a contrast examiners ask students to draw.
Two Acts rewrote the electoral map just before the 1885 election, and Parnell’s organised party was the main beneficiary.

The Representation of the People Act 1884 (the Third Reform Act) gave the vote to male householders and lodgers in the counties on the same terms as the boroughs, ending the old gap between town and country.
In Ireland the electorate rose from roughly 220,000 to roughly 740,000, more than tripling; the new voters were mostly small farmers and agricultural labourers (estimates vary).
The Redistribution of Seats Act 1885 abolished many small boroughs and divided the counties into single-member constituencies, though Ireland kept its 103 seats.
Single-member rural seats favoured a party organised in every parish, and the Irish National League had branches across the country, often led by priests.
Candidates were chosen at constituency conventions, and from 1884 each had to pledge to sit, act and vote with the Irish Party.
Voting remained in secret under the 1872 Ballot Act, so tenants could vote against their landlords without fear.
The Catholic hierarchy, led by Archbishop Walsh of Dublin and Archbishop Croke of Cashel, supported the party on the understanding that it would press for denominational education.
Parnell’s aim was to bargain with both British parties and to give Home Rule to whichever offered more.
At Cork in January 1885 Parnell declared that no man had the right to fix the boundary to the march of a nation, a demand for more than a limited local parliament.

In 1884 Conservatives such as Lord Randolph Churchill joined the Irish MPs in attacking the Liberal Lord Lieutenant, Earl Spencer, over the Maamtrasna murders (August 1882), where Myles Joyce was hanged despite doubts about his guilt.
That common cause is sometimes called the Maamtrasna alliance, and it opened the way to co-operation between Parnell and the Conservatives.
On 9 June 1885 the Irish Party voted with the Conservatives against Gladstone’s budget and brought down his government; Lord Salisbury formed a minority Conservative ministry.
Salisbury’s Lord Lieutenant, Lord Carnarvon, met Parnell secretly in London in August 1885; the Crimes Act was allowed to lapse and the Ashbourne Act offered loans for tenant purchase.
Parnell’s manifesto of November 1885 told Irish voters in Britain to vote against Liberal candidates, because of Liberal coercion in 1881–82.
Joseph Chamberlain’s plan for an elected Central Board for Ireland, discussed in 1885 through Captain O’Shea, was rejected by Parnell and by the Cabinet and kept Home Rule on the table.
At Arklow in October 1885 Parnell set out a demand for a legislature with control of Irish domestic affairs, and he stressed that Ireland would not be satisfied with less.
The election produced a hung Parliament in which the Irish Party held the balance, and it split Ireland along religious and regional lines.
The Irish Party won 85 of the 103 Irish seats, with one more at Liverpool Scotland, giving 86 MPs in all.
It won every seat outside Ulster except the two for Dublin University and a few in Dublin suburbs, and it swept the south and west.
In Ulster the party won 17 of 33 seats, in the Catholic-majority counties of the south and west of the province, while unionists held the Belfast seats and most of east Ulster.

In Great Britain the Liberals won about 335 seats (counts vary by method), the Conservatives about 249, and the Irish Party 86, so the Liberals’ lead over the Conservatives was almost exactly the Irish total.
That gave Parnell the decisive vote: the Irish Party plus the Conservatives could equal the Liberals, and the Irish Party could keep either in or out of office.
The Irish vote in British cities, especially Liverpool, helped the Conservatives in some constituencies, though its effect is hard to measure.
Parnell chose the moment well: he could now say that Ireland’s demand was clear, and that Home Rule could not be refused to a nation that had voted for it in this way.
Contemporary Liberals saw the results as proof that Ireland, minus Protestant Ulster, wanted Home Rule; contemporary Conservatives and unionists replied that two Irelands had voted.
Gladstone moved to Home Rule within weeks of the election, took office again in February 1886 and introduced a bill in April.
On 17 December 1885 newspapers published the Hawarden Kite: reports, leaked by Gladstone’s son Herbert, that Gladstone (at Hawarden in Flintshire) favoured Home Rule.

Salisbury’s ministry was defeated in January 1886 on an amendment about allotments for labourers (Jesse Collings), with the Irish voting against it, and Gladstone formed his third ministry in February.
Joseph Chamberlain, who joined the cabinet, resigned in March 1886 along with Sir George Trevelyan, and Lord Hartington declined to serve.
Gladstone introduced the Government of Ireland Bill on 8 April 1886.
The bill would have set up an Irish legislature in Dublin with an executive responsible to it; the Crown, defence, foreign policy, trade and the customs remained with Westminster.
Ireland was to pay a fixed share (one fifteenth) of imperial expenditure, and the Irish members would no longer sit at Westminster.
The Irish legislature was to have two orders, sitting together, designed to reassure Protestants and property owners, and was forbidden to establish or endow any religion.
A companion Land Purchase Bill would have offered loans to buy out the landlords; it was unpopular in Britain and was dropped, and it weakened the main bill.
Parnell accepted the bill as a basis for a settlement, though he objected to its financial terms and its control of the police.
The Liberal split, not the Conservatives alone, defeated the First Home Rule Bill.
The bill was debated for several weeks in April–June 1886 and the vote came early on 8 June at second reading.
It was defeated by 341 votes to 311 (some sources give 343 to 313), a majority of 30.
About 93 Liberals, led by Hartington and Chamberlain, voted with the Conservatives against the bill; they became the Liberal Unionists.
Chamberlain argued that the bill would break up the empire and treat Ulster Protestants unfairly; the veteran radical John Bright also opposed it.
Conservatives such as Lord Randolph Churchill argued that Home Rule meant separation and the loss of the Protestant minority’s rights.
Gladstone’s supporters argued that coercion had failed and that Home Rule would give Ireland a settled government and reconcile it to the Crown.
After the defeat Gladstone dissolved Parliament and called a general election.
The crisis of 1886 created organised unionism in Ulster and the south.
Lord Randolph Churchill wrote in February 1886 that the Orange card was the one to play against Home Rule, and he spoke in the Ulster Hall, Belfast, on 22 February 1886.
A later letter of May 1886 gave him the phrase that Ulster would fight and Ulster would be right, a slogan unionists used for decades.
The Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union had been formed in 1885 by southern unionists, mainly landlords and professionals, to organise opposition to Home Rule.
Ulster Protestants established Loyalist Anti-Repeal organisations in 1886, and the Orange Order grew sharply; unionists feared that an Irish parliament would be a Catholic parliament.
The Belfast riots began on 4 June 1886 after the bill’s defeat was in prospect and continued into September.
At least 30 people were killed, and hundreds were injured; estimates of the death toll vary.
The Belfast violence deepened sectarian division, and both sides used it as evidence: nationalists blamed unionist mobs and the Orange Order, unionists blamed Home Rule agitation.
The voters rejected Gladstone, and the Conservatives governed for most of the next twenty years.
The July 1886 general election gave the Conservatives and Liberal Unionists a combined majority of more than 100 over the Gladstonian Liberals and the Irish Party.
Salisbury formed his second government, supported by the Liberal Unionists, who joined the Conservatives in coalition in 1895.
The Irish Party again won about 85 seats in Ireland, so the nationalist case was undiminished.
Home Rule was now the official policy of the Liberal Party, and the Liberal–Nationalist alliance was the central fact of Irish parliamentary politics until 1914.
Parnell was at the height of his power, with a disciplined party and a Liberal ally, until the Pigott forgeries and the O’Shea divorce.
The Liberal split turned Home Rule into a cause that could pass only when the Liberals had a majority independent of the Lords, which did not happen until the Parliament Act of 1911.
Unionism became a lasting organised force in Ireland and Britain, and the Conservative–Unionist alliance shaped policy up to the Ulster crisis.
Parnell was the central figure in the case study: he made the Irish Party decisive and tied Home Rule to the Liberals.
He turned the National League into an election machine and imposed the pledge, so the party could deliver its votes as a bloc.
He chose to keep both British parties guessing, bargaining with Carnarvon and then supporting Gladstone, an example of his tactical skill.
He imposed Captain O’Shea as candidate in the Galway by-election of February 1886 against Tim Healy’s objections, which showed his control but sowed resentment.
He was a participant who led the campaign, and nationalist contemporaries saw the 85 seats as a personal triumph and a national mandate.
Unionists and many Conservatives saw him as the leader of a movement linked to violence and the Land War, and The Times later published forged letters aimed at this reputation.

Strengths examiners ask about include his discipline, his tactical sense, his appeal to both Fenians and constitutionalists and his skill in the Commons; weaknesses include his reliance on the Liberal alliance, his aloofness and the secrecy of his private life.
Historians such as F.S.L. Lyons describe 1885–86 as Parnell’s zenith; others note that his strategy depended on Gladstone surviving the Liberal split.
Documents on this case study are speeches, newspaper reports and cartoons, and each can be placed by who produced it and when.
Nationalists (Freeman’s Journal, United Ireland) presented the 1885 result as a national verdict and the First Home Rule Bill as a just but limited settlement.
Unionists (Belfast News-Letter, the Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union) presented Home Rule as a threat to the empire, to property and to Protestants.
Gladstone’s speeches argued that Home Rule was a moral duty after the failure of coercion; his critics called it a surrender to agitators.
Liberal Unionist speeches, by Chamberlain and Hartington, argued that Irish self-government would endanger the union of the two islands.

Punch, drawn by John Tenniel and others, usually depicted Irish agitators as violent or ape-like, as in the Irish Frankenstein of 1882, and took an anti-Home Rule line; some Irish and radical papers published pro-Home Rule cartoons.
A cartoon can be placed by its date and symbols: Gladstone as the old man with an axe, Parnell as a tempter or bully, Hibernia as a woman, John Bull as a stout man.

Historians differ on why Gladstone took up Home Rule: genuine conviction after the 1885 result, or tactical manoeuvre to keep the Liberals together, as argued by A.B. Cooke and John Vincent in The Governing Passion (1974).
The elections were a triumph for the Irish Party and a defeat for Home Rule.
Achievement: the Irish Party won a national mandate, forced Home Rule onto the British agenda and won over a major British party.
Limit: the party could not pass a bill without a British majority, and Gladstone’s conversion split the Liberals and left the Conservatives in power.
Achievement: the bill’s defeat was narrow and the Liberal alliance gave nationalists a realistic route to Home Rule.
Limit: the elections showed that Ulster Protestants were opposed, a problem that Parnell’s party never solved.
Contemporary nationalists blamed the Liberal Unionists and the House of Commons; contemporary unionists said the vote showed the Union was safe.
Later historians see 1886 as the origin of the Ulster question as well as of the Liberal–Nationalist alliance, which makes it a turning point whatever its immediate failure.
After 1886 Parnell kept the Liberal alliance and kept his distance from agrarian violence; his enemies tried to destroy him with forged evidence, and failed.
The Plan of Campaign (October 1886) was launched by O’Brien, Dillon and Harrington; Parnell did not endorse it and feared that evictions and violence would alarm British Liberals.
Parnell’s main concern was the Liberal alliance, and he spent much of 1887–89 away from Ireland and the daily running of the party.
In March 1887 The Times began a series called Parnellism and Crime, and on 18 April 1887 it printed a letter, supposedly signed by Parnell, that excused the Phoenix Park murders.
The letter was one of several forged by Richard Pigott, a discredited Dublin journalist who sold them to The Times.
The government set up a Special Commission of three judges in 1888 to examine the charges against Parnell and sixty-odd Irish MPs.
Under cross-examination in February 1889 Pigott collapsed; he had misspelled the word hesitancy in the same way as in the forged letter, and he fled to Madrid, where he shot himself on 1 March 1889.
Parnell was cheered in the Commons, visited Gladstone at Hawarden in December 1889, and won £5,000 in damages from The Times in 1890.
The Commission’s report (February 1890) rejected the forged letters, though it criticised the Land League’s methods; Parnell stood at the height of his reputation.
The divorce case of November 1890 turned the Liberal alliance and the Catholic hierarchy against Parnell and split the party.
Parnell had lived with Katharine O’Shea for years; her husband Captain William O’Shea, a former Irish Party MP, filed for divorce in December 1889 and named Parnell as co-respondent.
The case was heard on 15–17 November 1890; Parnell did not contest it and a decree nisi was granted.
On 25 November the Irish Party re-elected Parnell as chairman, before Gladstone’s letter to John Morley (saying Parnell’s leadership would make his own position untenable) was published.
Non-conformist Liberals threatened to desert Gladstone, and Gladstone told the Irish Party that he would not lead the Liberals if Parnell stayed.
On 3 December 1890 the Catholic bishops, led by Archbishop Walsh, condemned Parnell as unfit to lead.
Parnell issued a manifesto To the People of Ireland (29 November) which revealed details of private talks with Gladstone and attacked the Liberals, and it deepened the bitterness.
The debate in Committee Room 15 at Westminster lasted from 1 to 6 December 1890; on 6 December about 45 MPs led by Justin McCarthy walked out, leaving about 28 with Parnell.
The anti-Parnellites, later organised as the Irish National Federation, included Dillon, William O’Brien and the fierce critic Tim Healy; the Parnellites kept the National League.
Parnell lost by-elections in North Kilkenny (December 1890), North Sligo (April 1891) and Carlow (July 1891), campaigning in vicious conditions.
He married Katharine on 25 June 1891 and died at Brighton on 6 October 1891, aged 45; about 200,000 people are said to have followed his funeral to Glasnevin.
This part covers his years of peak influence, his fall and the overall judgement; the strengths and weaknesses below are the usual basis for essays.
Between 1886 and 1890 he combined an alliance with Gladstone with firm control over a disciplined party of 85 MPs.
He was a participant in the Pigott and O’Shea affairs and lost control of events after the divorce, when his refusal to step aside split the movement.
Contemporary nationalists were divided: the Parnellites saw him as a leader betrayed by Liberals and bishops, and the anti-Parnellites as a leader who put himself above the cause.
Contemporary unionists saw him as a dangerous agitator, until the Pigott collapse made them look foolish.
Strengths: party discipline, tactical skill, ability to unite Fenians, land reformers and constitutionalists, and a clear command of Commons procedure.
Weaknesses: aloofness and autocratic style, dependence on the Liberals, ambiguity about violence in the Land War, and a private life that he did not manage.

Historians differ: F.S.L. Lyons in his 1977 biography stresses the tragic collision of ambition and scandal; Paul Bew in 1980 stresses Parnell as a conservative landlord politician whose strategy had limits.
His legacy was the idea of an independent Irish party; he also left the mythology of a martyr, which later separatists, including Yeats and Joyce, drew on.
Gladstone’s last attempt at Home Rule was killed by the House of Lords, and the Irish Party spent the 1890s in feud.
The Liberals returned to office in 1892 with a small majority that depended on the Irish MPs; Gladstone, aged 83, introduced the Second Home Rule Bill on 13 February 1893.
The Bill proposed a legislature of two houses, and it kept a reduced number of Irish MPs at Westminster, to meet the objection that they would be excluded.
The Commons passed the bill in September 1893 by 301 votes to 267, after eighty-two sittings.
The House of Lords threw it out on 8 September 1893 by 419 votes to 41, and Gladstone retired in March 1894.
Unionists had mobilised against it, notably at the Ulster Convention in Belfast in June 1892 (see the notes on unionism).
The Conservatives under Salisbury won the 1895 election, and the Unionists governed for most of the next ten years, trying to kill Home Rule with kindness.
In the 1890s the Irish National Federation (Dillon and McCarthy), Healy’s followers and Redmond’s small Parnellite group fought each other, and voters became disillusioned.
The United Irish League was founded by William O’Brien at Westport, Co. Mayo, in January 1898 to revive the land agitation in the west.
The parties reunited in January 1900, and Redmond was elected chairman in February 1900; Healy was excluded.
Redmond rebuilt the party, won land reform and then used the Liberals’ dependence on his votes to put Home Rule on the statute book.
Redmond and William O’Brien took part in the Land Conference of 1902–03, which led to the Wyndham Act (see the notes on land reform).
In May 1907 a national convention of the party rejected the Irish Council Bill, a limited devolution scheme introduced by Chief Secretary Augustine Birrell.
In 1910 two elections left the Liberals dependent on the Irish Party: in January the Irish had 82 seats, and in December 84.
After the Lords rejected the People’s Budget (1909), Redmond’s party backed the Liberals and the Parliament Act (1911) removed the Lords’ veto, leaving only a two-year delay.
Asquith introduced the Third Home Rule Bill in April 1912; it passed the Commons three times and became law on 18 September 1914 (see the notes on the Third Home Rule crisis).
The Act was suspended by a Suspensory Act for the duration of the war, which Redmond accepted.
Under pressure from the unionist threat, in March 1914 Redmond accepted a proposal that Ulster counties could opt out for six years, a concession he had previously refused.
In June 1914 Redmond forced the Irish Volunteers to accept 25 of his nominees on their provisional committee.
Redmond led the reunited party for eighteen years and believed that Home Rule could be won by constitutional methods and kept by loyalty to the empire.
John Redmond (1856–1918) was born at Ballytrent, Co. Wexford, into a Catholic gentry family, educated at Clongowes, and became a barrister and MP in 1881.
He stayed loyal to Parnell in 1890 and led the small Parnellite group after Parnell died in 1891; he sat for Waterford City from 1891 until his death.
He was a participant who negotiated the Land Conference, the 1911 Parliament Act and the 1912 Bill, relying on his control of the party’s votes.
Contemporary nationalists generally admired him as the leader who delivered Home Rule; critics such as Griffith and the IRB attacked his reliance on Liberal goodwill.
His pledge in August 1914 that the Volunteers should defend Ireland, and his Woodenbridge speech of 20 September 1914 urging them to fight in the war, split the Irish Volunteers.
About 170,000 followed him into the National Volunteers and about 11,000 stayed with Eoin MacNeill’s Irish Volunteers (estimates vary).
Strengths: party management, parliamentary skill, a genuine achievement in land and the Home Rule Act, and personal integrity.
Weaknesses: dependence on the Liberals, failure to resolve the Ulster problem, acceptance of partition in principle in 1914 and poor judgement of the new separatism.

Historians differ: older accounts such as Denis Gwynn’s sympathetic 1932 biography and Dermot Meleady’s more recent work present a statesman wrecked by war; others see a leader out of touch with the new generation.
Arthur Griffith proposed a separatist policy of abstention and economic self-reliance as an alternative to Home Rule.
Arthur Griffith, a Dublin printer and journalist, founded the newspaper The United Irishman in 1899 with William Rooney.
Cumann na nGaedheal was founded in 1900 to unite groups promoting Irish language, industry and the national cause.
In The Resurrection of Hungary (1904) Griffith argued that Ireland should follow Hungary, which had won its own parliament within a dual monarchy in 1867 by abstaining from the imperial parliament.

At a convention in November 1905 Griffith’s National Council adopted what became the Sinn Féin policy: abstention from Westminster, a national assembly in Dublin and protective tariffs for Irish industry.
Cumann na nGaedheal merged with the Dungannon Clubs of Bulmer Hobson in 1907 to form the Sinn Féin League; Griffith’s weekly Sinn Féin followed in 1906.
In the North Leitrim by-election of February 1908 the Sinn Féin candidate C.J. Dolan, a former Irish Party MP, was beaten by roughly three to one.
Sinn Féin lost support after 1908 and the party remained small, but its ideas about abstention and self-reliance were revived in 1917.
A younger generation of separatists revived the IRB and used the Ulster Volunteers as a model for armed nationalism.
Tom Clarke, a Fenian who had served fifteen years in prison, returned from the USA in December 1907 and opened a tobacconist’s shop in Dublin.
With Bulmer Hobson and Seán Mac Diarmada, Clarke took control of the IRB and founded the paper Irish Freedom (1910).
Eoin MacNeill’s article The North Began, published on 1 November 1913, argued that the Ulster Volunteers had shown that Irishmen could organise to defend their rights.
The Irish Volunteers were founded on 25 November 1913 at the Rotunda Rink in Dublin; MacNeill became chairman and the IRB had a hidden influence.
Cumann na mBan, a women’s organisation to support the Volunteers, was founded in April 1914.
The Howth gun-running on 26 July 1914 landed about 900 rifles from Erskine Childers’s yacht Asgard; British soldiers then fired on a crowd at Bachelor’s Walk in Dublin, killing four.
After Redmond’s Woodenbridge speech the Volunteers split in September 1914: the majority became the National Volunteers and a minority kept the name Irish Volunteers.
The period shows constitutional nationalism at its strongest and the first serious challenge to it.
Achievements of the Home Rule movement: a united parliamentary party, land reform and, by 1914, a Home Rule Act on the statute book.
Limits: Parnell’s fall wasted a decade, the Lords killed the 1893 Bill, and the Ulster question remained unsolved in 1914.
Sinn Féin and the IRB offered a separatist alternative, but before 1914 they were small and divided; their growth after 1914 owed more to war and the 1916 Rising than to their own efforts.
Contemporary unionists judged Redmond a threat to the Union; separatists judged him too moderate; most nationalists in 1914 supported him.
Historians now often argue that Home Rule was not doomed before 1914 and that its collapse came from the war, the Rising and the conscription crisis.
Unionism was a coalition of Protestants of all classes in Ulster with landlords and business people elsewhere in Ireland, united by opposition to a Dublin parliament.

Ulster had a slight Protestant majority (about 56 per cent in 1911), concentrated in the east: Antrim, Down, Armagh and Londonderry had Protestant majorities, while Tyrone and Fermanagh were narrowly Catholic.
Protestants of every class were unionist: landlords and gentry, industrialists, shopkeepers, Presbyterian tenant farmers and Protestant workers in Belfast.

Southern unionists were a small minority (Protestants were about a tenth of the population outside Ulster), made up of landlords, professionals, businessmen and Church of Ireland clergy, strongest in Dublin and parts of Munster and Leinster.
Most Ulster Presbyterians had supported the Liberals before 1886, and Gladstone’s conversion to Home Rule pushed many into the unionist camp.
Many Protestants had been alarmed by Gladstone’s disestablishment of the Church of Ireland (1869) and by the Land Acts, and saw Home Rule as the next step.
Colonel Edward Saunderson led the Irish Unionist MPs at Westminster from 1886 until his death in 1906, and was followed by Walter Long, then Carson in 1910.
Unionists opposed Home Rule for three linked reasons: religion, economics and identity.
Religion: Protestants feared that a parliament elected by a Catholic majority would be under Catholic Church influence; the slogan was that Home Rule is Rome Rule.
The Catholic hierarchy’s role in the Irish Party’s candidate selection in 1885, and later the Ne Temere decree of 1908, strengthened the argument.

Economy: Belfast’s linen, shipbuilding, engineering and rope-making depended on British and imperial markets and raw materials, and unionists feared tariffs and higher taxes under a Dublin parliament.
The agricultural south and west had a different economy from the industrial north-east, so unionists argued that an Irish parliament would favour agricultural interests.
Identity and empire: Ulster Protestants saw themselves as British, were proud of the empire, and believed that Home Rule was the first step towards separation.
Protestants also feared for their position as a minority in a self-governing Ireland, and many believed nationalists would dispossess them, as in the Land War.
Liberal unionists such as Chamberlain argued that Home Rule would threaten the union of the kingdoms, not only the Ulster minority.
Protestants held a disproportionate share of Ireland’s land, wealth and professions, and feared losing status in a state run by the Catholic majority.
Many Ulster unionists believed that the Land Acts and the Irish Party’s links with Fenians showed that nationalists would not respect property.
From 1885 unionists built organisations to match the National League.
The Orange Order, founded in 1795, revived in the 1880s and gave Ulster unionism a mass base of lodges across the province.
The Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union was founded in 1885 by southern unionists; the Ulster Loyalist Anti-Repeal Union followed in 1886.
The Belfast riots of 1886 sharpened sectarian division (see the notes on the 1885–86 elections).
The Irish Unionist Alliance was formed in 1891 to unite the Irish unionist bodies.
The Ulster Convention, held in the Botanic Gardens in Belfast in June 1892 with about 12,000 delegates, protested against the Second Home Rule Bill; a Dublin convention followed.
The Ulster Unionist Council was founded in March 1905 as a central body for Ulster, bringing together Orange lodges, constituency associations and unionist MPs.
Opposition to the Irish Reform Association’s devolution proposals in 1904–05 convinced Ulster unionists that they needed their own permanent body.
The Ulster Women’s Unionist Council, formed in January 1911 under Lady Londonderry, mobilised tens of thousands of women for the unionist cause.
Carson, a Dublin-born barrister, led the unionist campaign against the Third Home Rule Bill and made the threat of armed resistance credible.
Edward Carson (1854–1935) was born in Dublin, educated at Trinity College, and became a leading barrister, Solicitor General for Ireland in 1892 and Solicitor General for England in 1900–06.
He was MP for Dublin University from 1892, and in 1895 he cross-examined Oscar Wilde as counsel for the Marquess of Queensberry in the libel case that ruined Wilde.
In 1910 he became leader of the Irish Unionist parliamentary party, and he was the chief unionist campaigner from 1911 to 1914.
He was a participant: he led the Ulster Day rally on 28 September 1912, signed the Covenant first at Belfast City Hall, and led the Provisional Government plan of 1913.
His southern, Dublin background made him an unlikely leader of Ulster, but he spoke for all Irish unionists, which was the point of his campaign.
Contemporary unionists revered him as the defender of the Union; nationalists and many Liberals thought him a man ready to defy parliament, and Redmond denounced the threat of force.
Historians differ: some say he never intended to fight and bluffed to protect the Union; others that his threat made partition inevitable, and that he abandoned southern unionists.
He resigned the leadership in 1921, becoming a law lord, and lamented that unionism had been sacrificed in the creation of Northern Ireland.
After the Parliament Act of 1911 removed the Lords’ veto, unionists organised a campaign of mass resistance with Conservative backing.
The Parliament Act (August 1911) meant that the Third Home Rule Bill would become law within about two years, even if the Lords rejected it.
James Craig, a wealthy Belfast businessman and MP for East Down, became Carson’s chief organiser and planned the campaign.
A huge unionist demonstration was held at Craigavon, outside Belfast, in September 1911, with Carson as speaker.
Andrew Bonar Law, the Conservative leader since November 1911, spoke at Blenheim Palace on 27 July 1912, pledging the party to support Ulster in any resistance.
The Third Home Rule Bill was introduced on 11 April 1912; an amendment to exclude four Ulster counties was defeated in June 1912.
On Ulster Day, 28 September 1912, about 237,000 men signed the Solemn League and Covenant, pledging to use all means to defeat Home Rule, and about 234,000 women signed a separate declaration.
The total of about 471,000 signatures included many in Britain; some, especially younger Protestants, signed in their own blood or at the church door.
The Commons passed the Third Home Rule Bill in January 1913, the Lords rejected it, and the same happened in July 1913; a third Commons passage in 1914 overrode the Lords under the Parliament Act.
A British Covenant organised by the Union Defence League in 1914 gathered a very large number of signatures in Britain (about two million is often quoted).
The Twelfth of July Orange demonstrations and Presbyterian and Church of Ireland ministers gave the campaign a religious character, with many ministers joining Covenant services.
In 1913 unionist leaders organised an armed force and prepared to take over the government of Ulster.
The Ulster Volunteer Force was formed in January 1913 from earlier local drilling clubs, with Lieutenant-General Sir George Richardson as commander.
By 1914 the UVF had perhaps 90,000 to 100,000 men, organised in battalions, with many drilling openly and wearing uniform.
In September 1913 the Ulster Unionist Council announced that it would set up a Provisional Government of Ulster, with Carson as chairman, if Home Rule became law.
Unionists said that they were loyal to the king but not to a parliament they believed to be illegitimate.
The government did not prosecute, and Redmond warned that the failure to act encouraged separatist counter-organisation (the Irish Volunteers, founded November 1913).
The crisis peaked in the first half of 1914, with the army’s reluctance and the unionist arms landing.
On 9 March 1914 Asquith proposed that Ulster counties could vote themselves out of Home Rule for six years; Carson rejected this as a stay of execution.

On 20 March 1914, in the Curragh incident, Brigadier-General Hubert Gough and many of his officers offered to resign rather than act against Ulster; the Secretary for War, John Seely, and Sir John French resigned afterwards.
On the night of 24–25 April 1914 the UVF landed about 25,000 rifles and several million rounds at Larne, Donaghadee and Bangor, organised by Fred Crawford, and the police and army did not intervene.
The Larne landing prompted nationalists to organise their own gun-running at Howth and Kilcoole in July–August 1914.
The Buckingham Palace Conference (21–24 July 1914), opened by George V and chaired by the Speaker, brought Asquith, Lloyd George, Redmond, Dillon, Carson, Craig, Lansdowne and Bonar Law together.
The Conference failed over the area to be excluded, especially Tyrone and Fermanagh, with mixed populations.
The Home Rule Act received the royal assent on 18 September 1914 but was suspended for the duration of the war, leaving Ulster’s status unsettled.
The rifles had been bought in Germany by Fred Crawford and brought to Larne by the ship Clyde Valley, then distributed by car across Ulster in a night.
Redmond rejected permanent exclusion of Ulster as partition, while Carson rejected temporary exclusion; the gap between them was never closed before the war.
Judgements on unionism compare its success in blocking Home Rule before 1914 with its failure to hold the whole of Ireland in the Union.
Achievement: unionists defeated the first two Home Rule Bills, built effective organisation and by 1914 had forced the government to accept the principle of exclusion for Ulster.
Achievement: the UVF, the Covenant and Conservative backing showed that Home Rule could not be imposed on Ulster by force, and made Carson and Craig decisive in later negotiations.
Limit: unionists could not stop the Third Home Rule Bill becoming law, and southern unionists had no protection.
Limit: the Conservative alliance meant unionism was exposed when the Conservatives themselves compromised, as they did in 1920–21.
Contemporary nationalists thought unionist arms threatened democracy and parliament; unionists thought them a legitimate defence of rights.

Historians such as A.T.Q. Stewart (The Ulster Crisis, 1967) show how close Britain came to civil war in 1914; Alvin Jackson stresses unionist resilience and the divisions between Ulster and southern unionists.
Women’s suffrage began in Ireland as a small, respectable campaign among middle-class Protestant and Quaker women, linked to property rights, education and local government.

Women had no parliamentary vote and, under common law, a married woman’s property belonged to her husband; Married Women’s Property Acts (1870 and 1882) improved this, and Isabella Tod campaigned for them.
Isabella Tod organised a suffrage society in Belfast in the early 1870s (accounts give 1871 to 1873), the first in Ulster.
Anna Haslam, a Quaker, and her husband Thomas founded the Dublin Women’s Suffrage Association in 1876; it later became the Irish Women’s Suffrage and Local Government Association.
The early societies petitioned MPs, held drawing-room meetings and sent speakers, and they worked alongside the campaign for girls’ education and against the Contagious Diseases Acts.
Women ratepayers won the municipal vote in 1887, and women were first elected as poor law guardians in 1896.

The Local Government (Ireland) Act of 1898 gave women the vote in county and district council elections and the right to stand for district councils and boards of guardians, though not for county councils (opened by an Act of 1911).
Several prominent Irish suffragists, such as Tod, were unionists, while others supported Home Rule, so the movement avoided taking sides on it for decades.
The King and Queen’s College of Physicians in Dublin began licensing women in 1877, the first body in the United Kingdom to do so, opening medicine to Irish women.
Anna Haslam (1829–1922) led the Dublin society for over forty years and lived to see women gain the vote.
Tod was a Belfast Presbyterian reformer who campaigned on women’s education, property and votes within a unionist outlook.
Isabella Tod (1836–1896) was born in Edinburgh and settled in Belfast, where she lived until her death.

She was a participant in the campaigns that led to the Married Women’s Property Act (1882) and to the inclusion of girls in the Intermediate Education Act (1878) and the Royal University’s charter (1879).
She helped found the Ladies’ Institute in Belfast (1867), a society for girls’ education, and worked with Margaret Byers of the Ladies’ Collegiate School (later Victoria College).
She co-founded the Belfast Women’s Temperance Association (1874) and campaigned against the Contagious Diseases Acts.
As a Liberal Unionist she opposed Home Rule in 1886 and urged women to oppose it; she helped found the Irish Women’s Liberal Unionist Association.
Contemporaries respected her as a public speaker and organiser, though her unionism limited her influence among nationalists.
Historians present her as a pioneer who created the first sustained suffrage organisation in Ulster and broke the exclusion of women from Irish public debate.
Suffrage groups multiplied after 1900, but the Irish Party refused to back the cause.
The Irish Women’s Suffrage Federation, founded in 1911 under Louie Bennett and others, linked local societies and used peaceful methods.
The Irish Women’s Franchise League (1908) was more radical, and argued that no Home Rule settlement was legitimate without votes for women.
In Westminster, a Conciliation Bill proposing a limited vote for women was defeated in March 1912, with the Irish Party mostly voting against.
Redmond and Dillon feared that a franchise bill would complicate the passage of Home Rule, and Redmond personally opposed votes for women.
Suffragists tried to have an amendment in favour of women’s votes added to the Third Home Rule Bill, which the Irish Party and the government opposed.

Suffragists generally split on the national question: some, like Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington, argued that independence would be incomplete without women’s votes; others, notably in Ulster, were unionists.
From 1908 the League brought militant methods to Irish politics, and its campaign peaked in 1912–13.

The Irish Women’s Franchise League was founded in Dublin in 1908 by Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington, Margaret Cousins, her husband James Cousins and Francis Sheehy-Skeffington; its aim was votes for women on the same terms as men.
The League published the weekly Irish Citizen from May 1912 (edited at first by Francis Sheehy-Skeffington and James Cousins), which ran until 1920.
In June 1912 eight League members, including Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington and Margaret Cousins, were arrested for breaking windows at government buildings in Dublin, and were imprisoned.
During Asquith’s visit to Dublin in July 1912, English suffragettes of the WSPU disrupted his visit, and Mary Leigh threw a hatchet into the carriage in which he and Redmond were travelling.
Imprisoned suffragettes went on hunger strike, and the English prisoners were force-fed in Mountjoy, which provoked public protest.
Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington was jailed again in 1913 and released after a hunger strike under the Cat and Mouse Act.
Hostile crowds attacked suffragettes at public meetings, and many nationalists and trade unionists considered the militant tactics counter-productive.
Sheehy-Skeffington was the leading Irish militant suffragist, who tied women’s rights to nationalism and socialism.
Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington (1877–1946) was born in Kanturk, Co. Cork, the daughter of the nationalist MP David Sheehy, and took an MA from the Royal University in 1902.
She married the pacifist and feminist Francis Skeffington in 1903, and they each added the other’s surname.
She co-founded the Irish Women’s Franchise League in 1908, was imprisoned for window-breaking in 1912 and in 1913, and was a contributor and later editor of the Irish Citizen.

She was a participant, and her organisation shaped how the issue was seen in Ireland, but she was also a critic of the Irish Party and later of Cumann na mBan, which she saw as subordinating women to men.
Her husband was shot without trial by Captain Bowen-Colthurst in April 1916, and she campaigned for an inquiry and refused compensation.
Contemporaries admired her courage but many nationalists thought her tactics divisive; unionists and the Irish Party saw her as a nuisance.
Historians now see her as a key figure of Irish feminism who insisted that independence must include equality.
The suffrage cause was entangled with the national question, and women in each camp chose their side.
Unionist women in Ulster signed their own declaration on Ulster Day in September 1912, around 234,000 of them, and had a public role in unionism; suffragists such as Tod had been unionists.
Nationalist women formed Cumann na mBan in April 1914 to support the Volunteers; suffragists such as Sheehy-Skeffington objected to its auxiliary status.
Many suffragists argued that women should not be asked to postpone their claim until Home Rule or the Union had been settled.
The Irish Citizen pursued both aims, and it attracted writers from different political groups, from the pacifist movement to the trade unions.
Votes for women were granted in 1918 (women over thirty with property qualifications), after the First World War, and the Irish Party that had opposed the cause had by then been destroyed.
State funding of secondary schools began in 1878 and used examinations to decide payment; primary education was reformed in 1900.
The Intermediate Education (Ireland) Act (1878) set up an Intermediate Board that held public examinations (junior, middle and senior grades) for boys and girls from 1879.
Schools were paid results fees according to how many pupils passed, a system known as payment by results; prizes and exhibitions rewarded top candidates.
The system financed denominational schools without interfering in their management, so Catholic, Protestant and convent schools all grew.
Girls’ schools used the examinations to compete with boys; Alexandra College (Dublin, 1866), Victoria College (Belfast) and the Loreto and Dominican convent schools all prepared girls.
Critics said payment by results encouraged cramming, narrowed the curriculum to examinable subjects and neglected Irish and science.

National school teachers had been paid by results since the 1870s; the Revised Programme of 1900 ended this, broadening the curriculum to include drawing, practical work, nature study and Irish as an ordinary subject within school hours.
The bilingual programme of 1904 encouraged teaching through Irish in Gaeltacht schools.
Victoria College in Belfast, founded by Margaret Byers in 1859 as the Ladies’ Collegiate School, and Alexandra College, founded in 1866, were pioneers of girls’ secondary education.
The Royal University opened degrees to women and Catholics; the 1908 Act settled the university question with two new universities.
The Royal University of Ireland (1879) was an examining body that awarded degrees to students of any college or none; it replaced the old Queen’s University.
It admitted women to its examinations and degrees on equal terms, and the first women graduated in the early 1880s; Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington was among its later graduates.
Catholics complained that no university gave them a real Catholic institution; Trinity College Dublin was Protestant in ethos and the Catholic bishops forbade Catholics to attend it.

The Irish Universities Act (1908), prepared by Chief Secretary Augustine Birrell, dissolved the Royal University and created the National University of Ireland (constituent colleges at Dublin, Cork and Galway) and Queen’s University Belfast.
The NUI had a Catholic ethos, with Archbishop Walsh as first chancellor, and was open to women on equal terms.
The Gaelic League campaigned for compulsory Irish for matriculation: the NUI Senate decided in 1910 to require it, applied from 1913.
Reforms opened up public life to women and widened access to education, but the parliamentary vote came late and by a different route.
Achievement: by 1914 women could vote and stand in local elections, sit on boards of guardians, take degrees and run campaigns and newspapers.
Limit: Irish women had no parliamentary vote before 1918, none of the three Home Rule Bills gave them one, and militancy produced little change.
Achievement: the Intermediate system and the 1908 Act widened access to secondary and university education, especially for Catholics and girls.
Limit: payment by results encouraged cramming and the narrow curriculum, and denominational divisions over universities lasted for decades.
Contemporary Irish Party leaders saw suffrage as a distraction from Home Rule; suffragists saw it as a democratic right.
Historians stress that the movement was divided by nationalism and unionism, which weakened it, but that its organisation gave women experience used in later politics.
Dublin had few factories and a large pool of unskilled labour, and its working class lived in some of the worst housing in the United Kingdom.
Dublin’s tenements were old Georgian townhouses on the north side and in the Liberties, divided into single rooms; more than 20,000 families lived in one room each (1911 census).
Many houses were owned by landlords who collected high rents for rooms with no running water and a shared yard toilet, and some landlords sat on Dublin Corporation.
Dublin had a very high death rate, among the highest of any city in the United Kingdom, with tuberculosis and infant mortality especially severe.
Most unskilled men were casual labourers at the docks, in carting and building, hired by the day at the stand with no security and very low pay.
Women worked in laundries, textile mills, biscuit factories and as domestic servants for low wages.
On 2 September 1913 two tenement houses in Church Street collapsed, killing seven people and exposing the state of Dublin housing in the middle of the lockout.
A Local Government Board housing inquiry in 1913–14 reported on the conditions of tenement life.
Irish unions began as craft bodies for skilled workers; from the 1890s a new unionism reached unskilled workers.
Craft unions, mainly branches of British unions, organised skilled tradesmen such as printers, carpenters and engineers, and had little interest in the unskilled.
The Irish Trades Union Congress was founded in 1894 to give Irish unions a common voice, though most unions remained British-based.
New unionism, which spread from Britain in the 1880s, organised unskilled workers into general unions, and used the strike, including the sympathetic strike.
James Connolly founded the Irish Socialist Republican Party in Dublin in 1896, arguing that socialism and national independence were linked.

In 1907 James Larkin, then an organiser for the National Union of Dock Labourers, led a strike of Belfast dockers and carters that united Catholic and Protestant workers for a time; riots in August left two dead.
Larkin broke with the British union and founded the Irish Transport and General Workers’ Union in Dublin in 1909, with Liberty Hall as its headquarters.
The ITGWU won disputes in Dublin and Cork and fought a lockout in Wexford in 1911; Larkin founded the weekly Irish Worker in 1911.
The Irish Labour Party was founded in 1912, at the Irish TUC meeting in Clonmel, to represent workers in parliament.
Larkin was the charismatic organiser who built the ITGWU and led the Dublin workers in 1913.
James Larkin was born in Liverpool in the 1870s (he gave 1876; some sources say 1874) to Irish parents, and worked as a docker before becoming a union organiser; he died in 1947.
He was a participant: he led the Belfast strike of 1907, founded the ITGWU in 1909 and was the main figure in the Dublin events of 1913.
His tactics, known as Larkinism, included the sympathetic strike and the refusal of union members to handle goods from firms in dispute (tainted goods).
He was a powerful speaker; he appeared in disguise on the balcony of the Imperial Hotel, Murphy’s property, on 31 August 1913, to address the banned meeting.
He was sentenced to seven months for sedition in October 1913 but released on 13 November after a public campaign.
He left Ireland for the United States in October 1914 and was imprisoned there in 1920 and deported in 1923; he later returned to Irish politics and died in 1947.
Contemporary employers, the conservative press and Archbishop Walsh’s supporters condemned him as an agitator, while Dublin workers revered him as a champion.
Historians credit him with the first mass organisation of unskilled Irish workers, though some argue that his temper and tactics made compromise harder in 1913.
Connolly was the thinker of the Irish labour movement, who argued that socialism and national freedom were inseparable.
James Connolly (1868–1916) was born in Edinburgh to Irish parents, served in the British army, and became a socialist organiser in Edinburgh before moving to Dublin in 1896.
He founded the Irish Socialist Republican Party in 1896 and edited its paper, the Workers’ Republic.
He lived in the USA from 1903 to 1910, organising for socialist bodies and the Industrial Workers of the World, and wrote Labour in Irish History (1910).
He returned in 1910, became Ulster organiser of the ITGWU and helped found the Labour Party in 1912.
During the lockout he was Larkin’s lieutenant; when Larkin was jailed and then left for the USA, Connolly led the union and the Irish Citizen Army, becoming its commander in 1914.
Contemporaries on the left admired him, while the Church and employers distrusted his socialism; many nationalists saw him as a distraction from the national cause until 1916.
Historians judge him the leading Irish socialist thinker, with debate over whether his turn to the Rising in 1916 showed that he put nation before class.
William Martin Murphy led the employers’ attempt to destroy the ITGWU before it could win recognition.
William Martin Murphy (1844–1919) was Dublin’s leading capitalist: chairman of the Dublin United Tramways Company, owner of the Irish Independent, and an Irish Party supporter turned critic.
He was president of the Dublin Chamber of Commerce and the leading figure of the Dublin Employers’ Federation, which had hundreds of members.
Murphy argued that the ITGWU’s sympathetic strikes and boycotts were tyranny over business and workers, and that employers had the right to manage without interference.
In July and August 1913 Larkin’s union had won gains from several Dublin firms, and Murphy decided to challenge it on the trams and in the Independent’s despatch department.
In mid-August 1913 Murphy dismissed workers at the Independent and DUTC who were members of the ITGWU.
A tram strike on the first day of Horse Show week grew into the lockout of thousands of workers.
On Tuesday 26 August 1913, the first day of Horse Show week, tram drivers and conductors walked off their cars, causing chaos in the city.
Murphy replaced strikers with other workers and the police protected them; the ITGWU responded by calling out other workers who handled tram-related goods.
Larkin burned a police proclamation banning a meeting and promised to speak in Sackville Street (now O’Connell Street) on Sunday 31 August 1913.
