On 30 August baton charges in Ringsend and the city killed two men; on 31 August police baton-charged the crowd in O’Connell Street, injuring hundreds in what was called Bloody Sunday.
On 3 September about 400 employers agreed that all workers must sign the Document, a pledge to leave the ITGWU and not support it, and many locked out those who refused.
About 20,000 workers were out of work by autumn (estimates range up to 25,000), which meant many thousands more dependants were affected.
The Board of Trade’s Askwith inquiry (late September–October 1913) condemned the Document, but the employers refused its proposals.
George Russell (AE) published an Open Letter to the Masters of Dublin in the Irish Times on 7 October 1913, attacking the employers for starving workers into submission.
Help from British unions kept the workers going, but the British TUC refused to take the sympathetic action Larkin wanted.
British trade unions sent food: the first food ship, the Hare, arrived in Dublin on 27 September 1913, and money and supplies continued to arrive from British unions.
Strike pay and relief were distributed from Liberty Hall, with soup kitchens and food parcels.

The Save the Kiddies scheme, promoted by Dora Montefiore and others in October 1913, planned to send strikers’ children to homes in Britain; Archbishop Walsh condemned it as a threat to the children’s faith, and priests and the Ancient Order of Hibernians prevented children leaving.
On 23 November 1913 the Irish Citizen Army was founded at Liberty Hall to protect pickets from police, drilled by Captain Jack White.
A special British TUC congress in December 1913 rejected calls for a sympathetic strike or a boycott of Dublin goods, a heavy blow to the ITGWU.
By January 1914 hunger was driving workers back, and the ITGWU advised them to return; the dispute formally ended around 18 January 1914, many men returning without signing the Document.
Employers kept the right to bar ITGWU members in some firms and some workers were blacklisted, so the outcome favoured the employers.
The union lost the lockout but survived, and the dispute left a lasting mark on Irish labour and politics.
Many strikers returned without recognition of the union, and the ITGWU lost members, but it survived and grew during the First World War.
The Irish Citizen Army, born of the lockout, took part in the Easter Rising of 1916 under Connolly.
The dispute made labour a political force in Dublin and began the alliance of labour and nationalism that Connolly favoured.

It split nationalist opinion: Griffith’s Sinn Féin and the Irish Party were largely unsympathetic to the strikers, while Connolly, Pearse’s circle, Yeats, AE and Constance Markievicz expressed support.
The Church sympathised with the poor but condemned the tactics and the Save the Kiddies scheme, and opposed socialism.
The housing inquiry and public sympathy increased pressure for slum clearance in Dublin.
Documents on 1913 include employer statements, newspaper reports, Church statements, poems and cartoons.
Murphy’s Irish Independent portrayed Larkin as a dangerous agitator and the strike as an attack on trade and liberty.
The Irish Worker and Connolly’s writings portrayed the employers as aggressors starving workers into submission.
Archbishop Walsh criticised the housing conditions but warned against socialist ideas and condemned the removal of children.

Yeats’s poem September 1913 (published 8 September) was written in the dispute over Hugh Lane’s gallery, in which Murphy’s Independent opposed funding, and it attacks the narrow, commercial Dublin middle class.
AE’s Open Letter to the employers is a strong middle-class voice for the workers, written by a poet, not a trade unionist.
Cartoons in the Irish Worker and in Dublin papers show Murphy and the police as oppressors, or Larkin as a demagogue, depending on the paper.
To place a document, identify the stage (tram strike, Bloody Sunday, the Document, the food ships, the end), the author’s interest and the audience.
Judgements on 1913 compare the strength of organised labour with the cost of defeat.
Achievement: the ITGWU organised thousands of unskilled workers, kept a mass movement alive for five months and won widespread sympathy.
Limit: it failed to defeat the employers, lacked British union support for sympathetic action and ended with hunger forcing a return.
Larkin’s strengths were inspiration and organising ability; his weaknesses were intransigence and the extension of the dispute into a general conflict.
Murphy’s strengths were unity and resources; his weaknesses were hardness that cost him public sympathy and drew the attention of the British government.
Contemporaries disagreed: employers called it a defence of liberty, workers a defence of the right to organise.
Historians see 1913 as a defeat that strengthened the labour movement, and as a source of the Citizen Army and the radicalisation that fed 1916.
The co-operative movement tried to improve farming by self-help at a time when the land question was moving towards settlement.
Horace Plunkett (1854–1932), the son of Lord Dunsany, was an Anglo-Irish landowner who ranched in Wyoming in the 1880s and returned to Ireland convinced that farmers needed better organisation.
He was a Unionist MP for South Dublin from 1892 to 1900, though he worked with nationalists in his reform schemes.
Irish farmers suffered from poor marketing, dependence on local shopkeepers and moneylenders, and competition from Danish butter, which was better made and graded.
Plunkett took the Danish model of farmer-owned co-operative creameries, where farmers pooled milk and used a mechanical separator, giving higher quality at lower cost.
The first co-operative creamery is usually dated to 1889 at Dromcollogher, Co. Limerick, and the model then spread in Munster and elsewhere.
Plunkett’s supporters included Fr Tom Finlay, a Jesuit, and the poet George Russell (AE), who later edited the movement’s paper, the Irish Homestead.
The Irish Agricultural Wholesale Society was founded in 1897 and the Irish Homestead began in 1895 as the movement’s weekly paper.
In 1894 Plunkett founded a central body to promote co-operative societies across the country.
The Irish Agricultural Organisation Society (IAOS) was founded in 1894 to organise, advise and inspect co-operative societies.
Its motto was better farming, better business, better living, a statement of its self-help philosophy.
Co-operative creameries multiplied in the 1890s, giving small dairy farmers a market and a share of profits.
Credit societies, modelled on German Raiffeisen banks, lent small amounts to members on the guarantee of their neighbours, reducing dependence on gombeen men (local moneylenders and shopkeepers).
Other societies supplied seeds and fertiliser and sold eggs and poultry; the Irish Agricultural Wholesale Society was founded in 1897.
By the First World War there were close to 1,000 societies with roughly 100,000 members, though they were strongest in Munster and weakest in Ulster (estimates vary).
Co-operative creameries introduced mechanical cream separators and bought milk by its fat content, which rewarded quality and raised the standard of Irish butter.
Plunkett brought nationalists and unionists together in 1895 to call for state help for farming and industry.
The Recess Committee met during the parliamentary recess of 1895, and brought together unionist and nationalist members.
Its report in 1896 studied Danish, French and German methods and recommended a government department with a minister responsible for agriculture and technical education.
The Department of Agriculture and Technical Instruction (DATI) was established in 1899, with Plunkett as its first vice-president (the effective head).
DATI supported agricultural education, instructors, research, technical schools and fisheries, and the Chief Secretary was its president.
Plunkett lost the vice-presidency in 1907 after hostility from the Irish Party.
The Department was financed by the Treasury and the Chief Secretary was its nominal president, with T.W. Russell succeeding Plunkett as vice-president in 1907.
Co-operation brought clear economic gains, but political suspicion limited it.
Many nationalists suspected Plunkett, a unionist, of trying to turn farmers away from the land and national questions; others, like AE, saw the movement as national self-help.
Many unionists, especially Ulster farmers, were slow to join, partly through suspicion of Plunkett’s dealings with nationalists.

The Catholic clergy often supported local creameries, but Plunkett’s book Ireland in the New Century (1904) criticised the Church’s influence on Irish initiative, and a clerical campaign contributed to his defeat in 1900 and his later problems.
Private creamery owners and shopkeepers resented the competition from co-operatives.
Results: the co-operatives improved the quality of Irish butter, raised farm incomes, spread the idea of self-help and trained a generation of local leaders.
The movement did not solve the problems of poor western farmers, who were helped more by the Congested Districts Board (see the notes on land reform).
Belfast grew from a town of about 20,000 around 1800 into Ireland’s industrial capital.
Belfast’s population grew fast: about 255,000 at the 1891 census (when it passed Dublin city), 349,000 in 1901 and 387,000 in 1911.
Linen, spun and woven in mills, was the first great industry; Belfast was nicknamed Linenopolis and employed tens of thousands, most of them women and girls.
The Belfast Ropeworks at Connswater was among the largest ropeworks in the world.
Tobacco manufacture grew with Gallaher and other firms, and engineering firms such as Sirocco Works produced machinery for export.
Other trades included whiskey distilling (Dunville) and aerated waters.
Catholic workers from the countryside moved into west Belfast, around the Falls Road, so that by 1911 about a quarter of the city was Catholic.
The American Civil War cut cotton supplies in the 1860s and boosted linen, and power-loom mills replaced handloom weaving.
Belfast’s population was only about 20,000 around 1800, so the later growth was rapid.
The Belfast Ropeworks, founded in 1873, supplied rope to shipping across the world.
Shipbuilding on Queen’s Island made Belfast famous and tied its prosperity to the empire’s shipping trade.
Edward Harland, an English engineer, bought a small yard on Queen’s Island in 1858 and went into partnership in 1861 with Gustav Wolff, a German-born engineer from Hamburg.
William Pirrie, born in Quebec to Ulster parents, joined the yard as an apprentice, became a partner in 1874 and chairman after Harland’s death in 1895; he was made Lord Pirrie in 1906.
The firm built ships for the White Star Line, including the Olympic-class liners Olympic, Titanic and Britannic, the biggest ships in the world when launched.
Titanic was launched on 31 May 1911 and sank on her maiden voyage on 15 April 1912 with the loss of about 1,500 lives.
Workman Clark, founded in 1880 by Frank Workman and George Clark, was the second Belfast yard and built cargo and passenger ships.
Together the yards employed tens of thousands, with Harland and Wolff alone employing about 15,000 men by 1912.
The Arrol Gantry, built over the slipways in 1908–09, allowed Olympic and Titanic to be built side by side.
Industrial Belfast offered work but also hard conditions and a religious divide that fed unionism.
Mill workers, mostly women and girls, worked long hours in hot, damp rooms full of flax dust, which caused lung disease, and wages were low.
Shipyard work was dangerous and casual labourers were laid off between contracts.
Skilled jobs in the shipyards and engineering were mainly held by Protestants, often through family and Orange Order connections, while Catholics tended to be labourers.
Sectarian riots occurred in 1857, 1864 and 1886, and the riots of 1886 involved attacks on Catholic workers at the shipyards (see the notes on the 1885–86 elections).

In July 1912, during the Home Rule crisis, Protestant workers drove Catholic workers and some Protestant labour sympathisers out of Workman Clark and Harland and Wolff, thousands in all by some estimates.
Larkin’s 1907 strike briefly united Catholic and Protestant workers but did not last.
Many Protestant workers feared that Home Rule would bring tariffs and Catholic dominance, and this linked industrial interests to unionism.
Many mill women were the main earners in their families, and half-time child workers also worked in the mills until reforms limited this.
The two cities had different economies, which shaped their politics.
Belfast depended on export manufacturing, mainly linen and shipbuilding, linked to the British and imperial markets; Dublin depended on administration, trade, brewing and distilling.
Dublin had large employers such as Guinness at St James’s Gate and Jacob’s, but many of its workers were casual and poorly paid.
Belfast wages for skilled men were higher than in Dublin, and its tenements were less bad (Belfast had back-to-back terraces), though disease and low wages still afflicted the mill districts.
Belfast was strongly Protestant and unionist; Dublin was nationalist, with a strong labour movement.
Belfast’s industrial development depended on its link with Britain, which was a major reason for unionist opposition to Home Rule.
Belfast’s Catholic minority and Protestant majority lived in separate districts, such as the Falls and the Shankill, so the city’s politics were territorial as well as economic.
Both developments brought prosperity to part of Ireland, but each left problems unsolved.
Achievement: the co-operatives improved farmers’ incomes and quality of produce and encouraged self-reliance; Belfast became an industrial city of international importance.
Limit: the co-operatives hardly reached the poorest western farmers and Ulster, and Belfast’s prosperity relied on cheap female labour and sectarian divisions.
Contemporary nationalists were suspicious of Plunkett as a unionist, while unionists admired Belfast as proof of the Union’s benefits.
Historians see Plunkett’s movement as a significant success of self-help, though it is often judged less influential than land reform in modernising Irish farming.
In the early 1880s organised sport in Ireland followed English rules and was dominated by the gentry and middle class, while the native game of hurling had declined.
Athletics was organised by bodies that followed English amateur rules; these rules excluded artisans and labourers, so most working people and farmers could not compete.
Rugby, cricket and later soccer were played in schools, garrison towns and among the gentry; the Irish Rugby Football Union was founded in 1879 and the Irish Football Association in 1880.

Hurling had declined since the Famine, as landlord patronage ended and rural communities shrank, though it survived in parts of Galway, Clare, Tipperary, Kilkenny, Cork and Limerick, played under varying local rules.
Michael Cusack founded the Metropolitan Hurling Club in Dublin in 1882 and tried to standardise rules, while Trinity College students also played hurling.

The cultural background included the Gaelic Union (1880), formed to preserve the Irish language, and a growing sense that English habits were replacing Irish ones, which later writers called anglicisation.
The political background was the Land War, the rise of the Irish Party and Parnell, and a Fenian revival; the new association emerged in a period of intense national feeling.
Cusack’s Metropolitan Hurling Club in Dublin held a match in 1883 under agreed rules and used the Irish Times to argue for a native game.
The Gaelic Athletic Association was founded at Thurles on 1 November 1884 by a small group led by Michael Cusack and Maurice Davin.

Michael Cusack (1847–1906) was born in Co. Clare, trained as a teacher and ran a cramming academy in Dublin; he was a forceful, abrasive enthusiast, later the model for the Citizen in James Joyce’s Ulysses.
Maurice Davin (1842–1927) was a champion weight-thrower and rower from Carrick-on-Suir, Co. Tipperary, who was respected for his fairness and became the first president.
In October 1884 Cusack published an article, A Word about Irish Athletics, in United Ireland, calling for a national body to revive Irish sports.
Cusack and Davin sent invitations to a meeting at Hayes’ Hotel in Thurles, Co. Tipperary, on 1 November 1884.
Seven men attended, including Cusack, Davin, John Wyse Power, a journalist, and others; Davin was elected president and Cusack, Wyse Power and J.K. Bracken were elected secretaries.
The Association aimed to revive Irish games, to open athletics to all classes, and to promote physical fitness and national pride.
The Association’s full title was the Gaelic Athletic Association for the Preservation and Cultivation of National Pastimes.
Cusack won the support of the most powerful figures in nationalist Ireland, who gave the GAA legitimacy and publicity.
Archbishop Thomas Croke of Cashel, a nationalist and supporter of the land movement, agreed to be patron in a letter of December 1884.
Croke attacked the imitation of English games and manners, and urged the revival of Irish sports as an act of national self-respect.
Charles Stewart Parnell and Michael Davitt also agreed to be patrons, which linked the GAA to the Home Rule and land movements.
Croke’s letter was widely printed and made the GAA respectable, and many priests became club presidents and organisers.
Davitt saw the GAA as a way of drawing working people and farmers into the national movement, and he wrote and spoke in support.
Croke, Archbishop of Cashel from 1875, had supported the tenants during the Land War and was a known nationalist, so his name carried weight with farmers.
John Wyse Power, a journalist and IRB man, was one of the first secretaries, showing that Fenians were involved from the start.
The GAA set rules that separated Irish sport from English sport and built a structure on the parish.
Davin drew up the first rules for hurling and Gaelic football in 1885, reducing the old local variations to a national code.
Competition was open to all classes; the old amateur rules that excluded manual workers were rejected.
In the early years the GAA banned members from playing or attending foreign games such as cricket, rugby and soccer, the so-called foreign games ban.
Members of the Royal Irish Constabulary and the British armed forces were also barred, because they represented British rule.
Clubs were organised by parish, with county committees and a Central Council above them, and an annual convention that was usually held in Thurles.
The parish structure suited the Catholic Church’s organisation, which made it easy for priests to take part.
The GAA was strictly amateur in principle, and it set out to keep money and professionalism out of sport.
The GAA spread quickly and in 1887 held the first All-Ireland championships.
The GAA spread to the south and west and then to the midlands and Leinster; within a few years hundreds of clubs had affiliated.
Hurling and football matches drew large crowds, often with bands and processions, and club matches became local occasions.
The first All-Ireland championships began in 1887, with open draws and no provincial stage.
The first hurling final was played at Birr, Co. Offaly, on 1 April 1888, when Thurles (Tipperary) beat Meelick (Galway); the score is variously reported.
The first football final was played in April 1888 and was won by Limerick (represented by the Commercials club) against Louth.
Cusack founded the weekly The Celtic Times in 1887 to promote Gaelic games.
The GAA’s success made it a target for Fenians and a worry for the Church, and its leaders fell out.
Members of the Irish Republican Brotherhood joined the GAA in large numbers, using clubs and county boards to recruit and to gain influence.
Dublin Castle watched the GAA closely, and RIC reports described it as a front for Fenianism.
Cusack, who disliked the secret society, quarrelled with Davin and other officers, and was removed as secretary in 1886.
The annual conventions of 1886 and 1887, held in Thurles, were contests between moderates and IRB-linked delegates for control of the Central Council.
Archbishop Croke and other bishops grew uneasy, and clergy withdrew from clubs in some places; Davin stepped down as president in 1889.
The IRB hold on the Central Council was strong by the later 1880s, and the more it grew the more the Church held back.
Two blows in quick succession, an expensive overseas tour and the split in Irish nationalism, almost destroyed the association.
In autumn 1888 a party of about fifty hurlers and athletes, known as the American Invasion, toured the United States, with Irish-American support in cities such as New York and Boston.
The tour lost money, left debts and disrupted the 1888 championships, which were left unfinished; some of the athletes stayed in America.
The O’Shea divorce and the split in the Irish Party in December 1890 divided GAA members, with the IRB generally favouring Parnell and Church-minded members opposing him.
Parnell’s death in October 1891 left the association demoralised.
By 1891 membership and the number of clubs had collapsed, and a few county boards were all that remained in many areas.
The GAA recovered slowly in the 1890s, with a new generation of leaders and the support of the Gaelic revival.
Examiners ask how the GAA dealt with its difficulties to 1891; the main answers are organisation, patronage and compromise.
The parish-based club system meant that local clubs could continue even when the Central Council quarrelled.
The patronage of Croke and the clergy gave the association moral authority, and priests helped to restore order in clubs.
The appeal of hurling and football and of local rivalry was strong in itself and did not depend on politics.
The removal of Cusack and the departure of Davin showed an attempt to settle disputes by changing leaders rather than breaking up the body.
Connections with the nationalist movement, through Parnell, Davitt and the IRB, gave it energy but also exposed it to the Parnell split.
The GAA’s identity as an Irish-only, amateur body made it a symbol of de-anglicisation, a core part of the Irish Ireland ideas later developed by the Gaelic League.
Documents on the GAA are letters, speeches and reports, and they reflect the aims and tensions of the movement.
Cusack’s article of October 1884 and his invitations are founding documents, expressing the aim of opening athletics to all classes.
Croke’s letter of December 1884 is the best-known statement of the GAA’s national purpose, and it should be read as a clerical and nationalist appeal against English fashions.
Davitt’s letters and speeches of support show the GAA’s links with the land movement; Parnell’s patronage brought political prestige.
Unionist newspapers and the Dublin Castle reports describe the GAA as seditious or as a cover for the IRB.
Reports of conventions and county board meetings are evidence of the dispute between moderates and the IRB, though they are written by partisans.

Historians such as Marcus de Búrca (The GAA: A History) and W.F. Mandle (The Gaelic Athletic Association and Irish Nationalist Politics) emphasise the connection between the GAA and nationalism, with Mandle stressing political motives and de Búrca the sporting ones.
The GAA’s early years show both a cultural achievement and the cost of political entanglement.
Achievement: it created a national organisation open to all classes, standardised the rules of hurling and football and built a parish network.
Limit: IRB infiltration, the quarrel with the Church, the American tour and the Parnell split almost destroyed it by 1891.
Contemporary nationalists saw it as a school for national feeling; unionists and the authorities saw it as Fenian; bishops saw it as useful but dangerous.
Historians now see the GAA as a central part of the cultural nationalism of the 1880s, which anticipated the Gaelic League of 1893.
Hyde’s lecture of 1892 gave the cultural revival its programme: Irish people should stop imitating England and revive their own language and customs.
Douglas Hyde delivered The Necessity for De-Anglicising Ireland to the National Literary Society in Dublin on 25 November 1892.
Hyde argued that Ireland had been anglicised in language, names, dress, games and ideas, and that the Irish were failing both to be English and to be Irish.
He insisted the aim was to preserve what was distinctive about Ireland, and that this was compatible with a political view that was not separatist.
He pointed to the decline of Irish as a spoken language, which had fallen sharply since the Famine, and asked for it to be cultivated and used in schools.
The lecture influenced the GAA’s earlier example, and led within a year to the founding of the Gaelic League.
The Gaelic League, founded in 1893, built a mass movement to revive the Irish language.
The Gaelic League (Conradh na Gaeilge) was founded in Dublin on 31 July 1893 by Douglas Hyde, Eoin MacNeill and others, with Hyde as president.
It was officially non-political and non-sectarian, and it welcomed Catholics, Protestants, nationalists and unionists.
Branches ran Irish classes, and travelling teachers (timirí) were sent to rural areas; there were several hundred branches by 1904.
The League organised feiseanna (festivals of music, dance and language competitions) and, from 1897, the annual Oireachtas.
Its weekly paper An Claidheamh Soluis began in 1899; Patrick Pearse edited it from 1903 to 1909.

Successes: Irish was allowed in primary schools by the Revised Programme of 1900, and the League won a campaign to make Irish compulsory for matriculation to the National University, decided in 1910 and applied from 1913.
St Patrick’s Day became a national holiday for the League, with processions from 1903, and people also took Irish names and used Irish-language signs.
From about 1910 a growing number of IRB members joined the League and pushed it towards politics; Hyde resigned as president in 1915 when the League declared for Irish independence.
Hyde was the scholar who launched the language revival and gave it a non-sectarian, non-political character.
Douglas Hyde (1860–1949) was born in Castlerea, Co. Roscommon, the son of a Church of Ireland rector, and learned Irish from the people around him in Frenchpark.
He studied at Trinity College Dublin, published collections of Gaelic songs and folktales, including Love Songs of Connacht (1893), and wrote under the name An Craoibhín Aoibhinn.
He was a participant: he gave the 1892 lecture, co-founded the League in 1893 and led it for twenty-two years.
Contemporaries admired his scholarship and his appeal across religious lines, but Moran and other Irish Irelanders thought him too genteel and too tolerant of Anglo-Irish culture.
Hyde resigned as president in 1915 when the League adopted an explicitly political aim; he later became a senator and the first President of Ireland (1938–45).
Historians credit him with launching the revival and mass interest in the language, while recognising that its political use after 1900 went beyond his intentions.
Moran gave the revival a sharper edge by defining the Irish nation as Gaelic and Catholic.
David Patrick Moran founded the newspaper The Leader in 1900 and used it to argue for an Irish Ireland.
He urged support for Irish language, industry and games, and attacked the Anglo-Irish literary movement and the Irish Party as West Britons.
In his view the nation was Gaelic and Catholic, and Protestants could be accepted only if they adopted this identity.
Moran’s book The Philosophy of Irish Ireland (1905) gathered his articles and set out his creed.
The Leader promoted boycotts of English goods and entertainment, and attacked music-hall and English newspapers.
Moran’s influence divided the revival between Hyde’s inclusive approach and a narrower Catholic and Gaelic nationalism.
A group of mainly Protestant writers in English drew on Irish myth, folklore and peasant speech to create a national literature and theatre.
The National Literary Society was founded in Dublin in 1892 with Hyde and Yeats among its leaders.
The Irish Literary Theatre was founded in 1899 by W.B. Yeats, Lady Gregory and Edward Martyn; its first production, Yeats’s The Countess Cathleen, was in May 1899.
Yeats and Lady Gregory’s Cathleen ni Houlihan was first staged on 2 April 1902, with Maud Gonne in the title role.
The Abbey Theatre opened on 27 December 1904, funded by Annie Horniman, with Yeats, Lady Gregory and J.M. Synge as directors.
Lady Gregory (1852–1932) wrote plays and collected folklore; Synge (1871–1909) used the speech of the Aran Islands and the west of Ireland.
Synge’s The Playboy of the Western World provoked riots at the Abbey in January 1907, as nationalist audiences objected to its picture of rural Irish life as immoral.
Yeats, a Protestant poet and dramatist, tried to give Ireland a literature that would shape a national identity.
William Butler Yeats (1865–1939) was born in Sandymount, Dublin, the son of the painter John Butler Yeats, and spent much of his childhood in Sligo and London.
He was a participant who co-founded the National Literary Society, the Irish Literary Theatre and the Abbey, and who campaigned for a national theatre.
His early poetry, such as The Wanderings of Oisin (1889), drew on Irish mythology, and his friendship with the nationalist Maud Gonne linked him to political circles.
Contemporary nationalists admired his work but distrusted his Anglo-Irish background; Moran mocked his Celtic note, while the Catholic Church attacked The Countess Cathleen in 1899.

September 1913, published in the Irish Times on 8 September 1913, grew out of the Hugh Lane gallery dispute and condemned the narrow Catholic middle class for lacking the generosity of earlier Irish rebels.
He later served as a senator (1922–28) and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923.
Historians such as R.F. Foster see him at the centre of Irish cultural life, while critics find an elitist attitude to democracy in his politics.
The revival was marked by public disputes about who defined Irish identity.
The Countess Cathleen (1899) was attacked as heretical by Catholic critics, and Cardinal Logue condemned it without seeing it.
The Playboy riots of January 1907 showed the clash between the Abbey’s artistic freedom and the nationalist demand for flattering images of Irish life.

The Hugh Lane dispute began in 1912, when Dublin Corporation hesitated to fund a gallery for Lane’s collection of French paintings; Lane withdrew the offer and lent the pictures to the National Gallery in London in 1913.
After Lane died on the Lusitania in May 1915, a codicil left the pictures to Dublin, leading to a long dispute that was only settled in 1959.
Nationalists argued that Irish culture should be Gaelic and Catholic, while the Anglo-Irish writers claimed a place for English-language literature and for Protestant traditions.
Tension between the two visions, Anglo-Irish and Irish Ireland, ran through the revival and remained after independence.
After the Famine the Catholic Church tightened its hold on Irish life, and from the 1880s Catholic and nationalist identity increasingly overlapped.
Historians speak of a devotional revolution: from the 1850s Mass attendance rose, with parish missions, retreats, confraternities and devotions such as the Rosary and the Sacred Heart.
New churches and cathedrals were built across the country, funded by a more prosperous farming and trading middle class.
The Church controlled most national schools through clerical managers and ran secondary schools through religious orders such as the Christian Brothers, Jesuits and convent teaching orders.
Maynooth trained a large clergy, which held a high social position in rural communities and was often involved in politics and the GAA.
Sodalities and confraternities organised lay devotion, and the Pioneer Total Abstinence Association was founded by Fr James Cullen, a Jesuit, in 1898 to fight drunkenness.
The Ne Temere decree, in force from Easter 1908, required the children of mixed marriages to be raised as Catholics and angered Protestants.
The land reforms and expanding education produced a Catholic middle class, which provided the personnel of the nationalist movement.
The bishops generally supported Home Rule after 1885, which tied Catholic identity to nationalism, and the Irish Party was largely Catholic.
Unionists reacted by presenting Home Rule as Rome Rule; the Church’s role in the Parnell split and Ne Temere reinforced the fear.
The GAA recovered in the 1890s and the two bodies became partners and rivals.
The GAA recovered slowly after 1891, reorganised its county boards and resumed competitions; it bought grounds at Jones’s Road in Dublin in 1908, later Croke Park.
The IRB remained influential in its leadership, and in the early 1900s it formalised a ban on foreign games.
The GAA was mass, rural, male and sport-based; the League drew women, teachers and the urban middle class, and its work was language and education.
The GAA was politically committed from the start; the League was non-political until 1915.
Both were created by cultural nationalists and shared the aim of de-anglicisation and many members.
Fr Michael O’Hickey, professor of Irish at Maynooth, was dismissed by the bishops in 1909 after campaigning for compulsory Irish, showing limits to Church support for the League.
The revival gave Ireland a cultural identity but left argument about who belonged to it.
Achievement: the League, GAA and theatre created lasting institutions and symbols, and gave self-confidence to the nationalist movement.
Limit: the language did not revive as an everyday tongue, and the Catholic and Gaelic emphasis excluded many Protestants and unionists.
Contemporary unionists saw the revival as a disguise for separatism; Irish Irelanders such as Moran saw the Literary Revival as too Anglo-Irish.
Historians differ on whether the revival caused the revolution of 1916, as Pearse and the IRB claimed, or merely provided a language for politics that had other causes.
History is the past itself, the evidence that survives of it, and the written accounts historians build from that evidence.
The past itself is gone; no one can examine the Dublin lockout of 1913 directly, only what it left behind.
Evidence is whatever survives: documents, objects, images, buildings and recorded memories.
A written history is a historian’s account, shaped by the questions asked and the evidence found, so two historians can offer different histories of the same events.
Historical knowledge is provisional: new evidence or new questions can revise an account, as when the Pigott forgeries collapsed in 1889 and showed the letters against Parnell to be false.
A source is the item itself, such as a speech by Gladstone; it becomes evidence only when a historian uses it to answer a particular question, such as why Liberals split in 1886.

Public records (census returns, parliamentary papers, police reports) show official policy and statistics; private institutions’ records (union minute books, company papers, the GAA’s convention reports) show the interests of their members.
Letters, memoirs and eyewitness accounts give personal views, for example Davitt’s Leaves from a Prison Diary or accounts by participants in Bloody Sunday.
Newspapers, speeches and pamphlets show how events were presented to the public at the time.
Maps, photographs and political cartoons are visual evidence; oral testimony and radio or television transcripts are usually recorded long after events.

Repositories include archives (state records and the papers of organisations), libraries (printed books, newspapers and pamphlets) and museums (objects, banners and photographs), and each holds different kinds of source.
A historian cross-examines every source with the same set of questions before using it.
Who made it: a nationalist MP, a unionist editor, a bishop or a trade unionist each saw events from a position that shaped what they recorded.
Why it was made: to inform, persuade, defend an interest, record an event or claim credit afterwards.
When it was made: a report written during the election campaign of 1885 differs from a memoir written decades later.
In what circumstances: a statement made under pressure, in secret or before an inquiry may differ from a public speech.
For what audience: a speech to supporters aims to rally them; a letter to an opponent aims to persuade or warn.
Stages of research: choose a question, locate sources, evaluate them, compare them with each other, form an interpretation and test it against the evidence.
Primary sources were produced at the time of the events (a speech, a letter, a newspaper report, a cartoon); secondary sources are later accounts based on them (a modern book on Home Rule).
Primary does not mean reliable: a participant’s account is close to events but may be biased, and a secondary source may be more balanced but further from the facts.
A source can be both: a historian’s book is secondary for the period it describes but primary evidence for the thinking of the time it was written.
Documents mix checkable facts with opinion and persuasion, and the historian has to separate them.
A fact can be checked against other evidence, for example that Lord Frederick Cavendish and Thomas Burke were killed in Phoenix Park on 6 May 1882.
An opinion is a judgement that evidence cannot settle, for example that the Land Act of 1881 was a betrayal of the tenants.
Bias is a consistent tilt in how a source presents events, shown by loaded words, selective detail and omission, for example a unionist newspaper describing a nationalist rally as a mob.
Propaganda is material designed to persuade a mass audience, using emotion, slogans and selected facts; Home Rule is Rome Rule is a unionist slogan that works this way.
A biased source is not worthless: it is good evidence of what its author and audience believed, even when poor evidence of what happened.
Objectivity is the aim of fair, evidence-based judgement, although no historian is free from all assumptions.

Strengths of a source include closeness to events, first-hand knowledge, precision and corroboration by others; limitations include bias, a narrow viewpoint, gaps, later revision and the survival of only some records.
Revising a view: historians change their accounts when new sources appear, when old ones are tested harder, or when new questions are asked, such as women’s roles in the suffrage movement.
Question 1 on the paper is the documents-based question on the prescribed topic, with four parts: comprehension, comparison, criticism and contextualisation.
Question 1 is worth 100 marks of the 400: part (a) comprehension 20, part (b) comparison 20, part (c) criticism 20 and part (d) contextualisation 40.
The documents, written or visual, come from one of the topic’s three case studies: the elections of 1885–86, Dublin 1913 or the GAA to 1891.
With four equal questions in about 170 minutes, plan roughly 40 minutes for Question 1: a few minutes each for parts (a) to (c) and the biggest share for part (d).
Part (a) asks what a document says or shows; the answer must come from the named document alone.
Step 1: read the source note giving the author, date and publication, then the document.
Step 2: underline the exact points the question asks for, and find the line for each.
Step 3: put each point in your own words with a detail from the document (a name, date, place or figure).
Step 4: do not add outside knowledge; part (a) is marked on what the document tells you, and extra background earns nothing.
Example approach: for a speech on Home Rule, list each argument the speaker gives, in order, with a short reference to each.
Comparison asks how two documents are alike or different on a stated point, and every point needs evidence from both.
Choose the exact point the question names, such as attitude to Home Rule, to the strikers or to the GAA’s bans.
State what the first document says on that point, quoting or referring to a line.
State what the second says, then say whether they agree, differ or agree only in part.
A specific similarity or difference in both documents earns marks; a description of each document separately does not.
Explain the difference where you can, using the authors’ positions: for example a nationalist paper and a unionist paper describing the same crowd would use different words and numbers.
Compare like with like: a private letter and a public speech can differ because of audience rather than disagreement.
Use linking words such as whereas, both and unlike to keep every sentence a comparison.
Criticism asks how far a document can be trusted or how useful it is, and the answer tests provenance, purpose, viewpoint and reliability.
Provenance: who produced the document, when and where; a name and date alone are not an evaluation.
Purpose: why it was produced and for whom; a speech meant to rally supporters will present facts in their favour.
Viewpoint: the author’s party, religion, class or nationality, for example a landlord, a tenant, a priest or an employer.
Reliability: whether the claims are specific and supported by other evidence, or general and unsupported.
Cite a line from the document for each judgement, for example an emotional phrase as evidence of bias.
Balance the answer: say what the document is good evidence for as well as what it cannot show; a biased source can still be useful evidence of attitudes.
Usefulness questions ask how useful a document is for a stated enquiry, so measure it against that enquiry.
Questions on fact and opinion ask you to pick out one example of each, and questions on propaganda ask how the language and imagery persuade the audience.
Visual sources are read with the same questions as written ones, with extra attention to symbols and captions.
Identify every figure and what it stands for: Hibernia or Erin for Ireland, John Bull or Britannia for Britain, a statesman drawn from his known appearance.
Read the caption, labels and dates, because the meaning often rests on the words.
Note the exaggeration: caricature of faces, size, dress or animal imagery shows the artist’s attitude to a person or group.
Identify the message and the target audience: a cartoon in Punch addressed British readers, while one in a nationalist or unionist paper addressed supporters.
A cartoon is opinion, not record: use it as evidence of attitudes and propaganda, not of the facts of an event.
Ask whether a cartoon is hostile to Irish people or to a politician, and support the answer with a detail such as the way a figure is drawn.
A photograph shows what stood in front the camera, but the choice of subject, framing, staging and caption can mislead.
Example: a photograph of the Church Street ruins of September 1913 is good evidence of the state of Dublin housing, but does not show who was to blame.
Part (d) is a short essay on the subject of the case study, using your own knowledge; it is not a retelling of the documents.
Part (d) carries 40 marks, twice as much as any other part, and is marked like a short essay on cumulative relevant points.
It asks about the case study’s subject, such as a leader’s strengths and weaknesses, how an organisation dealt with difficulties, or the causes and outcome of a dispute.
Open with the background and context, then deal with events in order, with dates, names and numbers, then outcomes and significance.
Use the documents sparingly as supporting evidence, referring to them by letter, but do not summarise them.
Cover both sides: for example the arguments of nationalists and unionists in 1885–86, employers and workers in 1913, or the Church, the IRB and the founders in the GAA.
Finish with a judgement that answers the question set, such as how far a leader succeeded or how significant an event was.
Draw on the rest of the topic for context: Home Rule and land for the elections, labour and Dublin’s poverty for 1913, and cultural revival and the Parnell split for the GAA.
Every document can be dated by the people, events and language it contains, and dating it is the first step in using it.

Elections of 1885–86: mention of the Third Reform Act or the new voters points to 1884–85; the balance of power, the Hawarden Kite or Salisbury points to late 1885; a bill, Chamberlain or the Liberal Unionists points to April–June 1886; the Orange card, Belfast rioting or the July poll points to mid-1886.
Typical voices for 1885–86: Parnell and Irish Party speakers, Gladstone, Chamberlain, Hartington, Lord Randolph Churchill, the Freeman’s Journal, the Belfast News-Letter, and Punch.

Dublin 1913: trams and Horse Show week point to late August; O’Connell Street, batons and a banned meeting point to 31 August; the Document, Askwith or AE’s letter to September–October; food ships, Save the Kiddies and the Citizen Army to October–November; return to work to January 1914.
Typical voices for 1913: Larkin, Connolly, William Martin Murphy, Archbishop Walsh, the Irish Worker, the Irish Independent, the TUC and the Dublin Metropolitan Police.

The GAA to 1891: Thurles and Hayes’ Hotel point to November 1884; Croke, Parnell and Davitt as patrons to 1884–85; Cusack’s removal and IRB influence to 1886–87; the first championships to 1887–88; the American tour to 1888; the Parnell split and collapsing membership to 1890–91.
Typical voices for the GAA: Cusack, Davin, Croke, Davitt, Parnell, the nationalist press, the RIC and Dublin Castle.
Once dated, ask who gains from the document’s version of events, and what it leaves out.
Marks separate answers that use the evidence precisely from those that retell it or ignore it.
Strong comprehension answers use only the document and give precise details; weak ones add outside facts or copy whole passages.
Strong comparison answers name a point and give a line from each document; weak ones describe the two documents one after the other.
Strong criticism answers judge provenance, purpose and viewpoint with cited lines and reach a balanced verdict; weak ones say only that the source is biased.
Strong part (d) answers combine dated detail, two or more viewpoints and a clear judgement; weak ones paraphrase the documents or offer a general essay.
A strength of the format is that it rewards close reading; a limit is that it rewards answers that are tied closely to the case study and its documents.
Contemporary views and later historians’ views are both useful in part (d), for example how contemporaries saw Parnell or Larkin and how historians now judge them.
Home Rule became a real prospect because the Liberal government depended on the Irish Parliamentary Party and had removed the House of Lords' power to block bills for good.
After the two general elections of 1910 the Liberals needed the votes of John Redmond's Irish Parliamentary Party to stay in office, and Redmond's price was Home Rule.
The Parliament Act 1911 replaced the Lords' veto with a delaying power of two years: a bill passed by the Commons in three successive sessions became law without Lords' consent.
Asquith introduced the Third Home Rule Bill on 11 April 1912.
The Bill set up an Irish parliament in Dublin of a Senate of 40 and a House of Commons of 164, with an executive responsible to it.
Westminster kept the Crown, war and peace, the army and navy, foreign relations and customs; most taxation remained under Westminster, and the police stayed under British control for six years.
Under the Bill Ireland would send 42 MPs to Westminster, down from the 103 Irish seats of the time.
The Commons passed the Bill in January 1913 and again in July 1913, and the Lords rejected it each time (30 January and 15 July 1913).
The Commons passed it a third time in May 1914, which meant it could become law without the Lords.
Unionists answered the Bill with mass protest and then armed organisation, and nationalists formed their own volunteers in reply. The detail is in the notes on the movements for reform before 1914.
Edward Carson, a Dublin-born barrister, led Irish unionists, and James Craig organised the campaign in Ulster.
On Ulster Day, 28 September 1912, about 237,000 men signed the Ulster Covenant pledging to resist Home Rule, and about 234,000 women signed a parallel Declaration.
The Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) was formed in January 1913 to resist Home Rule by force; it drilled tens of thousands of men.
In March 1914 the Curragh incident, in which British cavalry officers said they would rather be dismissed than act against Ulster, showed that the army could not be relied on to coerce the unionists.
The UVF landed about 25,000 rifles at Larne, Co. Antrim, on the night of 24–25 April 1914 and the government did not stop it.

The Irish Volunteers were founded at the Rotunda in Dublin on 25 November 1913, with Eoin MacNeill as their public leader; the IRB (Bulmer Hobson and others) helped organise them from behind the scenes.
On 26 July 1914 the Volunteers landed about 900 German rifles at Howth, Co. Dublin, from Erskine Childers's yacht Asgard.

That afternoon soldiers of the King's Own Scottish Borderers fired on a jeering crowd at Bachelor's Walk in Dublin and killed three civilians; nationalists contrasted this with the lack of action at Larne.
By mid-1914 Home Rule was about to become law, but exclusion of Ulster was unresolved and the outbreak of war removed the issue from the agenda.
Asquith offered county option (each Ulster county voting on exclusion for six years) in March 1914; Carson rejected temporary exclusion and Redmond reluctantly accepted it as a concession.
In June 1914 Redmond forced the Irish Volunteers' committee to admit 25 of his own nominees, so he could control the movement.
The Buckingham Palace Conference of 21–24 July 1914 failed to agree a border for excluded counties; the sticking point was Tyrone and Fermanagh.
An Amending Bill to provide for Ulster was introduced in the House of Lords in June 1914 and was changed there to exclude all nine counties of Ulster; it never became law.
Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914, and on 18 September 1914 the Home Rule Act received royal assent.
A Suspensory Act, passed at the same time, postponed the operation of Home Rule until the end of the war, with an undertaking that Ulster would get special treatment by an amending Act.
Redmond tied the Home Rule cause to the British war effort. The result was a split in the Volunteers and, over time, a loss of confidence in his party.
On 3 August 1914 Redmond offered the Irish Volunteers to defend Ireland alongside the Ulster Volunteers.
At Woodenbridge, Co. Wicklow, on 20 September 1914, Redmond urged the Volunteers to join the British army and fight in the war.
The Volunteers split: about 170,000 followed Redmond as the National Volunteers, while about 11,000 stayed with MacNeill as the Irish Volunteers.
About 200,000 Irishmen served in the British forces during the war, and estimates of Irish deaths range from about 30,000 to about 50,000.
The 10th (Irish) Division fought at Suvla Bay, Gallipoli, in August 1915.
The 16th (Irish) Division, raised mostly from nationalist recruits, fought at Guillemont and Ginchy on the Somme in September 1916; the nationalist MP Tom Kettle was killed at Ginchy.
The 36th (Ulster) Division, drawn from the UVF, attacked at Thiepval on the first day of the Somme, 1 July 1916, and suffered over 5,000 casualties in two days.
Farmers gained from high food prices, and shipbuilding and engineering in Belfast boomed, but prices rose faster than wages in the towns, and Dublin's poor suffered.
Redmond's party lost influence because it had delivered a suspended Home Rule Act, and anti-war feeling among separatists grew as the war dragged on.
The Rising was organised by a secret group inside the IRB, which treated Britain's war as the opportunity to strike. German help was promised but badly co-ordinated.

The IRB's Supreme Council set up a Military Council in 1915; it ended up with seven members: Patrick Pearse, Joseph Plunkett, Éamonn Ceannt, Tom Clarke, Seán MacDiarmada, James Connolly and Thomas MacDonagh.
Connolly of the Irish Citizen Army, who had been planning a rising of his own, was brought in by the Military Council in January 1916.
The funeral of the Fenian Jeremiah O'Donovan Rossa on 1 August 1915 was organised as a show of strength and gave Pearse a platform.
Roger Casement went to Germany in autumn 1914 to seek arms and an Irish Brigade from Irish prisoners of war; very few prisoners joined.

A German ship, the Aud (disguised as a Norwegian vessel), carried about 20,000 rifles for the Rising; it was meant to land them in Tralee Bay, Co. Kerry, but arrived without a pilot or signals and was intercepted by the Royal Navy on Good Friday, 21 April 1916.
The Aud's captain scuttled the ship in Cork Harbour on 22 April, and the arms were lost.

Casement landed from a German submarine at Banna Strand, Co. Kerry, on 21 April 1916 and was arrested within hours; three Volunteers drowned that night when their car drove off Ballykissane pier on the way to meet him.
MacNeill, who had been misled about the plans, learned of the Aud's loss and issued a countermand; it was published in the Sunday Independent on Easter Sunday, 23 April.
The Military Council met and put the Rising back by one day to noon on Easter Monday, 24 April, so only a part of the Volunteers turned out.
About 1,200 Volunteers and Citizen Army members took over strong points in Dublin and proclaimed a republic. They were out-gunned and out-numbered, and the fighting was confined mostly to Dublin.

On Monday 24 April the rebels seized the General Post Office (GPO) in O'Connell Street as their headquarters, with Pearse as President and Commandant-General and Connolly commanding the Dublin forces.

Pearse read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic outside the GPO; it was addressed to ‘Irishmen and Irishwomen’, guaranteed religious and civil liberty and equal rights, and was signed by the seven members of the Military Council.

The main garrisons were Boland's Mill (Éamon de Valera), the South Dublin Union (Ceannt), Jacob's biscuit factory (MacDonagh), St Stephen's Green and the College of Surgeons (Michael Mallin and Countess Markievicz), and the Four Courts (Edward Daly).
The rebels failed to take Dublin Castle and did not seize the main British barracks, and Trinity College, the Castle and the docks stayed in British hands.
Martial law was proclaimed in Dublin on 25 April and General Sir John Maxwell was sent to take command on 28 April.
British reinforcements arrived from the Curragh and from Britain; at Mount Street Bridge on 26 April a handful of Volunteers inflicted heavy casualties on the Sherwood Foresters.
The gunboat Helga shelled Liberty Hall, and artillery shelling and fires wrecked much of O'Connell Street.
Outside Dublin, Thomas Ashe's Volunteers won a fight at Ashbourne, Co. Meath, on 28 April, Enniscorthy was held for several days, and Liam Mellows led a poorly armed rising in Galway.
The GPO was evacuated on Friday 28 April after fire; the garrison retreated to Moore Street, where The O'Rahilly was killed.
Pearse surrendered to Brigadier-General Lowe on Saturday 29 April and the other garrisons surrendered on Sunday.
About 485 people died: about 260 civilians, about 140 British soldiers and police, and about 80 rebels, with thousands wounded; the figures are research estimates.
The Rising was at first unpopular in Dublin. The speed and manner of the executions, and mass arrests, turned opinion towards the rebels.
As rebel prisoners were marched away, some Dubliners jeered them, and the Irish Parliamentary Party and most newspapers condemned the Rising.
About 3,500 people were arrested and about 1,800 were interned in Britain, many at Frongoch camp in north Wales.
Ninety men were sentenced to death by courts-martial, and 15 were shot between 3 and 12 May 1916: 14 at Kilmainham Gaol, and Thomas Kent at Cork.
Pearse, Tom Clarke and Thomas MacDonagh were shot on 3 May; Joseph Plunkett married Grace Gifford in the prison chapel the night before his execution on 4 May.

James Connolly, wounded in the fighting, was shot on 12 May while seated in a chair, together with MacDiarmada; the other 75 death sentences were commuted, including those of de Valera and Markievicz.
Bishop O'Dwyer of Limerick publicly refused Maxwell's demand to discipline priests and criticised the executions.
Augustine Birrell resigned as Chief Secretary on 3 May 1916, and Asquith visited Dublin.

Lloyd George's attempt to settle the Irish question in June and July 1916, with Home Rule at once and temporary exclusion of six counties, failed when Unionist ministers insisted on permanent exclusion.
Casement was tried for treason and hanged at Pentonville Prison on 3 August 1916; the British used his diaries to damage his reputation.
The Frongoch prisoners were released at Christmas 1916, and a general amnesty followed in June 1917; many of them became the core of the new Sinn Féin.
Pearse was the chief ideologue of the Rising and its leading public figure. He is judged both as an educator and cultural figure and as an advocate of armed sacrifice.
Pearse (1879–1916) was born in Dublin to an English father and an Irish mother, joined the Gaelic League in 1896 and qualified as a barrister, though he hardly practised.
He edited the League's paper An Claidheamh Soluis from 1903 and founded St Enda's, a bilingual school, in 1908; his essay The Murder Machine attacked the state education system.
He joined the IRB in 1913, became Director of Military Organisation of the Irish Volunteers, and joined the Military Council in 1915.
In his graveside oration for O'Donovan Rossa on 1 August 1915 he said Ireland unfree would never be at peace; this speech remains his best-known statement.
His 1915 writings praised war as cleansing; he described bloodshed as a cleansing and sanctifying thing, and critics later called this ‘blood sacrifice’, a phrase he did not himself use as a slogan.
He was President of the Provisional Government and Commandant-General in 1916, read the Proclamation, and ordered the surrender on 29 April.
He was executed in Kilmainham Gaol on 3 May 1916 at the age of 36, along with his brother Willie on 4 May.
Contemporaries were divided: Redmond's supporters and many Dubliners condemned him in April 1916, while by autumn he was honoured as a martyr.

Historians differ: Ruth Dudley Edwards's biography (1977) treated him as a gifted but troubled figure, Conor Cruise O'Brien criticised the cult of sacrifice, and Joost Augusteijn (2010) stressed his development as an educator and a revolutionary.
Markievicz was a participant in the Rising and its most prominent female combatant. Her later career is covered in the notes on the second Sinn Féin and the War of Independence.

Constance Gore-Booth (1868–1927) was born in London and brought up at Lissadell, Co. Sligo; she studied art at the Slade School in London and in Paris, and married the Polish count Casimir Markievicz in 1900.
She joined Inghinidhe na hÉireann and Sinn Féin in 1908 and in 1909 helped Bulmer Hobson found Fianna Éireann, a republican youth organisation.
She joined the Irish Citizen Army and in the 1913 Lockout ran the soup kitchen at Liberty Hall.
In the Rising she was second-in-command to Michael Mallin at St Stephen's Green and the College of Surgeons, and she surrendered with the garrison.

At court-martial on 4 May 1916 she was sentenced to death, and General Maxwell commuted it to penal servitude for life on account of her sex; she was held in Aylesbury Prison until the amnesty of June 1917.
Contemporaries admired her courage and also mocked her aristocratic background; Sean O'Casey was critical of her.
Later historians stress her place as an early woman in revolutionary politics and her commitment to labour and women's causes.
Judgements of the Rising depend on whether it is measured by its military result, by the aims of the Proclamation, or by its political effects.
Military failure: the rebels held no major target outside their garrisons, were contained within a week, and had few arms.
Political success: the executions, internment and the Proclamation's republican claim gave the survivors a moral authority the Parliamentary Party could not match.
Contemporary view: unionists and Redmond's party called it a German-backed rebellion; the Catholic press, which at first condemned it, shifted after the executions.
Later view: revisionist historians stressed its small support, secret planning and the fact that civilians were the largest group of dead; others stressed the effect of the British reaction.
Yeats's line ‘A terrible beauty is born’ from his poem Easter, 1916 summed up the sense that Irish politics had changed.
Home Rule was overtaken by events: the suspended Act never came into force, and partition came instead through the Government of Ireland Act of 1920.
The Rising set up a debate over legitimacy that shaped later republican claims, and its fiftieth anniversary in 1966 and centenary in 2016 became public occasions.
Sinn Féin was a small party before 1916, but the British called the Rising the ‘Sinn Féin rebellion’ and survivors used the name. In 1917 it became the vehicle for separatists of every kind.
Arthur Griffith founded Sinn Féin in 1905; it stood for economic self-reliance, abstention from Westminster and a dual monarchy of Britain and Ireland on the Austro-Hungarian model.
Count Plunkett, father of the executed Joseph Plunkett, won the North Roscommon by-election in February 1917 as an independent separatist and then abstained from Westminster.
Joseph McGuinness, a prisoner in Lewes, won South Longford in May 1917 by 37 votes, helped by the slogan ‘Put him in to get him out’.
De Valera won East Clare in July 1917 by a large majority, and W.T. Cosgrave won Kilkenny City in August 1917.

Thomas Ashe, one of the 1916 leaders, died on 25 September 1917 after being forcibly fed during a hunger strike in Mountjoy, and his funeral drew huge crowds; Michael Collins gave the graveside oration.
At the Sinn Féin Ard Fheis of 25–26 October 1917 de Valera was elected president, with Griffith standing aside.
The new constitution was a compromise: the aim was an independent Irish republic, and once that was achieved the people could choose their own form of government.
Sinn Féin now drew in ex-Volunteers, the IRB, Gaelic Leaguers and many younger priests, and its clubs spread through the country; at the same time, de Valera was elected president of the Volunteers.
Conscription united nearly all Irish nationalist opinion against the government and gave Sinn Féin credit for leading the resistance.
The German spring offensive began in March 1918 and Britain was desperately short of men, so the Military Service Act of 18 April 1918 allowed conscription in Ireland.

An all-party anti-conscription conference met in Dublin on 18 April, with Dillon, de Valera, Griffith, William O'Brien, Tim Healy and Labour representatives, and the Catholic bishops, meeting at Maynooth, backed resistance.
A national pledge to resist conscription was signed at church doors on 21 April, and on 23 April a one-day general strike closed most of the country outside Belfast.

The government never applied conscription, but it replaced the Viceroy with Lord French and in May 1918 arrested about 70 Sinn Féin leaders on the claim of a ‘German Plot’, citing the landing of Joseph Dowling from a German submarine.
De Valera, Griffith, Count Plunkett and Markievicz were among those arrested and held in Britain, and Collins and Harry Boland avoided arrest.

The arrests removed the older leaders and strengthened the radicals; Sinn Féin won by-elections in the summer and Redmond's party, which had been weakened by Redmond's death on 6 March 1918, lost ground.
The first election after the end of the war was fought on a franchise that roughly tripled the electorate, and it transformed the Irish party system.
The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave the vote to all men over 21 and women over 30, and the Irish electorate rose from about 700,000 to about 1.9 million.
The election was held on 14 December 1918 and counted on 28 December.
Sinn Féin won 73 of Ireland's 105 seats; the Unionists won 26 and the Irish Parliamentary Party won only six.
Sinn Féin took about 47 per cent of the votes, and 25 of its seats were won without a contest.
The IPP kept some seats, such as Joe Devlin's in Belfast, thanks to an arrangement with Sinn Féin in a few constituencies.
Unionists won most of the seats in the north-east, and Belfast and Ulster supplied the evidence for partition.
Constance Markievicz won St Patrick's, Dublin, while in Holloway prison, and became the first woman elected to the House of Commons; she did not take her seat.
De Valera was elected for East Clare and East Mayo, and many successful Sinn Féin candidates were in prison.
Sinn Féin carried out its election promise to set up its own parliament and began to run a government in competition with Dublin Castle.
The First Dáil met at the Mansion House on 21 January 1919; only 27 of the elected deputies attended because many were in jail.

It adopted a Declaration of Independence, a message to the free nations of the world and the Democratic Programme, which put the nation's claim to its resources and the right of every citizen to a living above private property.
De Valera escaped from Lincoln Gaol on 3 February 1919 with the help of Collins, and was elected Príomh Aire on 1 April 1919.
The ministry included Griffith (Home Affairs, later Foreign Affairs), Collins (Finance), Cathal Brugha (Defence), Count Plunkett (Foreign Affairs) and Markievicz (Labour).
The Dáil Loan (the National Loan), organised by Collins, raised over £350,000 in Ireland and more than 5 million dollars in the United States.
Sinn Féin won most of the councils in the 1920 local elections, and local authorities then pledged loyalty to the Dáil.
The Dáil set up arbitration courts in 1919, which developed into Dáil courts from mid-1920, and republican police replaced the RIC in many areas.
In August 1920 the Volunteers swore an oath of allegiance to the Dáil, and from then on they were known as the Irish Republican Army (IRA).
The government banned the Dáil in September 1919, and in 1920 many of the republican ministers worked in hiding.
The IRA waged a guerrilla war on the RIC and the army. A few thousand active men tied down many times their number.
The first shots came at Soloheadbeg, Co. Tipperary, on 21 January 1919, when Seán Treacy, Dan Breen and others killed two RIC constables guarding gelignite; the attack was not ordered by the Dáil.
The RIC withdrew from many isolated barracks in 1919–20, and the IRA burned the empty buildings and attacked others.
Active service units, known as flying columns, ambushed patrols and barracks; Tom Barry's West Cork column and Seán Hegarty's Cork forces were among the best known.
Collins was Director of Intelligence and used moles in Dublin Castle and the police, such as Ned Broy, to get information.
His Squad, formed in 1919, killed detectives of the Dublin Metropolitan Police's G Division and other agents.
Tomás Mac Curtain, Lord Mayor of Cork, was murdered by police in March 1920, and Terence MacSwiney, his successor, died on hunger strike in Brixton on 25 October 1920.
Kevin Barry, an 18-year-old medical student, was hanged on 1 November 1920 for his part in an ambush that killed three soldiers.
On Bloody Sunday, 21 November 1920, the Squad killed 14 men, mostly British officers and intelligence agents, in Dublin.
That afternoon Auxiliaries and RIC opened fire on the crowd at a football match at Croke Park, killing 14 civilians, including a player, Michael Hogan.
At Kilmichael, Co. Cork, on 28 November 1920, Tom Barry's column killed 17 Auxiliaries and lost three men.
In May 1921 the IRA burned the Custom House in Dublin but lost five men killed and about 80 captured, a heavy blow to the Dublin Brigade.
About 2,000 people were killed in the war, including soldiers, police, IRA men and civilians.
The British added to the police and the army but could not defeat the IRA, and the reprisals cost them support at home and abroad.
The Black and Tans, recruits from ex-soldiers who were short of police uniforms and so wore mixed khaki and dark green, began arriving in March 1920; about 10,000 served.
The Auxiliary Division of the RIC (ADRIC), about 2,000 ex-officers, was formed in July 1920 and operated in companies with considerable independence.
The Restoration of Order in Ireland Act (August 1920) allowed courts-martial for civilians, and martial law was declared in several southern counties from December 1920.
Reprisals included the sacking of Balbriggan in September 1920 and the burning of Cork city centre on the night of 11–12 December 1920, after an IRA ambush at Dillon's Cross.
The Labour Party, the press and many Church leaders in Britain criticised reprisals, and the Liberal and Labour leaders called for talks.
The Government of Ireland Act of 1920 set up a Northern parliament, and the elections of May 1921 confirmed Sinn Féin's hold on the south and unionist control in the north-east.
In June 1921 George V's speech at the opening of the Northern parliament called for reconciliation, and Lloyd George invited de Valera to talks on 24 June.

Britain went to the negotiating table because reprisals damaged its reputation, the IRA could not be crushed without a much larger force, dominion premiers and American opinion urged a settlement, and the cost of the war was rising.
De Valera spent June 1919 to December 1920 in the United States raising money and seeking recognition for the republic; this is covered in the notes on the diaspora.
Collins was the organiser of the IRA's intelligence war and of the republican finances. He was a participant in the Rising and the war and then a negotiator of the Treaty.
Collins (1890–1922) was born near Clonakilty, Co. Cork, worked in London in the post office and in a financial firm from 1906 to 1916, and joined the IRB there.
He fought in the GPO in 1916 as aide to Joseph Plunkett and was interned at Frongoch, where he built a network of future activists.
After his release he became a leader of the Volunteers and the IRB; he organised the National Aid funds and spoke at Ashe's funeral.
He was Minister for Finance from April 1919, organised the Dáil Loan, and as Director of Intelligence ran the Squad and the spy network.
He escaped capture throughout the war and was the most wanted man in the country.
His role in the Treaty talks and the Civil War is covered in the notes on those subjects.
Contemporaries: republicans admired him as the man who won the war; British officials regarded him as a ruthless organiser of murder, yet Churchill and others came to respect him in London.
Historians: Tim Pat Coogan (1990) portrayed a hero of the revolution, while Peter Hart (2005) gave a more critical account of the killings in which he was involved.
This part covers de Valera's leadership of Sinn Féin and the Dáil before the Treaty talks. His later career is in the notes on the Free State and the Republic.
De Valera (1882–1975) was born in New York, raised in Bruree, Co. Limerick, and was a maths teacher who joined the Volunteers in 1913.
He commanded the garrison at Boland's Mill in 1916; his death sentence was commuted, partly because he was born in America.
He was released in June 1917, won East Clare in July, and became president of Sinn Féin and of the Volunteers in October 1917.
He was arrested in the German Plot in May 1918, escaped from Lincoln on 3 February 1919, and was elected head of the Dáil in April 1919.
He was in America from June 1919 to December 1920, where his disputes with the Irish-American leaders John Devoy and Judge Cohalan limited his success.
After his return he took the lead in the talks with Lloyd George in July 1921.
Contemporaries: supporters saw him as the leader who held the movement together, while critics said he was rigid and out of touch with the IRA's campaign.
Historians: Tim Pat Coogan (1993) and Diarmaid Ferriter (Judging Dev, 2007) debate whether he was a pragmatist or an ideologue.
This part covers Markievicz after her release in 1917, as a Sinn Féin politician and Dáil minister.
After her release in June 1917 she joined Sinn Féin and the Volunteers' public campaign, and she was elected to the executive.
She was arrested in the German Plot of May 1918 and held in Holloway, where she was elected in December 1918; she was released in March 1919.
She was Minister for Labour in the Dáil ministry from April 1919 to January 1922, the only woman in the cabinet, and one of the first women in Europe to hold cabinet rank.
In September 1920 she was arrested again and sentenced to two years' hard labour; she was released in July 1921, after the Truce.
Her work as minister was limited by the fact that she was in jail or on the run for much of the time.
She opposed the Treaty in the Dáil vote in January 1922; her later career is covered in the notes on the Civil War.
Contemporaries admired her bravery but some Sinn Féin colleagues distrusted her socialism and her flamboyance.
Historians now emphasise her importance as a pioneer of women's participation in revolutionary politics.
Judgements depend on whether the 1918 election, the Dáil and the IRA are credited with winning the settlement or blamed for its costs.
Achievement: the 1918 result gave Sinn Féin a democratic mandate, and the counter-state showed Irish people could run their own affairs.
Achievement: the IRA campaign made Ireland costly and hard to govern and, with Dáil diplomacy, brought Britain to talks.
Limit: the IRA never controlled much territory, and it was short of arms and men by mid-1921.
Limit: the election was won on a minority share of the vote, and Sinn Féin's mandate said nothing about methods; many voters wanted an end to Home Rule rather than war.
Contemporary view: nationalists saw a legitimate government defending itself, while the British government called the Dáil and IRA a ‘murder gang’ before changing course.
Later view: historians debate how far the war was supported by the majority and how far it involved intimidation of informers and loyalists, as in Peter Hart's work on Cork.
The dual strategy of Dáil and IRA left the movement with two sources of authority that the Treaty split in 1922.
Partition was the result of unionist resistance, British failure to find an all-Ireland settlement and the pattern of the 1918 vote.
Unionist resistance: the Ulster Covenant of 1912 and the UVF made clear that Home Rule for all Ireland could be enforced only by force.

Exclusion debates: county option for six years (March 1914), the failed Buckingham Palace Conference (July 1914) and the failed Lloyd George proposals of 1916 all assumed the exclusion of some Ulster counties.
The 1916 plan collapsed because unionist ministers in the cabinet insisted that exclusion be permanent, while nationalists were told it would be temporary.
The war and the Rising changed nationalist politics, and the Irish Convention of 1917–18 failed to produce agreement.
The 1918 election confirmed the divide: Sinn Féin won most of the island, while unionists won 26 seats, mostly in the north-east.

Only four of the nine Ulster counties had unionist majorities (Antrim, Down, Armagh and Londonderry), and Tyrone and Fermanagh had narrow nationalist majorities; the chosen six counties gave a safer unionist majority than nine.
Northern Ireland had about 1.25 million people, of whom about two-thirds were Protestant and about one-third Catholic.

British policy: Lloyd George's coalition, with a large Conservative element, was unwilling to coerce Ulster, and the Government of Ireland Act of 1920 gave the unionists the offer of their own parliament.
The Act of 1920 created two Home Rule parliaments. Only the northern one worked, and the Treaty then allowed it to stay out of the Free State.

The Government of Ireland Act (December 1920) set up a parliament for the six counties of Northern Ireland and one for the other 26 counties of Southern Ireland, with a Council of Ireland to link them.
In the Northern election of 24 May 1921 the Unionists won 40 of 52 seats, and Sinn Féin and the Nationalists won six each but would not recognise the parliament.
Craig became Prime Minister in June 1921, and George V opened the Northern parliament in Belfast on 22 June 1921.
Southern Ireland's parliament never worked, since Sinn Féin won 124 of 128 seats and treated the election as one for the Dáil.
Under the Treaty Northern Ireland could opt out of the Free State, and it did so on 7 December 1922, the day after the Free State came into being.
The Treaty provided for a Boundary Commission, chaired by Richard Feetham, with Eoin MacNeill for the Free State and J.R. Fisher for Northern Ireland, since Craig refused to nominate.
The commission's expected report was leaked to the Morning Post in November 1925; MacNeill resigned, and on 3 December 1925 the three governments agreed that the border would stay as it was.
The Tripartite Agreement also released the Free State from its share of the imperial debt and ended the Council of Ireland.
The founding of the state was accompanied by sectarian rioting and an IRA campaign, to which the government responded with exceptional powers.
After the killing of an RIC officer in Cork in July 1920, thousands of Catholic and some Protestant labour supporters were expelled from the Belfast shipyards and engineering works.
Riots in Derry in June 1920 and in Belfast through 1920–22 killed about 500 people, most of them Catholics, and drove many families from their homes.
The Dáil organised a boycott of Belfast goods in 1920, which hurt Catholic workers and shopkeepers more than it hurt the unionist economy.
The Ulster Special Constabulary, formed in late 1920, had full-time A Specials, part-time B Specials and reserve C Specials; it was recruited almost entirely from Protestants.
The Royal Ulster Constabulary replaced the RIC in June 1922; on paper a third of its places were reserved for Catholics, but they never filled them.
The Craig–Collins pacts of January and March 1922 failed, and the IRA offensive on the border in May 1922 led the government to intern republicans.

The Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act of April 1922 allowed internment, curfews, the banning of meetings and the arrest of suspects without warrant; it was renewed annually and made permanent in 1933.
Several hundred men were interned in 1922, including some held on the prison ship Argenta.
The Ulster Unionist Party governed without interruption and changed the electoral rules to keep it in power. Nationalists took little part in the system.
Nationalists abstained from Stormont at first; the Nationalist Party under Joe Devlin took its seats in 1925, but Sinn Féin remained abstentionist.
Tyrone and Fermanagh county councils and many other nationalist-controlled councils, which refused to recognise the Belfast government in 1920–22, were dissolved and replaced by commissioners.
The Local Government Act of 1922 abolished proportional representation in local elections and redrew electoral areas.
Proportional representation for Stormont elections was abolished in 1929 and single-member constituencies introduced, which helped the Unionists and weakened Labour and independents.
Derry Corporation stayed under unionist control from 1923 until 1969 even though Catholics were a majority of the city's population; this is the best-known case of gerrymandering.
