The Unionist Party held every Stormont election from 1921 to 1969 by large margins, and a bloc vote on border issues kept Protestant workers within it.
Stormont Parliament Buildings, on the outskirts of Belfast, were opened by the Prince of Wales in 1932, a symbol of the permanence of the state.
Nationalists said that the state discriminated against Catholics. Unionists denied it, arguing that Catholics refused to take part in the state.
Catholics were about a third of the population but held a small share of senior posts in the civil service, the judiciary, and local government.
The shipyards and heavy industry employed few Catholics, and Protestant workers' networks and the Orange Order helped to secure employment.
Local councils controlled by unionists allocated public housing, and nationalists argued that houses were allocated to Protestant families first.
In the mid-1930s Basil Brooke urged unionists not to employ Catholics, a statement widely quoted as evidence of the attitudes of leading unionists.

On 24 April 1934 Craig told the Stormont parliament that he boasted of a Protestant parliament and a Protestant state; he said this in reply to southern Catholic claims, and it is the best-known statement of the attitudes of the unionist government.

Critics of the system, such as Michael Farrell in The Orange State (1976), see systematic discrimination, while others accept discrimination in some fields but stress that it was not centrally planned.
Nationalist abstention in the early years and the Catholic Church's separate schools left the minority with a limited voice in the state.
Northern Ireland entered the 1920s with high-value industries that depended on export markets, and the post-war slump and the Depression hit them hard.
Shipbuilding at Harland and Wolff and linen were the two big employers, and both fell back after the post-war boom ended in 1920–21.
Unemployment was around 20 per cent for much of the 1920s and reached around 25 per cent in the early 1930s, among the highest in the United Kingdom.
Agriculture remained important, with small farms exporting cattle and eggs to Britain.
The government followed a policy of ‘step by step’ with Britain on welfare benefits, which kept pensions and unemployment pay in line with British levels, financed with an imperial contribution.
Housing in the slums of Belfast was poor and overcrowded, and the government built little until the late 1930s.

In October 1932 unemployed Catholic and Protestant workers joined in the Outdoor Relief strike and riots in Belfast against the harsh relief rules; police shot dead two people, and the Board of Guardians increased the relief.
Partition broke up an economy that had been built on all-Ireland trade and weakened both parts.
Customs controls on the border from 1923 interrupted the flow of goods and cattle, and the Free State's tariffs and Economic War of the 1930s made smuggling common.
Belfast's linen, shipbuilding and engineering, which had sold to a UK and world market, lost the southern market they had counted on.
The Free State lost the industrial north-east, which had provided the bulk of Irish manufactured exports, and was left with an economy dependent on agriculture.
Dublin and Belfast, once part of a single banking and railway system, were run from different centres, and railways such as the Great Northern crossed the border.
Society divided as well: Catholics in the North were cut off from the southern state's institutions, while Protestants in the South felt the pressure of the Catholic ethos.
Politically the border became the main theme of Northern nationalism and southern foreign policy, as seen in Articles 2 and 3 of the 1937 constitution.
Craig was a leader of Ulster resistance to Home Rule and the first Prime Minister of Northern Ireland. He is judged as the builder of a stable state and also as a leader of a sectarian one.
Craig (1871–1940) was born in Belfast, the son of a wealthy whiskey distiller, and worked as a stockbroker; he served in the Boer War and became MP for East Down in 1906.
He organised the UVF and the Larne gun-running of April 1914 alongside Carson.
He was a junior minister in the British government from 1916 to 1921, ending as Parliamentary and Financial Secretary to the Admiralty.
He succeeded Carson as Unionist leader in February 1921 and became Prime Minister of Northern Ireland in June 1921, serving until his death on 24 November 1940.
He was made Viscount Craigavon in 1927.
He negotiated with Collins in 1922 and with Lloyd George, but insisted that the border was settled; he refused to nominate to the Boundary Commission.
His government created the RUC and the Special Powers Act, and abolished proportional representation, so critics see him as a sectarian figure.
His defenders note that he held the state together against IRA violence and economic crisis and that his government copied British social policy.
Contemporaries: unionists revered him as their founder, while nationalists considered him responsible for their exclusion.

Historians: Patrick Buckland's biography (1980) stressed his cautious, conservative leadership and his failure to reach out to Catholics, while others criticise the lack of any attempt to win minority consent.
Bates was the minister who ran the machinery of control for more than 20 years, and his name is associated with the security system and electoral changes.
Richard Dawson Bates (1876–1949) was a Belfast solicitor who was secretary of the Ulster Unionist Council from 1906 to 1921 and helped to organise the UVF.
He was Minister of Home Affairs from 1921 to 1943, responsible for the RUC, the Special Constabulary, the Special Powers Act and local government and elections.
He introduced the Local Government Act of 1922 that abolished PR for local elections and the 1929 change for Stormont elections.
He used his powers to ban republican parades and organisations, to arrest and intern suspects and to censor some publications.
Contemporaries: nationalists described him as the architect of the system of control, and many unionists praised his efficiency.
Historians: Buckland, in The Factory of Grievances (1979), describes how his department's decisions, even if cautious, left a legacy of grievances; Bates left office in 1943 in ill health.
Judgements depend on whether the state is measured by survival and stability or by its treatment of the minority.
Achievement: it survived the violence of 1920–22 and the Depression and secured the position of Northern Ireland within the United Kingdom.
Achievement: it maintained British standards in education, health and welfare through its step-by-step policy.
Limit: it relied on emergency powers, a largely Protestant police and manipulated electoral rules, so the minority never accepted it.
Limit: a one-party government with a permanent majority did not develop real opposition, and unemployment policy was timid.
Contemporary view: unionists regarded it as a bulwark against a Catholic all-Ireland state, while nationalists saw a Protestant state.
Later view: historians disagree on how far the system was planned discrimination, but accept that its legacy shaped the Troubles.
The Truce of 11 July 1921 opened talks about Ireland's status. Months of correspondence were needed before a formal conference could meet, and the central question was already clear: the Crown.
Lloyd George had invited de Valera to talks on 24 June 1921, after George V's call for reconciliation at Belfast, and the Truce came into force at noon on 11 July.
De Valera met Lloyd George in London four times between 14 and 21 July 1921, and neither side could shift the other on principle.
The British proposal of 20 July offered dominion status with restrictions: British control of defence and the ports, free trade, and no change to the position of the six counties.

The Dáil cabinet rejected the offer on 10 August; de Valera's counter-proposal was ‘external association’, in which Ireland would be a separate republic linked to the British Commonwealth, with the Crown recognised only as head of the association.
In an exchange of letters through the late summer Lloyd George insisted that Ireland accept the Crown and remain within the Empire, and de Valera insisted on the right of self-determination.

Lloyd George's invitation of 29 September proposed a conference to see how the association of Ireland with the Empire might be reconciled with Irish national aspirations; the Irish accepted it, and the conference opened on 11 October 1921.

Britain wanted a settlement because the war was costing money and reputation, the Empire's dominion premiers urged compromise, and the cabinet knew that a full-scale reconquest would need a very large army and martial law over the whole island.
The Irish side wanted a settlement because the IRA was short of arms and ammunition, and because of the cost to civilians in the war zones.
The decision to send plenipotentiaries and keep de Valera in Dublin shaped the whole outcome and the debate about it afterwards.
The Irish delegation was agreed by the Dáil cabinet in September 1921: Arthur Griffith (chairman), Michael Collins, Robert Barton, George Gavan Duffy and Éamonn Duggan.
Erskine Childers was the delegation's chief secretary, with Diarmuid O'Hegarty, John Chartres and others as staff.
The delegation lived at 22 Hans Place in Knightsbridge, while Collins stayed separately at Cadogan Gardens.
De Valera stayed in Dublin, saying that as head of state he should be held in reserve and that he had to keep the more extreme republicans on side; Cathal Brugha and Austin Stack also stayed at home.
Critics, including Collins, argued that it was a mistake: the man with most authority and most experience of Lloyd George was absent and later disowned the result.
The delegates' credentials described them as plenipotentiaries, which meant they had full power to negotiate and sign.
Their written instructions were different: they should report to Dublin on the text of any proposed treaty before signing; the exact meaning of this instruction was later disputed.

The British team was Lloyd George (Prime Minister), Austen Chamberlain (Lord Privy Seal), Lord Birkenhead (Lord Chancellor), Winston Churchill (Colonial Secretary), Sir Laming Worthington-Evans (War Secretary), Sir Hamar Greenwood (Chief Secretary for Ireland) and the Attorney General, Gordon Hewart.
Lionel Curtis and the cabinet secretary Tom Jones acted as advisers and go-betweens for the British.
Plenary sessions at Downing Street gave way to small sub-conferences where Griffith and Collins argued about the Crown, Ulster, defence and finance.
The plenary sessions of 11–24 October produced no agreement, and after that small groups met, so most of the bargaining was done privately.

The Crown and the oath: the British demanded an oath of allegiance to the Crown and membership of the Commonwealth, and the Irish tried to substitute external association and an oath to the constitution.

Ulster: the Irish argued that Ireland was one nation and that the six counties should not be allowed to opt out; Lloyd George said he could not coerce them, and he suggested a Boundary Commission, which Griffith and Collins took as a way of reducing the North so much that it could not survive.
Defence: Britain demanded control of Irish ports and coastal defence for naval reasons, which the Irish saw as a limit on sovereignty.
Trade and finance: the British wanted free trade between the two islands and a share of the British public debt, while the Irish claimed offsetting counter-claims for overtaxation.
Craig and the Northern government refused to join the talks, and Lloyd George tried to extract concessions from Craig on the basis of a united Ireland within the Empire.
The delegates travelled to Dublin to consult the cabinet in November and December, so the process was not entirely independent of de Valera and the cabinet.
Throughout, Tom Jones and Lionel Curtis passed messages between Lloyd George and Griffith, and Collins formed a good relationship with Birkenhead.
The final week was a negotiation under deadline pressure. The decision to sign without referring back to Dublin is the central controversy.

On 2 December Griffith privately gave Lloyd George a written assurance that he would not allow the talks to break on the Ulster question, provided the Boundary Commission was set up; Lloyd George later treated this as a commitment and republicans saw it as a concession made without the cabinet's knowledge.
At a cabinet meeting in Dublin on 3 December the cabinet instructed the delegates not to accept the oath as drafted, and the delegates returned to London with that line.

On 4 and 5 December the British pressed for signature; on 5 December Lloyd George told Griffith and Collins that there would be a break and war unless the Treaty was signed that night, and he said his courier was ready to take letters to Craig either way.
Barton later recalled that Lloyd George warned of ‘immediate and terrible war’, and the British minutes described a threat of war within days; whether the threat was a bluff is still disputed.
The delegates returned to Hans Place, where Collins and Griffith argued that the alternative to signing was war, and Barton, who had at first refused, gave way.
The Treaty was signed at Downing Street at about 2.10 am on 6 December 1921 by all five Irish delegates, with the British team.
Collins said afterwards that he had signed his own death warrant, a remark he made in private letters of that month.
De Valera was not told in advance; he learned of the signing on 6 December and was angry that the delegation had not sent the final text to Dublin.
The Treaty created the Irish Free State as a self-governing dominion in the Empire, with the Crown, an oath, British naval bases and partition qualified by a Boundary Commission.
Article 1: the Irish Free State was to have the same constitutional status as Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa.
The King was represented by a Governor-General, and the Free State's parliament and government were to be responsible to the Dáil.
The oath: members of the Free State parliament had to swear to be faithful to the Constitution and to the King, ‘in virtue of the common citizenship of Ireland with Great Britain’.

Defence: Britain would defend the coasts, and kept the use of the ports of Berehaven, Queenstown (Cobh) and Lough Swilly, with the right to use others in war; the Free State army was to be limited in proportion to population.
Finance: the Free State took on a share of the British public debt, subject to counter-claims; the Treaty said nothing of land annuities.

Ulster: Northern Ireland could opt out of the Free State within one month, and a Boundary Commission would then settle the border in line with the wishes of inhabitants, as far as compatible with economic and geographic conditions.
A Provisional Government would take over from the British administration until the Free State was established.
The Treaty had to be approved by the Dáil, and by the British Parliament; it was also to be ratified by a meeting of the House of Parliament of Southern Ireland.
The Dáil debated the Treaty at length. The split that followed divided cabinet, army and families, and led to the Civil War.
On 8 December the Dáil cabinet met and divided four to three in favour of the Treaty; de Valera, Brugha and Stack were against.
De Valera issued a statement to the press saying that he could not recommend the Treaty to the Dáil.
The Dáil debated in private from 14 to 17 December, where de Valera put forward his own alternative text, Document No. 2, based on external association; it was never presented to the British.
The public debate ran from 19 December to 10 January 1922, with an adjournment over Christmas; speakers included Griffith, Collins, Brugha, Mary MacSwiney and Childers.
Collins described the Treaty as giving ‘the freedom to achieve freedom’, a stepping stone to full independence, while Brugha attacked Collins's reputation.
Opponents argued that the oath and the Crown betrayed the republic proclaimed in 1916 and declared in 1919; supporters argued that the people did not want more war.
All six women deputies voted against the Treaty.
The Dáil approved the Treaty on 7 January 1922 by 64 votes to 57.
De Valera resigned as President on 9 January and lost a vote to be re-elected, and Griffith became President of the Dáil on 10 January.
A Provisional Government under Collins was formed on 14 January and took over from the British administration in Dublin Castle on 16 January.
Griffith was the chairman of the delegation, the senior negotiator and the first president of the Dáil to head a pro-Treaty government.
Griffith (1871–1922) was a Dublin printer and journalist who founded the United Irishman and, in 1905, Sinn Féin; he advocated a dual monarchy and economic self-reliance.
He was not a participant in the Rising but was interned afterwards, and he stepped aside for de Valera as Sinn Féin president in 1917.
He was acting head of the Dáil during de Valera's American tour in 1919–20 and was Minister for Foreign Affairs in 1921.
In London he led the negotiations on the Crown and Ulster, and he was prepared to accept dominion status within the Empire with the Boundary Commission.
He was a shy, scholarly man, in poor health after months in prison, and he was widely seen as the most honest of the delegates.
After his election as President of the Dáil in January 1922 he led the pro-Treaty side until his death from a cerebral haemorrhage on 12 August 1922.
Contemporaries: supporters of the Treaty praised his courage and integrity; republicans condemned him as having abandoned the republic.
Historians: Michael Laffan and Colum Kenny stress his role in creating the political movement that won independence and his realism in 1921.
Collins was reluctant to go to London, but his reputation as the man who had defeated the British gave the delegation influence and made it hard for the Dáil to reject the result.

Collins was Minister for Finance and head of the IRB, and he warned the cabinet that he would be a poor negotiator; he believed that his name was needed for the military side but that the politicians should lead.
In London he handled the military and financial issues and built relationships with Birkenhead and Churchill.
He accepted the Boundary Commission clause in the expectation that Tyrone, Fermanagh and parts of Armagh and Down would be transferred, and he believed Northern Ireland could not survive after that.
He argued on the night of 5 December that the IRA could not win another round and that the Treaty gave the means to build up the army and the state.
He saw the Treaty as giving freedom to achieve freedom, and he signed it as a first step.
He was chosen as chairman of the Provisional Government in January 1922; his death in August 1922 is described in the notes on the Civil War.
Contemporaries: anti-Treaty republicans accused him of using his IRB position to override the cabinet, while his supporters said he was honest about the Treaty's limits.
Historians: Tim Pat Coogan sees him as a pragmatic realist, while Peter Hart draws attention to his ruthlessness.
De Valera set the strategy and then rejected the outcome. Historians still argue about whether his decision to stay at home was shrewd or a mistake.
De Valera's talks with Lloyd George in July 1921 showed that the British would not allow an Irish republic, yet he remained committed to external association.
He chose the delegation and wrote its instructions, but did not join it; his reasons were to keep a power in reserve and to avoid committing the head of state.
He sent messages to London advising delegates to hold out on the Crown and oath, and kept in touch with Dublin cabinet colleagues.
After the signing he opposed the Treaty on the grounds that the delegates had signed without the cabinet's approval of the final text.
His Document No. 2 would have accepted the Crown as head of an association with the Commonwealth in the matter of common concern, with an oath to the constitution only; the Dáil did not adopt it.
Contemporaries: supporters of the Treaty said that he had set a trap for Collins and Griffith, and republicans said that he was upholding the Republic.

Historians: Lord Longford's Peace by Ordeal (1935) defended the delegates, while later biographers such as Coogan and Ferriter see him as a politician who used ambiguity to hold the movement together.
Judgements depend on whether the Treaty is measured against the republic of 1916 and 1919 or against the realistic alternatives of December 1921.
Achievement: Britain withdrew its army and administration from 26 counties, and the Free State got its own parliament, police, army and civil service.
Limit: the Treaty kept the Crown, the oath, British bases and partition, which republicans said betrayed the declared republic.
Pro-Treaty view: it gave the freedom to achieve freedom, and a refusal would have meant war in 1922 with the IRA short of arms.
Anti-Treaty view: the delegates were bullied into signing, and the Dáil had no right to give away the republic.
Public opinion: most newspapers, the Catholic bishops, farmers and business supported the Treaty, and the pro-Treaty side won about three-quarters of the votes in the June 1922 election.
Unionists saw the Treaty as removing the threat to the North, but the Boundary Commission disappointed nationalists in 1925.
Later view: historians debate whether the delegates were out-manoeuvred, whether the ultimatum was a bluff, and whether de Valera's absence made a bad outcome more likely.
Ratification of the Treaty divided the Dáil, Sinn Féin and the IRA, and for five months two rival authorities existed side by side.
After the Dáil vote of 7 January 1922 the Provisional Government under Collins took over from the British, and a new National Army was recruited, while the Dáil continued to meet under Griffith.
The IRA divided: most of its senior officers, led by Rory O'Connor and Liam Lynch, rejected the authority of the Dáil in March 1922 and held their own convention.
British troops left Dublin from January 1922, and both pro- and anti-Treaty forces took over barracks, which led to local clashes.
The anti-Treaty IRA seized the Four Courts in Dublin on 14 April 1922 and held it as a headquarters.
The Collins–de Valera pact of 20 May 1922 proposed a joint panel of pro- and anti-Treaty Sinn Féin candidates in the election; Collins repudiated it on the eve of the poll.

In the general election of 16 June 1922 pro-Treaty candidates won 58 seats and anti-Treaty candidates 36, with Labour 17 and others making up the rest; the draft Constitution was published on the day of the poll.

On 22 June 1922 two London IRA men shot Field Marshal Sir Henry Wilson, a unionist MP and adviser to the Northern government, and the British government pressed Collins to act against the Four Courts garrison.
The kidnapping of a National Army general, J.J. ‘Ginger’ O'Connell, by the Four Courts garrison on 26 June was a further trigger.
The National Army, using British artillery and supplies, took Dublin and then the towns, and the war became a guerrilla campaign that the anti-Treaty side could not win.
On 28 June 1922 the National Army shelled the Four Courts with British field guns; the garrison surrendered on 30 June after an explosion in the Public Record Office destroyed centuries of records.
Fighting in Dublin lasted until early July, and Cathal Brugha was killed in action on 7 July.
The National Army held the larger forces and the better arms; it took Limerick and Waterford in July, and landed at Fenit, Co. Kerry, and at Cork in August.
By the end of August the anti-Treaty forces had lost the towns and turned to guerrilla warfare, ambushes and the destruction of roads, bridges and railways.
Arthur Griffith died of a cerebral haemorrhage on 12 August 1922, and Michael Collins, then commander-in-chief, was shot dead at Béal na Bláth, Co. Cork, on 22 August 1922.
Richard Mulcahy became commander-in-chief, and W.T. Cosgrave became head of the government.
The Army Emergency Powers Resolution of September 1922 let military courts impose the death penalty for possession of arms.
The first four executions took place on 17 November 1922, and Erskine Childers was shot on 24 November after being found with a pistol.
On 8 December 1922 the government shot Rory O'Connor, Liam Mellows, Joe McKelvey and Dick Barrett, in reprisal for the killing of the TD Seán Hales the day before.
In total the Free State government executed about 80 anti-Treaty prisoners; the exact number is disputed by historians.
Free State soldiers in Kerry killed prisoners with landmines, as at Ballyseedy on 7 March 1923, in a reprisal that shocked many in the pro-Treaty side.

Liam Lynch, the anti-Treaty chief of staff, was killed in the Knockmealdown Mountains on 10 April 1923; his successor Frank Aiken ordered the arms dump on 24 May 1923, with a message from de Valera supporting the order.
Estimates of the dead range from about 1,500 to several thousand, and the war left a legacy of bitterness that shaped party politics for generations.
Cumann na nGaedheal, founded in 1923, set up the main institutions of the state. The emphasis was on continuity and law and order.

The Constitution of the Irish Free State came into force on 6 December 1922; it provided for a two-chamber Oireachtas, proportional representation, an Executive Council responsible to the Dáil, a Governor-General and the Treaty oath.
The Governor-General was Tim Healy from 1922 to 1928, followed by James McNeill.
The Civic Guard was founded in 1922 and renamed the Garda Síochána in 1923; it was unarmed, led by Eoin O'Duffy as Commissioner, and absorbed the Dublin Metropolitan Police in 1925.
The Courts of Justice Act 1924 set up a new court system of District, Circuit, High and Supreme Courts, replacing both the British and the Dáil courts.

The civil service and local government were kept largely as in British times, which gave the new state continuity and efficiency; the Ministers and Secretaries Act 1924 set up the government departments.
The Free State joined the League of Nations in 1923 and opened a legation in Washington in 1924.
The Land Act 1923 completed the transfer of land to tenants by compulsory purchase of untenanted land.
The Shannon Scheme was approved in 1925 and built by the German firm Siemens-Schuckert; the Electricity Supply Board was created in 1927 and the Ardnacrusha power station opened in 1929.
Within five years the government faced the army mutiny, the Boundary Commission crisis and the assassination of a leading minister.
The Army Mutiny of March 1924 came from a group of former IRA and IRB officers around Liam Tobin and Charles Dalton, who objected to demobilisation and to the influence of ex-British army officers.

The mutiny ended with the resignation of the Army Council and the Minister for Defence, Richard Mulcahy; the government reorganised the army under Kevin O'Higgins, which established civil control over the army.

The Boundary Commission crisis of November 1925 followed the leak of its expected findings to the Morning Post; Eoin MacNeill resigned and the Free State government agreed the Tripartite Agreement of 3 December 1925, which left the border unchanged.
Kevin O'Higgins, Minister for Justice and External Affairs, introduced the Public Safety Acts, which gave the government special powers against armed opposition.
O'Higgins was shot dead by three anti-Treaty IRA men on his way to Mass at Booterstown on 10 July 1927.

In response the government passed the Public Safety Act of 1927 and the Electoral Amendment Act, which required candidates to promise to take the oath, so Fianna Fáil had to decide whether to enter the Dáil or leave politics.
Constitutional republicanism, led by de Valera, replaced armed resistance and the Free State's parliamentary system gained legitimacy.
De Valera and his supporters left Sinn Féin in March 1926 over abstention and founded Fianna Fáil on 16 May 1926, arguing that the oath could be treated as an empty formula.
In the June 1927 election Fianna Fáil won 44 seats and Cumann na nGaedheal 47, and in the second election in September 1927 Cumann na nGaedheal won 62 and Fianna Fáil 57.
After O'Higgins's murder Fianna Fáil entered the Dáil on 12 August 1927, signing the oath book as a formality.
The Referendum and Initiative clauses of the Constitution were removed in 1928 and the Governor-General's role was left unchanged.
The Depression and the government's spending cuts reduced the support of Cumann na nGaedheal, and Fianna Fáil promised protection, land annuity relief and the abolition of the oath.
In the February 1932 election Fianna Fáil won 72 seats and Cumann na nGaedheal 57; de Valera was elected President of the Executive Council on 9 March 1932 with Labour's votes.
Cosgrave's government handed over power peacefully, and the army and police accepted the change; this was the first democratic transfer of power in the new state after a civil war.
The Civil War shaped party politics and the way the state was remembered for generations.
The two sides became the two main parties: Fine Gael descended from the pro-Treaty side and Fianna Fáil from the anti-Treaty side.
The 1923 general election, held in August, gave Cumann na nGaedheal 63 seats and the Republicans 44, though the republicans abstained.
De Valera was arrested in August 1923 and released in July 1924.
Anti-Treaty prisoners numbered in the thousands in 1923, and a hunger strike in October 1923 ended without success.
Both sides committed atrocities, and families and communities were divided, which made the war a subject of silence in Irish public life.
Cosgrave led the pro-Treaty side from 1922 to 1932 and built the state's institutions. He is judged as a cautious administrator who secured democracy.
William Thomas Cosgrave (1880–1965) was a Dublin publican's son, a Sinn Féin councillor from 1909 and a member of the South Dublin Union garrison in 1916; his death sentence was commuted.
He won Kilkenny City in August 1917 and served as Minister for Local Government in the Dáil ministry from 1919.
He became head of government after the deaths of Griffith and Collins in August 1922, and was President of the Executive Council from December 1922 to March 1932.
He led Cumann na nGaedheal and, after 1933, became first leader of Fine Gael, which merged his party with others, until 1944.
His government held the state together through the Civil War, the mutiny and the assassination of O'Higgins, and favoured rule of law and balanced budgets.

Contemporaries: supporters admired his determination and honesty, but critics called him a conservative who relied on a narrow group of ministers and who allowed the government to be seen as pro-British.

Historians: Tom Garvin (1922: The Birth of Irish Democracy, 1996) stresses his defence of democracy against militarism, while John Regan (The Irish Counter-Revolution, 1999) argues that the government was too conservative and authoritarian.
Judgements depend on whether the test is survival and legitimacy or social and economic performance.
Achievement: the state survived civil war, mutiny and assassination, and had working institutions by 1927.
Achievement: the peaceful transfer of power in 1932 showed that democratic institutions had become accepted.
Achievement: the Shannon Scheme and the ESB gave the state a modern electricity system.
Limit: the government used military courts, executions and public safety laws that opponents described as repression.
Limit: its economic policies, based on low spending and low taxation, did little for urban poverty and unemployment.
Limit: the Boundary Commission outcome of 1925 showed that the Treaty's northern hopes had been unrealistic.
Contemporary view: supporters saw the government as the defender of law, while opponents called it the Treaty government.
Later view: historians disagree about whether it was a successful counter to militarism, or a conservative counter-revolution.
The Cosgrave governments accepted the Treaty but used the Commonwealth to widen the Free State's independence step by step.
The Free State registered the Treaty with the League of Nations in 1924, treating it as an international agreement rather than an internal British matter; Britain objected.
The Boundary Commission crisis ended with the Tripartite Agreement of December 1925, which released the Free State from its share of the imperial debt, and so put the border question aside.

The Imperial Conference of 1926 produced the Balfour Declaration, which described Britain and the dominions as autonomous communities, equal in status and freely associated; Kevin O'Higgins was one of its principal advocates.
The Statute of Westminster (December 1931) gave the dominions legislative independence, and removed the British Parliament's power to override dominion laws.
Cosgrave's government accepted the oath, the Governor-General and the Treaty ports, and held that independence should come by agreement with Britain.
The Free State continued to pay the land annuities, the repayments that tenant farmers owed for land bought under the Land Acts, to the British Exchequer under the financial arrangement of 1923–25.
Fianna Fáil's election pledge was to remove the oath and the Treaty's symbols. De Valera did this by legislation, relying on the Statute of Westminster and the Free State's own Dáil majority.
De Valera became President of the Executive Council on 9 March 1932 and also took the post of Minister for External Affairs.
In 1932 he dismissed James McNeill as Governor-General (in October) and appointed Domhnall Ua Buachalla, a Fianna Fáil figure with no official role, in his place in November.
The Constitution (Removal of Oath) Act became law in May 1933 and ended the oath of fidelity to the King for members of the Oireachtas.
The Constitution (Amendment No. 22) Act 1933 ended the right of appeal to the Privy Council.

The abdication of Edward VIII in December 1936 gave de Valera his opportunity: on 11 December the Constitution (Amendment No. 27) Act removed all references to the Crown and the Governor-General from the Constitution.
On 12 December 1936 the Executive Authority (External Relations) Act gave the King a role only in the appointment of diplomats and signing of international agreements.
Britain accepted these changes without military or economic action, partly because the Statute of Westminster supported de Valera's constitutional argument.
De Valera's decision to stop the land annuities became a trade conflict, which was only ended by the agreements of 1938.
The annuities amounted to about £3 million a year; de Valera argued that they were a debt owed to the Irish government, not to Britain, and he stopped paying them in mid-1932.
Britain regarded the payments as obligatory under the 1925 agreement and imposed special duties on Irish cattle, beef, butter and other exports from July 1932.
The Free State responded with duties on British goods such as coal, cement and iron and steel products, and began a policy of self-sufficiency.
The Coal–Cattle Pact of 1935 allowed an exchange of Irish cattle exports for British coal, and slightly reduced the damage.
The farm economy and its effects are covered in the notes on economy and society.
Fianna Fáil argued that the conflict was a price for sovereignty, and in rural constituencies it kept its voters, while Cosgrave's party attacked the policy as damaging.
The first years of Fianna Fáil rule saw a challenge from the right, which strengthened the government's hand and led to the creation of a new opposition party.
The Army Comrades Association was founded in February 1932 by pro-Treaty ex-officers to protect Cumann na nGaedheal meetings from IRA disruption.
In February 1933 de Valera dismissed Eoin O'Duffy as Garda Commissioner, and O'Duffy took over the ACA in July 1933, when it adopted a blue shirt and a stiff-armed salute.
The movement was renamed the National Guard in July 1933, a planned march on Dublin was prohibited, and the organisation was banned in August 1933.
In September 1933 Cumann na nGaedheal, the Centre Party and the Blueshirts merged as Fine Gael under O'Duffy; he was forced out within a year, and Cosgrave became leader in 1935.
De Valera banned the IRA in June 1936, after the murder of Vice-Admiral Somerville, and removed the Blueshirt and IRA challenge to the state.
O'Duffy later led an Irish Brigade of about 700 men to fight for Franco in Spain in 1936–37.
The new constitution replaced the 1922 Constitution and gave the state a more Irish and Catholic character, while avoiding the word republic.
It was drafted by de Valera with civil servants John Hearne and Maurice Moynihan, and with advice from clergy including the Archbishop of Dublin.
It was approved by a plebiscite on 1 July 1937 by 56 per cent to 44 per cent and came into force on 29 December 1937.
Article 4 named the state Éire, or in English Ireland, and Article 5 declared it a sovereign, independent, democratic state.
Articles 2 and 3 claimed the whole island of Ireland as the national territory, while limiting the exercise of the state's laws to 26 counties until reunification.
The head of state was a President elected for seven years, and the head of government was the Taoiseach.
Article 41 recognised the family as the foundation of society, spoke of the woman's life within the home, and banned divorce.

Article 44 recognised the special position of the Catholic Church as the guardian of the faith of the majority and also named other denominations, including the Jewish congregations; it was removed in 1972.
Unionists, women's groups and some nationalists criticised the document; Douglas Hyde was inaugurated as first President on 25 June 1938.
Three agreements signed in London on 25 April 1938 settled the main disputes between the two governments and removed the Treaty's last military restriction.
The defence agreement transferred the Treaty ports at Berehaven, Cobh (Spike Island) and Lough Swilly to Ireland, and the handover took place in July 1938.
The financial agreement ended the land annuities dispute for a single payment of £10 million, far less than Britain had claimed.
The trade agreement ended the special duties on both sides.
Neville Chamberlain's government agreed partly to improve relations as war approached, and Churchill opposed the surrender of the ports.
De Valera had linked the ports to partition in the talks, but Britain would not move on the border.
The ports allowed Ireland to remain neutral in 1939, a policy examined in the notes on the Second World War.
The inter-party government formally ended the External Relations Act and left the Commonwealth, while the British guaranteed Northern Ireland's position.

Fianna Fáil lost its majority in the election of February 1948, and John A. Costello of Fine Gael became Taoiseach on 18 February 1948 in a coalition including Labour, Clann na Poblachta, Clann na Talmhan and others.
Seán MacBride, the Minister for External Affairs, wanted to repeal the External Relations Act, which he regarded as an anomaly.
Costello announced the decision while on a visit to Canada in September 1948.
The Republic of Ireland Act was passed in December 1948 and came into force on Easter Monday, 18 April 1949, repealing the External Relations Act and ending the state's link with the Commonwealth.
The British Ireland Act 1949 recognised that Ireland was no longer a member of the Commonwealth, but said Irish citizens would not be treated as foreigners.
It also declared that Northern Ireland would not cease to be part of the United Kingdom without the consent of the Parliament of Northern Ireland, which strengthened the unionist position.
The southern parties united in an anti-partition campaign in 1949, but it achieved little.
De Valera dominated the 1930s and 1940s and shaped the state's constitution, relations with Britain and neutrality. Judgements about him are divided.
He led Fianna Fáil in government from 1932 to 1948 and again in 1951–54 and 1957–59, and was President of Ireland from 1959 to 1973; he died in 1975.
He removed the oath, the Governor-General and the Privy Council appeal, drafted the 1937 constitution and secured the ports in 1938.
He kept Ireland neutral in the Second World War and banned the IRA in 1936.
He did not end partition, and the Economic War cost the farming economy dearly.
The social and economic record was weak: high emigration, unemployment, a conservative Catholic constitution and wartime censorship.

Contemporaries: supporters, especially small farmers and workers, saw him as the man who finished the work of independence, while opponents in Cumann na nGaedheal and the Blueshirts called him a dictator.

Historians: Joe Lee (Ireland 1912–1985) credits him with consolidating democracy and with strong political skills, while criticising the economy; Deirdre McMahon (Republicans and Imperialists, 1984) examined his diplomacy with Britain.
Biographers such as Tim Pat Coogan (1993) and Diarmaid Ferriter (Judging Dev, 2007) stress his stubbornness and also his pragmatism.
Both leaders increased Irish independence, but by different methods and at different costs.
Cosgrave's strengths: he secured the Free State's international recognition, used the Commonwealth to widen independence and avoided economic conflict with Britain.
Cosgrave's limits: he left the oath, the Governor-General and the ports in place, and the Boundary Commission failed.
De Valera's strengths: he removed the symbols of the Treaty, secured the ports and the annuities settlement and created a constitution that Britain accepted in practice.
De Valera's limits: the Economic War, the failure to end partition and the fact that most of his changes relied on the groundwork laid by Cosgrave at the Imperial Conferences.
Contemporary view: Fianna Fáil supporters said de Valera achieved real sovereignty; Fine Gael said he damaged the economy for the sake of symbols.
Later view: the Republic of 1949 is often judged mainly a formal act, as de Valera's earlier changes had already made the state independent in practice.
The Free State took over a small, mainly agricultural economy tied to Britain, and partition removed its industrial region.
Agriculture was the main employer, and more than 90 per cent of exports, mainly cattle, butter, bacon and eggs, went to Britain.

Partition left the Belfast shipyards, the linen mills and most heavy engineering in Northern Ireland, so the Free State had little industry beyond Dublin brewing, biscuits, and food processing, and the Ford factory at Cork.
The Free State set up its own customs controls on the border in 1923, interrupting trade in cattle and manufactured goods, and creating a smuggling economy.
The Irish pound remained tied to sterling: the Currency Act of 1927 created the Saorstát pound at parity with sterling, so Irish monetary policy followed Britain's.
The Free State had a population of under three million, and a small home market limited the scope for industrial growth.
The civil service, taxation and financial institutions were largely inherited from British rule, and the Department of Finance took over the cautious Treasury approach.
The Cumann na nGaedheal governments believed that the farm sector could carry the economy and that low taxes and free trade were the best policy.
Patrick Hogan, Minister for Agriculture from 1922 to 1932, concentrated on quality exports of beef, butter and bacon to Britain.
The Dairy Produce Act and the Creamery Act of 1924 and the Live Stock Breeding Act of 1925 improved standards, and the Agricultural Credit Corporation was founded in 1927 to lend to farmers.
Ernest Blythe, Minister for Finance from 1923, kept taxes and spending low, and the 1924 budget cut the old age pension from 10 shillings to 9 shillings a week.
Public-sector pay was also cut, and the government aimed for balanced budgets as a priority.
A Tariff Commission was set up under the Tariff Commission Act of 1926 to examine applications for protection, but it recommended tariffs on only a limited number of goods.
The Shannon Scheme was the chief exception to the policy of low state spending, and it was justified as providing cheap power for industry.
Critics said that the policy favoured large farmers and left cities, labourers and small farmers with little help.
The government set up the Agricultural Credit Corporation and promoted co-operative creameries as part of its farm policy.
McElligott was a civil servant, not a politician, but as Secretary of the Department of Finance he was one of the most influential figures in economic policy for a quarter of a century.
James J. McElligott (1893–1974) joined the Department of Finance in 1923, as an Assistant Secretary, and was Secretary of the Department from 1927 to 1953.
He later served as Governor of the Central Bank, from 1953 to 1960.
He worked with Blythe and then with Fianna Fáil's Finance Minister Seán MacEntee in the 1930s, and he advised ministers on the budget, spending and taxation.
His approach was financial orthodoxy: balanced budgets, low taxes, limited state borrowing and strict control of spending by other departments.
He was sceptical of high-spending social programmes and of industrial protection as practised by Seán Lemass, and Finance regularly opposed the cost of new schemes.
Contemporaries in other departments, especially Industry and Commerce, saw Finance as a block on development.
Historians such as Ronan Fanning, in The Irish Department of Finance (1978), argue that Finance's caution shaped policy for decades and held back growth until the reappraisal of the late 1950s.
The Wall Street Crash and the Depression cut the prices of farm exports and closed foreign markets just as Britain turned away from free trade.
The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 began a worldwide slump, and farm prices fell sharply.
The Free State's farmers lost income, and the number of those emigrating to the United States dropped as the American economy shut its doors.
In September 1931 Britain left the gold standard, but the Free State kept its currency tied to sterling.
In 1932 Britain introduced general import duties and imperial preference, which hurt Irish exports and showed the weakness of dependence on a single market.
Unemployment rose in the towns, and the Cumann na nGaedheal government cut spending and did not bring in tariffs on a large scale.
The crisis helped Fianna Fáil, which promised protection and self-sufficiency, win the election of 1932.
Irish farm prices fell steeply in the early 1930s, and the cost of the annuities became harder to bear.
Fianna Fáil, with Lemass as Minister for Industry and Commerce, abandoned free trade and tried to build industry behind tariff walls.
Tariffs and quotas were imposed on a wide range of imports, from clothing and shoes to household goods.
The Control of Manufactures Acts of 1932 and 1934 required that majority ownership of manufacturing firms in the Free State be Irish.
The Industrial Credit Company, set up in 1933, provided capital to new Irish firms.
The Irish Sugar Company was founded in 1933 to run the beet industry and the sugar factories.
The Turf Development Board (1934), Aer Lingus (1936) and the ESB were examples of the state's creation of semi-state bodies.
Wheat and beet growing were encouraged, and the wheat acreage rose roughly tenfold in the first years of the policy.
Industrial employment grew by tens of thousands over the 1930s, but many of the new firms were small, inefficient and depended on the home market.
Critics said protection raised prices and did not lead to exports; supporters said it created jobs which free trade would never have provided.
The policy of self-sufficiency was reinforced after 1939 by the Emergency, when imports were cut off.
The trade war with Britain over the land annuities hit the largest group of farmers hardest. The causes are covered in the notes on Anglo-Irish relations.
British duties on cattle, beef and butter from 1932 cut the price of cattle and made many exports uneconomic.
Cattle exports to Britain, the single largest item, fell sharply, and large and small cattle farmers saw their incomes drop.
The government paid bounties on exports and subsidised wheat and beet to make up for lost income, financed by higher taxes.
The Coal–Cattle Pact of 1935 allowed more Irish cattle into Britain in return for British coal.
Farmers in Munster and Leinster, with their large cattle farms, were hit more than small western farmers.
The 1938 agreement ended the dispute, but exports did not return to their former level before the war.
Dairy farmers and small farmers were affected by the fall in prices, and the cost of the trade war fell on the whole rural economy.
Fianna Fáil spent more than its predecessor on housing and welfare, but resources were limited and poverty remained widespread.
The Housing Acts of 1932 and 1936 raised state subsidies, and local authorities built tens of thousands of new houses, helped by slum clearance in Dublin.
The Unemployment Assistance Act of 1933 gave relief to those who had run out of insurance benefit.
The Widows' and Orphans' Pensions Act of 1935 introduced a contributory pension scheme.
Tenements in Dublin remained overcrowded, and the tuberculosis death rate was high.
Emigration fell in the early 1930s as the Depression closed American and British job markets, then rose again in the late 1930s and during the Second World War.
A marriage bar for national teachers, introduced in 1932, obliged women teachers to resign on marriage; a similar bar already applied in the civil service from the 1920s.
Emigrants' remittances were an important source of income for families in the west, and their reduction in the Depression hurt small farmers.
Neither free trade nor protection produced rapid growth. Judgements depend on whether the aim is stability, self-sufficiency or living standards.
Cumann na nGaedheal's achievement: financial stability, a sound currency, an efficient farm export trade and the Shannon Scheme.
Cumann na nGaedheal's limit: dependence on the British market and low spending left little help for the poor when the Depression came.
Fianna Fáil's achievement: new industries and jobs, a larger state role through semi-state companies and more social housing.
Fianna Fáil's limit: the Economic War, a small and protected market, continued emigration and low living standards.
Why success was hard: a small home market, few natural resources, dependence on Britain, the Depression and then the Second World War.
Contemporary view: supporters of protection held that it was necessary for independence; critics held that it hurt consumers and farmers.
Later view: historians such as Mary Daly and Joe Lee say that protection created jobs but not an efficient industry, while the Finance Department's caution restricted investment.
Ireland stayed out of the Second World War, which the government called the Emergency. Neutrality was seen as the proof of independent statehood.
The Dáil declared a state of national emergency on 2 September 1939, and Britain declared war on Germany on 3 September.
Neutrality demonstrated sovereignty: a state that followed Britain into war would look like a dominion in practice.
Partition was a reason: Ireland could not ally with Britain while Britain held Northern Ireland.
The return of the Treaty ports in 1938 made neutrality possible, since Britain no longer held the bases.
The Defence Forces were small and poorly equipped, and bombing of Irish cities was feared.
Civil War divisions meant that joining the war might have split the country again.
Most of the public supported neutrality, and the main parties, Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and Labour, accepted it, though James Dillon of Fine Gael argued for entering the war on the Allied side.
Neutrality was a benevolent one in practice, leaning towards Britain, but it was never formally broken.
The government took wide powers over the economy and public opinion, and used them to control information and public debate.
The Emergency Powers Act was passed on 3 September 1939 and let ministers make orders with the force of law, covering prices, supplies, movement and censorship.
Frank Aiken was Minister for the Co-ordination of Defensive Measures and was responsible for censorship.
Press censorship forbade reports on troop movements, ship sinkings, weather and criticism of neutrality.
Weather forecasts were banned from the radio and the press, since they might help the belligerents.
Letters and telegrams were opened and censored, and the Censorship of Publications Board, active since 1929, continued to ban books.
Radio Éireann avoided comment that might offend any belligerent, and war news was heavily controlled.
The war was called the Emergency, and the censorship policy also served to maintain public conformity with the official line.
The government expanded the army and created reserves for defence against invasion, while dealing firmly with the IRA.
The regular army grew from under 20,000 men to about 40,000 by 1941, with Reserve forces added.
The Local Defence Force (LDF) was founded in June 1940 after the fall of France as a volunteer reserve, and tens of thousands joined.
The Local Security Force worked with the Garda in civil defence.
The government made secret contingency plans for co-operation with Britain if Germany invaded.
The IRA was banned in 1936, and the Offences Against the State Act of 1939 reinforced the law against it.
The IRA's S-Plan bombing campaign in Britain began in January 1939; the Coventry bomb of August 1939 killed five people.
On 23 December 1939 the IRA raided the Magazine Fort in the Phoenix Park and removed the army's reserve ammunition, and the government recovered most of it.
The Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act of 1940 introduced internment without trial, and hundreds of IRA men were held at the Curragh.
Several IRA men were executed during the war for the killing of Gardaí, and others died on hunger strike.
Shipping losses and British restrictions meant shortages of coal, petrol, tea and wheat. The government controlled production and distribution.
Seán Lemass was Minister for Supplies from 1939 to 1945, and the Department of Supplies controlled imports, prices and rationing.
Tea, sugar, butter, flour, bread and fuel were rationed, and petrol was restricted so that private motoring almost stopped.
Compulsory tillage orders required farmers to plough more land, and the wheat harvest increased, though bread became darker and coarser.
Coal imports collapsed, and turf production grew; huge turf stacks were built in the Phoenix Park and elsewhere, and trains ran on turf.
Gas supplies were limited to certain hours, and inspectors, known as glimmer men, checked on households.
Irish Shipping Ltd was set up in 1941 to buy and run ships, since British shipping was unavailable, and its ships sailed unescorted under the Irish flag.
Irish merchant seamen died when ships were sunk by submarines and aircraft despite their neutral markings.
The Wages Standstill Order of 1941 froze most wages while prices rose, so real incomes fell, and the Trade Union Act of 1941 was aimed at the unions.
Exports of cattle to Britain continued, and farmers gained from guaranteed prices for produce, though industry suffered from lack of raw materials.
Neutrality led to repeated pressure from Britain and, later, the United States.
In June 1940, after the fall of France, Malcolm MacDonald brought de Valera an offer: if Ireland joined the Allies, Britain would declare for a united Ireland in principle.
De Valera rejected the offer in early July 1940, because he doubted that Britain could deliver unity and because the Northern government was not consulted.
Churchill, who had opposed the return of the ports in 1938, publicly complained about the loss of the bases in the battle of the Atlantic.
The British considered occupying the ports in 1940–41 but decided against it.
The Irish government complained when Britain restricted supplies of coal, wheat and shipping to Ireland.
David Gray, the American Minister in Dublin, was strongly critical of neutrality, and the United States pressed the government after it entered the war in December 1941.
In February 1944 the United States and Britain presented the American Note, asking the government to expel the German and Japanese diplomats before the D-Day landings.
De Valera refused, and Britain restricted travel to Ireland in the following months.
In practice neutrality was benevolent towards the Allies. At the same time, the state suffered from German bombing.
Irish military intelligence (G2) shared information with British intelligence and the Garda watched German agents; the spy Hermann Görtz was caught and interned.
Allied aircraft were allowed to fly over Donegal to the Atlantic, and Allied airmen who crashed in Ireland were quietly released, while Germans were interned in the Curragh.
Weather reports from Blacksod Point lighthouse, Co. Mayo, in June 1944 contributed to the decision on the date of D-Day.
About 50,000 to 70,000 people from the Free State served in the British forces; soldiers who deserted from the Irish army to join them were barred from public employment in 1945.
German aircraft bombed Wexford (Campile creamery, August 1940, three killed) and other places.
On the night of 31 May 1941 German bombers dropped bombs on the North Strand in Dublin, killing about thirty people (estimates range from 28 to 34), and destroying or damaging many houses.
The government protested to Germany; Germany said it was an error, and West Germany paid compensation after the war.
Dublin and other fire brigades went north to help Belfast in April 1941, with the approval of de Valera.
De Valera's insistence on diplomatic correctness to the end brought a public attack from Churchill.
On 2 May 1945, after Hitler's death was announced, de Valera called on the German minister Eduard Hempel to express condolences.
He had paid a similar visit to the American Minister on the death of Roosevelt in April 1945.
De Valera defended the visit as diplomatic protocol that a neutral state had followed throughout the war, but many Irish and Allied commentators criticised it.
In his victory broadcast of 13 May 1945 Churchill attacked Irish neutrality and referred to the ports.
De Valera replied on Radio Éireann on 16 May, saying that Churchill's speech had shown how a great power might justify infringing a small state's rights, and that Ireland had stood alone.
The broadcast was widely praised in Ireland and strengthened de Valera's reputation, though it did not improve relations with Britain.
The war closed Irish ports and imposed austerity, but opened the British labour market.
Tens of thousands of workers went to Britain each year to work in factories and construction, and sent money home.
The Irish economy suffered from shortages, and unemployment remained high for those who stayed.
Prices rose faster than wages, and the poor in Dublin and other towns suffered most.
The government used its emergency powers to maintain control of the press and labour, with little organised protest.
The Children's Allowances Act of 1944 and the creation of a separate Department of Health (1947) showed the first steps in post-war social policy.
Many Irish women and men served in the British forces, and the Irish government gave them little recognition after the war.
Judgements depend on whether the priority is sovereignty and survival or the moral and economic costs.
Achievement: the state avoided invasion and bombing on the scale of Belfast and kept its independence.
Achievement: neutrality was popular and strengthened national unity after the Civil War.
Limit: shortages, wage controls and censorship reduced living standards and freedom of expression.
Limit: the policy isolated Ireland from the Allies and left it without a voice at the end of the war.
Contemporary view: supporters called it a principled defence of independence; critics said it was selfish, as Churchill suggested.
Later view: historians such as Joe Lee and Brian Girvin stress the practical advantages of neutrality and its pro-Allied bias, but also question the moral cost.
As part of the United Kingdom, Northern Ireland was at war from 3 September 1939, in contrast to the neutral South, and unionists treated the war effort as proof of their loyalty.
Unionists contrasted Northern Ireland's loyalty with the South's neutrality, which strengthened the unionist case against a united Ireland.
Nationalists in the North were divided: some supported the war, many Catholics served in the forces, while others resented unionist rule.

Conscription was not applied to Northern Ireland, though Britain introduced it in 1939; in May 1941 Churchill's government considered extending it and dropped the idea after opposition from nationalists, the Catholic bishops and the Dublin government.
The IRA was active in Belfast: Tom Williams was hanged at Crumlin Road Gaol on 2 September 1942 for killing a policeman, and the case deepened nationalist resentment.
James Craig died on 24 November 1940, and John Miller Andrews succeeded him as Prime Minister.
Andrews was criticised for an elderly cabinet and slow response to the Blitz, and he resigned in April 1943; Basil Brooke took over and led until 1963.
Brooke, an energetic unionist, had been Minister of Commerce and Production and pushed war production and agriculture.
The war brought full employment to a region that had suffered mass unemployment since the 1920s.
Harland and Wolff built warships and merchant ships and repaired thousands of vessels for the Admiralty.
Short Brothers in Belfast built Stirling bombers and other aircraft.
Engineering firms made munitions, tanks parts and aircraft parts, and rope works and the linen mills made parachutes, tents and uniforms.
Farmers were ordered to plough more land and the region became an important food supplier to Britain.
Unemployment fell sharply as war contracts came in, and women entered factories in large numbers.
Wages rose, but industrial unrest occurred over pay and conditions in the shipyards and engineering works.
Belfast's linen, rope and engineering firms were all busy, and the city's population was swollen by workers moving in for war jobs.
The Northern Ireland government worked closely with the Ministry of Aircraft Production and the Admiralty in London.
The Northern government assumed that Belfast was too far from German airfields to be attacked, and its civil defence was weak.
Belfast was an obvious target because of the shipyard, the aircraft factory, the docks and the engineering works.
Before April 1941 the city had few public air-raid shelters, and many working-class houses had no shelter at all.
Anti-aircraft defences were small: the city had only a handful of heavy guns and no night-fighter cover.
A German reconnaissance flight over Belfast in November 1940 showed that the city was within reach, but the government did not accelerate preparations.
Fire services were small and under-equipped, and the authorities depended on outside help.
Overcrowded terraced housing near the docks and mills increased the risk of casualties and fire.
Four raids hit Belfast in spring 1941. The Easter Tuesday raid was the deadliest night of the Blitz in any British city outside London.
A smaller raid on the night of 7–8 April targeted the shipyard and killed about a dozen people.
The main raid took place on the night of 15–16 April 1941, Easter Tuesday, when around 180 German bombers attacked the city.
About 900 people were killed, and the working-class districts of north and east Belfast were worst hit.
The raid of 4–5 May 1941 was an incendiary attack on Harland and Wolff, Short Brothers and the docks; about 150 people were killed.
In all the Blitz killed about 1,000 people, and more than half of the city's houses were damaged.
Tens of thousands of people were left homeless, and in the days after the raids up to 100,000 people left the city each night to sleep in the countryside, known as ditchers.
After the raid of 15–16 April, fire brigades from Dublin, Dún Laoghaire, Dundalk and Drogheda crossed the border at de Valera's authorisation to help, a remarkable act of cross-border help.
Many bodies were laid out in public buildings such as the Falls Road baths, and some were buried in mass graves.
Many of the dead were in the streets around York Street and the Antrim Road, and the city mortuaries were overwhelmed.
The raids showed up the city's poverty and the weakness of its public services.
Children and mothers were evacuated to country areas, and many people took refuge in barns and church halls.
Host families in rural areas were shocked by the poor health, clothing and hygiene of some evacuees from the slums.
The condition of the children became a theme in debates on housing and public health, as it had in Britain in 1939.
The Unionist government was criticised for its slow response, and the Blitz contributed to the fall of Andrews in 1943.
Many evacuees drifted back to Belfast within weeks, and housing remained scarce for years.
Churches, schools and halls in towns such as Lisburn and Antrim took in refugees, and the authorities opened emergency rest centres.
From 1942 Northern Ireland became a staging area for the Allied build-up, and the American presence changed daily life.
The first American troops landed at Dufferin Quay, Belfast, on 26 January 1942.
By 1944 there were well over 100,000 American servicemen in Northern Ireland, in camps, airfields and ports.
They brought money, goods unavailable in rationed Britain and a new popular culture, including dances and cinema.
Black American soldiers served in segregated units, and many local people treated them with more welcome than the US authorities.
Northern Ireland's ports and airfields supported the Atlantic convoy escort and the preparation for D-Day.
The war raised expectations that the state should provide better housing, health and employment.
The Beveridge Report of 1942 shaped discussion of a post-war welfare state, and Northern Ireland followed British legislation after 1945 under the policy of parity.
The destruction of housing made housing an urgent political issue after the war.
In February 1943 Jack Beattie won a Belfast West by-election at Westminster against the Unionist candidate, a sign of working-class discontent.
Labour candidates made gains in 1945, but the Unionist Party held power at Stormont.
The Education Act (Northern Ireland) 1947 and Health Services Act of 1948 came out of the wartime reform climate.
Sectarian divisions remained, and the Unionist government made no changes to the electoral system or policing.
The war changed Belfast's economy and politics but not its religious division.
Unemployment, high in 1939, was low in 1945 because of war contracts.
Large areas of housing had been destroyed or damaged, and many families lived in temporary housing.
Industries such as shipbuilding and aircraft were running at full capacity, but depended on wartime orders.
The Unionist Party was still in control, though challenged by Labour and criticised for the failures of civil defence.
The links with Britain were stronger, because of wartime co-operation and the promise of welfare reform.
Catholic and Protestant communities remained separate, and the border and the division from the South were more entrenched.
Judgements depend on whether economic and social change or political continuity is stressed.
Achievement: war production ended mass unemployment and raised living standards for many workers.
Achievement: the war strengthened Northern Ireland's place in the United Kingdom and prepared it to take part in the welfare state.
Limit: the Blitz exposed poor preparation and housing, and the government had to answer for it.
Limit: the Unionist Party's control and the Catholic minority's exclusion were unchanged.
Contemporary view: unionists praised the contribution, and nationalists were critical of both the war role and the unionist government.
Later view: historians such as Brian Barton and Jonathan Bardon argue that the war was a turning point for the economy and social policy but not for politics.
The Free State made the revival of Irish a central aim of cultural policy and used schools and the civil service to achieve it.
Irish was made a compulsory subject in national schools in 1922, and many infant classes were taught wholly through Irish.
A pass in Irish became necessary for State examinations at second level and for entry to the civil service and the Garda, so that language knowledge was tied to jobs.
Ernest Blythe, Minister for Finance, was a strong advocate, and the civil service was required to learn Irish.
The Gaeltacht Commission was set up in 1925 and reported in 1926, defining the Irish-speaking districts and recommending economic and educational support.
An Gúm was founded in 1926 to publish books in Irish, including translations of foreign works, to supply school texts and readers.
Taibhdhearc na Gaillimhe, an Irish-language theatre, opened in Galway in 1928.
Preparatory colleges were set up to train teachers who could teach through Irish.
Irish was recognised as the first official language by the 1937 constitution.
The policy raised the number of people who could say they knew Irish, but few used it in daily life.
Census returns showed a rise in the share of the population able to speak Irish, from about 18 per cent in 1926 to about a quarter in 1936, mostly as a result of schooling.
The Gaeltacht, the real Irish-speaking districts, continued to shrink because of emigration and poverty.
Many parents and teachers resented the compulsion, and some pupils learned little.
Irish remained a symbol of national identity, and the state kept it as a school subject even where it failed as a spoken language.
The Church ran most schools, and the state accepted its role.
National schools were managed by clergy of the local denomination, and the state paid salaries and set the curriculum.
The School Attendance Act of 1926 made school attendance compulsory for children from 6 to 14.
Secondary schools were mostly fee-paying and run by religious orders, and few working-class children reached them.
The Vocational Education Act of 1930 set up vocational committees to provide technical education.
The Church influenced the content of teaching, and the 1937 constitution recognised the family and the Church's role.
The Catholic Archbishop of Dublin, John Charles McQuaid, from 1940 was an influential voice on social and educational issues.
Legislation reflected Catholic teaching on morality, and critics saw the result as an enforced conformity.
The Censorship of Films Act of 1923 set up a film censor who could cut or ban films.
In 1925 the Dáil changed its standing orders so that private bills for divorce could no longer be introduced; W.B. Yeats made a famous speech in the Seanad in defence of the Protestant minority.
The Censorship of Publications Act of 1929 set up a board with the power to ban books and periodicals considered indecent or immoral.
Among the writers banned were Samuel Beckett (More Pricks Than Kicks, 1934) and, later, Kate O'Brien and Seán Ó Faoláin.
The Public Dance Halls Act of 1935 required licences, in response to clerical concerns about dances.
The Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1935 banned the sale and import of contraceptives.
Article 41 of the 1937 constitution banned divorce, and Article 44 recognised the special position of the Catholic Church.
The Protestant population of the Free State fell in the 1920s and 1930s, partly through emigration, the Ne Temere rule on mixed marriages and Civil War violence.
The state promoted a national culture through games, theatre and broadcasting, and the GAA enforced a cultural boundary.
The Tailteann Games were held in Dublin in 1924, 1928 and 1932, a festival of sport and the arts modelled on the ancient games, and open to people of Irish descent abroad.
The Abbey Theatre received a state subsidy from 1925, the first for a national theatre in the English-speaking world.
The Gate Theatre was founded in 1928 by Hilton Edwards and Micheál Mac Liammóir to stage international plays.
The state radio station 2RN began broadcasting from Dublin on 1 January 1926, and a high-power transmitter at Athlone from 1932 was followed by the name Radio Éireann in 1938.
The Irish Folklore Commission was established in 1935 under Séamus Ó Duilearga, and the Schools' Collection of 1937–38 had children collect local folklore.
The GAA's Rule 27, in the rulebook from 1905, banned members from playing foreign games such as soccer and rugby, and was later extended to attending them; it was repealed in 1971.
In 1938 the GAA removed President Douglas Hyde as patron after he attended an international soccer match in Dublin.
Culture was linked to nationalism by the idea of a Gaelic and Catholic Ireland, which excluded many Protestants and urban people.
Education was contested between the Unionist government, which wanted a non-denominational state system, and the churches.
The Lynn Committee was appointed in 1921 to review education under the first Minister of Education, Lord Londonderry, and reported in 1923.

The Education Act (Northern Ireland) 1923, known as the Londonderry Act, created county education committees and placed schools under local education authorities, with public elementary schools to be free of church control.

Protestant churches objected to the exclusion of religious instruction, and the Act was amended in 1925 to allow Bible instruction, and the Orange Order and the Protestant clergy gained a voice in management.
The Catholic Church refused to transfer its schools to state control, and Catholic schools stayed outside the system with only partial public funding.

The 1930 Amendment Act allowed transferred Protestant schools to have four representatives of the transferors and two of the local authority on their committees, which Catholics saw as favouring Protestant interests.
The result was a divided school system, which remained a source of segregation and a grievance for Catholics.
Unionist and nationalist communities expressed separate identities in a state that favoured the first.
Orange Order parades on 12 July and loyalist bands were central to unionist culture and enjoyed official protection.
The Protestant ethos of the state was symbolised by the flag, the Union Jack, and by the royal visits and ceremonies at Stormont.
Nationalists supported the GAA, Irish-language classes and Catholic schools, but the Irish language received little state support.
Under the Special Powers Act the authorities could ban processions and republican emblems, and nationalist parades were more likely to be banned.
Craig's statement of 1934 that Northern Ireland was a Protestant state was matched in the South by the Catholic emphasis of the 1937 constitution.
Hone was a leading modernist painter who turned to stained glass and became the best-known Irish stained-glass artist of her time.
Evie Hone (1894–1955) was born in Dublin, and studied art in London and later in Paris under André Lhote and Albert Gleizes.
With Mainie Jellett she was one of the first Irish painters to work in a cubist style.
In the 1930s she turned to stained glass, learned from Wilhelmina Geddes, and worked with An Túr Gloine, the studio founded by Sarah Purser in 1903 to revive Irish stained glass.
She converted to Catholicism in 1937, and much of her work was for churches.
My Four Green Fields, a window symbolising the four provinces, was made for the Irish pavilion at the 1939 New York World's Fair and won first prize for stained glass.
The Crucifixion east window of Eton College Chapel was commissioned in 1949 to replace glass destroyed by a bomb in 1940, and was installed in 1952.
Contemporaries praised her work as a modern Irish art with international standing.
Historians such as Nicola Gordon Bowe place her in the movement to give Ireland a modern cultural identity after independence.
Cultural policy gave the new state a distinct identity, but it also narrowed the range of what was acceptable.
Achievement: institutions such as An Gúm, the Folklore Commission, the Abbey and Radio Éireann preserved and promoted Irish culture.
Limit: compulsory Irish did not make it the daily language of most people, and the Gaeltacht continued to decline.
Achievement: arts and crafts, including the work of Hone, flourished with state and church patronage.
Limit: censorship and moral legislation restricted writers and individual choice, and minorities felt excluded.
In the North the divided education system and separate cultural traditions deepened the communal division.
Contemporary view: supporters saw cultural policy as defending Irish identity; critics, including writers such as Ó Faoláin, saw a narrow and conformist vision.
Later view: historians stress the tension between revival and restriction, and the influence of the Church.
The Eucharistic Congress was an international Catholic gathering, held in Dublin in 1932 to mark an anniversary that tied Catholicism to Irish identity.

An International Eucharistic Congress is a gathering of Catholics from many countries to honour the Eucharist, the sacrament in which Catholics believe bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ; the first was held in 1881 and each is held in a different city.
The 31st Congress was awarded to Dublin, and 1932 was chosen as the 1,500th anniversary of the traditional date of St Patrick's arrival in Ireland in 432.
The invitation and the early planning were made while Cosgrave's government was in office, and the Church and the state treated the event as a national occasion.
Archbishop Edward Byrne of Dublin headed the organising effort, and the Pope sent a legate, Cardinal Lorenzo Lauri.
The Congress was an opportunity for the new state to show itself to the world, ten years after independence and a civil war.
The Catholic Church had a strong position in Irish life: the vast majority of the population was Catholic, and clergy managed schools and hospitals.
The Congress was planned under Cosgrave, but it took place under de Valera, who had come to power in March 1932.
Fianna Fáil won the February 1932 election and de Valera became head of government on 9 March 1932, three months before the Congress.
De Valera, who was known for his personal piety, took a leading part and his government gave the planning full support.
Dublin was prepared with altars, decorations, flags and illuminations, and the streets of poorer districts were decorated too.
A large altar was built in the Phoenix Park for the final Mass, and the arrangements for transport, accommodation and crowd control were extensive.
A radio station was set up at Athlone to coincide with the Congress, so that the ceremonies and the Pope's message could reach listeners around the country.
Visitors came from the United States, Britain and Europe, and thousands of pilgrims came from Northern Ireland.
A national committee raised money by public subscription, and parishes organised local groups for the processions.
Thousands of volunteers acted as stewards, and special first-aid and catering services were arranged for the Phoenix Park.
The Congress showed close co-operation between the Catholic hierarchy and the new Fianna Fáil government, and it exposed the unresolved question of the Crown's representative.
De Valera and Archbishop Byrne received Cardinal Lauri at Dún Laoghaire on his arrival on 21 June 1932, and he was escorted through crowds to Dublin.
