Some 36,000 schoolchildren lined the route from Dún Laoghaire to the Pro-Cathedral.

The Governor-General, James McNeill, representing the Crown, was not invited to the reception for the legate at Dublin Castle, and press reports say that Fianna Fáil ministers would have walked out if he had attended.
McNeill responded by holding a dinner to which de Valera and the ministers were not invited, and wrote to de Valera on 7 July 1932 complaining of discourtesy.
The affair was part of the conflict that led to McNeill's dismissal in October 1932.
De Valera used the occasion to present his government as both Catholic and independent of the Crown.
Five days of Masses, processions and services culminated in an open-air Mass in the Phoenix Park and a procession to O'Connell Bridge.
The Congress ran from 22 to 26 June 1932 and opened at the Pro-Cathedral in Dublin.
On 25 June a children's Mass was held in the Phoenix Park, attended by around 100,000 children.

On Sunday 26 June the closing Mass was celebrated at an altar in the Phoenix Park before a crowd often put at around a million, though the estimate may be exaggerated; it is described as about a quarter of the population of the state.
John McCormack, the famous Irish tenor, sang César Franck's Panis Angelicus at the Mass.
A message from Pope Pius XI was broadcast live by radio from the Vatican to the crowd.
After the Mass four processions went from the park to O'Connell Bridge, where Cardinal Lauri gave the closing benediction to a crowd of up to half a million people.
The legate's party left, and the Congress ended on 26 June with large crowds along the quays.
Ceremonies during the week included Masses in city churches and a procession of the Blessed Sacrament.
Cardinal Lauri addressed the crowds and the Pope's blessing was conveyed to the people of Ireland.
The closing Mass began at 1 pm on 26 June at an altar designed by the architect John J. Robinson, and the celebrant was Archbishop Michael Curley of Baltimore.
Cardinal Lauri, who had been made a cardinal in 1926, presided as the Pope's representative throughout.
The size of the event tested the state's administration and brought international attention.
Special trains, buses and sailings brought crowds from all over Ireland and abroad, and the Garda and the Army managed the crowds.
The use of loudspeakers allowed huge crowds to hear the ceremonies, and radio carried the broadcast to the country.
Foreign newspapers reported the event, and it gave the Free State international publicity as a Catholic country.
The event was a success for de Valera, whose prestige grew at home and abroad.
The Congress passed off without major disorder in the Free State, which was a strong demonstration of public order only ten years after the Civil War.
Archbishop Byrne and the organising committee had to coordinate bishops from around the world, and papal flags and Irish flags were flown together.
The Athlone station that began broadcasting for the Congress later became Radio Éireann, in 1938.
Reports at the time and since claimed that the crowds exceeded those at Pope John Paul II's Phoenix Park Mass in 1979.
In the North the Congress was seen very differently, and it highlighted the religious divide on the island.

Catholic pilgrims travelling by train and bus to and from Dublin were attacked in Northern Ireland; trains were stoned at places such as Portadown, Lisburn and Belfast, and at Ballymena a special train was attacked and some pilgrims were injured.
Police made baton charges at some stations to protect pilgrims.
Unionists saw the Congress as proof that the Free State was a Catholic state, which reinforced their view that partition was necessary.
Protestant newspapers and Orange leaders criticised the scale of Catholic display, and the attacks on pilgrims added to sectarian tension.
For Northern nationalists, the Congress was a source of pride and reinforced their sense of belonging to an Irish Catholic nation.
The Congress is usually assessed through three themes: relations between Church and state, Catholic identity, and Ireland's image abroad.
Church and state: it showed the alliance between the hierarchy and the political leadership which shaped the 1937 constitution and social legislation.
Catholic identity: it presented Ireland as a Catholic nation, in line with the Gaelic and Catholic ideal of the 1930s.
International image: it presented the Free State as stable, devout and independent, and made de Valera well known abroad.
Sovereignty: the Governor-General dispute showed the government's desire to downgrade the Crown's representative.
Unionist view: it confirmed fears of a state dominated by the Catholic Church.
Contemporary view: the Catholic press and most of the public regarded it as a great national triumph.

Later view: historians describe it as the high point of the Church's public influence, and a sign of the conformity that marked the 1930s; some stress the Congress as a political success for de Valera.
De Valera's critics in Cumann na nGaedheal noted that the Congress had been planned by Cosgrave's government but that Fianna Fáil gained the credit.
The Congress also gave de Valera's new government a chance to show it could work with the Church.
The Congress is often compared with the 1979 papal visit as the largest religious gathering in Irish history.
The Congress was a great public success, but its effect was largely symbolic.
Achievement: it showed the state could organise a major international event soon after the Civil War.
Achievement: it united people across party lines at a time of political change.
Limit: it did not change any laws or institutions, and its influence was cultural and political.
Limit: it deepened the distrust between North and South, and Catholic and Protestant, on the island.
Contemporary view: a triumph for the Church and the nation.
Later view: a moment when church, state and nation appeared identical, which later generations judged more critically.
Emigration was already an established feature of Irish life before 1845, but it changed in who left and where they went.
Ulster Presbyterians were the first large group of Irish emigrants to North America, sailing to the American colonies through the 18th century.
After 1815 the flow widened: about one million people left Ireland between 1815 and 1845, with estimates ranging up to 1.5 million.
Pre-Famine emigrants were often Protestant small farmers, weavers and tradesmen from Ulster and the midlands who could pay their own fares and had some capital.
From the 1830s Catholic emigrants from the south and west made up a growing share, and they were poorer and less skilled than earlier emigrants.
British North America (Canada) was the main transatlantic destination before 1845 because fares there were the cheapest, and many emigrants then walked or sailed on into the United States.
Britain received the largest number of the poorest emigrants, because the crossing to Liverpool or Glasgow cost only a few shillings.
The 1841 census counted about 420,000 Irish-born people in Britain, concentrated in Liverpool, Glasgow, Manchester and London.

Seasonal migration: tens of thousands of labourers from Mayo, Donegal, Galway and other western counties crossed each summer to work on English and Scottish harvests and returned home with cash to pay the rent.
Irish labourers in Britain worked as navvies on canals and railways, as dockers, as building labourers and in textile mills.
Irish districts grew in the poorest parts of British cities, such as Little Ireland in Manchester and St Giles in London.
In North America Irish men dug canals such as the Erie Canal (opened 1825) and built roads and early railways, while Irish women went into domestic service.

Push factors: subdivision of holdings into tiny plots, a population that had risen to about 8.2 million by 1841, dependence on the potato, the decline of domestic linen and wool spinning, and evictions for rent arrears.
Pull factors: higher wages and demand for labour in industrial Britain and North America, cheap land in Canada, and letters from earlier emigrants describing work abroad.
Timber ships carried Canadian timber to Britain and Ireland and returned westwards nearly empty, so they took emigrants cheaply as human ballast.
Repeated failures of the potato turned a steady flow into a mass exodus.
Potato blight, caused by the water mould Phytophthora infestans, destroyed about a third of the crop in 1845 and almost all of it in 1846.
The 1847 crop was largely free of blight but very small because little seed had been planted, and blight returned in 1848; 1847 is remembered as Black 47 for its deaths and fever.
About one million people died of starvation and famine-related disease between 1845 and 1851; estimates vary.
Between 1.5 and 2 million people emigrated between 1845 and 1855 (estimates vary), the great majority to the United States, with several hundred thousand to British North America and to Britain.
The census showed Ireland's population falling from about 8.2 million in 1841 to about 6.5 million in 1851.

Famine emigrants were mostly Catholic, poor, unskilled and Irish-speaking in many cases, and came heavily from the west and south-west; many travelled as whole families rather than as single young adults.
Emigration was panic flight rather than planned movement: in 1847 about 300,000 destitute Irish people landed at Liverpool alone, and many stayed there.
By 1851 the number of Irish-born in Britain had risen to about 730,000, and about a fifth of Liverpool's population was Irish-born.
Public works were the main relief in 1846, but the pay was low and late and heavy labour weakened starving workers.
The Temporary Relief Act of 1847 replaced the public works with soup kitchens, which fed about 3 million people a day at their peak in the summer of 1847 before closing that autumn.

The Poor Law Extension Act of June 1847 made the Poor Law unions pay for relief, and its Gregory clause (quarter-acre clause) denied relief to anyone holding more than a quarter acre unless they gave up the land.
Rising poor rates gave landlords a reason to clear smallholders, and evictions rose sharply between 1847 and 1852.
Assisted emigration: some landlords paid passages because shipping tenants abroad was cheaper than paying rates to support them in the workhouse.

Major Denis Mahon of Strokestown, Co. Roscommon, sent 1,490 tenants via Liverpool to Quebec in 1847; hundreds died on the crossing or soon after at Grosse Isle, and Mahon was shot dead on 2 November 1847.

Lord Palmerston sent about 2,000 tenants from his Sligo estate to Canada in 1847, and many arrived destitute; Lord Lansdowne paid passages for several thousand tenants from Kenmare, Co. Kerry, in the early 1850s.
The Earl Grey scheme (1848–1850) shipped about 4,000 orphan girls from Irish workhouses to Australia as domestic servants.
The Encumbered Estates Act of 1849 allowed bankrupt estates to be sold, and many new owners cleared tenants to consolidate farms.
Pre-paid passages: relatives already abroad bought tickets from shipping agents in America and posted them home, so people with no money could still leave.
Much Famine emigration was funded this way rather than by landlords or the state; assisted emigration paid for only a small minority of those who left.
Chain-emigration: the first member of a family to settle abroad sent money and tickets for the next, who in turn paid for others, so whole families and parishes moved in stages.
Emigrants from the same district tended to settle in the same streets and parishes abroad, where kin found them lodgings and work.
Letters home described wages, prices and fares and were read aloud in villages, spreading information about where to go.
Most transatlantic emigrants first crossed to Liverpool, which had the most frequent sailings; others sailed direct from Cork harbour, Dublin, Limerick, Sligo, Derry, Galway and smaller ports.
Fares to Quebec were cheaper than to New York, so the poorest emigrants went to British North America.
The US Passenger Acts of 1847 limited the number of passengers per ship and raised fares on the US route, diverting more of the poorest and sickest emigrants to Canada.
Steerage passengers were crammed into the lower decks of sailing ships for a voyage of six weeks or more, with poor ventilation, little water and food often below what the law required.
Typhus (ship fever), spread by lice, and dysentery killed thousands at sea; ships with high death rates became known as coffin ships.
Of about 100,000 people who sailed for British North America in 1847, an estimated 17,000 or more died at sea, in quarantine or soon after arrival.
Ports of arrival included New York, Boston, Philadelphia, Quebec and Saint John, where fever sheds and quarantine stations were set up.
Grosse Isle (Grosse Île) was the quarantine station for the port of Quebec and the first North American landfall for tens of thousands of Famine emigrants.
Grosse Isle is an island in the St Lawrence River about 48 km downstream from Quebec City.
The quarantine station was opened in 1832 to stop cholera reaching Quebec from emigrant ships.
Every ship bound for Quebec had to stop there; a medical officer inspected passengers, and the sick were landed at the hospital while the healthy were held in sheds or on board.
The medical superintendent was Dr George Mellis Douglas, who had been its medical superintendent since 1836.
The station was built for the normal flow of a season, and its hospital sheds held only a few hundred patients when the 1847 emigration began.
The first ship of the season, the Syria, arrived in mid-May 1847 with fever on board, and the hospital was full within days.
By 31 May 1847 about 40 ships carrying some 12,500 passengers lay at anchor off the island, in a queue stretching down the river.
Ships waited days or weeks for inspection, and the sick and dead lay in the holds alongside the healthy, so fever spread among people who had been well.
Tents and new sheds were put up, but sick and dying people lay on the ground and on the beaches; healthy passengers were crowded into sheds where many caught typhus.
Dr Douglas warned the authorities in advance and asked for more help, and his reports are a major source on the season; several doctors on the island caught typhus and some died.
Catholic priests from the diocese of Quebec, many of them French-Canadian, and Anglican clergy took turns on the island; several caught typhus and some died.
More than 5,000 people were buried on the island in 1847, most of them Irish; some estimates of the deaths on the island are higher.

Passengers passed as healthy carried typhus up the river: about 6,000 Irish emigrants died in the fever sheds at Montreal in 1847, and Montreal's mayor John Mills died of typhus while helping the sick.
Hundreds of children orphaned at Grosse Isle and in the fever sheds were adopted by French-Canadian families, many of whom let them keep their Irish surnames.
Partridge Island, the quarantine station at Saint John, New Brunswick, faced a similar fever crisis in 1847 with ships from Ireland and Liverpool.

New York received far more Famine emigrants than Quebec, but the poorest and sickest were more often diverted to Canada by the dearer US fares; New York's emigration commissioners opened the Castle Garden landing depot in 1855 to protect arriving emigrants.
The medical staff erected a monument on the island in 1853 to the dead of 1847.

The Ancient Order of Hibernians erected a large Celtic cross on the island's highest point, unveiled on 15 August 1909, with inscriptions in Irish, English and French; the Irish text blames the Famine on British rule more bluntly than the English text.

The quarantine station closed in 1937, and the island became a Canadian national historic site; after Irish-Canadian campaigning it became, in the 1990s, Grosse Île and the Irish Memorial National Historic Site.

Nationalists from John Mitchel onwards used Grosse Isle as evidence that British policy, not only the blight, killed the Irish poor; others stressed landlord clearances and the limits of colonial resources.
Grosse Isle shows the human cost of unregulated mass emigration, the failure of governments on both sides of the Atlantic to prepare, and the generosity of French-Canadian Quebec.
Relief versus loss: emigration saved hundreds of thousands from starvation, but it emptied the poorest districts and began a century of population decline.
Choice versus force: pre-paid tickets show emigrants making their own family decisions, while clearances and assisted schemes such as Mahon's show tenants being pushed out.
Contemporary view: officials, landlords and many economists welcomed emigration as a cure for overpopulation; John Mitchel and the Young Irelanders saw it as extermination.
Later view: Kerby Miller (Emigrants and Exiles, 1985) argued that emigrants saw themselves as exiles banished by England, a view that shaped Irish-American nationalism.

Revisionist historians of the 1950s to 1970s played down British blame, while Cormac Ó Gráda, Christine Kinealy and others since the 1990s have stressed failures of relief policy alongside the natural disaster.
Grosse Isle has become the leading memorial to the Famine dead outside Ireland, though the great majority of Famine emigrants went to the United States and Britain.
After the Famine emigration did not stop; it became a settled part of Irish rural life, with a steady outflow in good years and bad.
About 4 million people left Ireland in the six decades after the Famine (estimates vary), and the population of the whole island fell from about 6.5 million in 1851 to about 4.4 million in 1911.
The United States took about four out of five emigrants; Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand took most of the rest.
The number of Irish-born people in the United States peaked at about 1.87 million in the census of 1890.
Emigrants were mostly young and single, aged roughly 15 to 30, and Ireland was unusual in Europe in sending about as many women as men; in some decades women outnumbered men.
Emigration was heaviest from the west and south-west, and the poorest counties of the west sent the highest proportion of their people.
After the Famine farms were no longer subdivided: one son inherited the holding (impartible inheritance) and one daughter received a dowry, so the other children had to emigrate or stay unmarried.
Late marriage, the shift from tillage to cattle grazing, and the lack of industry outside the north-east pushed young people out.
Agricultural depression and evictions around 1879 to 1882 caused a fresh surge, especially from the west; the Land War was partly a response to the insecurity that fed it.
The crossing and the farewell both changed in this period.
The American wake was a farewell gathering with music, dancing, food and drink as well as tears, held on the night before an emigrant left, because most emigrants never came back.
Steamships replaced sail from the 1860s, cutting the Atlantic crossing from about six weeks to about two weeks by the 1870s and making the voyage far safer.
Liners called at Queenstown (Cobh) and at Moville near Derry to pick up emigrants travelling steerage.
In New York emigrants landed at Castle Garden from 1855 and at Ellis Island from 1892; the first person processed at Ellis Island, on 1 January 1892, was Annie Moore from Cork.

Colonial governments in Australia and New Zealand paid or subsidised passages to attract settlers, so Irish emigration there was largely assisted, while emigration to America was paid for privately, often with money sent from relatives.
In the USA the Irish settled overwhelmingly in cities of the north-east and Midwest: New York, Boston, Philadelphia, Chicago and the mill and mining towns of New England and Pennsylvania.
Irish men mostly began as unskilled labourers on docks, railways, canals and building sites and in mines and factories, and many moved up into skilled trades, police forces and fire departments.
Irish women dominated domestic service in cities such as New York and Boston; the job gave board, lodging and wages that could be saved and sent home.
Irish Americans moved into city politics through the Democratic Party, and by 1900 the second generation was entering teaching, clerical work and the professions.
In Britain the Irish settled in Liverpool, Glasgow, London, Manchester and the industrial towns of Lancashire and west-central Scotland, working on the docks, in building, in mills and in mines.
Irish nurses, teachers and domestic servants were prominent among women emigrants to Britain, and Irish harvest labourers continued to cross seasonally.
In Australia Irish-born people and their descendants made up roughly a quarter of the European population, settling as farmers, labourers and gold-miners in New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland.
Emigrants also went to Canada, where many Protestants settled in Ontario, and to New Zealand, and some went to Argentina.
Emigrants' remittances: money and pre-paid tickets sent home by emigrants, amounting to well over a million pounds a year in the later 19th century.
Much of the money came from servant girls and labourers, who sent home a large share of their wages.
Remittances paid for the passages of younger brothers and sisters, so one emigrant could bring out a whole family over a few years.
Remittances also paid rent, shop debts and dowries and helped families keep their holdings, which made emigration a support for the rural economy as well as a drain on it.
The American letter, often containing dollars, was a regular event in western households, and it kept relatives informed of jobs and wages abroad.
Chain-emigration meant that new arrivals stayed with kin, found work through them, and settled in the same parishes, so emigrant communities reproduced the networks of home.
Letters collected by historians such as David Fitzpatrick (Oceans of Consolation, 1994, on the Irish in Australia) show how strongly emigrants kept family ties.
The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 limited immigrants of each nationality to 3 per cent of that nationality's foreign-born population in the 1910 US census.

The Immigration Act of 1924 (Johnson-Reed Act) set quotas at 2 per cent of each foreign-born group in the 1890 census, a base chosen to favour north-western Europeans over southern and eastern Europeans.
The Irish Free State received a quota of 28,567 a year under the 1924 Act, cut to 17,853 from 1929 when the national-origins formula took effect; Northern Ireland came under the British quota.
The quotas redirected rather than ended emigration: emigration to the USA fell sharply from the 1920s, and Britain became the main destination.
The Great Depression after 1929 cut American demand for labour and reduced Irish emigration to the USA still further, and some emigrants returned.
Britain was easy to enter, jobs were close and the fare was low, and the Irish moved to Britain in large numbers in the 1930s.
The Free State governments did not try to restrict emigration, which they treated as an economic problem they could not quickly solve.
During the Emergency (1939 to 1945) Irish people needed travel permits and identity documents to go to Britain, and both governments controlled who could travel.

Britain recruited Irish workers for war factories, building and farm work, and well over 100,000 people from the Irish state went to work in Britain during the war; tens of thousands more joined the British forces.

The Ireland Act of 1949 confirmed that Irish citizens in the United Kingdom were not treated as aliens and could live, work and vote there freely, and the Common Travel Area allowed free movement between the two islands.
Irish people were also exempted from the controls of the Commonwealth Immigrants Act of 1962.

Post-war reconstruction created huge demand for labour in Britain: Irish men worked as navvies on roads, building sites and power stations, while Irish women trained as nurses in the new National Health Service (1948) or worked in factories and offices.
The Irish in Britain clustered in London (Kilburn, Camden Town, Cricklewood), Birmingham, Coventry, Luton, Manchester and Liverpool.

The US Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 abolished the national-origins quotas from 1968 and favoured family ties and skills, which made it harder for Irish people without American relatives to enter.
The government set up the Commission on Emigration and Other Population Problems in 1948, and it reported in 1954.

The Commission found that emigration was caused mainly by economic factors such as low incomes, unemployment and small farms, but also by the attractions of better living standards and a livelier social life abroad.
It accepted that emigration could not be ended quickly and urged economic development and improved rural conditions rather than any ban on leaving.
Emigration peaked in the 1950s: about 400,000 people left the state between 1951 and 1961 (net), most of them for Britain.
The 1961 census recorded the lowest population in the history of the state, about 2.8 million.
The Vanishing Irish (1953), a collection of essays edited by the American priest John A. O'Brien, warned that the Irish nation was dying out through emigration and late marriage.

Economic Development (1958), drawn up by T.K. Whitaker, and the First Programme for Economic Expansion, pursued by Seán Lemass as Taoiseach from 1959, brought growth that cut emigration sharply in the 1960s.
Many young emigrants arrived in Britain with no training and lived in lodging houses or navvy camps where hard drinking and long hours were common.
Navvy work was often arranged through subcontractors who paid cash in hand, leaving workers without insurance or job security.
Notices reading No Irish are widely remembered from lodging-house windows in the 1950s and 1960s, though historians disagree about how common they were.
Catholic chaplaincies, the Legion of Mary and Irish centres in London and other cities helped new arrivals find lodgings and work.
Irish dance halls such as the Galtymore in Cricklewood and the Gresham on the Holloway Road became centres of emigrant social life.

Assimilation in the USA was helped by the English language, the Democratic Party, the Catholic parish and its schools, and the size of the Irish community; by 1914 the second generation increasingly thought of itself as American.

In Britain the Irish were also English-speaking but remained a visible Catholic working-class minority, and Catholic schools and parishes helped to keep a distinct identity; Irish-born people could return home easily, so many saw their stay as temporary.
Enda Delaney (The Irish in Post-War Britain, 2007) argued that Irish emigrants to Britain kept strong ties with home while integrating into British working life.
Irish-speaking emigrants from the Gaeltacht tended to lose the language within a generation abroad.
Domhnall (Dónall) Mac Amhlaigh (1926–1989) was an Irish-language writer whose diary of navvy life is the best-known first-hand account of 1950s emigration to Britain.
Born in Galway in 1926 and raised in Co. Kilkenny, he was a native of the west who wrote in Irish.
Facing poor prospects at home he went to England in 1951 and worked as a labourer on building sites and roads, based in Northampton.
His diary of 1951 to 1957, Dialann Deoraí (An Exile's Diary), was published in 1960; Valentin Iremonger translated it as An Irish Navvy: The Diary of an Exile (1964).
It describes the work, the lodgings, the pubs and dance halls, homesickness, the company of other Irish navvies and the mixture of welcome and prejudice the Irish met in England.
He was a participant, not an observer: he lived the life he described and stayed in England for the rest of his life, dying in Northampton in 1989.
He also wrote novels and short stories in Irish, including Schnitzer Ó Sé (1974), and journalism.
Contemporaries in Ireland valued the diary as a frank picture of a life that official Ireland preferred not to discuss.

Historians now treat it as a key source on the Irish in post-war Britain, showing a generation that worked, socialised and kept its identity in an Irish world inside English cities; as a single author's account it cannot stand for every emigrant's experience.
Safety valve versus drain: emigration relieved rural poverty and unemployment and brought in remittances, but it took the young and kept the population falling until 1961.
Opportunity versus exile: many emigrants gained better wages and lives, while others, as Mac Amhlaigh shows, felt themselves exiles doing the hardest work.
US restriction redirected rather than stopped emigration: Britain's open door absorbed the flow after the 1930s.
Contemporary view: churchmen and politicians spoke of the vanishing Irish and blamed modern attractions as well as poverty; the Commission of 1954 placed the cause in economic weakness.

Later view: Kerby Miller stressed exile and banishment, while historians such as Enda Delaney see emigration to Britain as a choice by individuals within family strategies, not simply as forced exile.
Hostility to the Irish rested on religion, poverty and competition for work, and it was reinforced by stereotypes that were widely printed.
Religion: most Irish emigrants were Catholic, and Protestant Americans and Britons often saw Catholicism as foreign and a threat to their institutions, with the Pope as a rival authority.
Poverty and disease: the Irish who arrived in the Famine years were poor, crowded into slums, and outbreaks of cholera and typhus were blamed on them.
Crime and drink: Irish migrants were blamed for crime, drunkenness and disorder in the cities where they lived, and they were over-represented in arrest figures.
Competition for work: Irish labourers and servants competed with native-born and other workers, and willingness to accept low wages created resentment, including strike-breaking tensions.
Racial stereotypes: the Irish were portrayed as a separate and inferior race, and in cartoons they were often drawn with apelike features.
Political fear: Protestants feared that Catholic voters would take orders from their priests and that Irish nationalists would involve the host country in Irish quarrels.
American nativism, the movement against immigrants and Catholic influence, reached its height in the 1840s and 1850s and continued in cartoons and job notices afterwards.
The Philadelphia riots of 1844 were anti-Catholic disturbances in which Irish Catholic churches and homes were attacked by nativist mobs after a dispute about the use of the Bible in schools.
Nativism grew into a political movement, and the Know-Nothings, formally the American Party, won major state victories in 1854, including Massachusetts.
The Know-Nothings took their name from the secrecy of their members, who were told to say they knew nothing when questioned about the movement.
The Know-Nothings wanted longer waiting periods before immigrants could become citizens and voters, and to bar Catholics from public office; the movement broke up before the Civil War over slavery.

Job advertisements and signs in the 19th century are said to have stated No Irish Need Apply; historians such as Richard Jensen have argued that written signs were rarer than later memory suggests, while Rebecca Fried's research found real examples, so the extent is debated.
Thomas Nast's cartoons in Harper's Weekly in the 1870s portrayed Irish Catholics, and especially Irish politicians, as ape-like and corrupt.
Irish Americans responded by building their own parishes, schools, newspapers and societies, and by using the vote.
In Britain anti-Irish feeling was mixed with sectarian rivalry, and it flared at moments of Fenian threat.
Punch magazine caricatured the Irish in the 1840s and 1860s, presenting them as simian, violent and backward.
The Stockport riots of 1852 saw Irish Catholic homes and churches attacked in Stockport after a Catholic procession in the town.
The Murphy riots of 1867 followed the anti-Catholic lectures of William Murphy and brought attacks on Irish districts in towns such as Birkenhead and Wolverhampton.
In Liverpool and Glasgow, Protestant Orange lodges and Catholic Irish communities clashed, and sectarian rivalry shaped local politics and street life.

After the Manchester Martyrs were executed in November 1867 and the Fenian bomb at Clerkenwell prison in London that December killed about a dozen people, fears grew that all Irish people in Britain were a security threat.
Fenian scares led to heavy policing of Irish districts, and Irish nationalists claimed that the state treated the whole community as suspect.
Writers blamed the Irish for typhus, low wages and crime in industrial towns, and the Victorian press often presented them as a separate race.
Irish Americans turned their numbers into political power through the Democratic Party and the city machines.
Most Irish Americans voted Democratic, because the party defended immigrants against nativist attacks and offered jobs and help.
Ward politics: local party organisers in each ward gave immigrants jobs, housing and legal help in return for votes.
Tammany Hall, the Democratic organisation in New York City, controlled city politics through patronage, jobs and contracts; it was led by Irish bosses from 1872, beginning with John Kelly.
William R. Grace, born in Ireland, became the first Irish Catholic mayor of New York in 1880, and Hugh O'Brien became the first Irish Catholic mayor of Boston in 1885.
John F. Fitzgerald (Honey Fitz) and later James Michael Curley dominated Boston politics in the early 20th century.
Al Smith, a New York Catholic of Irish descent, became governor of New York and the Democratic presidential candidate in 1928.
Irish men were prominent in urban police forces and fire companies, and these jobs were a route into local politics.
Irish-American political success was built on group loyalty, and it gave immigrant communities a voice in city government.
Richard Croker turned Tammany Hall into the most powerful political machine in New York City.
Richard Croker was born in Co. Cork in 1843 and was taken to New York as a child, where he grew up in a poor Irish district.
He rose through the Fourth Avenue gang, the fire companies and the local Democratic clubs, and he held minor city offices such as alderman and coroner.
He became the leader of Tammany Hall in the mid-1880s and ran it until 1902, using patronage, jobs in city departments and contracts to build support among immigrants and the poor.
He controlled Democratic nominations and placed his allies in office, including Mayor Robert Van Wyck (1898 to 1901).
Investigations by the Lexow Committee (1894) into police corruption and the Mazet Committee (1899) exposed the system, and he left the leadership after Tammany lost the mayoral election of 1901.
He retired to Ireland, where he lived at Glencairn near Dublin and bred racehorses; his horse Orby won the Epsom Derby in 1907.
Contemporary reformers and much of the respectable press condemned Croker's corruption, while many Tammany voters regarded him as a friend of the poor.

Historians now present him as the clearest example of machine politics, in which immigrant political success came with corruption, though they also see his career as a route of upward mobility for an immigrant.
Joseph P. Kennedy showed how an Irish-American could rise to the top of business and then government, and his career was marked by controversy.
Joseph P. Kennedy was born in Boston in 1888, the son of Patrick J. Kennedy, a Boston politician and businessman, and he married Rose Fitzgerald, daughter of Mayor John F. Fitzgerald.
He built a fortune in banking, the stock market and the film industry before entering government.
He was the first chairman of the US Securities and Exchange Commission, from 1934, set up to regulate the stock market after the crash of 1929.
In 1937 he led the US Maritime Commission, and in 1938 President Roosevelt appointed him ambassador to Britain, the first Irish Catholic to hold the post.

As ambassador from 1938 to 1940 he supported Neville Chamberlain's policy of appeasement and doubted that Britain could win a war with Germany, and he resigned in late 1940 after an interview that was widely seen as defeatist about Britain.
Contemporary Irish-American opinion was divided: some were proud of his success, while others distrusted his conservative views and his closeness to the British government.
Historians judge him a self-made businessman and an appeaser whose pessimism damaged his career, and whose ambitions shaped his sons, including John F. Kennedy (see the notes on John F. Kennedy).
Paul O'Dwyer combined a career as a New York lawyer with campaigns for civil rights and for Irish causes.
Paul O'Dwyer was born in Bohola, Co. Mayo, in 1907 and emigrated to New York in 1925, becoming a lawyer there in the 1930s; he was the brother of William O'Dwyer, mayor of New York from 1946 to 1950.
He defended trade unionists and took on civil rights cases and causes for working people and immigrants, and supported the civil rights movement.
He was a Democratic politician who ran unsuccessfully for the US Senate in 1968 as an opponent of the Vietnam War and later served as president of the New York City Council in the mid-1970s.
He was active in Irish causes, and in later decades he supported civil rights for Catholics in Northern Ireland and criticised British policy there.
Contemporaries saw him as a liberal and a critic of the establishment, and some criticised his views on Northern Ireland as too sympathetic to the republican cause.
Historians place him in the tradition of liberal Irish-American politics, in which civil rights and Irish nationalism were linked.
The Irish vote in British cities was strongest in Liverpool and Scotland, and it was used by nationalist and Labour politicians.
The Irish National League of Great Britain, founded in 1883, organised Irish voters behind the Irish Parliamentary Party.
In the general election of 1885 Parnell told Irish voters in Britain to vote against the Liberals, and they voted Conservative.
T. P. O'Connor was elected MP for Liverpool Scotland in 1885, and he held the seat until 1929 as a nationalist and a journalist.
O'Connor founded newspapers in London, including The Star, and he used the press to support Home Rule and Irish causes.
After Gladstone's first Home Rule Bill in 1886 Irish voters in Liverpool and Glasgow largely supported the Liberal Party as the party of Home Rule.
From the early 20th century Irish voters in Britain increasingly backed the Labour Party, which also drew support from the working class.
Irish-born men could vote and stand for Parliament as British subjects, so their political participation was easier than in the USA, where naturalisation was needed.
The Molly Maguires were a secret society among Irish miners in the Pennsylvania anthracite coalfields, whose conflict with mine owners ended in executions.

The society operated in the anthracite coalfields of eastern Pennsylvania, especially in Schuylkill County, in the 1860s and 1870s, and drew on the tradition of the Ribbonmen and the name of an Irish agrarian secret society.
Irish miners worked in dangerous conditions for low pay, and many members belonged to the Ancient Order of Hibernians.
Violence against mine bosses and police was blamed on the Mollies, who were accused of murders and arson.
The owner of the Reading Railroad, Franklin B. Gowen, hired the Pinkerton detective James McParland, who infiltrated the society under the name James McKenna.
After the failed Long Strike of 1875 the miners' union was broken, and the trials took place in 1876 to 1878, with convictions depending heavily on the evidence of informers and of McParland.
Twenty men were hanged between 1877 and 1879; ten were hanged on a single day, 21 June 1877, known as the Day of the Rope, and the leader Jack Kehoe was hanged in 1878.

Labour historians see the Mollies as victims of an employer-backed frame-up, while others see a real secret society using violence; Kevin Kenny (Making Sense of the Molly Maguires, 1998) argued that they were a genuine society, rooted in Irish agrarian violence, but that the trials were unfair.
Jack Kehoe was pardoned after his death, by the Governor of Pennsylvania in 1979.
Judgements on Irish political life in America and Britain turn on whether the Irish gained real influence despite discrimination, or only built machines and patronage.
Achievement: Irish politicians built lasting power in American cities and in some British seats, and they gave immigrants a route into public life.
Limit: machine politics relied on patronage and corruption, and reform movements challenged it from the 1880s onwards.
Success against discrimination: by the early 20th century Irish Americans were prominent in the police and city government, a sign that discrimination was being overcome.
Contemporary view: nativists and reformers condemned Irish politicians as corrupt, while Irish communities defended them as champions of immigrants.
Later view: historians disagree on whether Irish political success advanced assimilation or delayed it, because machine politics kept communities separate.
Britain versus the USA: the Irish in Britain had votes sooner, but their political voice was channelled into the Irish Parliamentary Party and Labour rather than into city machines.
Irish nationalism became an international force through emigrant organisations in the United States, Canada and Britain, which raised money and planned rebellion.
The Irish Republican Brotherhood was founded in Dublin on 17 March 1858 by James Stephens, aiming at an independent Irish republic by armed force.
The Fenian Brotherhood was founded in New York in 1858 by John O'Mahony as the American wing of the movement, and it drew on Irish emigrants and veterans of the American Civil War.
Fenian money came from Irish emigrant workers in American cities and paid for preparations for the Irish rising of 1867, which failed.
In June 1866 Fenians crossed the Niagara River into Canada and won a skirmish at Ridgeway, Ontario, before withdrawing under pressure from the US government.
A second Fenian raid into Canada in 1870 was defeated, and the raids damaged the movement's reputation in America and strengthened the case for Canadian confederation.

Clan na Gael was founded in New York in 1867 as a secret republican society for Irish Americans, and after the Fenian Brotherhood declined it became the strongest republican body in the United States.

The last convict ship to Australia, the Hougoumont, carried about 60 Fenian prisoners in 1867 to 1868, and an American campaign for the release of imprisoned Fenians drew support from Irish-American opinion.
Jeremiah O'Donovan Rossa's Skirmishing Fund, launched in New York in 1876, paid for the dynamite campaign in English cities in the 1880s, extending the use of American money for violence.
John Devoy was the most important Irish-American republican of his generation, and his career links the Fenians of the 1860s with the rising of 1916.
John Devoy was born in Co. Kildare in 1842 and joined the Irish Republican Brotherhood in the 1860s, recruiting Fenians in the British Army.

He was arrested in 1866 and sentenced to 15 years' penal servitude for treason-felony, and he was released in 1871 on condition that he went into exile; he sailed to New York with other prisoners on the Cuba.
In America he became a leading figure in Clan na Gael and used Irish-American newspapers to argue for an independent Irish republic.
In 1876 Devoy and Clan na Gael organised the rescue of six Fenian prisoners from Western Australia, carried out by the American whaler Catalpa.
In 1878 he proposed the New Departure with Michael Davitt, a plan for Fenians to cooperate with Charles Stewart Parnell's constitutional nationalists for land reform and self-government.
He founded the Gaelic American newspaper in New York in 1903, and he edited it for many years to keep Irish-American opinion behind the republican cause.

In 1914 he and Judge Daniel Cohalan met the German ambassador in Washington, Count Bernstorff, to ask for German help for an Irish rising, and Clan na Gael sent money to the IRB before the Rising of 1916.
After 1919 he quarrelled bitterly with de Valera, and he supported the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921; he visited the Irish Free State in 1924 and died in 1928.

Contemporaries in Britain regarded Devoy as a dangerous revolutionary, while many Irish Americans saw him as an elder statesman of the republican cause; de Valera's supporters saw him as an obstinate old man.

Historians, such as Terry Golway in his biography Irish Rebel (1998), present him as a central link between Fenian conspiracy in Ireland and organised Irish-American support in the twentieth century; his memoir Recollections of an Irish Rebel was published in 1929.
Irish nationalists raised money in America for the land agitation of 1879 to 1882, and American support gave the movement a wide base.

Michael Davitt, a Fenian released from prison in 1877, visited America in 1878, and his work with Devoy produced the New Departure that linked physical-force republicans with constitutional nationalists.
The Irish National Land League was founded in Dublin in 1879, with Parnell as president and Davitt as a founder, to campaign against rack-renting and eviction.
Parnell toured America in early 1880, raising funds among Irish Americans in cities across the country and addressing the House of Representatives in Washington.
Patrick Ford's newspaper the Irish World raised large sums for the Land League and for evicted tenants.

American money paid for relief to evicted tenants and for the Land League's campaign when the League was suppressed in 1881, and the American Ladies' Land League, led by Fanny Parnell, was founded in New York in 1880.
The Land League funds helped to sustain tenants who had been evicted, and this made American money a direct force in Irish agrarian politics.
Irish nationalist organisations in Britain and Australia gave the movement support beyond the United States, though their influence was smaller.
The Irish National League of Great Britain, founded in 1883, organised Irish voters in Liverpool, Glasgow and other British cities behind the Irish Parliamentary Party.
The Irish Self-Determination League of Great Britain, founded in 1919, campaigned for the Irish Republic among Irish emigrants in Britain during the War of Independence.

Irish Catholic communities in Australia, especially in Melbourne and Sydney, supported Home Rule through their churches and press, and Irish Parliamentary Party delegates, including the Redmond brothers in 1883, toured Australia to raise funds.
After 1916 Irish Australians, led by Archbishop Mannix, opposed conscription and supported the cause of Irish independence (see the notes on the Catholic Church abroad).
The Fenian prisoners transported to Western Australia and the Catalpa rescue gave Australia a place in Fenian memory.
Irish-American organisations gave money and support to the 1916 Rising, and their divisions shaped Irish politics after 1918.
Clan na Gael supported the 1916 Rising with money and contacts, and Devoy and Cohalan sought German help through the German embassy in Washington.
The Irish Race Convention held in New York in March 1916 launched the Friends of Irish Freedom, led by Judge Daniel Cohalan and Devoy.
The arms ship Aud, sent from Germany for the Rising, was intercepted by the Royal Navy and scuttled off Cork harbour in April 1916.
After the Rising and the executions of its leaders Irish-American opinion moved strongly behind the Irish Republic, and the Friends of Irish Freedom raised money and lobbied Congress.
An Irish Race Convention in Philadelphia in February 1919 called on the Paris Peace Conference and President Wilson to support Irish self-determination.

Divisions among Irish-American leaders, especially between Devoy and Cohalan on one side and Éamon de Valera on the other, weakened the unity of the movement after 1919 (see the notes on de Valera in America).
After the partition of Ireland, nationalists sought international support against the border, and Irish America was a key source of lobbying.
The Government of Ireland Act of 1920 created Northern Ireland, and the border with the Irish Free State was confirmed after the Boundary Commission collapsed in 1925.
The Anti-Partition League was formed in Northern Ireland in 1945 to unite nationalists, and it sought support in Ireland, Britain and America.
Éamon de Valera, then leader of the opposition, toured the USA and other countries in 1948 to press the anti-partition case, though the tour did not win any US government move to end partition.
In September 1948 Taoiseach John A. Costello announced in Canada the intention to repeal the External Relations Act, and the Republic of Ireland Act took effect on 18 April 1949.
Britain answered with the Ireland Act of 1949, which guaranteed that Northern Ireland would remain in the United Kingdom unless its parliament decided otherwise.
Ireland declined to join NATO in 1949 because of partition, and Seán MacBride, as Minister for External Affairs, appealed to American politicians and press.
Congressman John Fogarty of Rhode Island proposed in 1950 that American aid to Britain be linked to ending partition; the proposal failed, and the Irish government's campaign faded after 1951.
Ulster Unionists sought support among emigrants of Ulster Protestant descent in North America and the Dominions, and their identity rested on a shared Scots-Irish heritage.

Ulster-Scots identity: the descendants of Ulster Presbyterians in the United States and Canada, often called Scotch-Irish, kept a sense of Ulster origins; a Scotch-Irish Society of America held its first congress in 1889.
Several US presidents, including Andrew Jackson and Woodrow Wilson, were claimed as Ulster-Scots.
The Ulster Covenant of 28 September 1912 was signed by about half a million Ulster Unionists to oppose Home Rule, and it became the symbol of loyalist resistance.
The Orange Order in Canada, with lodges in Ontario and Toronto, was politically significant and gave moral support to Ulster unionism during the Home Rule crisis.
In Australia Orange lodges in Victoria and New South Wales supported the British connection and opposed Home Rule for Ireland.

Ulster Unionist lobbying abroad relied on the Scots-Irish and Orange networks and on figures like Bonar Law, a Canadian-born Ulster-Scot; it had moral and some financial value, but little direct influence on British policy.
Bonar Law was born in Canada to an Ulster Presbyterian father, and he led the Conservatives in the Home Rule crisis before becoming prime minister in 1922.
Andrew Bonar Law was born in Kingston, New Brunswick, in 1858, the son of a Presbyterian minister, the Rev. James Law, who came from Ulster.
The family moved to Glasgow in 1870, and Bonar Law went into the iron trade there before entering Parliament in 1900.
He became leader of the Conservative Party in November 1911, succeeding Arthur Balfour.
At Blenheim Palace in July 1912 he told a rally he could imagine no length of resistance to which Ulster could go that he would not support.
He was a leading Unionist in the Home Rule crisis of 1912 to 1914, and his support for the Ulster Unionists made the exclusion of Ulster a Conservative goal.
He served in the wartime coalition governments and was Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1916 to 1919 in Lloyd George's government.
He became Prime Minister in October 1922, resigned in May 1923 because of cancer, and died in October 1923.
Contemporary opinion was divided, with Liberal and nationalist newspapers portraying him as a reckless partisan, while unionists praised his loyalty.
Historians such as Robert Blake (The Unknown Prime Minister, 1955) stress his role in shaping Conservative policy on Ulster, and they debate how far his stand made partition more likely.
Achievement: Fenian and Clan na Gael networks funded and armed the nationalist movement, and Land League funds sustained the agitation of 1879 to 1882.
Limit: the Fenian rising of 1867 and the raids into Canada failed, and factional splits in America weakened support.
Anti-partition campaigners won sympathy in America after 1945 but failed to end partition.
Unionist networks gave moral and financial support through Orange and Scots-Irish links, but they had little direct effect on British policy.
Contemporary view: British officials regarded Irish-American networks as threats to security, while Irish-American leaders saw themselves as allies of the Irish cause.
Later view: historians debate whether diaspora money decided events, and many stress that the decisive politics took place in Ireland and Britain.
Éamon de Valera went to America in June 1919 as head of the Dáil government, after escaping from prison in England, to win recognition for the Irish Republic.
De Valera was born in New York in 1882 to an Irish mother and a Spanish father, and he was raised in Co. Limerick.
He commanded the Volunteer garrison at Boland's Mill in Dublin during the 1916 Rising, and his death sentence was commuted to imprisonment.
Sinn Féin won 73 of the 105 Irish seats in the general election of December 1918, and its MPs set up Dáil Éireann in January 1919 and declared an Irish Republic.
He was arrested in May 1918 in the round-up that followed the so-called German Plot, and he was held in Lincoln Gaol in England.
He escaped from Lincoln Gaol on 3 February 1919, in an escape arranged by Michael Collins and Harry Boland.
In April 1919 the Dáil elected him head of its ministry, as Príomh Aire, usually translated as President.

An Irish Race Convention in Philadelphia in February 1919 sent three Irish-American delegates, Frank P. Walsh, Edward F. Dunne and Michael J. Ryan, to Paris to ask Wilson to hear Ireland's case; they later visited Ireland.

The Dáil had sent envoys to the Paris Peace Conference, but President Woodrow Wilson did not press Britain on Irish self-determination, and the Irish delegates, including Seán T. O'Kelly, were not heard.
His aims in America were to win US recognition of the Republic, to raise funds for the Dáil government, to influence the 1920 presidential election, and to bring pressure on Britain.
De Valera arrived in America in June 1919 and toured cities with large Irish populations, where he was greeted by crowds, receptions and parades.
He left Ireland secretly in May 1919 as a stowaway on a ship from Liverpool, and he arrived in New York in June 1919, where Harry Boland had already arrived to prepare the way.
His public appearance in New York later in June 1919 launched a tour of the cities with the largest Irish communities, and he addressed a huge rally at Fenway Park in Boston on 29 June 1919.
His meetings in cities such as Boston, Chicago and New York drew large Irish-American audiences, who gave him receptions and donations.
A few days before his arrival, on 6 June 1919, the US Senate passed a resolution asking the Peace Conference to hear Irish representatives, which showed sympathy but did not commit the government.
Irish-American organisations and parishes arranged his meetings, and local branches raised money and sent subscriptions to Dublin.
His message was recognition of the Republic, support for the Dáil, and funds for the struggle in Ireland.
The reception was enthusiastic among Irish Americans, while the American government and most of the press treated the mission with caution.
British officials objected to his tour, which they regarded as propaganda against British rule in Ireland.
The tour continued through 1919 and into 1920, and de Valera also visited Irish communities in western states, where Irish-American organisations arranged his meetings and receptions.
The bond drive was meant to raise a large sum for the Dáil government, and it was the most successful part of the mission.

The Dáil authorised a loan, and bond certificates in the Irish Republic were sold to Irish Americans in a campaign launched in January 1920, so that supporters could invest in the struggle for independence.
The aim was to raise five million dollars, and the drive reached roughly that amount by 1921, though sources differ on the exact total.
The drive used the networks of Irish-American organisations, parishes and clubs to reach donors in cities across the United States.
Disputes arose over who controlled the money, and Irish-American leaders disagreed with de Valera about how the funds should be spent.
The bond drive gave the Dáil government a financial base in the diaspora, which was used alongside the National Loan raised in Ireland by Michael Collins as Minister for Finance.
Francis M. Carroll's study of the money raised, Money for Ireland (2002), stresses its importance for the Republic's finances.
De Valera's mission divided Irish America, and his clash with Devoy and Judge Cohalan weakened the unity of the movement.
John Devoy and Judge Daniel Cohalan led the Friends of Irish Freedom, which had supported Irish independence since 1916.
They quarrelled with de Valera over the control of funds and of the American movement, and the conflict was carried out in the press.
Devoy and Cohalan saw de Valera as trying to take control of an organisation they had built, while de Valera wanted an organisation that answered to the Dáil.
Harry Boland, who had organised the American side of the mission, backed de Valera, and the two camps traded accusations in the Gaelic American and other papers.
The split reduced the unity of Irish America, and de Valera turned to a new organisation of his own.
The quarrel showed the difficulty of running a movement from America when the leaders in Ireland had their own priorities.
De Valera's public statements in early 1920 caused controversy among his own supporters.

In February 1920 de Valera gave an interview to the Westminster Gazette in London, in which he suggested that Britain's security fears could be met by treating Ireland as the United States treated Cuba.
The comparison with Cuba, which accepted American influence over its foreign policy, caused controversy among republicans at home and abroad, who felt it offered a compromise on full independence.
Cohalan and Devoy used the interview to attack him.
De Valera himself argued that he was only showing that the Irish demand was reasonable to American opinion.
In 1920 de Valera tried to win a commitment to recognition from both major American parties, and neither convention gave one.
The Republican National Convention met in Chicago in June 1920, and the Democratic National Convention met in San Francisco in June and July 1920.
De Valera approached delegates and party leaders at both conventions, seeking a plank recognising the Irish Republic.
The Republican platform ignored the request, and the Democrats adopted only a resolution of sympathy with Irish aspirations for self-government.
The Republican candidate Warren G. Harding won the presidential election in November 1920, and his administration did not recognise the Republic.
Many Irish Americans, angered by the Wilson administration's refusal to back Irish self-determination, voted Republican in November 1920.
After the failure of the conventions the campaign was reorganised.

The American Association for the Recognition of the Irish Republic (AARIR) was founded in November 1920 as a new organisation for campaigning for recognition, which replaced the Friends of Irish Freedom for de Valera's supporters.
The new association grew rapidly and claimed several hundred thousand members, and it organised rallies and lobbied members of Congress.
An American Commission on Conditions in Ireland, set up in December 1920, investigated British reprisals in Ireland and increased American sympathy.
The death on hunger strike of Terence MacSwiney, Lord Mayor of Cork, on 25 October 1920 received wide American press coverage, and it helped the Irish cause.
While de Valera was in America, the Anglo-Irish War intensified, and the British government passed a Government of Ireland Act that divided the island.
The Soloheadbeg ambush on 21 January 1919 marked the start of the Anglo-Irish War, which lasted until 1921.
The British government banned the Dáil on 12 September 1919, and the Dáil's ministers went underground.
Michael Collins, as Minister for Finance and director of IRA intelligence, ran much of the war in Ireland while de Valera was in America.

From March 1920 the British government reinforced the Royal Irish Constabulary with the Black and Tans and, from July, the Auxiliaries, and reprisals against civilians were widely reported in American newspapers.
On 21 November 1920, known as Bloody Sunday, IRA gunmen killed British intelligence officers in Dublin, and British forces then fired on a crowd at Croke Park, killing 14.
Kevin Barry, an 18-year-old IRA Volunteer, was hanged in Dublin on 1 November 1920, and Auxiliaries burned part of Cork city in December 1920.
The Government of Ireland Act, passed in December 1920, created separate parliaments for Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland.
De Valera returned to Ireland in December 1920, when the Government of Ireland Act was being passed, and Harry Boland stayed on in America.
The mission secured publicity and money for the Republic, but not the recognition its leaders wanted.
No American government recognised the Irish Republic during the mission or in the years that followed.
The mission raised money for the Dáil government, which helped to pay for the war and the Dáil's administration.
The mission raised the profile of the Irish Republic in American newspapers and at public meetings.
The split among Irish-American organisations weakened the Friends of Irish Freedom and led to a new body, the AARIR.
De Valera's absence left the Dáil government without its president at a time of war, and relations between him and Collins were strained.
The mission was one of the first major efforts by the Irish Republic to win international recognition, and it shows both the possibilities and the limits of diaspora politics.
Harry Boland remained in the United States after de Valera left, and the AARIR carried on the campaign into 1921.
Achievement: the mission brought the Irish Republic's case to large American audiences and raised about five million dollars for the Dáil government.
Limit: the American government never recognised the Republic, and the Irish-American movement was divided by the mission.
Contemporary view: supporters called the mission a triumph, while the British government and its allies called it dangerous and divisive.
Contemporary view in Ireland: some nationalists argued that the time spent in America would have been better used at home.
Later view: historians stress that the mission was a propaganda and fundraising success but a diplomatic failure, because the recognition it sought was never granted.
Irish priests, bishops and religious sisters shaped Catholic communities overseas, and their institutions kept a sense of Irishness alive.

Irish-born and Irish-American priests and bishops dominated the American Catholic hierarchy for much of the 19th and early 20th centuries, because Irish emigrants formed the largest Catholic group and spoke English.
John Hughes, born in Co. Tyrone, became archbishop of New York in 1850, and John McCloskey of New York, of Irish parentage, became the first American cardinal in 1875.
Irish communities built parish churches, and many were dedicated to Irish saints such as Patrick and Brigid.
St Patrick's Cathedral in New York, built from the 1850s, was dedicated in 1879, and it became a symbol of the Irish-led Catholic presence in the city.
The Third Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1884 required every parish to establish a school for Catholic children, which made parochial schools central to Catholic life.
Religious orders with Irish members, including the Sisters of Mercy and the Christian Brothers, ran schools, hospitals and charitable houses.

Catholic fraternal societies such as the Ancient Order of Hibernians and the Knights of Columbus, founded in 1882 by an Irish-American priest, Michael McGivney, offered insurance, funeral benefits and social life.
The parish gave emigrants a social centre with dances, sodalities and sport, and the priest acted as an adviser and community leader.
Irish-born priests served many of the Catholic parishes in Liverpool, Glasgow and other British cities, where they built churches and schools for poor congregations.
The Catholic hierarchy was restored in England and Wales in 1850, at a time when Famine emigration was swelling Catholic numbers.
The Education (Scotland) Act of 1918 brought Catholic schools in Scotland into the state system while keeping their religious character, which secured their place in Scottish education.

Brother Walfrid, a Marist from Co. Sligo, founded Celtic Football Club in Glasgow in 1887 to raise money for poor Irish Catholic families, and the club became a symbol of the Irish community in Scotland.
Irish nuns ran hospitals, orphanages and schools in British cities, and their work reached poor Irish districts that the state had not served well.
In Australia the Catholic Church was led largely by Irish-born clergy and bishops, and Irish orders such as the Christian Brothers and the Sisters of Mercy staffed its schools.
When the Australian colonies ended state aid to church schools in the 1870s and 1880s, the Catholic Church built its own school system, funded by the Irish Catholic community.
The Catholic community in Britain and Australia was a visible minority, and its institutions were a focus for both loyalty to the Irish cause and sectarian suspicion.
Irish Catholics were the largest Catholic group in English-speaking Canada, and the church built parishes, schools and hospitals in Montreal, Toronto and Ontario towns.
St Patrick's Basilica in Montreal, opened in 1847, was built to serve the city's growing Irish Catholic congregation.
Michael Power, the first Catholic bishop of Toronto and the son of Irish emigrants, died of typhus in October 1847 after caring for Famine emigrants.
In Newfoundland people of Irish Catholic descent formed a large share of the population, and the church was central to their community life.
In Ontario Catholic and Orange rivalry was constant, and disputes over separate Catholic schools were a recurring political issue.
Daniel Mannix was an Irish-born Catholic archbishop in Melbourne, whose opposition to conscription and support for Irish independence made him a controversial figure.
Daniel Mannix was born in Charleville, Co. Cork, in 1864, trained at Maynooth, and was president of Maynooth College from 1903 until 1912.
He was appointed coadjutor archbishop of Melbourne in 1912, and he became archbishop in 1917.
As archbishop he opposed conscription in Australia during the First World War, and he took a leading part in the campaign in the referendums of 1916 and 1917, both of which were defeated.
His stand brought him into conflict with the prime minister, Billy Hughes, and with imperial loyalists, who called him disloyal.
He supported Irish independence and criticised British policy in Ireland after 1916, which made him a target for British loyalist opinion in Australia.

In August 1920, on a voyage from the USA to Ireland, he was taken off his ship at sea by a British naval vessel and landed in England, and he was banned from entering Ireland; he went on to speak to Irish Catholic communities in Britain.
He clashed with the Orange Order and other Protestant organisations in Victoria, and sectarian disputes shaped Melbourne politics in his time.
In the 1950s he supported the anti-communist Catholic Movement led by B. A. Santamaria, which contributed to the Labor split of 1955.
Contemporary attitudes were sharply divided: Irish Australians and many Catholics admired him, while imperial loyalists and Protestant organisations in Australia called him disloyal.

Historians present him as a major figure in Australian Catholic and political life, and they debate how far his nationalism was an Irish-Australian response to anti-Catholic prejudice; he died in November 1963, aged 99.
The Gaelic Athletic Association was founded in Ireland in 1884, and it reached Irish communities overseas through clubs and tours.
The GAA was founded at Hayes's Hotel in Thurles, Co. Tipperary, on 1 November 1884, and its founders included Michael Cusack and Maurice Davin.
The GAA promoted Gaelic football and hurling, and it also organised athletics, as a way of building a distinctly Irish sporting culture.

In 1888 a party of Irish athletes, hurlers and footballers toured the United States, playing exhibition matches and athletics before Irish-American crowds; the tour lost money, and some of the party stayed in America.

Irish-American clubs playing Gaelic football and hurling appeared in New York, Chicago, Boston and other cities with large Irish populations, and New York became the GAA's main centre in North America, with Gaelic Park in the Bronx opening in 1926.
A London GAA board was established in the 1890s, and clubs in Britain and Australia gave Irish emigrants a regular social life built around their identity.
The 1947 All-Ireland football final between Cavan and Kerry was played at the Polo Grounds in New York, to mark the Irish diaspora's place in the association.
The GAA linked sport with nationalism: it banned its members from playing or attending foreign games, a rule formalised in 1905, and clubs abroad were part of the same nationalist culture.
Protestant emigrants from Ulster, often called Scotch-Irish, kept a Presbyterian and Methodist identity that was distinct from Irish Catholic nationalism.
Ulster Presbyterians settled in Pennsylvania and along the Appalachians in the 18th century, and Francis Makemie, from Co. Donegal, helped found the Presbyterian church in the American colonies.
Their descendants in the USA became known as Scotch-Irish, a term that was widely used from the 19th century to distinguish them from Catholic Irish, especially after the Famine.
Presbyterian and Methodist congregations in the USA and Canada kept links with the churches in Ireland and recruited ministers from them.

Methodism in America and Canada was spread by Irish Palatine emigrants from Co. Limerick, such as Philip Embury and Barbara Heck, who helped found the first Methodist society in New York in the 1760s.
The Ulster-Scots identity stressed Protestant descent, loyalty to the British Crown and a sense of a separate heritage from the Irish Catholic majority.
Many Protestant emigrants assimilated quickly into American and Canadian denominations, and their sense of Irishness faded more quickly than that of Catholics.
In Canada Ulster-Scots and Presbyterian identity was strong in Ontario, and it was linked to loyalty to the British connection.
The Orange Order was founded in Ireland in 1795, and it carried a Protestant and loyalist identity to Canada and Australia, where it was politically significant.
The Orange Order was founded in Co. Armagh in 1795, after the Battle of the Diamond between Protestant and Catholic groups.
Lodges reached Canada early in the 19th century with soldiers and settlers, and the Grand Orange Lodge of British America was formed in 1830 to coordinate them.
Orange lodges in Toronto and Ontario were politically influential, and Toronto, sometimes called the Belfast of Canada, was long governed by Orangemen as mayors.
Sir John A. Macdonald, Canada's first prime minister, was an Orangeman, and Mackenzie Bowell, prime minister from 1894 to 1896, was a Grand Master.
Orange parades on 12 July, known as the Twelfth, marked the Battle of the Boyne and were occasions of public display and occasional violence in Canada.
Orange lodges were established in colonial New South Wales from the 1840s and spread to Victoria, and they opposed Catholic influence and Home Rule.
In Australia the Orange Order was part of a loyalist and anti-Catholic culture, and it clashed with Catholic institutions in Melbourne and Sydney.
Orange parades in New York in 1870 and 1871 led to riots with Irish Catholics in which dozens died, which showed that Irish sectarian rivalry was carried to America.
Church, sport and community life worked together to sustain a sense of Irishness abroad, though many emigrants and their children took part in only some of them.
Priests and nuns acted as community leaders, and parish events such as dances, picnics and fundraising kept Irish life visible in the city.
St Patrick's Day parades in New York date back to 1762, and they became a major public display of Irish identity in America.
Church schools taught Catholic children their faith and gave the second generation a grounding in parish and community life.
The second generation often moved towards American or Australian culture, and the church and GAA supported Irishness for those who wanted it.
Catholic and Orange rivalry in Canada and Australia shaped the public life of Irish communities, and sectarian tension was a constant feature.
The Catholic Church encouraged loyalty to the new country as well as faith, so it was a vehicle of assimilation as well as of Irishness.
Achievement: the Catholic Church and GAA gave Irish emigrants a community, a social life and an Irish identity that lasted for generations.
Limit: many emigrants' children assimilated, and the institutions reached only part of the emigrant population.
Contemporary view: Irish nationalists praised the church and the GAA as guardians of Irishness, while nativists and imperial loyalists regarded them as divisive.
Later view: historians argue that the Catholic Church and the GAA sustained identity but also helped Irish communities to organise and gain power in their new societies.
Protestant and Orange identity achieved political influence in Canada and Australia, but it was often a sign of loyalty to the British connection, not of Irish nationalism.
Ireland sent Catholic missionaries to Africa and Asia out of proportion to its population, and this effort was given a national meaning.

The Catholic Church in Ireland was strengthened after the Famine by the reforms of Archbishop Paul Cullen, a change that Emmet Larkin called the devotional revolution, and this produced a large supply of priests, brothers and nuns.
Irish seminaries and novitiates, such as St Patrick's College, Maynooth, trained far more clergy than the Irish church needed, and the surplus went to the Irish diaspora and then to the missions.
The phrase Ireland's spiritual empire described the reach of Irish missionaries across Africa and Asia, and it gave missionary work a national identity.
Irish writers linked the missions to the monks of the early church, such as Columbanus, and to Ireland's reputation as an island of saints and scholars.
Irish nationalism and Catholicism were closely linked, so a country that had no empire of its own could present itself as a leader in spreading the faith without the taint of colonialism.
Irish parishes raised money through collections, missionary magazines and mission exhibitions, which linked congregations at home with the work abroad.
Edel Quinn, a Legion of Mary envoy to East Africa from 1936, who died in Nairobi in 1944, became a lay symbol of Irish missionary dedication.
Mission work gave Irish women a leadership role in nursing, teaching and medicine that was hard to find at home.
The Maynooth Mission to China was founded in 1916, and it became the Missionary Society of St Columban, with its headquarters at Dalgan Park, Navan, from 1918.
The Columbans worked in China, then in Korea, Japan, the Philippines and Latin America.
The Missionary Society of St Patrick, founded at Kiltegan, Co. Wicklow, in 1932 by Father Patrick Whitney, sent priests to Nigeria and later to Kenya and other African countries.
The Society of African Missions (SMA), founded in France in 1856, had an Irish province in Cork, and its Irish members worked in West Africa, including Nigeria and Ghana.
The Holy Ghost Fathers, called Spiritans, were a French-founded congregation with a large Irish province that took on the missions of Nigeria, Kenya and Sierra Leone.
The Missionary Sisters of the Holy Rosary, founded by Bishop Joseph Shanahan in 1924 at Killeshandra, Co. Cavan, taught and nursed in Nigeria and other parts of Africa.
Other Irish groups included the Loreto sisters in India and the Presentation Sisters, and Irish Jesuits in Zambia and India.
Edward Galvin was a Cork priest who founded the Maynooth Mission to China and became a bishop in Hanyang, central China.
Edward Galvin was born in Co. Cork in 1882 and was ordained for the diocese of Cork in 1909.
He went to China in 1912 as a missionary priest, and in 1916 he returned to Ireland, where with Father John Blowick he founded the Maynooth Mission to China, approved by the Irish bishops.
The first Irish missionaries went to China in 1920, and Galvin led the mission in the Hanyang area of Hubei province in central China.
He became prefect apostolic in 1924 and vicar apostolic of Hanyang in 1927, when he became a bishop; Hanyang became a diocese in 1946.
The mission ran churches, schools, orphanages and clinics, and it trained Chinese catechists and priests, though few Chinese priests were ordained before the 1940s.
He led the mission through the civil conflicts of the 1920s and 1930s and the Japanese invasion, in which Hanyang was bombed.
After the Communist takeover of 1949 the missionaries faced restrictions, and Galvin was placed under house arrest, tried and expelled in 1952; he died at Dalgan Park in 1956.
Contemporaries in Ireland saw Galvin and the China mission as heroes of the Catholic church, and their letters and talks raised vocations and money.
Chinese Communist authorities criticised the missionaries as agents of foreign influence, and this view shaped their expulsion.
Historians place the Columbans in the wider history of Western missions in China, and they debate how far missionary work helped or hindered local communities.
Mary Martin founded the Medical Missionaries of Mary, whose sisters combined nursing and medicine with mission work in Africa.
Mary Martin was born in Dublin in 1892 and trained as a nurse and midwife; she went to Nigeria in the 1930s to work in mission medicine.
Until 1936 the Catholic Church forbade religious sisters to practise obstetrics and surgery, and a Vatican instruction of that year lifted the restriction, making her order possible.
She went to Nigeria and founded the Medical Missionaries of Mary, which is dated to 1937 in Nigeria; the order's mother house was at Drogheda, Co. Louth.
The order trained doctors, nurses and midwives, and it set up hospitals and clinics in areas where few medical services existed.
Its sisters worked in Nigeria, and the order's mission hospitals and nursing schools became central to its work there; it later worked in other African countries.
Martin directed the order's expansion and the training of its members, and she became known as Mother Mary of the Incarnation.
She was the first woman to receive the Freedom of the Borough of Drogheda, in 1966, and she died in 1975.
Contemporary Irish Catholic opinion praised the order and its work, and the sisters were presented as models of the mission spirit.
Historians present the Medical Missionaries of Mary as a pioneer of women-led medical missions, and they ask how far medical work served colonial aims.
The Holy Ghost Fathers, called Spiritans, were a French-founded congregation whose Irish members led much of the mission in south-eastern Nigeria.
