The Holy Ghost Fathers (Spiritans) began work at Onitsha on the lower Niger in 1885, before Britain's colonial control had been established in the interior.
The mission area was south-eastern Nigeria, where the Igbo people were the largest group, in the British colony and protectorate of Southern Nigeria and later the Eastern Region.
Joseph Shanahan, an Irish Spiritan born in Co. Tipperary in 1871, arrived in Nigeria in 1902 and made the school the main instrument of conversion, building village schools staffed by catechists.
He became prefect apostolic in 1920 and a bishop, appealed to Irish seminaries for recruits, and founded the Holy Rosary Sisters in 1924.
He left Nigeria in 1931 because of ill health, and he died in 1943; his remains were reburied in Onitsha Cathedral in 1956.
Methodist and Anglican missionaries competed with the Catholics for converts, and rivalry over schools was a feature of the region.
By 1945 the mission had a network of parishes, schools and a few hospitals in the region, which the postwar expansion built on.
Between 1945 and 1966 the mission grew into a large network of schools, hospitals and parishes, staffed by Irish missionaries and increasingly by Nigerians.
After 1945 the mission opened new parishes, schools, hospitals and training colleges across south-eastern Nigeria.

The Archdiocese of Onitsha was created in 1950 when the Catholic hierarchy was established in Nigeria, with the Irish Spiritan Charles Heerey as its archbishop, and Joseph Whelan became the first bishop of Owerri.
The number of Irish priests, brothers and sisters working in the mission rose in the 1950s, with recruits from Irish seminaries and novitiates.
Mission schools became the main route to education in the region, and the Catholic mission ran a large share of primary and secondary schools.
Teacher training colleges prepared local teachers, which created a growing educated class in the region.
Hospitals and dispensaries run by the Holy Rosary Sisters and Medical Missionaries of Mary provided medical care in rural areas where government services were few.
The Catholic population of the region grew strongly, and local vocations to the priesthood and religious life increased; Michael Tansi, an Igbo, was ordained in 1937 and beatified in 1998.
Nigerians were trained as priests, teachers and nurses, and in 1965 Francis Arinze, aged 32, became auxiliary bishop of Onitsha.
The mission depended on the colonial government for funding and cooperated with it, though the two sometimes disagreed over schooling and policy.
The colonial government paid grants towards mission schools under a grant-in-aid system, in return for inspection and standards.
The grants made education cheaper for the mission and for families, but they also tied the schools to government requirements.
Missions and colonial officials sometimes disagreed over curriculum, language and the role of religious teaching in schools.
In the 1950s the regional government of Eastern Nigeria introduced free primary education, which increased demand for schools and strained mission resources.
Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960, and the mission adapted to a new state in which Nigerians held most public offices.
After independence the mission's leadership passed increasingly to Nigerian priests and bishops, a process known as localisation.
Many of the educated Nigerians who served in the new state had passed through mission schools, which gave the mission a lasting role in the country's élite.
The mission's achievements in education and health can be set against criticisms of its cultural influence and against the damage of the Biafran war.
Achievements: the mission built schools, hospitals and churches, trained many local teachers and nurses, and helped create a Catholic church with Nigerian leadership.
Criticisms: mission education promoted Christian and Western values, and critics argued that it weakened local culture and languages.
Critics also said the mission was paternalistic, because Irish missionaries held the leadership long after local people were qualified for it.
Rivalry between Catholic and Protestant missions over schools and converts also divided communities.
On 30 May 1967 the eastern region declared itself the Republic of Biafra, and a civil war followed until January 1970.

During the war many mission stations, schools and hospitals were damaged, closed or abandoned, and missionaries were displaced; Irish Holy Ghost Father Anthony Byrne helped organise the relief airlift to Biafra.
The famine in Biafra moved many Irish people, and the Irish relief agency Concern was founded in 1968 in response to it.
After the war many foreign missionaries left the east, including Bishop Whelan of Owerri, and the state took over mission schools.
Irish Catholics saw the missions as a sign that Ireland was a nation with a mission of its own, not only a country that exported people.
The idea of an Irish spiritual empire combined Irish nationalism with the universal claims of the Catholic Church.
The missions raised money and vocations at home, and they linked Irish parishes to the lives of people overseas.
Later historians have questioned the empire idea, and they see it as a self-image that was closely tied to Irish Catholic identity and to the colonial world.
The decline in Irish vocations after the 1960s and the localisation of the churches in Africa and Asia ended the era of large-scale Irish mission work.
Achievement: the Holy Ghost mission built schools, hospitals and parishes that outlasted colonial rule and produced educated Nigerian leaders.
Limit: the mission was tied to the colonial state through grants, and it was slow to hand leadership to local clergy.
Contemporary view: Irish Catholics praised the missionaries as heroes of the faith, while some African critics questioned their paternalism and cultural impact.
Later view: historians stress both the practical contribution of missions to health and education and the cultural and political costs of their work.
Galvin and Martin compared: both founded mission institutions in the 1910s and 1930s, but Galvin's China mission ended in expulsion in 1952, while Martin's medical order grew in Africa.
Hollywood shaped the world's picture of Ireland, often through sentimental and comic stereotypes built on the older stage Irishman.
The stage Irishman was a 19th-century theatrical stereotype of the Irish as drunken, quick-tempered, sentimental and comic, and Hollywood inherited it.
Harrigan and Hart's Mulligan Guard comedies in New York in the 1870s and 1880s and the Irish-American stage of Chauncey Olcott made the stage Irishman familiar to American audiences.
John Ford, an American director of Irish descent born in Maine in 1894, whose parents came from Spiddal, Co. Galway, and the Aran Islands, made many films about Irish themes and Irish-American life.
Ford's The Informer, released in 1935, won him the Academy Award for Best Director, and it dealt with the Irish revolutionary period in Dublin.
Hollywood films often showed the Irish as rural, Catholic and emotional, and urban or industrial Ireland was rarely shown.
Going My Way, released in 1944, presented an Irish-American priest in New York, and it became one of the popular images of Irish Catholicism in America.
Irish-American priests, policemen and fighting Irishmen became stock characters, played by actors such as Pat O'Brien and Barry Fitzgerald.
Disney's Darby O'Gill and the Little People (1959) presented Ireland as a land of leprechauns and banshees.
The Quiet Man was filmed in the west of Ireland in 1951 and released in 1952, and it became the most influential film image of rural Ireland.
The Quiet Man was directed by John Ford and starred John Wayne and Maureen O'Hara, with Barry Fitzgerald and Victor McLaglen, and was based on a story by the Irish writer Maurice Walsh.
It was filmed around Cong in Co. Mayo and in Connemara in 1951, with Ashford Castle as one of its main locations.
The film won Academy Awards at the 1953 ceremony for Ford's direction and for the colour cinematography of Winton C. Hoch and Archie Stout.
The film's locations, including the Quiet Man Bridge in Cong, drew American visitors who wanted to see the places they had seen on screen.
Irish critics objected to the film's portrayal of rural people as comic and drunken, and they argued that it stereotyped Irish life.
The film helped to make Cong a tourist destination, and it shaped the expectations that many American visitors brought to Ireland.
The film's rural, comic, romantic Ireland suited the tourist board, even though real Ireland in 1952 was suffering mass emigration.
Maureen O'Hara was a Dublin-born actress who became a Hollywood star and was closely identified with Irish heroines on screen.
Maureen O'Hara was born Maureen FitzSimons in Ranelagh, Dublin, in 1920, and she trained as an actress in Dublin at the Abbey Theatre school before moving to Britain and then America.
Her first Hollywood film was Jamaica Inn, released in 1939 and directed by Alfred Hitchcock, and she went on to a long Hollywood career.
She appeared in How Green Was My Valley in 1941 and in Miracle on 34th Street in 1947, which established her as a major star.
She worked repeatedly with John Ford, and their films included Rio Grande in 1950 and The Quiet Man in 1952, in which she played the fiery Mary Kate Danaher opposite John Wayne.
Contemporary Irish-American audiences embraced her as an Irish star, while Irish critics debated whether her roles presented a true picture of Irish women.
Historians note that her screen image of the Irish woman as spirited and independent was partly a Hollywood creation, and that her own sense of Irishness was shaped by her Dublin upbringing.
She became a US citizen, received an honorary Academy Award in 2014, and died in 2015; her career is often used as an example of how Irish stars helped to build a screen image of Ireland.
Music carried Irish images to audiences abroad, from the concert tenor of the early 20th century to the folk revival of the 1960s.

Sentimental songs such as When Irish Eyes Are Smiling (1912) and Danny Boy, written in 1910 by an English lyricist to an Irish air, were products of the Irish-American song industry and shaped an image of Ireland as a land of exile and longing.
John McCormack, born in Athlone in 1884, became an internationally famous tenor and recorded Irish ballads that were popular with Irish audiences abroad; he died in 1945.
McCormack's concerts in America and Britain made Irish songs part of mainstream concert repertoire, and he was a leading figure in Irish-American cultural life.
Céilí bands played traditional Irish dance music, and they performed for dancers in Irish halls and clubs in America and Britain.
Irish-American song and dance were kept alive in parish halls, clubs and dance halls, which gave emigrant communities a shared cultural life.
The Clancy Brothers, from Carrick-on-Suir, Co. Tipperary, and Tommy Makem, from Co. Armagh, became popular in America after appearing on the Ed Sullivan Show in 1961.

The folk revival of the 1960s brought Irish songs to a young audience in America and Britain, led by groups such as the Clancy Brothers and, from 1962, the Dubliners, and it changed how Irish music was seen abroad.
The Irish state and private groups promoted tourism to attract visitors, including descendants of emigrants who wanted to see the places their families had left.
Bord Fáilte, the Irish Tourist Board, was set up under the Tourist Traffic Act of 1952 to promote tourism and to develop tourist facilities.
An Tóstal, a national festival of Irish culture and heritage, was launched in 1953 to draw visitors and to promote Irish events and traditions.
Shannon Airport opened in 1945 as a transatlantic stop for aircraft, which brought American travellers through Ireland.
Shannon Airport opened the world's first duty-free shop in 1947, which made it a point of contact between Irish life and travellers from America.
Aer Lingus began transatlantic flights between Dublin, Shannon and New York in 1958.
Heritage tourism grew in the 1950s and 1960s, with visits to ancestral places, church records and genealogy services for descendants of emigrants.
Roots tourism, the visiting of ancestral homes by people of Irish descent, linked the Irish state's promotion of tourism with the emigrant communities abroad.
Tourism was valued as an export industry that brought in dollars and sterling, and it fitted the economic planning of the late 1950s.
Carol Reed's film Odd Man Out (1947), set in Belfast and starring James Mason, showed the Irish revolutionary underworld to international audiences.
The Irish Hospitals' Sweepstake, run from 1930, sold tickets in large numbers in the USA and Britain, where it was illegal, and made the name of Ireland widely known.
Ireland's pavilion at the New York World's Fair of 1939 presented a national image to American visitors.
An Coimisiún le Rincí Gaelacha, set up in 1929 to standardise Irish dancing competitions, helped spread feiseanna and Irish dance classes among Irish communities abroad.
Gael-Linn, founded in 1953, promoted Irish-language recordings and cultural projects that reached emigrant audiences.
John F. Kennedy's election and his visit in 1963 changed how Irish Americans and the Irish public saw one another.

Kennedy's great-grandfather Patrick Kennedy left Dunganstown, Co. Wexford, in 1849, and the family's Irish origins were well known in Ireland; his mother's family, the Fitzgeralds, also had Irish roots.

Kennedy was elected president in 1960, becoming the first Catholic president of the United States, and many Irish Americans saw his election as acceptance of Irish Catholics in public life, after the defeat of Al Smith in 1928.
Kennedy visited Ireland from 26 to 29 June 1963, going to Dublin, Wexford and Dunganstown, Cork, Galway and Limerick.
On 28 June 1963 he addressed the Oireachtas, the Irish parliament, in Dublin.
The visit drew large crowds and intense press coverage in Ireland, and it was widely celebrated as a moment of Irish pride.
Kennedy's image in Ireland combined ancestry with success in American politics, and it encouraged Irish people to see their emigrant relatives as part of a shared story.
His assassination on 22 November 1963 was mourned widely in Ireland, and his portrait hung in many Irish homes.
Historians argue that the visit fitted the self-confidence of Seán Lemass's government as the economy opened to the world, rather than causing it.
Kennedy's father's career is covered in the notes on Joe Kennedy, whose business and diplomatic career shaped the family's public profile.
Ireland had little film production of its own before the late 1950s, and foreign productions and state censorship shaped what images reached Irish cinemas.
The Censorship of Films Act of 1923 gave the Irish state power to ban films, and the film censor removed or refused films on moral grounds.
Ardmore Studios opened at Bray, Co. Wicklow, in 1958 as the main film studio in Ireland.
Foreign productions, including Hollywood films, were shot in Ireland in the 1950s, and they brought Irish scenery and Irish actors to the screen.
Irish cinema-goers saw mostly Hollywood and British films, so the American image of Ireland reached Irish audiences as well as Americans.
Robert Flaherty's documentary Man of Aran (1934) presented a romantic picture of life on the Aran Islands that many islanders did not recognise.
Achievement: Hollywood films, music and tourism made Ireland widely known abroad, and they attracted visitors and strengthened ties with emigrant descendants.
Limit: the images were often sentimental, rural and stereotyped, and they left out industrial and urban Ireland.
Contemporary view: the state's tourism bodies welcomed the images, while Irish critics objected that they stereotyped Irish people as comic or drunken.
Later view: historians see these images as a version of Ireland made for export, and they debate how far the Kennedy visit changed Irish self-image or only celebrated it.
Film versus music: films fixed a rural, comic image, while the folk revival gave Irish culture a younger and more confident voice abroad.
Northern Ireland had its own parliament at Stormont from 1921, but its place in the United Kingdom was the central question for both communities.
The Government of Ireland Act 1920 created Northern Ireland from six counties, with a devolved parliament at Stormont in Belfast; the other twenty-six counties got a separate settlement.
The Republic of Ireland Act 1948 took effect on 18 April 1949, ending Ireland's membership of the Commonwealth and formally declaring the twenty-six counties a republic.
The Ireland Act 1949, passed at Westminster in response, declared that Northern Ireland would not cease to be part of the United Kingdom without the consent of its parliament.
This guarantee gave unionists a legal safeguard against a united Ireland imposed by Westminster without their consent.
Unionists held a majority in the Stormont parliament at every election from 1921 to 1972, so nationalists formed a permanent opposition.
Local government elections used first-past-the-post after the 1922 abolition of proportional representation, which helped unionists win control of councils in mixed areas.

Local election voting was restricted to ratepayers and their spouses, and company directors had extra votes, until the franchise was reformed in the late 1960s; nationalists called this the business vote.

The Stormont general election of 10 February 1949, sometimes called the chapel-gate election, was fought on the border question after the declaration of the Republic, and the Unionist Party won 37 of the 52 seats.

The Flags and Emblems (Display) Act (Northern Ireland) 1954 allowed the police to remove an Irish tricolour if its display was thought likely to cause a breach of the peace, which nationalists resented.
Sir Basil Brooke, later Lord Brookeborough, led the Unionist government for twenty years and put stability and loyalty to the Crown first.
Basil Brooke became Prime Minister of Northern Ireland in 1943 and was succeeded by Terence O'Neill in 1963.
His government resisted reform of local government and the franchise, and it saw no need to change a system that kept unionists in power.

As Minister of Agriculture in the 1930s Brooke urged loyalists to employ Protestants rather than Catholics, speeches that nationalists cited for decades as evidence of sectarian attitudes at the top of the Unionist Party.
The Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act (Northern Ireland) 1922 stayed in force, allowing detention without trial and the banning of organisations.
The Ulster Special Constabulary, including the part-time B Specials, was kept as an armed reserve alongside the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and it was almost wholly Protestant.
The Royal Ulster Constabulary was the main police force, and Catholics made up only a small minority of its ranks.
The Nationalist Party abstained from Stormont for long periods and accepted the role of official opposition only in 1965, so there was little effective challenge to the government in the 1950s.
Brooke retired in March 1963 at the age of 74 and Terence O'Neill succeeded him.
Stormont adopted the British welfare settlement for schooling, but the system kept religious divisions and set a selection test at age eleven.
The Education Act (Northern Ireland) 1947 provided free secondary education for all pupils, extending the opportunities available to children from poorer families.
It set up a tripartite system of grammar, technical and secondary intermediate schools.
Pupils moved on at about age eleven after the eleven-plus examination, which decided who went to a grammar school.
Voluntary schools, mostly Catholic, kept their own management and received a state capital grant towards building costs of 65 per cent, while controlled schools were run by the education authorities.
The Act also extended state scholarships and grants for university study, so more Catholic students reached Queen's University Belfast from the 1950s.
Free secondary education gave Catholic children access to a wider range of qualifications, and by the 1960s a new educated Catholic middle class was emerging.
Education remained segregated by religion, so Protestant and Catholic children grew up in separate schools.
The National Health Service and the state housing programme reached Northern Ireland, but local councils controlled the allocation of council houses.
The National Health Service began in Northern Ireland on 5 July 1948, the same day as in England, Scotland and Wales.
The Northern Ireland Housing Trust, set up in 1945, built houses and estates in towns and cities across the province.

The Housing Trust allocated its houses on a points system and was regarded as fair, but most council houses were allocated by local councils, and many unionist-controlled councils allocated houses in ways that favoured Protestant families.

Londonderry Corporation was controlled by unionists even though Catholics formed a majority of the city's population, because the ward boundaries were drawn in 1936 to place most Catholic voters in one ward.
Gerrymandering was the drawing of electoral boundaries so that one group's voters were concentrated in a few wards, and unionists won more seats than their share of the vote.
Catholic and Protestant families were increasingly housed in separate estates, which later made segregated housing a feature of Belfast and Derry.
In Fermanagh and Tyrone, where Catholics were roughly half the population, unionist-controlled councils also held power, a pattern nationalists cited in the 1960s.
The welfare reforms of the 1940s were extended to Northern Ireland on a basis of parity with Britain.
National Insurance, unemployment benefit and pensions were run on a UK-wide basis, so benefits in Northern Ireland matched those in Britain.
The welfare reforms of the 1940s followed the Beveridge Report (1942) and the post-war Labour government's legislation of 1945 to 1948.
The principle of parity meant Stormont was expected to follow British social policy, which limited its freedom to set different rules.
The welfare state was therefore a shared British settlement, and its cost in Northern Ireland was met largely by the British Treasury.
The Social Services Agreement of 1949 formalised parity, and the British subsidy paid for public services that Northern Ireland could not fund from its own tax revenue.
Welfare parity meant that the Catholic minority benefited from the same services as Protestants, but it did not remove discrimination in allocation and jobs.
Northern Ireland's economy depended on shipbuilding and linen, which declined from the 1950s, while new industry was concentrated in unionist areas.
Harland and Wolff, Belfast's main shipyard, had built the Titanic, completed in 1912, but its workforce shrank in the post-war decades as shipbuilding declined.
Linen manufacturing, once a major employer in County Antrim and the Lagan valley, declined as cheaper foreign competition and synthetic fibres spread.
Unemployment in Northern Ireland stayed above the UK average and was the highest of any UK region for much of the period.
The Stormont government offered grants and incentives to attract new industry, including man-made fibre plants and aircraft production at Short Brothers.
Most new industrial investment was placed in the Belfast area and towns east of the River Bann, leaving the largely Catholic west, including Derry, with fewer jobs.
Emigration drained the province of young people, and the economy lagged behind Britain throughout the Brookeborough years.
Agriculture remained a large employer, and the farming economy was supported by British agricultural subsidies.
Catholics made up about a third of the population but were under-represented in public employment, policing and senior posts.
Catholics made up about a third of the population of Northern Ireland, 35 per cent in the 1961 census.
Catholics were under-represented in the Royal Ulster Constabulary and in senior civil service posts.
Some large private employers, especially in Belfast's shipyards and engineering works, employed very few Catholics.
Nationalists argued that Stormont treated the minority as second-class citizens and that discrimination was systematic.
Unionists argued that discrimination was exaggerated and that Catholics had equal access to state services and to the vote.
Unionist governments saw the Specials and the RUC as essential defences against republican violence, not as sectarian forces.
Local councils in Unionist hands were also major employers, and nationalists complained that they too hired few Catholics for senior posts.
The IRA's Border Campaign was an attempt to end partition by force, and it failed to win popular support.
The IRA launched its campaign, codenamed Operation Harvest, in December 1956, with attacks on RUC barracks, customs posts and border installations.
The campaign aimed to end partition by force, but it attracted little support from the nationalist community.
Stormont introduced internment without trial in 1957, and the Dublin government also acted against IRA activity in the Republic.

The campaign began with raids such as the attack on Brookeborough RUC barracks on 1 January 1957, in which the IRA men Seán South and Feargal O'Hanlon were killed; both became republican martyrs and South was remembered in song.
The IRA Army Council called off the campaign in February 1962, after which the movement was weak for several years.
The failure led some republicans to rethink their strategy, and in the 1960s a faction turned towards left-wing politics and social campaigns.
The campaign was mostly confined to the border counties, and its members were largely rounded up under internment north and south of the border.
Sectarianism was the hostility between Protestants and Catholics that shaped jobs, housing, marriage and social life in Northern Ireland.
The Belfast riots of 1920 to 1922 killed hundreds of people and left lasting memories of violence on both sides.
The Orange Order and the Ancient Order of Hibernians were the main Protestant and Catholic fraternal bodies, each with a political dimension.
Religious segregation in schools, housing and workplaces meant that most people had little regular contact with the other community.
Mixed marriages were uncommon, and religious differences were a factor in many social and personal decisions.
Sectarian prejudice was strongest in working-class areas where jobs and houses were scarce and rival communities lived side by side.
Parades and the display of flags marked out territory, so symbols of identity were also symbols of division.
Achievement: the welfare reforms in health, education and housing raised living standards for citizens across Northern Ireland.
Achievement: Stormont kept political stability through the 1950s, with no sustained challenge to the Union, and it defeated the IRA border campaign.
Failure: the Catholic minority continued to face discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting, and this grievance was later taken up by the civil rights movement.
Failure: the economy stayed weak, with unemployment and emigration above the UK level, and new industry was poorly distributed between east and west.
Contemporary view: unionists praised Brooke's stability and his loyalty to the Crown, and his supporters saw his government as the guardian of the Union.
Contemporary view: nationalists condemned the Special Powers Act and discrimination as proof that the state was sectarian.
Later view: historians stress that the welfare reforms were real, but that the failure to share power meant they could not satisfy the Catholic community.
Achievement: the 1947 education reforms and the NHS gave Catholic and Protestant families alike better health and wider opportunities.
Terence O'Neill came to power in 1963 with a programme of economic modernisation and gestures towards Catholics and the Republic.
Terence O'Neill succeeded Brookeborough as Prime Minister in March 1963, having been Minister of Finance since 1956.

He promoted economic planning, drawing on the Matthew Report (1963) on regional planning around Belfast and the Wilson Plan (1965) on economic development, which led to the new city of Craigavon in County Armagh.
He made symbolic visits to Catholic schools and hospitals, which unionist hardliners resented as concessions.

On 14 January 1965 he received the Taoiseach, Seán Lemass, at Stormont, a meeting widely described as the first between the heads of the two governments since partition; O'Neill had not told most of his cabinet in advance.
O'Neill returned the visit to Dublin in February 1965, and his policy of improving relations with Catholics and the Republic became known as bridge-building.
Government-backed projects such as Craigavon and the new university at Coleraine were part of a wider plan to show that Northern Ireland could be modern and prosperous.
Catholics welcomed the gestures but judged that real change in housing, jobs and voting was too slow.
Nationalists responded in 1965 when the Nationalist Party under Eddie McAteer agreed to become the official opposition at Stormont for the first time.
O'Neill's reforms split his own party, and hardline unionists saw the Lemass meeting as the first step towards a united Ireland.
Ian Paisley founded the Free Presbyterian Church in 1951, and by the mid-1960s he was the leading Protestant critic of O'Neill's policies.
Paisley and other hardliners opposed the Lemass meeting, arguing that it undermined the Union and Protestant identity.

William Craig, Minister of Home Affairs, was a hardline figure in the cabinet who banned the Derry march of 5 October 1968; O'Neill dismissed him in December 1968 after he spoke in favour of a unilateral declaration of independence.
Unionist MPs in the Stormont parliament and in the party organisation argued that O'Neill was giving away too much to nationalists.
The 'O'Neill must go' campaign, led by Paisley and others from 1966, sought the Prime Minister's removal from office.
O'Neill's position weakened as unionist opposition grew and as violence on both sides increased in 1968 and 1969.

In 1966 Paisley set up the Ulster Constitution Defence Committee and the Ulster Protestant Volunteers, and he was jailed for three months in 1966 for refusing to be bound over after a protest at the Presbyterian General Assembly.
The Ulster Volunteer Force, a loyalist paramilitary group, murdered three people in 1966, including Peter Ward, a Catholic barman, and its leader Gusty Spence was convicted of murder.
O'Neill was the reforming Prime Minister whose policies drove the civil rights movement and whose authority collapsed under its pressure.
He was born in London in 1914 into a landed family with its seat at Shane's Castle, County Antrim, was educated at Eton and became Prime Minister in 1963 after a career in the Stormont cabinet.
He held the post of Minister of Finance from 1956 to 1963, where he developed the economic planning that later shaped his premiership.
He made modernisation and reconciliation the centre of his programme, and he tried to build contact with Catholics and with Dublin.
In 1968 and 1969 he came under pressure from London, from the civil rights movement and from within his own party, and he conceded reforms step by step.
He announced a five-point reform package on 22 November 1968 and explained his policy in the 'Ulster at the Crossroads' broadcast on 9 December 1968.
He resigned as Prime Minister on 28 April 1969 after a crisis in his party, a poor showing in the February election and a series of bomb attacks on water and electricity installations.
He was made a life peer in 1970 as Baron O'Neill of the Maine.
Contemporaries were divided: some hardline unionists accused him of betraying the Union, while nationalists welcomed the gestures but judged them too slow.

Historians generally judge him a modernising economic planner who wished to reform on his own terms; they note that he did not see Catholic grievances as primarily political and that his authority was constrained by his own party.
The McCluskeys founded the Campaign for Social Justice, which turned evidence of discrimination in Dungannon into a national campaign.

Conn and Patricia McCluskey founded the Campaign for Social Justice in Northern Ireland in January 1964 in Dungannon, County Tyrone; it grew out of the Dungannon Homeless Citizens League which they set up in 1963.
Conn McCluskey was a local doctor, and the campaign gathered evidence on discrimination in housing allocation and local jobs, especially by councils in Tyrone and Fermanagh.
It published its findings and lobbied British MPs, which helped to lead to the formation of the Campaign for Democracy in Ulster at Westminster in 1965.
The McCluskeys were participants in the campaign, and their work provided models and evidence for the civil rights movement that followed.
Some unionists dismissed the campaign as a front for republicans, a charge the McCluskeys rejected; they described their aim as equal treatment of citizens.
Historians credit the Campaign for Social Justice with turning discrimination into a public issue before the Civil Rights Association was formed.
The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association was founded in 1967 to campaign for equal rights for Catholics on the British model.
NICRA was founded in January 1967 and drew together nationalists, socialists, trade unionists and some liberal Protestants.
Its demands included one man, one vote in local elections, an end to gerrymandering, fair allocation of council houses on a points system and laws against discrimination by public bodies.
It also demanded the repeal of the Special Powers Act and the disbanding of the B Specials.
Its first march was from Coalisland to Dungannon on 24 August 1968, and it was followed by marches in Derry, Newry and Belfast.
The movement used peaceful marches and sit-ins to draw attention to discrimination, and it sought British support for reform.

The authorities banned or obstructed many marches, which led to confrontations with the police and loyalist counter-demonstrators, as when supporters of Paisley blocked a march in Armagh on 30 November 1968.
Westminster elections already used one man, one vote, so the demand applied to local elections, where the franchise was restricted to ratepayers and their spouses.
The banned civil rights march in Derry was broken up by police, and the footage shown on television turned the movement into an international story.
The Derry march of 5 October 1968 was organised by NICRA and was banned by the Minister of Home Affairs, William Craig.
Marchers who defied the ban were confronted by RUC officers, who used batons on the crowd in the Duke Street area.
Television footage of the violence, in which the Westminster MP Gerry Fitt was among those struck, was broadcast widely and shocked opinion in Britain and Ireland.
The event is seen as the start of the civil rights crisis of 1968 and 1969, as it moved the movement from marches to confrontation.
Nationalists in Derry saw the police action as proof of discrimination, while unionists blamed the civil rights organisers for provoking disorder.
The Derry disturbances led to the formation of the Derry Citizens' Action Committee, with John Hume as vice-chairman, and to pressure from the British government on O'Neill to introduce reforms.
The five-point package of 22 November 1968 promised a points system for allocating council houses.
It promised an ombudsman, a Parliamentary Commissioner, to investigate complaints against government departments.
It promised that Londonderry Corporation would be replaced by a development commission.
It promised to withdraw the Special Powers Act when the situation allowed, and to end the company vote in local elections while reviewing the wider franchise.
One man, one vote in local elections was not in the package, and O'Neill's party accepted it only in April 1969.
The People's Democracy march to Derry was attacked at Burntollet, and the violence that followed brought O'Neill's government to its end.
People's Democracy was formed in October 1968 by students at Queen's University Belfast, including Bernadette Devlin, in the wake of the Derry march.
The People's Democracy march from Belfast to Derry began on 1 January 1969, a few dozen marchers aiming to protest against discrimination and to press for one man, one vote.
On 4 January 1969 the marchers were attacked by a loyalist crowd near Burntollet Bridge, among whom were off-duty B Specials, and many marchers were injured.
That night RUC officers entered the Catholic Bogside, and residents built barricades and declared the area Free Derry.
Marchers and civil rights supporters accused the RUC of failing to protect the march, which damaged confidence in the police among Catholics.
The Stormont general election of 24 February 1969 left the Unionist Party divided, and O'Neill held his own seat at Bannside against Paisley by 1,414 votes.
The Mid Ulster by-election of 17 April 1969 returned Bernadette Devlin, and in the same month O'Neill's party agreed to accept one man, one vote in local elections.
O'Neill resigned on 28 April 1969 and was succeeded by James Chichester-Clark, who defeated Brian Faulkner in the party vote by a single vote.

Bombs at water and electricity installations in March and April 1969 were first blamed on the IRA, but were later attributed to loyalists of the Ulster Volunteer Force, and they undermined O'Neill's position.
Devlin was a student leader and civil rights activist who became the youngest woman elected to Westminster at the time.
Bernadette Devlin was born in 1947 in Cookstown, County Tyrone, and studied psychology at Queen's University Belfast.
She became a leader of People's Democracy and a prominent speaker in the civil rights campaign in 1968 and 1969.
She was elected MP for Mid Ulster at a by-election in April 1969, aged twenty-one, as a candidate of the unity and civil rights movement.
She was a participant in the People's Democracy campaign that organised the Belfast to Derry march of January 1969.
She wrote a memoir, The Price of My Soul, published in 1969, which presented the civil rights struggle from her own perspective.
Contemporary nationalists saw her as a symbol of youth and defiance, while unionists regarded her as a dangerous agitator.
Historians tend to view her as a key figure who brought the civil rights movement into Westminster politics.
She was convicted of incitement to riot after the Battle of the Bogside in August 1969 and served a prison sentence in 1970.
On 31 January 1972, the day after Bloody Sunday, she struck the Home Secretary Reginald Maudling in the House of Commons.
She lost her Westminster seat in February 1974, and in January 1981 she and her husband were seriously wounded by loyalist gunmen at their home.
Paisley's opposition to O'Neill made him the most visible unionist critic of reform before 1969.
Ian Paisley was born in 1926 in Armagh and founded the Free Presbyterian Church in 1951.
Before 1969 he was a minister and public campaigner, who organised rallies and protests against O'Neill's policies.
He opposed the Lemass meeting and argued that the Prime Minister was undermining Protestant identity and the Union.
He was a participant in the 'O'Neill must go' campaign, and his rallies mobilised grassroots Protestant opinion.
Contemporaries saw him as the voice of hardline unionism, and many moderate unionists were uneasy about his methods.
Historians argue that his campaign against O'Neill helped to shift unionist politics towards the hardline position of the 1970s.
In 1966 he was jailed for three months, and in April 1970 he won the Bannside seat at Stormont that O'Neill had vacated.
Success: O'Neill's reforms conceded much of the civil rights programme, including a points system for housing, an ombudsman and, by April 1969, one man, one vote in local elections.
Limit: the reforms came late, after the Derry march of October 1968 and British pressure, and many civil rights leaders judged them concessions forced by protest.
Success: the movement put discrimination on the British political agenda and brought the question of Northern Ireland's government into the open.
Failure: O'Neill could not carry his party or the unionist community, and his resignation in April 1969 showed the limits of reform from above.
Contemporary view: nationalists welcomed the movement's gains but argued that the state had not yet ended discrimination.
Contemporary view: unionists were divided, with hardliners blaming the civil rights movement for provoking violence.
Later view: historians differ on whether O'Neill was a sincere reformer who was undermined, or a leader whose reforms were too limited and too late.
Derry had a college but not a university, and its nationalist majority saw the choice of a new university site as a test of fair treatment.
Magee College in Derry had been founded in 1865 by the Presbyterian Church, taught degrees of Trinity College Dublin, and did not have full university status.
The Robbins Report of 1963 recommended a large expansion of higher education across the United Kingdom, and Northern Ireland began planning a second university alongside Queen's University Belfast.
Derry's population was mostly Catholic, and the city had higher unemployment and more emigration than the Belfast area.
Nationalists in Derry argued that the city, the second largest in Northern Ireland, deserved the new university after decades of neglect, and many Derry unionists also wanted it.
The question of location was therefore not only academic: it was a test of whether Stormont treated the west of the province fairly.
Derry's grievances over the university were part of the wider 'west of the Bann' complaint about public investment.
The new university was planned as a single institution, so choosing one town meant that no other town could host it.
The Lockwood Committee was set up to advise on the site, and a cross-community campaign in Derry pressed for the city to be chosen.
The Lockwood Committee, chaired by Sir John Lockwood, was appointed in 1963 to advise on the development of higher education in Northern Ireland, including the siting of the new university.
The University for Derry Committee was formed to campaign for the city, and it was chaired by John Hume, then a young teacher.
The campaign drew support from across the community, including some Protestant and business figures in Derry, as well as nationalists.
The campaign argued that Derry had the population, the existing college buildings and the need for jobs that justified a university.
The Lockwood Committee reported in February 1965 and recommended Coleraine rather than Derry.
After the report, Derry supporters organised a motorcade to Stormont in February 1965 to protest against the decision.
The committee heard evidence from the Derry campaign and from other towns competing for the university.
The government accepted the Lockwood recommendation, and the decision was carried by the unionist majority in the Stormont parliament.
The government accepted the Lockwood recommendation that the new university be sited at Coleraine, County Londonderry, a smaller town about 30 miles from Derry.
Derry's representatives argued that the choice had been made on political grounds, and the allegation that 'faceless men' had shaped it became a popular slogan.
The Stormont debate and vote produced a unionist majority in favour of Coleraine, while nationalist members and some Derry unionists opposed the decision.
The government argued that Coleraine offered a central site, good access and room for expansion, and that Derry's case had been fully considered.
The Derry campaign continued after the decision, and the controversy remained a live issue in Derry politics for several years.
The decision was widely seen in Derry as a sign that Stormont would not give the city equal treatment in public investment.
Hume was the chair of the University for Derry campaign and became the nationalist leader who pressed for reform through constitutional politics.
John Hume was born in Derry in 1937, trained as a teacher at St Patrick's College, Maynooth, and taught in Derry.
He chaired the University for Derry Committee, bringing together nationalists and some unionists behind a single campaign for the city.
He was a participant in the campaign, and he led deputations and public protests for the university in 1964 and 1965.
Contemporaries saw him as a moderate and effective campaigner who could organise across the community, though some unionists saw him as a nationalist agitator.
Historians regard the campaign as an early step in his career, and as a sign of his commitment to constitutional and cross-community politics.
The campaign shaped his later politics, which combined social grievances with constitutional nationalism, and led to his later role in the SDLP.
Hume was elected to Stormont for Foyle in 1969 and to Westminster for Foyle in 1983.
He was also a founder of the credit union movement in Derry and a leader of the Derry Citizens' Action Committee formed after 5 October 1968.
1963: the Robbins Report prompts the search for a site for a second university in Northern Ireland, and the Lockwood Committee is appointed.
1963 to 1965: the Lockwood Committee investigates possible sites, while the University for Derry Committee campaigns for Derry.
February 1965: the Lockwood Committee reports in favour of Coleraine, and Derry supporters travel to Stormont by motorcade.
1965: the Stormont government accepts the recommendation after a debate and a unionist majority vote.
1965 to 1968: planning and building of the new university at Coleraine proceed while the Derry campaign continues.
1968: the New University of Ulster opens at Coleraine, with its first students arriving that autumn.
October 1968: the Derry civil rights march of 5 October and the formation of the Derry Citizens' Action Committee link the university issue to housing and voting grievances.
Both sides used the controversy to make arguments about fairness, and the decision became a symbol of regional and religious inequality.
Derry campaigners used posters, pamphlets and public meetings to present the case for the city, and their message was that Derry had been overlooked.
The government and its supporters presented Coleraine as a sound academic and economic choice, and they rejected charges of sectarian motives.
Critics linked the decision to other public investment decisions, including the choice of Craigavon, a new city between Lurgan and Portadown, designated in 1965.
The 'west of the Bann' grievance held that new industry and public bodies were located east of the Bann, leaving Derry and the west with fewer jobs.
The University controversy therefore fed a wider belief that discrimination was built into government decisions, not only into local councils.
The controversy helped nationalists argue that they had no fair share of public investment, a view that the civil rights movement later made central.
The university decision was one of several decisions of the mid-1960s that Derry nationalists saw as favouring the east.
The Benson Report of 1963 recommended closing unprofitable railway lines, and the Derry Road line from Portadown through Omagh to Derry was closed in 1965.
The closure left Derry without a direct rail link to Belfast and, nationalists argued, reinforced its isolation.
The Matthew Report of 1963 proposed new growth centres around Belfast, and the new city of Craigavon in County Armagh was seen in Derry as drawing investment east.
Derry had traditional industries such as shirt-making, which employed mainly women, while male unemployment was high.
The Londonderry Corporation boundaries drawn in 1936 gave unionists control of a council in a majority Catholic city, so the city's own representatives could not influence these decisions.
Housing in Derry was overcrowded, which in 1968 produced direct action by housing protesters.
These grievances together created the sense that the university decision was one in a series of decisions against the west.
For Derry, the decision confirmed a sense of neglect and gave the city's nationalists a clear example of unfair treatment by Stormont.
The university campaign gave Hume experience of cross-community organisation, which he later used in the SDLP and in the power-sharing debates.
Derry's grievances over the university fed directly into the demands of the civil rights movement in Derry in 1968 and 1969.
The controversy showed that economic and educational investment could become a political issue in its own right.
Unionists regarded the decision as a rational choice of site and an example of the government's modernising programme.
Historians view the decision as one of several episodes that deepened nationalist distrust of Stormont in the mid-1960s.
Magee became part of the University of Ulster formed in 1984, giving Derry a university presence that the campaign had sought.
Strength of the nationalist case: Derry had the larger population, existing college buildings, and high unemployment, which gave a strong economic argument.
Strength of the government's case: Coleraine offered a central site and room to grow, and the Lockwood Committee had made its recommendation on those grounds.
Limit of the nationalist case: the 'faceless men' allegation was not backed by proof, and the decision followed a formal committee process.
Limit of the government's case: the choice of Coleraine, with a small population, weakened the argument that public investment was evenly spread.
Contemporary view: Derry nationalists saw the decision as proof of discrimination, while unionists saw it as a planning matter.
Later view: historians tend to see the controversy as a symbol of the wider inequality in public investment, rather than as proof of a single plot.
Both sides accepted that Derry needed higher education, so the dispute was over the site rather than the principle.
The Apprentice Boys' parade in Derry in August 1969 led to street fighting, and British troops were sent in to restore order.
On 12 August 1969 the Apprentice Boys' parade passed close to the Bogside, and stone-throwing and clashes with the RUC began.
The Battle of the Bogside lasted from 12 to 14 August 1969, and residents erected barricades that became the 'Free Derry' area.
British troops were deployed in Derry on 14 August 1969, the start of the army's long involvement in internal security.
Rioting in Belfast on 14 and 15 August 1969 saw Catholic streets such as Bombay Street burned and several people killed, most of them Catholics.
Thousands of families, most of them Catholic, fled their homes in Belfast, and refugee centres were set up in the Republic and in Catholic parishes.
The events of August 1969 are often treated as the start of the Troubles in their most violent form.
The Hunt Report, published on 10 October 1969 by a committee led by Lord Hunt, recommended a reformed, unarmed RUC under a police authority.
It recommended that the B Specials be disbanded, and the Ulster Special Constabulary was stood down in April 1970.
The Ulster Defence Regiment, formed in 1970 as a part-time regiment of the British army, replaced the B Specials in local security duties.

After the August rioting the British government issued the Downing Street Declaration of 19 August 1969, which reaffirmed that Northern Ireland would not cease to be part of the United Kingdom without the consent of its people, and promised reforms.
Chichester-Clark's two years as Prime Minister saw reform under pressure from London and a rising tide of violence.
James Chichester-Clark became Prime Minister on 1 May 1969, defeating Brian Faulkner in the party vote by 17 to 16.
He presided over the Battle of the Bogside and the disbanding of the B Specials, and was pressed by London to carry out the reforms of the Hunt Report.
His government announced a points system for housing allocation, the creation of a Housing Executive (established in 1971) and reform of local government.
Unionist hardliners saw these steps as surrender, while nationalists said they came too late.
He resigned on 20 March 1971 after the British government refused to send more troops and reinforce the security policy he wanted.
Brian Faulkner succeeded him as Prime Minister on 23 March 1971.
The split in the IRA at the end of 1969 created the Provisional IRA, which argued that the Catholic community needed armed defence.
The IRA split in December 1969 into the Provisional IRA, led by figures such as Seán Mac Stíofáin, and the Official IRA, led by Cathal Goulding.
The Provisionals argued that the IRA must defend Catholic areas and that British forces should be driven out, a position that gained support after August 1969.
Provisional Sinn Féin was set up in January 1970 to match the new military wing.
The Falls Road curfew of 3 to 5 July 1970 saw troops search houses for weapons, and four civilians were killed during the operation.
The Social Democratic and Labour Party was founded on 21 August 1970 by nationalist politicians including Gerry Fitt, John Hume, Austin Currie and Paddy Devlin, with Fitt as leader.
The Alliance Party was founded in April 1970 as a cross-community party, and it later chose Oliver Napier as leader.
The Official IRA, which stressed a left-wing political strategy, declared a ceasefire in May 1972, and the Provisionals became the main republican force.
The SDLP withdrew from Stormont in July 1971 after the army shot dead two men in Derry, Séamus Cusack and Desmond Beattie.
Loyalist paramilitary groups grew in response to the republican campaign, and they attacked Catholic civilians and republicans.
The Ulster Volunteer Force was revived in 1966, and in the early years of the Troubles it carried out attacks on Catholic targets.
The Ulster Volunteer Force was revived in 1966 and murdered three people that year, and in the early years of the Troubles it carried out attacks on Catholic targets.
The Ulster Defence Association, a loose umbrella of loyalist groups, was formed in 1971 and grew rapidly in working-class Protestant areas; it was a legal organisation until 1992.

The bombing of McGurk's Bar in Belfast on 4 December 1971 killed 15 Catholic civilians; the police first blamed the IRA, but the Police Ombudsman concluded in 2011 that the Ulster Volunteer Force was responsible.
Loyalist groups claimed that their violence defended the Union and Protestant areas, but most of their victims were Catholic civilians.
William Craig founded the Ulster Vanguard movement in 1972, which held large rallies against the loss of Stormont's powers.
Loyalist paramilitaries killed hundreds of people between 1969 and 1993, the great majority of them civilians, mostly Catholics.
Faulkner was the Prime Minister who introduced internment and then saw the government collapse under the pressure of violence and British policy.
Brian Faulkner, born in 1921, had been Minister of Home Affairs in 1959–63 and Minister of Commerce under O'Neill until he resigned in 1969; he became Prime Minister in March 1971.
He succeeded James Chichester-Clark on 23 March 1971, winning a party vote against William Craig.
He asked London to authorise internment, which began on 9 August 1971, and he defended it as necessary to stop the IRA.
He participated in the talks with Westminster on the control of security, and he insisted that Stormont should keep its powers over policing and order.
Contemporary unionists praised his firmness on security, while nationalists saw internment as a deliberate attack on the Catholic community.

He resigned on 24 March 1972 when Westminster took over security, and historians generally see him as a pragmatic, able politician whose attempts at reform were swamped by violence he could not contain.
He offered the opposition committee chairmanships at Stormont in 1971, and the SDLP rejected the offer and left Stormont after the July 1971 shootings in Derry.
Internment was introduced on 9 August 1971 and was applied mainly to republicans, and the violence that followed killed civilians.
Internment, the detention of suspects without trial, began on 9 August 1971 in Operation Demetrius, which arrested about 340 people in its first sweep.
Those arrested were almost entirely Catholic, and many had no paramilitary links; no loyalist was interned until 1973.
Interrogation methods known as the five techniques, which included hooding and sleep deprivation, were used on fourteen internees, known as the Hooded Men.
The Compton and Parker inquiries examined the methods, and in 1978 the European Court of Human Rights found that the techniques were inhuman and degrading, but not torture.

At Ballymurphy in west Belfast, eleven civilians died during army operations of 9 to 11 August 1971, including a priest, Father Hugh Mullan; a coroner's inquest in 2021 found that those killed were innocent.
Nationalists saw internment as proof of bias, and it increased recruitment to the Provisional IRA; 1971 was the first year in which Troubles deaths passed 100.
A civil rights march in Derry against internment ended with British paratroopers killing thirteen civilians, an event that deepened the conflict.
The NICRA march of 30 January 1972 in Derry protested against internment and was banned by the authorities.
Soldiers of the 1st Battalion, Parachute Regiment, entered the Bogside, and they fired on marchers and bystanders, killing thirteen people on the day.
A fourteenth man who was wounded died some months later, and most of the dead were shot while unarmed or while fleeing.
The Widgery Report of 19 April 1972, by the Lord Chief Justice, largely accepted the army's account, and nationalists widely rejected it.

The Saville Inquiry, reporting in June 2010, found that the soldiers' firing was unjustified and unjustifiable and that none of the casualties had posed a threat; the Prime Minister, David Cameron, apologised.
The killings led to the burning of the British embassy in Dublin on 2 February 1972, and they increased recruitment to the Provisional IRA.
Stormont was suspended and government was taken over by Westminster after the British government refused to hand security powers to Stormont.
Faulkner demanded control of security from Westminster, but the British government under Edward Heath refused.
Faulkner and his ministers resigned on 24 March 1972 in protest, and Westminster suspended the Stormont parliament from 30 March.
The Northern Ireland (Temporary Provisions) Act 1972 introduced Direct Rule from 30 March 1972, placing the province under a Secretary of State.
William Whitelaw was the first Secretary of State for Northern Ireland and governed with civil servants, two ministers of state and the army.

Direct Rule was meant to be temporary, but apart from the brief power-sharing executive of 1974 it lasted throughout the period to 1993, because the parties could not agree a power-sharing settlement acceptable to both communities.
The Stormont parliament was formally abolished in 1973 by the Northern Ireland Constitution Act.
Whitelaw granted special category status to paramilitary prisoners in June 1972, and he met leaders of the Provisional IRA in London on 7 July 1972 during a short ceasefire, talks which failed.

Direct Rule lasted because unionists would not accept an assembly with nationalist participation, nationalists would not accept a return to majority rule, and London wished to avoid a return to the old system.
The IRA bombings of 21 July 1972 killed nine people in Belfast, and the army's Operation Motorman broke the IRA's no-go areas.
On 21 July 1972, the Provisional IRA set off about twenty bombs in Belfast in the space of about an hour and a half, a day that became known as Bloody Friday.
Nine people died in the bombings, and about 130 were injured, and the attacks shocked public opinion in Britain and Northern Ireland.
Operation Motorman, launched on 31 July 1972 with more than 12,000 soldiers, moved into the no-go areas in Belfast and Derry, including the Creggan and the Bogside.
The operation dismantled the barricades and restored government control over areas that the IRA had controlled.
The IRA's campaign continued after Motorman, and 1972 was the deadliest year of the Troubles, with nearly 500 deaths.
By the end of 1972 about 700 people had died in the conflict since 1969.
Discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting gave the civil rights movement a sustained base of grievance.
The state's security forces, the B Specials and the RUC, were seen by Catholics as partisan, which turned protest into a security issue.
The Provisional IRA gave the Catholic community a military organisation, and its campaign drew the British army into the conflict.
Loyalist paramilitaries defended Protestant areas and attacked Catholic civilians, which increased the cycle of reprisal.
Internment and Bloody Sunday hardened attitudes on both sides and made political compromise harder.
Stormont's inability to share power with nationalists meant there was no political institution capable of containing the violence.
The decline of Stormont had many causes: civil rights protest, the failure to reform fast enough, the IRA campaign, and the British government's decision to take over security.
Achievement: the end of Stormont removed an institution that nationalists had rejected since 1921, and it opened the way for new political settlements.
Failure: the Stormont government could not contain the violence, and its reliance on internment alienated the Catholic community.
Contemporary view: unionists saw the suspension of Stormont as a betrayal by Westminster, while nationalists welcomed it as the end of an unfair system.
Later view: historians argue that the 1972 settlement was forced by violence, and that the Unionist government's decline was a product of its own policies as well as republican action.
Contemporary view: the British government saw Direct Rule as a temporary measure, but it proved to be a long-term arrangement.
After the suspension of Stormont, the British government held a border poll and published a plan for a devolved Assembly based on power sharing and an Irish dimension.
A border poll held on 8 March 1973 asked voters whether Northern Ireland should remain part of the United Kingdom or join a united Ireland, and nationalists boycotted it.
About 98.9 per cent of those who voted chose to stay in the United Kingdom, but turnout was only about 59 per cent because of the boycott.
The poll did not settle the constitutional question for nationalists, since the boycott left their view unrecorded.

The White Paper of March 1973, Northern Ireland Constitutional Proposals, proposed a new Assembly elected by proportional representation, with an executive in which unionists and nationalists shared power.
The White Paper also proposed a Council of Ireland linking Belfast and Dublin, which many unionists regarded as a first step towards a united Ireland.
The Northern Ireland Constitution Act of July 1973 abolished the old Stormont parliament and provided for the new Assembly, with the Secretary of State keeping control of security.
The Assembly election of June 1973 produced a power-sharing executive that took office on 1 January 1974, led by Brian Faulkner.
The Assembly election of 28 June 1973 used the single transferable vote, and it returned unionists, nationalists and Alliance members.
The Ulster Unionist Party was split between Faulkner's supporters, who accepted power sharing, and unionists who opposed it, including Paisley's Democratic Unionists and William Craig's Vanguard.
Brian Faulkner became Chief Executive of the power-sharing executive, with Gerry Fitt of the SDLP as his Deputy Chief Executive.

John Hume of the SDLP became Minister of Commerce, and Oliver Napier of the Alliance Party was Head of Legal Affairs; other SDLP members included Austin Currie (Housing) and Paddy Devlin (Health and Social Services).
The executive took office on 1 January 1974, and the Assembly began to operate in the same month.
The Assembly had 78 members, and the election gave the SDLP 19 seats and Alliance 8, while anti-agreement unionists took about as many seats as Faulkner's supporters.
The Sunningdale conference of 6 to 9 December 1973 produced an agreement on the Council of Ireland, the status of Northern Ireland and policing.
The conference was held at Sunningdale Park in Berkshire from 6 to 9 December 1973, attended by the British Prime Minister Edward Heath and the Taoiseach Liam Cosgrave.
The Northern Ireland parties present were Faulkner's Unionists, the SDLP represented by Fitt and Hume, and the Alliance Party.
The agreement set up a Council of Ireland with a council of ministers, seven from each side, and a consultative assembly of 60 members drawn equally from the Dáil and the Northern Ireland Assembly.

The Irish government accepted that Northern Ireland's status would not change without the consent of a majority there, and the British government stated that it would support a united Ireland if a majority wished it.
A Law Enforcement Commission was set up to examine how to deal with fugitive offenders and a possible all-Ireland court, and both governments promised policing acceptable to both communities.
The agreement was signed on 9 December 1973, and the British government said it was committed to implementing it through the Assembly.
Opponents noted that the Irish government did not formally change Articles 2 and 3 of its constitution at Sunningdale, and the Boland case reinforced that concern.

Kevin Boland, a former Fianna Fáil minister, challenged the Irish government's declaration on status in the courts, and the Irish government's defence that the declaration did not alter the constitutional claim damaged Faulkner's position among unionists.
The Ulster Unionist Council voted by 427 to 374 on 4 January 1974 to reject the Council of Ireland, and Faulkner resigned as party leader on 7 January 1974.
Harry West replaced Faulkner as leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, and Faulkner later formed the Unionist Party of Northern Ireland.
The executive's work on housing, health and education was overshadowed by the arguments over the Council of Ireland, which Faulkner tried to postpone.
The Conservative government of Edward Heath lost the February 1974 election, and Harold Wilson formed a Labour government in March 1974, with Merlyn Rees as Secretary of State.

Harold Wilson, the Prime Minister, said in a televised broadcast on 25 May 1974 that the strikers and their backers were 'sponging' on Westminster and British democracy, a remark that became known as the 'spongers' broadcast and angered unionists.
Faulkner resigned as Chief Executive on 28 May 1974 after his proposal to delay the Council of Ireland's later stages was rejected by his SDLP and Alliance colleagues, and the executive collapsed.
Unionist opponents of Sunningdale united against it, and a general strike in May 1974 brought the executive down.
The United Ulster Unionist Council (UUUC) was formed in January 1974 by unionist parties and groups opposed to Sunningdale, including Paisley's supporters and the Vanguard movement.
In the Westminster general election of 28 February 1974, the UUUC won eleven of the twelve Northern Ireland seats, and Gerry Fitt kept Belfast West for the SDLP.

The Ulster Workers' Council, led by Harry Murray and others and backed by loyalist paramilitaries, called a general strike that began on 15 May 1974, and it cut electricity supplies and paralysed services.
Merlyn Rees, the Secretary of State in Harold Wilson's Labour government, and the army did not confront the strikers directly, and the power-sharing executive was unable to govern.
The Dublin and Monaghan bombings of 17 May 1974, two days after the strike began, killed 33 people in the Republic; see the notes on terrorism and the Republic's response.
Faulkner resigned as Chief Executive on 28 May 1974 after the other unionist members of the executive were unwilling to negotiate with the strikers, and the executive collapsed.
The strike drew on workers in power generation and essential industries, and it was enforced by roadblocks and intimidation.
The Assembly had voted by 44 to 28 on 14 May 1974 to support the Sunningdale policy, the day before the strike began.
Unionists rejected the Council of Ireland as a step towards a united Ireland, which many believed was the aim of nationalists in the executive.
The Assembly's power-sharing arrangements were not supported by a majority of unionists, and the Unionist Party's own members split over the agreement.
The Ulster Workers' Council strike showed that a determined protest by loyalist workers could paralyse Northern Ireland's economy and government.
The British government's reluctance to use force against the strikers signalled to unionists that London would not defend the executive.
Republican violence continued during the executive's term, and it made moderate unionists more fearful about security and nationalist intentions.
The executive had no mechanism to build consent among the unionist community, which was essential to any settlement that depended on majority support.
Unionist opponents of the agreement argued that it was imposed on the majority, and they used this claim to justify the strike.
Faulkner accepted power sharing at Sunningdale and paid the political price, and his record shows both courage and a misreading of unionist opinion.
Faulkner served as Chief Executive from January 1974, after leading the Unionist Party into the Sunningdale settlement.
He took part directly in the Sunningdale conference and was the main unionist negotiator in the talks with the British and Irish governments.
He was a Unionist who accepted a Council of Ireland, which was a deliberate and costly decision that split his party and cost him the support of many unionists.
He resigned on 28 May 1974 when the Ulster Workers' Council strike made the executive impossible to run, and he never returned to office.
Contemporaries were divided: loyalist opponents denounced him as a traitor, while nationalists and the British government regarded him as a leader who had taken a serious risk for peace.
Historians give him credit for courage and realism, but they argue that he underestimated the depth of unionist opposition and that he lacked consistent British support.
He died in 1977 after a fall from his horse in a hunting accident, and he had been made Baron Faulkner of Downpatrick earlier that year.
He resigned the leadership of the Ulster Unionist Party in January 1974 and later founded the Unionist Party of Northern Ireland, which failed to attract wide support.
Hume was a key architect of the power-sharing executive and argued that cross-community government was the only realistic path to peace.
John Hume served as Minister of Commerce in the power-sharing executive from January 1974, and he was a leading negotiator for the SDLP at Sunningdale.
He argued for power sharing and an Irish dimension, and he believed that a Council of Ireland would give nationalists a stake in the settlement.
He was a participant in the executive, and he defended it against unionist and republican critics during the strike of May 1974.
Contemporaries saw him as one of the most capable nationalist negotiators, although his position was attacked by republicans who rejected any settlement within Northern Ireland.
Seamus Mallon, Hume's SDLP colleague, later called the Belfast Agreement of 1998 'Sunningdale for slow learners', and historians often make this connection between the two settlements.
Hume continued as an SDLP figure after the executive's collapse and became party leader in 1979; see the later notes on the search for a settlement.
The Constitutional Convention, elected on 1 May 1975, tried to restore devolved government, but it collapsed in March 1976 without agreement.
The failure of Sunningdale led Westminster to rely on Direct Rule, with security policy and the administration of the province run from London.
The Anglo-Irish Agreement of 1985 returned to the principle that the Irish government should have a formal role, but it did not restore power sharing.
Sunningdale became the reference point for later debate on whether any settlement could be imposed without majority unionist consent.
Achievement: Sunningdale produced the first power-sharing executive in Northern Ireland, with unionists and nationalists in government together.
Achievement: the agreement set out principles, including consent and an Irish dimension, that later settlements built on.
Failure: the executive lasted only five months, from 1 January to 28 May 1974, and it could not survive a general strike.
Failure: the agreement lacked the consent of the majority of unionists, and the Council of Ireland was rejected as a threat to the Union.
Contemporary view: the British and Irish governments and the SDLP regarded Sunningdale as a sound basis for peace.
Contemporary view: the UUUC and the Ulster Workers' Council regarded it as a betrayal of the Union and a surrender to republicans.
Later view: historians see Sunningdale as a failure that showed both the possibility and the difficulty of a settlement that needed unionist consent.
Later view: the collapse showed that no executive could survive without the support of a majority of unionists, a lesson applied in the Anglo-Irish Agreement and in later talks.
Direct Rule continued after 1974 except for the brief power-sharing executive, and the Peace People brought a popular peace movement onto the streets in 1976.
Direct Rule was restored after the collapse of the executive in 1974, with the Secretary of State and the Northern Ireland Office responsible for government.

The Secretaries of State included Merlyn Rees (1974 to 1976), Roy Mason (1976 to 1979), Humphrey Atkins (1979 to 1981), Jim Prior (1981 to 1984), Douglas Hurd (1984 to 1985), Tom King (1985 to 1989), Peter Brooke (1989 to 1992) and Patrick Mayhew (1992 to 1997).

The Constitutional Convention, elected on 1 May 1975, was meant to find a devolved settlement; its unionist majority recommended a return to majority rule, Westminster rejected this for lacking cross-community support, and it was dissolved in March 1976.
Under 'Ulsterisation' from 1976, the security role of the British army was reduced in favour of the Royal Ulster Constabulary and the Ulster Defence Regiment.
On 10 August 1976 three children of Anne Maguire were killed in Belfast when a car driven by a Provisional IRA volunteer, Danny Lennon, who had been shot by soldiers, crashed into them.
Betty Williams, a Belfast woman who witnessed the crash, and Mairead Corrigan, the children's aunt, led the first peace march, with the journalist Ciaran McKeown as a third founder.
The movement organised large peace rallies in Belfast and across Northern Ireland, and it appealed to both communities to end the violence.
The Peace People were a movement of ordinary people, and they called for an end to paramilitary violence on all sides.
Williams and Corrigan were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for 1976, which was announced in 1977.
Contemporaries praised the movement, but some republicans and loyalists dismissed it as naive, and its support faded after 1977 as the violence continued.

Criminalisation was the policy of treating paramilitary offenders as ordinary criminals: special category status for prisoners was ended on 1 March 1976, and Diplock courts, trials without a jury, had been introduced in 1973.
The prison protests over political status at the Maze prison, known as the H-Blocks, led to the 1981 hunger strikes, which made Bobby Sands a symbol across Ireland.
After special category status ended on 1 March 1976, republican prisoners refused to wear prison uniform, beginning the blanket protest, and in 1978 the protest escalated into the dirty protest.
Bobby Sands began a hunger strike on 1 March 1981 to demand the restoration of political status, and he died on 5 May 1981 after 66 days.
Sands was elected MP for Fermanagh and South Tyrone in April 1981, while he was on hunger strike, and his election gave the protest wide publicity.
Nine further hunger strikers died between May and August 1981, including Francis Hughes, Patsy O'Hara and Kieran Doherty, making ten in all.
The hunger strike ended on 3 October 1981 without political status, although concessions were later made on clothing and remission.
Sinn Féin adopted an electoral strategy in 1981, summed up in the phrase 'the armalite and the ballot box', used by Danny Morrison at the party's October 1981 Ard Fheis.
Owen Carron, Sands's election agent, won the Fermanagh and South Tyrone by-election in August 1981 as an Anti H-Block candidate.
Sinn Féin won five seats in the October 1982 Northern Ireland Assembly election, and Gerry Adams was among those elected, though the members abstained.
In June 1983 Gerry Adams won the West Belfast seat at Westminster, which Gerry Fitt had held since 1966, and Sinn Féin members refused to take their seats there.
The strategy was a deliberate move to build political support, and critics saw it as a cover for continued IRA violence.
Margaret Thatcher declared that 'crime is crime is crime; it is not political', and her government refused to concede political status.
Prisoners had begun an earlier hunger strike in October 1980, which ended on 18 December 1980, and two prisoners were elected to the Dáil in June 1981, including Kieran Doherty.
Adams was the Sinn Féin leader who turned the party into an electoral force, and he became the main republican interlocutor with the British and Irish governments.
Gerry Adams was born in 1948 in Belfast and grew up in a republican family in West Belfast.
He was interned in the early 1970s and in July 1972 was released to take part in the secret talks between the Provisional IRA and William Whitelaw in London.
He was elected president of Sinn Féin in November 1983, a post he held until 2018, and he led the party's move into electoral politics.
He was a participant in the republican movement's talks with the SDLP's John Hume from 1988 and again from 1991 to 1993.

Contemporaries saw him as the political face of the republican movement; in October 1988 the Home Secretary, Douglas Hurd, banned the broadcast of the voices of spokespeople for Sinn Féin and other groups, including Adams, and broadcasters used actors' voices; the ban ended in 1994.

Supporters credit him with leading republicans from armed struggle towards negotiation; critics, including unionists, argued that he used Sinn Féin's electoral strategy to complement the IRA campaign.
Adams has always denied membership of the IRA, though many historians and security sources identify him as a senior republican figure.
He was shot and wounded by loyalist gunmen in Belfast in March 1984, lost his Westminster seat to Joe Hendron of the SDLP in 1992, and regained it in 1997.
The New Ireland Forum brought together the constitutional nationalist parties of Ireland, and its three options were rejected by the British Prime Minister.
The New Ireland Forum was set up in 1983 by the Dublin government, and it included Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael, Labour and the SDLP, while Sinn Féin was excluded.
The unionist parties declined to take part, which meant that its report reflected the views of nationalist parties and the Dublin government.
