The Forum's report, published on 2 May 1984, set out three options: a unitary Irish state, a federal or confederal state, and joint authority by Britain and Ireland, and it said that the unitary state was the preferred option.
At a press conference on 19 November 1984, Margaret Thatcher rejected all three options, saying 'Out, out, out'.
Thatcher's rejection of the Forum's options marked the limits of British willingness to change Northern Ireland's constitutional position in the mid-1980s.
On 12 October 1984 the IRA bombed the Grand Hotel in Brighton, where the Conservative Party conference was being held.
Five people were killed in the bombing, and Margaret Thatcher escaped; the IRA said it would try again, and Patrick Magee was later convicted of planting the bomb.
The Hume–Adams dialogue began in 1988, when the SDLP leader and the Sinn Féin president held talks that were publicly acknowledged.
The talks were controversial, with unionists and some nationalists objecting to contact between the SDLP and Sinn Féin while the IRA campaign continued.
The dialogue resumed in 1991 and produced joint statements in 1993, and historians see it as an important precursor to the peace process.
Thatcher was the British Prime Minister who led the government through the hunger strikes and signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement, a shift in British policy.
Margaret Thatcher was Prime Minister from May 1979 to November 1990, and she made security and the defeat of terrorism central to her policy in Northern Ireland.
She refused to grant political status to the hunger strikers, saying 'crime is crime is crime', and her government held firm during the 1981 protest.
She signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement with the Taoiseach Garret FitzGerald at Hillsborough Castle on 15 November 1985, giving the Irish government a formal consultative role.
She took part in the negotiations at Chequers and Hillsborough, and she signed the Agreement despite strong opposition from unionists.
Contemporary unionists regarded her as having betrayed the Union, while nationalists welcomed the Agreement as a sign of British recognition of an Irish interest.

Historians differ on her motives: some stress the hope of improved security cooperation with Dublin, others the aim of preventing Sinn Féin's growth after 1981, and in her memoirs she acknowledged that security cooperation did not improve as she had hoped.
Her Northern Ireland years saw the IRA killing of Lord Mountbatten on 27 August 1979, the same day as the Warrenpoint ambush that killed eighteen soldiers, and the Brighton bombing.
Molyneaux led the Ulster Unionist Party through the period of the Anglo-Irish Agreement and was the main voice of mainstream unionist opposition.
James Molyneaux was born in 1920, was MP for South Antrim from 1970 and for Lagan Valley from 1983, and he became leader of the Ulster Unionist Party in 1979.
He led the unionist opposition to the Anglo-Irish Agreement, and he worked with Ian Paisley on the 'Ulster says No' campaign.

He took part in the unionist campaign of 1985 and 1986, which included the 'Ulster says No' rally at Belfast City Hall on 23 November 1985 and the resignation of fifteen unionist MPs from Westminster in January 1986.
Contemporaries valued his caution and his commitment to the Union, although some unionists felt he was too passive in opposing the Agreement.
Historians regard him as a steady leader of mainstream unionism who opposed the Agreement without the confrontational style of Paisley.
He favoured the integration of Northern Ireland into the United Kingdom's system of government rather than devolution, and he led the party until 1995.
He cultivated good relations with British ministers in the 1990s, and John Major's government at times relied on Ulster Unionist votes at Westminster.
Hume led the SDLP from 1979 and became the leading constitutional nationalist voice, with his dialogue with Sinn Féin reshaping the search for peace.
John Hume became leader of the SDLP in 1979 and was elected to the European Parliament the same year.
He supported the Anglo-Irish Agreement, arguing that it gave nationalists a role in Northern Ireland's government.
He began the dialogue with Gerry Adams in 1988 and argued that the IRA campaign must end if nationalists were to achieve their goals by dialogue.
He took part in the Brooke–Mayhew talks of 1991 and 1992, which tried to set up a new devolved settlement.
Contemporaries saw him as a moderate and effective nationalist leader, while unionists criticised him for talking to Sinn Féin.

Historians credit him with shaping the nationalist case for a peace process based on consent and dialogue, and his work with Adams and with the Irish government influenced the Downing Street Declaration.
He described the conflict as a problem of three relationships, within Northern Ireland, between North and South and between Ireland and Britain.
The Anglo-Irish Agreement gave the Republic a formal consultative role in Northern Ireland, and it was the biggest British policy shift since Sunningdale.
The Agreement was signed on 15 November 1985 at Hillsborough Castle by Margaret Thatcher and Garret FitzGerald.
It set up an Intergovernmental Conference of ministers, with a permanent joint secretariat at Maryfield near Belfast, through which the Irish government could put forward views on Northern Ireland.
Article 1 affirmed that there would be no change in the status of Northern Ireland without the consent of a majority of its people, and the Irish government's role was consultative only.
Unionists responded with the slogan 'Ulster says No', a large rally at Belfast City Hall on 23 November 1985 and a day of action in March 1986.
Fifteen unionist MPs resigned their Westminster seats in January 1986 to force by-elections, but the Agreement remained in force.

Republicans rejected the Agreement because it did not end British jurisdiction, and Fianna Fáil under Charles Haughey opposed it in the Dáil, but nationalists in the SDLP saw it as a limited but real step towards Irish involvement.
Thatcher's motives included improving cross-border security and winning back nationalist support from Sinn Féin, while the Irish government wanted to protect the SDLP.
The Enniskillen bombing of 1987 became one of the best-known atrocities of the Troubles and increased pressure for peace.
On 8 November 1987, Remembrance Sunday, an IRA bomb exploded at the war memorial in Enniskillen, County Fermanagh, killing eleven people.
The victims were civilians, mostly elderly, who had gathered for the ceremony, and a twelfth person died in 2000 after a long coma.
The IRA said it had intended to attack soldiers, but it admitted that the bombing was a mistake and was widely condemned.
Gordon Wilson, whose daughter Marie was killed, forgave the bombers in a famous BBC interview and called for an end to violence.
The bombing was condemned in Britain, in Ireland and in the United States, and it damaged the IRA's standing.
The talks of 1991 and 1992 failed to produce a settlement, and the Downing Street Declaration of 1993 set out the principles on which later peace efforts were built.
Peter Brooke, as Secretary of State, said in November 1990 that Britain had no selfish strategic or economic interest in Northern Ireland.
The Brooke initiative of 1991 and the Mayhew talks of 1992 brought the parties together in multi-party talks, but they did not produce agreement.
The Downing Street Declaration was issued on 15 December 1993 by Prime Minister John Major and Taoiseach Albert Reynolds.

The declaration said that the Irish people as a whole had the right to self-determination, which could be exercised by agreement between North and South, and it said that a united Ireland would require the consent of a majority in Northern Ireland.

It said that the British government had no selfish strategic or economic interest in Northern Ireland, would legislate for a united Ireland if a majority wished it, and invited republicans to renounce violence and join talks.
It also contained a commitment by the Irish government to establish a forum for peace and reconciliation, and to examine Articles 2 and 3 of its constitution.
Achievement: the Anglo-Irish Agreement gave the Irish government a formal consultative role in Northern Ireland's affairs, a larger role than Sunningdale had given it.
Achievement: the Downing Street Declaration set out principles of consent and self-determination that became the basis for later agreements.
Limit: between 1974 and 1993 no devolved government was restored, and Direct Rule remained the basis of British policy.
Limit: the Hume-Adams dialogue and the Brooke and Mayhew talks did not end the IRA campaign, and violence continued throughout the period.
Contemporary view: nationalists and the Irish government saw the Anglo-Irish Agreement and the Declaration as steps towards justice and peace.
Contemporary view: unionists regarded the Agreement as an infringement of their constitutional rights and denounced the Declaration as a sign that Britain was moving towards a united Ireland.
Later view: historians see the period as one in which the framework for peace was built gradually, through dialogue, agreements and the acceptance of consent as a principle.
The Provisional IRA aimed to force British withdrawal and a united Ireland, and its campaign included bombings in Northern Ireland and Britain.
The Provisional IRA's aim was to end British rule in Northern Ireland and to bring about a united Ireland through a campaign of armed attacks.
Its attacks targeted British soldiers, members of the RUC and UDR, and civilians in bombings, shootings and car bombs.
Bloody Friday on 21 July 1972 saw more than twenty bombs in Belfast city centre, killing nine people.

The Birmingham pub bombings of 21 November 1974 killed 21 people; they were attributed to the Provisional IRA, which never claimed them, and the Birmingham Six convicted of them were freed in 1991 when their convictions were quashed.
The Guildford pub bombings of October 1974 killed five people and were attributed to the Provisional IRA; the Guildford Four convicted of them were freed in 1989.

Lord Mountbatten was killed with three others by an IRA bomb on his boat off Mullaghmore, County Sligo, on 27 August 1979, the same day that eighteen British soldiers were killed in an ambush at Warrenpoint, County Down.
The Brighton bombing of 12 October 1984 killed five people and targeted the Conservative government.
The Enniskillen bombing of 8 November 1987 killed eleven people at a Remembrance Day ceremony.
The Warrington bombing of 20 March 1993 killed two boys, Johnathan Ball and Tim Parry, and injured many more.
The IRA bombed Hyde Park and Regent's Park in London on 20 July 1982, killing eleven soldiers and bandsmen, and Harrods in December 1983, killing six people.
Republican attacks on Protestants in Northern Ireland included the La Mon House bombing of 1978, which killed twelve people, and Teebane in January 1992, where eight Protestant workmen were killed.
The Irish National Liberation Army, formed in 1975, killed 17 people in the Droppin' Well bar bombing in Ballykelly in December 1982, 11 of them soldiers.
Responsibility for deaths during the Troubles was spread across republican and loyalist paramilitaries and the security forces.
About 3,500 people were killed between 1969 and 2001, and about half of them were civilians.
Republican paramilitaries were responsible for about 60 per cent of the deaths, loyalist paramilitaries for about 30 per cent and the security forces for about 10 per cent.
The Provisional IRA was responsible for the largest number of killings, followed by loyalists of the UDA and UVF.
The worst year was 1972, with nearly 500 deaths, and the number of deaths fell sharply in the 1980s.
In 1992 to 1994 loyalist groups killed more people than republican groups, many in sectarian attacks on Catholics.
On 5 February 1992 the UFF killed five Catholic civilians at Sean Graham's bookmakers on the Ormeau Road, Belfast.
The Miami Showband massacre of 31 July 1975 saw UVF members kill three members of a popular band at a fake checkpoint in County Down.
On 23 October 1993 an IRA bomb in a fish shop on the Shankill Road killed ten people, including one of the bombers, and loyalists responded a week later at Greysteel.
The Kingsmill massacre of January 1976 saw ten Protestant workmen shot dead in South Armagh by republicans, who claimed it as a response to earlier loyalist killings of Catholics.

The Loughgall ambush of 8 May 1987 saw the SAS kill eight IRA members and a civilian passer-by when the IRA attacked a police station, and it became central to allegations of a 'shoot to kill' policy.
The Gibraltar shootings of 6 March 1988 saw the SAS kill three unarmed IRA members who were planning an attack, and the incident raised questions about the use of lethal force by the security forces.
The British army and RUC carried out searches, arrests and surveillance operations that disrupted IRA units, but the IRA continued to recruit and attack.
Republican prisoners in the 1970s and 1980s were held in special category and later in the H-Blocks, where their protests kept the issue of political status in the public eye.
Republicans argued that the army's arrests and searches in Catholic areas increased recruitment to the IRA.
The Stalker and Sampson inquiries of 1984 to 1986 investigated allegations that the RUC had shot unarmed republicans in 1982, and the claims fed the 'shoot to kill' controversy.
A cargo of arms from Libya on the ship Eksund was seized by French customs in November 1987, showing how the IRA was supplied for its campaign.
Loyalist paramilitaries opposed British withdrawal and the power-sharing settlements, and they attacked Catholic civilians as well as republicans.
The Ulster Volunteer Force was revived in 1966 and carried out attacks in the early years of the Troubles, including bombings and shootings.
The Ulster Defence Association was formed in 1971 as an umbrella for local loyalist groups, and its killing wing, the Ulster Freedom Fighters, was formed in 1973.
The bombing of McGurk's Bar in Belfast on 4 December 1971 killed 15 Catholic civilians; police first blamed the IRA, but the Police Ombudsman concluded in 2011 that the UVF was responsible.

The UVF carried out the bombings in Dublin and Monaghan on 17 May 1974, which killed 33 people and an unborn child and are the largest loss of life in a single day of the Troubles; claims of security force collusion were never proven.
The Greysteel massacre of 30 October 1993 saw the Ulster Freedom Fighters kill eight people at a Halloween dance in the Rising Sun bar, County Londonderry, a week after the Shankill bomb.
Loyalist paramilitaries claimed to be defending the Union, but most of their victims were Catholic civilians with no paramilitary links.
UVF and UDA gunmen carried out attacks on Catholic bars and homes in Belfast during the 1970s, and attacks on Catholic workers on the roads.
Some loyalist groups carried out sectarian murders of Catholics that were marked by torture and brutality, and the Shankill Butchers were the most notorious.
The Shankill Butchers were a UVF gang based on the Shankill Road in west Belfast, who abducted and killed Catholics at night between 1975 and 1977.
The gang was led by Lenny Murphy, and eleven members were convicted in 1979 of a series of murders, receiving many life sentences.
Many victims were killed with knives and hatchets, which led to widespread revulsion in both communities.
The gang's activities showed how sectarian violence could develop outside the formal paramilitary chains of command, and Murphy himself was shot dead in 1982.
Both republicans and loyalists used murals, publications and political statements to shape public opinion, and the British government sought to restrict broadcasts.
Republican murals in the Falls and Bogside celebrated IRA volunteers and the hunger strikers, and they became a central feature of the political landscape.
Loyalist murals in Protestant areas celebrated the UVF and UDA and presented their violence as a defence of loyal communities.
Republicans used publications such as An Phoblacht to present their case, and their statements were sought by international media.

In October 1988 the British government banned the broadcast of the voices of spokesmen for Sinn Féin and ten other organisations, including loyalist groups, and broadcasters used actors' voices; the ban was lifted in 1994.
The ban was intended to deny publicity to terrorist groups, and critics said it restricted freedom of expression.
Irish-American support for republicans provided funds and publicity for the republican campaign.
In the Republic, Section 31 of the Broadcasting Authority Act barred broadcasters from interviewing spokesmen for the IRA and, from 1977, Sinn Féin, and it was allowed to lapse in 1994.
The republican movement published An Phoblacht, and its propaganda stressed the British occupation and the hunger strikers as martyrs.
The Republic's government responded to the violence of August 1969 with a broadcast, emergency aid and a border presence, but the Arms Crisis of 1970 divided the Fianna Fáil government.

On 13 August 1969 the Taoiseach Jack Lynch broadcast that the Irish government 'can no longer stand by' while Catholics were attacked in Belfast and Derry, and he called for a United Nations peacekeeping force.
The Irish army set up field hospitals at the border and the government provided relief for refugees fleeing Belfast and Derry, with camps at Gormanston and elsewhere.

The Arms Crisis of May 1970 followed allegations that ministers had planned to import arms for Northern nationalists using money voted for relief, and Lynch dismissed Charles Haughey and Neil Blaney from the government on 6 May 1970.
Haughey, Captain James Kelly, John Kelly and Albert Luykx were tried for conspiracy to import arms and acquitted in October 1970.

After Bloody Sunday the Irish government declared a day of mourning and recalled its ambassador from London, and the British embassy in Dublin was burned on 2 February 1972 by a crowd, which the government condemned.
The IRA was declared an unlawful organisation in the Republic in 1936, and membership remained illegal under the Offences against the State Act 1939.
The Offences against the State (Amendment) Act 1972 allowed a Garda chief superintendent's belief to be evidence of IRA membership, and it was passed in December 1972 after bombs in Dublin.
The Special Criminal Court was reactivated in 1972 to try offences connected with paramilitary violence without a jury.
The Republic's government under Liam Cosgrave supported the Sunningdale settlement and its Council of Ireland, which was intended to show Dublin's commitment to cross-border cooperation.
Garda cooperation with the RUC increased, but extradition from the Republic of people wanted in Northern Ireland remained a point of tension between Dublin and London.
The Criminal Law (Jurisdiction) Act 1976 allowed some cross-border offences to be tried in the Republic.

The Emergency Powers Act 1976 followed the IRA killing of the British ambassador, Christopher Ewart-Biggs, and led President Cearbhall Ó Dálaigh to refer the bill to the Supreme Court and then resign.
The Extradition (European Convention on the Suppression of Terrorism) Act 1987 was passed after the Enniskillen bombing.
Garret FitzGerald, Taoiseach from 1981 to 1982 and from 1982 to 1987, pursued the New Ireland Forum and signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement with Margaret Thatcher in 1985.
Charles Haughey, Taoiseach from 1987 to 1992, returned Fianna Fáil to power and kept the Anglo-Irish Agreement's framework in place.
Unionists complained that the Republic had too much influence through the Agreement's Intergovernmental Conference.
Extradition and cross-border security cooperation were recurring issues, and the Anglo-Irish Agreement put security cooperation on a formal footing.
Haughey and Thatcher held a summit in Dublin in December 1980 that agreed to study the 'totality of relationships' between the two islands.
Fianna Fáil under Haughey opposed the Anglo-Irish Agreement in the Dáil in 1985, but kept its framework when he returned to government in 1987.
Impact: terrorism killed large numbers of civilians and security force members, and it made political compromise harder by hardening attitudes on all sides.
Impact: republican and loyalist campaigns shaped British policy, with security measures and political initiatives both shaped by the need to contain violence.
Failure: neither the IRA nor the loyalist groups achieved their stated aims, and the main ceasefires came in 1994, after the period covered here.
Failure: terrorism deepened sectarian divisions, and its victims in both communities created lasting grievances.
Contemporary view: the British and Irish governments condemned terrorism and sought to isolate paramilitaries from political influence.
Contemporary view: republicans argued that the IRA was defending the Catholic community and fighting an occupying power, while loyalists claimed to defend the Union.
Later view: historians point out that most of the killing was done by paramilitary groups, not the state, and that the long campaign persuaded many in each group that violence could not win.
The Troubles caused thousands of deaths and injuries, and the violence fell most heavily on the working-class areas of Belfast and Derry.
Between 1969 and 1993 the Troubles caused about 3,000 deaths, and the total for the whole conflict to 2001 is about 3,500; figures vary by source.
1972 was the deadliest year of the Troubles, with nearly 500 deaths.
About half of the dead were civilians, and members of the security forces, republican paramilitaries and loyalist paramilitaries also died in large numbers.
Tens of thousands of people were injured, and hospitals in Belfast developed specialist expertise in treating gunshot and blast injuries.
The violence was concentrated in Belfast, Derry and the border counties, and in working-class areas where both communities lived side by side.
Most deaths took place in Northern Ireland, though bombings in Britain and the Republic also caused deaths, including the Dublin and Monaghan bombings of 1974.
Deaths were concentrated in north and west Belfast, and working-class districts such as Ardoyne, the Falls and the Shankill suffered most.
The violence deterred investment and tourism, and the cost of insurance and security rose for businesses across the province.
Foreign investors were reluctant to build factories in Northern Ireland because of the risk of bombing and disruption.
Tourism fell sharply, as visitors avoided the province, and bomb attacks and the security cordon around central Belfast, the so-called ring of steel, harmed the city's trade.
Businesses faced high insurance premiums to cover damage from bombs, and some companies moved their operations to Britain or the Republic.
The security measures, including checkpoints and searches, increased the time and cost of moving goods and people.
Business closures and relocations put further pressure on local jobs.
Compensation for criminal damage was paid under government schemes, which added to public spending.
Traditional manufacturing kept shrinking, while the public sector and security jobs grew, and the province became more dependent on the British state.
Manufacturing employment continued to decline, with the shipyards, linen and engineering losing jobs through the 1970s and 1980s.
Public-sector employment grew, with jobs in health, education, local administration and the security services increasing as a share of the workforce.
The Ulster Defence Regiment, the RUC and the prison service provided large numbers of jobs in the security sector.
British subvention, the public money transferred from the Treasury, rose and kept the public sector and living standards above what local output alone could support.
Dependence on the public sector meant that Northern Ireland's economy was exposed to changes in British government spending.
Harland and Wolff was taken into public ownership in 1975 and Short Brothers in 1977, because the government wished to protect jobs.
Several man-made fibre plants promoted in the 1960s cut back or closed in the 1970s and 1980s.
The De Lorean factory at Dunmurry, Belfast, was a government-backed investment that collapsed in 1982 and cost the taxpayer heavily.
The De Lorean Motor Company built a car factory at Dunmurry, near Belfast, which began production in 1981, with large grants and loans from the British government.
The factory was intended to create about 2,000 jobs in an area of high unemployment, and it was sited between Catholic and Protestant districts of west Belfast.
The De Lorean car's production was limited and its sales were poor, and the company went into receivership in 1982.
John De Lorean was arrested in the United States in October 1982 and charged with drug trafficking, and he was acquitted in 1984.
The collapse left the British government with heavy losses, and the episode became a symbol of the difficulty of attracting investment to Northern Ireland.
Unemployment stayed well above the UK average, and Catholic unemployment was consistently higher than Protestant unemployment.
Unemployment in Northern Ireland was the highest of any UK region for much of the period, and it stayed above the UK average through the 1970s and 1980s.
Catholic unemployment was consistently higher than Protestant unemployment, and in some surveys it was roughly twice as high.
The Fair Employment (Northern Ireland) Act 1976 set up a Fair Employment Agency to investigate discrimination in employment.
The Fair Employment Act of 1989 strengthened the law, created a Fair Employment Commission and required employers to monitor their workforce.
Areas of west Belfast and Derry suffered the highest levels of deprivation, with families who had lost jobs and had few alternative sources of income.
Unemployment among young Catholic men was especially high in the 1980s, and was a factor in recruitment to paramilitaries.
The MacBride Principles of 1984 were a code of fair employment practice promoted by Irish-American campaigners for US firms operating in Northern Ireland.
The Northern Ireland Housing Executive took control of public housing, and the violence accelerated the segregation of Protestant and Catholic communities.
The Northern Ireland Housing Executive was established in 1971 to take over public housing from the local councils and the Housing Trust.
The Executive introduced allocation procedures based on a points system, intended to end the discrimination that the civil rights movement had criticised.
Intimidation drove families to move to areas where their own community was the majority, and an estimated tens of thousands of people left their homes in Belfast between 1969 and 1973.
Peace walls, barriers built between Protestant and Catholic streets from 1969 onwards, separated some neighbourhoods in Belfast and later in Derry.
Segregation of housing made communities more distinct and it made it harder for people from different backgrounds to meet.
Some families moved from mixed areas into segregated estates, despite the Housing Executive's allocation policy.
Schools remained largely segregated by religion, and a small integrated movement began in the 1970s and 1980s.
Most children continued to be educated in schools that were either Catholic or Protestant, and the system reflected the religious divisions of the province.
The integrated education movement began in the 1970s, when parents in both communities formed All Children Together in 1974 to campaign for mixed schools.
Lagan College, opened in Belfast in 1981 with a small intake, was the first integrated secondary school in Northern Ireland.
The Education Reform (Northern Ireland) Order of 1989 gave statutory support to integrated schools and placed a duty on the government to encourage them.
Integrated schools were few at first and depended on parental campaigns and charitable funding.
Teacher training was also separated, with Catholic teachers trained mainly at St Mary's College and Protestants at Stranmillis College.
Catholic voluntary schools continued to get state support, and the Catholic Church defended its right to control schools.
The health service coped with trauma and gunshot injuries, and the violence caused long-term stress that affected the population.
The Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast developed expertise in treating gunshot wounds and blast injuries, skills that many hospitals in Britain had little need for.
The health service had to treat large numbers of injured civilians and members of the security forces, and this placed heavy demands on staff.
Mental health problems, including stress and trauma, were widespread among people who had lived through bombings, shootings and displacement.
The security measures and fear of attack affected daily life, including health care, through delays and restrictions on movement.
Ambulance crews and hospital staff faced danger when responding to bomb incidents.
The health service was reorganised in 1973 into four Health and Social Services Boards.
Security checkpoints, searches and vehicle checks were a feature of daily life in Belfast and Derry, and they changed the routines of shopping and travel.
Some town centres were closed to traffic or sealed off after bombings, and shoppers had to pass through checks to enter them.
Divided towns and estates meant that some people avoided areas where the other community lived, which limited social contact.
Children grew up with the sound and presence of security forces and with memories of violence in their local areas.
Car bombs prompted security checks and car-park controls in city-centre shopping areas.
Cost: the violence deterred investment and tourism, and the economy became dependent on public money and the security sector.
Cost: segregation of housing and schooling deepened the social divisions between the communities.
Achievement: the Fair Employment Acts and the Housing Executive were steps towards equal treatment in jobs and housing.
Limit: unemployment and deprivation remained high, and the reforms did not close the gap between Catholics and Protestants.
Contemporary view: unionists pointed to the public investment and the British subvention as evidence that the state supported the province.
Contemporary view: nationalists argued that discrimination and deprivation were rooted in the state's policies and that the Troubles had made them worse.
Later view: historians stress that the Troubles were both a cause and a consequence of economic and social inequality, and that the economic costs were heavy for both communities.
Religion and political allegiance overlapped, so that most unionists were Protestant and most nationalists were Catholic, though the boundaries were not absolute.
Catholics made up about a third of the population of Northern Ireland, 35 per cent in the 1961 census, and Protestants made up the majority.
The Presbyterian Church in Ireland was the largest Protestant denomination, with the Church of Ireland and the Methodist Church also significant.
Unionist identity combined Protestantism, loyalty to the British Crown and attachment to the Union with Great Britain.
Nationalist identity combined Catholicism, Irish cultural heritage and support for a united Ireland, though many nationalists were not practising Catholics.
Religious affiliation shaped schooling, marriage patterns and social networks, and many people had little regular contact across the divide.
Denominational identity was passed on through baptism and schooling, so divisions were reinforced across generations.
The Orange Order was the largest Protestant fraternal organisation, and its parades became a focus of unionist identity and of conflict.
The Orange Order was founded in 1795 after the Battle of the Diamond, near Loughgall in County Armagh, between Protestant and Catholic groups.
The Order's annual parades on 12 July, marking the Battle of the Boyne of 1690, are its central public ritual.
Members of the Order were required to be Protestant, and its lodges were organised in local communities across the province.
The Order was closely linked to the Ulster Unionist Party through its delegates to the Ulster Unionist Council, and many unionist politicians were members.
Parades through Catholic areas were a source of tension, and the Order's marches were often restricted or rerouted to avoid confrontation.
Orangemen were forbidden to marry Catholics or attend Catholic services, which reinforced the separation of the communities.
The Twelfth of July, the main Orange parade day, is a public holiday in Northern Ireland, and bands, banners and bonfires on the eleventh night are part of the tradition.
The Black Preceptory and the Apprentice Boys are related Protestant institutions with their own parades.
Catholic identity drew on the Church, the Irish language and the Gaelic Athletic Association, and the GAA ban on British security forces was a key symbol of separateness.
The Gaelic Athletic Association was founded in 1884 and promoted Gaelic games as an expression of Irish identity.
The GAA's Rule 21 banned members of the British security forces, the RUC and the British army, from membership, and it remained in force until 2001, a point of contention with unionists.
The Ancient Order of Hibernians was a Catholic fraternal body that paralleled the Orange Order in its social and political role.
The Irish language had a small but active community in Northern Ireland, and in 1971 the first Irish-medium primary school opened at Shaw's Road in Belfast.
Catholic churches and schools were central to community life in nationalist areas, and the Catholic Church was a major provider of education.
In Catholic areas the GAA clubs, parish halls and the Church were the main centres of social life.
Nationalists regarded the Irish language and Gaelic games as expressions of an Irish identity that the Stormont state had not respected, for example in the Flags and Emblems Act.
Ecumenism is the movement for dialogue and cooperation between churches, and it gained momentum from the Second Vatican Council and from local initiatives in Northern Ireland.
The Second Vatican Council, held from 1962 to 1965, encouraged dialogue between the Catholic Church and other Christian churches.
The Corrymeela Community was founded in 1965 by the Presbyterian minister Ray Davey, who had been chaplain at Queen's University, at Ballycastle, County Antrim, as a centre for reconciliation.
The Irish School of Ecumenics was founded in 1970 in Dublin by the Jesuit priest Michael Hurley to promote reconciliation and interchurch dialogue.
Leaders of the Catholic and main Protestant churches held their first formal inter-church meeting at Ballymascanlon, County Louth, in 1973.
Ecumenism was supported by moderate church leaders, but it faced hostility from hardline Protestant and Catholic traditions.
In December 1974 a group of Protestant clergy met IRA leaders at Feakle, County Clare, and the IRA declared a Christmas ceasefire soon afterwards.
Pope John Paul II appealed for an end to violence during his visit to Drogheda in September 1979.
Hardline Protestant opposition to ecumenism, led by Ian Paisley and the Free Presbyterian Church, portrayed ecumenism as a betrayal of the Protestant faith and the Reformation.
Catholic and Protestant clergy who joined joint initiatives were sometimes denounced by their own congregations or hierarchies.
Mixed marriages and joint worship faced disapproval in both communities, which limited the practical impact of ecumenism.
Violence and sectarian killing undermined trust between the churches, and clergy were themselves targets of attacks.
The ecumenical movement succeeded in building contacts and dialogue, but it did not change the political division between unionists and nationalists.
The Catholic Church's rules on mixed marriages, which required the children to be brought up as Catholics, caused resentment among Protestants until they were relaxed in 1970.
Paisley protested when the Presbyterian General Assembly considered links with the World Council of Churches in 1966.
Paisley combined religious and political leadership, and his opposition to ecumenism and to Catholicism shaped the hardline unionist position of the 1970s and 1980s.
Ian Paisley was the founder and moderator of the Free Presbyterian Church, and he combined his ministry with a political career from 1970.
He founded the Democratic Unionist Party in 1971 and led it until 2008; he won the Bannside seat at Stormont in April 1970 and the North Antrim seat at Westminster in June 1970.
He opposed ecumenism and any dialogue with the Catholic Church, and he attacked the Papacy and the Catholic Church in public speeches.
He took part in the unionist opposition to Sunningdale, supporting the 1974 strike, and he led protests against the Anglo-Irish Agreement.
Contemporaries saw him as a powerful and divisive figure, admired by his supporters and condemned by his opponents for his rhetoric.
The sociologist Steve Bruce argued that evangelical Protestant belief was central to Paisley's politics, and historians note that his religious politics made ecumenism more difficult.
In October 1988 he shouted at Pope John Paul II in the European Parliament in Strasbourg, calling him the Antichrist, and was removed from the chamber.
He was elected to the European Parliament in 1979, topping the poll in Northern Ireland.
Seamus Heaney was the leading poet of the Troubles, and his work explored violence, identity and the inheritance of the past.

Seamus Heaney was born in 1939 at Mossbawn, near Castledawson in County Derry, the eldest of nine children of a Catholic farming family, and he was educated at St Columb's College, Derry, and Queen's University Belfast.
His early collections included Death of a Naturalist (1966), Door into the Dark (1969) and Wintering Out (1972).
North, published in 1975, drew on Iron Age bog bodies, including 'Punishment', to reflect on the violence in Northern Ireland, and its poems made the bog body a symbol of ritual killing.
He moved to County Wicklow in the Republic in 1972, and later taught at Harvard and Oxford; he was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1995.
Field Work (1979) and Station Island (1984) continued his engagement with violence, memory and the Catholic tradition.
Critics such as Ciaran Carson argued that North mythologised violence and made it seem inevitable, while others praised the poems as a major contribution to literature.
Historians see his work as a key cultural response to the Troubles, one that gave expression to grief, guilt and the search for an identity beyond sectarianism.
In his 1983 poem 'An Open Letter' he objected to being described as British in an anthology, writing that his 'passport's green'.
Writers, playwrights and artists responded to the Troubles in many forms, and the Field Day Theatre Company was a leading cultural initiative.
Field Day Theatre Company was founded in 1980 by the playwright Brian Friel and the actor Stephen Rea, with Seamus Heaney, Seamus Deane and Tom Paulin among its directors.

Friel's play Translations, the company's first production, opened at the Guildhall in Derry in September 1980, and it dealt with the English renaming of Irish placenames and the loss of the Irish language.
Other Northern poets, including Derek Mahon, Michael Longley and John Montague, explored identity, landscape and violence in their work.

Novels such as Bernard MacLaverty's Cal (1983) and Brian Moore's Lies of Silence (1990), plays such as Frank McGuinness's Observe the Sons of Ulster Marching Towards the Somme (1985), and songs such as Stiff Little Fingers' Alternative Ulster (1978) dealt with life in the Troubles.
Cultural production in both communities reflected a desire to express identity, but it also reinforced the sense of separate traditions.
Field Day's critics, such as the critic Edna Longley, argued that its emphasis on a shared Irish culture downplayed the unionist tradition.
Murals in Catholic and Protestant areas of Belfast and Derry became popular forms of political expression, as did the painted gable end in the Bogside reading 'You are now entering Free Derry'.
The Cultural Traditions Group was set up in 1988 to promote mutual understanding of the different cultural traditions in Northern Ireland.
The Cultural Traditions Group was set up in 1988 by the government's Central Community Relations Unit, and was later part of the Community Relations Council formed in 1990.
Its purpose was to recognise both unionist and nationalist traditions, and to encourage sharing of culture across the community divide.
Critics on both sides questioned whether equal recognition of traditions could replace political agreement on the constitutional question.
The Group's work centred on cultural events, education and shared activity across the community.
The Education Reform Order of 1989 made Education for Mutual Understanding and Cultural Heritage cross-curricular themes in schools.
Strength: ecumenism created channels of dialogue between churches and clergy, which gave some moderates a voice during the Troubles.
Limit: hardline religious opposition, led by Paisley, restricted the impact of ecumenism and made dialogue politically costly.
Strength: Heaney's poetry and the Field Day movement gave a shared cultural language to the violence and to the search for identity.
Limit: cultural initiatives reached mainly educated and middle-class audiences, and they did not change the political divisions between the communities.
Contemporary view: unionists saw religious and cultural traditions as central to their British identity and resisted anything that appeared to dilute them.
Contemporary view: nationalists saw their culture and religion as the basis of a distinct Irish identity, which they wanted recognised within a united Ireland.
Later view: historians argue that cultural responses to the Troubles were genuine and productive, but that they were not sufficient on their own to resolve the political conflict.
The siege of Derry was the defining event for the Apprentice Boys, and its memory has shaped Protestant identity in the city ever since.
In December 1688, during the Williamite-Jacobite conflict, thirteen apprentice boys shut Derry's gates against a regiment loyal to the Catholic King James II.
Governor Robert Lundy favoured negotiating with James and was distrusted by the defenders; he left the city in April 1689, and his name became a byword for betrayal among Protestants.
The siege proper began in April 1689 and lasted 105 days, during which the city's population suffered severe hunger and disease; George Walker and Henry Baker were among the defence leaders.
The relief ship Mountjoy broke the boom across the River Foyle on 28 July 1689, bringing supplies to the starving garrison.
The Jacobite army withdrew at the end of July and the start of August 1689, and the defence of the city became a central Protestant story of resistance; the Battle of the Boyne followed in 1690.
The city walls were built between 1613 and 1619, and they gave Derry its distinctive fortified character.
Food shortages in the city were severe, and accounts describe the garrison eating horses and other animals in the last weeks of the siege.
The defenders flew a crimson flag from the cathedral tower as a sign of defiance, and the cannon Roaring Meg on the walls became a symbol of the siege.
The relief ship Mountjoy was accompanied by the Phoenix, and the pair broke the boom across the Foyle on 28 July 1689.
The Apprentice Boys of Derry was founded in 1814 as a club to commemorate the siege, and its members were drawn largely from Protestant tradesmen and businessmen.
The Apprentice Boys of Derry Club was established in 1814 by Protestants in Derry to commemorate the siege, and the No Surrender Club followed in 1824.
The organisation was named after the apprentices who shut the gates in 1688, and its members took the apprentices as their symbol.
The Memorial Hall in Society Street, opened in 1877 in honour of the thirteen apprentice boys, became the centre of the organisation's activities.
The Apprentice Boys spread to other places in Northern Ireland and Britain through branches founded by Derry members, and a governing General Committee was set up in 1861.
Membership was open to Protestant men, and the organisation was part of the wider network of Protestant loyal and fraternal bodies.
Membership grew through the nineteenth century as the commemorative tradition spread among Protestant tradesmen.
The Dublin Apprentice Boys of Derry Society formed in December 1813, shortly before the Derry parent club.
The Apprentice Boys' parades and commemorations in August and December marked the siege, and their route along the walls gave them a particular meaning.
The Relief of Derry commemoration takes place in August, traditionally on 12 August and now the second Saturday, marking the lifting of the siege.
The August parade follows a route around the city walls, and it is the largest Apprentice Boys event in the calendar.

The December commemoration of the Shutting of the Gates, now on the first Saturday, includes a service at St Columb's Cathedral and the burning of an effigy of Governor Lundy, a custom said to date from 1832.
The parades include bands, banners, the firing of a cannon, the hoisting of crimson flags, wreaths for those who died and speeches, and they draw large crowds of visitors and members.
The walls and the Diamond at the centre of the city are the main focus of the parade's route and its symbolism.
The Apprentice Boys' symbols and slogans expressed a sense of threat and loyalty, and critics saw them as triumphalist.
The siege mentality, a term used by historians, describes a community's sense of being surrounded and under threat, which the siege story reinforced for unionists.
The slogan 'No Surrender' came to express defiance of Catholic and nationalist demands, and it was used at parades and in political rhetoric.
For unionists the relief of 1689 represented the defence of Protestant civil and religious liberty against a Catholic monarch.
For nationalists the parades and their route past the Bogside symbolised a celebration of military conquest and of the Protestant ascendancy.
The term triumphalism, used by critics, describes celebrations that display victory over another community, and it was applied to the Apprentice Boys' parades.
The Apprentice Boys' banners and slogans linked the siege to loyalty to the Crown and to the Protestant monarchy of 1689.
The phrase 'No Surrender' is also the name of the No Surrender Club of 1824 and has been a unionist slogan since the siege.
The Bogside lies below the city walls on the west bank of the River Foyle, and it was largely Catholic and working class.
Derry had a Catholic majority in its population, but unionists controlled the Londonderry Corporation through gerrymandering.
Parades past the Bogside were a source of tension, and the route of the August parade was a recurring point of dispute.
Civil rights campaigners in Derry in 1968 and 1969 raised housing and voting grievances, and nationalists saw the Apprentice Boys' parades as part of the city's unionist power structure.
Derry's Catholic population was concentrated in the Bogside, the Creggan and the Brandywell.
The Apprentice Boys' parade of 12 August 1969 passed the Bogside, and the clashes that followed led to the Battle of the Bogside and British army deployment.
On 12 August 1969 the Apprentice Boys' parade marched along the walls near the Bogside, and stone-throwing and clashes with the RUC began.
The Battle of the Bogside lasted from 12 to 14 August 1969, with residents and police in running confrontation.
Residents built barricades and the area became known as 'Free Derry', a symbol of nationalist resistance.
British troops were deployed in Derry on 14 August 1969, and the army's presence in the city became a long-term feature of life.

The events of August 1969 are seen as a turning point in the Troubles, and the parade is associated with the outbreak of violence; unionists point out that the parade itself was legal and traditional.
Nationalists said the parade was a provocation, while the Apprentice Boys said they were holding their traditional march and that disorder was started by others.
After 1969 the authorities restricted or rerouted the Apprentice Boys' parades in Derry in some years of the early 1970s, and the parades resumed as security improved.
The Apprentice Boys and their supporters argued that parades were a legitimate expression of their culture and loyalty.
The IRA blew up the Walker Pillar, a monument to the siege's governor George Walker, on the city walls in 1973.
The organisation negotiated parade routes with the authorities and, later, with residents' groups.
Derry's population shifted markedly in these years as many Protestants left the west bank for the Waterside, which reduced the Protestant presence within the walls and sharpened the sense of siege.
The Apprentice Boys were central to contrasting interpretations of Derry's history, and the parades were a symbol of the wider divide.
For unionists the Apprentice Boys' parades celebrate the defence of Protestant liberty, and they keep alive the memory of the siege as a foundation of loyalty.
For nationalists the parades are associated with the Protestant ascendancy and with the history of exclusion in the city.
The dispute over the parades was part of the wider civil rights agenda in Derry, linking cultural symbols to questions of discrimination and power.
Historians see the Apprentice Boys' tradition as an example of how a commemoration of a past event can take on contemporary political meaning.
Both communities in Derry developed their own traditions, and the tension between them shaped the city's politics from the 1960s onwards.
The dispute over parades was one of the issues raised by the Derry civil rights movement, alongside housing and voting.
The 1969 parade and the Battle of the Bogside brought the civil rights crisis in Derry to a violent climax.
The events in Derry in 1969 led to British army deployment and to a sustained period of conflict in the city.
The Apprentice Boys retained a central place in Derry's civic and cultural life, and the Memorial Hall remained a focus of commemoration.
The disputes over parades and routes contributed to the lasting division between unionist and nationalist interpretations of Derry's history.
Major Apprentice Boys events continued to need police and security planning, which kept the parades in the public spotlight.
Unionists in the city worried about their place within the walls as Protestant numbers on the west bank fell during the Troubles.
Achievement: the Apprentice Boys preserved a commemorative tradition that gave Protestant Derry a shared public identity over more than a century.
Limit: the parades' route past the Bogside made them a point of conflict, and they became a symbol of division in the city.
Contemporary view: unionists regarded the parades as a legitimate expression of heritage and loyalty, and they resisted restrictions as an attack on their culture.
Contemporary view: nationalists saw the parades as triumphalist, and they argued that the route past the Bogside was a provocation.
Later view: historians stress that the tradition was both a genuine commemoration and a political statement, and that its meaning changed with the political conflict.
After sixteen years of Fianna Fáil rule, a coalition of the parties of opposition took office in February 1948 and governed until 1951.
Fianna Fáil had been in power since 1932 and remained the largest party in the February 1948 general election, but it lost its majority.
Clann na Poblachta, a new republican party founded in 1946 by Seán MacBride, took only a small number of seats in 1948 but held the balance of power in the Dáil.
The first Inter-Party Government united Fine Gael, Labour, the National Labour Party, Clann na Poblachta, Clann na Talmhan and some independents.
Richard Mulcahy, the Fine Gael leader, stood aside because of his Civil War record, and John A. Costello became Taoiseach.
William Norton of Labour was Tánaiste, Seán MacBride was Minister for External Affairs and Noël Browne of Clann na Poblachta became Minister for Health in 1948.
The coalition had no common economic programme beyond ending Fianna Fáil's long hold on office, and it contained both conservative and radical members.
The government's best-known act was constitutional, but it also made economic and health decisions that mattered.
Costello announced during a visit to Canada in September 1948 that the government would repeal the External Relations Act of 1936 and declare a republic.
The Republic of Ireland Act 1948 came into force on 18 April 1949 (Easter Monday), ending the state's last formal link with the Crown and its Commonwealth membership.

Britain responded with the Ireland Act 1949, which guaranteed that Northern Ireland would not cease to be part of the United Kingdom without the consent of its parliament, and which said that the Republic was not a foreign country and that Irish citizens in Britain were not aliens (see the notes on Anglo-Irish relations).
Ireland declined an invitation to join NATO in 1949, with MacBride citing partition as the obstacle.
The Industrial Development Authority (IDA) was set up in 1949 to encourage new industry, including investment from abroad, though in the 1950s it had little money or power.

Ireland took part in the Marshall Plan (the European Recovery Programme) and received about 146 million dollars, much of it as loans; a large share went on land reclamation and agriculture rather than industry, which later critics saw as a missed chance.
The government expanded house building and nationalised the public transport companies into Córas Iompair Éireann in 1950.

Noël Browne led a campaign against tuberculosis, a major killer; the state built new sanatoria, funded partly from the Hospitals Sweepstake, and a BCG vaccination programme was begun. Deaths from TB fell steeply in the 1950s.
The scheme became the clearest example of the Catholic hierarchy's power over social policy in the 1950s.
Browne drew on the Health Act 1947 to propose free care for mothers before and after childbirth and for children up to the age of 16, available to all without a means test.
The Irish Medical Association opposed the scheme as a threat to doctors' private practice and independence.

The Catholic hierarchy objected that the scheme gave the state too much power over family life, that it might lead to state-provided education in sexual matters, and that it undermined the rights of parents.

Archbishop McQuaid advised Browne and Costello on the church's objections, and the bishops wrote to Costello in late 1950 and again in April 1951 that the scheme was contrary to Catholic social teaching.
Seán MacBride, who wanted to protect his government from a clash with the church, asked Browne to resign, and Browne resigned on 11 April 1951 and then published the correspondence.
Costello and the cabinet accepted the hierarchy's view; Costello told the Dáil that the government was bound to accept the bishops' decision on a matter of Catholic moral teaching.
The affair helped bring down the government: Clann na Poblachta lost ground, the coalition lost support in the Dáil and Costello called a general election for May 1951.
The Fianna Fáil government that took office replaced the scheme with the Health Act 1953, which was means-tested and so left many people without free care.
McQuaid was Archbishop of Dublin from 1940 to 1972 and the most influential churchman in the state in the 1950s.
John Charles McQuaid was born in 1895 in Cootehill, Co. Cavan, joined the Holy Ghost Fathers and was president of Blackrock College before he became Archbishop of Dublin in 1940.

He was a participant in the Mother and Child crisis, as the leading churchman to advise the government on the scheme and as the author of the argument that it conflicted with Catholic teaching on the family.
His objections did not stop at medical detail: he objected to the principle that the state, not parents and the church, should decide how mothers and children were cared for.
His influence rested on personal contact with ministers, notably with de Valera, whom he had advised on the Constitution of 1937 and its article on religion.
Contemporaries who agreed with him saw him as a defender of Catholic social teaching; Browne and his supporters saw him as an interfering prelate who used his power to defeat a good scheme.

Historians who studied the church-state relationship after the 1951 events, such as John Whyte, concluded that the government deferred to the hierarchy; later work using archives suggests that Browne's own political weakness and the doctors' opposition were also important, but that the bishops' stance was decisive.
De Valera returned as Taoiseach, but without a majority and with an economy short of foreign currency.
Fianna Fáil formed a minority government in 1951 with de Valera as Taoiseach, Seán Lemass as Tánaiste and Minister for Industry and Commerce, and Seán MacEntee as Minister for Finance.
MacEntee's 1952 budget was deflationary: it cut subsidies on basic foods and raised duties, which pushed prices up, in order to reduce imports and the balance of payments deficit.
The budget was unpopular, and in the 1954 general election Fianna Fáil lost seats.
The government passed the Underdeveloped Areas Act 1952, which gave grants for new industry in the poorer western counties.
The Health Act 1953 provided a framework of means-tested maternity, child and hospital care in place of the Mother and Child Scheme.
Emigration continued at a high level throughout these years, and unemployment stayed high.
The minority government depended on the votes of independent deputies, which limited how far it could go with unpopular measures.
Costello returned as Taoiseach in 1954 at the head of a coalition that again had no programme for growth.
The second coalition contained Fine Gael, Labour and Clann na Talmhan, with Clann na Poblachta supporting it from outside government.
Gerard Sweetman, the Minister for Finance, was a strong believer in private enterprise and low state spending.
A balance of payments crisis built up in 1955 and 1956 because imports ran well ahead of exports and foreign currency reserves fell.
The government responded with higher taxes, credit restrictions and cuts in current spending, which reduced demand and pushed up unemployment.
A Capital Investment Advisory Committee reviewed proposals for public capital spending in the mid-1950s; it was an early step towards planning public investment.
In December 1956 the IRA began its Border Campaign, and the government faced pressure from Clann na Poblachta over its response.
Clann na Poblachta withdrew its support in January 1957, and Costello called an election.
While most of western Europe boomed, the Irish economy grew only slowly and people left in large numbers.
The census showed a population of 2,960,593 in 1951 and 2,818,341 in 1961, a fall of about 140,000 despite a high birth rate.
Net emigration in the 1950s was about 400,000, roughly 200,000 in each half of the decade, and most of those who left were young people heading for Britain.
Britain offered work in construction, factories, the health service and transport, and the British economy was growing faster than the Irish.
Agriculture still employed about 40 per cent of the workforce, mostly on small farms of low productivity, and cattle exports to Britain were the main earner.

Industry was behind protective tariffs and the Control of Manufactures Acts, which required that most shares in new firms be held by Irish citizens and so discouraged foreign investment (see the notes on the First Programme for Economic Expansion).
Irish growth in the 1950s was a fraction of the growth in western Europe, and the gap with other countries widened.
The Irish pound was tied to sterling, so Irish interest rates and trade followed British conditions, including the British government's 'stop-go' cycles.
The 1957 election ended the second coalition, and the decade is remembered as one of missed opportunities.
In the March 1957 general election Fianna Fáil won 78 seats and an overall majority, and de Valera became Taoiseach for the last time.
Lemass returned to Industry and Commerce and also served as Tánaiste, and James Ryan became Minister for Finance.
T.K. Whitaker had become Secretary of the Department of Finance in 1956 and began the work that led to Economic Development (see the notes on economic planning).
Historians such as J.J. Lee and Tom Garvin criticise the leaders of the 1950s for lacking ambition and for preferring stability to change, which gave rise to the term 'wasted years'.
Others point to constraints: a small economy that depended on the British market and the sterling link, and the weak foreign exchange position.

A third view is that the Inter-Party governments did lay groundwork, through the IDA, the Underdeveloped Areas Act and public investment, that Fianna Fáil later built on, and that policy-makers then lacked planning tools that were developed only in the late 1950s.

Achievements: the Republic of Ireland Act completed the move to a republic; the IDA, the Underdeveloped Areas Act and Marshall Aid laid foundations for later industrial policy; the anti-tuberculosis campaign saved lives.
Limits: no government drew up a long-term plan, and each balance of payments crisis led to deflation that made unemployment and emigration worse.
The Mother and Child affair showed the limits of state action in social policy when the church and the medical profession opposed it.
Contemporary view: voters punished each government in turn for high taxes and emigration, and the sharp swings between coalition and Fianna Fáil governments reflected that dissatisfaction.

Later view: historians generally accept that the decade was one of slow growth and missed opportunities, but they differ about how far this was caused by policy mistakes rather than by Ireland's dependence on Britain.
By 1957 the policy of protection that Fianna Fáil had begun in the 1930s was widely seen to have run out of steam.
Tariffs and the Control of Manufactures Acts of 1932 and 1934 had created many small factories that sold only on the home market, and the home market was too small to support efficient industry.
The Control of Manufactures Acts required that a majority of the shares in a new company be held by Irish citizens, which discouraged foreign firms from setting up in Ireland.
Exports were mostly live cattle and farm produce sold to Britain, so the economy depended on one customer.
Net emigration in the 1950s was about 400,000 and the population was falling, while the rest of western Europe was growing fast.
The balance of payments crises of 1951–52 and 1955–56 had been met by deflation, which cut demand without improving productive capacity (see the notes on alternating governments).
Fianna Fáil returned to government in March 1957 with Seán Lemass at Industry and Commerce and James Ryan at Finance, and they were ready to listen to new ideas from officials.
Economic Development was a report by civil servants, led by Whitaker, that changed the direction of policy.
Thomas Kenneth Whitaker became Secretary of the Department of Finance in 1956 at the age of 39, and he gathered a group of younger officials to examine the economy.
In May 1958 he published Economic Development, a study prepared in the Department of Finance and presented under the authority of the government.
It argued that protection had failed to produce growth or jobs and that emigration was a symptom of an economy that was not expanding.
It recommended shifting public investment from social projects such as housing and hospitals towards directly productive investment in agriculture, industry and tourism.
It welcomed foreign capital and technology, a break with the Control of Manufactures Acts, and it argued for export-led growth.

The government accepted its analysis, and in November 1958 it published the Programme for Economic Expansion, usually called the First Programme, which turned the proposals into a policy with targets.
The First Programme ran for five years from 1959 to 1963 and set out an agenda for growth.
Aim: to raise national output and living standards and to halt emigration by creating jobs in export industry and farming.
Target: a modest rise in gross national product of about 2 per cent a year, set deliberately low so that it could be achieved.

The Industrial Development (Encouragement of External Investment) Act 1958 and related measures removed the rule that Irish citizens must hold most of the shares in new firms, opening the way to foreign-owned factories.
Export Profits Tax Relief, first introduced in 1956, was extended so that profits from increased exports were exempt from tax.
Grants were offered through the IDA, which was given a larger role, to firms setting up new plant, with the best terms in the poorer western areas.
The Shannon Free Airport Development Company was set up in 1959 and built an industrial estate at Shannon to attract foreign firms.
In agriculture, An Foras Talúntais (the agricultural research institute) was established in 1958 and farmers were encouraged to raise productivity and exports.
The state shifted its capital spending towards productive investment, though spending on housing and health rose again as growth took hold.
Judged by its own targets, the First Programme succeeded, and it did so by a wide margin.
Real national output grew by about 4 per cent a year between 1958 and 1963, roughly double the target, and the growth was faster than in the previous decade.
Exports of manufactured goods rose sharply, and industrial production grew as new, mostly foreign-owned firms began to operate.
Net emigration fell to about 80,000 in 1961–66, from about 200,000 in 1956–61.
The 1966 census recorded a population of about 2.88 million, up from 2.82 million in 1961 and the first rise since the early 1950s.
Unemployment fell but remained a serious problem, and total employment grew only modestly because jobs in farming continued to decline.
The balance of payments remained a concern, and by the mid-1960s wage claims and inflation were raising difficulties.
Part of the success lay outside Ireland: the late 1950s and 1960s were years of strong growth in Britain and Europe, which raised the demand for Irish exports.
The Programme was the start of regular economic planning in Ireland, followed by a Second Programme published in 1963 and a Third Programme for 1969–72.
Contemporaries welcomed it as a sharp break with the pessimism of the 1950s, and the idea of a plan for growth was supported across the parties and by the trade unions and employers.
Those who see it as a turning point stress the end of protection, the openness to foreign investment and the change in public confidence.

Sceptical historians stress that the world economy was booming, that the Programme built on measures begun by the Inter-Party governments, such as Export Profits Tax Relief, and that its targets were modest.
Critics on the left argued that foreign firms took profits out of the country and that the growth was uneven, with the west benefiting least.
Whitaker himself stressed that the Programme was a framework and that its success depended on private investors and on a favourable international climate.
Lemass became Taoiseach in June 1959, when de Valera was elected President, and he carried the Programme through.
Lemass had been a minister since 1932 and a pragmatic modernizer; he was Taoiseach until November 1966, when he was succeeded by Jack Lynch.

His style was practical and businesslike: he built a closer relationship with the trade unions and employers, and the national wage rounds, in which unions, employers and the government bargained over general pay increases, were an example.
The Second Programme for Economic Expansion, published in 1963, aimed for growth of about 4 per cent a year to 1970, but it was abandoned in 1967 after wage rises and a balance of payments deficit.
The government set up the Committee on Industrial Organisation and, from 1963, adaptation councils to help industries prepare for competition from free trade.
Ireland joined the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) in 1967, which committed it to lower tariffs.
He used the new television service, Telefís Éireann, to explain government policy and to project an image of a modern state (see the notes on the impact of RTÉ).
He is also remembered for easing the state's attitude to Northern Ireland, as in his meetings with Terence O'Neill.
Lemass saw that the future of Irish industry lay in competing in open markets, not in protection.
Ireland applied to join the European Economic Community on 31 July 1961, nine days before Britain did, because Britain was the market for most Irish exports.

President de Gaulle vetoed British entry on 14 January 1963, which ended the negotiations for the time being, although Ireland's application remained on the table (see the notes on the UN and the EEC).
With EEC entry delayed, Lemass turned to a trade agreement with Britain: the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement was signed on 14 December 1965 and took effect on 1 July 1966.
The agreement provided for the removal of tariffs on trade between the two countries over ten years and kept access for Irish farm exports to the British market.
Free trade threatened protected Irish firms in textiles, footwear and other consumer goods, and many small firms closed over the next decade.
Supporters argued that free trade would bring cheaper inputs, larger markets and new investment, and that protected industries could not survive in the long run.

Lemass visited Terence O'Neill at Stormont on 14 January 1965, and O'Neill visited Dublin on 9 February 1965; these were the first meetings of the leaders of the two parts of Ireland since partition (see the notes on Anglo-Irish relations).
Whitaker was a civil servant, not a politician, and the most influential public official of his generation.
Whitaker was born in 1916 in Rostrevor, Co. Down, and joined the civil service in 1934.
As Secretary of the Department of Finance from 1956 to 1969 he was the main author of Economic Development and the First Programme, working with Lemass and with ministers such as James Ryan.
He was a participant in the change of policy, using the authority of the Department of Finance, which had traditionally resisted spending, to argue for investment.

He later served as Governor of the Central Bank from 1969 to 1976, as a senator from 1977 to 1982 and as chairman of several commissions, including the Constitution Review Group of the 1990s; he died in 2017 at the age of 100.
Contemporaries praised his clarity and courage in questioning protection, though some in his own department doubted how far growth could be planned.

Historians see him as the architect of the new approach, while stressing that Lemass and de Valera supplied the political will, and some argue that his role has been overstated by the idea that planning alone made the economy grow.
Lemass was the minister and then Taoiseach who turned the new thinking into government policy.
Lemass was born in Dublin in 1899, fought in the Rising in 1916 and on the anti-Treaty side in the Civil War, and his brother Noel was killed in 1923.

He was a founder of Fianna Fáil in 1926 and was Minister for Industry and Commerce from 1932 to 1939, from 1941 to 1948, from 1951 to 1954 and from 1957 to 1959, and Minister for Supplies from 1939 to 1945.
As the architect of the protectionist industrial policy of the 1930s, he was able later to argue that protection had served its purpose and should now give way to competition.
As Taoiseach he backed the First Programme, applied to join the EEC and signed the Free Trade Agreement.
Contemporaries saw him as a practical, impatient leader who got things done, though some in Fianna Fáil mistrusted his break with protection.
Historians and biographers judge him a modernizer who changed the tone of Irish politics, but they note that he left rural poverty, urban housing problems and partition unresolved.
Whitaker supplied the analysis and Lemass the political leadership; the Programme needed both, and their partnership is the central reason for the change of direction.
Whitaker was cautious by temperament and was more sceptical than Lemass about the Second Programme's ambitious targets, which were abandoned in 1967.
Achievements of the First Programme: growth about twice the target, falling emigration, rising exports and a shift in confidence.
Limits: total employment barely increased, farming and the west lagged, and the balance of payments remained fragile.
Contemporary view: the Programme was a success, and Fianna Fáil regained an overall majority in the 1965 election.
Later view: historians accept that it was a turning point but debate how much of the growth came from policy and how much from the European boom.
Until the 1960s the state left most second-level education to the churches and to parents who could pay.

Before 1967 most children left school at 14 with only a primary education; secondary schools charged fees and were mostly owned by religious orders, while vocational schools, set up under the 1930 Vocational Education Act, were run by local committees and had lower status.
Ireland had no state policy for the expansion of education before the 1960s, and the Department of Education was seen as a passive administrator.
Planning for economic growth after 1958 raised the question of whether the country was educating enough people with the skills it needed.
Patrick Hillery, Minister for Education from 1959 to 1965, commissioned a survey with the help of the OECD.
Investment in Education, published in 1965, showed wide differences in participation by social class and region and a shortage of trained teachers and technical skills.
The report argued that education was an investment in growth and not only a cultural or religious matter, and it recommended expanding second-level and technical education.
Two ministers, Hillery and then Donogh O'Malley, turned the report's findings into reforms.
In 1963 Hillery announced a new type of second-level school, the comprehensive school, which would offer both academic and practical subjects to pupils of all abilities and be funded by the state.
The first comprehensive schools opened in 1966, among them schools at Carraroe, Co. Galway, and Cootehill, Co. Cavan, in areas that lacked second-level schools.
Donogh O'Malley became Minister for Education in July 1966 and announced on 10 September 1966 that free second-level education would be introduced the following year.
O'Malley is remembered for announcing the scheme boldly, and it is often said that he did so without having settled the cost with the Department of Finance.
The scheme began in September 1967 and abolished fees in schools that joined it, and it was accompanied by free school transport, which allowed rural pupils to reach a school.
Most secondary schools joined, and enrolment at second level rose steeply in the years that followed.
O'Malley died in March 1968 aged 47, and Brian Lenihan and then Pádraig Faulkner as Ministers for Education continued the work.
The Primary Certificate examination was abolished in 1967, and the school-leaving age was raised from 14 to 15 in 1972.

Community schools were introduced from the early 1970s, usually by merging a local secondary school and a vocational school, so as to offer a full range of subjects to all pupils and to serve adults in the area.
Regional Technical Colleges, which offered certificate and diploma courses in technology and business, opened from 1970 in towns such as Carlow, Dundalk, Athlone and Waterford.
The Higher Education Authority was set up in 1968 to advise the government on university funding and to plan expansion.
A higher education grants scheme was introduced in 1968 to help students from poorer homes to attend university or college.
The National Institute for Higher Education in Limerick opened in 1972 with an emphasis on technology and business.
The number of students in third-level education grew strongly through the 1970s, and more women and more students from rural and working-class homes reached university than before.
A new curriculum for primary schools was introduced in 1971 after years of planning by a committee of teachers, inspectors and others.
It replaced a curriculum built on memorisation and examination with one that emphasised the needs and interests of the individual child.
It gave more attention to activity-based learning, to art, music and drama, and to the teaching of Irish through speaking rather than drill.
Teachers needed retraining, and some, along with some parents, found the change difficult in large classes and poor buildings.
Health policy moved gradually from a means-tested service towards wider public provision, with continuing disputes over who should provide it.
The Health Act 1953 replaced the Mother and Child Scheme with means-tested maternity and child services and set out eligibility for public hospital care according to income.
Before the health boards, rural primary care was provided mainly through the dispensary system run by the county authorities, with dispensary doctors treating medical card holders.
The Voluntary Health Insurance Board was set up in 1957 to offer private health insurance, mainly to people who earned too much to qualify for free hospital care.
The Fitzgerald Report of 1968 on hospital services recommended fewer, larger regional hospitals, a change that proved controversial in local communities.
The Health Act 1970 created eight regional health boards, which began work in 1971 and took over the functions of the old county health authorities.
Comhairle na nOspidéal, set up in 1972, regulated the appointment of consultants and the structure of hospital services.
Medical cards, which gave lower-income families free GP care and medicines, remained the main way of providing free primary care, while better-off patients paid for visits.
Hospital building was funded partly by the Hospitals Sweepstake, and large projects such as Beaumont Hospital in Dublin were delayed for years by cost and planning disputes.
Welfare payments grew in range and level, especially after 1965, as the economy grew and the state's role in family support expanded.
Children's allowance, first introduced in 1944, was paid to families and its value and coverage were raised over the following decades.
The Social Welfare Act 1952 gathered the existing social insurance schemes into a single system covering unemployment, illness, widowhood and old age.
Contributory old age pensions were introduced in 1961 for insured workers, in addition to the non-contributory pension.
Free travel for old age pensioners was introduced in 1967 and an electricity allowance followed in 1968.
Deserted wife's benefit was introduced in 1970, and an unmarried mother's allowance followed in 1973, recognising mothers who had children outside marriage as claimants in their own right.
Pay-related benefit for unemployed and sick workers was introduced in 1974, tying payments to previous earnings.
