Welfare spending rose as a share of national income in the 1970s, partly because unemployment grew after the oil crises (see the notes on the economic challenges of the 1970s and 1980s).
Local authorities built large numbers of houses and flats from the 1950s onwards, replacing city-centre tenements and slums and housing families on new estates at the edge of the cities.
The Housing Act 1966 allowed tenants to buy their local authority houses, which increased home ownership.

Ballymun, in north Dublin, was built by Dublin Corporation between 1966 and 1969 as a large estate of flats, including seven fifteen-storey towers named after the leaders of 1916; poor facilities, unemployment and decay later gave it a bad name, and it was demolished and rebuilt from the late 1990s.
Planners in the late 1960s recommended new towns at Tallaght, Clondalkin and Blanchardstown around Dublin, and suburban growth transformed the edges of Dublin, Cork and Limerick.
The ESB's rural electrification scheme, begun in 1946, had connected nearly all rural homes by the mid-1970s, bringing lighting, radio, television and appliances to farms.
Group water schemes, supported by state grants from the 1960s, brought piped water to rural homes that had relied on wells and pumps.
Electricity and running water changed daily life, especially for women, and they made it easier to keep young people on the land or in rural towns.

Patrick Hillery, from Miltown Malbay, Co. Clare, was Minister for Education from 1959 to 1965, then Minister for Industry and Commerce, for Labour and from 1969 to 1973 for External Affairs, before becoming President in 1976.
Hillery's contribution was the planning: he commissioned the survey that became Investment in Education and announced the comprehensive schools in 1963.
Donogh O'Malley, a Limerick TD, was Minister for Health in 1965 and 1966 and Minister for Education from 1966 until his death in March 1968.
O'Malley's contribution was the political decision: his announcement of free second-level education turned a long-term plan into an immediate promise.
Historians generally credit Hillery with the groundwork and O'Malley with the public breakthrough, and note that the headline of 'free education' was a simplification because some costs remained.

The churches kept control of management in most primary and secondary schools, and the hierarchy was wary of comprehensive and community schools, so compromises gave the bishops representation on boards of management.
Many schools were small, overcrowded and short of qualified teachers when enrolment rose after 1967.
Tension between the academic secondary tradition and the practical vocational tradition continued, since the Leaving Certificate points for college places favoured academic subjects.
Free fees did not remove other costs such as books, uniforms and travel, so poorer families still faced barriers.
Rural areas, especially in the west, still had fewer second-level and third-level places than the east.

Achievements: free post-primary education and transport widened access, a state-wide hospital and health board structure was created, and social welfare protected more families, including lone mothers.
Limits: class differences in educational attainment persisted, the VHI and the dual system left health care unequal, and some large housing schemes, notably Ballymun, created new social problems.
Contemporary view: parents, teachers and unions welcomed the reforms, while the churches accepted the expansion but were concerned to keep control of their schools.

Later view: historians stress that the reforms were driven as much by the economic need for skills as by social ideals, and that the benefits went first to the middle classes, but they accept that they were a major change of direction.
The decade that began with EEC entry brought a series of external shocks that exposed the weaknesses of the Irish economy.
Ireland imported almost all of its oil, so it was badly exposed when the Arab members of OPEC cut supplies and raised prices after the Yom Kippur War of October 1973.
The oil price rise of 1973 pushed up inflation in the mid-1970s and ended the long post-war boom in Europe, reducing demand for Irish exports.
The Fine Gael-Labour coalition of 1973 to 1977 under Liam Cosgrave faced recession, rising unemployment and a large balance of payments deficit.
The Iranian Revolution of 1979 caused a second oil shock, which raised fuel costs and prices again, and inflation reached about 20 per cent in 1981.
Ireland joined the European Monetary System in March 1979 and broke its link with sterling for the first time since the 1820s; the link had been a feature of the Irish pound since the 1920s.
Governments responded to rising unemployment by raising public spending and borrowing, since the state hoped that growth would return, and the national debt rose rapidly.
By the early 1980s a large share of tax revenue was being spent on interest on the national debt (see the notes on unemployment and emigration in the 1980s).
Lynch succeeded Lemass and led Fianna Fáil through the first years of the Troubles, then returned to power in 1977.
John Mary Lynch was born in Cork in 1917 and became a famous hurler, winning six All-Ireland medals in a row; he qualified as a barrister before entering the Dáil in 1948.
He was Minister for Education from 1957, for Industry and Commerce from 1959 and for Finance from 1965, and became Taoiseach on 10 November 1966 as a compromise choice between rival candidates.
He won the 1969 general election with a majority of seats but lost power in 1973 to the National Coalition of Fine Gael and Labour.

In August 1969, after violence in Derry and Belfast, he said in a broadcast that the state could not stand by, and the army set up field hospitals near the border, but he ruled out military intervention.

His policy on Northern Ireland was to seek unity by consent and to oppose violence; he condemned internment in August 1971 and recalled the Irish ambassador from London after Bloody Sunday in January 1972.
In December 1972, after bombs in Dublin, his government secured passage of amendments to the Offences Against the State Act to deal with the IRA.
Strengths: he was popular and conciliatory, kept the party together and stopped the state from being drawn into the conflict in the North.
Weaknesses: critics said he was indecisive, that he was slow to remove Haughey and Blaney from his cabinet, and that the 1977 programme he led was financially reckless.

Contemporaries admired his decency and moderate approach but doubted his firmness; historians assess him as a skilful manager of the party, whose time was dominated by the crisis in the North and the Arms Crisis.
The Arms Crisis was the most serious split in Fianna Fáil in the Troubles and tested Lynch's authority.
In April 1970 the Special Branch told Lynch that senior ministers might be involved in a plan to import arms for Northern nationalists.
On 6 May 1970 Lynch dismissed Charles Haughey, Minister for Finance, and Neil Blaney, Minister for Agriculture, and Kevin Boland resigned from the cabinet in protest.
Haughey, Blaney, Captain James Kelly of army intelligence, John Kelly from Belfast and the Belgian businessman Albert Luykx were charged with conspiracy to import arms illegally.
The charge against Blaney was dropped before the trial, and Haughey and the other accused were acquitted in October 1970.
Haughey always maintained that the government had known about the plan; Lynch's version was that he acted as soon as he had evidence; the question of who knew what is still disputed by historians.
The crisis left a lasting division between Lynch's supporters and Haughey's in Fianna Fáil, which continued into the 1980s.
Fianna Fáil's manifesto for the June 1977 general election promised to abolish domestic rates and the tax on cars and to create jobs by increasing spending.
The party won 84 of the 148 seats, the largest majority in the history of the state.
The new government cut taxes and increased public spending, financed by borrowing, in the hope of lifting growth; the current budget deficit and the national debt rose sharply.
Growth was strong at first, but inflation, a second oil crisis and the cost of the manifesto turned the position into a crisis by 1979.
Fianna Fáil lost two by-elections in Cork in November 1979, which weakened Lynch's authority, and he announced his resignation in December 1979.
Haughey defeated George Colley for the leadership of the party by 44 votes to 38 and became Taoiseach on 11 December 1979.
Haughey dominated Irish politics in the 1980s and divided opinion more than any other leader.

Charles Haughey was born in 1925 in Castlebar, Co. Mayo, trained as an accountant, married Maureen Lemass, a daughter of Seán Lemass, and became very wealthy; he was Minister for Justice, for Agriculture and, from 1966 to 1970, for Finance.
He was dismissed in the Arms Crisis, spent the 1970s rebuilding his support in the party and returned as Minister for Health and Social Welfare in 1977.
In a television address on 9 January 1980 he told the country that it was living beyond its means and called for sacrifice, but his government's spending and borrowing continued to rise.
His first government lasted until June 1981; he returned briefly in March 1982 and held office again from March 1987.
In 1987 he led a minority government that, with the support of Fine Gael under Alan Dukes (the Tallaght Strategy), cut public spending sharply under his Minister for Finance Ray MacSharry.
The Programme for National Recovery, agreed in October 1987 with the unions, employers and farmers, held pay increases to low levels in return for a commitment to reduce the deficit.
Strengths: charisma, drive, loyalty from followers and a talent for tactics; weaknesses: secrecy, extravagance and the use of power for personal advantage.

Contemporaries divided between those who saw him as a bold nationalist who got things done and those who saw him as a corrupting influence; the tribunals of the 1990s and 2000s later found that he had received large sums from businessmen.

Historians now generally judge him a gifted but flawed leader whose record on the public finances was poor before 1987, and whose later cuts, along with the PNR, helped to prepare recovery in the 1990s.
Three general elections in eighteen months produced weak governments and a sense of crisis.
The June 1981 election produced a Fine Gael-Labour coalition under Garret FitzGerald, which depended on independent TDs.
That government fell in January 1982 when its budget, which proposed VAT on children's clothes and shoes, was defeated, and a new election followed in February 1982.
Haughey returned to office in March 1982 with the support of the Workers' Party, some independents and Tony Gregory, who secured investment for inner-city Dublin in return.

In 1982 a series of scandals followed: phone-tapping of journalists, a leadership challenge against Haughey, and the arrest in August of the murderer Malcolm MacArthur in the apartment of the Attorney General, Patrick Connolly.

A description of these events as grotesque, unbelievable, bizarre and unprecedented was turned into the acronym GUBU by Conor Cruise O'Brien, and it became shorthand for the political culture of the time.
Haughey's government fell in November 1982 when the Workers' Party and Tony Gregory withdrew their support, and the third election in eighteen months brought FitzGerald back to power.
FitzGerald, an economist and Fine Gael leader, headed two coalitions with Labour and tried to modernise the state.

Garret FitzGerald was born in 1926, the son of Desmond FitzGerald, a minister in the first Free State government; he worked as an economist and lecturer before becoming Minister for Foreign Affairs from 1973 to 1977.
He became leader of Fine Gael in 1977 and was Taoiseach from June 1981 to March 1982 and from December 1982 to March 1987.

In 1981 he announced a constitutional crusade to make the Republic more pluralist and thereby more attractive to Northern unionists, with divorce reform and the removal of Catholic influences from the law.

The crusade had limited results: the 1983 referendum inserted a constitutional ban on abortion, the Eighth Amendment, which FitzGerald had not wished to see written in that form, and the 1986 divorce referendum was defeated.
In 1985 his government liberalised the law on contraceptives, allowing sale without prescription to people over 18.
He established the New Ireland Forum in 1983, and negotiated the Anglo-Irish Agreement with Margaret Thatcher in 1985 (see the notes on Anglo-Irish relations).
His economic record was weak: his coalition tried to reduce the deficit but unemployment and the debt kept rising, and Labour left the government in January 1987 over spending cuts.
Strengths: intellect, integrity and a vision of a modern, tolerant Ireland; weaknesses: a tendency to overreach and difficulty in holding a coalition together on economic policy.
Contemporaries admired his honesty and energy but saw him as unworldly; historians credit him with helping to open Irish politics to new ideas, but judge his economic record the weakest part.
The Eighth Amendment, which recognised the right to life of the unborn, was approved on 7 September 1983 by about two to one in a referendum.
It was promoted by anti-abortion groups, and both Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael leaders gave way to the pressure, although FitzGerald had concerns about the wording.
The divorce referendum of 26 June 1986 sought to remove the constitutional ban on divorce and was defeated by about two to one.
The results showed that the church still had great influence over social questions in the 1980s, and that liberalisation had not progressed as FitzGerald had hoped.
Debates about pluralism and the Constitution in the 1980s are an important background to the changes of the 1990s (see the notes on culture and religion).
Unemployment rose from about 7 per cent in 1979 to over 15 per cent by the mid-1980s, with the numbers on the live register approaching a quarter of a million.

Emigration returned on a large scale, with about 200,000 more people leaving than arriving over the decade, many of them well-educated young people heading for Britain, the United States and continental Europe.
The public debt rose to more than 100 per cent of national income by 1987, and interest payments absorbed a large part of tax revenue.
Tax rates rose to pay for services, which discouraged investment and made the burden on workers heavy.
Cuts in spending in 1987 and the PNR brought the deficit down, laying the base for the recovery of the 1990s.
Lynch: kept the state out of the Northern conflict and held the party together, but left the economy in difficulty after 1977.
Haughey: showed drive, and in 1987 presided over a turn towards financial discipline, but his earlier government was marked by deficits and scandal.
FitzGerald: put pluralism and the Northern question on the agenda, but was unable to deliver social change in referendums or economic recovery.
Contemporary view: voters repeatedly turned governments out, partly because each had to impose or defend painful measures.

Later view: historians describe the 1980s as a lost decade for growth, though they see the late 1980s as the beginning of the recovery, and debate how far credit belongs to Haughey, MacSharry, Dukes and the European funds.
The declaration of a republic completed the separation from Britain in the South but hardened partition in British law.
The Republic of Ireland Act 1948 came into force on 18 April 1949 and ended the External Relations Act link with the Crown; Ireland formally left the Commonwealth.
Britain responded with the Ireland Act 1949, which declared that the Republic was not a foreign country and that Irish citizens in Britain would keep the right to vote, work and receive benefits.
The Act also stated that Northern Ireland would not cease to be part of the United Kingdom without the consent of the Parliament of Northern Ireland, which gave unionists a veto over any change.
The Irish government saw this as a guarantee of partition and a betrayal of nationalists, and Dublin protested that the Northern Ireland parliament was unrepresentative.
The Common Travel Area allowed free movement between the two islands and continued after 1949, which mattered to the large number of Irish emigrants in Britain.
Articles 2 and 3 of the 1937 Constitution claimed the whole island as the national territory, which unionists and the British government cited as proof that Dublin did not accept Northern Ireland.
The coalition government of 1948 to 1951 launched an anti-partition campaign with support from all the main parties, aiming to win international sympathy for Irish unity.
The campaign included speeches abroad, especially in the United States, and the argument that Northern Ireland's nationalists were treated unfairly.
Britain and the unionist government at Stormont refused to discuss the question, and the campaign had no practical result.
The IRA's Border Campaign, from December 1956 to 1962, had little support in the Republic; Fianna Fáil interned IRA suspects at the Curragh from 1957 to 1959.
By the late 1950s Irish governments moved to a more pragmatic approach, concentrating on economic recovery.
In the late 1950s roughly three-quarters of Irish exports, mainly live cattle and other farm produce, went to Britain.
Britain was also the main source of imports, and the Irish pound was tied to sterling, so Irish prices and interest rates followed British conditions.
This dependence explains why Irish policy-makers sought to join the EEC only when Britain did, and why the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement of 1965 mattered.

Once both countries were in the EEC from 1973, and Ireland joined the European Monetary System in 1979 without Britain, the share of exports to Britain fell steadily, to less than half by the early 1980s.
In 1965 relations between Dublin, Belfast and London became more cooperative than at any time since partition.
Lemass travelled to Stormont on 14 January 1965 and met Terence O'Neill, the Northern Ireland Prime Minister, who then visited Dublin on 9 February 1965.
The meetings were the first between the heads of government of the two parts of Ireland for decades, and the discussions concentrated on trade, tourism and electricity rather than on partition.
Lemass's approach implied that the North would not change without the consent of its people, which marked a change from the anti-partition rhetoric of the 1950s.
Ian Paisley and other unionists denounced the meetings, and some in O'Neill's own party mistrusted them.
The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement was signed on 14 December 1965 and began to remove tariffs on trade between Ireland and Britain from 1966.
Violence in Northern Ireland tested relations between the Irish and British governments from 1969.

After rioting in Derry and Belfast in August 1969, Lynch said that the state could not stand by, but he refused to send troops across the border, and the British government sent the army onto the streets.
The Arms Crisis of 1970 showed the division inside Fianna Fáil over how to respond (see the notes on Lynch, Haughey and FitzGerald).

In 1971 Lynch met Edward Heath, the British Prime Minister, and Brian Faulkner, the Northern Ireland Prime Minister, at Chequers, where Lynch argued that only an Irish dimension could end the violence.

The introduction of internment on 9 August 1971 was condemned by the Irish government, which took Britain to the European Court of Human Rights; in 1978 the court found that interrogation methods used on internees had been inhuman and degrading.

On Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972, soldiers of the Parachute Regiment shot dead thirteen civilians in Derry, and a fourteenth died later; the Irish government recalled its ambassador and declared a day of mourning.
On 2 February 1972 a crowd burned the British embassy in Merrion Square, Dublin, and the British government protested.
Heath suspended Stormont and introduced direct rule in March 1972, which the Irish government welcomed as a step towards a new settlement.

In August 1969 the Minister for External Affairs, Patrick Hillery, visited the Falls Road in Belfast and the Irish government asked the United Nations to consider sending a peacekeeping force, a request Britain blocked.
Ireland and Britain joined the EEC together on 1 January 1973, and their ministers began to meet regularly in Brussels, which improved personal contacts.
A Fine Gael-Labour coalition under Liam Cosgrave took office in March 1973, with Garret FitzGerald as Minister for Foreign Affairs.
The Sunningdale Agreement of December 1973 was agreed by Heath, Cosgrave and the leaders of the Ulster Unionists, the SDLP and the Alliance Party.
It provided for a power-sharing executive with Brian Faulkner as chief executive and Gerry Fitt as deputy, and a Council of Ireland to give the Republic a say in North-South cooperation.
The Irish government accepted that the status of Northern Ireland would not change without the consent of a majority there.
Loyalists opposed the Council of Ireland, and the Ulster Workers' Council strike from 15 to 28 May 1974 brought down the executive.
On 17 May 1974, during the strike, loyalist bombs in Dublin and Monaghan killed thirty-three people, and no one was convicted.

In August 1979 the IRA killed Lord Mountbatten at Mullaghmore, Co. Sligo, on the same day as eighteen British soldiers died at Warrenpoint, and Lynch and Thatcher agreed to improve security cooperation.
Margaret Thatcher became Prime Minister in May 1979 and met Haughey in London in May 1980 and in Dublin on 8 December 1980.

The Dublin summit produced a joint statement that studies would be made of the totality of relationships within these islands, which Haughey presented as a major step towards a new relationship and Thatcher treated as limited.
The 1981 hunger strikes, in which ten republican prisoners died, including Bobby Sands, strained relations between the two governments.
In November 1981 FitzGerald and Thatcher set up an Anglo-Irish Intergovernmental Council.

During the Falklands War in 1982 Ireland, which sat on the UN Security Council, at first supported EEC sanctions on Argentina, but in early May, after the sinking of the General Belgrano, Haughey's government withdrew its support and called for a ceasefire.
Thatcher was angered and saw it as a breach of solidarity, and trust between the two leaders did not recover while Haughey was in office.
Earlier, in July 1976, the IRA killed Christopher Ewart-Biggs, the British ambassador to Ireland, near Dublin, and the Irish government responded with emergency powers legislation.
The agreement signed at Hillsborough was the main achievement of Anglo-Irish diplomacy in this period.

The New Ireland Forum, which met in Dublin from May 1983, brought together Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael, Labour and the SDLP, and its report in May 1984 offered three options: a unitary state, a federal or confederal state, and joint authority.
Thatcher publicly rejected all three options in November 1984, but the Forum had strengthened the SDLP and shown that nationalists had a common position.
Negotiations between officials followed, and FitzGerald and Thatcher signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement at Hillsborough Castle, Co. Down, on 15 November 1985.
In it both governments affirmed that the status of Northern Ireland would not change without the consent of a majority of its people.

It set up an Intergovernmental Conference, co-chaired by the Northern Ireland Secretary and the Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs, with a permanent secretariat at Maryfield, near Belfast, through which the Irish government could put forward views on Northern Ireland affairs.
Unionists protested strongly: a rally in Belfast drew a huge crowd, and fifteen unionist MPs resigned their seats in January 1986 to force by-elections.
Fianna Fáil opposed the agreement in the Dáil, and Desmond O'Malley, expelled from the party for supporting it, founded the Progressive Democrats in December 1985.
Thatcher accepted the agreement partly for security reasons: she wanted closer cooperation with Dublin against the IRA and hoped that a role for Dublin would strengthen the SDLP against Sinn Féin.
By 1989 the Intergovernmental Conference met regularly and cooperation on security and cross-border matters had grown, although unionists continued to boycott it.
Disputes over extradition, over alleged miscarriages of justice in cases of Irish people in British courts and over the British army's actions in Northern Ireland continued to cause friction.
The IRA's campaign continued, and the North remained divided and violent.
Haughey, who had opposed the agreement in 1985, left it in place when he formed a coalition with the Progressive Democrats after the 1989 election.

Joint membership of the EEC, the growth of North-South contacts and the habit of regular meetings meant that relations were closer than in 1949, even though the fundamental dispute over Northern Ireland remained.
Achievements: from the Ireland Act of 1949, an Irish government moved to accept the consent principle, gained a formal consultative role in 1985 and built regular channels of contact with London.
Limits: Sunningdale collapsed within five months, the 1985 agreement did not end the violence, and each government kept different aims.
Contemporary view: nationalists saw the Anglo-Irish Agreement as recognition of their rights; unionists saw it as a threat to the union made without their consent.

Later view: historians see the agreement as a foundation for later developments such as the Downing Street Declaration of 1993 and the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, although some judge that its immediate effect was limited.
Ireland had been outside international organisations since the League of Nations and wished to join the UN as soon as it was founded.

Ireland applied for UN membership in 1946, but the Soviet Union used its veto in the Security Council, citing Ireland's neutrality in the Second World War and the lack of diplomatic relations between the two states.
The deadlock over new members lasted until 1955, when a package deal in the General Assembly allowed sixteen states to be admitted together.
Ireland was admitted on 14 December 1955, alongside states as varied as Italy, Spain, Austria, Hungary and Jordan.
Ireland was neutral in the Cold War sense of belonging to no military bloc, but it was a Western, Christian democracy and generally sympathetic to the West on issues of communism.
Membership gave a small state a voice on world affairs and a means of showing independence of Britain.
Frank Aiken, Minister for External Affairs from 1951 to 1954 and from 1957 to 1969, used the UN to pursue a policy not tied to the Western powers.
Aiken was a veteran of the War of Independence and Civil War who had been in de Valera's governments since 1932, and he led the Irish delegation to the General Assembly nearly every year.
From 1957 Ireland would not support the American-led move to block debate on the seat of the People's Republic of China, a position that irritated Washington.
In 1959 Ireland and Malaya sponsored a resolution at the UN criticising the Chinese suppression of human rights in Tibet.
Ireland backed discussion of Algeria's self-determination and later opposed apartheid in South Africa, which reflected an anti-colonial approach.

Aiken's main contribution was in the effort to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons: Irish resolutions were introduced from 1958, and Resolution 1665 of 4 December 1961 called on all states to agree not to transfer or acquire nuclear weapons.
That resolution led to negotiations on the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, which opened for signature in 1968, and Ireland was the first state to sign it.
Critics said the Irish line was naive or inconsistent with Ireland's position in the West; supporters said it showed that a small state could influence world opinion.
Irish soldiers served in UN peacekeeping from 1958, and the Congo was the first major test.

Irish officers served as UN observers in Lebanon from 1958, and Irish troops joined the UN force in the Congo (ONUC) in July 1960, soon after the Congo gained independence from Belgium and fell into disorder.
On 8 November 1960 an Irish patrol was ambushed at Niemba in Katanga, and nine soldiers were killed, the first big loss of Irish life in UN service.

In September 1961, 155 men of A Company, 35th Battalion, under Commandant Pat Quinlan, were besieged at Jadotville by Katangese forces and foreign mercenaries; after five days, with ammunition and water short, they surrendered, and were held for weeks before being released (see the notes on the decolonisation of Africa).
About 6,000 Irish soldiers served in the Congo until 1964, and twenty-six lost their lives.
Irish troops joined the UN force in Cyprus (UNFICYP) from 1964, to keep apart the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities.
From 1978 an Irish battalion served with the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), set up after Israel's invasion of southern Lebanon.
Peacekeeping linked Ireland's identity as a neutral state to practical service, and it gave the Defence Forces an important role and good reputation abroad.
Frederick Boland, formerly Secretary of the Department of External Affairs and ambassador in London, was Ireland's permanent representative at the UN from 1956.
He was elected President of the fifteenth session of the General Assembly, which began in September 1960, an honour for a small state that had joined only five years earlier.

The session was dominated by the crisis in the Congo and by Cold War tension, and in October 1960 Boland broke his gavel while trying to restore order during a heated exchange involving the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev.
Boland's election showed the respect Ireland had gained, and the session brought more African states into the UN as colonies became independent.
Ireland also served on the Security Council in 1962, the first of several terms.
The Treaty of Rome in 1957 created a common market of six states, and Irish policy-makers soon saw that staying outside it carried risks.
The European Economic Community was founded by France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg in 1957, with a customs union and a common external tariff.
When Britain, Ireland's main market, applied to join, Irish ministers feared that a British entry would leave Ireland outside a market where its farm exports would face barriers.
Ireland formally applied on 31 July 1961, and the Dáil and the main parties and farmers' groups supported the application.
Supporters hoped to gain access to a large market for beef and dairy goods and to attract investment, and Lemass argued that membership would help to modernise Irish industry.
French president Charles de Gaulle vetoed British entry on 14 January 1963, which stopped negotiations, although the Irish application remained on the table.
To prepare, the government set up bodies to improve industrial competitiveness and signed the free trade agreement with Britain in 1965 (see the notes on economic planning).
Ireland, Britain, Denmark and Norway applied again in 1967, but de Gaulle vetoed British entry a second time in November 1967.
After de Gaulle resigned in 1969, the Hague summit of December 1969 agreed to enlarge the community, and negotiations opened in Luxembourg in 1970.

Patrick Hillery, as Minister for External Affairs, led the Irish negotiating team; Ireland won a five-year transitional period for industry and agreed terms on farm prices and a limited fisheries arrangement.
The Treaty of Accession was signed in Brussels on 22 January 1972.
The government held a referendum on 10 May 1972 to amend the Constitution to allow membership; about 83 per cent of those who voted were in favour, on a turnout of about 71 per cent.
Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and farmers' organisations supported entry, while Labour, Sinn Féin and some trade unionists opposed it on the grounds of loss of sovereignty and neutrality.
Ireland, Britain and Denmark became members on 1 January 1973; Norway's voters had rejected membership in September 1972.
Hillery became Ireland's first member of the European Commission in 1973.
The Single European Act, signed in February 1986, aimed to complete the single market by the end of 1992 and extended qualified majority voting to more decisions.
It also gave a legal basis to European political cooperation, the effort of member states to coordinate foreign policy.
Raymond Crotty, an economist, challenged the government's plan to ratify the Act, and the High Court rejected his case on 12 February 1987.

On 9 April 1987 the Supreme Court ruled that the provisions on political cooperation limited the state's freedom to conduct its foreign policy, and that ratification therefore required an amendment to the Constitution.
The Tenth Amendment, approved by referendum on 26 May 1987 by about 70 per cent to 30 per cent, on a low turnout of about 44 per cent, allowed ratification.
The Crotty judgment established that major transfers of power to the EEC and the EU would require a referendum in Ireland.
Ireland refused to join NATO in 1949, with partition as the stated reason, and kept to a policy of military neutrality in the Cold War.
The Defence (Amendment) Act 1960 allowed the government to send Irish contingents abroad on service under the United Nations, which provided the legal basis for the Congo mission.
Irish troops served only under UN command and with the approval of the Dáil, a condition that later became formalised in policy.
Peacekeeping allowed a neutral state to take part in world affairs without joining an alliance, and it became a source of national pride.
The question of whether EEC membership would affect neutrality was raised by opponents in 1972, and the government replied that membership did not require Ireland to join a military alliance.
Economic motives: the failure of protection, the need for markets for beef and dairy goods beyond Britain, and the hope of attracting industry looking for access to a large market.
Political motives: membership would end the dependence on the British market and give a small state a seat among the major European powers.
The Common Agricultural Policy, which would pay guaranteed prices, was the strongest attraction for farmers and the Irish Farmers' Association.

Opponents, grouped in the Common Market Defence Campaign, argued that entry would cost sovereignty and neutrality, force small firms and farms out of business and give control of the economy to foreign companies.
Labour opposed entry in 1972, as did Sinn Féin and parts of the trade union movement, but the main parties and employers' and farmers' organisations campaigned for a yes vote.
Raymond Crotty, who later challenged the Single European Act, was a prominent economist critic of the EEC.
The size of the yes vote in 1972 showed how strongly the public linked membership to economic hopes.
The UN gave Ireland international recognition, a platform for independent policies on China, nuclear weapons and decolonisation, and a respected peacekeeping role.

The EEC had greater practical effect: it gave farmers guaranteed prices and access to a large market, brought regional and social funds, attracted foreign investment and reduced Ireland's dependence on Britain.

Contemporary view: supporters of the UN saw it as the best guarantee of Irish independence and neutrality; supporters of the EEC saw it as the only way to modernise the economy and end dependence on Britain.

Later view: historians generally judge that EEC membership had the deeper impact on Irish society and economy, while the UN involvement shaped Ireland's self-image and foreign policy and has remained an important part of its identity.
From 1 January 1973 Ireland was part of a common market with free movement of goods and a common external tariff, and a member of its institutions.
Tariffs on trade with other member states were phased out over a transitional period that ended in 1977, and Ireland adopted the common external tariff on goods from outside the community.
EEC law took precedence over Irish law in the areas covered by the treaties, and the Third Amendment to the Constitution, approved in 1972, made this possible.
Irish ministers sat on the Council of Ministers, Irish members sat in the European Parliament, and Patrick Hillery served as the first Irish member of the Commission from 1973.
Ireland held the presidency of the Council of Ministers for the first time in the first half of 1975.
Membership reduced dependence on Britain: the share of Irish exports going to Britain fell as trade with the continent grew.
Net payments from the EEC budget to Ireland amounted to several per cent of national income by the 1980s, which helped to pay for farm support, training and infrastructure.
Membership was the context for Ireland's decision in March 1979 to join the European Monetary System, which ended the link between the Irish pound and sterling.
The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) guaranteed minimum prices for products such as beef, milk and cereals, and bought surplus produce into intervention stores.
Irish farm prices were raised towards EEC levels during the transition, and farm incomes rose sharply in the early years of membership, especially for beef and dairy farmers.
Land values rose and farmers invested in machinery, buildings and drainage, helped by grants.
The benefits were uneven: larger and more productive farms in the east and south gained most, while small farms on poor land in the west gained less.
Guaranteed prices encouraged overproduction, and in 1984 the EEC introduced milk quotas, limiting output on Irish dairy farms.
The number of people working on the land continued to fall, and agriculture's share of employment and output declined.
The European Regional Development Fund was created in 1975, partly because Britain, Ireland and Italy pressed for help for poorer regions, and Ireland received a considerable share of it.
The European Social Fund paid for training and employment schemes for young and unemployed people.
Funds were spent on roads, water and sewerage schemes, telecommunications and industrial estates, mainly under the direction of the Irish government.
A reform of the structural funds in 1988, linked to the Single European Act, doubled the money available, with Ireland as a major beneficiary of the programmes for 1989 to 1993.
The Social Fund helped to pay for the training schemes of AnCO, the state training authority.

American and other foreign firms set up factories in Ireland to sell into the EEC, drawn by IDA grants, a young English-speaking workforce and low taxes; in 1981 a 10 per cent rate of corporation tax on manufacturing profits was introduced.
Electronics, pharmaceuticals, chemicals and engineering became leading sectors, with firms such as Digital in Galway and, later, Intel at Leixlip.
Protected Irish industries such as clothing, textiles and footwear lost their tariff protection and many firms closed, with heavy job losses.

Employment in traditional manufacturing fell, and the rise in unemployment of the late 1970s and 1980s showed that membership did not by itself solve the economy's weaknesses (see the notes on the economic challenges of the 1970s and 1980s).
Irish exports became more diversified, with manufactured goods overtaking farm produce in the value of exports.

EEC directives on equal pay (1975) and equal treatment in employment (1976) required changes in Irish law, and they reinforced the Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 and the Employment Equality Act 1977 (see the notes on the status of women).
The marriage bar in the public service was lifted in 1973, and a directive on equal treatment in social welfare, adopted in 1978, forced changes to payments to married women in the 1980s.
Irish citizens gained the right to live and work in other member states, which eased emigration, and young people had more contact with continental Europe.
Irish judges were obliged to apply EEC law, and the European Court of Justice became a route for individuals to challenge Irish law.
Critics argued that membership cost Ireland some of its independence, and the debate over sovereignty returned in the Crotty case and the later referendums on European treaties.
Irish fishing was small and under-developed, but it was important to coastal communities and became a sensitive issue in the accession negotiations.
Irish waters were rich in fish, but the industry was small: most boats were old, small and inshore, and the fleet lacked the capacity to fish far from land.
Fishing employed only a few thousand full-time fishermen, concentrated in Donegal, Kerry, Cork, Galway and parts of the east coast, and many combined it with farming.
Irish consumers ate little fish outside Fridays, and the home market was small, so the industry exported little.
Foreign trawlers from France, Spain, Belgium, the Netherlands and Britain fished close to the Irish coast under historic rights, because the exclusive Irish limit was narrow.
Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM), the state fisheries board, was created in 1952 to develop the industry through grants and loans for boats, training and marketing.
In the 1960s and early 1970s BIM helped to build a more modern fleet, including larger boats able to catch herring, whitefish and shellfish.
Fish made up a tiny share of Irish exports and national output before 1973, which is why governments treated the fishing terms as less important than the farming terms.
The EEC had agreed a principle of equal access for all member states' fleets to community waters in 1970, just before the applicant states opened negotiations.

Irish negotiators argued that fishing was important to poor coastal communities, and Ireland obtained a derogation: an exclusive six-mile zone for Irish boats and a 12-mile zone in parts of the coast, for ten years to the end of 1982.
Critics said the government gave away too much in order to secure the farming terms, and that the fishing industry was treated as expendable.
In 1976, at The Hague, member states agreed to extend their fishing limits to 200 nautical miles from 1977 and recognised that Ireland needed preferential treatment.
Negotiating a new common policy took until January 1983, when member states agreed on a Common Fisheries Policy (CFP).

The CFP set annual total allowable catches (TACs) for the main species, divided into national quotas according to the principle of relative stability, based on past catches, with some preference for Ireland.
It kept a 12-mile coastal belt reserved for local fishermen, and the arrangements were to be reviewed after ten years.
Irish fishermen and ministers complained that Ireland's quotas were small compared with the value of the fish in its waters.
With EEC and state grants, BIM financed new and larger vessels, and the Irish fleet grew in the late 1970s and 1980s.
Killybegs, Co. Donegal, developed into Ireland's leading fishing port, with a fleet of larger trawlers and pelagic boats and with processing factories and a growing service industry.
Castletownbere, Co. Cork, became a major whitefish port, with boats landing fish for sale and export.
Other ports such as Dunmore East, Howth, Rossaveel and Kilmore Quay also received investment in piers and harbours.
Foreign fleets from Spain, France and elsewhere fished in Irish waters, and the Irish Naval Service was used to inspect and arrest vessels that broke the rules.
Disputes over illegal fishing, over the size of quotas and over the shares given to other states recurred through the 1980s.
Benefits: investment in harbours, boats and processing plants created jobs in some coastal towns, and the 200-mile limit gave Ireland a large area of sea to manage.
Costs: quotas limited what Irish boats could land, small inshore fishermen often lost out to larger vessels and fewer ports, and young people left declining harbours.
Fishermen's organisations claimed that Ireland received a small share of the fish caught in its own waters, and argued that the government treated fisheries as secondary to farming.
The government replied that the 12-mile zone and the preferences obtained at The Hague were the best terms available and that Ireland, as a small state, could not manage the waters alone.
Supporters of EEC membership pointed to the new money for the industry; critics, including the Common Market Defence Campaign, pointed to the loss of control over a national resource.
The fishing industry remained a source of grievance, and its history became a standard example in debates on the costs of membership.
Fish processing and exports to continental markets expanded through the 1980s.
Achievements: secure and better-priced markets for farmers, large transfers from Europe, foreign investment in new industries, equality legislation and a wider international outlook.
Limits: protected firms closed, unemployment rose in the 1980s, small farms and the west benefited least, and the fishing industry gained less than farming.
Contemporary view: supporters said membership was the only way to modernise an economy that relied on protection and emigration; opponents said it threatened sovereignty and traditional industries.

Later view: historians generally accept that membership underpinned the transformation of the economy and society, while stressing that the full benefits came later, from the 1990s, and that farmers and fishermen did not all gain equally.
A century of decline ended in the 1960s, and the population then grew faster than at any time since the Famine.
The census recorded 2,960,593 people in 1951 and 2,818,341 in 1961, a fall of about 140,000 caused by emigration.
The population rose to about 2.88 million in 1966 and about 2.98 million in 1971, as net emigration fell and the birth rate remained high.
It then grew rapidly, to about 3.44 million in 1981 and about 3.54 million in 1986, the highest figure since the 1860s.
Births reached a peak of about 74,000 around 1980, and the population was young, with a large proportion under 25.
The increase slowed after 1986, when heavy emigration returned, and the 1991 census recorded a small fall.
Net emigration was about 400,000 in the 1950s, and most emigrants were young people going to Britain for work.
Economic expansion in the 1960s cut net emigration to about 100,000 over the decade.
In the 1970s the flow reversed: about 100,000 more people arrived than left, many of them Irish emigrants returning home as Britain suffered recession and Ireland joined the EEC.

Emigration returned in the 1980s, with around 200,000 net emigrants over the decade, as unemployment passed 15 per cent; these emigrants were often well educated and went to Britain, the United States, Australia and continental Europe.
Emigration was a continuing feature of Irish society, and it shaped family life, rural depopulation and attitudes to politics (see the notes on the economic challenges of the 1970s and 1980s).
The urban population passed half the total around 1971, and more than a quarter of the people lived in the Dublin area by 1981.
New suburbs and towns such as Tallaght, Clondalkin and Blanchardstown absorbed people moving from the countryside, while small farms and rural villages lost population.
Marriage rates rose in the 1960s and 1970s, and people married at a younger age than in the 1950s, when late marriage and non-marriage were common.
Large families were the norm in the 1960s, but the fertility rate fell steadily afterwards, to close to replacement level by the late 1980s.
Falling family size was linked to more use of contraception, which was illegal to sell until the late 1970s, and to women's rising education and employment.
The marriage bar required women in the civil service and other public posts to resign when they married; it was removed for primary teachers in 1958 and for the civil service in 1973.
Women were also paid less than men for similar work, and many employers, including banks, imposed their own bars on married women.
The Commission on the Status of Women, chaired by Thekla Beere, was set up by the Lynch government in 1970 after pressure from women's organisations.
Its interim report in 1971 recommended equal pay, and its final report in December 1972 made 49 recommendations on equal pay, employment, education, family law and social welfare.
The report provided a programme for reform, and many of its recommendations were implemented during the 1970s and 1980s.

The Irish Women's Liberation Movement was formed in 1970 by journalists and activists including Mary Kenny, Nell McCafferty, June Levine and Nuala Fennell, and its manifesto Chains or Change (1971) demanded equal pay, equal education, contraception and legal changes for unmarried mothers and deserted wives.

On 22 May 1971 dozens of members travelled by train from Dublin to Belfast, bought contraceptives that were illegal to import into the Republic and returned openly to Connolly Station, challenging customs officers to stop them.
The action attracted wide media attention, including coverage on The Late Late Show, and made contraception a public issue.
Later groups such as Women's Aid, founded in 1974 to help victims of domestic violence, and the Well Woman Centre, opened in 1977, provided services that the state did not.
Women's organisations also used the trade unions and the Council for the Status of Women to lobby ministers.
The law on contraception was the most controversial issue in the status of women in the 1970s.
Mary McGee, a mother of four who was medically advised against another pregnancy, took a case against the State after customs seized contraceptive jelly sent to her from abroad.

In McGee v Attorney General, decided in December 1973, the Supreme Court found by four to one that the ban on importing contraceptives was unconstitutional as it infringed the right to marital privacy.
The Fine Gael-Labour government introduced a bill to regulate contraceptives in 1974, but it was defeated when Taoiseach Liam Cosgrave himself voted against it.

The Health (Family Planning) Act 1979, introduced by Haughey as Minister for Health, allowed contraceptives to be sold on prescription to people with a genuine need for family planning, described by Haughey as an Irish solution to an Irish problem.
The Act took effect in 1980; in 1985 sale to people over 18 without prescription was allowed (see the notes on Lynch, Haughey and FitzGerald).
The Catholic Church officially opposed artificial contraception, a position reaffirmed by Pope Paul VI in 1968, but surveys suggested that many Irish married Catholics ignored the rule.
Equal pay for the public service was introduced in 1973, shortly after the removal of the marriage bar.
The Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 required equal pay for men and women doing the same or similar work, with the principle taking effect from the end of 1975 in line with the EEC directive.
The Employment Equality Act 1977 made it unlawful to discriminate on grounds of sex or marital status in recruitment, training and promotion.
The Employment Equality Agency was set up under the 1977 Act to promote equality, investigate complaints and advise the government.

Other measures included the Juries Act 1976, which ended the exclusion of women from jury service, and the Family Home Protection Act 1976, which stopped a husband selling the family home without his wife's consent.

The Maternity Protection of Employees Act 1981 gave women the right to leave and to return to their jobs, and social welfare was reformed in the 1980s to give married women equal treatment, under pressure from EEC law.
Women remained a small minority in the Dáil: only a handful sat in the 1970s, six after the 1977 election, and the number reached 14 by 1987.
Eileen Desmond of Labour became Minister for Health and Social Welfare in 1981, the first woman in a cabinet since Constance Markievicz.
Gemma Hussey of Fine Gael was Minister for Education from 1982 to 1987, and Nuala Fennell was a Minister of State for women's affairs from 1982.
More women entered the workforce, particularly married women, whose participation rate rose from about 5 per cent in 1961 to about 17 per cent in 1981.
Mary Robinson, a senator from 1969, was the most prominent woman in public life outside government.
Meehan was a trade unionist and campaigner who became the first head of the Employment Equality Agency.

Sylvia Meehan was born in Dublin in 1929, worked as a teacher, and was vice-president of the Association of Secondary Teachers, Ireland and chairperson of the women's committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions.
She was appointed in 1977 as the first chairperson of the new Employment Equality Agency, a post she held until 1992.
She was a participant in the enforcement of the equal pay and equal treatment laws, supervising research, investigations and advice on discrimination at work.
The agency's research into the position of girls and women in education, pay, maternity leave and childcare helped to shape later legislation.
Contemporaries regarded her as an effective and determined advocate, though employers and some politicians resisted the agency's findings.
Historians see her as a key figure in turning the 1970s equality laws into practice, though they stress that the agency's powers were limited; she died in 2018.
Robinson was a lawyer and senator who used the courts and the Oireachtas to challenge discriminatory law.

Mary Robinson was born in Ballina, Co. Mayo, in 1944, graduated from Trinity College Dublin, was called to the bar in 1967, studied at Harvard and became Reid Professor of Law at Trinity at the age of 25.
She was elected to the Seanad for the University of Dublin in 1969 and served until 1989, as an independent.

She introduced private members' bills in the early 1970s to liberalise the law on contraception, which the Seanad refused to debate, and later sought reform of the law on homosexuality; neither became law at the time.
She campaigned for women to serve on juries, a change enacted in the Juries Act 1976.

As a barrister she took cases on behalf of individuals against the State, including a tax case brought by a married couple, which the Supreme Court decided in their favour in 1980, and the long-running case of the campaigner David Norris against the law criminalising homosexual acts.
She joined the Labour Party in 1976 and left it in 1985 in protest at the Anglo-Irish Agreement, and she was a Dublin city councillor from 1979 to 1983.
Contemporaries saw her as a liberal reformer and an able lawyer; she was attacked by conservatives and the church for her views, but respected for her persistence.
Historians credit her with creating a legal and political basis for reform in the 1970s and 1980s that prepared the way for the changes of the 1990s and for her election as President in 1990.
Achievements: the marriage bar ended, equal pay and employment equality were legislated, contraception became legally available and women gained new organisations, rights and visibility.
Limits: women remained scarce in politics and senior jobs, pay gaps persisted, divorce and abortion remained prohibited and the church kept its influence.
Contemporary view: conservatives argued that the reforms threatened the family and Catholic values; reformers saw the changes as too little and too slow.

Later view: historians see the period as the beginning of social liberalisation, driven by economic change, EEC law and campaigning, but argue that change was uneven and that Ireland remained more conservative than many European states in the 1980s.
The language was the first official language of the state, but it was losing ground as a community language, and by the 1960s public attitudes were turning against compulsion.
The 1937 Constitution declared Irish the national and first official language, and successive governments backed its revival through schools, the civil service and the Gaeltacht.
Irish was a compulsory subject in school, a pass in Irish was required for the Leaving Certificate and Irish was needed for entry to the civil service.
Gael Linn, founded in 1953, tried to promote the language through popular means, including records, the Amharc Éireann newsreel from 1956 and the feature film Mise Éire in 1959.
The Gaeltacht was in decline in the 1950s because of emigration, and the state set up Gaeltarra Éireann in 1957 to encourage industry in Irish-speaking areas.
The Commission on the Restoration of the Irish Language reported in 1963, and a government White Paper of 1965 accepted the aim of restoration but proposed a more flexible approach.
The Language Freedom Movement, founded in 1966, campaigned against compulsory Irish, arguing that it turned pupils against the language, and it provoked counter-campaigns.

In 1973 the Fine Gael-Labour government, with Richard Burke as Minister for Education, ended the rule that students must pass Irish to gain the Leaving Certificate, and the requirement for civil service entry was also relaxed.
The Gaeltacht Civil Rights Movement, formed in 1969, demanded better services and Irish-language radio, and in 1970 it ran a pirate station, Saor Raidió Chonamara.
Raidió na Gaeltachta began broadcasting from Connemara on Easter Sunday, 2 April 1972, giving Irish speakers a regular service in their own language.
Bord na Gaeilge was set up in 1975 to coordinate efforts to promote Irish.
Údarás na Gaeltachta, created in 1980, took over responsibility for economic and social development in the Gaeltacht.
The Irish language retained its symbolic status, but the number of everyday speakers continued to decline outside the Gaeltacht, which itself was shrinking.
Ó hEithir was a writer, journalist and broadcaster whose work in Irish and English brought the culture of the Gaeltacht and the Irish language to a modern audience.
Breandán Ó hEithir was born on 18 January 1930 on Inis Mór, one of the Aran Islands, and died on 26 October 1990.
He was a journalist and a broadcaster with RTÉ, presenting and reporting on current affairs and on cultural and sporting matters in Irish and English, and wrote a regular newspaper column.
His novel Lig Sinn i gCathú (1976), a satirical novel about the life of a Galway student, was widely read in Irish, and he translated it himself as Lead Us into Temptation in 1978.
His Over the Bar (1984) was a personal history of the GAA, and The Begrudger's Guide to Irish Politics (1986) was a witty account of political life in English.
He was a participant in the cultural change of the period rather than a leader of a movement: he wrote about the Irish language as a living medium for modern subjects, not as a duty.
Contemporaries valued him as a bridge between the Gaeltacht and the English-speaking world and as a rare Irish-language writer with a wide readership.
Later critics and his biographer Liam Mac Con Iomaire see him as one of the most accomplished bilingual writers and broadcasters of his generation.
Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann was founded in Mullingar in 1951, and the fleadh cheoil competitions held from 1952 helped to spread traditional music and dance.
Seán Ó Riada composed the score for Mise Éire (1959), and from 1961 his group Ceoltóirí Chualann played traditional music in a concert style, which brought it to a wider audience.
Ó Riada's Ceol an Aifrinn (1968), an Irish-language Mass set to sean-nós style music for the church at Cúil Aodha, linked the music revival to the changes brought by Vatican II.
The Chieftains were formed in 1962, and the Clancy Brothers, The Dubliners and later groups such as Planxty made Irish ballads and traditional music popular at home and abroad.
The revival gave Irish culture a modern commercial and international dimension and reduced the old divide between a rural traditional culture and urban popular culture.
The Second Vatican Council, held in Rome between October 1962 and December 1965, changed Catholic worship and the church's relationship with other Christians and the modern world.
Pope John XXIII opened the council on 11 October 1962 and it closed on 8 December 1965 under Paul VI; Irish bishops, including McQuaid, attended.
The council allowed the Mass to be said in the vernacular instead of Latin, and the first Masses in English in Ireland were celebrated in 1965.
Priests now faced the congregation, laypeople could be readers and distribute communion, and parish councils and lay organisations were encouraged.

The council promoted ecumenism, dialogue with other Christian churches: the Catholic ban on attending Trinity College Dublin was lifted in 1970 and the first inter-church talks were held at Ballymascanlon, Co. Louth, in 1973.
It declared that religious freedom was a right, which weakened the claim that a Catholic state should have a special position in law.
Many Irish Catholics welcomed the changes, but others, mostly older, felt unsettled by the loss of Latin and old devotions.
Vatican II also encouraged people to think for themselves on moral questions, which contributed to a questioning of church authority.
McQuaid, Archbishop of Dublin from 1940 to 1972, was the most powerful churchman in Ireland and was cautious about the changes brought by the council.
McQuaid attended Vatican II and, on returning in December 1965, assured Dubliners that the council would not disturb their faith, a message of reassurance in tune with his conservative outlook.
He implemented liturgical reforms in Dublin, but slowly, and he was wary of ecumenism, which he regarded as risky for Catholic doctrine, and of lay initiatives outside the control of the clergy.
He was a participant in church-state relations, with direct access to ministers, and had been involved in the Mother and Child dispute of 1951 (see the notes on alternating governments).
He was also involved in education, social work and the building of new churches and schools in the Dublin suburbs, and founded charitable bodies such as the Catholic Social Service Conference.
He retired in January 1972 and died in 1973; he was succeeded by Dermot Ryan.
Contemporaries admired his efficiency and devotion to the church, but critics complained of his authoritarian style and his readiness to intervene in politics and in people's lives.

Historians, notably John Cooney in his biography of 1999, portray him as the ruler of Catholic Ireland whose style came to seem out of date; other historians stress his role in building schools and welfare services and argue that the decline of church power was the result of social change as much as of his policies.
A survey in 1973 and 1974 found about nine in ten Catholics attending Mass weekly, so practice remained high even as other signs of change appeared.
Pope Paul VI's encyclical Humanae Vitae in 1968 reaffirmed the ban on artificial contraception, and many Irish married Catholics found it difficult to accept.
Vocations to the priesthood and religious life began to fall from the late 1960s, and fewer young people entered seminaries and convents.
Pope John Paul II visited Ireland from 29 September to 1 October 1979, and a mass in the Phoenix Park drew more than a million people, but the visit did not halt the long-term shift.

Secularisation, the decline in the influence of religion on public life and private behaviour, advanced through the 1970s and 1980s, helped by education, television, emigration and contact with Europe.

Pluralism, the idea that the state should respect different beliefs and not enforce one, was at the centre of the 1983 referendum on abortion and the 1986 referendum on divorce, and the results showed that traditional views remained strong (see the notes on the leadership of the 1970s and 1980s).

The Censorship of Publications Act 1929 set up a board that could ban books for being indecent or obscene, and the Act of 1946 added an appeals board; thousands of books were banned, including works by leading Irish writers.
John McGahern's novel The Dark was banned in 1965, and McGahern lost his teaching job after the Archbishop of Dublin's intervention, which became a symbol of the censorship of the time.

The Censorship of Publications Act 1967, introduced by the Minister for Justice, Brian Lenihan, provided that a ban lasts twelve years, after which a book is freed unless banned again, and thousands of titles were released.
Film censorship became more liberal during the 1960s and 1970s, as television and cinema showed material from abroad.
Contraceptives and publications about them were covered by separate laws until the Health (Family Planning) Act 1979 (see the notes on the status of women).
Censorship in broadcasting took a different form, through the powers of the minister over RTÉ (see the notes on the impact of RTÉ).
The number of cars on the road rose several times over between 1960 and 1980, and better roads, bus services and air travel reduced rural isolation.
Telephone services, once poor and slow to expand, were improved and in 1984 Bord Telecom Éireann was set up to run them as a separate state company.

Television reached most households in the 1960s and early 1970s, and RTÉ 2 started in 1978, bringing more programmes and choice; British channels could be received in much of the east and north (see the notes on the impact of RTÉ).
The Irish Times under the editor Douglas Gageby, from 1963, became a forum for new ideas, and magazines such as Magill, founded in 1977, expanded political journalism.
Pirate radio stations grew in the 1970s and 1980s, challenging RTÉ's monopoly, and the Radio and Television Act 1988 licensed independent local radio.
Computers were adopted in business and government from the 1970s, and American firms such as Digital opened plants in Ireland, laying the base for the electronics industry.
These changes exposed people to a wider range of ideas and lifestyles, and helped to break down the isolation on which traditional authority had rested.

Achievements: the Irish language gained broadcasting and institutions, traditional music was revived and reached a world audience, the church embraced liturgical reform and ecumenism, and censorship was relaxed.
Limits: the language continued to decline as a community language, the compulsion debates left many pupils indifferent, and the church's leadership, especially under McQuaid, was slow to adapt.
Contemporary view: traditionalists feared that television and liberal reform threatened Irish identity and Catholic values, while reformers saw the changes as overdue.
Later view: historians see the period as the start of the shift to a more secular and pluralist society, with the church retaining strong influence on law and public life well into the 1980s.
Irish television began late, after a long debate about whether and how the state should run it.
Radio had been run by the state since 2RN opened in Dublin in 1926, and by the 1950s it was called Radio Éireann and was part of the Department of Posts and Telegraphs.

Before 1961 viewers in the east, the north and along the coast could pick up BBC and Ulster Television signals from Britain and Northern Ireland, and these showed that Irish demand for television was growing.

The government decided to set up a national service, financed by licence fees and advertising, and the Broadcasting Authority Act 1960 created the Radio Éireann Authority, soon known as the Radio Telefís Éireann (RTÉ) Authority, to run radio and television.
The members of the Authority were appointed by the government, which also set the framework in law.
Telefís Éireann began broadcasting on 31 December 1961; President de Valera spoke at the opening and warned that television had a great power for good and evil.
Television reached most of the country within a few years as transmitters were built, and by the early 1970s most households had a set.
The Minister for Posts and Telegraphs could direct the Authority in certain matters under the 1960 Act, and Section 31 allowed him to require it to refrain from broadcasting specified material.
RTÉ was a statutory body, not a government department, and the Act required it to be impartial in news and current affairs; how far it was independent in practice was a source of conflict.

Seán Lemass saw television as a means of national development and public information, and he said that RTÉ was an instrument of public policy, which meant it should support the national goals of the government without being its mouthpiece.
Critics, including many in RTÉ, held that a broadcaster could serve the public only if it was free to criticise the government.
The tension between the two views shaped the history of RTÉ in the 1960s and the crisis of 1971 and 1972.
Much early output was imported from Britain and the United States, including westerns, comedies and films, and imported programmes gave Irish viewers a view of life elsewhere.
Home-produced programmes covered news, sport, current affairs, drama, light entertainment and Irish-language material; coverage of Gaelic games drew large audiences.
The Riordans, a drama about a farming family that began in 1965, was a hit with viewers, especially in rural Ireland, and it dealt with real issues of farming life and change.
Telefís Scoile, which began on 4 February 1964, broadcast lessons for secondary school pupils and was one of the earliest schools television services in Europe.
Irish-language programmes and news bulletins in Irish were broadcast from the start, though they took a small share of airtime and often had a small audience.
RTÉ also raised standards for Irish drama and music, and helped writers, actors and entertainers to reach a national audience.
The Late Late Show, first broadcast in July 1962, became the best-known programme on Irish television and a forum for national debate.
The programme was a live Friday night talk show with guests, music and audience participation, and it started as a summer filler before it became a fixture.
Gay Byrne presented it from 1962 until 1999, and his skills as a chat-show host brought viewers an open-minded, humorous but probing style.
The show discussed subjects that were rarely talked of in public, including sex, marriage, contraception, unmarried mothers and the church.

In 1966 a quiz item for married couples led to the episode known as the Bishop and the Nightie: when Gay Byrne asked a wife, Eileen Fox, what she had worn on her honeymoon night, she said she had not worn a nightdress; the remark caused uproar.
Bishop Thomas Ryan of Clonfert condemned the programme, and other clergy and some viewers complained, while many viewers defended Byrne and the show.
The incident showed that television could provoke public arguments about morality and the limits of church authority, and it brought the Late Late Show to national attention.
Seven Days, a current affairs series launched in 1966, used young producers and reporters to investigate housing, poverty, emigration and other social issues.
Ministers resented programmes that criticised policy, and complaints were made to the RTÉ Authority, which was under pressure to restrain current affairs.
A Seven Days programme on illegal moneylending in 1969 led to a government-ordered inquiry and a row about RTÉ's independence, after which current affairs coverage was reorganised.
From the end of the 1960s the Troubles made coverage of Northern Ireland a major source of conflict between RTÉ and the government, which feared that broadcasts would encourage violence.
The government held financial and legal power over the broadcaster, as it appointed the Authority and could change the law.
Television altered how evenings were spent, since people stayed at home to watch rather than go to dances or visit neighbours, and it reduced the isolation of rural communities.
It brought national and international news and sport into every home, and gave people in the countryside access to the same culture and entertainment as city people.
Programmes on social issues exposed viewers to arguments about contraception, divorce and the church that censorship had kept out of print.
Church leaders such as McQuaid were concerned about the effects of television on faith and morals, but the church also used television to broadcast Mass, the Angelus and religious programmes.
Politicians had to learn to use the medium: party leaders appeared on television to speak directly to voters, and campaigns began to focus on television appearances and image.
Viewers' reactions varied: many welcomed the new window on the world, while others, including some clergy and traditionalists, saw it as a threat to Irish values.
Coverage of the Northern conflict led to the first serious use of the government's powers over broadcasting.

On 1 October 1971 the Minister for Posts and Telegraphs, Gerry Collins, issued the first order under Section 31, directing RTÉ not to broadcast material that could promote or incite to crime or tend to undermine the authority of the State.
RTÉ journalists protested that the order restricted reporting of the Troubles and argued that the public had a right to hear different views.
On 19 November 1972 the radio programme This Week broadcast an interview by Kevin O'Kelly with Seán Mac Stíofáin, chief of staff of the Provisional IRA, who was arrested the same day.
The government regarded the broadcast as a breach of the Section 31 order, and in late November 1972 Collins dismissed the whole RTÉ Authority and appointed a new one.
O'Kelly was later jailed for refusing to identify Mac Stíofáin's voice in court.
The sacking caused protests by journalists and in the Oireachtas, and it raised the question of whether a state broadcaster could report freely.
Section 31 restrictions were extended and widened in the 1970s and 1980s, and they were not ended until 1994.
Byrne was the presenter of The Late Late Show and the best-known broadcaster in Ireland for decades.
Gay Byrne was born in Dublin in 1934, worked in Britain in the 1950s and returned to join Radio Éireann in the late 1950s, becoming a presenter on Telefís Éireann in its first years.
He presented The Late Late Show from 1962 to 1999 and a morning radio programme from 1973, which gave him a wide audience in every part of the country.
He was a participant in the change of the 1960s: his questions to guests and audience on sex, marriage and religion set the agenda for debate.
He generally avoided taking sides, presenting himself as a neutral host, but his willingness to air subjects that the church or the government preferred to avoid had a liberalising effect.
Contemporaries were divided, with many welcoming him as a modern voice and others, including some clergy, seeing his programme as an attack on morals.

Historians and commentators regard him as a major influence on how Irish people talked about sexuality, the church and social issues, while noting that television reflected changes that were already under way; he died in 2019.
The government and Lemass: RTÉ should help to modernise the country, explain official policy and support national aims, and ministers expected a degree of cooperation from its Authority.
RTÉ journalists and producers: a national broadcaster should be free to investigate and criticise, and many saw ministerial pressure as censorship.

The Catholic Church: television was a powerful influence on the young that needed to be watched, and bishops and priests objected to some programmes, though the church also valued the airtime given to religion.

Language activists: Irish-language output was too small a share of the schedule, and imported English-language programmes, mostly from Britain and the United States, risked weakening the language further.
Rural viewers: programmes such as The Riordans showed their own lives, while others thought the city-based producers misrepresented the countryside.
Politicians outside government: opposition parties complained of bias in favour of the government, and some felt that the Authority was too ready to give way to ministers.

Historians such as Robert Savage, in his study of television and Irish society in these years, show that RTÉ both reflected changes already under way and helped to speed them, and that its relationship with the state was complicated rather than simply one of control.
Entertained: it brought sport, drama, light entertainment and music to a national audience, and many programmes, such as The Riordans and The Late Late Show, were hugely popular.
Challenged: current affairs and chat shows questioned authority and exposed issues that were taboo, such as contraception, poverty and the Northern conflict.
Changed: viewers had a wider view of the world, attitudes to church and state became more questioning, and the habit of national debate grew.
Limits: the government held strong powers, Section 31 and the dismissal of the Authority showed that independence was fragile, and Irish-language programmes struggled for audiences.
Contemporary view: viewers welcomed the entertainment and new voices, while the church and government saw risks in the programmes.

Later view: historians argue that television both entertained and challenged, and that it speeded up changes in attitudes to religion, sexuality and authority, while acknowledging that other factors such as education, emigration and EEC entry mattered too.
The powers that defeated Napoleon met at Vienna to redraw the map of Europe. Their aims were to contain France, restore the old order and prevent another bid for European domination.
The Congress met from autumn 1814, and its Final Act was signed on 9 June 1815, nine days before the battle of Waterloo (18 June 1815).
Its leading figures were Metternich for Austria, Castlereagh for Britain, Tsar Alexander I for Russia, Hardenberg for Prussia and Talleyrand for restored France.
Legitimacy: rulers deposed by Napoleon were restored, with the Bourbons returned to the thrones of France, Spain and Naples.

Balance of power: a ring of buffer states was built around France: the Kingdom of the Netherlands, enlarged to include Belgium; Piedmont-Sardinia, strengthened by gaining Genoa; and a neutral Switzerland.
Austria gave up the Austrian Netherlands but gained Lombardy-Venetia in northern Italy, and Habsburg relatives ruled Tuscany, Modena and Parma, making Austria the dominant power in the peninsula.
Prussia gained the Rhineland and Westphalia, which made it guardian of the Rhine frontier against France, together with about two-fifths of Saxony and Swedish Pomerania.
Russia gained most of the Duchy of Warsaw as the Congress Kingdom of Poland, with the Tsar as its king.
Britain kept colonies and bases taken during the wars, including Malta, Heligoland, Ceylon and the Cape Colony, and Castlereagh pressed for a moderate peace that did not humiliate France.
The Papal States were restored to the Pope.
Nationalist and liberal hopes awakened by the French Revolution and Napoleon were ignored: Germans, Italians, Poles and Belgians were placed under rulers chosen by the great powers.
The Congress replaced the Holy Roman Empire, dissolved in 1806, with a German Confederation (Bund) of 39 sovereign states, set out in the Federal Act of June 1815.
Its only institution was a Diet (Bundestag) at Frankfurt made up of delegates sent by the member governments, with Austria presiding; there was no elected national parliament.
Important decisions needed large majorities or unanimity, and the member states kept their own rulers and armies, so the Bund could act only when Austria and Prussia agreed.
