Its main purpose was the security of its members against France and against revolution, not German unity.

Article 13 of the Federal Act promised each state a constitution based on assemblies of estates; Bavaria and Baden (1818) and Württemberg (1819) granted constitutions, but Austria and Prussia did not, which angered liberals.
Austria and Prussia were the two dominant members, and their rivalry shaped German politics until 1866.
After 1815 the great powers met at congresses to manage crises. Metternich turned these meetings into a means of suppressing revolution.
The Quadruple Alliance of Britain, Russia, Austria and Prussia (November 1815) bound the four to uphold the settlement, keep France in check and meet at intervals.

The Holy Alliance (September 1815), proposed by Alexander I and signed by Russia, Austria and Prussia, pledged rulers to govern by Christian principles; Britain refused to join, and Metternich called it empty but used it to bind the eastern monarchies together.
Aix-la-Chapelle (1818) ended the allied occupation of France and admitted France to the Concert of Europe.
Troppau (1820): Austria, Prussia and Russia signed the Troppau Protocol, claiming the right to intervene against revolutions that threatened other states; Britain and France refused to sign.
Laibach (1821) authorised Austrian troops to crush the revolution in Naples, and Austria also put down the Piedmontese rising that year.

Verona (1822): the eastern powers backed a French invasion of Spain to restore Ferdinand VII, which went ahead in 1823; Britain, whose foreign secretary was now Canning after Castlereagh's death in August 1822, refused and left the Congress System.
Britain's withdrawal, and its later support for Latin American and Greek independence, left the system as an alliance of the three eastern autocracies.
Metternich's aim was to preserve the 1815 settlement and the multinational Habsburg Empire, which liberalism and nationalism threatened to break apart.

Austria was an autocracy under Emperor Francis I (to 1835) and then the feeble Ferdinand I: there was no constitution or parliament, and power rested with the emperor, his ministers, the army and the bureaucracy.
Inside Austria, police, informers, postal interception and strict censorship of books, newspapers and the theatre watched and silenced critics.

The Carlsbad Decrees followed the murder in March 1819 of the conservative writer August von Kotzebue by Karl Sand, a radical student; they were drawn up at a ministers' conference at Carlsbad in August and adopted by the Diet in September 1819.
The Decrees banned the Burschenschaften, put the universities under government supervisors, allowed liberal professors to be dismissed and imposed censorship on newspapers and shorter publications.
A Central Investigating Commission at Mainz was set up under the Decrees to hunt down revolutionary conspiracies across the German states.

The Six Articles of June 1832, passed by the Diet after the Hambach Festival, reasserted the princes' authority: state parliaments could not refuse taxes to force concessions, and the Diet could intervene in states where order broke down.
Further measures in July 1832 banned political associations and public meetings and tightened press controls.
Abroad, Metternich used the congresses and the alliance with Russia and Prussia to justify intervention, and Austrian troops crushed risings in Italy in 1821 and 1831.
The system relied on Prussia's cooperation inside the Bund and on Russia's support in Europe, so it was weakened when either went its own way.
The Burschenschaften, student fraternities founded at Jena in 1815, spread liberal and nationalist ideas and adopted the black, red and gold colours later used by German nationalists.
The Wartburg Festival (October 1817) gathered students to mark the 300th anniversary of Luther's Reformation and the 1813 victory at Leipzig, called for German unity and burned conservative books.
The revolutions of 1820–21 in Spain, Naples and Piedmont forced kings to grant constitutions, but Austrian troops restored absolutism in Italy and French troops did so in Spain in 1823.

The Greek War of Independence (from 1821) broke the principle of non-intervention for the powers: philhellenism, boosted by Byron's death at Missolonghi in April 1824, led Britain, France and Russia to destroy the Turkish-Egyptian fleet at Navarino (1827).

The London Protocol (February 1830) recognised an independent Greece, and the Convention of London (1832) made it a monarchy under Otto of Bavaria; Metternich had opposed this support for rebels against a legitimate ruler.
The July Revolution in France (1830) overthrew Charles X, the last Bourbon king, after his July Ordinances, and brought Louis-Philippe of Orléans to the throne.

The Belgian revolt of August 1830 separated Belgium from the Netherlands; the London Conference recognised its independence, Leopold of Saxe-Coburg became king in 1831, and the Treaty of London (1839) guaranteed its neutrality.
The November Uprising (1830–31) in Russian Poland was crushed, and Nicholas I abolished the Polish constitution in 1832.
Risings in Modena, Parma and the Papal Legations in 1831 were put down by Austrian troops.
The Hambach Festival (May 1832) brought about 20,000–30,000 people to the Palatinate to demand German unity, a free press and popular sovereignty under black, red and gold flags.
Prussia's Customs Law of 1818 abolished internal tariffs inside its scattered territories and set a low external tariff.
Neighbouring states joined Prussia's system, and the Zollverein (German Customs Union) took effect on 1 January 1834 with 18 states, under treaties agreed in 1833.
Members traded freely with each other behind a common external tariff and shared the customs revenue.
Austria stayed outside because its protected industries and separate tariff system could not fit a low-tariff union, and Metternich warned that the union was building Prussian influence.
Leadership of the Zollverein gave Prussia an economic and political lead in Germany and accustomed the smaller states to looking to Berlin rather than Vienna.
News of the February 1848 revolution in Paris sparked demonstrations in German and Austrian cities.
On 13 March 1848 students and workers demonstrated in Vienna, troops fired on the crowd, and the court made Metternich resign that evening; he fled and went into exile in England.
His fall removed the main defender of the 1815 settlement and coincided with revolutions across the Habsburg lands and the German states.
The Habsburg Empire then faced a crisis of nationalities, with Hungarian, Czech and Italian demands for self-rule (see the notes on the 1848 Revolution in Germany).
Prince Clemens von Metternich, a Rhineland aristocrat, guided Habsburg foreign policy from 1809 to 1848 and gave his name to the conservative order of 1815–1848.
Born in Koblenz in 1773, he saw his family's Rhineland estates overrun by the French revolutionary armies, which shaped his lifelong hatred of revolution.
He became Austrian foreign minister in 1809 and state chancellor in 1821, and hosted and dominated the Congress of Vienna.
He believed that liberalism and nationalism would destroy the multinational Habsburg Empire, so he defended monarchy, legitimacy and the balance of power.
He was a direct participant: he drafted the Carlsbad Decrees and the 1832 measures, led the congresses of Troppau and Laibach and sent Austrian troops into Italy.
His policy was shaped by events he could not control: Greek independence, the 1830 revolutions and the Zollverein all showed the limits of his power.
He famously dismissed Italy as a geographical expression (1847), meaning it was not a nation.
He returned to Vienna in 1851 and died in 1859; his memoirs, edited by his son and published from 1880, presented him as the defender of order against revolution.
Contemporaries: conservative rulers praised him as the guardian of peace, while liberals and nationalists saw him as the symbol of reaction, censorship and police rule.

Historians: Heinrich von Srbik's biography (1925) and Henry Kissinger's A World Restored (1957) praised him as a statesman who gave Europe a stable peace; critics argue that he only repressed the causes of unrest, which returned with greater force in 1848.
Success: the great powers fought no general war between 1815 and the Crimean War (1853–56).
Limit: the peace owed much to exhaustion after 1815 and to Britain's naval power, not only to Metternich.
Success: revolutions in Italy (1821, 1831) and liberal movements in Germany (1819, 1832) were crushed, and the Habsburg Empire survived intact until 1848.
Limit: the Congress System broke up in the 1820s, and Greek independence and Belgian independence overturned parts of the 1815 settlement.
Success: in the German Confederation, Austria kept its presidency and the smaller states usually followed its lead before 1848.
Limit: Prussia's Zollverein built a German economic unit without Austria, laying a foundation for Prussian leadership.
Overall: the system delayed liberal and national change for over thirty years but did not remove its causes, and it collapsed within days of the Vienna rising of March 1848.
Revolution began in Palermo in January 1848 and in Paris on 22–24 February, when Louis-Philippe fell and the Second Republic was declared.
Within weeks risings followed in Vienna (13 March), Milan (the Five Days, 18–22 March), Venice, Berlin (18 March), Budapest and Prague.

Common causes: the crop failures and economic depression of 1846–47; middle-class liberal demands for constitutions; nationalist demands from Germans, Italians, Hungarians and Czechs; and the example of Paris, spread quickly by newspapers, railways and the telegraph.
Britain and Russia escaped revolution, and by 1849 nearly every rising had been defeated by the old monarchies and their armies.
The German revolution grew out of economic distress, liberal frustration with the system of 1815 and the wish for a united German nation.
Potato blight from 1845 and poor grain harvests in 1846 and 1847 sharply raised food prices and caused hunger riots in many areas.

A commercial and industrial depression in 1847 brought bankruptcies and unemployment, hitting artisans already threatened by factory competition; the Silesian weavers' rising of 1844 had shown the desperation of hand workers.
Liberals, mostly educated middle-class men, wanted constitutions, freedom of the press and assembly, trial by jury and a German national parliament.
Nationalists wanted a German nation state, but disagreed whether it should include the German lands of the Habsburg Empire.
Peasants in the south and west wanted an end to the remaining feudal dues and services owed to landlords.
Liberal opposition had grown in the southern state parliaments and in Prussia's United Diet of 1847, which refused to vote a railway loan without constitutional concessions.
Within weeks of the Paris revolution, rulers across the German states gave way to crowds rather than risk being overthrown.
A mass meeting at Mannheim in Baden on 27 February 1848 demanded a free press, trial by jury, citizens' militias and a German parliament, and these March demands spread across the states.
Rulers appointed liberal March ministries, promised constitutions and lifted censorship in Baden, Württemberg, Hesse, Saxony and Hanover.
In Bavaria, Ludwig I, already discredited by his affair with the dancer Lola Montez, abdicated in March 1848.
In Berlin, troops fired on a crowd on 18 March, and a night of barricade fighting left about 300 civilians dead.
On 19 March Frederick William IV withdrew the troops from Berlin and was forced to bare his head before the bodies of the dead in the palace courtyard.
On 21 March he rode through Berlin wearing the black, red and gold colours and declared that Prussia would merge into Germany.
He appointed a liberal ministry under the Rhineland businessmen Camphausen and Hansemann and called a Prussian National Assembly, elected in May 1848.
Peasant risings in the south-west forced governments to begin abolishing feudal dues.
The Vorparlament (pre-parliament), a self-appointed gathering of liberal politicians, met at Frankfurt from 31 March to 3 April 1848.

It rejected the radicals' call for a republic and arranged elections to a national assembly by broad manhood suffrage, although each state set its own rules and some excluded servants and men on poor relief.
Disappointed radicals in Baden, led by Friedrich Hecker and Gustav Struve, launched a republican rising in April 1848, which federal troops defeated at Kandern on 20 April.
The Frankfurt National Assembly opened on 18 May 1848 in the Paulskirche (St Paul's Church).

About 585 deputies were elected, and some 800 men sat at some point including substitutes; most were lawyers, judges, civil servants, teachers and professors, so it was nicknamed the professors' parliament.
Craftsmen were few, and there were almost no peasants or workers among the deputies.
The Assembly elected Heinrich von Gagern, a moderate liberal from Hesse-Darmstadt, as its president.

On 29 June 1848 it chose Archduke John of Austria as Reichsverweser (imperial regent) at the head of a Provisional Central Power, but this government had no army, civil service or tax revenue of its own.
The Basic Rights of the German People, passed in December 1848, guaranteed equality before the law, freedom of the press, speech, religion, assembly and movement, and trial by jury.
They abolished the nobility as a privileged estate, landlords' private courts and feudal dues, and abolished the death penalty except under martial law.
Grossdeutsch (Greater German): a Germany including the German-speaking Habsburg lands, favoured by Catholics, Austrians and many southerners.
Kleindeutsch (Lesser German): a Germany united under Prussia without Austria, favoured by Gagern and most Protestant northern liberals.

The Grossdeutsch plan failed when Austria's new chief minister, Prince Felix Schwarzenberg, insisted in March 1849 that the whole multinational Habsburg Empire must enter any German state or none of it would.
The Assembly also claimed mixed areas ruled by others, such as parts of Prussian Poland (Posen), showing that liberal nationalism could deny other nations' rights.

The duchies of Schleswig and Holstein were ruled by the King of Denmark; Holstein, wholly German, belonged to the German Confederation, while Schleswig had a mixed Danish and German population and did not.
When the new Danish king, Frederick VII, moved to incorporate Schleswig into Denmark in March 1848, the German population rose and set up a provisional government at Kiel.
Prussian troops under General Wrangel invaded on the Confederation's behalf, which the Assembly hailed as a national war.
Under pressure from Britain and Russia, Prussia signed the Malmö armistice in August 1848 without consulting Frankfurt.
The Assembly first rejected the armistice and then, having no army of its own, accepted it on 16 September 1848.

Radicals rioted in Frankfurt on 18 September and murdered two conservative deputies, Prince Felix Lichnowsky and General Hans von Auerswald, and the Assembly had to be saved by Prussian and Austrian troops.
Fighting resumed in 1849, but Prussia made peace with Denmark in 1850, the duchies' army was defeated at Idstedt that July, and the London Protocol of 1852 confirmed the Danish king's rule.
By late 1848 the old governments had regained control of their capitals through force, while the liberals at Frankfurt were still debating.
In June 1848 the Austrian general Windischgrätz bombarded Prague and crushed the Czech rising, and in July Radetzky defeated Piedmont at Custoza.
A radical rising in Vienna in October 1848 was crushed when Windischgrätz and the Croatian commander Jelačić retook the city on 31 October.
Robert Blum, a radical Frankfurt deputy from Saxony, was shot in Vienna on 9 November 1848, despite his immunity as a member of the Assembly.
Schwarzenberg became Austrian chief minister in November, and on 2 December 1848 the 18-year-old Franz Joseph replaced Emperor Ferdinand.
In Berlin, Frederick William IV appointed a conservative ministry under Count Brandenburg, and General Wrangel's troops entered the city on 10 November 1848 without resistance.
On 5 December 1848 the king dissolved the Prussian National Assembly and imposed a constitution of his own, which kept royal control of the army and ministers.

In May 1849 Prussia brought in the three-class franchise, which divided voters into three classes by the taxes they paid; each class chose a third of the electors, so a small wealthy minority had a vastly greater say than the poor majority.

The Frankfurt constitution, completed on 27–28 March 1849, created a federal German Empire with a hereditary emperor, a lower house elected by manhood suffrage and an upper house representing the states.
On 28 March 1849 the Assembly elected Frederick William IV Emperor of the Germans by 290 votes, with 248 deputies abstaining.

Frederick William gave an evasive answer to the Assembly's delegation on 3 April and formally refused the crown on 28 April 1849, because he would not accept a crown from an elected assembly rather than from his fellow princes.
In private he scorned it as a crown picked up from the gutter of revolution.
Austria rejected the constitution and recalled its deputies in April 1849.
Twenty-eight smaller states accepted the constitution by mid-April, but Prussia, Bavaria, Saxony and Hanover rejected it, so it never came into force.
In May 1849 radicals rose in Saxony, the Palatinate and Baden to force the princes to accept the constitution; Richard Wagner and Mikhail Bakunin took part in the Dresden rising.
Prussian troops crushed the Dresden rising in May and the Baden and Palatinate risings by July 1849, when the fortress of Rastatt surrendered and many rebels were executed.
The moderates left Frankfurt, and about 100 radical deputies moved to Stuttgart as a rump parliament until Württemberg troops dispersed them on 18 June 1849.
Thousands of revolutionaries emigrated, many to the United States, where the Forty-Eighters included Hecker and Carl Schurz.
Prussia's Erfurt Union plan, drawn up by Joseph von Radowitz, tried in 1849–50 to unite Germany under Prussia by agreement of the princes, and an Erfurt Parliament met in March–April 1850.
Austria, backed by Russia, threatened war, and by the Punctation of Olmütz (29 November 1850) Prussia abandoned the union; Prussians remembered it as a humiliation.
The old Confederation and its Diet were restored in 1851 under Austrian presidency, with Bismarck as Prussia's delegate at Frankfurt from that year.
The Frankfurt Assembly had no army, money or administration, so it depended on the very governments it was trying to limit.
The rulers kept control of their armies and bureaucracies, which stayed loyal and were used to retake Prague, Vienna and Berlin once the shock of March had passed.
Liberals were divided from radicals and workers: middle-class deputies feared a social revolution and a republic more than they feared the princes.
Peasants lost interest once governments abolished most feudal dues in 1848, as Austria did in September 1848.
Months of debate on the Basic Rights and the Grossdeutsch–Kleindeutsch question gave Austria and Prussia time to recover.
National rivalries with Danes, Poles and Czechs split the revolutionaries and gave the Habsburg army willing allies, such as Jelačić's Croats.
The refusal of the crown by Frederick William IV left the constitution without the one state strong enough to enforce it.
Failure: no united Germany was created, the Basic Rights were repealed by the restored Diet in 1851, and the old Confederation returned.
Achievement: feudal dues and serfdom were abolished, and Prussia kept a constitution and parliament after 1850, however limited.
Failure: liberals were discredited as impractical, and many concluded that unity would come only through Prussian power, which Bismarck's later methods confirmed.
Achievement: the Assembly was Germany's first national parliament, created political parties and provided a model for the constitutions of 1919 and the Basic Law of 1949.
Contemporary views: conservatives celebrated the restoration of order, while radicals and exiles, including Marx and Engels, blamed the cowardice of the liberal middle class.

Later views: A. J. P. Taylor wrote that in 1848 German history reached its turning point and failed to turn, a view linked to the idea of a German special path (Sonderweg) away from democracy; more recent historians stress the revolution's lasting gains in political culture and participation.
After the failure of 1848, the balance between Prussia and Austria within the German Confederation turned on economic power and on the ability of each state to manage its own affairs.
The Zollverein, which by the 1850s included most German states except Austria, gave Prussia control of a large common market and a share of the tariff revenue.
The Ruhr and Silesia provided coal and iron, and the growth of railways linked the Prussian industrial regions to Berlin and to the Rhineland.
Krupp's steel works at Essen, expanded from the 1850s, produced guns and rails and symbolised Prussia's industrial power.
Austria's finances were weak and its government remained centralised and conservative, with the Habsburg monarchy heavily in debt.
Austria's defeat in the Second Italian War of Independence (1859), when it lost Lombardy at the battles of Magenta and Solferino, exposed its military weakness.
Austria's proposed reform of the Confederation, the Frankfurt Princes' Congress of August 1863, collapsed after Prussia, on Bismarck's advice, refused to attend.
Austria had alienated Russia by its stance in the Crimean War (1853–56), so it lacked a friend when Prussia challenged it.
Prussia's 1862 commercial treaty with France set a low-tariff course that the Zollverein states followed, which Austria's protectionist system could not match.

William became regent in 1858 and king in 1861; the army reform planned by Roon kept three-year service, enlarged the regular army and reduced the role of the citizen Landwehr, which the liberal majority in the Prussian Landtag opposed.
The liberals refused to vote the army budget, the king considered abdicating, and the constitutional crisis deepened.
Albrecht von Roon, War Minister from 1859, and Helmuth von Moltke, chief of the general staff from 1857, were the leading figures behind the army reforms.
In September 1862 William I appointed Otto von Bismarck as Minister-President and Foreign Minister of Prussia to break the deadlock.
Bismarck's government declared that it was entitled to continue collecting taxes during the conflict, which lasted until the Indemnity Bill of 1866.
The duchies of Schleswig and Holstein were ruled by the Danish king, but the German population of Holstein and parts of Schleswig wanted links with the German Confederation.
In November 1863 Denmark adopted a constitution that brought Schleswig closer to Denmark, which broke an earlier agreement and provoked the German states.
Prussia and Austria jointly invaded Denmark in February 1864, defeated it in the battles of Düppel and Als, and forced the Treaty of Vienna (October 1864).
Denmark gave up Schleswig, Holstein and Lauenburg to the two victors, and the question of their future was left to be settled between Prussia and Austria.
The Convention of Gastein (August 1865) gave Austria the administration of Holstein and Prussia the administration of Schleswig, which set up the conflict of 1866.
Christian IX succeeded to the Danish throne in November 1863 and signed the new constitution, which contravened the London Protocol of 1852 that had settled the succession to the duchies.
Bismarck secured Italian support for the war by an alliance with Italy in April 1866, which promised Venetia to Italy if Prussia won.
Prussia declared the Gastein arrangements at an end and occupied Holstein in June 1866, and most German states sided with Austria in the Confederation.
Prussia's breech-loading needle-gun, Moltke's planning and rapid rail mobilisation allowed its armies to advance quickly into Bohemia.
The battle of Königgrätz (also called Sadowa), fought on 3 July 1866, was the decisive Prussian victory of the war.
The Treaty of Prague (August 1866) dissolved the German Confederation and excluded Austria from German affairs.
Prussia annexed Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau, Frankfurt and Schleswig-Holstein, and the southern states signed secret military alliances with Prussia.
Austria was required to accept the dissolution of the Confederation and gave up Venetia, which passed to Italy, and the Habsburg lands lay outside any German state.
The North German Confederation was formed in 1867 by the states north of the River Main, under Prussian leadership.

Its constitution, which took effect in 1867, made the king of Prussia president of the Confederation, with Bismarck as its Chancellor, and gave the president control of foreign policy and the armed forces.
The Reichstag of the Confederation was elected by universal male suffrage, while the Bundesrat, the upper house of the states' governments, was dominated by Prussia.
The National Liberal Party was founded in 1867, and many liberals accepted Bismarck's leadership in return for national unification.
A Customs Parliament (Zollparlament) met in 1868 with deputies from the southern states as well as the north, although the south elected many opponents of Prussia.
After Königgrätz, Bismarck persuaded William I to halt at the Nikolsburg preliminaries (July 1866) and not to march on Vienna or take Austrian territory, to keep Austria as a future friend.
The Indemnity Bill of 1866 asked the Landtag to approve retrospectively the years of government without a budget, and it split the liberals into those who gave way and those who stayed in opposition.
In 1870 Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, a relative of the Prussian king, was offered the vacant Spanish throne, which alarmed France, which feared encirclement.
Leopold's candidacy was withdrawn on 12 July 1870 after French pressure, but France then demanded a guarantee that it would never recur.
On 13 July 1870 King William I at Bad Ems refused to give that guarantee, and his telegram to Bismarck was edited by Bismarck and published in a shortened form.
The edited Ems telegram made the exchange seem an insult to France, and France declared war on Prussia on 19 July 1870.
The southern German states, Baden, Württemberg and Bavaria, joined the war on the Prussian side under the terms of their treaties with Prussia.
The French army was defeated at Wörth and Spicheren in August 1870 and at Sedan on 2 September 1870, where Napoleon III was captured.
The siege of Paris lasted from September 1870 to January 1871, and the French government of National Defence continued the war until the city surrendered.

Napoleon III led the army to the front, and Moltke's armies, using railways and superior artillery, won quickly; after Sedan the Second Empire fell on 4 September 1870 and Gambetta's Government of National Defence carried on the war.
The French army at Metz surrendered in October 1870 and Paris capitulated in January 1871, with an armistice signed on 28 January.

In November 1870 treaties brought the southern states into the new union, and in late 1870 King Ludwig II of Bavaria sent a letter, drafted with Bismarck's help, inviting William I to accept the imperial title.
The German Empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871 in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, with William I as German Emperor.

The Treaty of Frankfurt (May 1871) ended the war, transferring Alsace (except Belfort) and part of Lorraine, including Metz, to Germany and requiring France to pay an indemnity of five billion francs.

The constitution of the German Empire, adopted in spring 1871 and based on that of the North German Confederation, created a federal state with a Reichstag, a Bundesrat and an emperor who was also King of Prussia.
The Chancellor answered to the emperor, not to the Reichstag, and Prussia, with its own conservative franchise, dominated the new state.

Bismarck was a Prussian conservative and Junker landowner who used war and diplomacy to create the German Empire. This part covers his role in the unification process; his later career is covered in the notes on the Second Reich and the Bismarckian system.
Born in 1815 into a Junker landowning family in the Prussian province of Saxony, Bismarck sat in the United Diet of 1847 as an ultra-conservative and in the Prussian Landtag from 1849.
He was Prussian representative at the restored German Diet in Frankfurt from 1851 to 1859, and then ambassador in St Petersburg and Paris before becoming Minister-President in 1862.
In his speech to the Budget Committee on 30 September 1862 he said that the great questions of the day would be decided not by speeches and majority votes but by blood and iron.

As Minister-President he argued that the constitution had a gap on what happened when king and Landtag disagreed (the gap theory), and so collected taxes and carried through the army reform without an approved budget.
He acted as a participant at each stage of unification, managing the Danish War, the Gastein settlement, the alliance with Italy and the Ems telegram.
Contemporaries were divided: conservatives admired his success, while many liberals saw him as an authoritarian who had broken the constitution.

Historians disagree: admirers in the Prussian school saw a master plan, A. J. P. Taylor portrayed an opportunist improvising, and Lothar Gall called him a white revolutionary who used revolutionary means to preserve conservative power.
He became Chancellor of the North German Confederation in 1867 and Imperial Chancellor in 1871, holding office until 1890.
Realpolitik, a word coined by Ludwig von Rochau in 1853, meant pursuing state interests through power and diplomacy rather than through principles or ideology.
Bismarck used liberal demands for national unity to win support for his policies, while keeping the army and the monarchy under royal control.

He isolated Austria diplomatically: Russian goodwill after the Alvensleben Convention of 1863 against the Polish rising, Napoleon III's neutrality after their meeting at Biarritz in 1865, and the alliance with Italy in 1866.
He set out limited war aims and avoided humiliating Austria in 1866, which made it easier for Austria to become a partner later.
He used the Ems telegram to create a public crisis that drew the southern states into the war, which showed his readiness to exploit an opportunity.
Italy was unified between 1859 and 1871, with the Kingdom of Italy proclaimed in 1861 and Venetia and Rome added in 1866 and 1870.

Both unifications were led by a strong kingdom (Piedmont or Prussia) that won wars with the help of diplomacy: Piedmont used French help against Austria in 1859, while Prussia relied on the neutrality of Russia and France.
Italy's unification was driven by a mix of Piedmontese leadership and Garibaldi's volunteers, while Germany's was directed by the Prussian state and its army.
Italy won Venetia thanks to Prussia's victory in 1866, but Rome was blocked until the French garrison left in 1870.
Italy's unity came partly from below, through Garibaldi's volunteers and plebiscites, while Germany's came from above, through the Prussian army and the princes.
Italy left Italian-speaking Trentino and Trieste in Austria, while Germany placed Poles, Danes and Alsatians inside the Empire.
Unity, the aim of the liberals of 1848, was achieved by 1871, but from above by Prussian arms rather than by a parliament.
The settlement left Austria, with its millions of Germans, outside the Empire (the Kleindeutsch solution), and the Empire contained Polish, Danish and, after 1871, French-speaking minorities.
The new Empire was dominated by Prussia, and the Reichstag, though elected by manhood suffrage, had no control over the Chancellor and less power than the liberals had hoped.
Liberal supporters of unification saw the Empire as a national triumph, while later critics argued that it was a Prussian-led autocracy built on militarism.
The Congress of Vienna left Italy divided into several states, most of them under Austrian influence or Habsburg relatives, with the Pope ruling the central lands.
The Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia, ruled by the House of Savoy, was the largest independent state in the north-west and the only major Italian state ruled by a native dynasty.
Austria directly ruled Lombardy and Venetia in the north, and Habsburg princes ruled Tuscany, Modena and Parma.
The Papal States covered central Italy from Rome to Bologna, and the Pope's government was an absolute monarchy with clerical control of administration.
The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, ruled by the Bourbons from Naples, covered the south and Sicily.
Secret societies, most notably the Carbonari, spread liberal and nationalist ideas among army officers, students and professionals in the 1820s.
The Carbonari took part in the revolts of 1820 in Naples and 1821 in Piedmont, which were crushed by Austrian troops, leaving the leaders imprisoned or exiled.
Revolts in 1831 in Modena, Parma and the Papal Legations of central Italy were defeated with Austrian help, and the Modenese rising's leader Ciro Menotti was executed.
Napoleonic rule had introduced the Code Napoleon, a single administration and the idea of a united Italy, which restored rulers could not entirely undo.
Mazzini was the most influential theorist and organiser of Italian nationalism before 1848. His ideal of a republican, unified Italy shaped the movement even when his methods failed.
Mazzini was born in Genoa in 1805, trained as a lawyer and joined the Carbonari before his arrest and exile in 1830.
In 1831 he founded Young Italy at Marseille, a secret society that aimed at a unified republic and whose members were mostly young.

He wanted a unitary republic, with the people as the sovereign, and his motto was God and the People (Dio e Popolo); his later book The Duties of Man (1860) stressed duty to the nation over individual rights.
He organised a failed invasion of Savoy in 1834 with other exiles, which was easily defeated, and he later founded Young Europe (1834) to link revolutionary movements.
Mazzini lived in exile in Switzerland, France and England, and from 1837 he remained based in London, where he ran his network of exiles and conspiracies.
In 1848 he returned to Italy and took part in the Roman Republic of 1849, where he was one of the triumvirs who governed the city.
Mazzini was a participant in the revolutionary movement rather than a witness: he planned risings and sent agents into Italy, but his ideas also inspired ordinary followers.
Contemporaries were divided: radicals and republicans admired him, while Cavour and the monarchists disliked his republicanism, and the Pope and Austria saw him as a dangerous conspirator.
Mazzini remained a republican and rejected the monarchical Italy of 1861 as a betrayal; in 1870 he was arrested in Sicily while trying to start a republican rising, and he died in Pisa in 1872.
Historians now see Mazzini as a key ideologue of Italian nationalism whose ideas shaped the Risorgimento, though his conspiracies largely failed and his republic was not achieved.
Mazzini's national ideas relied on the people's own insurrection and education, not on foreign help or kings, and his Young Italy members swore an oath to work for an independent, united republic.

Revolutions broke out across Italy in early 1848, starting at Palermo in January; after the February revolution in Paris, risings followed in Milan and Venice, and Pius IX granted a constitution in the Papal States.
The Five Days of Milan (18–22 March 1848) drove the Austrian garrison out of the city before Radetzky withdrew to the fortresses of the Quadrilateral.
Charles Albert of Piedmont declared war on Austria in March 1848, the first of the Italian wars of independence, and Piedmont's army was defeated at Custoza in July 1848.
Pope Pius IX, who had won a liberal reputation in 1846, withdrew from the war against Austria in April 1848 and fled to Gaeta in November 1848 after the murder of his minister Pellegrino Rossi.
The Roman Republic was proclaimed in February 1849, and Mazzini, Saffi and Armellini governed the city, with Garibaldi commanding its defence.
The Republic of San Marco in Venice, led by Daniele Manin, held out against Austria until August 1849.
Charles Albert was defeated at Novara in March 1849, abdicated and was succeeded by his son Victor Emmanuel II, who made peace with Austria.
French troops sent by Louis-Napoleon, then President of France, captured Rome in July 1849, restored the Pope and kept a garrison there.
Piedmont kept the Statuto Albertino, a constitution granted by Charles Albert in 1848, with an elected chamber, and it was the only Italian state to keep its constitution after 1849.
The Siccardi Laws of 1850 removed the separate church courts and some clerical privileges, causing conflict with the Papacy.

Count Camillo di Cavour, a landowner and journalist who had served as minister of agriculture and then finance, became Prime Minister of Piedmont in November 1852 and pursued economic modernisation, free trade and railway building.
Cavour made Piedmont a credible leader of the national cause by sending about 15,000 troops to the Crimean War in 1855, which gave it a seat at the Congress of Paris in 1856.
At the Congress of Paris, Cavour raised the Italian question and the problem of Austria's presence in the peninsula before the Great Powers.

Cavour and Napoleon III met secretly at Plombières in July 1858, agreeing that France would support Piedmont in a war against Austria, provided Austria appeared the aggressor, in return for Nice and Savoy; the plan also envisaged a marriage between Princess Clotilde of Savoy and Napoleon III's cousin Prince Napoleon.
The cession of Nice and Savoy to France in 1860 angered some nationalists, including Garibaldi, who was born in Nice.
The Italian National Society, founded in 1857 by Manin, La Farina and Garibaldi among others, backed Piedmont's leadership in place of Mazzini's republicanism.
Austria, goaded by Piedmontese mobilisation, issued an ultimatum and declared war on Piedmont in April 1859, and France came to Piedmont's support under Napoleon III.

The French and Piedmontese armies won at Magenta on 4 June 1859 and at Solferino on 24 June 1859, bloody battles that, together with Prussian mobilisation on the Rhine and Catholic anger at home, led Napoleon III to seek peace.
Napoleon III made the armistice of Villafranca with Austria on 11 July 1859 without consulting Cavour, who resigned in anger; Lombardy went to Piedmont but Venetia stayed under Austrian rule.
The Treaty of Zürich (November 1859) gave Lombardy to Piedmont, while Austria kept Venetia.
Tuscany, Modena, Parma and the Romagna held plebiscites in March 1860 and voted to join Piedmont, which Napoleon III accepted in return for Nice and Savoy.
Nice and Savoy were ceded to France by the Treaty of Turin (March 1860).
Garibaldi led about 1,000 volunteers, the Thousand, who sailed from Quarto near Genoa on 5 May 1860.
They landed at Marsala in Sicily on 11 May 1860, won the battle of Calatafimi, and took Palermo, where Garibaldi governed as dictator in the name of Victor Emmanuel II.
Garibaldi crossed to the mainland and entered Naples on 7 September 1860, as the Bourbon king Francis II withdrew.

The Piedmontese army invaded the Papal Marches and Umbria in September 1860, and Garibaldi handed his conquests to Victor Emmanuel II near Teano in October 1860, with plebiscites in the south approving annexation.
The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861, with Victor Emmanuel II as king.
Cavour died on 6 June 1861, months after the proclamation, and his successors struggled to resolve the southern question.
Garibaldi's attempt to march on Rome in 1862 was stopped at Aspromonte by Italian troops, and his 1867 attempt was defeated at Mentana by French troops.
Italy allied with Prussia in April 1866 and fought Austria in the Third War of Independence, but its defeats at Custoza and Lissa did not stop the Prussian victory.
Austria ceded Venetia to Napoleon III, who passed it to Italy under the Treaty of Vienna (October 1866) and a plebiscite.
The French garrison in Rome was withdrawn in August 1870 after the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian War.
Italian troops entered Rome on 20 September 1870 after a brief bombardment, and a plebiscite in October 1870 approved the annexation of Rome.

Rome became the capital of the Kingdom of Italy in 1871 (after Turin and then Florence from 1865); the Law of Guarantees offered the Pope privileges, but Pius IX rejected it and declared himself a prisoner of the Vatican.
Austrian control of Venetia and its military strength in the Quadrilateral were the main obstacles until 1866.
French protection of the Papacy, and the garrison in Rome, prevented the unification of the peninsula until 1870.
Regional rivalries, the strength of local identities and the lack of a common language among most people made national unity hard to achieve.
The divisions between republicans, led by Mazzini, and monarchists, led by Cavour and the Savoy dynasty, weakened earlier attempts.
After 1852 Piedmont offered a constitutional model, a modern economy and a professional army, which made it the leader of the movement.
Cavour used diplomacy to isolate Austria and to gain French support, while the Crimean War helped Piedmont gain a place among the Great Powers.
Garibaldi's volunteers provided the military force that could move quickly through the south, which the regular army alone could not have achieved.
Achievement: by 1871 the peninsula was united under a single monarchy, with Rome as its capital, which had been the aim of the Risorgimento since the 1820s.
Limit: the new state was a centralised monarchy under Piedmontese control, with a franchise so narrow that only about 2 per cent of the population could vote.
Achievement: the Piedmontese model of constitutional monarchy and a modern economy was adopted in the new Kingdom.
Limit: the southern peasantry gained little from unification, and brigandage in the south was suppressed by the army after 1861.

Historians differ: some stress Cavour's diplomacy and Piedmont's leadership, Denis Mack Smith saw Cavour and Garibaldi as rivals as well as partners, and Antonio Gramsci described the Risorgimento as a passive revolution that left the peasants out.
Overall: unity came through Piedmontese diplomacy, French support and Garibaldi's volunteers, but fell short of Mazzini's republican and popular ideal, and he was left disappointed.
The Ottoman Empire ruled the Balkans and Greece in 1815. The decline of its authority over Christian subjects raised the Eastern Question: which Great Power would benefit when the Ottomans weakened.
The Ottoman Sultan ruled the Balkan Christians through local officials and the millet system, which gave religious communities some legal autonomy but no political rights.
Russia claimed to protect Orthodox Christians in the Balkans and gained influence over the Danubian principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia after its wars with the Ottomans.

Austria feared Russian expansion into the Balkans and wanted the Ottoman Empire kept intact as a barrier, while Britain also wanted to protect its route to India through the Mediterranean and the Straits.
The Treaty of Adrianople (1829), which ended a Russo-Ottoman war, gave Russia control of the mouths of the Danube and obliged the Sultan to honour Serbian autonomy.
The Ottoman Hatt-i Humayun of 1856 promised equal treatment for non-Muslim subjects, a reform the Great Powers had pressed for at the end of the Crimean War.
The First Serbian Uprising began in 1804, led by Karadjordje (Karađorđe) Petrović, against the Janissary garrison that had terrorised the Serbs.
The Ottomans crushed the first rising in 1813, and Karadjordje fled, but a second rising in 1815 was led by Miloš Obrenović.
Miloš negotiated autonomy with the Ottoman government, which a decree of the Sultan recognised in 1830, and he became hereditary prince.

Miloš ruled in an autocratic manner and rivals were removed, among them Karadjordje, murdered in 1817 on his orders according to most accounts; the liberal constitution of 1835 limited his power and was suspended within weeks under pressure from Russia, Austria and the Ottomans.
Serbia remained under Ottoman suzerainty and paid an annual tribute to the Sultan, which was the price of its autonomy.

After the Ottomans imposed a new statute in 1838, which gave power to a council of notables, Miloš was forced to abdicate in 1839 and was followed by his sons Milan, who died within weeks, and then Mihailo.

Serbia remained a tributary principality, with Ottoman garrisons in its fortresses until 1867, and gained full independence only in 1878; its example of autonomy under a local prince influenced other Balkan nationalists.
In 1844 Ilija Garašanin's Načertanije drew up a plan for a larger South Slav state under Serbian leadership.
The Philiki Etaireia (Friendly Society), founded in Odessa in 1814, planned an armed rising against the Ottomans and recruited among Greek merchants and intellectuals.
Alexander Ypsilantis launched an uprising in the Danubian principalities in March 1821, and it was defeated by the Ottomans.
A rising in the Peloponnese began in March 1821 and spread to central Greece, with a national assembly at Epidaurus declaring independence in January 1822.
The Ottoman response included massacres, such as the massacre on the island of Chios in 1822, which created a wave of sympathy for the Greek cause in Europe.
Philhellenism, the European enthusiasm for Greek independence, brought volunteers and money, and the English poet Lord Byron joined the cause and died at Missolonghi in April 1824.
The Egyptian ruler Muhammad Ali sent his son Ibrahim Pasha to the Peloponnese in 1825, who brought a new wave of destruction and reduced much of the region.
The battle of Navarino (20 October 1827), fought by British, French and Russian fleets against the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet, destroyed most of that fleet and made Greek independence possible.
The fall of Missolonghi to the Ottomans in April 1826 after a long siege strengthened European sympathy, and Delacroix's paintings of Chios and Missolonghi gave the cause a lasting image.
Britain, France and Russia had signed the Treaty of London (1827) to force an armistice on the Ottomans and Egypt, and Navarino was fought as a result.
The London Protocol of 1830 recognised Greece as an independent state, under a Great Power guarantee, with its borders set in the south.
The Treaty of London (1832) made Greece a monarchy under Otto, a young prince of Bavaria, who arrived as king in 1833.
Ioannis Kapodistrias, the first head of the Greek state, was assassinated in 1831 by members of the Mavromichalis family, whose leader he had imprisoned.
Athens became the capital of Greece in 1834, after the king's government moved there from Nafplio.
Otto's government was dominated by Bavarian officials and ruled autocratically until a revolt in 1843 forced him to grant a constitution; many Greeks also wanted a larger state, the Megali Idea.
Otto was deposed by a revolt in 1862, and the Powers chose a Danish prince as King George I in 1863.
Greece's first frontier, set in 1832, ran from Arta to Volos and left most Greeks outside the kingdom.
Balkan nationalism threatened the Ottoman Empire and invited Russian and Austrian intervention, which turned the Balkans into a focus of Great Power rivalry.
The Crimean War (1853–56) began over the protection of Christians in the Holy Places and Russian claims on the Ottoman Empire, and Britain and France went to war against Russia.
Moldavia and Wallachia elected the same prince, Alexander Ioan Cuza, in 1859, and the union was formally recognised by 1862; Cuza was deposed in 1866 and replaced by Carol of Hohenzollern.
The Treaty of Paris (1856) guaranteed the territorial integrity of the Ottoman Empire and neutralised the Black Sea, which removed Russian naval power from the region for a time.
Balkan crises in the 1850s and 1860s kept the Great Powers in a state of tension, and the Eastern Question was a permanent source of conflict.
Russian attempts to claim a protectorate over the Sultan's Orthodox subjects, pressed by Menshikov's mission of 1853, set off the Crimean War.
The Greek nationalist programme of the Megali Idea, voiced by Ioannis Kolettis in 1844, aimed to bring all Greeks into one state.
Russia was an autocracy in which the Tsar had unlimited authority, with no constitution, no elected national assembly and few restrictions on the Crown.
Alexander I (reigned 1801–25) promised reform but took little action on serfdom, and he was involved in the Holy Alliance and the Congress System after 1815.
His Law on Free Cultivators (1803) allowed some serfs to buy their freedom with their landlord's consent, but very few took advantage of it.
Nicholas I (reigned 1825–55) founded the Third Section, a political police force, in 1826 to monitor opponents of the regime.
In 1833 the minister Count Sergei Uvarov proposed the official doctrine of Orthodoxy, Autocracy and Nationality to define Russian identity.
The autocracy kept rigid control of the press, universities and education, and censorship was tight under Nicholas I.
Nicholas I presided over a codification of Russian law under Speransky (1833) and the reform of the state peasants under Kiselev (1837–41), but did not tackle private serfdom.
Serfs were peasants bound to the land of their noble owners, who controlled their labour, marriage and movement and could buy, sell or mortgage them.
By the late 1850s privately owned serfs made up more than a third of Russia's population, and serfdom had largely disappeared from western Europe by this time.
The main obligations were labour dues (barshchina), when serfs worked on the lord's land for several days a week, and quitrent (obrok), a payment in money or goods.
Serfs were subject to corporal punishment and the lord's courts, and their lives were controlled by their owners through the estate system.
Serfdom held back agricultural productivity, since landlords had little incentive to invest in improved methods and serfs had little interest in improving land they did not own.
Many of the workers in Russian factories, especially in the Urals, were serfs or peasants tied to their villages by passports, which limited the growth of a free labour force.
The Decembrists, a group of young officers and nobles, rose in St Petersburg on 14 December 1825 demanding a constitution and the end of serfdom.
The revolt was suppressed by Nicholas I within a day, and five leaders, including Pavel Pestel and Kondraty Ryleev, were hanged in July 1826, while others were exiled to Siberia.
The Decembrist revolt shaped Nicholas's rule, which was built on repression and strong censorship.
Serfdom was debated in official committees under Nicholas, but the government took no decisive action before the Crimean War exposed the weaknesses of the system.

The rising followed the confusion over the succession, when Constantine refused the throne after Alexander I's death in 1825; the Northern Society in St Petersburg and Pestel's Southern Society were its main groups.
Russia's defeat in the Crimean War showed the economic and military backwardness of the empire, and Alexander II (reigned 1855–81) made emancipation a priority.

The fall of Sevastopol in September 1855 forced Russia to accept peace in 1856, and Alexander told the Moscow nobility that it was better to abolish serfdom from above than wait for it to be abolished from below.
The emancipation edict was issued on 19 February 1861, freeing the serfs from personal bondage, after editorial commissions had drafted its terms from 1859.
Serfs received legal freedom, the right to marry and move, and a share of land, but landlords kept much of the best land.
Peasants had to pay redemption payments to the government over 49 years, to repay what the state advanced to landlords as compensation, with the peasants paying a part to the landlord directly.
The peasants were organised into village communes called the mir, which held the land collectively and were responsible for the redemption payments.
Until they completed redemption, peasants remained temporarily obligated to their former lords, paying dues for the land they used.
The mir made it difficult for peasants to leave the village, and the redemption payments made the peasants poor and indebted for decades.
Redemption payments continued until they were cancelled in 1907, after the 1905 revolution.
Alexander II's other reforms followed, including elected local councils (zemstva) and a new judicial system, both in 1864.
Achievement: Greece and Serbia gained autonomy or independence, and the Greek kingdom became the first independent Balkan state within the Ottoman lands.
Limit: Greek independence was achieved only with Great Power intervention, and the new state's borders were set by the Powers, leaving many Greeks outside it.
Achievement: the 1861 emancipation ended personal serfdom and gave the peasants a legal status and some land.
Limit: in many areas the peasants received less land than they had worked and were burdened by redemption payments and the mir system, which kept many in poverty.
Overall: Balkan nationalism created new states but fed Great Power rivalry, while the 1861 emancipation was a major reform that left the peasants with real grievances.
After Napoleon's first abdication the Bourbon monarchy was restored, but it accepted a constitution. Its later refusal to respect that constitution brought the July Revolution of 1830.

Louis XVIII returned to the throne in 1814 and issued the Charter (Charte constitutionnelle) in June, which kept many Napoleonic institutions and set up a two-chamber legislature, with the king alone proposing laws.
The franchise under the Charter was very narrow: only men who paid high direct taxes could vote, so the electorate was a small minority of wealthy property owners.
Louis XVIII's government carried out a White Terror in 1815 against Bonapartists and Revolutionaries, with summary violence and reprisals, especially in the south.
Charles X succeeded in 1824 and tried to restore the authority of the Church and the nobility, passing a law on sacrilege (1825) and compensating the émigrés for lands lost in the Revolution.
The elections of 1827 returned a liberal opposition majority against the government, and in August 1829 Charles X appointed Prince Polignac, whose ministry lacked support in the chamber.
On 25 July 1830 Charles X issued the July Ordinances, which dissolved the Chamber, restricted the press and changed the electoral rules.
Paris rose on 27–29 July 1830 (the Three Glorious Days), and Charles X abdicated on 2 August and went into exile in Britain; his one lasting success was the conquest of Algiers in 1830.
The liberal deputies chose Louis-Philippe, Duke of Orléans, as King of the French, which made the monarchy a constitutional one with a middle-class character.

The 1831 electoral law lowered the tax qualification, which raised the electorate from roughly 100,000 to about 170,000, and it had reached about 240,000 by 1848, still under 1 per cent of the population.
François Guizot, the leading minister from 1840 to 1848, opposed any further extension of the vote and urged the middle class to enrich themselves through work and thrift.
The opposition used the banquet campaign of 1847–48, public dinners at which reform was demanded, to put pressure on the government.
Guizot banned a banquet planned for Paris in February 1848, and the ban led directly to the crowds that brought down the July Monarchy.
Opposition came from legitimists, Bonapartists and republicans, and the regime met workers' risings in Lyon (1831 and 1834) and an assassination attempt in 1835 that led to repressive press laws.
An economic crisis in 1846–47, with poor harvests and unemployment, weakened the regime before the banquet campaign.
Fighting in Paris on 22–24 February 1848 brought barricades, the defection of much of the National Guard and the dismissal of Guizot, and Louis-Philippe abdicated on 24 February.
A provisional government was proclaimed the Second Republic on 24 February 1848, with the poet Alphonse de Lamartine as one of its leading members.
The provisional government granted universal male suffrage on 2 March 1848, which raised the electorate from about 250,000 to about 9 million men.
National Workshops (Ateliers nationaux) were set up in late February 1848 to give work to the unemployed, which became a heavy cost to the government and a target for conservatives.
The National Workshops were closed in June 1848, and workers resisted the closure with the June Days (23–26 June 1848), an insurrection in Paris.
General Louis-Eugène Cavaignac, given emergency powers, crushed the June Days with troops, leading to many deaths and thousands of arrests.
A constitution of November 1848 established a president elected by universal male suffrage for a single four-year term, with a single-chamber Legislative Assembly.
Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, nephew of Napoleon I, was elected president on 10 December 1848 with about three-quarters of the vote, beating Cavaignac.
Louis-Napoléon had been imprisoned at Ham after an attempted rising at Boulogne in 1840, and he had lived in exile in Britain and elsewhere.
The Party of Order, made up of monarchists and conservatives, won a large majority in the Legislative Assembly elections of May 1849.
The Falloux Law (March 1850) gave the Catholic Church a major role in education, and in May 1850 the conservative majority restricted the franchise, removing about three million voters.
Louis-Napoléon's campaign to change the constitution to allow his re-election failed in the Assembly in July 1851.
On 2 December 1851 Louis-Napoléon carried out a coup d'état, arresting deputies and dissolving the Assembly, and armed resistance in Paris and the provinces was suppressed.

A plebiscite in December 1851 approved the coup by a very large majority and a new constitution of January 1852 gave the president a ten-year term and wide powers; the plebiscite of November 1852 approved the restoration of the empire.
Louis-Napoléon proclaimed the Second Empire on 2 December 1852 and took the name Napoleon III, with the title of Emperor of the French.
The Second Empire in its early years was authoritarian: the press was censored, political opponents were exiled, and elections were controlled by official candidates.
The Crédit Mobilier, founded in 1852 by the Pereire brothers, financed railways, industry and urban development, and rapid economic growth followed in the 1850s.
The Paris Exposition of 1855 and the rebuilding of Paris under Haussmann showed the regime's commitment to modern economy and prestige.
Napoleon III married Eugénie de Montijo in 1853, and the regime promoted railway building and large public works.
The Cobden–Chevalier Treaty of 1860 with Britain reduced French tariffs, opening French markets to British goods and encouraging French industry to modernise.
From 1860 the regime gave the legislature more freedom to debate, and in 1864 it legalised the right to strike, though trade unions remained illegal; the press law of 1868 relaxed censorship.
France fought in the Crimean War (1854–56) as Britain's ally and it helped Piedmont in 1859, which led to the French gains of Nice and Savoy in 1860.
Napoleon III's plan for a French-backed empire in Mexico under the Habsburg Archduke Maximilian collapsed, French troops withdrew by 1867, and Maximilian was executed by Mexican republicans.
Napoleon III's government lost prestige after the Austrian war of 1866 and the Prussian victory, which had changed the balance of power in Europe.
Émile Ollivier formed a liberal ministry in 1870, and a plebiscite in May 1870 approved the liberal reforms by a large majority.

Napoleon III was a participant in the political events of 1848 to 1870 and a symbol of the French regime. Contemporaries and historians disagree about whether he was a modernising leader or an autocrat who led France into disaster.
Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte was born in Paris in 1808, the son of Louis Bonaparte, King of Holland, and the nephew of Napoleon I.
He attempted coups in Strasbourg (1836) and Boulogne (1840), both of which failed, and he spent about six years in prison at Ham, where he wrote on social questions, before escaping in 1846.
As president of the Second Republic he won the election of December 1848 by appealing to peasants and to the memory of his uncle, and he was supported by conservatives who expected to use him.
His coup of December 1851 and the Second Empire that followed made him the central political figure in France until 1870.
In foreign policy he backed Piedmont in 1859, joined the Crimean War, supported the Mexican adventure and then led France into war with Prussia in 1870.
He was captured at Sedan on 2 September 1870, was held in Germany and then went into exile in England, where he died in 1873.
Contemporaries were divided: supporters praised economic growth and Paris, while republicans and liberals such as Victor Hugo denounced him as a usurper.

Hugo and Marx, in Napoléon le Petit and The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, depicted him as a usurper and a parody of his uncle; revisionist historians such as Theodore Zeldin and Roger Price stress his interest in social reform, his economic programme and his liberalising steps, though they judge his foreign policy a failure.
Hugo was a politician as well as a writer. His political role in this period was as a deputy and an opponent of the Empire; his literary work is covered in the notes on cultural nationalism.
Victor Hugo, born in 1802, was a leading Romantic writer and a monarchist in the 1820s, and he had become a republican by 1848.
He was elected to the Constituent Assembly of 1848 and the Legislative Assembly, where he defended freedom of the press and education and opposed the restriction of the franchise.
He supported Louis-Napoléon's candidacy in 1848 but broke with him, and by 1851 was a leader of the democratic opposition in the Legislative Assembly.
After the coup of December 1851 he was forced to leave France, first to Brussels, then to Jersey (1852–55) and Guernsey (1855–70).
His pamphlet Napoléon le Petit (1852) and his satirical poems Les Châtiments (1853) attacked Napoleon III and made him a symbol of republican resistance.
He refused the amnesty offered in 1859 and stayed in exile on Guernsey as a protest against the regime.

Hugo returned to Paris on 5 September 1870, the day after the Third Republic was proclaimed; during the Commune he criticised its excesses but opposed the repression and offered asylum to fugitives in Brussels.

Contemporaries saw him as a republican hero, while critics saw his shifts from royalism to republicanism as inconsistent; his funeral in 1885 drew huge crowds, and historians now see him as a principled defender of liberty and democracy.
After Sedan the Empire collapsed, and a republic was proclaimed in Paris on 4 September 1870 by deputies from Paris, including Léon Gambetta.

A Government of National Defence continued the war against Prussia, and Paris was besieged from September 1870 until the armistice of January 1871; Gambetta left the city by balloon to organise resistance in the provinces.
The National Assembly elected in February 1871 was dominated by monarchists, with Adolphe Thiers as head of the executive, and it sat at Bordeaux and then at Versailles, not in Paris.

The Paris Commune of 18 March to 28 May 1871 began when Thiers's troops tried to seize the National Guard's cannon on Montmartre; it was a revolutionary government of Parisian radicals and socialists, suppressed by government troops in the Bloody Week with many thousands killed.
The Third Republic was confirmed in 1875 by constitutional laws, which established a parliamentary system with a president.

Five regimes between 1814 and 1871 (the Bourbon Restoration, the July Monarchy, the Second Republic, the Second Empire and the Third Republic) reflected the lack of agreement about the basis of government.
The Bourbon and July regimes were limited by narrow franchises, and the exclusion of most men from political life made opposition likely.
The Second Republic showed that universal male suffrage could bring a president who would destroy the republic, and it deepened the divide between the urban poor and the conservative countryside.
The Second Empire gave France economic growth and prestige but depended on the personal authority of Napoleon III, and its foreign policy failures weakened it.

Overall: France's regimes were unstable because each one lacked a broad consensus, and the authority of the state rested on the personal position of its rulers rather than on a settled constitutional system.
From the eighteenth century, British farming was transformed by consolidation of land, new crops and machinery, which raised output and drove labourers off the land.
Enclosure replaced open fields and common land with consolidated farms; it was carried out largely through thousands of Acts of Parliament, most of them passed between 1750 and 1850.
The Norfolk four-course rotation of wheat, turnips, barley and clover kept the soil fertile without leaving land fallow, and turnips and clover fed livestock through winter.
Jethro Tull's seed drill, introduced in the early 1700s, sowed seed in rows at a regular depth and reduced the waste of broadcast sowing.
Selective breeding by Robert Bakewell in Leicestershire improved livestock, producing sheep and cattle with more meat and wool.
The General Enclosure Acts of 1801 and 1845 simplified the procedure, and the Corn Laws of 1815 protected British grain growers by keeping out cheap imports.
Mechanisation, including the threshing machine, reduced the need for hand labour at harvest, and anger over it fed the Swing Riots of 1830 in southern England.
Many agricultural labourers lost their common rights and their access to land, and they moved to towns or emigrated.
New fertilisers, including guano imported from Peru and the superphosphate produced by John Bennet Lawes from 1842, raised yields from the 1840s.
In France the Revolution of 1789 abolished feudal dues and divided many estates, so the peasantry owned much of the land by 1815, and farming was typically small-scale.
In Prussia the Stein–Hardenberg reforms from 1807 abolished serfdom in stages and allowed peasants to become owners of their land, though many had to give up part of it to the noble estates.
The big Junker estates of eastern Prussia were modernised with improved methods, and their owners grew grain for export and for the growing cities.
Poor harvests in the mid-1840s, including the potato blight that struck from 1845, caused high food prices and widespread hunger across much of western and central Europe.
The agricultural crisis of 1846–47 helped to create the economic conditions that fed the revolutions of 1848.
Emigration from the German lands to the United States grew strongly in the late 1840s and 1850s, as rural people and artisans sought work and land abroad.
Coal, iron and cotton textiles were the leading industries of the first industrial revolution, with the factory and steam power at its centre.
James Watt improved the steam engine in the 1760s and 1770s, and steam was applied to pumping water from coal mines and to powering machinery in factories.
Richard Arkwright's water frame and Samuel Crompton's spinning mule transformed cotton spinning, and Britain became the world's leading exporter of cotton goods.
Raw cotton for the Lancashire mills was imported in large quantities, mostly from the southern United States.
The coke-smelting process of Abraham Darby at Coalbrookdale produced iron on a larger scale, and iron was used for rails, bridges and machinery.
The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830 and was the first steam-hauled passenger railway with a timetable, and the rail network expanded rapidly in the 1840s.
George Stephenson's locomotive Rocket won the Rainhill Trials in 1829, showing that steam locomotives could haul trains effectively.
Henry Bessemer's converter (1856) made steel cheaply, and the Great Exhibition of 1851 presented Britain as the workshop of the world.
Belgium was the first country on the European continent to industrialise, with coal mines in Hainaut and Liège and early iron and textile works.
France industrialised more slowly, with the textile industry in Alsace and Normandy, and a railway network that was built largely from the 1840s.
The first French line, from Saint-Étienne to Andrézieux, carried coal in the late 1820s, and the Railway Law of 1842 set out a national network under state and company partnership.
In the German lands the Ruhr coalfield and the Silesian coalfield grew rapidly, and the first German railway, between Nuremberg and Fürth, opened in 1835.
The Zollverein's removal of internal tariffs encouraged trade and investment in the German lands, supporting industrial growth in Prussia and the Rhineland.
Krupp's steel works at Essen expanded from the 1850s, and the steel industry of the Ruhr was built on coal and iron from the region.
Industrial growth on the continent was often financed by banks and investment, while in Britain it was financed mainly from profits and private capital.
Factories concentrated labour under supervision, with workers working long hours at fixed times, often 12 to 14 hours a day in British cotton mills.
Children and women made up a large share of the textile workforce, and children could start work at an early age.
The Factory Act of 1833 barred children under nine from most textile factories and limited older children to shorter hours, with inspectors to enforce it.
The Mines Act of 1842 banned women and children under ten from working underground in coal mines.
The Ten Hours Act of 1847 limited the working day of women and young persons in British textile mills to ten hours.
Accidents, machinery injuries, poor ventilation and long shifts were common, and little compensation was paid to injured workers.
The Luddite attacks on machinery in 1811–16 showed the hostility of hand workers to the new machines, and the Sadler Committee of 1832 gathered evidence of the abuse of child workers.

Laissez-faire was the belief that markets should be left free from government control. It shaped British policy in the period, though the state increasingly intervened in working conditions and public health.
Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776) argued that free trade and competition produce prosperity, and laissez-faire ideas were widely accepted by British economists.
The Corn Laws, which kept British grain prices high by restricting imports, were repealed in 1846 under Peel, a change that marked a victory for free trade.
The Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 required the poor to enter workhouses to receive relief, reflecting the belief that the state should not support the able-bodied.
The state intervened in working hours and child labour through the Factory Acts, but it refused to regulate wages or the general conditions of industry.
Continental governments, notably Prussia and France, were more willing to use the state to promote industry through tariffs, railways and state-backed banks.
Thomas Malthus and David Ricardo gave laissez-faire a theoretical support, while Friedrich List argued in 1841 that German industry needed protective tariffs.
Manchester, the centre of cotton manufacturing, grew from about 75,000 people in 1801 to about 300,000 in 1851.
Industrial cities such as Liverpool, Leeds and Birmingham also grew quickly, and new towns grew up around coal and iron works.
Migration from the countryside, including Irish migrants fleeing the Famine, brought large numbers of workers into the cities in the 1840s.

In the German lands the Ruhr towns of Essen, Bochum and Dortmund expanded quickly during the 1850s and 1860s, drawing workers from rural Prussia, with migrants from the Polish-speaking east arriving in large numbers later.
Paris grew through migration from the provinces, and its population roughly doubled to about a million in the first half of the nineteenth century.
The 1851 census showed that for the first time more than half of the people of Britain lived in towns.
Overcrowded housing, poor sanitation and open sewers in the industrial towns caused high death rates and frequent epidemics.
Cholera reached Britain in 1831–32 and again in 1848–49, and it struck Paris in 1832 and 1849, killing thousands in each city.
Edwin Chadwick's Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population (1842) showed the links between poor living conditions and disease, and it led to public health reform.
The Public Health Act of 1848 created a General Board of Health in Britain, with powers over drainage, water supply and the removal of waste.
In 1854 the London physician John Snow traced a cholera outbreak in Soho to a contaminated water pump on Broad Street, supporting the link between water and disease.
Friedrich Engels described the conditions of the working class in Manchester in The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845), a witness account that influenced the debate on reform.
Industrial towns had back-to-back houses and cellar dwellings, such as Little Ireland in Manchester, with no drains and shared privies.
The Peabody Trust, founded in 1862, built model housing for London's poor, and the Public Health Act of 1875 made sanitary provision compulsory for local authorities.
The Guizot Law of 1833 required each commune in France to maintain a boys' primary school and encouraged teacher training, and it became the basis of the French primary system.
Prussia had required children to attend school since the eighteenth century (a decree of 1763), and the Prussian state supervised village schools and their teachers.
The British government made its first grant for education in 1833, and it gave grants to the voluntary religious schools run by the churches.
The Elementary Education Act of 1870 in Britain, introduced by W. E. Forster, set up school boards to provide schools where voluntary provision was inadequate.
Rising literacy spread the reach of newspapers and political ideas, which helped the spread of nationalism and political mobilisation among the middle and working classes.
Gains: industrial growth raised output and national wealth, and agricultural improvements increased food production in the long run.
Costs: the enclosure of common land and industrial work drove many people into poverty and urban slums in the short term.
Gains: factory legislation, public health reform and primary education improved the lives of many people by the 1870s.
Costs: child labour, unsafe factories and disease remained serious problems even after reform began.

Overall: the economic changes of the period brought real gains in wealth and education, but they were achieved at a heavy social cost, and governments responded slowly and unevenly to the problems they created.
Workers in the early industrial period first organised in craft societies and then in wider unions, which governments tried to restrict and later tolerated.
The Combination Acts of 1799 and 1800 made it illegal for workers to combine to raise wages or change conditions in Britain.
The Combination Acts were repealed in 1824, and a further act in 1825 restored the right to organise but limited strikes and violence.
Six Dorset farm labourers, the Tolpuddle Martyrs, were sentenced to transportation to Australia in 1834 for swearing an oath to a union; a public campaign secured their pardon in 1836.
The Grand National Consolidated Trades Union, founded in 1834 under Robert Owen's leadership, aimed to unite all trades but collapsed within months.
The Amalgamated Society of Engineers, founded in 1851, was a New Model union with a high subscription, a central fund and benefit payments for sick and unemployed members.

Trade unions in the 1850s were mostly confined to skilled workers, and unskilled labourers remained largely unorganised until later decades; the Trades Union Congress first met in 1868 and the Trade Union Act of 1871 gave unions legal recognition.
Socialism in the early nineteenth century meant common ownership of the means of production, and the term was used by early reformers before Marx gave it a scientific basis.
Utopian socialists such as Henri de Saint-Simon and Charles Fourier planned model communities based on co-operation, and they rejected competitive capitalism.
Robert Owen's ideas and his experiments at New Lanark and New Harmony in Indiana showed that cooperative communities could be run successfully in practice, a case treated in its own notes.

In France, Louis Blanc's Organisation of Labour (1839) urged state-backed workshops, and in London the Communist League was formed in 1847 from a society of German exiles, with Marx and Engels drafting its programme.
Marx was the most influential theorist of socialism. His ideas were written and developed in the 1840s and 1860s, and his followers only became a mass movement after his death.
Karl Marx was born in Trier in 1818, studied philosophy and became editor of the Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne in 1842.
He was expelled from Paris in 1845 and from Prussia in 1849, and he settled in London in 1849, where he lived until his death in 1883.

With Friedrich Engels he wrote the Communist Manifesto, published in London in February 1848, which declared that all history was a history of class struggles and ended with a call for working men of all countries to unite.
He was a participant in the revolutions of 1848 as editor of the Neue Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne, which was closed in 1849 when he was expelled from Prussia.
His theory of historical materialism held that class struggle drives history, and that capitalism would be overthrown by the working class.
The first volume of Das Kapital appeared in 1867, analysing how capitalists profit from surplus value produced by labour.
He helped to found the International Workingmen's Association (the First International) in London in 1864, wrote its inaugural address and was the dominant figure on its General Council.
Contemporaries in the 1850s and 1860s saw him as a dangerous exile, and most of the European governments kept him under surveillance.

Historians now judge Marx as a major social theorist whose predictions of revolution in advanced capitalist countries were not fulfilled, although his analysis of capitalism influenced later economics and politics.
Marx's collaborator Engels financed him and edited the later volumes of Das Kapital after his death.
Bakunin was a Russian revolutionary and the most influential anarchist of the period. His rivalry with Marx split the First International.
Mikhail Bakunin was born in 1814 into a noble family in Russia, and he left the army and became a revolutionary in the 1840s.
He was a participant at the Slav Congress in Prague in 1848, and he joined the Dresden rising of May 1849, after which he was sentenced to death, a sentence later commuted to life imprisonment.
He was handed over to Austria and then Russia in 1851, held in the Peter and Paul Fortress, exiled to Siberia in 1857 and escaped in 1861 by way of Japan and the United States to London.
