Bakunin argued for the abolition of the state and of all authority, a position that became known as anarchism, and he rejected Marx's belief in the need for a workers' state.

His rivalry with Marx within the First International led to the expulsion of Bakunin at the Hague Congress in 1872, after which the International's General Council moved to New York; Bakunin died in 1876.
Contemporary governments saw him as a dangerous conspirator, while some radicals admired him as a champion of the oppressed.
Historians now treat Bakunin as a major figure in the anarchist tradition, although his influence on the mass labour movement was less than Marx's.
Chartism was the first mass working-class political movement in Britain, demanding parliamentary reform through peaceful methods, with the People's Charter of 1838 as its programme.
The People's Charter of 1838 demanded universal male suffrage, secret ballots, annual parliaments, equal electoral districts, the abolition of the property qualification for MPs and payment of MPs.
The London Working Men's Association, formed in 1836 by the cabinet-maker William Lovett, drafted the Charter with the radical Francis Place and others.

Chartist petitions to Parliament in 1839, 1842 and 1848 were rejected each time; the 1842 petition had over three million signatures, while the 1848 petition claimed nearly six million but was found to have far fewer, some of them forged.
The Newport Rising of November 1839, led by John Frost, was an armed uprising in Wales that was suppressed by troops, and Frost was sentenced to death but transported to Australia instead.
The Plug Plot strikes of August 1842 spread through the industrial north and Midlands, and they were suppressed after mass arrests.
The National Charter Association, formed in 1840, organised local meetings and campaigns, and its newspaper, the Northern Star, reached a wide readership.

The National Land Company, founded in 1845, bought estates and let subscribers draw lots for smallholdings, which would give them a vote in the counties, but it ended in failure and was wound up in 1851.
Chartism grew from the depression of 1837, hatred of the New Poor Law of 1834 and disappointment that the 1832 Act had given workers no vote.

Chartists divided between moral-force leaders such as Lovett and physical-force leaders; the movement failed because of its divisions, government repression, the refusal of Parliament to listen and the better economic conditions after 1848.
O'Connor was the most prominent Chartist leader in the 1840s and the editor of the movement's newspaper. His leadership was enthusiastic but divided the movement.
Feargus O'Connor was born in Co. Cork in 1796, trained as a barrister and entered politics as a supporter of Daniel O'Connell.

He was elected MP for Co. Cork in 1832, lost the seat in 1835, and became the leading figure in Chartism in England and in the National Charter Association; he was imprisoned for seditious libel in 1840–41 and was elected MP for Nottingham in 1847.
He founded the Northern Star in Leeds in 1837, which became the most widely read radical newspaper in Britain.
He was a participant in the Chartist campaigns of 1839, 1842 and 1848, and he presented the 1848 petition to Parliament.
He led the National Land Company, which bought land for members and collapsed after financial mismanagement.
The Chartist demonstration on Kennington Common on 10 April 1848 was intended to present a petition, but it dispersed peacefully after the authorities banned a procession to Westminster.
Contemporaries split over him: many working-class radicals admired him, while government officials and middle-class reformers regarded him as reckless.

Older accounts blame his vanity and his quarrels with Lovett and the moral-force Chartists; Dorothy Thompson and other historians stress his gifts as an organiser and speaker for the rank and file; his mental breakdown in 1852 ended his influence and he died in 1855.

The Reform Act of 1832 gave the vote to male householders in the boroughs who paid rent of £10 a year and removed seats from rotten boroughs for the new industrial towns, but it still left only about one adult man in five with a vote.
The Second Reform Act of 1867 extended the vote to many urban working men, the secret ballot came in 1872, and universal male suffrage followed only in 1918.
The Second Republic in France gave universal male suffrage in 1848, and the North German Confederation adopted it for its Reichstag in 1867.
Sir Robert Peel, Conservative leader and Prime Minister in 1834–35 and again from 1841 to 1846, was a central figure in the reform of British government.
As Home Secretary he founded the Metropolitan Police in London in 1829, a professional force that became a model for others.
He conceded Catholic emancipation in 1829, with the Duke of Wellington, to avoid civil conflict in Ireland, and it angered many Tories.
The Tamworth Manifesto of December 1834 set out a moderate programme of reform within the Conservative tradition, which became the basis of the modern Conservative Party.
He reintroduced income tax in 1842 to pay for tariff reductions, and his budgets of 1842 and 1845 cut tariffs on many imports.
The Bank Charter Act of 1844 regulated the issue of banknotes by the Bank of England, and the Factory Act of 1844 limited hours for women and children.
Peel repealed the Corn Laws in 1846, partly in response to the Irish potato famine, which split the Conservative Party; he resigned in June 1846 and died after a riding accident in 1850.
The Corn Laws repeal was supported by free-trade reformers such as Richard Cobden and John Bright, who had campaigned through the Anti-Corn Law League.
The Conservative Party's critics, notably Disraeli, attacked him as a traitor in 1846; historians such as Norman Gash judge him one of the greatest British statesmen of the century.
Owen worked outside government to create model communities, while Peel reformed the state from within through legislation and institutions.
Owen's aims were co-operation and communal ownership, whereas Peel wanted to preserve private property and the existing social order, while making it more efficient.
Owen's reforms were confined to one community, while Peel's measures such as the Metropolitan Police and the Bank Charter Act affected the entire country.
Owen's ideas were rejected by most of the political establishment, while Peel's policies were accepted as sound by much of the middle class.
Achievement: trade unions lost their illegal status after 1824 and the New Model unions gave skilled workers lasting organisation.
Limit: the Combination Acts, the Tolpuddle sentences and the failure of the GNCTU showed how hard it was to organise workers in the early period.
Achievement: Chartism created a mass movement that kept parliamentary reform on the agenda, and several Chartist demands were later achieved.
Limit: Chartism's petitions were rejected, its leaders were divided, and the movement lost momentum after 1848.
Achievement: Peel's reforms modernised the police, the banking system and tariff policy, and they helped the British economy grow.

Overall: the responses to industrialisation included unions, socialist theory and Chartist agitation, yet the main political gains came from state reform led by Peel rather than from working-class movements, which won their goals only much later.
Robert Owen was a Welsh-born manager who learned the cotton trade in Manchester before taking charge of a much larger mill complex in Scotland.
Robert Owen was born in Newtown, Montgomeryshire, in 1771, and he left school at about nine or ten to work in a draper's shop.
He moved to Manchester as a young man and was managing a cotton-spinning mill by the age of about nineteen, before becoming a partner in the Chorlton Twist Company in the 1790s.
Owen's Manchester experience taught him how mill workers and their families lived, and it shaped his view that environment forms character.
In 1799 he married Caroline Dale, daughter of David Dale, the Glasgow merchant who owned the New Lanark mills.
In the same year the Chorlton partners bought New Lanark from Dale, and Owen took over as its manager in January 1800, when he was in his late twenties.
His outlook was shaped by the environmentalist ideas of Enlightenment thinkers, which held that character is formed by surroundings.
New Lanark stands on the River Clyde in Lanarkshire, Scotland, and was founded in 1785 by David Dale with the cotton pioneer Richard Arkwright.
The mills used water power from the Falls of Clyde, which was the reason Dale chose the site, and the cotton-spinning works were among the largest in Britain at the time.
The village around the mills housed about 2,000 people when Owen took over, including some 500 pauper children brought from workhouses in Edinburgh and Glasgow.
The pauper children lived in dormitories near the mills and were supervised by the mill managers; Dale was thought a comparatively humane employer, but the children still worked long days.
Owen's partnership was reorganised in 1813, when Owen and new backers, including the philosopher Jeremy Bentham and the Quaker William Allen, bought out the earlier partners.
The 1813 partners agreed to take a fixed 5 per cent return on their capital, leaving the remaining profit to be spent on the community.
The mill day was about thirteen hours, and children from the age of five or six worked in the mills before attending evening classes, when they were tired.
By Owen's account, the village houses were dirty and overcrowded, the streets were filthy and sanitation was poor.
Owen described the workforce as marked by drunkenness, theft and disorder, and the people distrusted a manager from outside.
Owen said that discipline relied on fines and physical punishment, and he set out to replace it.
He saw these conditions as the result of environment rather than of individual failings, and he set out to change the environment to change character.
Owen later argued that the conditions at New Lanark reflected the wider failings of the factory system rather than the particular fault of its managers.
Owen stopped taking pauper children as apprentices and raised the minimum age of employment, so that children under ten no longer worked in the mills.
By 1816 he had reduced the working day to ten and three-quarter hours, and he argued that this did not reduce output.
In the American embargo of 1806 he kept paying wages to idle workers for about four months, which won their loyalty.
Owen opposed physical punishment, and he replaced it with a system of reward and example.

The Silent Monitor was a block of wood with a different colour on each side (black, blue, yellow and white, from bad conduct to excellent), hung beside each worker and turned each day to show their conduct, so that behaviour was recorded without shouting or punishment.
He used profits to pay for schools and welfare, which he treated as a sound investment in the workforce.
The Institute for the Formation of Character, opened in 1816, was a meeting hall and school for adults, which offered dancing, music, lectures and classes.
The infant school, opened in 1816, took children from the age of about one or two to six, and it used songs, games and practical activities rather than rote learning.
The village store sold goods at close to cost price and of good quality, and the sale of strong drink was controlled.
Owen rebuilt and improved the village housing, cleaned the streets and encouraged cleanliness and orderly living.
A school for older children was set up, which gave them some education in reading and writing before they entered work.
The Institute and school had no formal religious instruction, a feature that drew criticism from clergy and from his Quaker partners, who also objected to the dancing and music.
The infant school was one of the earliest of its kind in Britain and attracted visitors from abroad.
Owen wrote A New View of Society (essays published 1813–1816), in which he argued that human character is formed by circumstances and that society should improve those circumstances.

The 1802 Health and Morals of Apprentices Act, promoted by the cotton manufacturer Sir Robert Peel (the elder), had already limited hours for pauper apprentices, so the state had begun to intervene before Owen's campaign.
Owen gave evidence to a parliamentary committee on factory conditions in 1816 and campaigned for a law to limit the employment of children.
The Cotton Mills and Factories Act of 1819 barred children under nine from working in cotton mills and limited the working hours of children aged nine to sixteen to twelve a day.
The Act was weaker than Owen wanted, because it had no factory inspectors and so depended on local magistrates, and it was poorly enforced.

In 1817 Owen presented his plan for self-supporting co-operative villages to the Committee for the Relief of the Manufacturing Poor in London, and in 1820 he set out a similar plan in a Report to the County of Lanark.
In August 1817 he damaged his reputation by denouncing all organised religions at a public meeting in London.
Owen claimed that New Lanark stayed profitable under his management, which he used to show that his reforms did not bankrupt the business.
His partners, especially the Quaker William Allen, objected to the cost of his community schemes and to his religious views, and these disputes caused conflict within the partnership.
Owen left for the United States in 1824 to found New Harmony, and he finally ended his connection with New Lanark in about 1829.
After Owen left, the mills carried on under his former partners, continuing to produce cotton until 1968, and New Lanark remained a reference point for later social reformers.
In 1825 Owen bought the town of Harmony in Indiana from a religious community and founded New Harmony, a co-operative experiment that failed within a few years.
Disputes among the members of New Harmony over its organisation led to its collapse, and Owen left the settlement in 1827.
Owen set up the Equitable Labour Exchange in London in 1832, which exchanged goods using labour notes, and it collapsed within a few years.
Owen's ideas influenced the Grand National Consolidated Trades Union of 1834, which he led, and his periodical of 1834 was titled The New Moral World.
Owen's writings inspired the co-operative movement, and the Rochdale Pioneers in Lancashire set up a co-operative store in 1844.
New Lanark was not widely copied because the reforms required a level of control that few owners were willing to accept, and the profits of most mills depended on low wages and long hours.
Later employers built model villages, such as Saltaire in Yorkshire in 1853, but these were usually paternalist rather than co-operative.
Contemporaries were divided: some manufacturers and reformers praised New Lanark as a model, while many employers and conservative critics attacked Owen's religious views and his socialism.
Visitors from Britain and abroad, thousands of them, including statesmen and royalty, toured New Lanark in the 1810s and 1820s to see the reforms for themselves.
Owen's critics said that his community schemes were impractical and that the reforms relied on his personal control of the mill.
Historians debate whether New Lanark was a genuine model of welfare or a paternalistic system that depended on Owen's authority.
Historians now treat New Lanark as a significant experiment in industrial welfare, and its reforms influenced the development of education and public health policies.
Owen died at Newtown in 1858, and New Lanark was made a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 2001.
Success: New Lanark showed that shorter hours, schooling and decent housing could be combined with profit.
Limit: its success depended on Owen's personal control, which made it difficult to copy in other mills or communities.
Success: it helped to shape the Factory Act of 1819 and the infant school movement and inspired the co-operative movement.
Limit: the 1819 Act was weak, Owen quarrelled with his partners and New Harmony failed.
Contemporary view: the reformer's friends saw a benevolent experiment; critics saw a paternalist whose religious views were dangerous.
Later view: historians see a pioneer of industrial welfare, though one whose methods of control were paternalistic.
Rapid urban growth in the nineteenth century created problems of overcrowding, disease, traffic and disorder that cities could no longer leave to chance.
Industrial and urban growth brought millions of people into cities, and existing streets, water supplies and housing could not cope with the numbers.
Narrow, winding medieval streets made traffic hard to move, and they were dangerous for pedestrians and for the carriages of the wealthy.
Overcrowded and unsanitary districts bred disease, and municipal authorities were slow to provide clean water and sewers.
Timber-framed and crowded housing in the older districts made fire a constant danger, and wider streets allowed fire engines to reach the buildings.
Governments feared revolution in crowded working-class districts, where barricades could be built quickly in narrow streets.
Planning was also a way of displaying the power and prestige of the state, with grand public buildings and open spaces.
Paris had about one million inhabitants by the early 1850s, and the city was divided between the wealthy west and the crowded working-class east and north.
The central districts around the Île de la Cité and Les Halles were a maze of narrow streets, with poor drainage and many old houses.
The city's water came from the Seine, the canal network and older aqueducts, and it was of poor quality in many districts.
The Hôtel-Dieu, the main hospital on the Île de la Cité, was overcrowded, and its wards held large numbers of sick patients in poor conditions.
The revolutions of 1830, 1848 and the June Days of 1848 had all been fought in narrow streets, which reinforced the case for broad avenues.
Napoleon III wanted to modernise Paris to improve health, reduce unemployment through public works and make the city easier to control.
Baron Georges-Eugène Haussmann, born in 1809, was appointed Prefect of the Seine, the official in charge of Paris and its department, in June 1853.
Haussmann served as Prefect for about seventeen years, working directly with the emperor and his ministers.
The expropriation law of 1841, extended by a decree of 1852, allowed the state to buy property compulsorily for public works, which gave Haussmann the legal power to clear whole blocks of houses.
Haussmann's methods were centralised, and he gave the Prefecture of the Seine large budgets and a large staff of engineers and architects.
The emperor wanted Paris to be the showcase of France, and it hosted the international exhibitions of 1855 and 1867.
The building programme employed large numbers of construction workers, one of the aims of the works, although much of the work was seasonal and uncertain.
Napoleon III had admired London's parks and squares during his exile there, and he drew up a plan marking the new streets he wanted.
The grands travaux (great works) were a series of projects to cut new avenues through the old city, which Haussmann directed.
The Rue de Rivoli was extended eastward from the 1850s, and the Boulevard de Sébastopol was cut north–south through the centre in the 1850s, linking the Seine with the railway stations to the north.
The Boulevard Saint-Germain and the Boulevard Saint-Michel were cut through the Latin Quarter, and they were lined with trees and uniform buildings.
The avenues were designed in straight lines to create vistas, and they were lined with uniform stone facades of similar height.
The military value of the boulevards was clear, since troops could move quickly through the city and artillery could fire along the straight streets.

The Avenue de l'Opéra was built in the 1860s and 1870s to frame the view of the new Opéra, and the Avenue de l'Impératrice was laid out in 1854 as a route to the Bois de Boulogne; the Étoile became the centre of twelve radiating avenues.
Building regulations fixed the height of facades along the new streets, giving the uniform look of Haussmann's Paris.
The engineer Eugène Belgrand built a new system of aqueducts and reservoirs that brought clean water into the city from sources in the Dhuis and Vanne valleys.
Belgrand's underground sewer network carried waste away from the centre, which improved sanitation and reduced disease.
The Bois de Boulogne, on the western edge of the city, was redesigned in the 1850s as a park with lakes, paths and a racecourse, on the model of London's parks.
The Bois de Vincennes, on the eastern edge, was converted into a park in the 1860s, to give the working-class east a counterpart to the Bois de Boulogne.
The Buttes-Chaumont, a former quarry and rubbish tip in the north-east, was transformed into a park with a lake and a cliff-top waterfall, which opened in 1867.
The Parc Monceau was redesigned in the 1860s, the Parc Montsouris was laid out in the south, and small squares were laid out in the city's districts, giving residents access to green space.
Jean-Charles Alphand, the engineer in charge of the city's parks and promenades, designed much of the planting and layout of the new parks.
Belgrand's new aqueducts brought spring water from the Dhuis (completed 1865) and Vanne (1874) valleys, with covered reservoirs in the city.
The Paris Opéra, designed by Charles Garnier, was begun in 1861 and opened in 1875, after the fall of the Empire, and became a symbol of the imperial city.
The new Les Halles, the central food markets, were built as iron-and-glass pavilions by Victor Baltard from the 1850s.
The Gare du Nord was rebuilt in the 1860s and the Gare de l'Est was enlarged, and the new boulevards linked the main railway stations.
Public fountains, lamps, kiosks and tree-lined squares were added to the new streets, giving the city a uniform appearance.
The new buildings were designed to frame the vistas of the boulevards and to create impressive views of major monuments.
In 1860 the suburbs of Paris were annexed to the city, and the number of arrondissements grew from twelve to twenty.
Among the annexed areas were Belleville, Montmartre and Passy, which brought large working-class populations into the enlarged city.
The annexation brought the population of the enlarged city to about 1.8 million by 1872, and it allowed Haussmann to plan the whole urban area.
The works were financed by municipal borrowing, large loans and taxes, and the city's debt grew considerably during the 1860s.
Critics such as the republican journalist Jules Ferry attacked the cost and the hidden borrowing in a pamphlet of 1868, The Fantastic Accounts of Haussmann.
Haussmann was dismissed in January 1870, when the new liberal ministry of Émile Ollivier refused to keep a prefect so unpopular with the opposition.
Haussmann published his Mémoires in 1890–93, defending his work, and he described himself as a demolition artist.
The demolition of old housing displaced many working-class families, who were forced into the outer districts of the east and north.
Rents rose in the new central districts, which were occupied by wealthier residents and businesses.
The result was a sharper division between the wealthy west and the working-class east of the city, an effect that Zola satirised in his novel La Curée.
Displaced workers settled in eastern districts such as Belleville and Ménilmontant, which later became centres of radical politics.
The new boulevards were criticised for their cost and for destroying the historic character of many districts; the poet Baudelaire mourned the vanishing old Paris in Le Cygne (1860).

Some contemporaries argued that the boulevards were designed to make the city easier to control, and the Commune of 1871 showed the limits of that control when barricades were built in the eastern districts.
Vienna's Ringstrasse, decreed in 1857, replaced the old city walls with a grand boulevard lined with public buildings, and it was built in the 1860s and 1870s.
Plots along the Ringstrasse were sold to private developers, who financed many of the new apartment blocks and houses.
In Barcelona the engineer Ildefons Cerdà produced a plan in 1859 for the extension of the city, the Eixample, with a regular grid of blocks.
In Britain the sanitary reform movement of the 1840s, led by Edwin Chadwick and others, pressed for drainage, water supply and public health legislation.
Haussmann's works were a response to the specific problems of a growing capital, and they were carried out by a centralised state authority with legal power over property.
Berlin's Hobrecht Plan of 1862 laid out the expansion of the city, and in the 1870s Joseph Chamberlain, mayor of Birmingham, cleared slums and built a new street, Corporation Street.
Success: the water and sewer systems greatly improved health and sanitation in the city, which had been among the worst-served capitals in Europe.
Success: the boulevards, parks and public buildings made Paris a model for city planners across Europe and the world.
Success: the works made Paris a safer, brighter city, with gas lighting and a more regular street plan, and raised property values in the central districts.
Failure: the displacement of the poor and rising rents created new social problems, and the working class was excluded from the new city.
Failure: the cost and debt of the works, and the way they were financed, provoked criticism that contributed to Haussmann's dismissal.

Overall: Haussmann's Paris solved many of the physical problems of a crowded city and became a model for modern planning, but it did so by displacing the poor and serving the interests of the regime and the wealthy.
Romanticism celebrated emotion, the past and the spirit of a people. Its artists and writers gave nationalist movements their myths, symbols and languages.
Romantic writers and artists rejected the rational order of the Enlightenment in favour of feeling, imagination and the national past.
The idea of a national spirit, the Volksgeist, was developed by the German thinker Johann Gottfried Herder in the late eighteenth century and was taken up by nationalists.
Folklore collection and the revival of medieval legends were central to cultural nationalism, since they claimed to reveal the true character of a people.
Cultural nationalism was most powerful where a nation lacked its own state, as in Italy, Germany, Poland and the Czech lands.
Artists and composers often worked with patrons and publishers in national capitals, and their audiences helped to shape national identity.
Victor Hugo's preface to his play Cromwell (1827) served as a manifesto for Romantic drama.
Frédéric Chopin wrote mazurkas and polonaises that drew on Polish dance rhythms, and his music became a symbol of Polish national feeling in exile after 1831.
Franz Liszt, born in Hungary, wrote the Hungarian Rhapsodies in the 1840s and 1850s, which drew on Hungarian and Romani music and presented Hungary's national identity to European audiences.
Giuseppe Verdi's opera Nabucco (1842) included the chorus Va, pensiero, sung by Hebrew exiles, which Italian audiences came to hear as a call for national liberation.
Around 1859 the cry 'Viva VERDI' was popularly said to be a coded slogan, since the letters could stand for Vittorio Emanuele Re d'Italia, the king the nationalists wanted.
Richard Wagner used German myths and legends in his operas, and his Ring cycle, first performed in full at Bayreuth in 1876, drew on the Nibelungen legend and Norse sagas.
Eugène Delacroix's painting Liberty Leading the People (1830) showed a personification of liberty leading the Parisian crowd over the barricades during the July Revolution.
Caspar David Friedrich's landscapes, such as Wanderer above the Sea of Fog (about 1818), expressed Romantic feeling for nature and the German spirit.
Romantic historical painting showed scenes from national history, which gave citizens a shared image of their past.
Bedřich Smetana's opera The Bartered Bride (1866) and his cycle of symphonic poems Má vlast (1874–79) drew on Czech folk music and landscape to express Czech national feeling.

The Brothers Grimm published their collection of folk tales, Children's and Household Tales, in 1812 and 1815, which presented German folklore as the expression of the German people; they also began a great German dictionary in 1838.

Alessandro Manzoni's novel I promessi sposi (The Betrothed), published in 1827, was set in Lombardy under Spanish rule, and Manzoni's revised edition of 1840–42, written in the educated Tuscan of Florence, became a model for standard Italian.
Adam Mickiewicz, the Polish poet, wrote Pan Tadeusz (1834), a national epic set in Lithuania, which celebrated the Polish national past.
Alexander Pushkin, author of Eugene Onegin, wrote in a Russian literary language that became the model for later writers, and his works were a central part of Russian national culture.

Standardising national languages, such as Italian and Czech, through grammars, dictionaries (Josef Jungmann's Czech dictionary of 1835–39) and schools helped to create a sense of a single national community; Elias Lönnrot's Kalevala (1835) did the same for Finland.
Hugo's literary work made him the most celebrated writer of French Romanticism. His political career and exile are covered in the notes on the French state.
Victor Hugo's play Hernani, staged in 1830, provoked a riot between Romantic supporters and classical critics, and it marked the victory of Romanticism in French theatre.
His novel Notre-Dame de Paris (1831) revived interest in the Gothic past of Paris and helped to inspire the restoration of medieval buildings.
His collection of poems Les Contemplations (1856) was written in part in memory of his daughter Léopoldine, who drowned in 1843, and it expressed grief and faith.

His novel Les Misérables (1862), written largely in exile on Guernsey, follows the convict Jean Valjean from 1815 to the Paris rising of 1832 and portrays the poor of France; it became one of the most widely read novels of the century.
Hugo was elected to the Académie française in 1841, a sign of his standing as a literary figure before his political career developed.
Contemporaries admired him as a national poet and a leader of Romanticism, while classical critics attacked his works for breaking the rules of form and taste.
Historians now regard Hugo as one of the greatest French writers, and his combination of literary and political engagement is seen as a model for later writers.
The Catholic revival of the early nineteenth century followed the anticlerical policies of the Revolution and Napoleon, and it restored the Church's role in education and public life.
Félicité de Lamennais founded the newspaper L'Avenir in 1830, which argued for a separation of Church and state and for freedom of the press and association.
Pope Gregory XVI condemned Lamennais's ideas in the encyclical Mirari vos in 1832, and Lamennais broke with the Church in 1834.
Frédéric Ozanam founded the Society of St Vincent de Paul in 1833, a lay Catholic charity that visited the poor and the sick in their homes.
The apparitions of the Virgin Mary to Bernadette Soubirous at Lourdes in 1858 gave rise to a major pilgrimage cult that spread through France.
The Falloux Law of 1850 allowed the Church to open secondary schools freely and gave bishops places on education councils.

Pius IX proclaimed the dogma of the Immaculate Conception in 1854 and issued the Syllabus of Errors, condemning liberalism, in 1864; his rule in Rome was protected by a French garrison under Napoleon III.
Methodism, founded by John Wesley in the eighteenth century, grew rapidly among workers in the industrial towns and the mining districts.
John Keble's assize sermon of 14 July 1833 launched the Oxford Movement, which sought to restore Catholic elements in the Church of England.
Christian Socialism, led by F. D. Maurice and Charles Kingsley from 1848, sought to apply Christian principles to the problems of industrial society.
Sunday schools and the ragged schools provided education to poor children, and they were run mainly by churches and charities.
Temperance societies campaigned against drunkenness, which was seen as a cause of poverty and family breakdown among the working class.
Churches in the industrial towns ran city missions and charitable work, and they responded to urban poverty with preaching, relief and education.
The religious census of 1851 revealed that large numbers of working people did not attend church, and the Salvation Army began in East London as the Christian Mission of William Booth in 1865.
Evangelical Christians such as Lord Shaftesbury led campaigns for factory reform, and the Preston teetotal movement of 1832 helped to launch the temperance cause.
Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, which made the electric generator and transformer possible.
Faraday's laws of electrolysis (1833–34) showed that the amount of substance deposited at an electrode is proportional to the electric charge passed through the solution.
The electric telegraph was developed in Britain by William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone, who patented their system in 1837, and it was first used on railways from the late 1830s.
Samuel Morse's telegraph system was demonstrated in 1844 on a line between Washington and Baltimore, and Morse code was widely adopted.
James Clerk Maxwell's 1865 theory of the electromagnetic field showed that light is an electromagnetic wave, unifying the theories of electricity and light.
A submarine telegraph cable was laid across the Atlantic in 1858, but it failed after a few weeks, and a lasting cable was completed in 1866.
Werner von Siemens's dynamo of 1866 made the large-scale generation of electricity possible.
Darwin was a naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection transformed biology. He was a witness to nature during his voyage and a theorist when he wrote his main work.
Charles Darwin was born in Shrewsbury in 1809, studied medicine at Edinburgh and then divinity at Cambridge, and joined the voyage of HMS Beagle as naturalist.
On the Beagle (1831–1836) he collected fossils, plants and animals in South America, the Galápagos Islands and Australia, and he observed the variation of species.

He developed the theory of evolution by natural selection in the years after his return, delayed publication for about twenty years, and published On the Origin of Species in November 1859, after Alfred Russel Wallace had reached the same idea.
The Origin argued that species change over time through variation and natural selection, and it proposed that all living things share common ancestors.
The Descent of Man, published in 1871, applied the theory to human origins.

Contemporaries were divided: scientists such as Thomas Henry Huxley defended him, while Bishop Samuel Wilberforce and many churchmen opposed his ideas at the Oxford debate of 1860, at which Darwin was not present.

Historians now regard Darwin as the founder of modern evolutionary biology, though his theory was later developed with genetics, which explained inheritance; he was buried in Westminster Abbey in 1882.
Gregor Mendel published his experiments on pea plants in 1866, showing that inheritance follows particular patterns, but his work was ignored until its rediscovery in 1900.
Louis Pasteur's experiments of the late 1850s showed that fermentation and decay are caused by micro-organisms, and his work developed the germ theory of disease.
Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments, published in 1861, showed that micro-organisms do not appear spontaneously in sterile broth, which undermined the theory of spontaneous generation.
The daguerreotype photographic process was announced in 1839, and Henry Fox Talbot's calotype process followed in 1841, establishing photography as a new medium.
The steam railway, the telegraph and the steamship transformed communication and trade, linking nations and empires in a faster network.
Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery in 1867 using carbolic acid, and chloroform anaesthesia was introduced by James Young Simpson in 1847.
Isambard Kingdom Brunel's iron screw steamship SS Great Britain (1843) and the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 transformed sea transport.
Achievement: cultural nationalism gave national movements powerful symbols, languages and histories, which helped to create a sense of national belonging.
Limit: cultural nationalism often idealised the past and excluded minorities, and national myths could be used to justify conflict.
Achievement: the Catholic revival and the churches' social work gave the poor relief and education, and it renewed the role of religion in public life.
Limit: the churches were divided between conservative and reforming wings, and their social work did not address the causes of poverty in industrial society.
Achievement: Darwin, Mendel and Pasteur transformed biology and medicine, and electricity and communication changed how people and states interacted.

Overall: the cultural and scientific developments of the period were major achievements that enriched national identities and expanded knowledge, but they also raised new questions about tradition, religion and national belonging that remained contested.

The German Empire was proclaimed in 1871 after Prussia's wars against Denmark, Austria and France. It combined a strong monarchy with an elected parliament, and it upset the old balance of power in Europe.

The German Empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871 in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, while Paris was still under siege in the Franco-Prussian War; King Wilhelm I of Prussia became German Emperor (Kaiser).

The Empire was a federation of 25 states: four kingdoms (Prussia, Bavaria, Saxony, Württemberg), smaller duchies and principalities, and three free cities. Prussia held about two thirds of the territory and population.
The Kaiser was hereditary King of Prussia, commanded the army, appointed and dismissed the Chancellor and could declare war with Bundesrat consent.
The Chancellor was responsible to the Kaiser, not to parliament. Bismarck held the office from 1871 to 1890 and was also Prussian Minister-President for almost all of that time.
The Bundesrat (federal council) represented the state governments. Prussia held 17 of its 58 votes in 1871, enough to block any proposed constitutional change.

The Reichstag was elected by universal male suffrage (men aged 25 and over) by secret ballot. It could pass or reject laws and the budget, but it could not appoint or dismiss the Chancellor or ministers.

The Treaty of Frankfurt (10 May 1871) made France pay an indemnity of 5 billion francs and cede Alsace and part of Lorraine, including Strasbourg and Metz; German troops stayed until it was paid, which France did by 1873.

A new Great Power in the centre of Europe, with a growing population and industry, changed the balance of power: France was weakened and embittered, while Britain, Russia and Austria-Hungary had to adjust to a united Germany.
Bismarck governed by managing parliament and identifying 'enemies of the Reich' in turn. The Kulturkampf against the Catholic Church is covered in the notes on church-state tensions.
Until 1878 Bismarck relied on the National Liberals in the Reichstag, who supported free trade and the Reich's unity.

After two attempts on the life of Wilhelm I in May and June 1878 (by Hödel and Nobiling), Bismarck used the fear of revolution to pass the Anti-Socialist Law in October 1878. It banned socialist organisations, meetings and newspapers but still let socialists stand for the Reichstag.
The law did not stop the SPD: the party's vote kept rising, and by the 1890 election it won about 1.4 million votes and 35 seats.

The tariff of 1879 ended free trade by protecting German iron and steel and agricultural products. It split the National Liberals, and Bismarck now relied on the Conservatives and the Catholic Centre Party.

To win workers away from socialism, Bismarck introduced state insurance: sickness insurance (1883), accident insurance (1884) and old age and invalidity insurance (1889). Germany was the first major state to create such a scheme.
Bismarck's mix of repression and welfare is often described as the 'carrot and stick'. The insurance schemes were limited in coverage and benefits, and they failed to reduce support for the SPD.

Bismarck won army funding by repeated confrontations with the Reichstag; in the 1887 election, held after the Reichstag rejected the army bill (the Septennate), the pro-government Kartell of Conservatives and National Liberals won a majority.
After 1871 Bismarck declared Germany a 'satiated' power that wanted no more territory in Europe. His aim was to keep the new Reich safe from a hostile coalition, above all one that included France.
French feeling after the loss of Alsace-Lorraine produced revanche, the desire for revenge and the recovery of the lost provinces; Bismarck assumed that France would never become a reliable friend.
His strategy was to keep France without allies by keeping the other powers friendly with Germany or at odds with each other. Contemporaries spoke of his fear of coalitions against Germany.

Bismarck wanted the Great Powers to feel that they needed good relations with Berlin more than with each other; he also steered rivalries towards the periphery of Europe, such as the Balkans and Africa.

In the War-in-Sight crisis of spring 1875 a German newspaper article suggested that Germany might attack France to stop its rearmament (France had passed a new army law). Britain and Russia warned Germany to hold back; historians disagree on whether Bismarck was really planning war or merely bluffing.
The crisis showed Bismarck that Britain and Russia would not allow France to be crushed a second time, and it fed his fear of a hostile coalition.

Franco-German tension flared again in 1886–87 under General Boulanger, a popular war minister who stirred up revanchist feeling, and in the Schnaebelé affair (April 1887), when a French frontier official was arrested by the Germans and later released.

Bismarck backed French colonial expansion, such as the occupation of Tunisia in 1881, and cooperated briefly with France against Britain over Egypt and Africa in 1884–85, to turn French attention away from Alsace-Lorraine.
The Three Emperors' League (October 1873) linked Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia as a conservative understanding to resist revolution and settle disputes among the three monarchies.
The League was only an understanding, and it came under strain in the Balkan crisis of 1875–78, when Christian peoples rose against Ottoman rule and Russia fought Turkey in 1877–78.
The Treaty of San Stefano (March 1878) created a large Bulgaria and gave Russia great influence in the Balkans. Austria-Hungary and Britain refused to accept it.
At the Congress of Berlin (13 June to 13 July 1878), chaired by Bismarck, who called himself an 'honest broker', the powers cut Bulgaria down and divided it into three parts.

The Congress recognised the full independence of Serbia, Montenegro and Romania. Austria-Hungary was allowed to occupy and administer Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Britain took Cyprus; Russia kept Bessarabia and gains in the Caucasus.
Russians felt that Bismarck had sided against them at Berlin and had cheated them of the fruits of their victory over Turkey; Russian newspapers attacked Germany, and the League lapsed.

The League was renewed secretly in June 1881 for three years (and again in 1884), with promises of neutrality if one member went to war with a fourth power and agreed Balkan spheres. It broke down in 1887 over the crisis in Bulgaria.

The Dual Alliance of 7 October 1879 was a secret defensive treaty between Germany and Austria-Hungary: each promised to help the other if attacked by Russia, and to stay neutral if attacked by another power, unless Russia joined that power.
Bismarck signed it to guard against a Russian attack and to bind Austria-Hungary to Germany; Wilhelm I accepted it reluctantly because it seemed to threaten his friendship with Tsar Alexander II.
The Dual Alliance lasted until 1918 and was the permanent core of Germany's alliance system.
The Triple Alliance (20 May 1882) added Italy, which was angered by France's occupation of Tunisia in 1881 and wanted support against France and recognition as a Great Power.

Under the Triple Alliance, Germany and Austria-Hungary promised help if Italy was attacked by France; Italy would help Germany if attacked by France, and all three would act together if any faced two or more Great Powers.
Italy declared that it would not fight Britain, and its relations with Austria-Hungary were poor because of the Italian-speaking territories (Trentino and Trieste) in Habsburg hands.
The treaty was renewed regularly until 1914; Italy stayed out of the war in August 1914 and joined the Allies in May 1915.

The crisis in Bulgaria (1885–87), where Russia and Austria-Hungary competed for influence after Prince Alexander of Battenberg was forced to abdicate in 1886, ended the Three Emperors' League in 1887.

Bismarck replaced it with the Reinsurance Treaty of 18 June 1887, a secret agreement between Germany and Russia for three years. Each promised neutrality if the other was at war with a third power, except if Germany attacked France or Russia attacked Austria-Hungary.
Germany also recognised Russia's interests in Bulgaria and promised diplomatic support over the Straits.
Bismarck did not tell Austria-Hungary or Italy of the treaty, and it can be argued that it conflicted in spirit with the Dual Alliance.

In November 1887 Bismarck banned the Reichsbank from accepting Russian bonds as security for loans (the Lombardverbot). Russia turned to France for loans, which helped to bring the two powers together.

Britain, Italy and Austria-Hungary signed the Mediterranean Agreements in 1887 to hold the status quo in the Mediterranean and Near East, with Bismarck's encouragement. This tied Britain loosely to the Triple Alliance powers.
The Reinsurance Treaty was not renewed in 1890 after Bismarck's fall, and Russia moved towards France (see the notes on the structures of European diplomacy).
Bismarck was not an enthusiast for colonies. He changed his mind in 1884, partly because of pressure from merchants and the colonial movement and partly for diplomatic reasons.
In 1884–85 Germany claimed South West Africa (Lüderitz), Togoland, the Cameroons, German East Africa and territory in the Pacific including north-east New Guinea.
Bismarck preferred protectorates run by chartered companies at their own cost rather than colonies governed by the state.

The colonial claims brought friction with Britain, especially over South West Africa and East Africa, and the Gladstone government protested; Bismarck used the disputes to build pressure on Britain and to cooperate with France.
Bismarck summoned the Berlin Conference (November 1884 to February 1885) on West Africa; it set rules for the partition of the continent (see the notes on the New Imperialism).

Relations with Britain improved after Lord Salisbury took office in 1885. Bismarck tried to keep Britain friendly through the Mediterranean Agreements and hoped that colonial quarrels would not damage the relationship.
Anglo-German tension was also dynastic: the future Frederick III's wife, Victoria, was Queen Victoria's daughter, and Bismarck distrusted the liberal influence of the English-born crown princess.
Bismarck is said to have told an explorer in 1888 that his map of Africa lay in Europe, meaning that colonies mattered to him mainly for their effect on European diplomacy.
Wilhelm I died on 9 March 1888 aged 90. His son Frederick III, a liberal who was fatally ill with throat cancer, reigned for 99 days and died on 15 June 1888.

The new Kaiser, Wilhelm II, aged 29, wanted to rule personally and disagreed with Bismarck about handling the workers; he wanted to ease the anti-socialist laws, which Bismarck wanted to make permanent.

The Anti-Socialist Law was due to expire in September 1890. After the Reichstag election of February 1890, in which the Kartell parties lost seats and the SPD vote grew, Bismarck mooted a coup d'etat to change the constitution.

Wilhelm II also objected to Bismarck's attempt to limit the ministers' access to the Kaiser through the Cabinet Order of 1852, and to the Chancellor's talks with the Catholic Centre leader Windthorst.
Bismarck offered his resignation on 18 March 1890, after the Kaiser made it clear that he would be dismissed otherwise. It was accepted two days later, and General Leo von Caprivi became Chancellor.
The British magazine Punch published the cartoon 'Dropping the Pilot' by John Tenniel on 29 March 1890, showing the Kaiser watching the old pilot leave the ship.
In the following months the Reinsurance Treaty was not renewed and Germany signed the Heligoland-Zanzibar treaty with Britain (July 1890).

Bismarck made the unification of Germany possible in the 1860s, and then governed it as Chancellor until 1890. This block covers the Chancellorship; his earlier career belongs to the notes on unification.
Bismarck (1815–98) came from a Junker landowning family at Schönhausen in Prussia, and became Minister-President of Prussia in 1862.

He was made Prince in 1871 and served as Chancellor under Wilhelm I, Frederick III and Wilhelm II. He controlled foreign policy personally, and most of the major policy decisions of the Empire were his.
He saw himself as a conservative protecting the monarchy and Prussian power; he used nationalism, tariffs and social insurance to keep the new Reich stable.

Contemporaries admired the 'Iron Chancellor' who had made Germany great: nationalists and conservatives adored him, while Catholics, Liberals and socialists suffered under his measures and called them persecution.
Foreign observers respected him as a master diplomat. Punch's cartoon of 1890 and the many Bismarck monuments erected after his death show how large he loomed.
After his dismissal he used the press to criticise Wilhelm II's governments, and published his memoirs, Thoughts and Recollections. He died on 30 July 1898 at Friedrichsruh.
Historians are divided. A.J.P. Taylor and others praised his skill as a diplomat who kept the peace; Lothar Gall called him a 'white revolutionary' who changed Europe from above.

Hans-Ulrich Wehler argued that Bismarck's rule was a kind of Bonapartist dictatorship that kept the old elites in power by 'negative integration', uniting the Reich against domestic 'enemies' such as Catholics and socialists; critics say it left Germany with a weak parliamentary tradition.
Foreign success: Germany fought no war after 1871 and avoided a two-front war while Bismarck was in office.

Foreign limit: the system was complicated and depended on Bismarck personally; the Reinsurance Treaty and the Dual Alliance pulled in opposite directions, and a successor could not keep all the balls in the air.

Foreign limit: the Dual Alliance committed Germany to Austria-Hungary in a Balkan region where Habsburg and Russian interests clashed, and the treatment of Russia in 1878 and 1887 helped to push it towards France.
Foreign success: the Congress of Berlin avoided a European war in 1878, and Bismarck was able to turn colonial rivalry to Germany's advantage.
Domestic success: he created a unified state, a national market, a common currency (the mark, 1873), a central bank (the Reichsbank) and the first national state insurance system in Europe.
Domestic failure: the Kulturkampf and the Anti-Socialist Law did not break the Catholic Church or the SPD; both emerged stronger, and the Reichstag remained weak.
Contemporary view: Germans in 1890 saw a statesman who had made Germany one of the strongest states in Europe.
Later view: historians stress the unfinished nature of his domestic settlement, which left his successors with an unreformed constitution and a divided society.
After Bismarck's fall, Germany's new leaders let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse. Russia and France, both isolated, drew together and ended France's isolation.

Chancellor Caprivi and the Foreign Office official Holstein decided not to renew the Reinsurance Treaty in 1890, believing it was incompatible with the Dual Alliance and with good relations with Britain.

Russia then turned to France: French banks began large loans to Russia from 1888 and the powers agreed to consult each other in a political understanding in 1891, after a French naval squadron visited Kronstadt.
A military convention was agreed in August 1892 and the Franco-Russian Alliance was formally ratified in January 1894. It was a defensive alliance directed at the Triple Alliance powers.

If France was attacked by Germany, or by Italy supported by Germany, Russia would attack Germany; if Russia was attacked by Germany, or by Austria-Hungary supported by Germany, France would attack Germany. Both would mobilise if any Triple Alliance member mobilised.
The alliance gave Germany the risk of a war on two fronts, the danger Bismarck had tried to avoid, and it later shaped the Schlieffen Plan.
The alliance was cemented by French investment in Russian railways and industry, and lasted until 1917.
Britain stayed outside permanent alliances until the early twentieth century. The Boer War showed it had few friends, and it began to settle quarrels with its imperial rivals instead.
Britain's policy of 'splendid isolation' lost its value after the Boer War, when most European opinion was hostile, and after Germany began to build a large navy.
The Anglo-Japanese Alliance (1902) gave Britain support in the Far East against Russia and allowed it to concentrate its navy nearer home; it was renewed in 1905 and 1911.
The Entente Cordiale (8 April 1904) settled colonial disputes: Britain was recognised in Egypt, France in Morocco, and the two settled questions over Siam, Madagascar, and the Newfoundland fisheries.

The Entente was not an alliance, but after the first Moroccan crisis British and French military staffs began secret talks in 1906, and in 1912 their navies agreed to divide responsibilities in the Channel and the Mediterranean.

The Anglo-Russian Entente (31 August 1907) settled rivalries in Asia: Persia was divided into a Russian northern zone, a British southern zone and a neutral middle; Afghanistan was recognised as a British sphere; both promised to stay out of Tibet.
The Triple Entente of Britain, France and Russia was therefore a loose understanding, without a common military commitment, facing the formal Triple Alliance.

The Triple Alliance was weaker than it seemed: Italy signed a secret agreement with France in 1902 (the Prinetti-Barrère agreement) promising neutrality if France was attacked, and attacked the Ottoman Empire for Libya in 1911–12.

From 1906 to 1914 each bloc grew more fearful of the other, and Germany spoke of 'encirclement' while Britain and France feared German ambitions; this made each crisis seem part of a struggle between the blocs.

From about 1880 the European powers competed to acquire territory in Africa, Asia and the Pacific. Historians group the causes into economic, strategic, nationalist, missionary and ideological motives.
Economic: industrial states needed raw materials such as rubber, cotton, palm oil, copper and later oil, and wanted protected markets when tariffs rose in Europe from the 1870s.

Economic theory: the British writer J.A. Hobson argued in Imperialism: A Study (1902) that capitalists invested overseas because of surplus capital at home; Lenin built on this in Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1916). Historians dispute it, since most trade and investment went to areas outside the empires.
Strategic: states sought naval bases, coaling stations and secure routes. Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 to protect the Suez Canal, the route to India, and then moved to control the Nile valley.

Nationalist: colonies were seen as a mark of Great Power status, and newspapers, colonial societies and the public cheered each acquisition. After defeat in 1871, France sought compensation overseas under Jules Ferry.
Missionary and humanitarian: churches wanted to spread Christianity and end the slave trade, and explorers such as David Livingstone and H.M. Stanley made Africa known to the public.

Ideological: ideas of racial and cultural superiority, including Social Darwinism, and a belief in a duty to 'civilise' other peoples (France's mission civilisatrice; Kipling's poem The White Man's Burden, 1899) were used to justify rule.
Technology made conquest easy: quinine against malaria, steamships, the telegraph and rifles and machine guns such as the Maxim gun gave Europeans overwhelming military advantage.
Competition fed on itself: once one power claimed territory, others felt that they had to do the same or be shut out.
In 1880 only about a tenth of Africa was under European control, mostly coastal areas such as Algeria, the Cape and Senegal; by 1914 about nine tenths of the continent had been taken.
The scramble was triggered by Leopold II's claims on the Congo, France's advance in West Africa and Tunisia (1881), and Britain's occupation of Egypt in 1882.

The Berlin Conference (November 1884 to February 1885), called by Bismarck and attended by fourteen powers including the United States, set rules for claims: notice to other powers, effective occupation, and freedom of trade on the Congo and Niger rivers.
No African ruler was represented at the Conference, and it did not itself divide Africa, but it made the partition faster and gave it a legal shape.
Britain's aim was a belt of territory from the Cape to Cairo, promoted by Cecil Rhodes, Prime Minister of the Cape Colony (1890–96); France sought to link its territories from Senegal to the Red Sea.
These two ambitions crossed at Fashoda in 1898. Germany took South West Africa, Togo, Cameroon and East Africa; Italy took Eritrea and Somaliland and, in 1911–12, Libya.
Africans resisted: Ethiopia defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa (1 March 1896), and only Ethiopia and Liberia were independent by 1914.
Leopold II, King of the Belgians, founded the International African Association in 1876 and used Stanley to claim the Congo basin for himself.
The Berlin Conference recognised the Congo Free State in 1885 as Leopold's personal possession, on the promise that he would end slavery and keep free trade.

From the 1890s the state forced Africans to collect wild rubber under quotas, as demand rose with the bicycle and the motor car; failure was punished by hostage-taking, beatings, mutilation and the burning of villages.
The Force Publique, the colonial army, enforced the system. Mortality rose sharply from violence, disease and starvation; the population fell by millions, though estimates vary widely.
E.D. Morel, a shipping clerk who noticed the Congo's trade figures, and the British diplomat Roger Casement (whose 1904 report documented the abuses) led the Congo Reform Association (1904).
Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness (1899) was based on his own time in the Congo, and Mark Twain wrote a satire on Leopold's rule.
International pressure forced the Belgian parliament to take over the colony in 1908, ending Leopold's personal rule.
France created French Indochina from Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos (1880s–1890s); Britain added Burma and Malaya; the Dutch held the East Indies.

China was defeated by Japan in the Sino-Japanese War (1894–95). The powers then forced concessions: Germany leased Kiaochow (Tsingtao), Russia Port Arthur, Britain Weihaiwei and France Guangzhouwan, and each claimed a sphere of influence.
The United States, which had defeated Spain in 1898 and taken the Philippines, Guam and Puerto Rico, proposed an 'Open Door' for trade in China (1899).
The Boxer Rising (1899–1901) was a Chinese uprising against foreigners and Christians, which besieged the foreign legations in Beijing in 1900; an eight-nation force relieved them.
Japan modernised after 1868, built a strong army and navy and defeated Russia in the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05), the first time an Asian power beat a European Great Power in modern times.
The defeat turned Russia's attention back towards the Balkans and Europe, and contributed to the revolution of 1905 (see the notes on Tsarist Russia).
Fashoda: in July 1898 a small French expedition under Captain Marchand reached Fashoda on the Upper Nile in Sudan, hoping to claim a French East-West belt of Africa.
In September 1898, after his victory at Omdurman, General Kitchener arrived with a far stronger force. Both sides refused to withdraw and war was feared.
France, isolated and facing the Dreyfus Affair at home, backed down in November 1898, and an agreement in March 1899 set the boundary between British and French spheres.
Fashoda poisoned Anglo-French relations until the settlement of 1904; but it also showed the danger of colonial clashes and encouraged both powers to solve their disputes.

The Boer War began in October 1899 after disputes over British claims on the Boer republics, the Transvaal and the Orange Free State, whose gold and rights of foreign settlers were at issue; the failed Jameson Raid of 1895–96 had already soured relations.
The Boers won early successes (Black Week, December 1899). Britain sent large reinforcements and, under Kitchener, burned farms and interned Boer civilians in camps, where over 20,000 died.
The Treaty of Vereeniging (31 May 1902) ended the war and the two republics were absorbed into the British Empire.
The war damaged British prestige, aroused hostility in Europe (Germany's Kruger telegram of 1896 had already caused outrage), and persuaded Britain to end its isolation.
After the Entente Cordiale of 1904, France moved to control Morocco, one of the last independent states in Africa.
Wilhelm II landed at Tangier on 31 March 1905 and spoke in support of Moroccan independence. Germany hoped to test the Entente and to win concessions from France.
German pressure forced the resignation of the French foreign minister Delcassé in June 1905, but the crisis ended at the Algeciras Conference (January to April 1906).

Algeciras was a diplomatic defeat for Germany: only Austria-Hungary supported it, Britain, Russia, Italy and the United States backed France, and France and Spain received the policing of Morocco's ports.
The crisis strengthened the Entente: British and French generals began secret staff talks.

In May 1911 France sent troops to Fez. Germany, in July 1911, sent the gunboat Panther to Agadir, demanding compensation, and Lloyd George warned in his Mansion House speech (21 July) that Britain would not be ignored.
The Agadir crisis was settled in November 1911: Germany accepted French control of Morocco in return for part of the French Congo (the 'New Cameroon' strip).
German opinion saw the settlement as a humiliation and Britain and France drew closer; the crisis led directly to the naval talks of 1912 between Britain and France.
Imperial rivalry created crises (Fashoda, the Boer War and Morocco) that raised tension and made Britain and Germany suspicious of each other.
Imperial agreements also reduced tension, as the Entente Cordiale and the Anglo-Russian Entente show; the powers were often able to settle colonial quarrels by compromise.
Imperialism made the alliance blocs more rigid: the Moroccan crises turned the Entente Cordiale from a colonial settlement into a quasi-alliance.
Imperial rivalries were mostly settled peacefully, so the war in 1914 came from the Balkans and Europe's own alliance system rather than from colonial clashes.
Contemporaries in Germany blamed British and French encirclement for their sense of insecurity, while the British and French blamed German pressure for the Moroccan crises.

Lenin and Hobson, writing from different positions, saw capitalism and imperialism as an underlying cause of the war; many later historians see imperialism as one factor alongside nationalism, militarism and alliances.
Wilhelm II was Kaiser from 1888 to 1918. His ambition to rule personally and his taste for a navy and a place in the world shaped German policy before 1914.
Wilhelm II was born on 27 January 1859, the eldest son of Frederick III and Victoria, the daughter of Queen Victoria. A difficult breech birth left him with a withered left arm.
He became Kaiser on 15 June 1888 at the age of 29 on his father's death, and forced Bismarck to resign in March 1890 because he wanted to rule personally.
He proclaimed a 'new course': he began by easing the Anti-Socialist Law and sponsoring workers' protection laws, then turned against the SPD when it kept growing.
He was first cousin to Tsar Nicholas II and George V and a grandson of Queen Victoria; he combined admiration for the Royal Navy with resentment of Britain.

He was impulsive and prone to indiscretion: his 'Hun speech' to troops departing for China (July 1900) and the Daily Telegraph interview (October 1908), which offended Britain, Japan and German opinion, damaged Germany's image.
After the Daily Telegraph affair the Reichstag demanded that the Kaiser submit to constitutional restraint, and Wilhelm withdrew from many public roles; Bülow resigned in 1909.
On 8 December 1912 he held a 'war council' with military leaders; historians disagree over whether it showed intent to start a war or merely a bellicose mood.

In 1914 he gave Austria-Hungary the 'blank cheque' on 5 July (see the notes on the outbreak of war) and he left for his annual cruise; he later tried to restrain Austria but could not stop the machinery of mobilisation.
He lost the confidence of the army in autumn 1918. His abdication was announced on 9 November 1918 and he went to the Netherlands, where he died at Doorn on 4 June 1941.

Contemporaries: nationalists and the navy admired him as the symbol of Germany's rise, while diplomats such as Holstein and politicians saw him as unpredictable and dangerous. Foreign cartoonists drew him as a menace.

Historians: John Röhl argues that Wilhelm exercised real personal rule and carries a heavy responsibility for 1914; Christopher Clark, in his biography and in The Sleepwalkers (2012), stresses his inconsistency and the shared responsibility of all the Great Powers.
Weltpolitik was the German drive, led by Wilhelm II, Bülow and Tirpitz, to turn Germany from a continental power into a world power through colonies, trade and a fleet.
Weltpolitik had economic roots: Germany was the leading industrial power in Europe, needed markets, raw materials and trade routes, and feared being shut out as Britain, France and Russia expanded.
It had domestic roots: conservatives and many liberals believed that imperial success would unite the classes behind the monarchy and distract from the rise of the SPD.
Bernhard von Bülow became Foreign Secretary in June 1897 and Chancellor in October 1900. In a speech to the Reichstag in December 1897 he claimed for Germany 'a place in the sun'.

Germany seized Kiaochow (Tsingtao) in China in November 1897 after two German missionaries were killed, and leased it for 99 years in 1898. It bought the Caroline, Marianas and Palau islands from Spain in 1899 and shared Samoa with the United States in the same year.
The Kruger telegram of 3 January 1896 congratulated the Transvaal president on defeating the Jameson Raid. It outraged British opinion and showed Germany courting anti-British feeling.

In 1898 Wilhelm II visited Constantinople and Damascus, declaring himself the friend of the world's Muslims. The Baghdad Railway concession (1899, expanded 1903) was meant to tie the Ottoman Empire to Germany and rival British and Russian influence in the Middle East.
Weltpolitik was backed by pressure groups: the Navy League, the Pan-German League (founded 1891) and the Colonial Society.
Attempts at Anglo-German alliance talks in 1898–1901 failed, and German pressure over Morocco (1905, 1911) gained little.
Germany had a small coastal navy in 1890. A decision to build a large battle fleet was taken in 1897-98 for reasons of power, prestige and domestic politics.
The Kaiser had long admired Britain's navy and wanted a fleet that matched Germany's new status; as a boy he had been impressed by Queen Victoria's fleet at Spithead.

Alfred Thayer Mahan's The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890) argued that national greatness depended on a strong battle fleet and command of the sea. Wilhelm II read it and ordered it placed on German warships.
Admiral Alfred von Tirpitz became state secretary of the Imperial Navy Office in June 1897 and drew up a plan for a battle fleet concentrated in the North Sea, not a cruiser fleet for overseas.

His 'risk theory' held that a German fleet strong enough to inflict serious damage on the Royal Navy would deter Britain from war, since even a British victory would leave it too weak against France and Russia.
Tirpitz also saw the fleet as a way of rallying the middle classes behind the Reich and of weakening the SPD; the navy would also give Germany bargaining power in colonial disputes.

The Navy Office launched a press campaign among professors and industrialists, and the German Navy League (Deutscher Flottenverein), founded in 1898, grew to over a million members and promoted the fleet.
Industrial interests such as Krupp (armour plate) and Blohm and Voss, as well as heavy industry in the Ruhr, stood to profit from orders.
The First Navy Law (1898) authorised a fleet of 19 battleships, 8 large cruisers and 12 small cruisers; the Reichstag voted the money for several years at a time.

The Second Navy Law (June 1900) was passed amid British anger over the Boer War. It increased the planned fleet to 38 battleships (four squadrons of eight, plus a flagship and reserve) and 20 large cruisers.
The Kaiser and Tirpitz hoped to reach a ratio of about two German ships to three British ones, which they judged was enough to make the risk theory work.

British leaders reacted at first by reorganising: Admiral Fisher, First Sea Lord from 1904, brought home ships from distant stations and concentrated fleets against Germany. The British naval estimates grew.

HMS Dreadnought was launched on 10 February 1906. She was faster than any other battleship and carried ten 12-inch guns. She made existing battleships obsolete, so Germany had to start again on the same footing as Britain.
Germany responded with its own dreadnought class (Nassau, launched 1908) and passed a supplementary law in 1908 which sped up building to four capital ships a year.

In 1909 the British public, alarmed at German progress, demanded eight new dreadnoughts with the cry 'We want eight and we won't wait'; the government laid down more than usual in the 1909-10 programme.
A supplementary law of 1912 added further battleships and a third squadron to the active fleet. The Kiel Canal was widened to take dreadnoughts and reopened in June 1914.
After 1912 Germany could no longer afford to compete both in the navy and the army, and in 1912-13 the army received large increases; Britain kept a clear lead in capital ships.
Britain ended its isolation by agreement with Japan (1902), France (1904) and Russia (1907), partly because of the German navy.
In 1904-05 Fisher redeployed the fleet to home waters, a change made possible by the agreement with France and Japan; the Royal Navy now faced the North Sea.
German proposals for naval talks in 1906-08 foundered on the fact that Germany would not accept limits on shipbuilding, while Britain would not give a promise of neutrality.
Bethmann Hollweg, Chancellor from 1909, wanted an agreement, and in 1911 and 1912 pursued the issue with British ministers.

The Haldane mission to Berlin (February 1912) failed because the Germans wanted a British promise of neutrality in a continental war, which would have left France and Russia to their fate, while Britain wanted a slowing of the building programme.

Churchill, First Lord of the Admiralty from October 1911, proposed a 'naval holiday' in 1912 and in 1912 the Royal Navy moved its Mediterranean battleships home, while France took on the Mediterranean (the Anglo-French naval agreement).
A détente on colonial and Baghdad Railway issues in 1913-14 brought some improvement, but the naval and military preparations of each side remained.
The fleet failed in its main aim: it did not deter Britain from war. Instead it turned Britain from a possible friend into an opponent, and helped push it into the Entente with France and Russia.
The fleet cost vast sums and absorbed resources that could have gone to the army, at a time when Germany's land frontiers were threatened by France and Russia.
The costs raised the national debt and taxation, led to the Reich's finance crisis of 1908-09 and sharpened disputes between Conservatives, who opposed inheritance tax, and the left.
The navy remained largely in harbour in the war. The only major battle, Jutland (31 May 1916), was indecisive, and the British blockade of Germany was never broken.

Many German sailors came to resent the fleet's inactivity and harsh discipline, and the mutinies at Wilhelmshaven and Kiel in 1918 triggered the revolution that overthrew the Kaiser (see the notes on war and revolution in Germany).
The war-time British blockade and the Allied claim to German ships at Scapa Flow (scuttled by the Germans in June 1919) completed the fleet's fate.
British contemporaries saw the German fleet as a challenge to the Empire; the Admiralty and press, including the Daily Mail and the Navy League in Britain, spread fear of invasion.
German contemporaries presented the fleet as essential for defence of overseas trade and as a symbol of national pride; Social Democrats and some Liberals objected to its cost.
Paul Kennedy, in The Rise of the Anglo-German Antagonism (1980), argues that the naval race was a major cause of the breakdown of relations between the two countries.
Fritz Fischer (Griff nach der Weltmacht, 1961) argued that Germany's leaders deliberately pursued world power by the fleet and then by war; critics say he exaggerated the coherence of German aims.
Others, such as Volker Berghahn, stress domestic motives: Tirpitz built the fleet to unite the right and to avoid reform at home, and the policy was a case of 'social imperialism'.
Some historians doubt that the naval race caused the war, noting that Anglo-German relations were improving in 1913-14 and that the Entente was formed first because of colonial concerns.
Achievement: Germany built the second-largest fleet in the world within about fifteen years and won prestige and domestic support for the Kaiser.
Limit: it never overtook Britain, and the cost of competing in both army and navy overstretched German finances.
Achievement: Weltpolitik gave Germany colonies and concessions such as Kiaochow, Samoa and the Baghdad Railway.
Limit: Weltpolitik was clumsy and provoked rival powers. Tangier (1905) and Agadir (1911) ended in humiliation, and Germany was left with its colonies small and unprofitable.
Achievement: the colonial and naval movement helped bring together Conservatives and National Liberals behind the government.
Limit: it deepened the sense of encirclement, which was a result of German policy, and made Britain more willing to stand with France and Russia in 1914.
Contemporary view: German nationalists regarded Weltpolitik as a necessity, while British opinion regarded it as a threat; later historians increasingly judge it a strategic mistake.
Serbia became fully independent in 1878. Its drive to unite the South Slavs threatened Austria-Hungary, and its link with Russia made a Serbian quarrel a Great Power matter.
The Congress of Berlin (1878) recognised Serbia's full independence from the Ottoman Empire and enlarged its territory. Serbia became a kingdom in 1882 under the Obrenović dynasty.
Austria-Hungary dominated Serbia's economy, which depended on exporting pigs and other livestock to the Habsburg market, and it kept Serbia in its sphere until the early 1900s.
Serbian nationalists dreamed of uniting the South Slavs (Serbs, Croats, Slovenes and the Slavs of Bosnia) in a single state. This threatened a Habsburg empire with millions of South Slavs.
In June 1903 a group of army officers murdered King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga in Belgrade. Peter I of the Karadjordjević dynasty became king.

The new regime turned away from Vienna and towards Russia and France. Russia, the great Slav and Orthodox power, saw itself as protector of the Balkan Slavs and wanted to prevent Austrian control of the Balkans.

The Pig War began in 1906, when Austria-Hungary closed its market to Serbian livestock to punish its trade links with France. Serbia found other markets, including Germany, Italy and France, and the war weakened Austrian influence.
Austria-Hungary feared that a strong Serbia could encourage the Slav nationalities of the empire to leave, and Chief of Staff Conrad von Hötzendorf repeatedly urged a preventive war against it.
Austria-Hungary had occupied and administered Bosnia-Herzegovina since 1878, though it remained under nominal Ottoman rule.
The Young Turk revolution of July 1908 in the Ottoman Empire raised the possibility that Bosnia would be reclaimed, so Austria acted.

In September 1908 the Austrian foreign minister Aehrenthal and the Russian foreign minister Izvolsky met at Buchlau and discussed a swap: Austria would annex Bosnia, and Russia would gain support for opening the Straits to its warships.
Austria announced the annexation on 6 October 1908, before Izvolsky had won agreement on the Straits, and Russia felt cheated.

Serbia, which regarded Bosnia as the heartland of Serb population, mobilised and demanded compensation; Serbian nationalism and anti-Austrian feeling grew, and the Narodna Odbrana society was formed to resist Austrian rule.

In March 1909 Germany told Russia to accept the annexation and drop its support for Serbia, or face consequences. Russia, still weak after the war with Japan and revolution of 1905, gave way; Serbia also had to accept.
The crisis humiliated Russia and Serbia, and left both resolved not to back down again. Russia accelerated its rearmament, and Austria-Hungary and Germany drew closer.
In 1912 Russia helped to build the Balkan League of Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece and Montenegro, aimed at the Ottoman Empire. Italy had just taken Libya from the Ottomans in 1911–12.
The First Balkan War (October 1912 to May 1913) saw the League defeat the Ottomans and take most of their European territory.
The Great Powers meeting at the London Conference (1912–13) created an independent Albania, supported by Austria-Hungary and Italy, which denied Serbia the Adriatic port it wanted.
The League then quarrelled over the spoils. In the Second Balkan War (June to August 1913) Bulgaria attacked Serbia and Greece and was beaten by them, with Romania and the Ottomans joining in.
By the Treaty of Bucharest (August 1913) Serbia doubled in size and took much of Macedonia, including Kosovo.
A stronger Serbia, backed by Russia and unsatisfied over the Adriatic, alarmed Austria-Hungary further, and Conrad pressed for war against it.

The Balkan Wars showed that a regional conflict could be contained by Great Power conference diplomacy (London 1912–13); but they left Austria-Hungary feeling that the next time it would have to fight.

The Black Hand (Unification or Death) was a secret society of Serbian army officers founded in May 1911. Its leader was Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as Apis, chief of Serbian military intelligence.
