It sought a Greater Serbia and trained and armed Bosnian nationalists, particularly those of the Young Bosnia movement, who wanted to end Habsburg rule over the South Slavs.

Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, went to Sarajevo to inspect army manoeuvres, on 28 June 1914. It was St Vitus's Day (Vidovdan), the anniversary of the Serbian defeat at Kosovo in 1389.

A first attempt in the morning, a bomb thrown by Nedeljko Čabrinović, failed to kill the Archduke. Later his driver took a wrong turn, and the car stopped near Gavrilo Princip, who shot Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie.
Princip was a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb. He and the other conspirators had been given weapons and training in Serbia, but how much the Serbian government knew of the plot is disputed.
The assassins were arrested; Princip was too young for the death penalty and died of tuberculosis in prison in 1918.
Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and decided to use the murder to destroy it, but first needed to know how Germany would respond.

On 5 and 6 July Germany gave Austria-Hungary its 'blank cheque', a promise of unconditional support in whatever action it took against Serbia. The Kaiser and Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg hoped for a short, localised war.
French President Poincaré and his prime minister visited St Petersburg from 20 to 23 July, reaffirming French support for Russia.

On 23 July Austria-Hungary presented an ultimatum to Serbia with ten demands and a 48-hour deadline. They included the suppression of anti-Austrian propaganda and a role for Austrian officials in the investigation within Serbia.
Serbia accepted most demands on 25 July but refused Austrian officials a role on its soil. Austria broke off relations and declared war on Serbia on 28 July.
Russia ordered partial mobilisation on 29 July and general mobilisation on 30 July. Germany demanded that Russia stop; when it did not, Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August.

Germany declared war on France on 3 August. Its Schlieffen Plan, which required a rapid defeat of France before Russia mobilised, meant it would attack France through Belgium whether or not France was the aggressor.

Germany invaded Belgium on 4 August after Belgium rejected an ultimatum. Britain, bound by the Treaty of London (1839) guaranteeing Belgian neutrality and concerned for the balance of power, declared war that day.
Bethmann Hollweg dismissed the treaty to the British ambassador as 'a scrap of paper'. Britain's entry made it a European war and, through the empires, a world war.

The Second International (1889) was a federation of socialist and labour parties. Its members believed that workers had more in common across borders than with their own ruling classes, but in 1914 national loyalty proved stronger.

It was founded in Paris in 1889, with a permanent International Socialist Bureau in Brussels from 1900. The largest member was the German SPD, which in 1912 won 110 seats and became the biggest party in the Reichstag.
Its parties disagreed over reform or revolution, and over how to act in a war. Rosa Luxemburg and Lenin argued for revolutionary action; Jean Jaurès of France backed a general strike against war.

The Stuttgart Congress (1907) resolved that socialists should do everything to prevent war, and if it came, to end it quickly and use the crisis to hasten the fall of capitalism. The last part was added after amendments by Luxemburg, Lenin and Martov.
The Basel Congress (24-25 November 1912), called during the first Balkan War, issued a manifesto against war and threatened that governments would face revolution if they started one.
Jaurès, the main French pacifist, was assassinated in Paris by a nationalist on 31 July 1914.
On 4 August 1914 the SPD Reichstag group voted for war credits. French socialists backed the 'sacred union' and joined the government, and British Labour largely supported the war.

The International collapsed. Socialists divided into those who backed their governments, pacifists, and a revolutionary minority (including Luxemburg, Liebknecht and Lenin) who opposed it as an imperialist war.
Anti-war socialists met at Zimmerwald (September 1915) and Kienthal (April 1916); the split led directly to the communist parties and the Third International (Comintern) in 1919.
Luxemburg was a Marxist theorist, speaker and journalist on the left of the SPD, a participant in the International's debates and a leading opponent of the war.
She was born into a Jewish family on 5 March 1871 in Zamość in Russian-ruled Poland, and studied at Zurich. Her disability, a limp from childhood illness, did not prevent her from speaking in public.
She helped found a Polish socialist party (later the SDKPiL) in 1893 and moved to Germany in 1898, where she gained German citizenship by marriage and joined the SPD.
In Reform or Revolution (1899) she attacked the revisionism of Eduard Bernstein, who wanted socialism by gradual reform. In 1905-06 she travelled to Warsaw to take part in the Russian revolution.
She taught at the SPD's party school in Berlin (1907-14) and wrote The Accumulation of Capital (1913), an economic study of imperialism.
She spoke against war before 1914 and was jailed in 1914 for urging soldiers to disobey orders. When the SPD voted for war credits on 4 August 1914 she was shocked by its capitulation.

With Karl Liebknecht she formed the International Group, later the Spartacus League (1916). From prison she wrote the Junius pamphlet (1915, published 1916), condemning the war as imperialist and the SPD's stance as betrayal.
She spent most of the war in prison or protective custody, from 1915 to 1916 and from July 1916 until November 1918, and was freed by the German revolution.
On the Russian Revolution of 1917 she welcomed the Bolsheviks' seizure of power but criticised their suppression of democracy and the Constituent Assembly.

She helped found the Communist Party of Germany (KPD) at the end of December 1918, but opposed the Spartacist rising of January 1919, which she thought premature. She was murdered by Freikorps soldiers on 15 January 1919 and her body thrown into a Berlin canal.
Contemporaries: the SPD leaders and conservatives viewed her as a dangerous agitator, 'Red Rosa'; to supporters, she was a courageous principled critic.
Historians now see her as a major Marxist thinker and a critic of both militarism and dictatorship, although they argue over whether her ideas would have worked in practice.
Alliances: Europe was divided into the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente, so a local quarrel could bring in all the Great Powers.
Militarism and plans: the powers built up large armies and conscription, and had mobilisation plans that left little time for diplomacy; the Schlieffen Plan required a swift attack on France.
Naval and colonial rivalry: the Anglo-German naval race and the Moroccan crises had poisoned relations between the powers.
Nationalism: South Slav nationalism threatened Austria-Hungary, French revanche aimed at Alsace-Lorraine, and pan-Slavism and pan-Germanism pushed Russia and Germany towards confrontation.
Short-term: the Bosnian crisis, the Balkan Wars, the assassination at Sarajevo, the blank cheque, the ultimatum and the sequence of mobilisations.
The Balkans were where the interests of Austria-Hungary and Russia collided, and each feared that backing down would cost it Great Power status.
Contemporary German view: Germany had been encircled and was forced into a defensive war by Russian mobilisation; this became the basis of German resistance to the war guilt clause later.
Contemporary Entente view: Germany and Austria-Hungary were aggressors, shown by the blank cheque, the ultimatum, and the invasion of Belgium.
Fritz Fischer (1961) argued that German leaders deliberately risked war in July 1914 to achieve world-power aims; his view raised an enduring debate about German war aims.

Christopher Clark, in The Sleepwalkers (2012), argues that the leaders of all the powers, including Serbia, Russia and France, stumbled into a war none fully intended, stressing the Balkans and contingency.

Austria-Hungary's decision to crush Serbia, Serbian-backed nationalism, Russian backing for Serbia and Germany's blank cheque were all necessary links in the chain; historians differ on the weight of each.
The war-guilt question became part of the peace settlement (see the notes on the Peace Settlement).

All the Great Powers expected a short war. Germany's plan was to defeat France in about six weeks and then turn on Russia, but the plan failed and the Western Front became a stalemate by the end of the year.
Germany invaded Belgium on 4 August 1914 and took Liège, then swept through Belgium and northern France under the Schlieffen Plan, modified by the younger Moltke, who weakened the right wing.
The British Expeditionary Force, a small professional army, fought its first major action at Mons on 23 August 1914 and retreated with the French.
The First Battle of the Marne (5-12 September 1914) halted the German advance about 40 kilometres from Paris. The Germans withdrew to the River Aisne and dug in.
Both sides then tried to outflank each other in the 'race to the sea', and the line of trenches reached the North Sea and the Swiss frontier by late 1914.
The First Battle of Ypres (October-November 1914) was a hard-fought defensive success for the British and French; the BEF lost much of its regular army and Britain had to rely on volunteers.
At Christmas 1914 troops along parts of the line took part in unofficial truces, which the high commands then forbade.

In the east, Russia invaded East Prussia, but General Hindenburg and his chief of staff Ludendorff destroyed the Russian Second Army at Tannenberg (26-30 August 1914), capturing about 90,000 men, and defeated the First Army at the Masurian Lakes in September.
Defensive weapons were stronger than the means of attack, so battles on the Western Front produced very high casualties for small gains.
Trench systems had a front line, support and reserve trenches linked by communication trenches, with barbed wire and the shell-torn ground of no man's land between the opposing lines.
Soldiers lived with mud, rats, lice, cold and the constant danger of shelling and snipers. Trench foot and shell shock (what we now call combat stress) were common.
The machine gun and quick-firing artillery made frontal attacks costly; most battle casualties were caused by shellfire.
Attackers relied on long preliminary bombardments, which warned the enemy and churned up the ground. From 1916 the 'creeping barrage' moved ahead of infantry as they advanced.

Poison gas was first used on a large scale by Germany at the Second Battle of Ypres (22 April 1915), when chlorine was released against French colonial and Canadian troops. Phosgene and mustard gas followed, and gas masks reduced its effect.
Tanks were first used by Britain at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916. They were slow and unreliable, but at Cambrai (November 1917) hundreds were used together with artillery and infantry.
Aircraft were used for reconnaissance, artillery spotting and, later, fighter combat and bombing. Germany used Zeppelins and Gotha bombers against British cities.
By 1918 both sides used combined arms: Germany developed stormtrooper infiltration tactics, and the Allies combined tanks, aircraft, artillery and infantry.
In a war of attrition each side tried to wear down the other's manpower and resources. Generals on both sides believed a breakthrough was possible, and they continued costly offensives.

In 1915 the Allies launched offensives at Neuve Chapelle, Artois and Loos, and the Germans used gas at Ypres. None broke the line, and shell shortages in Britain caused a political crisis in May 1915.

Verdun (21 February to 18 December 1916): the German chief of staff Falkenhayn attacked the symbolically important French fortress, intending, according to his later account, to bleed the French army white. Both sides lost hundreds of thousands of men.
The French commander at Verdun, General Pétain, rotated divisions through the battle, and the road known as the Sacred Way supplied the front. Verdun became a symbol of French endurance.

The Somme (1 July to 18 November 1916) was a joint British-French offensive planned partly to relieve Verdun. On the first day the British Army lost about 57,000 casualties, of whom about 19,000 were killed, the worst single day in its history.

The Somme advanced the Allied line only a few kilometres and cost over a million casualties in total across all armies. It was the first big battle for Kitchener's volunteer 'Pals' battalions, and wiped out the male population of some local communities.
Nivelle's offensive in April 1917 along the Chemin des Dames failed with heavy losses, causing mutinies in the French army; Pétain replaced Nivelle and restored morale by improving conditions.

Passchendaele (the Third Battle of Ypres, July to November 1917) was fought in the Ypres salient, partly to clear German submarine bases in Belgium. Heavy rain and shell damage turned the ground to mud, and the final gain was only about 8 kilometres.
At Cambrai (20 November 1917) Britain used hundreds of tanks in a surprise attack; the gains were mostly lost to a German counter-attack.
The Central Powers broke the Russian line at Gorlice-Tarnow in May 1915, forcing a great Russian retreat from Poland and Galicia.

The Brusilov Offensive (June 1916), led by General Brusilov against Austria-Hungary, was the most successful Allied offensive of the year. It took many prisoners and forced Germany to move troops east, but it cost Russia about a million casualties and could not be sustained.
Romania joined the Allies in August 1916 and was largely overrun by Germany and its allies by the end of the year.

Defeats, losses, shortages and the failure of the Tsar's government led to the February Revolution of 1917 (see the notes on Tsarist Russia). The Provisional Government continued the war, and the Kerensky Offensive of July 1917 collapsed.

After the Bolsheviks seized power in October 1917, they signed an armistice in December 1917 and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918, giving up large parts of Poland, the Baltic lands, Ukraine and Finland.
The treaty let Germany move over a million men west for the offensives of 1918, but it also tied down troops in the occupied east.

Gallipoli: after Ottoman entry into the war in October-November 1914, Britain and France tried to force the Dardanelles in March 1915. The land campaign began on 25 April 1915 with landings of British, French, Australian and New Zealand (ANZAC) troops. The campaign was stalemated and the troops were evacuated by 9 January 1916.
Gallipoli damaged the reputation of Churchill, who had promoted it, but helped to build the sense of national identity of Australia and New Zealand.

Italy joined the Allies in May 1915 under the Treaty of London, promised territory from Austria-Hungary. Eleven battles on the Isonzo brought little gain, and Italy suffered a disastrous defeat at Caporetto in October 1917 before recovering at Vittorio Veneto (October-November 1918).

In the Middle East, the British fought the Ottomans in Mesopotamia (surrender at Kut in April 1916) and in Palestine, where General Allenby captured Jerusalem in December 1917 and won at Megiddo in September 1918. The Arab Revolt was supported by T.E. Lawrence.

In the Balkans, Serbia was overrun by the Central Powers in 1915; the Allies maintained a front at Salonika. Bulgaria asked for an armistice on 29 September 1918, and the Ottomans and Austria-Hungary followed in October and November.
Germany's colonies were captured by the Allies, though German East Africa held out until the end of the war.
Britain used its fleet to blockade Germany, stopping imports of food and raw materials. Germany suffered shortages, and the winter of 1916-17, known as the turnip winter, was especially severe.

The German High Seas Fleet was cautious. The only major fleet engagement, Jutland (31 May to 1 June 1916), cost Britain 14 ships and about 6,000 men, and Germany 11 ships and about 2,500 men. The British fleet kept control of the North Sea and the German fleet remained mostly in port.
Germany turned to submarines. The sinking of the liner Lusitania on 7 May 1915, with almost 1,200 dead including 128 Americans, outraged American opinion, and Germany limited its campaign.

On 1 February 1917 Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, hoping to starve Britain into surrender within months. British shipping losses were very high in spring 1917, and Britain had food stocks for only weeks.
The adoption of the convoy system in 1917 and improved anti-submarine methods reduced losses, and the campaign failed to knock Britain out of the war while bringing the USA in.
Mass war needed mass armies. Continental states already had conscription, but Britain had relied on volunteers and had to change.
Germany and France called up all fit men under the pre-war system of conscription. Russia did the same.

In Britain, Kitchener's recruiting campaign raised over two million volunteers by the end of 1915. As losses grew and numbers fell, the Military Service Act of January 1916 introduced conscription for unmarried men aged 18 to 41; it was extended to married men in May 1916.
Conscientious objectors could appear before tribunals, and about 16,000 men claimed that status. Some were jailed or sent to non-combatant units.

The Military Service Act of 1916 did not apply to Ireland. A proposal in April 1918 to extend conscription to Ireland provoked the Conscription Crisis, a nationwide campaign of opposition, and was never put into effect.

The USA introduced conscription through the Selective Service Act of May 1917. Germany passed the Auxiliary Service Law in December 1916, which required all men aged 17 to 60 to work for the war effort.

Conscription and casualties raised the question of 'reserved occupations': governments had to keep skilled workers in munitions, mines and railways, and sometimes replaced them with women (see the notes on women in the workforce).
The Zimmermann Telegram, a secret German offer to Mexico of an alliance against the USA, was intercepted by British intelligence and published in the American press in March 1917.

The USA declared war on Germany on 6 April 1917, after the submarine campaign sank American ships and the Zimmermann Telegram, as an 'associated power' rather than a formal ally. Its troops under General Pershing arrived in strength during 1918.

With Russia out, Ludendorff planned the Spring Offensive (Kaiserschlacht), launched on 21 March 1918 with 'Operation Michael'. It made large gains and came close to Amiens, but did not break the Allied line.

In response, the Allies set up a unified command under Marshal Foch in April 1918. German troops were exhausted and short of supplies, and a counter-attack at the Second Battle of the Marne (July 1918) turned the tide.

The Hundred Days began with the Battle of Amiens on 8 August 1918, which Ludendorff called the 'black day of the German army'. Allied tanks, aircraft and artillery pushed the Germans back to the Hindenburg Line, which was broken in late September.

On 29 September 1918 Ludendorff told the Kaiser that Germany needed an armistice at once. Germany asked for terms using Wilson's Fourteen Points, and the armistice was signed in a railway carriage at Compiègne at 5 a.m. on 11 November, taking effect at 11 a.m.
Military deaths in the war are usually put at about nine to ten million, with many more wounded, and civilian deaths in the millions.
Douglas Haig commanded the British Expeditionary Force in France from December 1915 until the end of the war. He is the most controversial British commander of the war.
Born in Edinburgh in 1861 into a whisky-distilling family, Haig attended Sandhurst, joined the cavalry and served in the Sudan and the Boer War before becoming a corps commander in 1914.
He succeeded Sir John French as commander-in-chief of the BEF in December 1915 and was promoted field marshal in January 1917.
He commanded the Somme offensive of 1916, the Arras offensive and Passchendaele in 1917, and the defensive battles of 1918. On 11 April 1918 he issued his 'backs to the wall' order.
He led the Allied advance in the Hundred Days of 1918, in which British forces played the leading part and took many prisoners.
After the war he was made an earl and given a grant of money. He founded the British Legion in 1921 and supported the sale of poppies. He died in 1928, and his funeral was a national occasion.

Contemporaries: King George V and the army trusted him; Lloyd George distrusted him, thought his battles wasteful, and withheld reinforcements in early 1918. Many soldiers, and the public after the war, mourned him.
From the 1920s memoirs, notably Lloyd George's, criticised him. In the 1960s Alan Clark's The Donkeys popularised the phrase 'lions led by donkeys', which Clark misattributed to German generals.

Historians such as Denis Winter and Gerard De Groot depicted Haig as a callous and unimaginative butcher; John Terraine, Gary Sheffield and others argue that he adapted, learned from experience and led the army to victory in 1918.

Many historians now accept that his attritional strategy was shaped by circumstances: the strength of defences, the need to support France, and the poor communications that limited control over battles.
Allied success: the blockade, attrition and the arrival of American troops in 1918 wore down Germany's capacity to fight, and 1918's coordinated tank, artillery and air attacks broke its army.
Limit: the Western Front battles of 1915-17 produced casualties out of proportion to gains, and Passchendaele and the Somme became symbols of waste.
German success: Germany held the Western Front for four years, knocked Russia out of the war and nearly won in spring 1918.
German failure: the Schlieffen Plan failed in 1914, unrestricted submarine warfare brought in the USA, and the army was exhausted by 1918.
Contemporary view: the troops themselves, and many officers, criticised the high command; later views range from Clark's 'donkeys' to Sheffield's 'Forgotten Victory'.
By autumn 1918 the German army could not win and the home front was exhausted by blockade and hunger. Defeat, mutiny and revolution brought down the Kaiser.
On 29 September 1918, with the Hindenburg Line broken and Bulgaria out of the war, Ludendorff told the Kaiser that Germany needed an armistice at once.

To please Wilson, the Kaiser appointed the liberal Prince Max of Baden as Chancellor on 3 October 1918, with Social Democrats and Centre Party members in the government, and Germany asked Wilson for an armistice on the basis of the Fourteen Points.

Wilson's replies insisted that Germany must end its military autocracy, which encouraged calls for the Kaiser to go. The constitution was changed in late October to make the Chancellor responsible to the Reichstag.

Ludendorff resigned on 26 October. At the end of the month the naval command ordered the fleet to sail for a last battle; sailors at Wilhelmshaven refused, and a mutiny at Kiel spread from 3 November to ports and cities across Germany.
Sailors, soldiers and workers formed councils on the Russian model. Kurt Eisner declared a Bavarian republic on 7 November.

On 9 November, with a general strike in Berlin, Prince Max announced the Kaiser's abdication without his consent and handed the chancellorship to the Social Democrat Friedrich Ebert. Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a German republic from the Reichstag window, and Karl Liebknecht proclaimed a socialist republic from the Berlin palace.
Wilhelm II fled to the Netherlands on 10 November. On 11 November German representatives, led by the Centre politician Matthias Erzberger, signed the armistice at Compiègne.

The armistice required Germany to evacuate occupied territory, hand over weapons and ships, accept Allied occupation west of the Rhine, and gave up the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. The Allied blockade continued until the peace was signed.

A Council of People's Representatives of Majority and Independent Social Democrats ruled until elections. On 10 November Ebert made a pact with General Groener of the army: the army would support the government in return for its help in keeping order and respecting officers' authority.
Employers and trade unions agreed (the Stinnes-Legien agreement, November 1918) to recognise unions and introduce the eight-hour day.

The Communist Party of Germany (KPD) was founded around 30 December 1918 by Luxemburg, Liebknecht and others from the Spartacus League. The left wanted a council republic like Russia's; the SPD leaders wanted an elected parliament.

In the Spartacist rising or January uprising (5-12 January 1919), radicals occupied newspaper buildings in Berlin. The defence minister Gustav Noske crushed it with regular troops and Freikorps, volunteer units of ex-soldiers.

Luxemburg and Liebknecht were arrested and murdered by Freikorps officers on 15 January 1919. Communist risings in Bavaria, where a Soviet republic existed for a few weeks in April 1919, were also put down.

Elections to the National Assembly on 19 January 1919, the first in which women voted, made the SPD the largest party. The Assembly met at Weimar in February 1919 to avoid Berlin's unrest and adopted the Weimar constitution in August.

The republic began with the burden of defeat: right-wing nationalists spread the 'stab in the back' myth, that the army had been betrayed by socialists and Jews at home, though the army leadership itself had asked for an armistice.
Wilson set out the Fourteen Points in an address to Congress on 8 January 1918, as a statement of American war aims.

They called for open covenants of peace openly arrived at, freedom of the seas, free trade, reduction of armaments and an impartial adjustment of colonial claims, with the interests of the peoples concerned counting equally.

Points 6 to 8 dealt with the evacuation of Russia and Belgium and the return of Alsace-Lorraine to France. Points 9 to 13 set frontiers for Italy, Austria-Hungary, the Balkans, the Ottoman Empire and an independent Poland with sea access, broadly on national lines.
Point 14 called for a general association of nations to guarantee political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike. This became the League of Nations.

Germany's request for an armistice in October 1918 relied on the Fourteen Points. Britain and France accepted them as a basis in November, but Britain reserved its position on freedom of the seas and the Allies insisted on compensation for civilian damage.
Many Germans later felt that the Allies had broken the pre-armistice agreement by imposing the harsher Treaty of Versailles.
The conference opened in Paris on 18 January 1919. Over thirty states attended, but the defeated powers were excluded and the key decisions were taken by the Big Four.
The Big Four were Woodrow Wilson (USA), David Lloyd George (Britain), Georges Clemenceau (France) and Vittorio Orlando (Italy). The Council of Four took the main decisions.
Wilson wanted a just peace based on self-determination and a League of Nations, and he was the first US president to travel to Europe in office.
Clemenceau, nicknamed 'the Tiger', wanted security for France, which had been invaded twice in fifty years: a weak Germany, a Rhineland buffer, and heavy reparations.

Lloyd George had won the December 1918 election on slogans demanding that Germany pay, but he wanted a treaty that was not so harsh that it would provoke revenge, and he wanted to protect British trade and naval power and avoid French dominance on the continent.
Orlando wanted the territory promised to Italy in the secret Treaty of London (1915), and left the conference in April 1919 when Fiume was refused. Italians spoke of a 'mutilated victory'.
Japan, an ally, sought a racial equality clause, which was rejected, and gained German rights in Shandong. Russia, now Bolshevik, was not invited.
Ireland's Sinn Fein sent Seán T. O'Kelly to Paris to seek a hearing for Irish self-determination, but Wilson and the Allies refused to admit the Irish case.
Terms were drawn up by commissions and handed to the Germans in May 1919, with no negotiation, under a threat of resuming war if they refused to sign.
The treaty was signed by the German delegates in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, five years to the day after the assassination at Sarajevo.

Article 231, the war guilt clause, stated that Germany and its allies accepted responsibility for all loss and damage caused by the war that was imposed on the Allies by the aggression of Germany and its allies. It was the legal basis for reparations.

Territory: Alsace-Lorraine returned to France; Eupen-Malmedy went to Belgium; North Schleswig, after a plebiscite, to Denmark; and most of West Prussia and Posen to Poland, which gave Poland a corridor to the Baltic that split East Prussia from the rest of Germany. Germany lost about 13 per cent of its pre-war European territory and about a tenth of its population.

Danzig became a Free City under League of Nations protection, and Memel was placed under Allied control. The Saar was governed by the League for fifteen years, with its coal mines going to France, and a plebiscite was due in 1935.
Colonies: all of Germany's colonies were taken and became League of Nations mandates under Britain, France, Japan and others.

Military clauses: the army was limited to 100,000 volunteers, conscription ended, the navy limited to a few small ships and no submarines, there was no air force, no tanks or heavy artillery, and the Rhineland was demilitarised with Allied occupation for up to fifteen years.
Union of Germany and Austria (Anschluss) was forbidden.

Reparations: the sum was not set in the treaty. The Reparations Commission fixed a total of 132 billion gold marks in 1921, in a schedule of payments with three classes of bond; Germany was required to pay in practice about 50 billion.
Article 227 called for the trial of the Kaiser, but the Dutch refused to hand him over. The treaty also included the Covenant of the League of Nations.
Germans resented the treaty as a 'Diktat' because they were not allowed to negotiate. Scheidemann's government resigned rather than sign, and the Assembly accepted it under the threat of invasion.

Austria-Hungary broke up in October and November 1918, before the peace. Czechoslovakia declared independence on 28 October, and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (Yugoslavia) was proclaimed on 1 December. Poland, Hungary and Austria formed separate states.
Emperor Charles I withdrew from state affairs on 11 November 1918. Austria became a republic on 12 November.

The Treaty of St Germain with Austria (10 September 1919) recognised the new states, limited Austria's army to 30,000 and forbade union with Germany. Austria lost South Tyrol to Italy and the Sudeten German areas to Czechoslovakia.

The Treaty of Trianon with Hungary (4 June 1920) cut Hungary to about a third of its former territory, giving Transylvania to Romania, Slovakia to Czechoslovakia and Croatia to Yugoslavia. Over three million Hungarians were left outside its borders, causing bitter resentment.
The Treaty of Neuilly with Bulgaria (27 November 1919) took Western Thrace, which gave Bulgaria's Aegean outlet to Greece, imposed reparations and limited its army to 20,000.

The Treaty of Sèvres with the Ottoman Empire (10 August 1920) divided up the empire, with Armenia and a Kurdish area promised autonomy. Mustafa Kemal's nationalists rejected it and won the war against Greece, and the Treaty of Lausanne (1923) replaced it.
The Middle East was placed under League mandates: Britain received Palestine, Iraq and Transjordan; France received Syria and Lebanon.
Applied: the settlement created or restored Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia, and recognised Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, which had broken away from the Russian empire.

Plebiscites were held in some contested areas: North and Middle Schleswig (1920), Allenstein and Marienwerder, Upper Silesia (1921, split after a rising and a League decision in 1922) and Carinthia, and Burgenland went to Austria.
Denied: Germans and Austrians were forbidden to unite, though Austria's parliament had voted for union with Germany. About three million Germans of the Sudetenland were placed in Czechoslovakia.
Denied: South Tyrol, whose population was German-speaking, was given to Italy for strategic reasons; Hungarians in Romania, Slovakia and Yugoslavia were not given a choice.
Eastern Europe's new states were multi-ethnic: Poland and Czechoslovakia contained large German, Ukrainian, Slovak and other minorities, protected only by minority-rights treaties with the League.
The principle was not applied to colonies, which became mandates, nor to Ireland, Egypt or India, a fact noted by nationalists there.

The League of Nations came into being on 10 January 1920, with its seat in Geneva. Its main organs were the Assembly, the Council and the Secretariat, and it also had the Permanent Court of International Justice and the International Labour Organisation.

Its Covenant promised collective security: members agreed to respect each other's independence and to use arbitration, then economic sanctions and possibly force against an aggressor (Article 10 and Article 16).
The defeated powers and Soviet Russia were excluded at first. Germany joined in 1926 and the Soviet Union in 1934.
Wilson toured the USA in September 1919 to rally support, but suffered a stroke on 2 October 1919.

The Republican Senate, led by Henry Cabot Lodge, had objections to Article 10, which could oblige the USA to defend other states. The Senate rejected the treaty in November 1919 and again in March 1920.
The USA made a separate peace with Germany in 1921. Without the USA, the League lacked the strongest Western power, and France and Britain had to enforce the treaty alone.
Woodrow Wilson was President of the USA from 1913 to 1921. His Fourteen Points and the League of Nations shaped the Peace Settlement, but he could not win American support for it.

Wilson was born on 28 December 1856 in Staunton, Virginia. A historian and political scientist, he became president of Princeton University and Governor of New Jersey (1911-13) before winning the presidency in 1912.
He kept the USA neutral from 1914 and was re-elected in 1916 on the slogan that he had kept the country out of the war.

After the resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram, he asked Congress on 2 April 1917 to declare war so that the world might be made safe for democracy. Congress did so on 6 April.
He announced the Fourteen Points in January 1918 and was the leading figure at Paris, where he insisted that the League Covenant be part of the treaty.
He made compromises: he accepted reparations and Article 231, the Saar and Japanese gains in Shandong to win agreement on the League and mandates.

He refused to compromise with Republican senators led by Lodge, who wanted reservations to the Covenant, and the treaty failed in the Senate. His stroke in October 1919 left him incapacitated for the rest of his term.

Contemporaries: he was welcomed by huge crowds in Europe in December 1918 as a prophet of a new order, though Clemenceau is said to have mocked his idealism. Many Americans came to see him as having entangled the USA in European affairs.

Historians: admirers see him as the founder of liberal internationalism, whose ideas shaped the United Nations; critics find him self-righteous, inconsistent in applying self-determination, and politically inept in handling the Senate.
Achievement: new democratic states appeared where empires had ruled, and the League provided a forum for settling disputes, such as the Aaland Islands in 1921.
Limit: the new states contained large minorities, and revision was demanded by Germany, Hungary, Bulgaria and Italy, who felt cheated.

Limit: the treaty was too harsh to be accepted by Germany but not harsh enough to stop it from recovering. Enforcement depended on Britain and France, which disagreed, and the USA and Russia were outside the system.

Problems facing Europe after the war: economic dislocation, war debts and inflation, refugees and the influenza epidemic of 1918, the Russian Civil War and fear of Bolshevism, disputed borders such as the Polish-Soviet war of 1920, and the fragile new democracies.

Contemporary view: Keynes, a member of the British delegation who resigned, argued in The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919) that the reparations were unrealistic and would ruin European recovery; Marshal Foch is credited with saying that it was only an armistice for twenty years.

Later view: some historians say Germany's grievance was exaggerated and its terms were milder than Brest-Litovsk; others, such as Margaret MacMillan, see a serious attempt at a difficult task and argue that later failures, not the treaty itself, caused the Second World War.
After unification Germany combined abundant coal and iron with a large internal market, strong banks and a well-trained workforce. It overtook Britain in several industries before 1914.
Germany's population grew from about 41 million in 1871 to about 67 million in 1914, providing both labour and a large home market.
Coal and iron: the Ruhr coalfield was the heart of heavy industry, with further coal in the Saar and Silesia and iron ore in Lorraine, taken from France in 1871.

Political unification created a single market with a common currency (the mark, 1873), a central bank (the Reichsbank) and uniform commercial law. The Zollverein of the 1830s had already removed customs barriers between most states.

Railways, built mainly in the 1840s and 1850s, grew from about 21,000 km in 1871 to over 60,000 km by 1913, linking the Ruhr to ports, and later were run by the states, which kept rates low for industry.
Banks such as Deutsche Bank (1870) and Dresdner Bank (1872) were 'universal banks' that lent to industry for long periods and sat on company boards, so firms could raise capital for heavy investment.
Education: Germany's Technische Hochschulen, universities and technical schools trained engineers and chemists, and firms set up research laboratories.

The French indemnity of 1871 gave the new Reich a financial boost, and the boom of the early 1870s (the Gründerzeit) ended in a stock market crash in 1873. The long depression that followed encouraged cartels and tariffs.
Cartels, agreements among firms to fix prices and output, were common in coal, steel and chemicals. The Rhenish-Westphalian Coal Syndicate (1893) controlled most of the Ruhr coal supply.
By 1913 Germany produced more than twice as much steel as Britain, and was the world's second industrial power after the USA.

Hard coal output rose from about 30 million tonnes in 1871 to about 190 million tonnes in 1913, and German exports of machinery, chemicals and electrical goods competed with British goods across the world.
The Hamburg-America Line and the North German Lloyd of Bremen built up one of the largest merchant fleets in the world, supported by the growth of ports such as Hamburg.
From the 1880s new industries based on steel, chemicals and electricity grew faster than the older coal and textiles, and Germany was often the leader.
Steel: the basic (Thomas-Gilchrist) process of 1878 allowed the phosphoric iron ores of Lorraine to be turned into steel, and steel production expanded rapidly in the Ruhr.

Chemicals: BASF, Bayer and Hoechst, all founded in the 1860s, led the world in synthetic dyes and pharmaceuticals. Fritz Haber's ammonia synthesis, developed with BASF's Carl Bosch (1909-13), made artificial fertilisers and explosives possible.
Electricals: Werner von Siemens founded Siemens and Halske in 1847 and developed the dynamo and electric railway. Emil Rathenau founded the Deutsche Edison-Gesellschaft in 1883, renamed AEG in 1887.
Electric lighting, trams and power stations spread in cities in the 1890s, and by 1914 Siemens and AEG dominated German electrical engineering and exported across Europe.
Motor vehicles and engines: Karl Benz, Gottlieb Daimler and Rudolf Diesel developed the motor car and the diesel engine in the 1880s and 1890s (see the notes on the motor car).
Government patronage, the army and navy as customers, and the relationship between industry and science helped German firms to exploit new technology.
Germany's share of world manufacturing output passed Britain's in the years before 1914.
The Krupp works at Essen grew from a small steel workshop into the largest industrial enterprise in Europe, and became synonymous with German arms and industry.
Friedrich Krupp founded a cast steel works at Essen in 1811. His son Alfred Krupp (1812-87) took over as a teenager in 1826 and made it a major enterprise.

Alfred exhibited a flawless 2-ton cast steel ingot at the Great Exhibition in London in 1851, and won international attention. He developed seamless steel railway wheel tyres and, with the Bessemer process, steel rails.

He moved into artillery, producing breech-loading steel guns that Prussia adopted in the 1860s and which proved effective against France in 1870-71. He sold guns to many foreign governments, earning the nickname 'the Cannon King'.
Alfred built the Villa Hügel (1873) as the family's home and expanded the works to a workforce of tens of thousands by the time of his death in 1887.

Welfare and control: he built housing colonies for workers from the 1860s, and provided sickness and pension funds, schools and shops. He also expected loyalty and discouraged political activity, so historians describe this welfare as paternalism.

Friedrich Alfred Krupp (1854-1902) took over in 1887 and expanded into naval armour plate and, in 1902, shipbuilding by buying the Germania shipyard at Kiel. The Kaiser was a close friend and the fleet was a large customer.
A scandal over Friedrich Alfred's private life in Capri was reported in the press in November 1902, and he died that month; whether by suicide or stroke is disputed. Wilhelm II attended the funeral.
His daughter Bertha Krupp (1886-1957) inherited the firm at the age of 16 in 1902, and the firm was converted into a limited company (Fried. Krupp AG) in 1903, with Bertha as the main shareholder.
Bertha married Gustav von Bohlen und Halbach (1870-1950), a diplomat, in 1906. The Kaiser allowed him to take the name Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach. He chaired the board from 1909.

Under Gustav the firm grew with naval and army orders. In 1914 it produced the 42 cm 'Big Bertha' howitzer, named after Bertha Krupp, which was used against the Belgian fortresses at Liège and Namur in August 1914.
The firm made guns, shells, armour plate and submarines throughout the war and its workforce grew to well over 100,000, many of them women.

Contemporaries: Krupp was a national symbol of German industrial strength, admired by nationalists. Socialists attacked the family as 'merchants of death', and the Reichstag debated Krupp's profits and its bribery of officials in 1913-14.

Historians see the Krupps as a leading example of the links between heavy industry, the army and the state before 1914, and of industrial paternalism. The family's later role under the Nazis falls outside this period.
Industrial growth drew millions from the countryside, mostly from the east, to the cities and the Ruhr. By 1910 around 60 per cent of Germans lived in towns, up from about a third in 1871.
Berlin grew from under a million in 1871 to about two million by 1910, and Essen, Dortmund and other Ruhr towns grew many times over.
Working-class families lived in overcrowded tenements (Mietskasernen) in Berlin, often with several to a room. Disease and poor sanitation were common, though public health improved from the 1890s.

Factory work meant long hours, strict discipline and little security, though real wages rose slowly in the 1890s and 1900s. Women and children also worked, and a law of 1891 restricted Sunday work and limited the hours of women and children.
The Ruhr miners' strike of 1889 involved about 90,000 workers, and a second strike followed in 1905, forcing the state to intervene in mining conditions.
Catholic and Polish migrants, often in the Ruhr, added religious and ethnic tension to the class divisions.
The Social Democratic Party (SPD) was formed at Gotha in 1875 by uniting Marx's followers and Lassalle's General German Workers' Association.
The Anti-Socialist Law of 1878 banned the SPD's organisations and press until 1890, but socialists could still stand for the Reichstag, and their votes rose.

After the law lapsed, the SPD adopted the Erfurt Programme in 1891, which combined a Marxist analysis of capitalism with immediate demands for reform and democracy. Eduard Bernstein's revisionism, arguing for gradual reform, was rejected by the party in theory but accepted in practice.
In 1912 the SPD won about 4.25 million votes and 110 seats, becoming the largest party in the Reichstag, though the electoral system and the Bundesrat still excluded it from power.
The Free (socialist) trade unions grew to about 2.5 million members by 1913, bigger than the Christian and liberal unions.
Employers formed associations and used lockouts and blacklists in response, and the government used the courts and police against strikes.

The Junkers, the landowning nobility east of the Elbe, dominated the army officer corps, the Prussian civil service and the Prussian parliament, where the three-class voting system gave the rich more weight.

Cheap imported grain from the USA and Russia in the 1870s and 1880s threatened Junker profits. The tariff of 1879 protected grain and iron and led to an alliance of 'iron and rye' between heavy industry and landowners.

Tariffs raised food prices and angered workers and consumers, and the left and liberal industries, such as finished goods and exporters, opposed them. In 1902 Bülow's tariff raised duties on grain still further.
In 1897 the Prussian minister Miquel promoted Sammlungspolitik, a 'policy of rallying together' landowners and industrialists behind the monarchy, the navy and Weltpolitik, against the left.

Industrialists resented Junker privilege and the aristocratic dominance of the state, while many middle-class Germans tried to imitate the nobility. Historians such as Hans-Ulrich Wehler argue that this 'feudalisation of the bourgeoisie' blocked democratic reform.
Geoff Eley and David Blackbourn replied in The Peculiarities of German History (1984) that the German middle class was confident and the Reich was a modern society, not a flawed one.
Bismarck's insurance laws created sickness insurance (1883), accident insurance (1884) and old age and invalidity pensions (1889), partly to wean workers from the SPD.
Wilhelm II's 'new course' of 1890 started with factory laws on Sunday work, women and child labour, and a council to discuss labour matters, but he turned against the SPD when it kept winning votes.
Companies provided their own welfare. Krupp's housing, schools and funds are the best-known example, and other firms such as Siemens followed. Employers hoped for loyalty and an end to strikes.
Welfare did not stop the SPD vote from rising, and many workers were more loyal to their unions and party than to the state or firm.
Despite the growth in industrial wealth, workers had little political power in Prussia, where the three-class vote persisted until 1918.
Achievement: Germany became the leading industrial economy in continental Europe, strongest in steel, chemicals and electricals.
Limit: the growth was uneven. Agriculture and the east remained backward, and the economy was exposed to cycles of boom and slump.
Achievement: the Reich pioneered national social insurance, and real wages rose in the 1890s and 1900s.
Limit: welfare was paternalist and aimed at controlling the working class; political reform did not follow economic change.
Limit: heavy industry's dependence on arms orders linked the economy to militarism and the naval race.

Contemporary view: nationalists saw industrial power as proof of German greatness, while socialists saw it as exploitation. Later historians debate whether industrial Germany was a modern society with an unmodern politics.
Russia was the largest state in Europe, but it was poor, overwhelmingly rural and ruled by an autocratic tsar with no parliament.
Serfdom was abolished by Alexander II in 1861. Peasants had to pay redemption payments to the state over 49 years for the land they received, and these payments left many in debt.
Most peasants held land in the mir (village commune), which periodically redistributed strips among households. This discouraged investment, and farming methods were backward.
The census of 1897 showed a population of about 126 million, about 80 per cent of them peasants. Russia was an empire of many peoples, and Russians were less than half the population.
In 1871 Russia had little heavy industry, relatively few railways and a weak banking system; it exported grain and relied on foreign capital and technology.
Alexander II's reforms (zemstva, courts, army reform) were limited, and he was assassinated by the revolutionary group People's Will on 13 March 1881.

His son Alexander III (1881-94) and grandson Nicholas II (1894-1917) upheld autocracy, backed by the Orthodox Church, the nobility, the army and the secret police (the Okhrana), and pursued Russification of national minorities.

Nicholas II declared in 1895 that hopes for a constitution were 'senseless dreams'; revolutionary movements, including Social Revolutionaries (SRs) based on the peasantry and Marxist Social Democrats, developed underground.
Sergei Witte, Finance Minister from 1892 to 1903, led a state-directed 'great spurt' of industrial growth, paid for by foreign loans, taxation and grain exports.
Witte believed that Russia must industrialise to remain a Great Power, and the state built railways, ordered goods and protected industry with tariffs.
Railways were the key: the Trans-Siberian Railway began in 1891 and the main line to Vladivostok was open by about 1904 (completed in full in 1916). Rail mileage roughly doubled in the 1890s.
He put the rouble on the gold standard in 1897 to attract foreign investors. French and Belgian loans and investment paid for mines, ironworks and railways, helped by the Franco-Russian Alliance.

Coal, iron and steel grew in the Donbas in Ukraine, oil in Baku, and engineering and textiles in St Petersburg and Moscow. Output of pig iron and coal rose several times between 1890 and 1900, at a rate often put at about 8 per cent a year.
Industry was concentrated in huge factories such as the Putilov works in St Petersburg, which employed tens of thousands of workers, making labour organisation and protest easier.
The cost fell on the peasantry through high indirect taxes, and grain was exported even when people were hungry. Witte himself recognised the risk and warned about peasant discontent.

The industrial depression of 1900-03 caused unemployment and strikes. By 1914 Russia was the world's fifth industrial power by output, but its output per head was low and it relied on foreign capital.
The peasant economy suffered from small plots, outdated methods, rapid population growth and redemption payments. Land hunger grew as families increased.
A harvest failure in 1891 caused a famine across the Volga region and the black earth provinces. A cholera epidemic in 1892 killed hundreds of thousands.
Government relief was slow, and private and zemstvo volunteers, including Tolstoy and Chekhov, played a major part. The famine weakened trust in the regime.
The famine encouraged educated Russians to form opposition groups: the Union of Liberation (1903), liberals who wanted a constitution, and the SRs.
Peasant unrest grew in the early 1900s with attacks on landlords' estates in 1902 in Kharkov and Poltava provinces, and violence rose again in 1905-06.
Workers were mostly first-generation peasants who kept links with their villages, which spread discontent between city and countryside.
Russia and Japan were rivals in Manchuria and Korea. Russia had leased Port Arthur from China in 1898, and the Trans-Siberian Railway gave it a route to the Far East.
Interior minister Plehve is reported to have wanted 'a short victorious war' to stop revolution, but it did the opposite.
Japan attacked Port Arthur without warning on 8 February 1904. The Russian army suffered defeats at Mukden (February-March 1905), and Port Arthur surrendered in January 1905.
Russia's Baltic Fleet sailed around the world and was destroyed by the Japanese at Tsushima on 27-28 May 1905.
The Treaty of Portsmouth (5 September 1905), mediated by US President Theodore Roosevelt, gave Japan southern Sakhalin, Port Arthur and a free hand in Korea.
The defeat humiliated the autocracy, revealed the weakness of its army, transport and administration, and was the immediate trigger for the 1905 revolution.

On Sunday 22 January 1905 (9 January in the old Russian calendar) a peaceful procession led by the priest Georgy Gapon went to the Winter Palace in St Petersburg to present a petition for reforms to the tsar. Troops opened fire, killing and wounding hundreds, in 'Bloody Sunday'.

The massacre destroyed the people's trust in the tsar as their protector. Strikes, peasant risings, mutinies (the battleship Potemkin in June 1905) and national movements in Poland and the Caucasus followed.
In October 1905 a general strike paralysed the railways and cities. The Petersburg Soviet (council) of workers' deputies was formed, with Trotsky as a leading member.
Witte advised the Tsar to grant concessions. The October Manifesto (17 October 1905) promised civil liberties, an elected Duma with legislative powers, and a wider franchise.

The Manifesto split the opposition: liberals (Octobrists) accepted it, while socialists did not. The army stayed loyal, the Soviet leaders were arrested in December, and an armed rising in Moscow was crushed.
A large French loan in April 1906 helped the government to survive without relying on the Duma.

The Fundamental Laws (April 1906) kept the Tsar's title of autocrat, his control of the army, foreign policy and ministers, and his right to veto laws and to dissolve the Duma and rule by decree between sessions.
Peter Stolypin, Prime Minister from 1906 to 1911, combined repression with agrarian reform in a bid to create a conservative, prosperous peasant class.
The First Duma (May-July 1906) demanded land reform and ministers answerable to it, and was dissolved after 73 days. The Second Duma (1907) was also dissolved.
In June 1907 the Tsar and Stolypin changed the electoral law, so that landowners and the rich dominated the Third Duma (1907-12) and the Fourth Duma (1912-17).
Stolypin crushed disorder with field courts-martial from 1906, which executed over a thousand people. The hangman's noose was called 'Stolypin's necktie'.

The land reform of November 1906 let peasants leave the commune, claim their land as private property and consolidate their strips. The Peasant Land Bank helped them buy land, and resettlement in Siberia was encouraged.
By 1914 about two million households (about a quarter) had left the communes, but most peasants stayed in the mir. Stolypin said he needed twenty years of peace.
He was shot by a revolutionary who was also a police informer, Dmitri Bogrov, at the Kiev opera in September 1911, and died days later.
After 1912 workers' protest revived, with strikes following the shooting of miners at the Lena goldfields in April 1912, and strikes in St Petersburg in summer 1914.

Russia mobilised the largest army, but it was poorly led and short of rifles, shells and boots. Defeats at Tannenberg and the Masurian Lakes in 1914 and the great retreat of 1915 cost millions of casualties and prisoners. The Brusilov Offensive of 1916 was a success but cost heavily.

The war strained the economy: railways were overloaded, inflation rose as the government printed money, and food and fuel were short in the cities by winter 1916-17. Over fifteen million men were mobilised, reducing farm output.

Nicholas II took personal command of the army at the front in September 1915, leaving his wife Alexandra and Rasputin influential in government. Ministers changed rapidly. The Duma's Progressive Bloc demanded a government that had public confidence.
Grigori Rasputin, a peasant mystic whom the Tsarina trusted to ease the haemophilia of the heir, Alexei, was murdered by aristocrats in December 1916, a sign of the regime's isolation.

On 8 March 1917 (23 February in the Russian calendar), International Women's Day, women textile workers in Petrograd demanded bread. Strikes grew into a general strike, and the soldiers of the garrison joined the crowds instead of firing on them.

The Duma set up a Provisional Committee, and the Petrograd Soviet was revived. Army commanders told Nicholas to go, and he abdicated on 15 March 1917 (2 March in the Russian calendar), ending 300 years of Romanov rule. His brother Michael declined the crown.

The Provisional Government, headed first by Prince Lvov and from July by Alexander Kerensky, shared power with the Soviet, an arrangement known as 'dual power'. Order No. 1 of the Soviet told soldiers to obey the Soviet's orders.

The Provisional Government introduced civil liberties but continued the war and delayed land reform until a Constituent Assembly was elected. The Kerensky offensive in July 1917 failed, and desertions rose.

Lenin returned from exile in Switzerland in April 1917 and issued the April Theses, demanding 'all power to the Soviets', peace, land to the peasants and bread for workers. The Bolsheviks grew in strength in the Soviets.
A Bolshevik rising in the July Days failed, but in August-September General Kornilov's attempted coup against Kerensky was defeated with the help of the Bolsheviks, who gained arms and prestige.
The Bolsheviks won majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets by September. Trotsky chaired the Petrograd Soviet and organised the Military Revolutionary Committee.

On the night of 6-7 November 1917 (24-25 October in the old calendar) Bolshevik forces took bridges, stations and the telegraph, and the Winter Palace fell. Lenin announced the formation of a Soviet government under the Council of People's Commissars.

The new government issued decrees on peace and land and the right of nations to self-determination. In the Constituent Assembly election, the SRs won the most votes (about 40 per cent) and the Bolsheviks about a quarter; the Assembly met once in January 1918 and was dissolved by force.

Lenin signed an armistice in December 1917 and, after Trotsky's attempt to stall, accepted the harsh Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918. Russia gave up Poland, the Baltic provinces, Ukraine and Finland, a huge loss of land, population, coal and industry.
The Bolsheviks moved the capital to Moscow in March 1918 and created the Cheka (December 1917) to crush opposition. The Romanov family were shot at Ekaterinburg in July 1918.

The civil war (1918-20) was fought between the Reds (Bolsheviks), organised by Trotsky as War Commissar into the Red Army, and the Whites, a loose mix of generals, monarchists and liberals such as Kolchak, Denikin, Yudenich and Wrangel.
Britain, France, Japan and the USA sent troops to support the Whites and to guard supplies after 1918, but their effort was limited.
The Reds held central Russia with its railways, industry and capital and could move troops; the Whites were scattered and divided, and many peasants feared a return of the landlords.
War Communism (1918-21) meant seizing grain from peasants, nationalising industry and rationing, and the Red Terror targeted opponents.

The Red Army defeated Kolchak in Siberia (1919), Denikin and Yudenich (1919-20), and Wrangel in the Crimea in November 1920. In 1920 Poland defeated a Soviet advance on Warsaw. Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland became independent states.
Achievement: Witte's industrialisation built railways and heavy industry, and growth after 1906 was strong; Stolypin's reforms began to create a class of independent farmers.
Limit: industrial growth depended on foreign capital and on a poor peasantry, and it produced a discontented urban working class in huge factories.
Limit: political reform stopped short. The Dumas were weak, the autocrat could dismiss ministers, and Nicholas II mistrusted reformers and failed to use the chance of 1905-06.

Why the regime survived 1905 but not 1917: in 1905 the army stayed loyal and the opposition split; in 1917 the army was worn down by three years of defeat, the cities starved and the soldiers joined the strikers.

Historians' views: the optimists (such as Leopold Haimson and Hans Rogger in some respects) argue that Russia was modernising and that the war, not structural failure, caused collapse; pessimists argue that the autocracy was too weak to survive modernisation, and Orlando Figes stresses its failure to reform.

Contemporary views: liberals blamed the tsar's obstinacy; the Bolsheviks portrayed 1917 as a workers' revolution, though historians stress that it was also a coup by a disciplined party exploiting the failure of the Provisional Government.
The scale and length of the war forced governments to direct the economy and the lives of civilians, far beyond anything seen in earlier wars.

Britain's Defence of the Realm Act (DORA), passed in August 1914 and extended repeatedly, gave the government power over property, labour, the press and public behaviour. It restricted pub opening hours, censored news, and led to British Summer Time (1916).

The government took control of the railways at the start of the war in August 1914, and took over the coal mines in 1917 and shipping, to coordinate supplies. New ministries were created: Munitions (1915), Labour and Food (1916) and Shipping (1916).

The 'Shell Crisis' of spring 1915, when the army ran short of shells, brought down the Liberal government. Lloyd George led the new Ministry of Munitions that took charge of the supply of war material.

Germany organised the economy through the War Raw Materials Department (1914) under Walther Rathenau and the Hindenburg Programme (1916), which aimed to increase munitions production and mobilise labour.
Propaganda was used to recruit soldiers (the 'Your Country Needs You' poster), sell war bonds and encourage civilians to accept shortages. Governments also censored letters and newspapers.

Rationing: Britain introduced compulsory rationing of sugar, meat and butter in early 1918, after the submarine campaign cut supplies and queues grew. Germany introduced bread rationing from 1915 and a wider system of price controls.
Civilians became targets: Scarborough was bombarded by German warships in December 1914, and Zeppelins and Gotha bombers attacked British towns.
States paid for the war through borrowing, war loans and printing money rather than taxation alone, and the national debts of the belligerents multiplied several times over.
Britain, once the world's greatest creditor, became a debtor to the USA, and the USA took over as the leading financial power.
Inflation: prices rose faster than wages in most countries, and savings lost value. In Germany, where the war was funded mainly by loans and money creation, this laid the ground for later inflation.

Germany's blockade-hit economy suffered severe shortages. Harvest failure in 1916 caused the 'Turnip Winter' of 1916-17, and an estimated several hundred thousand civilians died of malnutrition-related causes by the end of the war.
Industry converted to war production, and new industries such as chemicals, aircraft and engineering expanded. Peacetime trade collapsed, and Europe lost export markets to the USA and Japan.
Areas fought over, such as northern France and Belgium, were devastated. Russia's economy collapsed under the strain, contributing to revolution.
Agriculture lost labour and horses to the army, but governments encouraged food production, with measures such as the Corn Production Act 1917 in Britain.

Casualties: about nine to ten million soldiers died, including around 1.4 million French and about 2 million German dead, and about 750,000 British (about 900,000 from the whole British Empire). Many survivors were disabled, and there were hundreds of thousands of war widows.

Class barriers loosened a little: shared danger in the trenches and a need for national unity, and a wider welfare provision. Rural and urban workers who served in the army gained experience of other regions.

Trade unions gained strength and recognition by governments that needed their cooperation. British union membership roughly doubled between 1914 and 1920, though strikes continued over pay and conditions.
Governments also made reforms: the British Education Act 1918 (Fisher Act) raised the school leaving age to 14, and promised housing for returning servicemen.
The influenza pandemic of 1918-19 killed tens of millions worldwide, with estimates ranging widely from 17 to 50 million or more, striking young adults weakened by the war.
Soldiers returned to unemployment and unrest, and demobilisation led to some strikes and mutinies in 1919.
Before the war most women who earned wages were young and unmarried, and worked in a narrow range of badly paid jobs. Only the war made it possible for them to do men's work on a large scale.

Domestic service was the largest single employer of women in Britain, with well over a million servants, and the next largest sectors were textiles and clothing. Pay was typically half or less than that of men.
In France many women worked on family farms and in textile and clothing workshops; in Germany about a third of women worked, mostly in agriculture, domestic service and textiles.
Women were largely excluded from skilled trades and the professions, and many trade unions refused them membership. Married women were expected to work in the home.

Politically, women could not vote in national elections in Britain, France or Germany. The suffragettes of Emmeline Pankhurst's Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU) used militant tactics from 1903, and the suffragists of Millicent Fawcett's NUWSS used peaceful campaigning.
In Germany women were banned from political associations until 1908, and the women's movement was divided between middle-class feminists and the SPD's women's organisation led by Clara Zetkin.
Men volunteered in huge numbers and recruitment for the army left gaps in the workforce. After the shell shortage, the Ministry of Munitions (1915) turned to women to fill the gap.

The Treasury Agreement of March 1915 between the government and unions accepted 'dilution' (employing unskilled workers on tasks done by skilled men) for the war's duration, and the Munitions of War Act of July 1915 supported dilution and banned strikes in munitions.

Hundreds of thousands of women worked in munitions by 1918, filling shells and fuses, making cordite and working in factories such as Woolwich Arsenal and the national filling factories. They were known as 'munitionettes'.

Conditions were hard: long shifts of 10 to 12 hours, shift work and the risk of explosion. At Chilwell in Nottinghamshire a huge explosion in July 1918 killed over 130 workers, and the Silvertown explosion of January 1917 killed 73.
TNT poisoning (toxic jaundice) turned skin yellow, earning women munition workers the name 'canary girls', and caused illness and some deaths.
The government appointed welfare supervisors, provided canteens and set up a Health of Munition Workers Committee, because poor conditions reduced output.
France lost its men to the army early in the war, and the harvest of 1914 was brought in largely by women, children and old men. Women ran family farms and businesses for the rest of the war.

From 1915 the French government under Albert Thomas, the undersecretary for munitions, encouraged women to work in the armaments industry. By the later war years, women made up a large share of the workers in French shell factories, including the Renault works at Billancourt. They were known as 'munitionnettes'.
Women in France also worked as tram conductors, postal workers and clerks, and as nurses in the army medical service.
In Germany the National Women's Service (Nationaler Frauendienst), organised in August 1914 by middle-class feminists such as Gertrud Bäumer, helped with food distribution and welfare.

As men were drafted, women increased in the metal and chemical industries, with Krupp, Siemens and other firms employing more women. The Hindenburg Programme and the Auxiliary Service Law of December 1916 mobilised male workers aged 17 to 60, increasing the pressure on women to fill gaps.
In Germany women bore the brunt of the food shortages, queuing for food, and women led food protests and riots in 1915-17.
Women replaced men in banks, government offices and shops, and the numbers of women clerks and typists rose greatly in Britain, France and Germany.
Women worked on trams, buses and railways as conductors, ticket collectors and porters, and as postal workers, firefighters and police auxiliaries in several countries.
The Women's Land Army was formed in Britain in 1917 as the submarine campaign made food a priority, and around 20,000 or more women worked as farm labourers.
Voluntary Aid Detachments (VADs, founded 1909) supplied nurses and ambulance drivers, including Vera Brittain, who wrote Testament of Youth. Women served in field hospitals near the front.

Edith Cavell, a British nurse who ran a training school in Brussels, was executed by a German firing squad on 12 October 1915 for helping Allied soldiers escape, and became a symbol of Allied propaganda.

Auxiliary services were created: the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps (1917), the Women's Royal Naval Service (1917) and the Women's Royal Air Force (April 1918), in which women worked as clerks, drivers, cooks, mechanics and telephonists, releasing men for the front.

Women were usually paid less than men even where they did the same work. Government rules in 1916 set women's rates for munitions below men's, though some women on piecework earned more than they had in domestic service.
Trade unions feared that employers would use women to undercut men's pay and skills. They agreed to dilution only on condition that pre-war practices were restored after the war.
In August 1914 Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst suspended the WSPU's militant campaign, and the government released suffragette prisoners.
The Pankhursts supported the war effort. In July 1915 the WSPU organised a 'Right to Serve' march in London, backed by government money, to demand that women be given war work.
Sylvia Pankhurst, in contrast, opposed the war and worked for women in London's East End. Christabel founded the Women's Party in 1917.

Contemporary opinion changed: ministers and newspapers praised women's war work, and Asquith said in 1917 that women had earned the vote by their war work, and recognised the importance of the contribution.

The Representation of the People Act of February 1918 gave the vote in Britain to all men over 21 and to women over 30 who met a property qualification, around 8 million women. The Act applied to Ireland, and in the 1918 election Constance Markievicz became the first woman elected to Westminster.
The Equal Franchise Act of 1928 gave women the vote on the same terms as men, at 21.

In Germany a decree of 12 November 1918 gave all women over 20 the vote and the right to stand. Women voted in the January 1919 election and 37 women were elected to the National Assembly. The Weimar constitution declared men and women equal in civic rights 'in principle'.
France did not give women the vote until 1944, though French women had done as much war work as British.

Demobilisation brought pressure on women to leave their jobs. German decrees of 1918-19 required women to give up jobs to returning soldiers, and the Restoration of Pre-War Practices Act (1919) in Britain reinstated the old trade rules. Many women were dismissed from munitions, and some returned to domestic service.

The Sex Disqualification (Removal) Act of 1919 opened some professions and jury service to women in Britain, but marriage bars persisted in many jobs, and domestic service remained a major employer in the 1920s.
Achievement: war work showed that women could do skilled and heavy jobs, increased their public presence and confidence, and helped win the vote in Britain and Germany.
Limit: most war jobs ended in 1918-19, women's pay remained below men's, and traditional views of women's roles returned. The vote was limited in Britain to women over 30.
Arthur Marwick (The Deluge, 1965) argued that war was a catalyst of social change, including the status of women.

Gail Braybon (Women Workers in the First World War, 1981) and others argued that change was limited and temporary and that the vote owed as much to pre-war campaigning and to political calculations as to war work.
Contemporary view: many people thought women's war work proved their worth as citizens; others, including many male workers, regarded it as a temporary emergency.
Differences between countries: war work and the vote were linked in Britain and Germany, whereas France's women gained neither political rights nor lasting economic ones until the 1940s.
Between 1871 and 1914 composers, writers, architects and painters presented national history, folk tradition and landscape as proof of a people's distinct identity.

Richard Wagner's operas drew on Germanic myth. His Ring cycle was first staged in full at his own theatre in Bayreuth in 1876, and the Bayreuth Festival continued after his death in 1883 as a shrine of German culture.

Germany's new national monuments expressed the Reich's identity: the Hermann Monument in the Teutoburg Forest (1875) honoured the Germanic leader who defeated the Romans, and the Monument to the Battle of the Nations at Leipzig was unveiled in 1913.

Bedřich Smetana's cycle of symphonic poems Má vlast (My Country, 1874-79), which includes The Moldau, celebrated Bohemian history and landscape at a time when the Czechs sought more autonomy within Austria-Hungary.
Jean Sibelius's Finlandia (1899-1900) became a symbol of Finnish resistance to Russian control, and Edvard Grieg used Norwegian folk music in Peer Gynt (1876).
Edward Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1 (1901) and the Coronation Ode (1902), with its 'Land of Hope and Glory', expressed British imperial confidence.

Rudyard Kipling celebrated British soldiers and the Empire in poems such as Recessional (1897) and The White Man's Burden (1899). His only son John was killed at Loos in 1915, and Kipling later wrote for the Imperial War Graves Commission.
Across Europe, governments and nationalist societies founded national museums, galleries and theatres, taught national history in schools and fostered national languages.
Writers' responses to the war moved from patriotic enthusiasm in 1914-15 to disillusionment and protest by 1917, and the post-war view of the war was shaped by the protest writers.

Rupert Brooke's 1914 sonnets, including The Soldier, expressed idealism about dying for England. Brooke died of blood poisoning on the way to Gallipoli on 23 April 1915 and was celebrated as a hero. Julian Grenfell and the Canadian John McCrae (In Flanders Fields, 1915) wrote in a similar spirit.

Siegfried Sassoon won the Military Cross, then in July 1917 published a statement condemning the prolongation of the war. Instead of a court martial, he was sent to Craiglockhart War Hospital in Edinburgh. His Counter-Attack (1918) used satire against generals and the home front.
Other soldier-poets included Isaac Rosenberg (killed in 1918), Edmund Blunden and Ivor Gurney. Robert Graves wrote the memoir Goodbye to All That (1929).
Henri Barbusse's novel Le Feu (Under Fire, 1916), which won the Prix Goncourt, described the lives of French infantry squad in the trenches and attacked the war's profiteers.
Ernst Jünger's Storm of Steel (1920) took the soldier's viewpoint of a German officer who found meaning in combat, and contrasts with later pacifist works.

Erich Maria Remarque's All Quiet on the Western Front (1929), a German bestseller, was a post-war novel that showed young soldiers ruined by war. Together with Graves and Vera Brittain's Testament of Youth (1933), it shaped later memory of the war.
Wartime censorship limited what could be published at the front, so the most critical works came out in 1918 or after.
Owen was a participant in the war who became its most famous poetic witness. Nearly all of his work was published after his death.
Wilfred Owen was born in Oswestry, Shropshire, on 18 March 1893, the eldest child of a railway official. He worked as a lay assistant to a vicar and as a teacher in France before the war.
He enlisted in the Artists Rifles in October 1915 and was commissioned in the Manchester Regiment in 1916. He fought on the Somme and in the Beaumont-Hamel area in January 1917.
After concussion and weeks in a shell-hole he was diagnosed with neurasthenia (shell shock) and sent to Craiglockhart War Hospital near Edinburgh in June 1917.
At Craiglockhart he met Siegfried Sassoon in August 1917. Sassoon read his drafts, advised him to write plainly and introduced him to literary circles, including Robert Graves.

Between autumn 1917 and 1918 he wrote or finished his best poems, including Dulce et Decorum Est (an attack on 'the old Lie' that it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country), Anthem for Doomed Youth, Strange Meeting, Futility and Exposure.
He used pararhyme (consonance in place of full rhyme) and graphic detail of gas, mud and death. He wrote in a draft preface that 'the poetry is in the pity'.

Owen returned to the front in 1918 and won the Military Cross for his actions near Joncourt in October. He was killed on 4 November 1918 in an attack on the Sambre-Oise canal, a week before the armistice, aged 25.
Only a few of his poems appeared in his lifetime. Sassoon and Edith Sitwell published a first edition in 1919-20, and Edmund Blunden produced a fuller edition in 1931.
Contemporaries: in the 1920s Owen was one of several war poets, and the public were drawn at first to Brooke. Interest grew after the 1930s as pacifist feeling spread.

Historians now regard Owen as the main English voice of the war's suffering. Some, such as Dominic Hibberd, have stressed his complex character. Others, like Jon Stallworthy, stressed his craft. Some critics note that the 'poets' war' view of 1914-18 was shaped by an educated officer class, and that most soldiers did not write such poetry.

The Reich was two-thirds Protestant, and about a third Catholic. After the First Vatican Council declared papal infallibility (1870), Bismarck feared that Catholics owed their loyalty to Rome and saw the Catholic Centre Party (founded 1870) as an enemy of the new state.

Bismarck also feared Polish Catholics in the east, and liberals welcomed an attack on the Church as a defence of modern secular society. The campaign was called Kulturkampf ('struggle for civilisation') by the liberal Rudolf Virchow.

In 1871 the pulpit law made it an offence for clergy to criticise the state in sermons, and the Catholic department of the Prussian ministry of culture was abolished. The Jesuits were expelled from Germany in 1872, and in March 1872 the School Supervision Law put schools under state inspection.
