The May Laws of 1873, piloted by the Prussian culture minister Adalbert Falk, required priests to study at state universities and pass state exams, and made state approval necessary for church appointments. Civil marriage became compulsory in 1875.

Pope Pius IX condemned the laws in 1875. Bishops were imprisoned or exiled, and by 1876 many parishes had no priest. Catholics resisted, and the Centre Party doubled its seats, becoming the second-largest party.

Bismarck turned to the Centre in 1878-79 for support for tariffs and against socialism. He opened talks with the new pope, Leo XIII (elected February 1878), and in 1880-83 and 1886-87 most laws were repealed or relaxed. The Jesuit ban lasted until 1917.
The Kulturkampf failed. It strengthened Catholic political unity, made the Centre Party a permanent force in the Reichstag, and showed the limits of Bismarck's power.
The Kingdom of Italy, created in 1861, took the Papal States, and on 20 September 1870 Italian troops entered Rome, completing unification. The Pope lost his temporal power.

The Law of Guarantees (May 1871) declared the Pope's person inviolable, gave him use of the Vatican and Lateran palaces and a yearly income. Pius IX rejected it and refused to recognise the Italian state, calling himself a prisoner in the Vatican.
This dispute was known as the Roman Question. The papacy's refusal to accept the loss of Rome divided Italians between the liberal, anticlerical state and the Catholic population.

The non expedit instruction (1868, reinforced in 1874) forbade Catholics from voting in or standing for parliamentary elections, so that most Catholics stayed out of national politics, while Catholics played an active role in local government and social action.
The state expanded civil marriage, secular education and the closure of religious orders, while Catholics built their own organisations: Catholic Action, banks, newspapers and cooperatives.

The ban was relaxed gradually; in the 1913 Gentiloni Pact Catholic voters supported Giolitti's liberal candidates, and in 1919 Don Luigi Sturzo founded the Catholic Popular Party. The Roman Question was only settled in the Lateran Treaties of 1929.
Leo XIII, pope from 1878 to 1903, tried to renew the church's relations with the modern world after the confrontational reign of Pius IX.
Vincenzo Gioacchino Pecci was born on 2 March 1810 and elected pope on 20 February 1878. He had been Archbishop of Perugia and a cardinal, and was a diplomat and scholar.
He ended the Kulturkampf by negotiation with Bismarck in the 1880s, and the Centre Party's cooperation with the government helped to repeal most of the laws.

In Rerum Novarum (15 May 1891) he addressed the 'condition of the working classes'. He defended private property and rejected socialism and class war, but upheld the right of workers to a just wage, decent conditions and to form trade unions, and called on states to protect the poor.
Rerum Novarum became the foundation of modern Catholic social teaching and encouraged Catholic trade unions and Christian democratic parties in Germany, Belgium, Italy and elsewhere.

His ralliement policy of 1890-92 urged French Catholics to accept the Third Republic and work within it. Monarchist Catholics largely refused, and the Dreyfus Affair and the anticlerical laws of the early 1900s, ending in the 1905 separation of church and state, undercut the policy.
He encouraged the study of Thomas Aquinas (Aeterni Patris, 1879) and opened the Vatican archives to scholars in 1883. In 1888 the Vatican condemned the Plan of Campaign and boycotting in Ireland.
He refused to accept the loss of the Papal States and kept the 'prisoner in the Vatican' stance, so the Roman Question remained open.

Contemporaries: liberals and many workers respected him as a thoughtful reformer, while conservative Catholics distrusted his accommodation with republics and the modern world. He died on 20 July 1903.
Historians: he is regarded as a pioneer of the modern papacy and of Catholic social thought, though critics argue that Rerum Novarum was cautious and that the ralliement failed in France.
Anti-Jewish prejudice was old in Europe, but after 1870 racial and political anti-Semitism spread. The word anti-Semitism was coined by Wilhelm Marr in Germany in 1879.

Economic anxiety, nationalism and the humiliation of 1871 in France led nationalists to blame Jews and Freemasons for the country's weakness. Édouard Drumont's La France juive (1886) was a bestseller portraying Jews as a threat to France, and in 1892 he founded the paper La Libre Parole.

In October 1894 Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish artillery officer from Alsace, was arrested and accused of passing secrets to Germany, convicted by a secret court martial in December 1894 and sent to Devil's Island in French Guiana.

In 1896 Colonel Picquart, head of army intelligence, found that the real author of the leaked memorandum (the bordereau) was Major Esterhazy. The army suppressed this and Esterhazy was acquitted in January 1898; a forgery by Colonel Henry was later exposed.
On 13 January 1898, Émile Zola published the open letter 'J'accuse' in the newspaper L'Aurore, accusing the army of covering up the truth. Zola was convicted of libel and fled to England.
France divided into Dreyfusards (republicans, socialists such as Jaurès, many intellectuals) and anti-Dreyfusards (the army, much of the Catholic Church, nationalists and monarchists).

A second court martial at Rennes in 1899 found Dreyfus guilty again, with 'extenuating circumstances'; President Loubet pardoned him. In 1906 the court of appeals cleared him and he was reinstated in the army.

The Affair weakened the army and the Church's reputation and led to the anticlerical measures of the early 1900s. It also influenced Theodor Herzl, who covered the case as a journalist and published Der Judenstaat (1896); the First Zionist Congress met at Basel in 1897.

About five million Jews lived in the Russian Empire in the late 1800s, the world's largest Jewish community. Most were confined to the Pale of Settlement, set up in 1791, and many were poor artisans and traders.

After Alexander II was assassinated in March 1881, rumours blamed Jews and pogroms (violent attacks) swept southern Russia, starting at Elizavetgrad in April 1881. Police and troops were slow to intervene.

The May Laws (Temporary Rules) of 1882 banned Jews from settling in rural areas of the Pale and from owning land. Quotas limited Jewish places in schools and universities from 1887, and Jews were expelled from Moscow in 1891-92.

Government officials such as Pobedonostsev, adviser to Alexander III and Nicholas II, supported discrimination and Russification, and the Orthodox Church and the Black Hundreds nationalist groups spread anti-Semitic propaganda.
The Kishinev pogrom (6-7 April 1903) killed 49 Jews and injured hundreds, and caused international outrage. More pogroms followed in 1905-06 during the revolution.

The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, which claimed a Jewish plot to dominate the world, was first published in Russia in 1903 and was later shown to be a forgery drawing on earlier fiction. It spread widely after 1917.

Between 1881 and 1914 about two million Jews emigrated from the Russian Empire, most to the USA, and others to Britain and Palestine. Many Jews also joined socialist movements such as the Bund (1897) and Zionism.

Cultural nationalism gave peoples without a state, such as the Czechs and Finns, a means of asserting their identity, but in Germany, Britain and Russia it also supported imperial and exclusive nationalism.

War literature: contemporaries read Brooke's patriotism in 1914-15 and the protest poets only after 1918; later readers see Owen and Sassoon as the war's authentic voices, but historians remind us that many soldiers still saw the war as justified.
Kulturkampf: a success in asserting state power over schools and marriage, but a political failure that strengthened Catholic unity and left Bismarck dependent on the Centre.
Italy: the Roman Question showed the limits of a liberal state's authority in a Catholic country, and kept Catholics out of national politics for decades.
Leo XIII: achievements in ending the Kulturkampf and in social teaching, but limits in the failure of the ralliement and the rejection of unification.

Anti-Semitism: the Dreyfus Affair ended in justice for one man and a republican victory, but the prejudice remained strong; in Russia state policy encouraged it, and the pogroms drove mass emigration.

Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who worked in France. Her research on radioactivity made her one of the most important scientists of the period and the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

Maria Skłodowska was born in Warsaw on 7 November 1867, when Poland was under Russian rule. Women could not attend university there, so in 1891 she went to study physics and mathematics at the Sorbonne in Paris.

In 1895 she married the physicist Pierre Curie. After Henri Becquerel found in 1896 that uranium gave off penetrating rays, she began research on them for her doctorate and coined the term 'radioactivity'.

She found that the mineral pitchblende was more radioactive than the uranium it contained and concluded that it must hold new elements. In July 1898 the Curies announced polonium, named after her homeland, and in December 1898 radium.
They processed tonnes of pitchblende in a shed to separate radium salt, which she achieved by 1902. Pure radium metal was isolated with André Debierne in 1910.
Marie Curie shared the 1903 Nobel Prize for Physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel for the study of radioactivity, becoming the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.
Pierre was killed in a street accident in Paris in April 1906. Marie took over his post and became the first woman professor at the Sorbonne.
She won the 1911 Nobel Prize for Chemistry for the discovery of polonium and radium. She is the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
In 1911 the French Academy of Sciences rejected her membership by a narrow vote, and the press attacked her over a relationship with the physicist Paul Langevin, partly on xenophobic grounds.

During the First World War she organised mobile X-ray units, known as 'petites Curies', for field hospitals and trained women to run them, with her daughter Irène. She also set up fixed radiological posts.
She founded the Radium Institute in Paris (opened 1914) and died on 4 July 1934 of aplastic anaemia, probably caused by long exposure to radiation. Her notebooks are still radioactive.

Contemporaries admired her as an exceptional scientist, though some were hostile to a foreign woman in a leading scientific position. Historians regard her as a founder of the study of radioactivity and a pioneer for women in science.
The discovery that microbes cause disease transformed medicine and surgery between 1870 and 1920.
Louis Pasteur showed in the 1860s that microbes cause fermentation and decay, and argued that they cause disease. Pasteurisation (heating liquids to kill microbes) was developed from this work.

He developed vaccines using weakened microbes against chicken cholera (about 1879), anthrax (1881) and rabies. In July 1885 he treated a nine-year-old boy, Joseph Meister, who had been bitten by a rabid dog, and the boy survived.
The Pasteur Institute was founded in Paris in 1887-88 to continue research and make vaccines.

Robert Koch in Germany developed methods to isolate bacteria in pure culture. He identified the anthrax bacterium (1876), the tuberculosis bacillus (announced on 24 March 1882) and the cholera bacterium (1883), and won the Nobel Prize for Medicine in 1905.
Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburo developed antitoxins against diphtheria and tetanus in 1890, and Behring received the first Nobel Prize for Medicine in 1901.
Paul Ehrlich developed Salvarsan, the first effective drug against syphilis, in 1909. It was the first modern chemotherapy.
Joseph Lister, a Scottish surgeon, used carbolic acid to clean wounds and instruments and spray the operating theatre from 1865-67. This antiseptic surgery cut deaths from infection.

Anaesthetics, ether (1846) and chloroform (1847, used by Queen Victoria in 1853), had made longer operations possible, and with asepsis (sterile conditions, developed in Germany in the 1880s-90s) surgery became much safer.
Public health measures such as clean water supplies and sewers, built from the 1850s, as well as better food and housing, did much to cut deaths from cholera and typhoid in European cities.
Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in Würzburg in November 1895. Doctors quickly used them to find broken bones and bullets, and he won the first Nobel Prize for Physics in 1901.
In the First World War X-ray equipment became standard in military hospitals, and Curie's mobile units brought it close to the front.
Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone in 1876, and telephone exchanges and networks spread rapidly in cities in the 1880s and 1890s.

Thomas Edison invented the phonograph in 1877 and developed a long-lasting electric light bulb in 1879. The first power stations followed in the 1880s, and electric lighting, trams and underground railways spread in cities.

Guglielmo Marconi, who had an Irish mother, Annie Jameson, sent wireless signals over longer distances from 1895-96. In December 1901 he claimed to receive a signal across the Atlantic in Newfoundland, sent from Poldhu in Cornwall. He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize for Physics.
Wireless became important at sea: it was used to call for help when the Titanic sank in April 1912, and it was used in military communication in the First World War.
The Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901 under the will of the Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel, who invented dynamite, and several early winners were German or French scientists.
Count Zeppelin built rigid airships from 1900, and the Wright brothers made the first controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air machine at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903.
Louis Blériot flew across the English Channel on 25 July 1909. Aviation meetings and prizes attracted publicity across Europe.
In the First World War aircraft were used for reconnaissance, artillery spotting, bombing and air combat. Production rose from hundreds to tens of thousands, and engines improved greatly.
John Alcock and Arthur Whitten Brown made the first non-stop transatlantic flight in June 1919, from Newfoundland to a bog near Clifden in Co. Galway.
Rudolf Diesel patented the diesel engine in 1892, and Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed the synthesis of ammonia (1909-13), which made artificial fertilisers and explosives possible.
Albert Einstein published the special theory of relativity in 1905 and the general theory in 1915.

The motor car emerged in Germany and France in the 1880s from the internal combustion engine, and from the bicycle and carriage industries. Steam and electric vehicles had been tried, but petrol won out.
Nikolaus Otto built the first practical four-stroke internal combustion engine in 1876, burning gas. It became the basis of the petrol engine.

Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach, who had worked for Otto's company, developed a small, light, high-speed petrol engine in the 1880s. In 1885 they fitted it to a wooden motorcycle, and in 1886 to a carriage.

Karl Benz founded Benz and Cie in Mannheim in 1883 and built a three-wheeled vehicle with a single-cylinder engine, running in 1885. He applied for a patent for his 'Motorwagen' on 29 January 1886, and it was granted in November 1886. It is regarded as the first practical car designed as a whole.
Benz and Daimler worked independently and never met. Their firms merged in 1926 to form Daimler-Benz.

Bertha Benz, with her sons Eugen and Richard, drove a Motorwagen from Mannheim to Pforzheim, about 106 km, in August 1888, without telling her husband. She bought fuel (ligroin) at a pharmacy in Wiesloch and made repairs on the way. The journey proved the car's usefulness and publicity helped sales.

In France, Panhard et Levassor and Peugeot began building cars in 1890-91 using Daimler engines. France led early car production, with races such as Paris-Rouen (1894) boosting interest. Louis Renault built his first car in 1898 and the Renault company followed in 1899.

John Boyd Dunlop, a Scottish veterinary surgeon in Belfast, patented the pneumatic tyre in 1888 for his son's tricycle. Dunlop tyres helped bicycles and cars run more smoothly, and the Michelin brothers brought out a detachable pneumatic tyre in 1891.

In Britain the 'red flag' law limited early vehicles to walking pace until 1896. The Locomotives on Highways Act of 1896 raised the limit to 12 mph and was celebrated by the Emancipation Run from London to Brighton in November 1896.

Daimler died in 1900. In 1901 the Daimler company produced the Mercedes, named after the daughter of the businessman Emil Jellinek, a car with a lighter engine and a lower body that set the pattern for later cars.
Charles Rolls and Henry Royce met in 1904, and the Rolls-Royce Silver Ghost (1906) made Britain a leader in luxury cars.
Early cars were handmade luxury goods for the rich. Henry Ford founded the Ford Motor Company in 1903 in Detroit with the aim of building a cheap car for ordinary people.
The Model T, launched in October 1908, was simple, strong and easy to repair. The price fell from about 850 dollars to under 300 dollars by the early 1920s as output rose.

In 1913 Ford introduced the moving assembly line at Highland Park, Michigan, in which the chassis moved past workers who each did one task. The time to build a chassis fell from over twelve hours to about ninety minutes.
Repetitive work caused high turnover. In January 1914 Ford announced a wage of five dollars for an eight-hour day, about double the usual pay, which kept workers and made them potential customers.
By 1920 the USA had millions of cars and produced most of the world's cars. Ford's mass production methods, later called Fordism, were studied and copied by European firms.
In Ireland the Gordon Bennett motor race was held in Co. Kildare and Carlow in July 1903, and the Motor Car Act 1903 introduced registration and a speed limit of 20 mph in Britain and Ireland.
The car industry drove demand for steel, rubber, glass, petrol and machine tools, and created work in manufacturing, garages and repair. Oil companies and tyre firms expanded.
Roads were improved and tarred for motor traffic, and governments passed traffic laws, licences and speed limits. Early motorists faced hostility from pedestrians, farmers and cyclists.
Cars were first status symbols for the rich. Motoring clubs and early tourism grew, and doctors, salesmen and country priests used cars before 1914.

In the First World War, motor lorries, cars and ambulances were vital. About 600 Paris taxis carried troops to the Marne battle in September 1914, and motor lorries supplied Verdun along the 'Sacred Way' in 1916.
War made engines and lorries more powerful, and the war also gave rise to the tank and armoured car, as well as aircraft engines.
After the war ex-army lorries and cheap cars allowed bus services and road haulage to compete with the railways in the 1920s.
Cars were still too expensive for most Europeans by 1920, and they were much less common than in the USA, where the Model T made them part of everyday life.
Achievement: germ theory, antiseptics and vaccines saved millions of lives, and new medical technologies such as the X-ray changed diagnosis.
Limit: knowledge of radiation danger came too late for many pioneers, including Curie, and the benefits of medicine reached the poor only slowly.
Achievement: electricity, the telephone and wireless changed communication, and the car and aeroplane transformed transport.
Limit: these technologies also served war. Aircraft, motor vehicles, chemistry and wireless were used in the First World War, producing deadlier weapons.
The car's early history: Germany and France invented it, but the USA, through the Model T and mass production, made it a mass consumer product.

Contemporary view: people saw science as progress and as a source of national prestige, as in Curie's French and Polish recognition. Later historians stress that the social effects of the car came mostly after 1920.
Fascism grew where parliamentary government seemed weak and where war, economic crisis and fear of revolution had left people frightened and angry.
Italy's war effort cost heavy casualties and debt, and the peace settlement gave Italy less than the Treaty of London (1915) had promised, feeding the sense of a 'mutilated victory'.

Italy had five prime ministers between 1919 and 1922 (Orlando, Nitti, Giolitti, Bonomi and Facta), and proportional representation, introduced in 1919, produced weak coalitions dependent on the Socialists and the Catholic Popolari.
The Biennio Rosso (1919-1920) brought strikes, peasant land seizures and factory occupations in the north, leading landowners, industrialists and the middle classes to fear a socialist revolution.
Inflation, unemployment and food shortages added to the anger of ex-servicemen, who believed the state had failed to reward them.
Fascism drew support from ex-servicemen, the lower middle class, large landowners in the Po valley and industrialists who wanted an end to strikes and socialist organisation.

The poet Gabriele D'Annunzio's seizure of Fiume with volunteers (September 1919 to December 1920) showed the weakness of the state and gave Fascism its style: black shirts, balcony speeches, the Roman salute and mass ritual.

Characteristics of fascism: extreme nationalism that places the nation above the individual, with power concentrated in one leader who embodies the nation (the leader principle) and is promoted by a personality cult.
A single party and a totalitarian state: Mussolini's own formula, from a 1925 speech, was 'everything within the state, nothing outside the state, nothing against the state'.
Fascists were hostile to communism, socialism and liberal democracy, which they blamed for class conflict and national weakness.

Fascism glorified violence, war and youth through uniformed squads and mass rallies, and promised corporatism, in which employers and workers would co-operate in state-controlled corporations instead of class conflict.

Comparison only: other interwar authoritarian regimes included Horthy's Hungary (1920), Primo de Rivera's Spain (1923-30), Piłsudski's Poland (1926), Salazar's Portugal (1932) and Metaxas's Greece (1936); most were conservative military or clerical dictatorships rather than mass fascist movements.
The Fascist movement gained power through organised violence against its opponents, often tolerated by local police and army commanders.
Benito Mussolini, a former editor of the socialist newspaper Avanti!, founded the Fasci di Combattimento in Milan in March 1919 with a programme that mixed radical and nationalist ideas.
The squadristi were armed squads, often led by ex-servicemen, who attacked socialist offices, trade union halls and Catholic People's Party premises, especially in the Po valley and Tuscany.
Fascist candidates won 35 seats in the May 1921 election, when Mussolini himself was elected, and Mussolini founded the National Fascist Party (PNF) that November.
Mussolini signed a Pacification Pact with socialist leaders in August 1921 to end the violence, but local squads ignored it and the pact collapsed.
Liberal leader Giovanni Giolitti included Fascists in his 1921 electoral bloc, underestimating their strength and believing he could control them.
The squads' violence was directed against the organisations that had led the 1919-1920 unrest, so Fascism presented itself as the defender of order against socialism.
By 1922 the Fascists had taken control of many local councils in northern and central Italy, giving them local bases of power independent of Rome.
The March on Rome was a show of force that persuaded the King to hand power to Mussolini rather than declare a state of siege.

Between 27 and 30 October 1922, about 30,000 Fascist squads converged on Rome under four leaders, the quadrumvirs (Balbo, De Bono, De Vecchi and Bianchi), while Mussolini waited in Milan; Prime Minister Luigi Facta asked for a state of siege.

King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign the state of siege decree, fearing civil war and doubting the army's loyalty; he invited Mussolini to form a government on 29 October and Mussolini took office on 30 October 1922.

Mussolini's first government was a coalition in which Fascists held only a minority of posts alongside Liberals, Popolari and nationalists, and parliament granted it emergency powers for a year in November 1922.
The Acerbo Law of 1923 gave two-thirds of the seats in the Chamber of Deputies to any list winning at least 25 per cent of the vote.
In the April 1924 election the Fascist-led national list won about 65 per cent of the vote, in a campaign marked by intimidation and violence against opponents.

The Fascist Grand Council (December 1922) became the party's governing body and the Fascist militia (MVSN, January 1923) turned the squads into a state-paid force loyal to Mussolini rather than the King.
The murder of a socialist deputy in 1924 threatened Mussolini's government and was followed by the removal of parliamentary and press freedom.
On 30 May 1924 Giacomo Matteotti, a Socialist deputy, denounced electoral fraud and violence in the Chamber of Deputies.
Matteotti was abducted in Rome on 10 June 1924 by men connected to the Fascist squads and was murdered; his body was found in August.
Opposition deputies walked out of the Chamber in what became known as the Aventine Secession, hoping the King would dismiss Mussolini; the King did not act.
On 3 January 1925 Mussolini told the Chamber that he accepted political responsibility for the violence, which marked the start of his open dictatorship.
Between 1925 and 1926 the government banned opposition parties, censored the press, and replaced elected mayors with appointed podesta.

The Leggi Fascistissime of 1925-26 made Mussolini responsible only to the King, let him rule by decree, set up a Special Tribunal for the Defence of the State (1926) and created the OVRA secret police; political prisoners were sent to internal exile (confino) on islands such as Lipari.
Violet Gibson, an Englishwoman, shot Mussolini in Rome on 7 April 1926 and wounded his nose; the attack was used to justify further repression.
A 1928 electoral law let the Grand Council draw up a single list of 400 candidates for voters to accept or reject, and the 1929 plebiscite approved it with about 98 per cent voting yes.
Mussolini aimed to bring the economy under state direction through fascist unions and corporations, but the system remained more theory than practice.
The Rocco Law of 1926 allowed only state-recognised syndicates to represent workers and employers, and it banned strikes and lockouts.
The Charter of Labour of 1927 set out the principles of the corporate system, in which employers and workers would be organised together under the state.
Corporations covering the main economic sectors were set up in 1934, and in 1939 the Chamber of Deputies was replaced by the Chamber of Fasces and Corporations.
The Battle for Grain (from 1925) aimed at self-sufficiency in wheat by raising tariffs and expanding cereal production on poor land.
The Battle for Births, promoted from about 1927, offered rewards for large families and penalised celibacy through taxation.
The Pontine Marshes south of Rome were drained and resettled in the 1930s, a project presented as a triumph of the regime.

Quota 90, announced in Mussolini's Pesaro speech of August 1926 and reached in 1927, revalued the lira to 90 to the pound sterling for national prestige; it made exports dearer, deflated the economy and cut wages.
After the 1929 crash the state rescued banks and industry through the Institute for Industrial Reconstruction (IRI, 1933) which left the state owning a large share of banking, shipbuilding and steel.
The regime used mass organisations, the press and film to create consent and an image of Mussolini as the embodiment of the nation.
The Opera Nazionale Balilla (1926) brought boys and girls into a state youth organisation, which was reorganised as the Gioventu Italiana del Littorio in 1937.
The Dopolavoro (after-work) organisation from 1925 provided sport, excursions and leisure for workers under fascist supervision.
The Istituto Luce, founded in 1924, produced newsreels and documentary films that showed Mussolini at work, at rallies and at public works.
The Ministry of Popular Culture, known as Minculpop, was set up in 1937 to control the press, radio, cinema and theatre.

Mussolini's image as Il Duce was promoted through posters, photographs of him harvesting grain or bare-chested, balcony speeches from the Palazzo Venezia in Rome, and slogans painted on walls such as 'Mussolini is always right' and 'Believe, obey, fight'.
The regime used the Catholic Church and public ritual to build legitimacy, although the Church kept its own youth and press organisations.
Elementary schools used a single state textbook from 1929, and university professors had to swear an oath of loyalty to the regime in 1931; only about 12 of some 1,200 refused.
Mussolini used foreign adventures to build prestige, and his ambitions led Italy into alliance with Germany and into the Second World War.

The Corfu incident of August 1923 began when General Enrico Tellini and members of an Italian boundary commission were murdered on the Greek-Albanian border; Italy bombarded and occupied Corfu until Greece paid compensation.
Italy annexed the port of Fiume in 1924 under a treaty with Yugoslavia, ending a long dispute left over from the peace settlement.
Italy invaded Abyssinia (Ethiopia) on 3 October 1935; the League of Nations imposed sanctions, but they did not stop the invasion or cut off oil supplies.
The Hoare-Laval Plan of December 1935, which would have given Italy much of Abyssinia, was abandoned after public protest in Britain and France.
Addis Ababa was captured on 5 May 1936, and Victor Emmanuel III was declared Emperor of Ethiopia.

Italy and Germany drew together after German support during the Abyssinian war and their joint intervention for Franco in Spain (1936-39); Mussolini announced the Rome-Berlin Axis in a Milan speech on 1 November 1936, joined the Anti-Comintern Pact in 1937 and accepted the Anschluss in 1938.

Mussolini posed as a peacemaker at the Munich Conference (September 1938), invaded Albania in April 1939 and signed the Pact of Steel with Germany on 22 May 1939, but declared Italy non-belligerent when war began in September 1939.
Italy declared war on Britain and France on 10 June 1940, when France was already beaten, but suffered defeats in Greece (from October 1940) and North Africa that made it dependent on German help.
Military defeats and an Allied invasion of Sicily brought the regime down in 1943, but Mussolini's rule in northern Italy continued under German control until 1945.
Allied forces landed in Sicily on 10 July 1943, and at a meeting on 24-25 July the Fascist Grand Council passed Dino Grandi's motion to return command of the armed forces to the King.
King Victor Emmanuel III dismissed Mussolini on 25 July 1943 and had him arrested; Marshal Pietro Badoglio formed a new government.
Italy's armistice with the Allies was announced on 8 September 1943, and German forces took control of much of the north and centre.
German paratroopers and SS commandos, among them Otto Skorzeny, rescued Mussolini from a mountain hotel at Gran Sasso on 12 September 1943.

Mussolini headed the Italian Social Republic, known as the Salò Republic after its seat on Lake Garda, a German puppet state that executed his son-in-law Ciano and other Grand Council members at Verona in January 1944.
Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci were shot by partisans near Lake Como on 28 April 1945, and their bodies were displayed in Piazzale Loreto in Milan.
Mussolini led Italy from 1922 to 1943 and was the founder and leader of the Fascist movement.
Born in 1883 at Predappio in the Romagna region, he trained as a teacher, became a socialist journalist, and edited Avanti! from 1912.
He was expelled from the Socialist Party in 1914 for supporting Italian entry into the First World War, and he served in the army and was wounded in 1917.
As founder of the Fasci di Combattimento (1919) and the National Fascist Party (1921), he led the movement that took power in 1922 and ruled as dictator from 1925.

He was a participant who shaped events: he organised the March on Rome from Milan, took personal responsibility for the violence in January 1925 and made the key decisions on Abyssinia, the Axis and entry into the war.

Contemporaries were divided: many conservatives, the Vatican and foreign statesmen admired his suppression of socialism (Churchill praised him on a visit to Rome in 1927), while Socialists, Popolari and liberals such as Giovanni Amendola, who died after a Fascist beating in 1926, denounced his violence.

Historians differ: Renzo De Felice argued that the regime enjoyed real popular consent in the years 1929-1936, while Denis Mack Smith portrayed Mussolini as an opportunist and propagandist more concerned with image than with real achievement.

Many historians now see Italian Fascism as an incomplete totalitarianism, since the King, the Church, the army and big business kept independent power, which is why the King was able to dismiss him in 1943.
Judgements of the regime turn on whether its stability and public works are weighed against its violence, economic failures and disastrous war.
Achievement: Mussolini ended parliamentary rule and established a one-party state by 1926 with little open resistance for most of the 1920s.
Limit: the corporate state existed largely on paper, as employers kept control of production and the corporations had little real power.
Achievement: the Lateran Treaties of 1929 settled the Roman Question, and the Pontine Marshes scheme, the autostrade motorways and rail electrification gave the regime visible successes.
Limit: the Battle for Grain did not make Italy self-sufficient in food, and the deflationary policy of Quota 90 damaged industry and jobs.
Achievement: Italy gained territory in Abyssinia and Fiume, which the regime presented as the fulfilment of national destiny.
Limit: the Abyssinian war was costly, the alliance with Germany drew Italy into a war it was ill-prepared to fight, and the regime collapsed in 1943 after defeats in North Africa and Sicily.

Contemporary view: many Italians and foreign conservatives saw Mussolini as the saviour of order who had defeated Bolshevism; later view: his regime is judged by its violence, its alliance with Hitler, the 1938 racial laws and the defeat it brought on Italy.
The Weimar Republic was founded in 1919 after the German Revolution and the end of the Kaiser's rule, and its constitution contained features that could be used to undermine it.

The National Assembly met at Weimar, away from the unrest in Berlin, and adopted a constitution on 31 July 1919 creating a federal republic with a President elected by the people for seven years and a Chancellor responsible to the Reichstag.
Proportional representation for the Reichstag produced many small parties and made stable majority government very difficult to form.
Article 48 allowed the President to issue emergency decrees and to rule without the Reichstag, a power that became central after 1930.

Many judges, civil servants, army officers and university teachers from the imperial era stayed in post and remained hostile to the republic, and the 'stab in the back' myth blamed the November 1918 politicians, not the army, for defeat.
Friedrich Ebert was the first President, from 1919 until his death in 1925; Paul von Hindenburg, a former field marshal, succeeded him in 1925.
The Treaty of Versailles of June 1919 imposed territorial losses, military limits and reparations, and Article 231 placed war guilt on Germany.
The London Schedule of 1921 set Germany's reparations at 132 billion gold marks, a sum that many Germans regarded as impossible and humiliating.
The republic faced armed challenges from left and right in its first years, and its judges and army officers were often sympathetic to the right.
The Spartacist rising of January 1919 and the murders of Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg were put down with the help of Freikorps units.

The Kapp Putsch of March 1920, led by Wolfgang Kapp with the Ehrhardt Freikorps brigade, seized Berlin while the army refused to defend the government; it collapsed after four days when trade unions called a general strike.
Political murders by the far right, including the killing of Matthias Erzberger in 1921 and of Walther Rathenau in June 1922, showed the weakness of the state's protection of its leaders.
The judiciary favoured the right: the statistician Emil Gumbel counted 354 political murders by the right and 22 by the left between 1919 and 1922, with far heavier sentences for left-wing killers.
Germany fell behind on reparations deliveries of timber and coal, and in January 1923 France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr, the main industrial region, to take coal and goods.
The German government under Chancellor Wilhelm Cuno called for passive resistance in the Ruhr, which the government funded by printing money.
The printing of money to pay for passive resistance caused hyperinflation in 1923, which wiped out savings and deepened distrust of the republic.

By November 1923 one US dollar was worth about 4.2 trillion marks, prices rose by the hour, workers were paid daily or twice daily and rushed to spend their wages, and barter replaced money in many places.
Middle-class savings, pensions and war loans were largely wiped out, leaving many people who had supported the old order resentful of the republic.
Debtors, speculators and large industrialists such as Hugo Stinnes, who borrowed to buy assets, gained from the inflation, while people on fixed incomes and savers lost most.
Gustav Stresemann became Chancellor in August 1923 and called off passive resistance in the Ruhr in September.

The Rentenmark, introduced on 15 November 1923 and backed by a mortgage on land and industry, ended the hyperinflation; Hjalmar Schacht, as currency commissioner and then Reichsbank president, kept its supply tightly limited, and it was replaced by the Reichsmark in 1924.

The Dawes Plan of 1924, drawn up by a committee chaired by the American Charles Dawes, set reparations payments that rose with Germany's capacity to pay, provided a loan of 800 million gold marks, and led the French to leave the Ruhr by 1925.
The Dawes Plan's loans made the German recovery of 1924 to 1929 dependent on American money, which was withdrawn when the Wall Street Crash began in October 1929.
Hitler's attempt to seize power in Bavaria in 1923 failed, but it gave him national publicity and a platform for his ideas.

Hitler joined the small German Workers' Party in Munich in September 1919; it was renamed the National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP) in February 1920 with a 25-point programme, and Hitler became its leader with dictatorial powers in July 1921.
The Nazi party's early support came from Bavarian ex-soldiers, anti-communist groups and the Sturmabteilung (SA), a paramilitary force founded in 1921.

On 8 to 9 November 1923 Hitler and Erich Ludendorff tried to seize power in Munich, starting in the Bürgerbräukeller beer hall, as a first step to a march on Berlin; Bavarian police fired on the marchers, killing sixteen Nazis, and four police officers died.

Hitler was tried for high treason in early 1924 and used the trial as a national platform; the sympathetic court gave him the minimum sentence of five years, and he served only about nine months at Landsberg prison.
He wrote Mein Kampf in prison, setting out his views on race, Lebensraum and the need to destroy Marxism and the Jews; the first volume was published in 1925.

The party had been banned after the putsch; Hitler refounded it in February 1925 and adopted a strategy of winning power legally through elections, but in the prosperous year of 1928 it won only 12 seats and 2.6 per cent of the vote.
Hitler's prominence in the 1929 campaign against the Young Plan, alongside Alfred Hugenberg's nationalist DNVP and its newspapers, gave the Nazis national publicity and respectability on the right.
Stresemann's foreign and economic policies brought Germany a period of relative prosperity and international acceptance, which many historians see as the republic's best years.
As Foreign Minister from 1923 to 1929, Stresemann pursued the revision of Versailles through negotiation rather than force.
The Locarno Treaties of October 1925 confirmed the western borders of Germany and led to Germany's entry into the League of Nations in 1926.
Stresemann shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926 with the French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand.
The Young Plan of 1929, chaired by the American Owen D. Young, reduced the total of reparations and spread payments to 1988.

Weimar governments built a welfare state: the eight-hour day (1918), large state-funded housing programmes in the later 1920s, and the 1927 Act creating national unemployment insurance, which was funded for far fewer claimants than the Depression produced and broke down after 1929.
Stresemann died in October 1929, and his successors could not secure the political support needed to continue his policies.
The Wall Street Crash and the Depression ended the economic recovery and brought the end of coalition government.
Unemployment in Germany rose from an annual average of about 1.9 million in 1929 to about 6 million registered unemployed by early 1932 as American loans were called in and exports fell.
The coalition of Social Democrats, Centre and liberal parties broke down in March 1930 over unemployment insurance contributions and the budget.
Heinrich Brüning, the new Chancellor from March 1930, governed through Article 48 emergency decrees, cutting wages, pensions and welfare to balance the budget.
Deflationary policies raised unemployment and gave the impression that the government was making the crisis worse, weakening support for the republic.
The banking crisis of July 1931, after the collapse of the Austrian Creditanstalt in May and of the Danat Bank in Germany, deepened the slump.

Brüning hoped deflation would prove that Germany could not pay reparations; Hoover's moratorium suspended them in 1931 and the Lausanne Conference of 1932, under his successor, effectively ended them.
Middle-class and farming groups, badly hit by falling prices, turned to parties that promised radical solutions.
The Nazi party's rapid electoral growth came from its appeal to unemployed people, farmers, small business owners and Protestant voters, especially in rural areas.

In the September 1930 Reichstag election the NSDAP won 107 seats and 18.3 per cent of the vote, up from 12 seats in 1928, becoming the second largest party after the SPD; the Communists also gained, winning 77 seats.
The Nazi party's propaganda combined attacks on the Versailles settlement, the Weimar parties and communism with promises of jobs, bread and national revival.

Goebbels, Gauleiter of Berlin from 1926, ran the party's propaganda with mass rallies, posters, newspapers such as Der Angriff and film, and in 1932 Hitler toured the country by aeroplane, speaking at several rallies a day.
The SA's street violence against communists and Social Democrats gave the party a reputation for strength and drew unemployed young men into its ranks.

In the July 1932 election the NSDAP won 230 seats and about 37 per cent of the vote, making it the largest party in the Reichstag, but Hitler refused any post below Chancellor and Hindenburg refused to appoint him in August.

Nazi voters were disproportionately Protestant, rural and small-town, middle-class (shopkeepers, farmers, white-collar workers, civil servants and pensioners) and young; Catholic areas loyal to the Centre Party and industrial workers loyal to the SPD and KPD were less receptive, though the Nazis did win many working-class votes.

Hitler became a German citizen in February 1932 so that he could stand for President; in March he won about 30 per cent to Hindenburg's 49.6 per cent, and in the run-off on 10 April Hindenburg won about 53 per cent to Hitler's 37 per cent.

Brüning banned the SA and SS in April 1932, but Hindenburg dismissed him in May, and Franz von Papen's government lifted the ban in June, leading to street battles such as the Altona 'Bloody Sunday' of July 1932.
Papen's government removed the Social Democrat government of Prussia in July 1932, in what became known as the Prussian coup.
In the November 1932 election the NSDAP lost about two million votes and 34 seats, falling to 196 seats and 33 per cent, although it remained the largest party; the party was also short of money.

Kurt von Schleicher became Chancellor on 3 December 1932 and tried to split the Nazis by offering the Vice-Chancellorship to Gregor Strasser and to win trade union support with job-creation schemes, but failed to build a majority and resigned on 28 January 1933.

Papen, after meeting Hitler at the banker Kurt von Schröder's house in Cologne on 4 January 1933, persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933 in a cabinet with only three Nazis (Hitler, Frick and Göring), believing that conservatives such as Papen as Vice-Chancellor and Hugenberg could control him.
This entry covers Hitler's route to the Chancellorship. His rule from 1933 is in the notes on the Nazi state in peace.
Born in 1889 at Braunau am Inn on the Austrian side of the border, he served in the German army in the First World War and was awarded the Iron Cross.
He joined the German Workers' Party in September 1919 while working as a political informant for the army in Munich, and became its most effective speaker.
As leader of the NSDAP from 1921, he used rallies, a private army and personal charisma to make the party the main vehicle of the far right.
He was a participant who learned from failure: after the Munich Putsch he chose the legal road to power through elections, while using the SA's street violence to show strength.

Contemporaries were divided: millions of voters saw him as a national saviour, the left saw him as a tool of big business, and conservatives such as Papen saw a demagogue whom they believed they had hired and could control.

Historians agree that he was appointed legally, but differ on why: Alan Bullock, in Hitler: A Study in Tyranny, stressed his opportunism and will to power, while Henry Ashby Turner, in Hitler's Thirty Days to Power (1996), showed that his appointment depended on intrigues among a few men around Hindenburg in January 1933.
Weimar governments faced war debts, housing shortages, inflation and then mass unemployment, and their responses moved from welfare spending to deflation to emergency job creation.

After 1918 the republic recognised trade unions and collective bargaining: the Stinnes-Legien agreement of November 1918 gave the eight-hour day and union recognition in return for employers' co-operation.
The Hauszinssteuer, a tax on house owners who had gained from inflation, funded large municipal housing estates in Berlin and Frankfurt in the later 1920s.

Stresemann's government ended hyperinflation in 1923 by ending passive resistance, balancing the budget and issuing the Rentenmark, but the middle classes who lost their savings were never compensated in full.
The 1927 Unemployment Insurance Act gave benefit to workers who paid contributions, but it was designed for about 800,000 claimants and was overwhelmed when unemployment passed three million.
Brüning's emergency decrees of 1930 and 1931 cut civil service pay, unemployment benefit and wages and raised taxes in order to balance the budget, a deflationary policy that deepened the slump.
The Voluntary Labour Service (Freiwilliger Arbeitsdienst) of 1931 gave unemployed young men work on public projects for pocket money, and it was widened under Papen and Schleicher.

Papen's September 1932 programme offered tax certificates to employers who hired extra workers, and Schleicher's emergency job-creation programme of December 1932 tried to win union support, but neither had time to take effect before January 1933.
Social strain was severe by 1932: millions of families lived on reduced benefit or on poor relief, and thousands of young unemployed men joined the SA, which provided uniforms, meals and shelter.
Judgements of the republic divide between blaming its structure and the Treaty of Versailles, and emphasising the impact of the Depression and the choices of its leaders.
Structural view: proportional representation, Article 48 and the lack of a stable parliamentary majority left the republic dependent on emergency government.
Versailles view: contemporaries on the right blamed the treaty for national humiliation, and this shaped the appeal of parties promising revision.
Achievement: Stresemann's policies produced a recovery between 1924 and 1929, with inflation defeated and Germany admitted to the League of Nations.
Limit: that recovery depended heavily on American loans, so the Wall Street Crash exposed its fragility and left no reserves to cushion the unemployment that followed.

Later historians such as Henry Ashby Turner stress that Nazi electoral support was falling by late 1932 and that Hitler's appointment was not inevitable but resulted from decisions by a small group of conservative politicians.
Contemporary left-wing and liberal critics blamed the conservative elite for undermining the republic, while the Nazi party presented itself as the only force able to restore order.
Within months of his appointment as Chancellor, Hitler removed legal and political limits on his power, using emergency decrees and intimidation.

The Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933 was blamed on a Communist plot (the Dutch communist Marinus van der Lubbe was found in the building) and used to justify the Decree for the Protection of People and State of 28 February, which suspended civil liberties such as freedom of the press and assembly.
Communists were arrested in large numbers after the fire, and the Communist Party was effectively destroyed in early 1933.
The Enabling Act of 23 March 1933 allowed the cabinet to make laws without the Reichstag for four years; only the Social Democrats voted against it.
Trade unions were abolished on 2 May 1933 and replaced by the German Labour Front, led by Robert Ley.
Gleichschaltung, the coordination of institutions, brought state governments, the civil service, the courts, universities and cultural bodies under Nazi control.
A law of 14 July 1933 made the NSDAP the only legal party in Germany.
The purge of the SA leadership in 1934 removed the last rival power bloc, and Hitler combined the offices of Chancellor and President after Hindenburg's death.
The SA under Ernst Röhm had grown to millions of members and wanted a second revolution and a larger role in the army.
Between 30 June and 2 July 1934, Hitler ordered the murder of Röhm and other SA leaders, and of political figures such as Gregor Strasser and former Chancellor Kurt von Schleicher.
The cabinet legalised the killings retrospectively on 3 July as acts of state self-defence, and the army leadership accepted the purge in return for the removal of the SA as a rival force.
President Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934, and Hitler combined the presidency and the chancellorship in the title of Führer and Reich Chancellor.
Soldiers swore a personal oath of loyalty to Hitler as Führer rather than to the constitution.
Hitler's authority rested on the Führer principle, in which decisions flowed down from the leader, and on the cult of his personal leadership in propaganda.
Heinrich Himmler, Reichsführer-SS from 1929, built up the SS and took control of the political police in most German states.
Reinhard Heydrich led the Security Service (SD) and, with Himmler, controlled the Gestapo, which had wide powers of arrest without legal challenge.
Dachau, opened near Munich in March 1933, was the first concentration camp, and others such as Sachsenhausen (1936) and Buchenwald (1937) followed.
Political opponents, trade unionists, Social Democrats and members of religious groups were the first people held in the camps.
Courts were restricted by the Special Courts and the people's court, which handed down political verdicts with little legal protection for defendants.
The Gestapo and the SS were given powers to detain people without trial, which the regime described as protective custody.
Nazi economic policy reduced unemployment through public works and rearmament, and prepared the economy for war.
Hjalmar Schacht, appointed president of the Reichsbank in 1933 and Economics Minister in 1934, financed rearmament through Mefo bills, which concealed military spending.
Public works, including autobahns (the first section opened in 1935), housing and military construction, reduced unemployment, which fell sharply between 1933 and 1936.
The Reich Labour Service became compulsory for young men in June 1935, and conscription was reintroduced in March 1935.
The New Plan of 1934 controlled foreign trade through bilateral agreements and exchange controls, which gave priority to imports needed for rearmament.
The Four Year Plan of September 1936, under Hermann Göring, aimed to make Germany ready for war within four years and to achieve economic self-sufficiency (autarky).
Schacht resigned as Economics Minister in 1937 after disagreements with Göring over the pace and cost of rearmament.
Hitler's first foreign moves rejected the Versailles restrictions and gained international acceptance of rearmament.
On 14 October 1933 Germany left the League of Nations and the Geneva Disarmament Conference, citing unequal treatment.
The Saar territory, governed by the League since 1920, returned to Germany after a plebiscite in January 1935 in which over 90 per cent voted for reunion.
On 16 March 1935 Hitler announced the reintroduction of conscription and an air force, in breach of the Treaty of Versailles.
The Stresa Front of Britain, France and Italy condemned the move in April 1935, but took no effective action against Germany.
The Anglo-German Naval Agreement of June 1935 allowed Germany a navy about 35 per cent the size of the British navy, and it was accepted by Britain without consulting France.
The agreement gave Hitler the diplomatic recognition that he had sought, and it encouraged him to test the western powers further.
Between 1936 and 1939 Hitler took territory by threat and by diplomacy, and each success made the western powers more reluctant to resist him.
On 7 March 1936 German troops reoccupied the demilitarised Rhineland, and the Locarno Treaties were breached without military resistance from Britain or France.

The Anschluss, the annexation of Austria, took place on 12 March 1938 after German pressure forced Austrian Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg to cancel a plebiscite on independence and resign, and German troops entered Austria.
Hitler's demands for the German-speaking Sudetenland in Czechoslovakia led to the Munich Agreement of 29 to 30 September 1938, which Britain and France signed with Germany and Italy.
Czechoslovakia was not consulted at Munich, and Britain's Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain described the agreement as securing "peace for our time".
German troops entered Prague on 15 March 1939, and Bohemia and Moravia became a German protectorate while Slovakia became a nominally independent client state.

Britain gave a guarantee to Poland on 31 March 1939, followed by France, but Germany and the Soviet Union signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact of 23 August 1939, with a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe between them.
Konrad Henlein's Sudeten German Party, funded from Berlin, demanded autonomy for the three million Sudeten Germans, giving Hitler a pretext to threaten Czechoslovakia in 1938.
Chamberlain flew to meet Hitler at Berchtesgaden on 15 September and again at Bad Godesberg on 22 September, where Hitler raised his demands; the Munich conference followed on 29 September.
The Munich Agreement required Czechoslovakia to hand over the Sudetenland to Germany between 1 and 10 October 1938; the Soviet Union, which had a treaty with Czechoslovakia, was not invited.
Hitler's occupation of Prague in March 1939 broke the Munich promises and ended the belief that his claims were limited to Germans, which led Britain to abandon appeasement and guarantee Poland.
The Nazi-Soviet Pact of 23 August 1939 removed the threat of a war on two fronts; Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939 and Britain and France declared war on 3 September.

Earlier steps included the German-Polish non-aggression pact of January 1934, a failed Austrian Nazi coup in July 1934 in which Chancellor Dollfuss was murdered, and the German Condor Legion's intervention for Franco in the Spanish Civil War from 1936.
Hitler's foreign policy was driven by racial ideology and the goal of Lebensraum in the east, which the intentionalist school of historians sees as a plan for war from the start.
In Mein Kampf Hitler argued that Germany needed Lebensraum (living space), to be won in Eastern Europe and settled by a racially pure population, with the Slavs to be subjugated.
The idea of a herrenvolk, a master race of Germanic people, underpinned both domestic policy and plans for the conquest and resettlement of Eastern Europe.

At a meeting of 5 November 1937, later recorded in the Hossbach Memorandum, Hitler told his military and foreign policy chiefs that Germany's space problem could be solved only by force, probably around 1943 to 1945.
Appeasement was British and French policy to satisfy Germany's grievances through concessions, based on the belief that Versailles had been unfair and that war must be avoided.
Historians disagree about whether Hitler planned a general war from 1933 (the intentionalist view) or responded to opportunities and his own followers' initiatives (the functionalist view).
A.J.P. Taylor's 1961 book argued that Hitler's aims were opportunist and similar to those of earlier German leaders, a view that was widely challenged by later historians.
Hitler's rule from 1933 to 1939 combined a consolidated dictatorship at home with a foreign policy of rearmament, expansion and war.
As Chancellor and then Führer, he set the direction of policy, while rival agencies competed for influence, a structure historians call polycracy.
He was a participant in the foreign policy decisions of 1933 to 1939, making the key choices about withdrawal from the League, rearmament, the Anschluss and Czechoslovakia.
Public opinion in Germany responded enthusiastically to his foreign successes, especially the Saar, the Rhineland and the Anschluss, which made his popularity high by 1938.
Foreign contemporaries were divided: some British politicians saw him as a revisionist who could be satisfied, while others, such as Winston Churchill, warned from the 1930s that he was a threat.
Later historians discuss how far he controlled events and how far his policies were shaped by pressure from the military, the party and the economy.
His foreign policy and the deaths of Jews, opponents and others in the camps are judged together by historians as the central crimes of his regime, a matter taken up in the notes on the Holocaust.
The regime aimed to unite Germans of 'pure' race in a national community under party control, and it reshaped work, education and family life to do so.

The German Labour Front under Robert Ley replaced the free unions; its Strength Through Joy (Kraft durch Freude) section organised cheap holidays, cruises and theatre trips, and its Beauty of Labour section improved factory conditions.

The Volkswagen savings scheme, in which workers paid weekly instalments towards a Strength Through Joy car, never delivered cars to the savers, because the factory was turned over to military production.

The Hitler Youth, led by Baldur von Schirach, became the only legal youth organisation under the Hitler Youth Law of December 1936, with boys in the Jungvolk and Hitler Youth and girls in the League of German Girls (BDM).
Schools taught racial science and nationalist history, textbooks were rewritten, and teachers were pressed to join the National Socialist Teachers' League.

Nazi ideology assigned women the roles of wife and mother (often summed up as Kinder, Küche, Kirche); marriage loans from 1933 were reduced by a quarter for each child born, and the Mother's Cross was awarded from 1938 to women with large families.
Women were pushed out of the civil service and professions such as law and medicine in 1933, although rearmament and labour shortages brought many back into work by the late 1930s.

Opponents, 'asocials' and people judged racially or biologically inferior were excluded from the community: Jews by the Nuremberg Laws of 1935, and disabled people by forced sterilisation under the law of July 1933.
Unemployment, officially about six million in early 1933, fell below one million by 1937 and gave way to labour shortages, although the figures excluded Jews and many women, and wages were held down.
The war gave the regime radical new powers; the course of the fighting is covered in the notes on the Second World War.
Albert Speer, Hitler's architect, became Minister for Armaments in February 1942 and raised output of weapons by rationalising production, even as Allied bombing increased.

After the defeat at Stalingrad, Goebbels called for total war in his Sportpalast speech in Berlin on 18 February 1943, leading to the closure of non-essential businesses and the conscription of women up to the age of 45 into war work.
Millions of forced labourers from occupied Europe, including prisoners of war and concentration camp inmates, worked in German factories and farms.

On 20 July 1944 Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg planted a bomb at Hitler's headquarters at Rastenburg (the Wolf's Lair), but Hitler survived and the plot, which involved army officers and conservative civilians, was crushed; thousands were arrested and several hundred executed.
Hitler remained in command to the end, committing suicide in Berlin on 30 April 1945.
Judgements of Hitler's foreign policy divide between seeing him as the driving force of a deliberate war and seeing the war as the product of wider forces and of appeasement.
Achievement: by 1939 Hitler had reversed the main Versailles restrictions, rebuilt the army and expanded German territory without a major war.
Limit: the expansion depended on the restraint of the western powers, which many German generals feared would fight, and the economy was strained by rearmament.
Intentionalist view: Hitler's Mein Kampf aims, the Hossbach Memorandum and the invasion of Poland show a deliberate plan for war.
Functionalist view: the policies of the Nazi state, the competition between agencies and the choices of Britain and France shaped how and when the war began.
Contemporary view: appeasement was supported by many British people who wanted to avoid another war, and Munich was welcomed at first as a rescue of peace.
Later view: Munich is generally judged a failure, because it removed Czechoslovakia's defences and left Hitler convinced that the western powers would not fight.
After the Bolsheviks seized power in 1917 (see the notes on the Russian Revolution), Lenin built a one-party state and fought a civil war that shaped the Soviet system.

The Cheka, the Bolshevik secret police set up in December 1917 under Felix Dzerzhinsky, used arrest and execution against opponents, including the Socialist Revolutionaries and Mensheviks, and after the attempt on Lenin it carried out the Red Terror from September 1918.

The Russian Civil War (1918-1921, with fighting continuing in the Far East until 1922) pitted the Red Army, led by Leon Trotsky as War Commissar, against the White armies and foreign intervention forces.
War Communism (1918-1921) nationalised industry and banks, forced peasants to hand over grain at fixed low prices, and rationed food to towns.
Peasant revolts and famine in 1920-1921, combined with the grain requisitioning, showed how unpopular the policy had become.
The Bolsheviks banned rival parties during the civil war, and the Communist Party became the only legal party in the Soviet state.
Lenin survived an assassination attempt in August 1918, after which the Cheka's use of terror was greatly expanded.
In March 1921 sailors and workers at the naval base of Kronstadt revolted against Bolshevik rule, demanding free elections and an end to the monopoly of power; the Red Army crushed the revolt.

At the Tenth Party Congress in March 1921 the Bolsheviks adopted the New Economic Policy (NEP), which allowed small private trade, peasant sales of surplus grain and some private small-scale industry.
The NEP restored food supplies and the economy recovered by the mid-1920s, while large industry and banking remained under state control.
The NEP was seen by many Communists as a retreat, and critics on the left argued that it produced a new class of traders and wealthy peasants called Nepmen and kulaks.
The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was formally created on 30 December 1922, bringing together Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and the Transcaucasian republics.
Lenin suffered strokes in 1922 and 1923, the first in May 1922, and died on 21 January 1924, leaving the party without a clear successor.
Stalin's rise as General Secretary, and his defeat of rival factions, decided who would lead the Soviet Union in the years of the Five-Year Plans.
Stalin had become General Secretary of the Communist Party in April 1922, a post that gave him control of party appointments.

Lenin's Testament, dictated in late 1922 and early 1923, criticised Stalin's rudeness and called for his removal from the post of General Secretary; the Central Committee did not publish it at the time.

Zinoviev and Kamenev first allied with Stalin against Trotsky in 1923-25; Trotsky's Left Opposition argued for rapid industrialisation and world revolution, and when Zinoviev and Kamenev joined him in the United Opposition of 1926 it was defeated, with its leaders expelled from the party by December 1927.
Trotsky was expelled from the party in 1927, sent to internal exile in Kazakhstan in 1928 and exiled from the Soviet Union in 1929; Stalin's agent killed him in Mexico in 1940.

The Right Opposition led by Nikolai Bukharin, Alexei Rykov and Mikhail Tomsky favoured the NEP and gradual growth, and was defeated in 1928-29 after Stalin, who had used it to beat the Left, turned to the Left's policy of rapid industrialisation and forced grain collection.
Stalin's defeat of rivals in the party allowed him to launch the First Five-Year Plan, and the Trotsky and Bukharin factions were both removed from political influence by 1929.
The First Five-Year Plan (1928-1932) set targets for heavy industry, and later plans extended the drive for rapid industrial growth.
Gosplan, the state planning agency, drew up the First Five-Year Plan, which was launched in October 1928 and aimed to transform the Soviet Union into an industrial power.
Targets were set for coal, steel, electricity, oil and machinery, with heavy industry given priority over consumer goods.
The steel city of Magnitogorsk was built in the southern Urals, becoming a symbol of the drive for industrialisation and of the labour that went into it.

Alexei Stakhanov, a Donbas coal miner, was reported to have cut 102 tonnes of coal in a single shift in August 1935, and the Stakhanovite movement was used to promote higher output, though the feat was prepared with help and made norms harder for ordinary workers.

Steel output rose from about 4 million tonnes in 1928 to about 18 million in 1940, but official statistics were inflated and the costs were very high: wages fell, housing was overcrowded, quality was poor and forced labour was used on projects such as the White Sea-Baltic Canal (1931-33).
The Second Five-Year Plan (1933-1937) and the Third (1938-1941) continued the emphasis on heavy industry, and the Soviet economy was militarised by the late 1930s.
Collectivisation aimed to bring peasant agriculture under state control, and its enforcement caused famine, mass deaths and the destruction of the kulaks as a class.

Collectivisation was launched in late 1929, when Stalin announced the 'liquidation of the kulaks as a class', and peasants were forced to join collective farms (kolkhozy) in which land and livestock were pooled and run to state orders.
Kulaks, the richer peasants, were described as enemies of the state and were deported or killed in a campaign of dekulakisation.
Peasants resisted by slaughtering livestock, and grain requisitions were set at levels that left villages short of food.
The harvest failures and forced requisitions of 1932 and 1933 produced a famine that killed several million people, mainly in Ukraine, the North Caucasus and Kazakhstan.
The Soviet authorities denied the famine and restricted movement to prevent starving peasants from reaching the towns.
Collectivisation transformed agriculture into a system of state-controlled production, but it produced lower output of meat and grain for several years.
The regime pursued a programme of social change that promoted literacy, changed family life and sought to replace religion with atheism and Marxist culture.
Literacy campaigns in the 1920s and 1930s raised reading levels greatly, and education was expanded to train workers and engineers.
The Bolsheviks legalised abortion in 1920 and promoted equality for women in work and politics, but abortion was restricted again in 1936.
The League of the Militant Godless, founded in 1925, campaigned against religion, and many churches and monasteries were closed or destroyed.
Socialist realism became the official style of art and literature in 1932, and the Union of Soviet Writers, formed in 1934, enforced its standards.
Cultural life was controlled by the party, and artists and writers who did not follow the official line faced censorship, expulsion or arrest.
The Soviet system promoted a new Soviet man and woman and a culture of collective achievement, expressed in parades, posters and public monuments.
Western visitors toured Soviet factories and collective farms in the early 1930s, and some returned with favourable reports about rapid industrial growth and the absence of unemployment.
The Webbs, Sidney and Beatrice, British socialists, published Soviet Communism: A New Civilisation? in 1935, which presented the Soviet system as a model for social planning.
The Depression made the planned economy look more attractive to some socialists, intellectuals and trade unionists in Britain, France and the United States.
Critics in the West, including many liberal and conservative commentators, pointed to the famine, the show trials and the absence of political freedom.
Contemporary opinion was therefore divided, and the Soviet alternative was a source of debate between supporters of planning and defenders of liberal democracy.
The Soviet Union's diplomatic recognition by the United States in 1933 and its membership of the League of Nations from 1934 gave the regime greater international standing.
The German invasion of June 1941 tested the Soviet system, and Stalin's wartime leadership combined the mobilisation of resources with terror against soldiers and civilians.
Germany invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941 in Operation Barbarossa, and the Red Army suffered heavy losses in the first months of the war.

Stalin chaired the State Defence Committee set up on 30 June 1941 to direct the war economy, and became Supreme Commander in August 1941; he stayed in Moscow during the German advance in the autumn of 1941.
Factories were moved east to the Urals and Siberia in 1941, and output of tanks, aircraft and munitions rose sharply by 1942.
The Battle of Stalingrad, from August 1942 to February 1943, marked the turning point on the Eastern Front, when the German Sixth Army was encircled and surrendered.
Stalin used the Red Army and the NKVD to enforce discipline, including executions of deserters and punishment of soldiers who had been captured.
The Soviet Union's victory in the war was used to strengthen Stalin's personal authority, and he was given the rank of Generalissimo in 1945.
Order 227 of July 1942, 'Not one step back', led to blocking detachments behind the front line and penal battalions for those who retreated.

Soviet industry relocated about 1,500 factories east of the Urals in 1941 and 1942, and Lend-Lease supplies from Britain and the United States, including trucks and food, supported the Red Army from 1941.
Soviet victories at Stalingrad (February 1943) and Kursk (July 1943) turned the war, and the Red Army reached Berlin in April-May 1945.
Soviet deaths in the war are usually estimated at about 27 million, military and civilian combined, far more than any other combatant.
Prisoners of war who returned from German captivity and whole nationalities such as the Chechens and Crimean Tatars, accused of collaboration, were punished by imprisonment or deportation.
In 1943 Stalin eased pressure on the Orthodox Church and appealed to Russian nationalism, calling the conflict the Great Patriotic War, to win popular support.
In 1945 Stalin joined Churchill and Roosevelt at Yalta and Potsdam, and the USSR emerged as a superpower with control over Eastern Europe.
Lenin led the Bolsheviks from 1903 to 1924, and he created the institutions that Stalin inherited.
Born Vladimir Ulyanov in 1870 at Simbirsk, he had an elder brother who was executed in 1887 for plotting against Tsar Alexander III.
He was a participant in the 1917 revolutions, returning to Russia in April 1917 and issuing the April Theses calling for the transfer of power to the soviets.
He led the Bolsheviks in seizing power in October 1917 and presided over the Council of People's Commissars, the first Soviet government.
As leader in the civil war, he authorised the use of terror, the grain requisitioning of War Communism and the suppression of the Kronstadt revolt.
Contemporaries in the party saw him as the authority on Marxist theory and tactics, and his death in 1924 was marked by an embalmed body displayed in a mausoleum in Moscow.
Historians judge him as the architect of the one-party state, though some stress that the NEP shows a pragmatic side, and others argue that his methods made the later terror possible.
Stalin's leadership from the late 1920s to his death in 1953 transformed the Soviet economy and society, and he built a cult of personality around himself.
Born Ioseb Dzhugashvili in 1878 at Gori in Georgia, he was trained for the priesthood before joining the revolutionary movement and taking the name Stalin.
As General Secretary he built a network of loyal appointees, and by 1929 he had defeated his main rivals in the party.
He directed the Five-Year Plans and collectivisation, and his decisions set the timetable and targets for the whole economy.
Stalin was the central figure of Soviet propaganda, with his portraits, statues and sayings displayed across the country, and cities such as Stalingrad were named after him.
Western admirers in the 1930s, such as the Webbs, praised his industrial achievements, while the famine, the show trials and the Terror provoked criticism from liberal and socialist opponents.

After Stalin's death, Nikita Khrushchev denounced the cult of personality in a secret speech to the 20th Party Congress in February 1956, and historians have since debated how far his policies reflected ideology, paranoia or the pressures of industrialisation.
A personality cult presented Stalin as the infallible successor of Lenin, and a system of terror and control gave the state its totalitarian character.
The cult began with the celebrations of Stalin's fiftieth birthday in December 1929, when Pravda hailed him as Lenin's heir and the 'leader' of the party.

Official history was rewritten: the History of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (Short Course) of 1938 gave Stalin the central role in the revolution, while Trotsky and other rivals were written out and removed from photographs.
Towns, factories and streets were named after Stalin, and poets, artists and film-makers portrayed him as the wise father of the people.
The 1936 Constitution, called the Stalin Constitution, promised universal suffrage, a secret ballot and civil rights, while the Communist Party's monopoly of power was left untouched.
The NKVD and the Gulag network of forced-labour camps held millions of prisoners, many of them peasants and political prisoners, who built canals, railways and mines.
Internal passports introduced in 1932 and 1933 and the registration of residence controlled movement, tying peasants to the countryside and keeping 'undesirables' out of the cities.
The Treaty of Rapallo with Germany (1922) restored relations between the two outcast states and allowed secret military co-operation on German rearmament on Soviet soil.
The Comintern, founded in 1919, directed foreign communist parties; its policy of denouncing Social Democrats as 'social fascists' split the German left in the early 1930s.
After Hitler took power, the USSR joined the League of Nations (1934), signed pacts with France and Czechoslovakia (1935) and backed the Popular Front policy of co-operation against fascism.
The USSR gave aid to the Spanish Republic in the Civil War from 1936, but was excluded from the Munich conference in 1938.

The Nazi-Soviet Pact of August 1939 gave Stalin time and a buffer: the Red Army entered eastern Poland on 17 September 1939, the USSR attacked Finland in the Winter War of November 1939, and the Baltic states were annexed in 1940.
The pact left the USSR unready when Germany attacked in June 1941, despite many intelligence warnings which Stalin discounted.
Judgements of the Soviet system balance its industrial and military achievements against the human costs of its methods.
Achievement: by 1941 the Soviet Union had built a large heavy industry base, and its war production helped defeat Germany.
Limit: collectivisation destroyed much of the peasant farming system and caused a famine that killed millions in 1932 and 1933.
Achievement: literacy and education expanded greatly, and women gained formal equality in work and the professions.
Limit: the cult of personality, the suppression of rival parties and the arrests of opponents removed any independent political life.
Contemporary view: many Western socialists and intellectuals saw the Soviet Union as a model for planning during the Depression.
Later view: historians after 1945 stressed the costs and the totalitarian features of the system, while more recent work has examined its social change and the views of ordinary people.
The trials of 1936 to 1938 followed a pattern set by earlier public trials, and they served several purposes for Stalin at once.

The Shakhty trial of 1928 tried engineers from a Donbas coal town on charges of sabotage and foreign conspiracy, and the Industrial Party trial of 1930 repeated the charges against leading technical specialists.
In April 1933 six British engineers of the Metropolitan-Vickers company were tried in Moscow for espionage and wrecking, a case that showed the regime blaming foreigners for industrial failures.
