The costs of the First Five-Year Plan and collectivisation, including shortages, accidents and the famine of 1932-33, created a need for scapegoats among managers, engineers and officials, who were accused of 'wrecking' and sabotage.

Stalin's rivals from the succession struggle, Trotsky in exile and former oppositionists such as Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin, still had prestige as old Bolsheviks and could be presented as a potential alternative leadership.
The 17th Party Congress of January and February 1934, known as the Congress of Victors, celebrated the success of the plans, yet most of its delegates did not survive the Terror.

Historians differ on motive: some stress Stalin's paranoia and desire for total personal power, while others point to real tensions over the pace of industrialisation, fear of foreign attack as Hitler rose, and the pressure on local officials to find enemies.
A party purge or chistka began in 1933, when members judged unreliable were expelled, and in 1935 a check on party documents led to further expulsions; these purges were not at first fatal.
The shooting of a leading Stalinist gave Stalin the pretext for the repression that followed.

Sergei Kirov, party leader in Leningrad and a member of the Politburo, was shot dead on 1 December 1934 at the Smolny Institute, the party headquarters in Leningrad, by Leonid Nikolaev, a young party member who had been dismissed from his job.
Nikolaev was tried in secret and shot in December 1934, and the NKVD at first blamed a plot by 'white guards' and then by former supporters of Zinoviev.

A decree of 1 December 1934, issued the day of the murder and apparently drafted by Stalin, ordered that terrorism cases be heard in days, with no defence lawyer, no appeal and immediate execution of death sentences.
Zinoviev and Kamenev were tried in secret in January 1935 and given prison terms of ten and five years; in 1936 they were brought back for a public trial on much graver charges.

Historians disagree about the murder: some, such as Robert Conquest, suspected that Stalin or the NKVD arranged it, while others, including J. Arch Getty and Matthew Lenoe, find evidence that Nikolaev acted alone; no document proving Stalin's involvement has been found.
Either way, Stalin exploited the killing: he claimed that a network of conspirators existed and that the opposition had been drawn into terrorism, and he used this claim to justify the show trials.
The Trial of the Trotskyite-Zinovievite Terrorist Centre opened the public series.

The trial was held from 19 to 24 August 1936 in the Hall of Columns of the House of Unions in Moscow, with sixteen defendants led by Grigory Zinoviev and Lev Kamenev, two of Lenin's closest colleagues and former members of the Politburo.
They were charged with forming a terrorist centre under Trotsky's direction, murdering Kirov, and plotting to kill Stalin and other leaders.

Before the trial Zinoviev and Kamenev had held out for months; Stalin reportedly promised that their lives and their families would be spared if they confessed, and the NKVD interrogators told them that confession would serve the party.
All sixteen defendants confessed in open court and all were sentenced to death; they were shot on 25 August 1936, within hours of the verdict, despite the promise.
Trotsky, living in Norway, and his son Lev Sedov were named as the organisers of the plot and were condemned in their absence.

The trial opened a campaign against 'Trotskyite-Zinovievite' enemies and led to the arrest of thousands of former oppositionists, and Mikhail Tomsky, a Right Oppositionist named during the trial, shot himself on 22 August 1936 before he could be arrested.
The trial of the so-called Anti-Soviet Trotskyite Centre moved the charges on to industrial sabotage.
It was held from 23 to 30 January 1937 and tried seventeen defendants, among them Yuri Pyatakov, a deputy commissar for heavy industry, and the journalist Karl Radek.

The defendants were accused of wrecking in factories and mines, causing railway accidents and plotting with Trotsky and with Germany and Japan to restore capitalism; the charges gave an explanation for the failures of the plans.

Pyatakov claimed to have flown to Oslo in December 1935 to meet Trotsky, but the Norwegian authorities reported that no foreign aircraft had landed there at the time, an inconsistency that foreign critics noticed.
Thirteen defendants, including Pyatakov, were shot; Radek and Grigory Sokolnikov received ten years in prison for co-operating with the prosecution, and two others received eight years.
Radek died in 1939 in prison; the circumstances are unclear, and the usual account is that he was killed by a fellow prisoner, probably on NKVD orders.
Sergo Ordzhonikidze, head of heavy industry and Pyatakov's superior, shot himself in February 1937, an event officially described as a heart attack.
The destruction of the army leadership took place largely in secret, unlike the public trials.
Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky, Deputy Defence Commissar and the leading advocate of modern mechanised warfare, was arrested in May 1937 with other senior officers.
They were tried by a closed military tribunal on 11 June 1937 on charges of treason and spying for Germany, and were shot the following day; the evidence was fabricated and relied on confessions.
Three of the five marshals of the Soviet Union, most army commanders and a large share of corps and divisional commanders were arrested, as were many naval and air force officers.
In total roughly 30,000 to 35,000 officers were dismissed or arrested between 1937 and 1939, although some were later released, and political commissars regained control of the army.

The purge left the Red Army poorly led at the time of the Winter War against Finland (1939-40) and the German invasion of June 1941, though historians debate how much the purge explains the defeats of 1941.
The Trial of the Right-Trotskyite Bloc was the last and the largest of the public trials.

It was held from 2 to 13 March 1938 and tried twenty-one defendants, including Nikolai Bukharin (former editor of Pravda and Comintern chairman), Alexei Rykov (former Prime Minister), the former NKVD chief Genrikh Yagoda, and Nikolai Krestinsky.

The defendants were charged with treason, spying for foreign powers, wrecking, planning to dismember the USSR, and conspiring to murder Lenin, Stalin, Kirov and the writer Maxim Gorky; Yagoda and a group of doctors were accused of causing deaths by medical murder.
On the first day Krestinsky retracted his confession, saying it was false, but he reversed himself the next day after a night in NKVD hands.

Bukharin accepted overall political responsibility for the 'bloc' but denied the specific charges of espionage and murder; this has been read as an attempt to signal his innocence to a careful reader.
Eighteen defendants, including Bukharin, Rykov and Yagoda, were shot on 15 March 1938; three others received prison terms.
Bukharin was rehabilitated by the Soviet government in 1988.
The trials were scripted from start to finish, and Stalin himself reviewed the charges and the testimony.
The prosecutor Andrei Vyshinsky, a former Menshevik and lawyer, prepared the cases with the NKVD and argued that a confession was sufficient proof of guilt.
The NKVD obtained confessions by sleep deprivation, long interrogations, threats against family members, false promises of leniency and, from 1937, with Stalin's approval, physical torture.
Defendants rehearsed their parts, and some seem to have been persuaded that confession served the party's interest, an argument used by interrogators on loyal communists.

The trials took place in public in the Hall of Columns or the October Hall of the House of Unions before an invited audience, with foreign journalists and diplomats present and the full transcripts published in several languages.
The presiding judge Vasily Ulrikh, a military judge, helped to keep the proceedings tightly controlled, and Soviet newspapers demanded the death penalty before the verdicts.

Weaknesses in the evidence, such as the Oslo flight, an alleged meeting in the Hotel Bristol in Copenhagen that had been demolished, and the near-identical wording of confessions, were noticed by foreign observers.

Joseph Davies, the American ambassador, who attended parts of the 1937 and 1938 trials, reported to Washington that the evidence appeared to establish guilt, and the German writer Lion Feuchtwanger, who visited Moscow in 1937, defended the trials in a book.
Some other diplomats and journalists were doubtful, and many liberals and socialists condemned the proceedings as a travesty of justice.

In 1937 an international commission chaired by the American philosopher John Dewey heard Trotsky's evidence in Mexico, in April, and in December reported that the charges were false; its report was titled Not Guilty.

Western communist parties defended the trials as necessary to destroy fascist agents, and some members left the party over the issue; the trials damaged the reputation of the Soviet system among liberals.
Stalin used the verdicts to discredit Trotsky, who was murdered in Mexico by an agent of the NKVD, Ramón Mercader, in August 1940.
Show trials were the visible tip of a mass campaign run by the NKVD and carried out largely in secret.
Nikolai Yezhov replaced Yagoda as head of the NKVD in September 1936, and the years 1937 and 1938 are often called the Yezhovshchina.

NKVD Order 00447 of 30 July 1937 set quotas by region for the arrest of 'former kulaks, criminals and anti-Soviet elements', with the first category to be shot and the second sent to camps; local officials asked for higher quotas, and the targets were exceeded.
National operations targeted ethnic groups with foreign connections, such as Poles, Germans and Latvians, and the Polish operation of 1937-38 was the largest.

NKVD records opened after 1989 show about 1.6 million arrests for 'counter-revolutionary' crimes in 1937 and 1938 and about 680,000 executions; some historians believe the true total of deaths was higher once camp deaths are added.
Many victims were ordinary workers, peasants and minorities rather than officials, and neighbours and colleagues were encouraged to denounce 'enemies of the people'.

According to Khrushchev's secret speech of 1956, 1,108 of the 1,966 delegates to the 1934 Congress were arrested and 98 of 139 members and candidates of the Central Committee elected at the Congress were shot.
By 1939 the Gulag held well over a million prisoners.
The Terror slowed in late 1938: Yezhov was removed in November 1938 and replaced by Lavrentiy Beria, and he was arrested in 1939 and shot in February 1940.
The trials illustrate three of the syllabus concepts.

Totalitarianism: the secret police, the control of the courts and the press, and the ability to make leading communists confess to invented crimes show a state that left no area outside political control.
Propaganda: newspapers, radio and public meetings across the USSR demanded death for the 'enemies of the people', and the confessions were used to explain shortages and accidents.
Personality cult: the trials presented Stalin as the vigilant leader who protected the people, Lenin's true heir, and denied the old Bolsheviks their share in the revolution.
The trials and the Terror were followed by the Short Course history of the party in 1938, which presented the defendants as agents of foreign powers from the beginning of the revolution.
The party's old guard was destroyed; Stalin's rivals and potential rivals were dead or in exile, and the new officials who replaced them owed their positions to him.
The economy lost managers, engineers and planners, and fear of being accused of wrecking made officials cautious and encouraged them to falsify results or avoid decisions.
The army and the security services were purged, and the scale of the loss of experienced officers is widely linked to the poor performance against Finland in 1939-40 and the German advance in 1941.
Society was affected through fear, denunciations and the arrest of relatives, and families of those arrested were stigmatised as relatives of enemies of the people.
Younger men promoted into the vacancies in the party, army and industry owed their careers to Stalin, which made the new elite loyal to him.
In 1956 Khrushchev condemned the Terror in his secret speech; mass rehabilitations followed, and Bukharin's was one of the last in 1988.
Judgements balance the consolidation of Stalin's personal power against the damage the Terror did to the state.
Achievement for Stalin: by 1939 the party, army and state were in the hands of officials loyal to him, and no organised opposition survived.
Limit for the regime: the loss of officers, managers and specialists weakened the army and the economy in the years before Barbarossa.
Contemporary supportive view: Soviet propaganda and foreign communists presented the trials as the exposure of real traitors, and visitors such as Davies and Feuchtwanger accepted the evidence.
Contemporary critical view: the Dewey Commission, liberal and socialist critics and many diplomats treated the trials as frame-ups.

Later view: after the opening of the archives in the 1990s historians treat the trials as stage-managed fabrications; they still debate how far Stalin planned the Terror, how much was driven from below by local officials, and how far it reflected paranoia or political calculation.
Later revisionist view: J. Arch Getty and others stress the disorder and local initiative in the Terror, while Robert Conquest and others emphasise central planning by Stalin.
France emerged from the First World War victorious but exhausted, and its governments were dominated by parties that demanded firm treatment of Germany.
The Third Republic, founded in 1870, was governed by an elected Chamber of Deputies and a President with limited powers.
The November 1919 election returned the Bloc National, a coalition of conservative, centre and Catholic parties, which governed until 1924.
France had lost about 1.4 million dead in the war, and many villages and farms in the north-east were devastated by fighting.
Reconstruction of the devastated areas was financed by German reparations, which the government expected Germany to pay in full.
Raymond Poincaré, Prime Minister in 1922 to 1924, pursued a hard line towards Germany and ordered the occupation of the Ruhr in January 1923.
The Ruhr occupation damaged French relations with Britain and the United States, which opposed it, and it ended in 1925 without securing full reparations.
The Cartel des Gauches, a coalition of Radicals and Socialists, won the May 1924 election and Édouard Herriot formed the first government of the Cartel.
The Cartel fell in April 1925 after a run on the franc and a financial crisis, and governments changed frequently in the following years.

Poincaré returned as Prime Minister in July 1926 with a national unity government and stabilised the franc in practice by the end of 1926 through tax increases and cuts in spending, and the Poincaré franc was fixed in law in 1928 at about a fifth of its pre-war value.
The Radical Party, a centre-left party with strong rural support, was the largest force in most governments of the 1920s and early 1930s.
The Chamber of Deputies held frequent votes of no confidence, and the government's ministers were often replaced after only a few months in office.
The constitution gave the President a largely ceremonial role, so policy was decided by the Prime Minister and the parliamentary majority.
France's economy was less affected by the Depression at first than Britain or Germany, but the slump arrived later and was prolonged by deflationary policy.
The French economy was built on small family farms and small businesses, which cushioned the country against the immediate effects of the Wall Street Crash.
Industrial production fell sharply from 1931, and unemployment rose more slowly than in Germany or Britain but remained a serious problem.
Governments kept the franc at its gold value until 1936, so deflation was used to defend the currency and lower prices, which hurt industry and farming.
The franc was devalued by the Popular Front government in October 1936, after which exports recovered slightly.
Heavy spending on the Maginot Line, a chain of fortifications along the German border built between 1930 and 1938, was one of the largest state investments of the period.

Alexandre Stavisky, a financier with political protection, was found shot dead in January 1934 after the collapse of his fraudulent bond sales; the police called it suicide but the left and right both suspected that he had been silenced.
The scandal forced the resignation of the Radical Prime Minister Camille Chautemps in January 1934, and right-wing leagues used it to attack the republic as corrupt.

On 6 February 1934 the leagues, including the Croix-de-Feu, Action française and the Solidarité française, marched on the Chamber of Deputies, and police opened fire; about fifteen people were killed and over a thousand injured.
The Daladier government resigned after the riots, and a national government under Gaston Doumergue was formed to restore order.

The left responded with a general strike and mass demonstration on 12 February 1934, and in July 1935 Socialists, Communists and Radicals united in the Popular Front against the threat of fascism, after the Comintern had reversed the Communists' hostility to other left parties.
The Popular Front won the 1936 election and introduced major social reforms, but its economic policies failed and it split over Spain.
In the elections of April and May 1936 the Popular Front coalition won a majority, and Léon Blum, a Socialist and the first Jew to hold the post, became Prime Minister in June 1936.

The Matignon Agreements of June 1936, negotiated between employers and unions under Blum's chairmanship, gave wage rises of about 7 to 15 per cent, union recognition, collective bargaining and elected workers' delegates, following a wave of sit-down strikes; laws that month brought in the 40-hour week and two weeks of paid holiday.
Around two million workers took part in strikes and factory occupations in May and June 1936, and the agreement was designed to end them.
The Popular Front's programme of nationalising armaments and the railways, and of spending on public works, was limited by financial pressure and capital flight.

Blum's government adopted a policy of non-intervention in the Spanish Civil War in August 1936, which was opposed by many on the left but supported by Britain, and it dissolved the far-right leagues in June 1936.

Blum paused the reforms in February 1937 and resigned in June 1937 when the Senate refused him emergency financial powers; after a brief second ministry in March and April 1938, Édouard Daladier became Prime Minister and the coalition ended, and in November 1938 his decrees undid the 40-hour week.
The Croix-de-Feu, led by Colonel François de la Rocque, was a veterans' league that attracted hundreds of thousands of members, and it became the Parti Social Français after it was dissolved in 1936.
Action française, led by Charles Maurras, was a monarchist and anti-Semitic movement which opposed the republic from before 1914.
Historians disagree on how far the leagues threatened democracy: René Rémond saw them as part of France's traditional right, while Zeev Sternhell argued that fascist ideas had deep roots in France.
Economic hardship and fear of war also split French opinion into left and right camps, and Communists and Socialists gained from the unity forged after February 1934.
France declared war on Germany in September 1939, but the defeat of its army in June 1940 ended the Third Republic and brought the Vichy state into being.

Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939 after the invasion of Poland, and the French army, commanded by General Maurice Gamelin, remained largely inactive during the Phoney War.
The German invasion of France and the Low Countries began on 10 May 1940, and German armoured divisions broke through the Ardennes to reach the Channel coast by late May.
The British Expeditionary Force and many French troops were evacuated from Dunkirk between 26 May and 4 June 1940.

Paris, declared an open city, was occupied on 14 June 1940; the government left for Bordeaux, Paul Reynaud resigned on 16 June, and Pétain became head of government and asked Germany for an armistice, before the government settled in the spa town of Vichy in July.
On 22 June 1940 an armistice was signed at Compiègne in the same railway carriage used for the 1918 armistice, dividing France into an occupied zone and an unoccupied zone.

On 10 July 1940 the National Assembly, the Chamber and Senate meeting together at Vichy, voted by 569 to 80, with about 20 abstentions, to give full powers to Marshal Philippe Pétain to draw up a new constitution, which ended the Third Republic.
The Maginot Line, named for the War Minister André Maginot, guarded the Franco-German border with deep forts, but it did not extend along the Belgian frontier or through the Ardennes.
French generals including Gamelin and Pétain believed that the Ardennes forest was difficult terrain for tanks, and the main French and British forces moved into Belgium in May 1940 on the Dyle plan.
France had as many tanks as Germany, but it spread them among infantry units instead of concentrating them in armoured divisions as Germany did.
German armoured units crossed the Meuse at Sedan on 13 and 14 May 1940 and reached the Channel coast by 20 May, cutting off the northern armies.
Contemporary explanations blamed political decadence under the Third Republic, but historians such as Ernest May stress poor intelligence, slow command and German skill rather than moral failure.
France lost about 90,000 killed in six weeks and well over a million men were taken prisoner.
Pétain's regime rejected republican and secular values in favour of authoritarian conservatism, which it called the National Revolution.
The regime renamed the state the État français and replaced the republican motto of Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité with Travail, Famille, Patrie (Work, Family, Fatherland).
Pétain's National Revolution blamed the Third Republic and the left for the defeat, and promoted traditional values, the Catholic Church and rural life.
Pierre Laval, dismissed in December 1940, returned as head of government in April 1942 and pursued a policy of close collaboration with Germany.
Pétain met Hitler at Montoire in October 1940 and announced that he had entered a path of collaboration with Germany.

The Vichy regime was an authoritarian state that relied on a veterans' organisation, the Legion of French Combatants, rather than a mass party, and it ended elections, banned strikes and dissolved the trade unions in favour of a Labour Charter in 1941.
Vichy's own press and radio supported the National Revolution, and its youth organisations aimed to instil discipline and loyalty to Pétain.

Under the armistice Germany occupied the north and the Atlantic coast, while the south stayed 'free' under Vichy until German troops occupied it in November 1942, after the Allied landings in North Africa.
France had to pay the costs of the German occupation, set at 400 million francs a day, and its food and industrial output were directed to Germany.
The British attack on the French fleet at Mers-el-Kébir on 3 July 1940 turned many Vichy supporters against Britain.
Food rationing, shortages and a black market affected daily life, and about 1.5 million French prisoners of war remained in Germany for years.
Vichy's sense of 'neutral' independence ended in 1942, as Laval's return led to closer co-operation, and the Germans occupied the whole country.

Collaboration took forms from economic cooperation and propaganda to active fascist parties such as the Parti Populaire Français of Jacques Doriot and the Rassemblement National Populaire of Marcel Déat.
The Vichy government took active steps against Jews, political opponents and resisters, and created a paramilitary force that fought against the Resistance.

Vichy passed the first anti-Jewish statute in October 1940, without German demand, excluding Jews from public office and many professions, and in 1942 it agreed to hand over foreign Jews in the unoccupied zone for deportation; about 76,000 Jews were deported from France and about 2,500 survived.

On 16 and 17 July 1942 French police arrested about 13,000 Jews in Paris, including about 4,000 children, and many were held at the Vélodrome d'Hiver cycling stadium before being sent via the Drancy camp to Auschwitz.
The Milice, a paramilitary force founded in January 1943, hunted members of the Resistance and carried out reprisals against civilians.

The Service du Travail Obligatoire (compulsory labour service), introduced in February 1943 after a voluntary scheme had failed, sent young French men to work in Germany, and many went into hiding in the maquis to avoid it.
Vichy's police and administration carried out many of the arrests and deportations, and collaboration extended to the economy, with supplies sent to Germany.
Historians since Robert Paxton's Vichy France of 1972 have argued that Vichy's collaboration was active and not merely a shield against harsher German policy.
Resistance to Vichy and the German occupation grew from a small group in London to an organised movement inside France by 1943.

Charles de Gaulle, a brigadier-general who had been Under-Secretary for War in Reynaud's government in June 1940, broadcast an appeal from London on 18 June 1940 calling on the French to continue the fight.
De Gaulle formed the Free French movement in London and was recognised by Britain, though his relations with Britain and the United States were often strained.
Jean Moulin united the main resistance groups in 1943 and presided over the first meeting of the National Council of the Resistance in May 1943.

Resistance activity included the production of underground newspapers, sabotage of railways, intelligence gathering and armed attacks on German troops by the maquis, groups of guerrillas in rural areas.
The Resistance was divided among Gaullists, Communists and other political groups, and the Communist-led Francs-Tireurs et Partisans, formed in 1942, became one of the largest armed groups.
Resistance groups carried out executions of collaborators and informers after the liberation, and these reprisals were a source of political tension.

Early groups such as Combat, Libération and Franc-Tireur ran underground newspapers and helped Allied airmen to escape, and Communists joined the armed struggle after Germany invaded the USSR in June 1941.
The maquis grew as young men avoided compulsory labour service in 1943 and 1944, and Resistance groups helped the Allied invasion by cutting railways.
The Germans took hostages and shot them in reprisal for attacks, and on 10 June 1944 SS troops massacred more than 600 civilians at Oradour-sur-Glane.
The village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, where Protestant villagers led by Pastor André Trocmé sheltered thousands of Jewish refugees, became a symbol of civilian rescue.

After the war the myth of a nation united in Resistance, promoted by de Gaulle, was challenged from the 1970s by historians and by the film The Sorrow and the Pity (1969-71), and in 1995 President Chirac acknowledged the state's responsibility for the Vél' d'Hiv round-up.
Allied landings in Normandy and southern France in 1944 led to the liberation of France and the collapse of Vichy.
The Allied invasion of Normandy began on 6 June 1944, and the Allies landed in southern France on 15 August 1944.

Paris was liberated on 25 August 1944 after an uprising by the Resistance and the arrival of General Leclerc's Free French armoured division, and on 26 August de Gaulle led a procession down the Champs-Élysées as head of the Provisional Government.
Pétain was taken to Germany in 1944 and was later tried in France, where he was sentenced to death in 1945; the sentence was commuted to life imprisonment by de Gaulle.
Laval was tried and shot in October 1945 after being convicted of treason.
An ordinance of April 1944 gave women the vote, first used in 1945, and the Fourth Republic was established after a new constitution was approved in 1946.
Judgements of the Third Republic weigh its stability and democratic survival against its inability to deal with the Depression or to resist invasion.
Achievement: the Third Republic survived the Depression and the leagues' challenge in 1934 without a coup, and its institutions held until 1940.
Limit: frequent government changes and the failure to modernise the army left France unprepared for the German attack of 1940.
Achievement: the Popular Front brought paid holidays and shorter working hours to French workers in 1936.
Limit: the Popular Front's economic policies failed to reduce unemployment, and it could not agree on how to respond to the Spanish Civil War.
Contemporary view: many French conservatives in 1940 saw the armistice and Pétain's rule as a necessary response to military defeat and the failures of the republic.
Later view: historians stress that Vichy was not forced into collaboration, and that its anti-Jewish policies went beyond German demands in some areas.
A brief post-war boom gave way to a sharp slump, and the government's cuts in public spending deepened unemployment in the early 1920s.
Demand for goods surged in 1919 and 1920 as wartime controls were removed, and prices rose sharply before collapsing in 1920 and 1921.
Unemployment rose above two million by mid-1921 as export markets were lost and industries shed workers.
The Geddes Axe of 1922, named after Sir Eric Geddes and his committee of economy, cut public spending on education, housing and the armed services.
Unemployment insurance, first introduced in 1911, was extended in 1920 to cover most workers, but benefits were limited and payments ended for many after a set period.

The coal industry was returned to private ownership in 1921, and the owners' attempt to cut miners' wages led to a lock-out; on 'Black Friday', 15 April 1921, the railwaymen and transport workers of the Triple Alliance refused to strike in support, leaving the miners to be defeated.
The decision to return to the gold standard at the pre-war rate made British exports more expensive, and its effect on the coal industry led to the General Strike of 1926.
In April 1925 the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Winston Churchill, returned sterling to the gold standard at the pre-war parity of about 4.86 dollars to the pound.

John Maynard Keynes criticised the decision in his 1925 pamphlet The Economic Consequences of Mr Churchill, arguing that the overvalued pound would make British exports uncompetitive and force down wages.
The coal owners announced wage cuts and longer hours, and the miners refused, leading to a lock-out in May 1926.
The Trades Union Congress called a General Strike from 4 to 12 May 1926 in support of the miners, and it was the only nationwide strike in British history.
The government mobilised volunteers and used the Organisation for the Maintenance of Supplies to keep essential services running, and the TUC called off the strike after nine days.
The miners stayed out for several months and were forced back to work on worse terms later in 1926.
Unemployment was concentrated in the older industrial regions of Wales, the north of England and central Scotland, while the south-east prospered.
The staple industries of coal, cotton, shipbuilding, iron and steel had been the basis of the Victorian economy, and they declined sharply in the inter-war years.
The coal industry lost jobs steadily from the mid-1920s, and South Wales, Durham and Northumberland were the most heavily affected coalfields.
The cotton industry of Lancashire lost export markets to Japan and India and suffered a long decline, with many mills closed by the 1930s.
Shipbuilding on the Tyne, Wear and Clyde was badly hit by the collapse of world trade and the lack of new orders, and many yards closed in the 1930s.

Unemployment in the distressed areas could remain above 30 per cent in many towns in the early 1930s, and higher still in places such as Jarrow and Merthyr Tydfil, while the south-east and the Midlands had relatively low unemployment.
Workers in the depressed regions often moved to the new industries of the south and Midlands, but many could not afford the cost of relocation or of housing.
The Wall Street Crash and the collapse of exports forced the Labour government to confront a budget crisis, leading to the formation of a National Government and the abandonment of gold.
Ramsay MacDonald led the second Labour government of 1929 to 1931, which lacked a majority and struggled with rising unemployment.

The May Committee on National Expenditure, reporting in July 1931, forecast a budget deficit of about 120 million pounds and recommended cuts of 20 per cent in unemployment benefit and public sector pay.

The Cabinet split over a 10 per cent cut in unemployment benefit, and MacDonald formed a National Government in August 1931 with Conservative and Liberal support; the Labour Party expelled him for doing so.
On 21 September 1931 Britain abandoned the gold standard, and sterling fell sharply against other currencies, which helped exports and allowed interest rates to fall.
The National Government won a landslide in the October 1931 general election, with Labour reduced to a small group of MPs.

The Invergordon mutiny of 15 to 16 September 1931, a few days before Britain left gold, in which sailors of the Atlantic Fleet protested against pay cuts, showed how the economy measures were resented in the armed forces.
The National Government moved away from free trade, introducing tariffs and imperial preference, and used cheap money to support recovery.
The Import Duties Act of February 1932 introduced a general tariff of 10 per cent on most imports, ending Britain's long commitment to free trade.
The Ottawa Agreements of 1932 gave preferential trade terms to the British Empire, and Britain kept a system of imperial preference until the 1970s.
Bank Rate was cut to 2 per cent in June 1932 and stayed there until 1939, a policy of cheap money that reduced the cost of borrowing and encouraged house building.
Protection helped industries such as steel and motor vehicles, but it raised the cost of food and materials for consumers.
The Ottawa system strengthened trade with the Dominions and colonies, but it reduced trade with the United States and with Europe.
The unemployed depended on insurance and then on means-tested assistance, and the most visible protest against the system came from hunger marches organised by local communities.
The National Unemployed Workers' Movement (NUWM), founded in 1921 by Communist-linked activists, organised protests, marches and resistance to evictions.

Hunger marches from the depressed regions to London, notably in 1922, 1932, 1934 and 1936, drew attention to the poverty of the unemployed; the National Hunger March of 1932 presented a petition with a million signatures to Parliament, which refused to receive it.

A household means test was introduced in November 1931, when benefit after 26 weeks passed to local Public Assistance Committees, and the Unemployment Act of 1934 created the national Unemployment Assistance Board to pay long-term unemployed people according to the same test of household income and savings.
The means test was unpopular because it looked at the income of all family members, and many families lost their assistance when a son or daughter earned money.

Local councils that paid relief in the depressed areas sometimes refused to apply the means test, and when the Board's new scales cut payments in early 1935, protests in South Wales and elsewhere forced the government to suspend them under the Standstill Act.

Before 1931 insured workers drew insurance benefit for limited periods and others relied on Poor Law relief, which the Local Government Act of 1929 transferred to local council Public Assistance Committees in 1930; both were blamed for stigma and hardship.
The government's policies for the depressed regions were limited, but house building and new light industries in the south and Midlands created jobs and transformed the economy.
The Special Areas (Development and Improvement) Act of 1934 designated the worst-hit areas and offered grants for new industries and public works there.
The Special Areas included South Wales, Tyneside, West Cumberland and parts of Scotland such as Clydeside, and the Commissioners appointed under the Act had limited funds.

About four million houses were built in Britain between the wars, roughly two-thirds of them privately built for owner-occupiers, with about a million council houses built by local authorities under acts such as Addison (1919) and Wheatley (1924), and the largest growth of suburban housing was in the south and Midlands.
The Housing Act of 1930 gave local authorities money to clear slums and build council housing, and the Housing Act of 1935 extended subsidies for slum clearance.
New light industries such as motor vehicles, electrical goods and consumer goods grew rapidly in the south-east and Midlands, with factories built on the outskirts of London and Birmingham.
The regional policy of the 1930s was modest in scale, and the depressed regions did not recover fully until rearmament created new demand at the end of the decade.
Keynes was an economist and government adviser whose ideas about public spending and demand became the basis of modern economic policy.
Born in Cambridge in 1883, he was a Fellow of King's College, Cambridge, and worked in the Treasury during the First World War.

He was a participant in the Versailles peace negotiations as a Treasury representative, resigned in protest at the reparations settlement, and wrote The Economic Consequences of the Peace in 1919, which condemned the settlement as unworkable.
In 1929 he co-wrote with Hubert Henderson the Liberal Party pamphlet We Can Conquer Unemployment, which proposed large public works programmes to reduce unemployment.
He argued in his General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money of 1936 that government spending could restore demand and employment when private investment was low.
Contemporaries disagreed about his ideas: the Treasury and the Bank of England were sceptical of deficit spending, while many Labour and Liberal politicians welcomed his arguments.
Historians judge his work as a turning point in economic thought, though they debate how far the 1930s recovery depended on his policies rather than on rearmament and cheap money.
In How to Pay for the War (1940) he proposed compulsory saving to prevent wartime inflation, and he returned to the Treasury as an adviser.

He led the British delegation to the Bretton Woods conference in 1944, where he argued for an international clearing union and a more flexible monetary system, and the agreement set up the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
Created Baron Keynes in 1942, he died in April 1946 after negotiating the American loan to Britain.
The interwar years brought rising living standards for those in work and persistent poverty in the depressed regions.
Real wages rose for those in work, prices fell in the early 1930s, and a growing number of families in the south-east and Midlands bought houses, cars, radios and electrical goods.
Trade unions were weakened after 1926, and the Trade Disputes Act of 1927 banned sympathetic strikes and made union members opt in to the political levy.

In the depressed areas, long unemployment brought malnutrition, overcrowded housing and high infant mortality, as shown by J.B. Priestley's English Journey (1934), George Orwell's The Road to Wigan Pier (1937) and the Pilgrim Trust's survey Men Without Work (1938).

Registered unemployment peaked at about three million, over 20 per cent of insured workers, in 1932 and 1933, and fell with recovery and rearmament after 1936 without ever dropping below a million before 1940.
Rearmament from 1936 increased demand for steel, shipbuilding and engineering and eased the problems of some depressed regions.
Mass leisure grew: cinema going, the BBC (founded 1922), dance halls and cheap holidays gave a shared culture, although families on the dole could afford few of these.
Judgements of the government's response weigh its success in restoring growth and stability against its failure to reduce unemployment in the depressed regions.
Achievement: the abandonment of gold and cheap money helped recovery in the south-east, and industrial production grew after 1932.
Limit: unemployment stayed above one million for most of the 1930s, and the depressed regions suffered long-term decline.
Achievement: house building and social provision expanded, and the National Government kept the parliamentary system working during a severe economic crisis.
Limit: the means test and the Special Areas policy were judged inadequate by critics on the left, who saw them as punishing the poor rather than creating jobs.
Contemporary view: the National Government's supporters argued that its policies had protected the currency and prevented a worse slump.
Later view: historians disagree about whether the 1930s recovery was caused mainly by monetary policy or by the expansion of consumer demand in the south-east.
Jarrow was a one-industry town on the south bank of the Tyne in County Durham, and the loss of its shipyard in the early 1930s left most of its working men without work.
Palmers Shipbuilding and Iron Company was founded in Jarrow in 1851 and grew into a yard and steelworks that dominated the town; it launched its thousandth ship in July 1930.
Almost the whole local economy depended on the yard, so when orders collapsed in the Depression, shops, trades and families that depended on its wages collapsed with it.
World shipbuilding was in slump: orders fell with world trade, and British yards had far more capacity than orders, which was the thinking behind the National Shipbuilders Security scheme.

National Shipbuilders Security Ltd (NSS) was formed in 1930, backed by the shipbuilders with the support of the Bank of England, to buy and close redundant yards, financed by a levy on the shipbuilding industry.
Palmers launched its last ship, the destroyer HMS Duchess, on 19 July 1932; creditors appointed a receiver in June 1933.
NSS bought the yard in 1934 and began to dismantle it, and sites sold by NSS were barred from shipbuilding for at least forty years, which ruled out any revival of the yard.

In 1934 the American businessman T. Vosper Salt proposed a modern steelworks on the Palmers site, but the British Iron and Steel Federation, which feared competition and a precedent for other areas, diluted the plan until it was unworkable; Wilkinson later said that it had been strangled at birth.

Unemployment in the town was far higher than the national average, with well over half of insured workers on the dole in the mid-1930s and figures of around two-thirds often quoted, compared with about 17 per cent in the north-east in 1936 and about 33 per cent in shipbuilding.

Jarrow had one of the worst records for poor housing, hunger and ill health in Britain, and Wilkinson later called it the town that was murdered; the Special Areas Act of 1934 had given it little help.
The march was run by the town council with cross-party support, and its public face was the town's Labour MP.
Ellen Wilkinson, known as Red Ellen, was a former Communist, a trade union organiser and Labour MP for Middlesbrough East from 1924 to 1931; she was elected for Jarrow in November 1935.

She backed the march as MP and did much of the publicity and parliamentary work, but she left it at Chester-le-Street to attend the Labour Party conference in Edinburgh and joined it again later, so she was not on foot for the whole way.
Councillor David Riley, the Labour leader on the council, was the leader and organiser of the marchers on the road.

Jarrow Borough Council backed the march, and Conservatives, Liberals and Labour on the council supported it, so it was presented as a cross-party appeal by the whole town, not a party or Communist protest.
Local clergy blessed the march at a departure service, and churches and Co-operative societies along the route provided food and beds.
The organisers called the march a crusade and prepared it carefully to give it a respectable character.
Their aim was a petition asking the government to bring new industry to Jarrow, above all a steelworks, and to end the distress of the town.
The marchers were chosen from more than a thousand volunteers; about 200 men set out, although records name fewer, and each was examined by a doctor for fitness.
The men carried a petition of over 11,000 signatures in an oak box, and a banner reading Jarrow Crusade, and a mouth organ band set the pace.
The marchers were disciplined, wore good boots donated by supporters, and were organised in a way to show that the unemployed were responsible citizens who wanted work.

The Labour Party and the TUC did not back the march, in part because they feared that it would be taken over by Communists and in part because they preferred parliamentary pressure; Labour's conference in Edinburgh in October 1936 gave it little support.
The Communist-led National Unemployed Workers' Movement had its own tradition of hunger marches, and the Jarrow organisers deliberately kept apart from it.
The men walked from the north-east to London, relying on the hospitality of towns along the way.
The marchers set out from Jarrow on 5 October 1936 after a service and a send-off by crowds.

They walked by way of Chester-le-Street, Darlington, Ripon, Harrogate, Leeds, Barnsley, Sheffield, Chesterfield, Nottingham, Leicester, Market Harborough, Northampton, Bedford, Luton and St Albans to London, a distance of about 290 miles.
They covered about 15 miles a day, slept in church halls, schools and workhouses, and ate at meals provided by supporters and local Co-operative societies.
In many towns, mayors, councils and Labour parties welcomed them, and the Liberal and Conservative leaders in some places joined in, although some local Conservatives distanced themselves.
They arrived at Marble Arch in London on 31 October 1936, after which the petition was handed to Parliament.
The press and newsreel coverage, much of it sympathetic, made the march a national story.
The government met the march with a refusal to act, but the petition itself was received.
Stanley Baldwin, the Prime Minister, declined to meet a deputation from Jarrow on 29 October 1936, and cited a fall in Jarrow's unemployment.
Wilkinson answered that the fall was due to combining the figures for Jarrow with those of South Shields, which hid the true numbers.
Wilkinson presented the petition in the House of Commons on 4 November 1936, but it was not debated and the government made no new commitment.
The Unemployment Assistance Board ruled that the marchers' benefit should be reduced on the grounds that they were not available for work while they marched.
The marchers went home by train on 5 November 1936, when crowds welcomed them in Jarrow.
The government's argument was that national recovery would restore jobs, and it questioned whether special help for one town was fair when many areas suffered.
The march brought no immediate results; recovery came with rearmament later in the decade.
Sir John Jarvis, a Conservative MP and businessman, helped to attract small firms to the Palmers site, and by 1939 about 100 men worked in a furniture factory and up to 500 in metal industries.
The Special Areas (Amendment) Act of 1937 provided tax reliefs for firms setting up in the depressed areas, but it was already being prepared and historians do not claim that the march caused it.
Rearmament and the Second World War brought real employment back to Tyneside, and Jarrow's recovery owed far more to war orders than to the march.
Wilkinson became Minister of Education in the Labour government of 1945 and died in 1947.
Many marchers felt they had failed; one called it a waste of time, and David Riley and some councillors briefly left the Labour Party after the march.
The march is remembered more than it achieved.
Contemporaries sympathetic to the march praised the discipline and dignity of the men, and Labour later adopted its banners as a symbol of the injustice of the 1930s.
Critics in the government and the press argued that the march was political theatre and could not solve structural problems.
The march helped to form the postwar belief that the 1930s were a time of government failure, which contributed to support for full employment policy and the welfare state after 1945.
The march was re-enacted in 1986 and 2011, and it remains one of the best-known symbols of the Depression in Britain.
As a documents-based topic, sources such as photographs of the marchers, newspaper reports, Wilkinson's speeches and government statements show how supporters and critics saw the same event.
The march took place in a month of major events, which affected how it was reported and received.

The National Government under Stanley Baldwin (Prime Minister since 1935) held a large majority, and ministers argued that general recovery, already well advanced in the south, would reach the distressed areas in time.

The march began in the same week as the Battle of Cable Street in London on 4 October 1936, when anti-fascists blocked a march by Oswald Mosley's British Union of Fascists, and it coincided with the Spanish Civil War, which dominated foreign news.
The abdication crisis over Edward VIII broke in December 1936, soon after the marchers had gone home, and pushed the Jarrow story out of the headlines.
Unemployment nationally was falling, to under two million by late 1936, which strengthened the government's argument that special help was unnecessary.
The Unemployment Assistance Board paid benefit by household means test, so the long-term unemployed of Jarrow depended on a rate set in London that took no account of local conditions.

Wilkinson was an experienced campaigner, and she used the march to dramatise the plight of her constituents in the Commons, where she argued that private industry could not be left to decide the fate of towns.
Sources on the march show differences of purpose and audience that are useful in a documents-based question.

Wilkinson, the council and the Daily Herald presented the march as a respectable appeal by a whole town, and photographs of the disciplined column with its banner and mouth organ band supported that image.
Government statements, including Baldwin's reference to falling unemployment, aimed to show that recovery was under way and that special action was not needed.
Labour and TUC leaders were cautious because they wished to avoid association with Communist-led marches and preferred political action through Parliament.
Conservative and some local newspapers questioned the march as a political stunt, while sympathetic papers described crowds and gifts along the route.
Wilkinson's book of 1939 was written after rearmament had begun to revive the town, so it combines a campaigner's anger with hindsight.

A cartoon or poster of the period usually shows the contrast between the needs of the distressed areas and the comfort of the south or of ministers, and the date helps to place whether it comes before or after the petition on 4 November.
The judgement depends on whether the march is measured by its immediate aims or by its long-term effect on opinion.
Failure: the government refused to meet the marchers, no steelworks or shipyard was secured, and the men lost benefit for the weeks they marched.
Failure: the real cause of recovery in Jarrow was rearmament and war, not the march.
Success: the march made Jarrow a national symbol, kept the problem of the distressed areas before the public, and showed that the unemployed were disciplined and honest.
Success: it was one of the few protests that won wide sympathy across party lines, and its memory shaped postwar attitudes to unemployment.
Contemporary view: supporters saw a moral victory; Conservatives and officials saw an exercise in publicity that offered no solution.
Later view: most historians see it as a failure in its immediate aims but a powerful moment in the politics of memory of the 1930s.
Blitzkrieg, or lightning war, combined fast armoured thrusts with air power and was first used on a large scale against Poland in September 1939.
Blitzkrieg relied on concentrated armoured divisions, close air support from dive-bombers such as the Junkers Ju 87 Stuka, and rapid breakthroughs that encircled enemy forces.
Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and the Polish army was defeated within about five weeks, with Warsaw surrendering at the end of September.
The Soviet Union invaded eastern Poland on 17 September 1939 under the terms of the Nazi-Soviet Pact, and the two powers divided the country.
Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, but their armies made no major attack on the Western Front during the Phoney War.
The Phoney War lasted from September 1939 until the German offensive in the west in May 1940.

Germany invaded Denmark and Norway on 9 April 1940; Denmark fell within hours, and Norway was conquered by June despite a failed Anglo-French landing, giving Germany Atlantic naval bases and Swedish iron-ore supplies.
In May and June 1940 German armoured forces defeated France in six weeks, and the Battle of Britain that followed was the first major campaign fought entirely in the air.
The German offensive in the west began on 10 May 1940, with an advance through the Netherlands, Belgium and the Ardennes, which bypassed the Maginot Line.
German armoured divisions reached the Channel coast at Abbeville by 20 May, cutting off the British and French forces in the north.
The Battle of Britain was fought from July to October 1940, as the Luftwaffe attacked RAF airfields and aircraft factories in an attempt to gain air superiority.
The RAF's Fighter Command, using Spitfire and Hurricane fighters and the radar early-warning Chain Home system, defeated the attempt to win air superiority.
Germany then switched to bombing London and other cities in the Blitz, which began on 7 September 1940 and continued into 1941.
Germany's invasion plan for Britain, Operation Sea Lion, was postponed in September 1940 and then abandoned.
The German invasion of the Soviet Union and the Japanese attack on the United States in December 1941 turned the war into a global conflict.
Operation Barbarossa, the German invasion of the Soviet Union, began on 22 June 1941 along a front of about 3,000 kilometres from the Baltic to the Black Sea.
German forces advanced rapidly in the first months and reached the outskirts of Moscow and Leningrad by late 1941, but were halted by the winter and Soviet counter-attacks in December.
The Japanese attack on the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941 brought the United States into the war, and Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on 11 December.
The Lend-Lease Act of March 1941 allowed the United States to supply Britain, and later the Soviet Union, with weapons and equipment without immediate payment.
Japan's attacks also took the Philippines, Malaya and Singapore, forcing Britain to surrender Singapore in February 1942.
Japan had been at war with China since 1937 and occupied French Indochina in 1940 and 1941; the United States responded with an oil embargo, which pushed Japan towards the attack of December 1941.
Within months Japan captured Hong Kong, Malaya, Singapore, the Dutch East Indies, the Philippines and Burma.
The American victory at Midway in June 1942, in which four Japanese carriers were sunk, ended Japan's advance, and the Guadalcanal campaign began the American counter-offensive.
The United States used an island-hopping strategy, backed by submarines and carrier air power, to approach Japan, and later bombed Japanese cities with B-29 bombers.
Japan surrendered after the atomic bombs and the Soviet declaration of war on 8 August 1945; the formal surrender was signed on 2 September 1945.
The Axis powers of Germany, Italy and Japan were linked by formal treaties, but their war aims were not coordinated and they often acted separately.
The Pact of Steel of 22 May 1939 bound Germany and Italy into a military alliance, although Italy was not ready for war when it entered in June 1940.
The Tripartite Pact of 27 September 1940 added Japan to the Axis, recognising the leadership of Germany and Italy in Europe and of Japan in East Asia.
Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and Slovakia later joined the Axis, and Finland fought alongside Germany against the Soviet Union.
Italy's defeats in Greece and North Africa in 1940 and 1941 forced Germany to intervene in the Balkans and in North Africa, drawing forces away from Barbarossa.
The Axis powers did not share a joint strategy, and Germany and Japan did not coordinate their attacks on the Soviet Union and the United States.
Britain, the Soviet Union and the United States formed a wartime coalition in which cooperation over strategy and the future of Europe was often strained.

Churchill and President Franklin Roosevelt issued the Atlantic Charter in August 1941, setting out shared principles including self-determination and the restoration of sovereignty to those deprived of it.
The Soviet Union joined the Allied coalition after Barbarossa, and Stalin repeatedly called for a second front in Western Europe to relieve pressure on the Red Army.
The Tehran Conference of November and December 1943 brought Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin together for the first time, and it set the plan for the invasion of France.
The Yalta Conference of February 1945 agreed the occupation zones of Germany, the principle of free elections in liberated Eastern Europe and the entry of the Soviet Union into the war against Japan.
Disputes over the timing of the second front, the future of Poland and the Soviet occupation of Eastern Europe foreshadowed the tensions of the Cold War.
The Allied victories of 1942 and 1943 reversed the Axis advance, and the Normandy landings of June 1944 opened the way to the defeat of Germany.
The Second Battle of El Alamein, from October to November 1942, defeated the Axis armies in North Africa under Erwin Rommel, and the Allies landed in Morocco and Algeria the same month.
The Battle of Stalingrad ended in February 1943 with the surrender of the German Sixth Army, and the Battle of Kursk in July 1943 became the last major German offensive in the east.
The Allies invaded Sicily in July 1943 and Italy's government surrendered in September 1943, but Germany occupied most of northern and central Italy.
The Normandy landings (D-Day) began on 6 June 1944, and Allied forces broke out of the beachheads and liberated Paris on 25 August 1944.
The Soviet Red Army advanced into Poland and the Balkans in 1944, and the Soviet offensive on Berlin began in April 1945.
Hitler killed himself in Berlin on 30 April 1945, and German forces surrendered in May 1945, with the surrender at Reims on 7 May and in Berlin on 8 May.
Technological developments shaped the war on land, at sea and in the air, and the decisive use of the atomic bomb ended the war against Japan.
Tanks: the German Panzer divisions used radio communication and combined armour with motorised infantry, while the Soviet T-34 and the American Sherman were produced in large numbers.

Aircraft: strategic bombing by RAF Bomber Command and the US Army Air Forces attacked German cities, causing fires and civilian deaths, with the bombing of Hamburg in July 1943 and Dresden in February 1945 among the most devastating raids.
Radar: the British Chain Home system and later airborne and ship-borne radar gave early warning of attacks and helped locate U-boats and aircraft.
Codebreaking: at Bletchley Park the British decrypted German Enigma messages, and the resulting intelligence, known as Ultra, was used in the Battle of the Atlantic and the North African campaign.
Submarines and convoys: German U-boats sank large numbers of Allied merchant ships in the Atlantic, but the convoy system and escort groups reduced losses from 1943.

Rockets and jets: Germany's V-1 flying bombs were launched against London from June 1944 and its V-2 rockets from September 1944, and later against Antwerp, and the Messerschmitt Me 262 jet fighter entered service in 1944, too late to change the outcome.

Atomic weapons: the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, and Japan announced its surrender on 15 August 1945; the bombs had been developed in the Manhattan Project, and the first test took place in New Mexico on 16 July 1945.
Churchill served as Prime Minister from May 1940 and led Britain through the war and the negotiations of the Grand Alliance.

Born in 1874 at Blenheim Palace into an aristocratic family, he entered Parliament in 1900 as a Conservative, joined the Liberals in 1904, was First Lord of the Admiralty from 1911 to 1915, and was Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1924 to 1929, then spent the 1930s out of office warning against Hitler.
He became First Lord of the Admiralty again in September 1939 and succeeded Neville Chamberlain as Prime Minister on 10 May 1940.
His speech of 4 June 1940 included the phrase 'we shall fight on the beaches', and his leadership in the Battle of Britain made him a symbol of national resistance.
He was a participant in the Allied conferences at Tehran and Yalta and negotiated closely with Roosevelt and Stalin, and he lost office in July 1945 after the general election.
Contemporaries, including some of his own party, criticised his part in the Gallipoli campaign in 1915 and his return to the gold standard in 1925, but his wartime leadership won wide admiration.

Historians have praised his resolve in 1940 and his strategic leadership, while criticising the bombing of German cities such as Dresden, the diversion of forces to the Mediterranean and Greece in 1941, and his attitude to colonial peoples, as in the Bengal famine of 1943.
He became Prime Minister at the head of a coalition including Labour leaders Clement Attlee and Ernest Bevin, and he also acted as Minister of Defence.
His speeches on the radio and in Parliament, including 'blood, toil, tears and sweat' (13 May 1940) and 'their finest hour' (18 June 1940), sustained morale after Dunkirk and during the Blitz.
Between 26 May and 4 June 1940, Operation Dynamo evacuated over 330,000 Allied troops from Dunkirk.
He built a close relationship with Roosevelt, meeting him at Placentia Bay, Washington, Casablanca (January 1943, where unconditional surrender was announced) and Quebec.
In October 1944 he met Stalin in Moscow and proposed the 'percentages agreement' on spheres of influence in the Balkans, which has been seen as a sign of wartime realism or of cynicism.
He attended the Potsdam Conference in July 1945 until the Labour election victory replaced him with Attlee.
The 1920s and 1930s produced the ideas and machines that were used in the Second World War.

Armoured warfare theory by British writers such as J.F.C. Fuller and Basil Liddell Hart, and by the German general Heinz Guderian in Achtung - Panzer! (1937), influenced the formation of German Panzer divisions from 1935.

Air power theorists such as Giulio Douhet argued that bombers would decide wars; the bombing of Guernica in April 1937 by the German Condor Legion in the Spanish Civil War, which tested aircraft and tactics, shocked world opinion.
Britain developed radar from 1935, when Robert Watson-Watt showed that radio waves could detect aircraft, and Chain Home stations were built along the east and south coasts from 1936.
Fighter design improved with the Hawker Hurricane (first flown 1935) and the Supermarine Spitfire (1936), and the Messerschmitt Bf 109 entered service in Germany.
Polish mathematicians broke the early Enigma machine in the early 1930s and passed their methods to Britain and France in July 1939.
Frank Whittle patented the jet engine in 1930, and the first German jet aircraft, the Heinkel He 178, flew in August 1939.
Rocket research by Wernher von Braun for the German army began in the early 1930s and led to the V-2 at Peenemünde.
Judgements of Churchill and the alliances weigh the British war effort and the coalition's success against its divisions and its costs.
Achievement: Britain's refusal to negotiate a peace in 1940 kept open a base from which the Allies could later invade Europe.
Limit: British strategy relied heavily on American resources after 1941, and the British Empire's position in Asia was lost in 1942.
Achievement: the Grand Alliance defeated the Axis powers and produced the United Nations as a post-war organisation.
Limit: the alliance concealed deep divisions over Eastern Europe, and these became the Cold War once Germany was defeated.
Contemporary view: many British people saw Churchill as the embodiment of national resistance, while critics on the left and in his own party questioned his judgement.
Later view: historians still debate how far Churchill's leadership was essential, with some stressing his role in 1940 and others emphasising the decisive contribution of Soviet and American forces.
Britain's government planned the evacuation of children and vulnerable adults from cities in anticipation of air attack, and the first movement took place in the first days of September 1939.
Operation Pied Piper began on 1 September 1939, moving schoolchildren, mothers with young children, the disabled and teachers from London, Birmingham, Liverpool and other cities to the countryside.
About 1.5 million people, most of them children, were evacuated in the first few days of the operation, and the government organised billeting of evacuees in private homes.
Evacuees were received unevenly in the countryside: some host families welcomed them, while others were shocked by poverty, poor hygiene and unfamiliar behaviour.
Many evacuees returned to the cities in late 1939 and early 1940 during the Phoney War, when the expected bombing did not come.
The evacuation exposed the gap between urban poverty and rural comfort, and its social findings were used by reformers to argue for improved health and education services.
Evacuation was repeated in the summer of 1940, when more children were sent away after the Blitz began and the fall of France threatened invasion.
Rationing spread the burden of shortages evenly, and the government's food policy aimed to keep the population healthy on limited supplies.
Rationing of bacon, butter and sugar began in January 1940, and rationing of meat followed in March 1940, with a fixed weekly allowance for each person.
The Ministry of Food, led by Lord Woolton from 1940, controlled food imports, set prices and organised the supply of basic foods such as National Loaf and National Dried Milk.
Clothing was rationed from June 1941 and furniture from 1943, and Utility schemes set minimum standards of design and quality for goods sold at controlled prices.
The Dig for Victory campaign encouraged families to grow vegetables in gardens, allotments and parks, and the Land Army recruited women to work on farms.
Shortages and rationing were accepted by most of the population because they were seen as fair; the government published ration allowances in the press to support confidence.
Rationing continued after the war, and meat was not freed from control until 1954.
The German bombing of British cities from September 1940 tested civilian morale and produced new forms of civil defence and public information.
The Blitz began on 7 September 1940 with the bombing of London's docks, and London was bombed on 57 consecutive nights between September and November 1940.
Anderson shelters, issued free to households from early 1939, Morrison shelters (from 1941) and Underground stations were used as shelters during raids.
The Local Defence Volunteers, renamed the Home Guard in July 1940, were formed in May 1940 to guard against invasion and to support civil defence.
Air Raid Precautions wardens, fire watchers and ambulance crews were among the civilian volunteers who worked during the raids.
The Ministry of Information and the BBC encouraged resilience through broadcasts and posters, and the Mass Observation surveys recorded public opinion and morale.

The Blitz of 1940 and 1941 killed about 40,000 civilians in Britain, over half of them in London, and other cities such as Coventry (14 November 1940), Liverpool, Birmingham and Belfast were heavily bombed.
The blackout, enforced from September 1939, raised road deaths sharply in the first winter, and air raid wardens enforced it.
Children were also sent abroad, and the sinking of the liner City of Benares by a U-boat in September 1940 with the loss of many evacuee children ended the overseas scheme.
Ernest Bevin, as Minister of Labour from 1940, directed workers into war industries, and from December 1943 some conscripts were sent to the coal mines as Bevin Boys.
The Women's Land Army put women to work on farms, and Land Girls helped to raise home food production.
Radio was central to civilian life, with news bulletins, Churchill's broadcasts, and morale shows such as ITMA, and the cinema newsreels and Ministry of Information films provided official messages.
V-1 flying bombs and V-2 rockets killed thousands of civilians in southern England in 1944 and 1945.
The shared experience of danger and rationing encouraged support for government planning and the welfare reforms after 1945.
The war brought women into industry, the armed services and civil defence, and the Beveridge Report of 1942 proposed a welfare state that became a post-war programme.
Women took up war work in factories making aircraft and munitions, and by 1943 women made up a large share of the industrial workforce.
The Auxiliary Territorial Service (ATS), the Women's Auxiliary Air Force (WAAF) and the Women's Royal Naval Service (WRNS) recruited women into the armed services.
The National Service (No. 2) Act of December 1941 required single women aged 20 to 30 to register for war work, and some were conscripted into factories or the services.
The Women's Voluntary Service organised civil defence and welfare work, including the provision of meals and clothing for bombed-out families.
The Beveridge Report, published in December 1942, identified five giants to be defeated: want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness.

The report proposed a comprehensive system of national insurance, family allowances and a national health service; it sold hundreds of thousands of copies, and its recommendations were largely carried out by the National Insurance Act of 1946 and the National Health Service of 1948 under the Labour government, along with the Education Act of 1944 and family allowances from 1945.
Germany's home front was shaped by the economic demands of war, the use of foreign workers and prisoners, and the strain of bombing from 1942.
Germany entered the war with a shortage of labour, and the regime was reluctant to ask German women to work in factories in large numbers before 1942.
After Goebbels's call for total war in February 1943, the regime extended the mobilisation of women and the workforce, though women's employment rose less than in Britain.
By 1944 about seven million foreign workers and prisoners of war from occupied Europe were used in German industry and agriculture, many living in camps under harsh conditions.
Forced labourers from the Soviet Union, known as Ostarbeiter, were treated more harshly than workers from western Europe, and many died from disease, overwork and mistreatment.
Rationing in Germany was tied to the status of the population: German civilians received higher rations than foreign workers and occupied populations.

Allied bombing of German cities caused heavy civilian deaths and the destruction of housing, as in the firestorm at Hamburg in July 1943, and children and families were evacuated from the cities to the countryside in a scheme called the Kinderlandverschickung.
War and occupation produced millions of refugees and displaced people, and their treatment reflected the policies of each government.
In May and June 1940 millions of French people fled from the advancing German army, crowding the roads of northern and central France.

Britain interned about 27,000 German, Austrian and Italian nationals as enemy aliens in 1940, including many refugees from Nazi persecution, and some were sent to the Isle of Man or overseas; over 800 died when the Arandora Star was sunk by a U-boat in July 1940.
The British government gave refuge to some Jewish refugees and to governments in exile, including the Polish, Norwegian and Dutch governments, which were based in London.
Displaced persons in Europe at the end of the war included forced labourers, prisoners of war, concentration camp survivors and people who had fled the Red Army.
Relief and repatriation of displaced people were organised after 1945 by the Allied military authorities and the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration (UNRRA), set up in 1943.
Many occupied peoples cooperated with the German occupiers, from the work of administrations to the active participation in persecution and deportations.
Vidkun Quisling, leader of the Norwegian fascist party Nasjonal Samling, headed a collaborationist government in Norway from February 1942, and his name became a term for traitors.
In the Netherlands the National Socialist Movement (NSB) under Anton Mussert cooperated with German authorities, and Dutch police helped round up Jews for deportation.
In Belgium the Rexist movement led by Léon Degrelle supported the German occupation, and Degrelle later fought in the Waffen-SS on the Eastern Front.
Vichy France under Pétain and Laval collaborated actively in the deportation of Jews and the supply of labour to Germany, and the Milice carried out reprisals against resisters.
Collaboration took many forms, including economic cooperation, the supply of workers and the provision of police and volunteers for German units on the Eastern Front.
Resistance movements ranged from underground newspapers and sabotage to armed partisan warfare and the rescue of persecuted people.
The Polish Home Army (Armia Krajowa), formed in 1942, was the largest underground army in occupied Europe and fought in the Warsaw Uprising of August to October 1944.
The Yugoslav partisans led by Josip Broz Tito fought German, Italian and Croatian forces from 1941, and they gained control of much of the country by 1945.
The White Rose group of Munich students distributed leaflets against the Nazi regime, and Hans and Sophie Scholl were executed in February 1943.
In Denmark, after a warning in early October 1943 of a German round-up, ordinary Danes helped to ferry most of the Jewish community across the Øresund to Sweden, more than 7,000 people in total.
Italian partisans fought the German occupation and the Salò Republic from 1943 to 1945, and the Italian resistance became a major political force after liberation.
The French Resistance and the Polish Home Army were both linked to Allied intelligence and special operations, which provided weapons, radio equipment and training.
For French civilians, occupation meant shortage, fear of reprisal and divided loyalties.
Ration cards were issued by age and work category, and bread, meat, fat and fuel were short; many city dwellers made trips to the countryside to buy food on the black market.
German soldiers requisitioned buildings and food, and curfews, identity checks and the taking of hostages made daily life uneasy.
Allied bombing of French industry and railways before and after D-Day killed tens of thousands of French civilians.
Families coped with the absence of around one and a half million prisoners of war in Germany, and many women had to take over family farms and businesses.
Attitudes changed over time: most people accepted Vichy at first, but the compulsory labour service and the German occupation of the south in November 1942 turned many against Vichy and the Germans.
Many civilians were passive 'attentistes' waiting on events, and only a minority joined the Resistance or actively collaborated.
Judgements of wartime society balance the solidarity and sacrifice of civilians against the wide scale of collaboration, and the limits of resistance.
Achievement: British society sustained the war effort through rationing, evacuation and civil defence, and the Beveridge Report reshaped post-war social policy.
Limit: Germany's home front relied on foreign labour and forced labourers, and its civilians were protected by systematic exploitation of occupied peoples.
Achievement: resistance movements in occupied Europe kept political opposition alive and provided the bases for post-war governments in France, Italy and Yugoslavia.
Limit: most people in occupied Europe neither resisted nor collaborated actively, and resistance remained a small minority of the population until 1944.
Contemporary view: the British public generally accepted the sacrifices of the war and supported the welfare plans that followed.
Later view: historians have examined the extent of collaboration and the myth of a unified resistance, with research since the 1970s showing a more complex and divided record.
Anti-Semitism had a long history in Europe, and the Nazi regime turned it into a racial doctrine that treated Jews as enemies of the German nation.

Anti-Semitism in Europe combined religious hostility, economic resentment and, from the late nineteenth century, racial theories that claimed Jews were a separate and inferior race (the notes on the period before 1914 cover its earlier growth).
Hitler's Mein Kampf of 1925 blamed Jews for Germany's defeat in 1918, for communism and for the Versailles settlement, and it set out the aim of removing Jews from German life.
The Nazi idea of a herrenvolk, a master race of Germanic people, required that Jews be defined as racially alien and excluded from the German community.
The Nazi party's propaganda, including the newspaper Der Stürmer, promoted anti-Semitic stereotypes and encouraged hostility towards Jewish neighbours.
Anti-Semitic thinking was not confined to Germany: in 1938 Italy introduced racial laws excluding Jews from schools, the professions and the armed forces.
Jews made up less than one per cent of Germany's population in 1933, and most had been fully integrated into German economic, cultural and civic life before the Nazi period.
From 1933 the regime excluded Jews from public life through boycotts, dismissals and legal definitions of race.
A national boycott of Jewish shops and businesses was ordered on 1 April 1933, although it was poorly supported and was called off after a day.
The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service of April 1933 dismissed Jewish officials, and later laws excluded Jews from the legal profession, medicine and journalism.
The Nuremberg Laws of 15 September 1935 defined Jews by descent and removed German citizenship from Jews, who became subjects with no political rights.
The Nuremberg Laws also banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and people of German or related blood, and their wording was used to define who was a Jew in later persecution.
Jewish businesses were 'Aryanised' by forced sale or confiscation, transferring their property to non-Jewish Germans at low prices.
