Many German Jews emigrated in these years, although the restrictions on emigrants' property and the difficulty of obtaining visas made flight hard for many.
Violence against Jews escalated in November 1938, and the international effort to find refuge for Jewish refugees failed to match the scale of the crisis.

Kristallnacht, the Night of Broken Glass, took place on 9 and 10 November 1938 after the shooting of the German diplomat Ernst vom Rath in Paris by Herschel Grynszpan, a young Jewish refugee whose family had been expelled to Poland; Goebbels used the news to launch the pogrom.

During the pogrom, Nazi supporters and the SA destroyed over 250 synagogues and damaged more than a thousand, wrecked thousands of Jewish shops and homes, and killed about 90 Jews; Jews were then fined a collective penalty of one billion marks.
About 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to the concentration camps of Dachau, Buchenwald and Sachsenhausen, and many were released only after agreeing to emigrate.
The Evian Conference of July 1938, called by the United States to discuss refugees, was attended by 32 countries, but few agreed to admit more refugees.
Many countries, including the United States and Britain, kept strict limits on immigration, and the quotas for Jewish refugees were not filled in many years.
The Kindertransport carried about 10,000 mostly Jewish children from Germany, Austria and Czechoslovakia to Britain between late 1938 and the outbreak of war.
After the invasion of Poland, the Nazis confined Jews in ghettos and used forced labour and mass shootings in the occupied east.

Following the invasion of Poland in 1939, Jews in occupied Poland were forced to wear an identifying badge, and the yellow star was imposed in Germany from September 1941; property was seized throughout the occupied territories.
Ghettos were set up in Polish cities, the largest being the Warsaw ghetto, sealed in November 1940, holding about 400,000 people, and the Łódź ghetto, sealed in 1940.
Conditions in the ghettos were marked by starvation, disease and overcrowding, and the Nazi authorities used forced labour in factories and on construction projects.
The Einsatzgruppen, mobile killing units of the SS and police, followed the German army into the Soviet Union from June 1941 and carried out mass shootings of Jews, Roma and political commissars.
At Babi Yar near Kiev, about 33,000 Jews were shot on 29 and 30 September 1941, one of the largest single massacres of the war.
The Nazi regime extended the persecution to Roma, people with disabilities and Soviet prisoners of war, who were also murdered in large numbers.
The murder of Jews in the occupied east was systematised in 1941 and 1942, and the Wannsee Conference set out the plan for the deportation and murder of European Jewry.
Historians date the decision for the systematic murder of the Jews to 1941, though no written order from Hitler survives; it was carried out through the Einsatzgruppen, deportations and death camps.
The Wannsee Conference, held on 20 January 1942 near Berlin and chaired by Reinhard Heydrich, coordinated the deportation of Jews from across Europe to camps in the east.

The plan was called the Final Solution of the Jewish Question, and the minutes of the conference record the Jewish population of each European country, about eleven million in all, including countries outside German control.
Gas vans were first used to murder Jews at Chelmno in December 1941, and the Operation Reinhard camps of Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka began operating in 1942.
Between 1942 and 1944 most of the Jews deported from occupied Europe were killed at Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno and Majdanek.
Historians have debated the role of Hitler's orders and the initiative of local officials, but agree that the genocide was a deliberate policy carried out by the state and its agencies.
Jews resisted the persecution in the ghettos and the camps, although the scale of armed resistance was limited by the German control of weapons and information.
The Warsaw ghetto uprising began on 19 April 1943 when Jewish fighters resisted the German attempt to deport the remaining inhabitants, and the fighting lasted until May 1943.
Armed resistance also took place at the Treblinka camp in August 1943 and at Sobibor in October 1943, where prisoners killed guards and escaped.
Jewish partisan groups fought in the forests of Eastern Europe, and the Jewish partisans of the Bielski group rescued families from the ghettos.
Many Jews resisted in quieter ways, including the smuggling of food and arms into the ghettos, the keeping of diaries and the maintaining of schools and cultural life.

Collaboration took the form of police units, local administrators and volunteers who helped round up and deport Jews in occupied countries, including the French police and the Dutch and Lithuanian authorities.
Many bystanders did nothing to stop the persecution, and in some countries neighbours profited from the seizure of Jewish property.
Rescuers hid Jews, forged documents and smuggled people across borders, and Yad Vashem in Jerusalem honours non-Jewish rescuers as the Righteous Among the Nations.
Oskar Schindler, a German industrialist in Krakow, employed Jewish workers in his factory and saved about 1,200 people from deportation to Auschwitz.

Denmark's rescue of most of its Jewish community in October 1943, when over 7,000 were ferried to Sweden, showed that large-scale protection was possible where the population and the local authorities were willing to act.
Soviet and Allied troops liberated the camps in 1944 and 1945, and the Nuremberg trials began the legal prosecution of the leaders responsible.
Soviet troops liberated the Majdanek camp in July 1944 and Auschwitz-Birkenau on 27 January 1945, where they found the remaining prisoners and evidence of the murders.
British and American forces liberated Bergen-Belsen and Dachau in April 1945, and their survivors were among the first witnesses to the camps' conditions.

The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg, which sat from November 1945 to October 1946, tried 22 leading German figures, and its judgments condemned the persecution of Jews as a crime against humanity.
Later trials at Nuremberg and in other countries prosecuted doctors, judges, industrialists and camp staff, and Adolf Eichmann was tried in Jerusalem in 1961.
The regime's racial ideology also led to the persecution and murder of other groups.
A law of July 1933 allowed compulsory sterilisation of people with hereditary conditions, and about 400,000 people were sterilised by 1945.

The Aktion T4 programme, begun in 1939, murdered about 70,000 disabled patients in gas chambers by August 1941, when public protests including Bishop Galen's sermon led to its formal end, although killing continued secretly.
Roma and Sinti, treated as racially inferior, were deported, imprisoned and murdered, with estimates of the dead ranging from about 200,000 to 500,000.
Millions of Soviet prisoners of war died in German captivity from starvation, disease and execution, about three million of the roughly 5.7 million captured.

Homosexual men were arrested under Paragraph 175, Jehovah's Witnesses were persecuted for refusing military service and loyalty oaths, and Slavs in Poland were treated as a labour reserve, with their intelligentsia targeted.
The camps were centres of killing run by the SS, and the Jewish victims came from every country the Germans controlled.

Auschwitz-Birkenau in occupied Poland combined a forced-labour camp with a gas chamber complex using Zyklon B; about 1.1 million people were murdered there, around 1 million of them Jews, and arriving prisoners were selected on the ramp for labour or immediate death.
Treblinka, Belzec and Sobibor were pure killing centres in which the great majority of arrivals were gassed within hours; Treblinka alone accounted for over 800,000 deaths.
In 1944 about 430,000 Hungarian Jews were deported to Auschwitz in under two months, once Germany had occupied Hungary in March, and most were murdered on arrival.

Jews in the occupied cities were ruled by Jewish Councils (Judenräte) that the Germans forced to administer the ghettos and select people for deportation, a role about which survivors and historians still disagree.
As Soviet forces advanced in late 1944 and 1945, the SS forced prisoners on death marches into Germany, in which tens of thousands died of exhaustion, cold and shooting.

National rates of loss varied: about 90 per cent of Polish Jews and a similar share of the Jews of the Baltic states were killed, about three-quarters of Dutch Jews (among them the diarist Anne Frank), and about a quarter of French Jews.
Allied governments knew of the mass killings by late 1942; the Allies declared in December 1942 that they would punish those responsible, but did not bomb Auschwitz or the railways leading to it.
Judgements of the Holocaust focus on its scale and its planning, and on the failure of most states and societies to act to prevent or stop it.
Scale: about six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust, and the murders were carried out across occupied Europe, with about three million Jews from Poland among the victims.
Planning: the Holocaust was a deliberate, state-organised genocide that developed over several years, with decisions taken at each stage of the war.
Failure: Allied governments received reports of the murders from 1942 and were slow to act, and the Evian Conference and Allied immigration quotas limited the rescue of refugees before the war.
Achievement: rescuers and resistance groups saved many Jews, and the Nuremberg trials established the principle that crimes against humanity could be prosecuted.
Contemporary view: many Europeans in the 1930s and 1940s saw the persecution as a domestic German matter or ignored it, and few governments treated it as a priority.
Later view: historians have debated the reasons for the Allied response, the role of the bystanders and the balance between intentions and circumstances in the decision for genocide.
Once in power the Nazis created a state propaganda ministry and brought the press, radio and public entertainment under central control.
The Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda was created on 13 March 1933 under Joseph Goebbels, and it took responsibility for the press, radio, film, theatre, music and the arts.
The Editors' Law of October 1933 required newspaper editors to be members of the Nazi-approved professional organisations, and Jewish journalists were excluded from the press.

Radio was brought under state control in 1933 when the ministry took over the broadcasting companies, and the Volksempfänger (People's Receiver), a cheap radio set costing 76 Reichsmarks, was launched at the Berlin radio exhibition in August 1933 to reach ordinary households; loudspeakers carried major speeches into factories and public squares.
The Reich Chamber of Culture, set up in September 1933 under Goebbels, controlled the members of the arts, and writers, painters, musicians and actors had to be admitted to it to work.
Propaganda used repetition of simple themes, such as national unity, the leader's authority, the threat from communism and the Jews, and the glory of the German nation.
Posters, parades, slogans and mass rallies were used to create a sense of community and to bind people to the leader and the party.
The regime used film and public spectacle to present an image of strength and unity, and it condemned art and literature that did not fit its ideology.
On 10 May 1933 students and party members burned books by Jewish, Marxist and liberal authors in public ceremonies in Berlin and other university towns.

The Degenerate Art exhibition in Munich in July 1937 displayed works by modernist painters, including Expressionists, as examples of decadence, while the Great German Art Exhibition showed approved art at the same time.
The 1936 Summer Olympics in Berlin were used to present Germany as a peaceful and modern nation, and the regime temporarily removed some anti-Semitic signs before the games.
German cinema was controlled through the Reich Film Chamber, which approved scripts and banned films that the regime judged unsuitable, and the state funded films with propaganda messages.
Feature films such as Jud Süß (1940) were made as explicit anti-Semitic propaganda, and they were shown to audiences in Germany and occupied countries.
Goebbels was the Gauleiter of Berlin and the head of Nazi propaganda from 1933 to 1945, and he was responsible for the regime's most important mass campaigns.
Born in 1897 in Rheydt, he studied literature and gained a doctorate before joining the Nazi party in 1924, when he worked for Gregor Strasser's wing of the party.
Hitler appointed him Gauleiter of Berlin in 1926, where he organised street campaigns, newspapers such as Der Angriff and mass meetings to build support in the capital.
He was a participant in the Reichstag election campaigns of 1930 and 1932, using modern techniques such as posters, loudspeaker vans and radio.
As Reich Minister of Propaganda from 1933, he shaped the regime's cultural policies and directed the Nazi response to the Jewish population through the media.
In his speech at the Berlin Sportpalast on 18 February 1943 he called for total war, and his speech was broadcast to the German public.

Historians differ in their view of his power: some see him as the regime's most effective propagandist and one of Hitler's most loyal followers, while others stress his rivalry with Himmler, Göring and Ribbentrop; his influence rose again from 1944 when he became Plenipotentiary for Total War, and he killed himself with his wife after poisoning their six children in Berlin on 1 May 1945.
Riefenstahl was a film-maker whose documentaries of the Nazi party's rallies and the 1936 Olympics gave the regime its most influential visual image.
Born in Berlin in 1902, she trained as a dancer and actress and made mountain films before Hitler commissioned her to film the party's rallies.
She was a participant in the Nazi film project, directing Triumph of the Will (Triumph des Willens) of 1935, which recorded the 1934 Nuremberg Rally.
Her documentary Olympia, released in 1938, covered the 1936 Berlin Olympics, and it used innovative camera techniques to present athletic achievement as a national triumph.

Contemporaries in Germany praised her technical achievement, Triumph of the Will won the German National Film Prize in 1935 and a gold medal at the Paris exposition of 1937, and foreign audiences saw her films as a powerful example of cinematic art, while critics abroad recognised their propaganda purpose.

After 1945 she claimed that her films were artistic documents rather than propaganda and denied knowing of the crimes of the regime; after several hearings she was classified as a fellow traveller (Mitläufer) in 1952, and she died in 2003 aged 101.
Historians have judged her films as among the most effective propaganda ever made, and they continue to debate the boundary between art and political propaganda in her work.
Nuremberg was chosen for the party's annual rally because of its historic association with German culture and its suitability for mass gatherings.
The Nazi party held its first large rally in Nuremberg in August 1927, and the city became the site of the annual party rally, known as the Reichsparteitag.
Nuremberg was a medieval imperial city with a strong sense of German history, and the Nazis used its historic buildings and traditions to link the regime with the German past.
The rally grounds were built on the Dutzendteich area to the south of the old city, and the largest planned building, the Congress Hall, was never completed.
The Zeppelin Field, with a grandstand designed by Speer, was used for mass parades and the appearance of the Führer before the party's formations.
The Luitpold Arena was used for the mass assemblies of the SA, SS and Hitler Youth, and the arena was designed to hold large numbers of marching men.
Speer's design for the rallies used massed banners, stone architecture and, from 1934, about 130 anti-aircraft searchlights pointed upwards at night, which became known as the cathedral of light.
Each year's rally had a theme that reflected the regime's stage of development, and the rallies expanded from party gatherings into national spectacles.
The 1933 rally, held in September, was the first held after Hitler became Chancellor, and it was called the Rally of Victory.

The 1934 rally of 4 to 10 September was filmed by Riefenstahl in Triumph of the Will, and it was the first after the Night of the Long Knives; it featured mass parades of the party, the SA and the SS, and army units, as a demonstration of unity.
At the 1935 rally, called the Rally of Freedom and held in September, the Reichstag met in Nuremberg, and the Nuremberg Laws were announced there on 15 September 1935.
The 1936 rally was called the Rally of Honour and the 1937 rally was called the Rally of Labour and included parades of workers and the Labour Service.
The 1938 rally, held in September just before the Munich Agreement, was called the Rally of Greater Germany, and it celebrated the Anschluss and the German expansion.

The 1939 rally, planned as the Rally of Peace, was cancelled at the outbreak of war, and after 1945 the rally grounds were used by the US Army and the city, with parts of the Zeppelin Field surviving today.
The rallies aimed to create emotional bonds between the leader, the party and the German people, and they were designed for both those who attended and the wider public.
Hundreds of thousands of party members, workers, soldiers and youths travelled to Nuremberg, and many found the rallies a powerful experience of collective belonging.
The rallies used ritual, including the consecration of party banners, torchlight processions and the oath of loyalty, to create a sense of sacred purpose.
Newsreels, radio and the press reported the rallies to the German public, and Riefenstahl's films extended their reach to cinemas in Germany and abroad.
Participants were organised into units and marched in disciplined formations, which created a visual impression of unity and order.
Foreign visitors and journalists were impressed by the rallies, and some saw them as evidence of the order and vitality of the new Germany.
The rallies also served to publicise the regime's laws and policies, including the 1935 Nuremberg Laws, and to present anti-Semitic ideas as part of the national community.

Riefenstahl's earlier film of the 1933 rally, Victory of Faith, was withdrawn after the murder of Ernst Röhm in 1934, which is one reason Triumph of the Will shows Hitler and the party as the sole leadership.
Triumph of the Will opens with Hitler's aeroplane descending through clouds over Nuremberg and is built on contrasts of the individual leader and the massed ranks, with music by Herbert Windt.
Control worked through licensing, daily instructions and a mixture of entertainment and political messages.

The Reich Press Chamber and the ministry's daily press conferences told editors what to print, and the Nazi publisher Max Amann bought up or closed many independent papers; the party paper Völkischer Beobachter and Goebbels's own Der Angriff were prominent.

Radio mixed light music and entertainment with news and speeches by Nazi leaders, and from 1939 listening to foreign broadcasts such as the BBC was a crime punishable by prison or, in serious cases, death.

The cinema was the most popular medium: entertainment films outnumbered political ones, but every programme included a newsreel, and from 1940 the single Deutsche Wochenschau newsreel was shown across occupied Europe.
Posters and slogans such as 'Ein Volk, ein Reich, ein Führer' were widely displayed, and youth and women's organisations, schools and the Labour Front were used for indoctrination.

The regime promoted the cult of Hitler as the saviour and father of the nation through the 'Heil Hitler' greeting, his birthday celebrations, portraits in public buildings and books of photographs by his photographer Heinrich Hoffmann.
A standard programme of set pieces over about a week made each rally a ritual of loyalty.
Each rally had days for particular groups: the party leadership, the Labour Service, the Hitler Youth, the SA and SS and, from 1935, the armed forces.

At the Luitpold Arena Hitler walked between ranks of tens of thousands of SA and SS men to lay a wreath at the war memorial, in 1934 with SA chief Viktor Lutze and Himmler, a staged image of the new order after the purge of Röhm.
In the consecration of the flags, Hitler touched new standards with the Blood Flag, said to have been carried in the Munich Putsch of 1923.
At the 1934 rally the Labour Service marched with spades, and the 'cathedral of light' made a night-time spectacle for the first time.
Hitler's speeches, usually delivered at night or in the evening when crowds were most receptive, expressed party doctrine and foreign policy, and at the 1936 rally the Four Year Plan was announced.
Rallies also had a popular side, with special trains, free food and accommodation in camps, and much of the cost was met by the party and by industry.
Judgements of Nazi propaganda weigh its success in creating consent and loyalty against the limits of persuasion and the role of terror in maintaining order.
Achievement: propaganda helped the Nazis build popular support in the 1930s, and the rallies and films gave the regime a powerful image of unity.
Limit: propaganda could not by itself sustain support, and the regime relied on the police, the courts and the camps to suppress opposition.
Contemporary view: many Germans responded to the rallies with enthusiasm, while exiled opponents and foreign critics saw them as an exhibition of dictatorship.
Later view: historians have debated how far the population believed the propaganda and how far it accepted the regime for other reasons, such as economic recovery and national pride.
Achievement: Riefenstahl's films remain among the most studied examples of film propaganda, and they have shaped the way later film-makers have used visual rhetoric.
Limit: after 1943 the propaganda effort focused increasingly on defence and national survival, and its credibility declined as the war turned against Germany.
The Lateran Treaties of 1929 ended the long dispute between the Italian state and the papacy and gave the Fascist regime Catholic support.
Since 1870 the popes had regarded themselves as prisoners in the Vatican, after the Italian state took Rome and ended the papal states.
The Lateran Treaties were signed on 11 February 1929 by Mussolini and Cardinal Pietro Gasparri, and they created the independent state of Vatican City.

The Italian state paid the Church compensation of 1.75 billion lire (750 million in cash and 1,000 million in government bonds) for the loss of the papal states, and the Church recognised the Kingdom of Italy with Rome as its capital.
Under the Concordat part of the treaties, Catholicism was recognised as the sole religion of the Italian state, and religious marriage was given civil effect.
Mussolini gained the support of the Catholic majority, and the Church's endorsement helped legitimise the regime in the eyes of many Italians.

The treaties were ratified in June 1929, and the Church gained religious teaching in state schools, state-paid priests and the recognition of Catholic marriage, in return for accepting the Italian state.
Relations between the regime and the Church worsened when the regime tried to control Catholic youth organisations, and the racial laws of 1938 caused further tension.

In 1931 the regime clashed with Catholic Action, the Church's lay organisation, over its youth and student groups, which the regime saw as rivals to the Fascist youth movement; Fascist squads attacked Catholic centres and the regime closed many of its branches, and in June Pius XI protested in the encyclical Non abbiamo bisogno.
An agreement of 1931 limited Catholic Action to religious, cultural and charitable activities, and it kept its youth groups out of politics and sport.
Apart from the 1931 encyclical, the Church's objections were mostly made in private diplomacy and in the Vatican's press, and Pope Pius XI rarely challenged Mussolini openly.

Mussolini's Manifesto of the Race, published in July 1938, defined the racial basis of Italian identity, and the racial laws of September to November 1938 excluded Jews from schools, the professions and the armed forces.
The Church opposed the racial laws in part, since they challenged the Catholic doctrine that all people shared a common humanity, but it did not break with the regime.
The Vatican's relationship with Italy was affected by the alliance with Germany, and the Church's independence was limited by the regime's pressure on the Catholic press and youth.
Hitler signed a Concordat with the Vatican in 1933, but he also planned to bring the Protestant churches under Nazi control through a single Reich Church.
The Reich Concordat between Germany and the Holy See was signed on 20 July 1933 and was intended to protect Catholic institutions and schools in return for the Church's withdrawal from politics.
The Centre Party, the main Catholic party, dissolved itself on 5 July 1933 as the Concordat was being concluded, and Catholic organisations in Germany lost much of their political role.

The German Christians, a pro-Nazi movement within German Protestantism, won about two-thirds of the seats in the Protestant church elections of July 1933, and they called for a single Protestant Reich Church under Nazi control.
Ludwig Müller, a German Christian, was appointed Reich Bishop of the new Protestant Reich Church in September 1933, but his leadership was challenged within the churches.

The Reichskirche plan sought to remove the independence of the Protestant regional churches, to exclude Jewish Christians from church office, and to replace Christian doctrine with an ideology of race and national blood.
The Nazi regime violated the Concordat within a few years, closing Catholic schools and youth organisations, and arresting Catholic priests and religious.
Opposition to the regime's control of the churches came from the Confessing Church among Protestants and from Catholic bishops and the papacy.
The Confessing Church was formed in opposition to the German Christians, and its founding Barmen Declaration of 31 May 1934 rejected the state's claim to control the Church's teaching.
Martin Niemöller, a Protestant pastor and former U-boat commander, led opposition to Nazi control, was arrested in 1937, and was held in concentration camps until 1945.
Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a Lutheran theologian, joined the Confessing Church's opposition and was later involved in the conspiracy against Hitler; he was executed at Flossenbürg in April 1945.

Pope Pius XI's encyclical Mit brennender Sorge (With Burning Anxiety) of 14 March 1937 criticised Nazi violations of the Concordat and the racial ideology, and it was read from pulpits in Catholic churches.

Clemens August von Galen, Bishop of Münster, preached sermons in July and August 1941 against the murder of people with disabilities under the euthanasia programme, and the programme was halted in August 1941.
The Church's protests were limited to defending its own institutions and to opposing the euthanasia programme, and the churches did not openly challenge the persecution of Jews on the same scale.
Radio became a mass medium in the 1920s and 1930s, and governments used it to inform, entertain and persuade listeners.
The British Broadcasting Company was founded in 1922 and became the British Broadcasting Corporation in 1927 under John Reith as its director-general, with a public service remit.
The American networks NBC, founded in 1926, and CBS, founded in 1927, were commercially financed and competed for advertisers and audiences.
President Franklin Roosevelt began his fireside chats on the radio in March 1933, speaking directly to listeners about the New Deal and, later, the war.
In Britain the BBC Home Service carried news, music and government information during the war, and Churchill made radio broadcasts to the nation at key moments.
The American Forces Network broadcast entertainment and news to Allied troops in Britain and Europe from 1942, and it played American popular music to a wide audience.
The German government used radio to reach the population, and William Joyce, known as Lord Haw-Haw, broadcast propaganda from Germany to Britain from 1939.
Cinema was the most popular mass entertainment of the 1930s, and Hollywood dominated the world market, while British and European film industries sought to protect their own production.
The Warner Brothers film The Jazz Singer, released in 1927, introduced synchronised sound to mainstream cinema and led to the rapid spread of talking pictures.
The Hollywood studio system of the 1930s, dominated by major studios such as MGM, Paramount, Warner Brothers and Fox, produced and distributed most of the films shown in Britain and Europe.
The Cinematograph Films Act of 1927 required cinemas in Britain to show a quota of British films, which aimed to protect the domestic industry against American competition.
Newsreels such as Pathé and British Movietone News brought the events of the 1930s to cinema audiences in Britain, and Germany and Italy used newsreels for propaganda.
In Germany American films were restricted from the mid-1930s and in effect excluded by 1940, and German cinema was dominated by home-made films and newsreels.
During the war Hollywood and British studios made films to support the war effort, including morale films and documentaries, while the American government used films to explain the war to the public.
Chaplin was a British-born comedian and film-maker whose Tramp character made him the most famous film star of the silent era, and whose later films criticised modern society and the dictators.
Born in London in 1889, he began on the stage as a child and was a member of a music hall troupe before he went to the United States in 1913 and joined the Keystone studio.
The Tramp character first appeared in 1914 and was developed in films such as The Kid (1921), The Gold Rush (1925) and City Lights (1931).
He was a participant in the Hollywood studio system, and he made Modern Times in 1936, a satire on industrial life and mechanisation, in which the Tramp is caught in the machinery of a factory.

In The Great Dictator, released in 1940 and his first full sound film, he played both a Jewish barber and Adenoid Hynkel, a parody of Adolf Hitler, ruler of Tomania, and it was a major commercial success in the United States; Chaplin, born four days before Hitler in April 1889, later said he would not have made it had he known the full horror of the camps.
Contemporaries admired his comic genius, but some American politicians and newspapers criticised his political views, and in the 1940s his leftist sympathies led to difficulties with the authorities.

Historians have judged Chaplin's work as a major achievement in silent and sound cinema, while debating the political content of his later films and the reasons for his departure from the United States in 1952.
Crosby was an American singer and actor whose radio shows, records and films made him the most popular entertainer of his age, and whose songs were heard across the world during the war.
Born in Tacoma, Washington, in 1903, he sang with a jazz band before becoming a radio singer in the early 1930s, when he developed his relaxed crooning style with microphone technique.
He made hundreds of records and starred in films, including the Road series with Bob Hope from 1940, and he won the Academy Award for Best Actor for Going My Way (1944) at the 1945 ceremony.

His recording of White Christmas, written by Irving Berlin, was released in 1942 for the film Holiday Inn and became one of the best-selling songs of all time; its longing for home made it hugely popular with troops.
Crosby entertained Allied troops during the war through radio broadcasts and USO tours, including a tour of Britain and France in 1944, and his popularity with the forces was very high.
Contemporaries in the United States and Europe saw him as an embodiment of American easy-going popular culture, and his music spread the sounds of American radio into Europe.
Historians tend to present Crosby as a key figure in the development of the modern popular music industry, and his role in wartime morale is studied alongside that of other entertainers.
Governments used entertainment to sustain morale and to explain the war.
Britain's Ministry of Information backed films such as In Which We Serve (1942), and radio shows such as ITMA (It's That Man Again) kept up spirits.
Vera Lynn's song We'll Meet Again (1939) became a symbol of separation and hope for servicemen and families.
The BBC's news bulletins gained a reputation for trustworthy reporting, in contrast to German propaganda, and BBC broadcasts to occupied Europe included coded messages to resisters.
Hollywood made films such as Mrs Miniver (1942), which won the Best Picture Oscar, and Casablanca (1942), and Frank Capra's Why We Fight series explained the war to American troops.
German troops and civilians popularised the song Lili Marleen, broadcast from a German-run station in Belgrade, which Allied soldiers also listened to.
By the late 1930s Hollywood films filled most of the screens in Britain and much of Europe, and the cinema was the weekly habit of millions, including young women and the working class.
Nazi Germany condemned jazz and swing as 'degenerate', but swing youth in Hamburg and other cities defied the ban, and the regime responded with arrests.
Fascist Italy imposed quotas on American films and used a state film body, Cinecittà, built in 1937, to boost home production.

In Britain, critics worried about the effect of Hollywood and American radio on language, taste and morals, and the Cinematograph Films Act and the BBC's public service ethos were partly a response to this.

American troops arriving in Britain from 1942 brought with them swing, chewing gum and cheap goods and sparked both admiration and resentment, summed up in the phrase 'overpaid, oversexed and over here'.
Lasting consequences were the dominance of American popular music and film in postwar Europe.

Judgements of church-state relations weigh the concordats and the Church's survival against the regimes' control of religious life, and judgements of popular culture weigh its appeal against state control and cultural reaction.
Achievement for Mussolini: the Lateran Treaties ended the dispute with the papacy and brought the Church's support to the Fascist regime for a decade.
Limit for Mussolini: the Church resisted the regime's attempt to take over Catholic youth, and it withdrew its support over the racial laws of 1938, though not openly.
Achievement for Hitler: the Concordat secured the Catholic institutions in Germany, and the regime avoided a rupture with the Catholic population in the early 1930s.
Limit for Hitler: the Reichskirche failed to unify the Protestant churches, and the Confessing Church and Catholic protests exposed the limits of Nazi control over religion.
Contemporary view: the Lateran Treaties were welcomed by Catholics around the world, while critics on the left saw them as a bargain that made the Church complicit in Fascism.

Later view: historians stress that American popular culture spread widely in Europe during the 1930s and became a key influence on European youth, despite attempts by the dictatorships to restrict it.
The wartime alliance of the USA, Britain and the Soviet Union held while Germany was defeated, but the aims of its members diverged once the war ended.

Yalta Conference (4–11 February 1945): Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin agreed that Germany would be divided into occupation zones and that Poland would have a government broadened to include non-communists, with free elections promised.
The occupation zones had been agreed by the Allies in 1944. The Soviet Union took the east, the USA the south and centre-west, Britain the north-west and France the south-west.
Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone and was itself divided into four sectors, one for each occupying power.
Potsdam Conference (17 July–2 August 1945): Truman, Stalin and, after the British election, Attlee, disputed reparations and the German–Polish border.
Stalin's security aim was a buffer of friendly governments along the Soviet western frontier, after invasions from the west in 1914 and 1941.
The USA tested its first atomic bomb on 16 July 1945 and used atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August; the Soviet Union tested its own bomb in August 1949, ending the American monopoly.

At Yalta the Allies also agreed that the Soviet Union would join the war against Japan, and the Declaration on Liberated Europe promised free elections in liberated states; Stalin's later disregard of it fed Western distrust.
In October 1944 Churchill and Stalin had informally split influence in the Balkans (the percentages agreement), giving the Soviet Union the lead in Romania and Bulgaria and Britain in Greece.
President Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945, and Harry Truman, who took a harder line towards Moscow, became president.
The Red Army occupied Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, eastern Germany and much of Czechoslovakia by May 1945, so Soviet power on the ground shaped what the West could demand.
Poland was the first flashpoint: the Soviet Union backed the communist-dominated Lublin government, while Britain and the USA backed the London-based government-in-exile.
The Allies agreed broad aims for a defeated Germany, but each occupying power ran its own zone, so the aims were never fully put into practice.
Potsdam set four aims for Germany: demilitarisation, denazification, democratisation and decentralisation, with the economy to be run as a single unit.
Each power took reparations from its own zone, and the Soviet Union also dismantled factories and shipped machinery east from its zone.
The Soviets wanted reparations from the industrial Ruhr in the west; the Western powers refused, because they wanted the western zones to recover.
The territory east of the Oder and Neisse rivers was placed under Polish and Soviet administration until a peace treaty, and German inhabitants were expelled from it.
Without a peace treaty, Germany remained under the control of the four occupying powers, which met as the Allied Control Council in Berlin.
By 1947 the zones were drifting apart economically, and the Western powers concluded that the single economy the Allies had agreed on could not be restored.
From 1946 the Western powers publicly named the Soviet Union as the threat and began to offer aid and military guarantees to Europe.
George Kennan, a US diplomat in Moscow, sent his 'Long Telegram' (22 February 1946) arguing that Soviet expansion would have to be contained by firm resistance at points of pressure.
Churchill's speech at Fulton, Missouri (5 March 1946) said that from Stettin on the Baltic to Trieste on the Adriatic an iron curtain had descended across the Continent.
Stalin answered in an interview in Pravda, presenting Churchill's speech as a call for war against the Soviet Union.
In February 1947 Britain told Washington that it could no longer afford to support Greece and Turkey, which created the opening for the USA to take on that role.

Truman Doctrine: on 12 March 1947 President Truman asked Congress for about 400 million dollars of aid to Greece and Turkey, which faced communist insurgency (Greece) and Soviet pressure over the Turkish straits; Congress approved it in May 1947.
Marshall Plan: announced by Secretary of State George Marshall in a speech at Harvard on 5 June 1947, it provided about 13 billion dollars of US aid through the European Recovery Programme (1948–52).
The Soviet Union and its eastern allies were pressed to refuse Marshall aid; Czechoslovakia and Poland had shown interest before withdrawing in July 1947.
The Cominform, founded in September 1947, linked the communist parties of Europe under Soviet direction.

The Greek Civil War (1946–49) between the royal government and communist guerrillas was the first test of the Truman Doctrine; the guerrillas were defeated in 1949 and Greece stayed in the Western camp.
Marshall's offer was open to all of Europe, but Stalin forbade eastern states to take part, and the Soviet delegation walked out of the Paris conference in July 1947.
Western Europe received Marshall aid as grants and loans, with 16 countries sharing it through the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation, set up in 1948.
Sovietisation was the process by which communist parties, backed by the Red Army and Soviet security police, took full control of states that had previously had mixed or non-communist governments.
In 1945–47 communist parties usually governed through coalitions with peasant, socialist and liberal parties, while controlling key posts such as the interior ministry and the police.

The Hungarian communist leader Mátyás Rákosi later boasted of slicing away his opponents one thin piece at a time; the phrase salami tactics is usually attributed to him and describes the method used across the region.
Poland: sixteen leaders of the Polish underground were arrested and tried in Moscow in 1945, and the peasant leader Stanisław Mikołajczyk left Poland in October 1947 after rigged elections.
Romania: King Michael was forced to abdicate on 30 December 1947 and a people's republic was proclaimed.
Czechoslovakia: in February 1948 non-communist ministers resigned over police control, and Klement Gottwald's communists took power without a general election.
Show trials and purges eliminated rivals, including the Hungarian foreign minister László Rajk, executed in 1949 after a trial in Budapest.
Land reform in 1945–47 broke up large estates in Poland, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and the Soviet zone of Germany, and gave land to small farmers, which helped the communists win support.
Soviet-style institutions followed: single-party rule, secret police, central planning, and collectivisation of farms in most states.
Yugoslavia under Tito was expelled from the Cominform in June 1948, showing that communist states could break from Moscow without ceasing to be communist.

Hungary: in the free election of November 1945 the communists won only about 17 percent against about 57 percent for the Smallholders; Rákosi then used the police and ministry of the interior to break the Smallholders, and fraud in the 1947 election gave the communists the largest share.
Bulgaria: the Fatherland Front government, dominated by communists, abolished the monarchy after a referendum in 1946, and the opposition leader Nikola Petkov was executed in 1947.
Czechoslovakia was the only eastern state to remain democratic until 1948; the death of the foreign minister Jan Masaryk on 10 March 1948, in a fall from a window, shocked Western opinion.
Poland: the Polish Workers' Party and Polish Socialist Party were merged into the Polish United Workers' Party in December 1948, ending independent socialist opposition.
Albania under Enver Hoxha and Yugoslavia under Tito had communist governments that came to power largely through their own wartime resistance rather than the Red Army.
The Soviet Union refused Marshall aid and built its own trade system, which later became the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance.
Eastern European states were bound to the Soviet Union by bilateral trade agreements in which their trade was directed towards Moscow.
A Soviet-led aid and trade offer to eastern Europe in 1947, often called the Molotov Plan, was the alternative to Marshall aid.
Comecon, the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance, was set up in January 1949 to coordinate trade and planning among the Soviet bloc states.
Eastern bloc states were not allowed to take part in the Marshall Plan, which divided Europe into two economic systems.
Soviet reparations and dismantling in eastern Germany slowed recovery there and made the Soviet zone economically dependent on Moscow.
The Western zones were merged and rebuilt, which the Soviet Union opposed, and the split between the two halves of Germany became permanent by 1949.
The American and British zones were merged into Bizonia on 1 January 1947, and the French zone was added in 1948–49 after the London talks, creating a single western area.
A currency reform in the Western zones on 20 June 1948 introduced the Deutsche Mark, which the Soviet authorities saw as a threat to their zone.
The Soviet Union blockaded road, rail and canal access to West Berlin from June 1948, cutting the Western sectors off from supplies.
The Western powers organised an airlift that flew in food, fuel and other supplies; it delivered over two million tons before the blockade was lifted on 12 May 1949.
The Federal Republic of Germany was founded on 23 May 1949 with a Basic Law drafted by a parliamentary council; Konrad Adenauer became its first chancellor in September 1949.

The German Democratic Republic was proclaimed on 7 October 1949 in the Soviet zone, where the Socialist Unity Party had been formed in April 1946 by merging the communist and social democratic parties.
Berlin stayed divided: West Berlin was run by the Western powers and closely tied to the Federal Republic, while East Berlin was declared the capital of the German Democratic Republic.
Stalin's aim in the blockade was to force the Western powers to abandon the new currency and their plans for a West German state, or to drive them out of Berlin.
General Lucius Clay, the American military governor, and the Berlin mayor Ernst Reuter led the Western and Berlin response; Truman refused to withdraw.
The airlift (Operation Vittles) flew into the Tempelhof, Gatow and Tegel airfields, with planes landing at times about every minute.
Each bloc formed an alliance for collective defence, and the Warsaw Pact was created largely in response to West German membership of NATO.
The Brussels Treaty of March 1948 linked Britain, France and the Benelux countries in a defensive alliance that became the basis for NATO.

The North Atlantic Treaty was signed in Washington on 4 April 1949 by twelve states, including the USA, Canada and most West European countries; its Article 5 treats an attack on one member as an attack on all.
West Germany joined NATO in May 1955, after its rearmament had been agreed.
The Warsaw Pact was signed in Warsaw on 14 May 1955 by the Soviet Union and seven eastern European states, and Soviet forces were stationed in member states.

The Warsaw Pact's founding members were the Soviet Union, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, East Germany and Albania; Albania stopped taking part in 1961 and formally withdrew in 1968.
NATO's first Secretary General was Lord Ismay, and the alliance's purpose was commonly summed up as keeping the Americans in, the Russians out and the Germans down.
Historians have disagreed about responsibility, and the opening of Soviet archives after 1991 changed the terms of the debate.
Traditional Western accounts blamed Stalin's ideological drive for expansion and the threat it posed to Western Europe.

Revisionist historians from the late 1950s, such as William Appleman Williams in The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959), argued that US economic expansion and the atomic monopoly provoked Soviet hostility.
Stalin's control of eastern Europe went far beyond a defensive buffer, through rigged elections, purges and one-party rule.
Western decisions such as the currency reform of June 1948 deepened the division of Germany, which Soviet leaders could regard as a threat.
Soviet archives opened after 1991 gave historians more evidence of Stalin's aims, but debate continues over how far he planned expansion beyond eastern Europe.
Historians who stress the defensive side point to the wartime invasions of Russia; those who stress the offensive side point to the speed with which communist rule was imposed in 1947–48.
Khrushchev led the Soviet Union from Stalin's death in 1953 to 1964 and set the terms of the Cold War between de-Stalinisation and nuclear confrontation.
Born in 1894 in Kalinovka, a village in Kursk province, he rose through the Communist Party under Stalin, becoming first secretary of the Moscow party in 1935 and of the Ukrainian party in 1938.
He was a participant in the Great Purge in Ukraine and Moscow in the late 1930s, which later made his attacks on Stalin's terror open to challenge.
After Stalin's death in March 1953 he became First Secretary of the Central Committee in September 1953, and he defeated rivals such as Georgy Malenkov and Lavrentiy Beria in power struggles.
In his secret speech to a closed session of the 20th Party Congress on 25 February 1956 he denounced Stalin's cult of personality and terror; the text was published in the West within months.
He argued at the same congress that war with the capitalist states was not inevitable, which became known as peaceful coexistence.
Contemporaries in the West saw him as unpredictable and aggressive, while Mao Zedong's China criticised him as a revisionist who had abandoned Marxist-Leninist purity.
Historians such as William Taubman, in Khrushchev: The Man and His Era (2003), describe a reformer whose policies were improvised and often failed, but whose de-Stalinisation opened Soviet society.

Rise to power, 1953–57: Beria was arrested in June 1953 and executed that December; Malenkov was forced to resign as premier in 1955; in June 1957 Khrushchev defeated the 'anti-party group' of Molotov, Malenkov and Kaganovich with help from Marshal Zhukov and the Central Committee, and in March 1958 he added the premiership to his party post.

Foreign initiatives of the thaw: he agreed to the Austrian State Treaty and withdrew Soviet troops from Austria in 1955, visited Tito's Yugoslavia in 1955 to mend the 1948 split, and attended the Geneva summit of July 1955.
At the 1959 American National Exhibition in Moscow Khrushchev and Vice-President Nixon held the 'kitchen debate' on the merits of communism and capitalism.
On 14 October 1964 the Central Committee removed him from the posts of First Secretary and chairman of the Council of Ministers, while he was on holiday in the Black Sea.
Leonid Brezhnev became First Secretary of the party and Alexei Kosygin chairman of the Council of Ministers.
His critics cited the Cuban humiliation, the failed agricultural and economic reforms, and his erratic style of leadership.
He was pensioned off and lived in retirement, largely at a dacha outside Moscow, until his death in 1971.
His fall confirmed that the Soviet leadership would not tolerate a single figure dominating policy, which shaped the more collective style of the Brezhnev years.
Khrushchev's domestic programme loosened Stalinist controls but its economic experiments produced mixed results.
De-Stalinisation released many political prisoners, reduced the role of the secret police and allowed more open discussion in literature.
The Virgin Lands campaign from 1954 ploughed up grassland in Kazakhstan and Siberia to grow grain, and it produced good harvests in its early years.
Droughts and poor management later brought failures, most seriously in 1963, when the harvest fell and grain had to be imported.
In 1957 industry was decentralised into regional economic councils, a reform that was later reversed by his successors.
The Novocherkassk strike of June 1962 over food prices and wages was suppressed by troops who fired on the crowd, a sign of the limits of his reforms.
Space achievements boosted prestige: Sputnik 1 was launched on 4 October 1957, and Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on 12 April 1961.
The crises before Khrushchev set the pattern of confrontation without direct war.
Berlin Blockade (1948–49): the first major crisis, ended by the airlift and followed by the founding of NATO.

Korean War (1950–53): the North Korean invasion of the South in June 1950 persuaded Western governments that communism was expansionist, and led to the rearmament of NATO, the creation of a unified NATO command under Eisenhower and the push to rearm West Germany.
Stalin's death on 5 March 1953 opened a more flexible phase; an armistice in Korea followed in July 1953.
Berlin was the most dangerous flashpoint in Europe, because West Berlin was an enclave inside East Germany and a window to the West.
On 27 November 1958 Khrushchev issued an ultimatum giving the Western powers six months to agree to a settlement that would end their occupation of West Berlin.
Khrushchev's visit to the USA in September 1959, including talks with Eisenhower at Camp David, produced a brief thaw that the U-2 incident later ended.
The Paris summit of May 1960 collapsed after the U-2 spy plane piloted by Francis Gary Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union on 1 May 1960.
At the Vienna summit in June 1961 Khrushchev pressed the new US president John F. Kennedy on Berlin, and the crisis deepened over the summer.
East German forces began building the Berlin Wall on 13 August 1961, closing the border between the two halves of the city.
The Western powers did not use force against the Wall, accepting it as the price of avoiding war; Kennedy is reported to have said that a wall was better than a war.
Between 1961 and 1989 the Wall and the border fortifications around it were guarded, and people who tried to cross were shot or arrested.
The Cuban Missile Crisis was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear war, and it was resolved by a compromise that Europeans watched closely.
In October 1962 US reconnaissance photographs showed Soviet medium-range missiles being installed in Cuba, within range of much of the USA.
President Kennedy announced a naval quarantine of Cuba on 22 October 1962 and demanded the removal of the missiles.

For about a week the two superpowers were on the brink of war; Kennedy sent former secretary of state Dean Acheson to brief the French president de Gaulle, who gave firm support, while most European governments learned of the crisis only as it unfolded.
On 28 October 1962 Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the missiles in return for a US pledge not to invade Cuba.
The secret part of the deal was a US promise to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey, which was not made public at the time.
The crisis shaped later arms control: a Moscow–Washington hotline was set up in 1963, and the Partial Test Ban Treaty followed in August 1963.
Khrushchev's motives were to defend Castro's Cuba after the Bay of Pigs invasion of 1961, to offset US missiles in Turkey and Italy, and to narrow the Soviet Union's weakness in long-range missiles.

The crisis began on 16 October 1962 when Kennedy was shown U-2 photographs; Kennedy's advisers (ExComm) weighed an air strike against a naval blockade and chose the blockade, described publicly as a quarantine.
Seen from Europe, the crisis showed that Berlin and Cuba were linked, and made West European leaders more aware that decisions on nuclear war would be taken in Washington and Moscow.
Each superpower relied on nuclear weapons to deter attack, and limited agreements grew out of the fear that deterrence could fail.
Nuclear deterrence meant that each side kept enough weapons to destroy the other after a first strike, a condition later called mutually assured destruction.
The Soviet Union tested the 50-megaton Tsar Bomba on 30 October 1961, the largest nuclear explosion ever set off.
The Partial Test Ban Treaty, signed in Moscow on 5 August 1963 by the USA, Britain and the Soviet Union, banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space and under water.
The Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968 committed non-nuclear states not to acquire nuclear weapons, while the nuclear powers agreed to pursue disarmament.
Western Europe depended on the US nuclear umbrella under NATO, and debates in France and Britain over independent deterrents reflected doubts about that protection.
France tested its first atomic bomb in 1960 and developed its own deterrent, which it kept outside NATO's military command from 1966.
The ideological dispute with Mao's China grew from the late 1950s and became open in 1960, when Soviet advisers were withdrawn from China.
The Sino-Soviet split meant the Soviet Union faced two rival communist powers and could not count on Chinese support in Europe.
Albania sided with China and in 1968 became the only member state to leave the Warsaw Pact.
Soviet leaders regarded the Berlin Wall as a means of stabilising the German Democratic Republic, which had lost about 2.7 million people to the West since 1945.
Détente was a period of easing tension, from about 1969 to the late 1970s, in which the superpowers and European states signed agreements on arms and borders.
Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik sought better relations with Eastern Europe; the Treaty of Moscow of 12 August 1970 renounced the use of force between the Federal Republic and the Soviet Union.
The Four Power Agreement on Berlin of 3 September 1971 guaranteed access between West Berlin and West Germany and confirmed the Western presence in the city.
The Basic Treaty of 1972 established relations between the Federal Republic and the German Democratic Republic, which led to both joining the United Nations in 1973.
SALT I, signed on 26 May 1972, limited anti-ballistic missile systems and placed interim limits on strategic offensive missiles.
The Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe produced the Helsinki Final Act on 1 August 1975, signed by 35 states including the USA, Canada and the Soviet Union.
The Final Act recognised existing borders in Europe and committed signatories to respect human rights, a commitment that later dissidents used to press their governments.
Détente broke down in the late 1970s, and a new arms race in Europe led to the deployment of intermediate-range missiles in the early 1980s.
On 24 December 1979 Soviet forces invaded Afghanistan, and the USA responded with a grain embargo and a boycott of the Moscow Olympics in 1980.
NATO's double-track decision of 12 December 1979 agreed to deploy Pershing II and cruise missiles in Western Europe unless arms talks with the Soviet Union succeeded.
The Soviet Union had deployed SS-20 intermediate-range missiles in the late 1970s, which threatened Western Europe.
Large peace demonstrations took place in West Germany, Britain and the Netherlands in 1981–83 against the deployment of the new missiles.
The Soviet leadership's fear of a Western first strike led to a serious misreading during the NATO exercise Able Archer 83 in November 1983.
The crisis was defused by arms negotiations, and the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty was signed in December 1987 under Gorbachev.
Examiners ask which events changed the course of the Cold War, so know the order and what each changed.
Berlin Blockade, 1948–49: confirmed the division of Germany and led to NATO.
Hungary, 1956: showed that the Soviet Union would use force to keep its bloc together.
Berlin Wall, 1961 and Cuba, 1962: the high points of confrontation, after which both sides sought safeguards such as the hotline and the Test Ban Treaty.
Prague Spring, 1968: the invasion of Czechoslovakia confirmed the Brezhnev Doctrine but did not end détente.
Helsinki, 1975: the high point of détente, which gave dissidents in the East a human rights standard.
Afghanistan and the Euromissiles, 1979: ended détente and began the second Cold War.
Reagan's election in 1980 brought a hard line: in March 1983 he called the Soviet Union an evil empire, and announced the Strategic Defense Initiative.

Gorbachev from 1985, the Reykjavik summit of October 1986 and the INF Treaty of 1987 reversed the arms race, and 1989 ended Soviet control of eastern Europe (see the notes on reform movements and the collapse of communism).
Khrushchev's record is judged by contrasting his bold moves with the setbacks that ended his rule.
Achievements: de-Stalinisation, the Partial Test Ban Treaty, the hotline, the Austrian State Treaty of 1955 and the space successes.
Failures: the Virgin Lands harvest crises, the reversal of his administrative reforms, and the Cuban settlement, which Soviet leaders saw as a retreat.
Contemporary Western views often focused on his unpredictability, while his Soviet colleagues attacked his rash 'hare-brained schemes' and his boasting.
Later historians have judged him as a reformer who opened the system but never built a lasting alternative to Stalinist planning.
The Berlin Wall, which his policy helped to produce, was for many observers the most lasting symbol of his era, and later assessments weigh it heavily against his reform record.
Nagy was a Hungarian communist who became the symbol of reform inside the party and was executed after the uprising.

Born in 1896, Nagy was a communist who spent much of the 1930s and early 1940s in the Soviet Union and returned to Hungary with the Red Army in 1944, serving as minister of agriculture in 1945 when land was distributed to peasants.
He was prime minister from 1953 to 1955, pursuing a New Course of consumer goods, relief for farmers and looser controls against the Stalinist policies of Mátyás Rákosi.
Rákosi had him removed in April 1955 and expelled from the party later that year, after Nagy had criticised collectivisation and heavy industry.

During the uprising he was a participant: he was reappointed prime minister on 24 October 1956, announced Hungary's neutrality and its withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact on 1 November, and appealed to the West for help.
Contemporaries in the Soviet bloc saw him as a traitor; Kádár's government branded him a counter-revolutionary, and he was tried in secret.

Nagy was executed on 16 June 1958, together with Pál Maléter and others, and buried in an unmarked grave; historians now treat him as a national martyr and a reformer who was the uprising's political leader.
He was reburied with a state ceremony on 16 June 1989, the thirty-first anniversary of his execution, as the regime was collapsing.
Hungary under Rákosi was one of the most rigidly Stalinist states of the Soviet bloc, and events in the Soviet Union and Poland in 1956 weakened its leadership.
Mátyás Rákosi led the Hungarian communists from the late 1940s and ran a one-party state with show trials, a powerful secret police (the AVH) and forced collectivisation of farms.
The Hungarian economy was run on Soviet lines, with heavy industry favoured and living standards falling, which fuelled resentment among workers and peasants.
Khrushchev's secret speech of 25 February 1956 exposed the crimes of Stalin's era and gave Hungarian reformers a precedent for criticising their own leaders.
Rákosi was forced to resign in July 1956 and was succeeded by Ernő Gerő, a Stalinist who lacked popular support.

The Polish October of 1956, when Władysław Gomułka returned to power after pressure from Poland's workers and party, encouraged Hungarian intellectuals in the Petőfi Circle and the Writers' Union to demand change.
Cardinal József Mindszenty, the head of the Hungarian Catholic Church, was jailed in 1949 in a show trial; the regime's attack on the Church added to resentment.

Nagy's New Course of 1953 followed Soviet pressure on the Hungarian leaders after Stalin's death; Rákosi stayed as party leader and used his control of the party to undermine Nagy, which divided the communists.
The AVH secret police, which spied on and arrested ordinary citizens, was the best-known instrument of Rákosi's rule and the main target of popular hatred.
Hungary also had large economic burdens: Soviet reparations in the late 1940s and obligations to supply the Soviet Union, which kept living standards low.
A student demonstration in Budapest turned into a national uprising within a day.
On 22 October students in Budapest drew up a list of sixteen demands, including free elections, the withdrawal of Soviet troops and the return of Imre Nagy as prime minister.
On 23 October a large crowd gathered at the statue of Stalin, which was pulled down, and a delegation tried to broadcast the demands on Radio Budapest.
The AVH secret police opened fire on the crowd outside the radio building, which triggered fighting across Budapest.
Soviet troops entered the city, and the Gerő government asked Moscow for help, which it received on the same night.
Armed civilians and army units joined the fighting, and the uprising spread to other towns in the following days.
For about a week Hungary had a reformed communist government and Soviet troops were pulling back, before the second intervention.

Nagy was reinstated as prime minister on 24 October 1956 and sought a ceasefire; he ordered Soviet troops out of Budapest, and the Soviet government announced on 30 October that it was prepared to negotiate the withdrawal of its forces.
On 30 October Nagy formed a coalition with non-communist parties, including the Smallholders and the Social Democrats, and the Communist Party was reduced to a minority role.
Workers' councils formed in factories and in Budapest, and some of them organised strikes and demanded genuine workers' control.
On 1 November Nagy declared Hungary neutral and announced its withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact, and he appealed to the United Nations.

Kádár, who had joined Nagy's government and become party leader on 25 October, left Budapest on 1 November, held talks with the Soviet leaders, and with their backing formed a rival government that was proclaimed on 4 November and based at Szolnok in central Hungary.

The Soviet leadership decided on 31 October to intervene again; fresh Soviet troops crossed the border from 1 November, and the main attack, Operation Whirlwind, began on 4 November, even as Soviet delegates were negotiating a withdrawal.
On 30 October a crowd attacked the party headquarters at Republic Square in Budapest and lynched several AVH men and party officials; the revolution's violence was used later by Soviet propaganda.
Cardinal Mindszenty was freed from house arrest on 30 October and returned to Budapest, and political prisoners were released.

Khrushchev and the Soviet Presidium at first leaned towards a negotiated settlement, but the declaration of neutrality, the end of one-party rule and the Suez crisis helped to convince them to intervene.
On 4 November 1956 Soviet forces returned in strength, crushed the fighting in Budapest and removed Nagy's government.
The second intervention began on 4 November 1956 with a large Soviet force that attacked Budapest and the provincial centres.
Nagy broadcast an appeal to the nation and the world that Soviet troops were attacking Hungary; he then took refuge in the Yugoslav embassy in Budapest.
Pál Maléter, the Hungarian minister of defence, was arrested while negotiating with the Soviet commanders and later executed alongside Nagy.
Kádár became prime minister on 4 November and formed a government that was backed by Soviet troops.
Nagy left the Yugoslav embassy on 22 November after a Soviet promise of safe passage, and he was taken away by Soviet forces that same day.
Fighting in Budapest continued until mid-November, with workers' councils calling a general strike that paralysed the country for weeks.
The uprising ended with a Soviet victory and a long repression, and the scale of the casualties and flight is the most widely quoted measure of its cost.
Commonly cited estimates put the Hungarian dead at about 2,500 to 3,000 and the Soviet dead at several hundred (often given as about 700); figures vary between sources and are approximate.
About 200,000 Hungarians fled to Austria and beyond, among them many young and skilled people; sources give varying figures, so the number is approximate.
Many thousands were arrested in the months after the uprising, and hundreds were executed in the years that followed under Kádár's government.
Nagy was lured from the Yugoslav embassy, taken to Romania, then returned to Hungary and tried in secret with Maléter and others; he was executed on 16 June 1958, with the verdict decided in advance.
Kádár's regime later moved to a policy of consolidation and limited reform, which in time became known as goulash communism.
The uprising coincided with the Suez crisis, and the Western powers did not intervene, which shaped Soviet calculations.

Israel invaded Egypt on 29 October 1956, and Britain and France bombed Egypt from 31 October and landed at Port Said on 5–6 November, drawing American and international attention away from Hungary at the crucial moment.
Radio Free Europe broadcast messages of encouragement to Hungarians, and Western politicians used the language of liberation, but no Western government intervened militarily.
The UN Security Council debated the Hungarian question but the Soviet Union vetoed action; the General Assembly condemned the Soviet intervention, but no UN force was sent.
Eisenhower publicly ruled out military intervention, reflecting the risk of a wider war and US caution over Soviet nuclear power.
The refugees who reached Austria were welcomed in the West, and their arrival was a propaganda victory for the West, though it did not change the outcome in Hungary.
Radio Free Europe's broadcasts were widely taken by Hungarians as promises of Western help, and the station was criticised afterwards for raising false hopes.
Western communist parties lost members and intellectuals after Hungary, and the uprising damaged the Soviet Union's reputation among the left.
The uprising was crushed because the Soviet Union was willing to use overwhelming force and the West would not act, but it left a lasting legacy in Hungary.
Soviet willingness to use force was decisive, because Moscow regarded Hungary's departure from the Warsaw Pact as unacceptable to its security.
The uprising had no organised armed leadership beyond local groups, and the negotiations with Soviet commanders failed to produce a lasting arrangement.
Its significance was that it confirmed the limits of de-Stalinisation in eastern Europe and showed that Soviet control would be defended by force.

Kádár's later policy of compromise (summed up in his 1961 saying that whoever is not against us is with us) and the New Economic Mechanism of 1968 allowed Hungarians more consumer goods and some market elements, as the price of political obedience.
The reburial of Nagy on 16 June 1989 and the later recognition of 23 October as Hungary's national day showed the collapse of communist authority in Hungary.
Contemporary views differed: Soviet and Kádár propaganda described a counter-revolution led by fascist elements, while Western reporting presented a national and largely anti-communist rising.

Hungary's declaration of neutrality and withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact crossed the line that the Soviet leaders would tolerate; Poland's Gomułka had stayed within the alliance and was allowed to survive.
Tito, who was consulted by Khrushchev before the second intervention, accepted the need to defeat the uprising but disliked Kádár's methods.

The memory of 1956 shaped later events: Czechoslovak reformers in 1968 promised to stay in the Warsaw Pact to avoid Hungary's fate, and Soviet leaders drew the lesson that force might be needed again.
Historians disagree about the uprising's character, and the answer shapes judgement of Nagy and of the West.
Achievements: within days the uprising forced Soviet withdrawal, a multi-party government and a declaration of neutrality, which no other satellite had achieved.
Limits: the uprising relied on the goodwill of Soviet commanders, and it had no means of defending itself once Moscow chose to use force.
Later historians differ between those who see a popular anti-communist revolution and those who see a reformist communist revolt that grew beyond its leaders.
Nagy's reputation was rehabilitated after 1989, but judgements of his communism, his tactics and his naivety about Soviet intentions remain debated.
Gorbachev was the Soviet leader whose reforms opened the way to the end of communist rule in eastern Europe and to the break-up of the Soviet Union.
Born in 1931 in Privolnoye in the Stavropol region, he studied law at Moscow State University, rose through the Communist Party in Stavropol, and became a full member of the Politburo in 1980.
He became General Secretary of the Communist Party on 11 March 1985, and in 1988 he became chairman of the Supreme Soviet, and in 1990 the first executive president of the USSR.
He pursued glasnost, which meant greater openness and criticism of the past, and perestroika, a restructuring of the economy that tried to combine market elements with planning.
He was a participant who chose not to use force in eastern Europe, and he withdrew Soviet troops from Afghanistan by February 1989.
Contemporaries in the West welcomed him: Margaret Thatcher, before he came to power, judged that he was a man she could do business with, and Reagan negotiated arms agreements with him.
Conservatives at home regarded him as having destroyed the Soviet system, while many Russians later blamed him for economic collapse.
Historians differ on whether he intended to end communism or to save it, and most agree that his reforms had consequences he did not foresee.

Gorbachev rose under the patronage of Yuri Andropov, and as General Secretary he drew on a generation of younger reformers, including Alexander Yakovlev and Eduard Shevardnadze (foreign minister from 1985).
His early slogan was uskorenie, acceleration of economic growth; when it failed he moved to perestroika and, at the 27th Party Congress in February 1986, to openness.
Democratisation: in 1989 the first partly free elections to the Congress of People's Deputies were held in March, and in 1990 the party gave up its constitutional monopoly of power.
He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990 for his role in ending the Cold War.
Karol Wojtyła, elected pope in 1978, supported the Polish opposition to communism and became a political figure as well as a religious leader.
Born in Wadowice in 1920, he was Archbishop of Kraków and became a cardinal in 1967 before being elected pope on 16 October 1978, the first non-Italian pope since 1523.
His visit to Poland from 2 to 10 June 1979 drew very large crowds, and it encouraged Poles to organise independently of the state.
He met Lech Wałęsa during his 1983 visit to Poland and gave moral support to Solidarity, which the Polish authorities tried to suppress.
He was shot in St Peter's Square on 13 May 1981 by Mehmet Ali Ağca, and he attributed his survival to divine intervention.
Contemporaries in the Polish and Soviet governments saw him as a threat, and the Polish state security services monitored the Church closely.

Historians disagree about how far he caused the 1989 revolutions; many see him as a moral leader who strengthened Polish civil society, while others stress the economic and political factors that made communism unsustainable.
During the 1979 visit he spoke in Warsaw's Victory Square in a Mass attended by hundreds of thousands, and many Poles took his call for the renewal of their land as encouragement to demand change.
Gdańsk strikers in August 1980 displayed the pope's portrait at the shipyard gate, and many Poles saw his election and visit as having given them the confidence to organise.
After martial law he visited Poland in 1983 and 1987 and used sermons to defend workers' rights without calling for revolt; in 1989 he received Gorbachev in the Vatican on 1 December.
Reform in eastern Europe repeatedly appeared and was suppressed, which showed the limits of Soviet tolerance.

East German workers rose on 17 June 1953 against increased work norms and shortages, and Soviet tanks suppressed the uprising in East Berlin and other towns; it spread to hundreds of towns before it was crushed.
Poznań workers protested in June 1956, and Władysław Gomułka returned to power in October 1956 after a confrontation with Moscow that was resolved without Soviet intervention.
Poland's October 1956 settlement allowed limited autonomy for the Church and for intellectuals, but the Polish party maintained one-party rule.
Czechoslovakia's Alexander Dubček became First Secretary of the Communist Party in January 1968, and he launched the Prague Spring reforms.
The Soviet response in each case combined concession and threat: Poland in 1956 won a new leadership, Hungary in 1956 was crushed, and Czechoslovakia in 1968 was invaded.
Poland's Gomułka ended forced collectivisation in 1956 and released Cardinal Wyszyński from internment, but by the 1960s he had reimposed tight controls.
The Prague Spring of 1968 tried to create socialism with a human face, and Soviet and Warsaw Pact forces ended it by force.
The Action Programme of April 1968 proposed freedom of expression, a looser press, the rehabilitation of victims of the 1950s and limits on the secret police.
Dubček's government also planned economic reforms that allowed more market mechanisms, and it promised a federal settlement between Czechs and Slovaks.

On 20–21 August 1968 Warsaw Pact forces from the Soviet Union, Poland, Hungary and Bulgaria invaded Czechoslovakia (East German units were mobilised but did not cross), and Dubček was arrested and taken to Moscow; Romania refused to take part.
Albania withdrew from the Warsaw Pact in protest against the invasion.

The Brezhnev Doctrine, set out in a Pravda article in September 1968 and in Brezhnev's speech to the Polish party congress that November, held that socialist states had a duty to intervene when socialism was threatened in another socialist state.
Gustáv Husák replaced Dubček and presided over a period of normalisation, in which many reformers were removed from office and purged from the party.
Charter 77, a document of Czechoslovak dissidents issued in January 1977 and led by Václav Havel, demanded that the state observe the human rights it had accepted.
Solidarity was the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc, and its rise forced the communist state to recognise an opposition.
Strikes at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk in August 1980 led to the Gdańsk Agreement of 31 August 1980, which recognised the right to form independent trade unions.
Solidarity was led by Lech Wałęsa, an electrician at the shipyard, and at its peak in 1981 it had about ten million members.
Its demands included free trade unions, the right to strike, better food supplies and access to the media.
On 13 December 1981 General Wojciech Jaruzelski declared martial law, arrested Solidarity leaders and banned the union.

The Polish authorities argued that martial law prevented a Soviet invasion; historians accept that Moscow had pressed for firm action but that Jaruzelski also acted to keep communist control, and Soviet archives show the Soviet leaders did not plan to send troops in.
Solidarity was legalised again in April 1989 after the Round Table talks between the government and the opposition from February to April 1989.
In 1989 communist rule collapsed across eastern Europe in a series of peaceful transfers and one violent revolution, largely without Soviet intervention.

In Poland, Solidarity won almost all of the seats it contested in the June 1989 elections, and in August 1989 Tadeusz Mazowiecki became prime minister of the first non-communist government in the Soviet bloc since 1948.

In Hungary the government began dismantling the border fence with Austria in May 1989, allowed East Germans to cross to Austria from September 1989, and Imre Nagy was reburied as a national hero in June 1989, while in the autumn the party accepted multi-party elections.
