East German citizens fled through Hungary and Czechoslovakia, and mass demonstrations in Leipzig and East Berlin forced Erich Honecker's resignation on 18 October 1989.
The Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November 1989 after an announcement that was misread as permitting unrestricted crossings.
In Czechoslovakia the Velvet Revolution began with a student demonstration on 17 November 1989, and Václav Havel was elected president on 29 December 1989.
In Bulgaria Todor Zhivkov was removed on 10 November 1989, and in Romania Nicolae Ceaușescu was executed on 25 December 1989 after a violent uprising.
Gorbachev's reforms at home and his non-intervention abroad removed the props that had kept communist states in power.
Chernobyl exploded on 26 April 1986 in Soviet Ukraine, and the official response was criticised for concealment, which strengthened the case for glasnost.
The INF Treaty of 8 December 1987 eliminated US and Soviet intermediate-range missiles, a landmark in arms control.
Gennady Gerasimov's remark in October 1989 that the Brezhnev Doctrine had been replaced by the Sinatra Doctrine meant that Eastern European states could choose their own path.
Lithuania declared independence on 11 March 1990, and other Soviet republics followed in demanding sovereignty.
The Warsaw Pact was dissolved on 1 July 1991 and Comecon was dissolved in June 1991.
A conservative coup against Gorbachev on 19–21 August 1991 failed after Boris Yeltsin rallied opposition in Moscow, and it accelerated the break-up of the union.
The Soviet Union was dissolved on 26 December 1991, a day after Gorbachev resigned as its president.
Gorbachev and Reagan met at Geneva (November 1985) and Reykjavik (October 1986), where they discussed deep cuts in nuclear weapons, and signed the INF Treaty at Washington in December 1987.
Gorbachev told the United Nations in December 1988 that the Soviet Union would cut its armed forces by 500,000 men and withdraw divisions from eastern Europe.
Boris Yeltsin was elected president of the Russian republic in June 1991 and became the main rival to Gorbachev's authority.
The eight leaders who staged the coup in August 1991 included the vice-president, the head of the KGB and the defence minister; it left Gorbachev weakened and the republics moved to leave the union.
The end of communism led to the reunification of Germany, the break-up of Yugoslavia and the new alignments of central Europe.
The German Democratic Republic and the Federal Republic were unified on 3 October 1990, under the Two Plus Four settlement signed in September 1990.

The Visegrád group of Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary was formed in February 1991 to coordinate their approach to integration with the West; its members later joined NATO (1999 for Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic) and the EU (2004).
Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991, and fighting followed in Slovenia and Croatia, while Bosnia and Herzegovina's independence led to war from 1992.
Czechoslovakia divided peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993, after the elections of 1992.
The Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania regained independence in 1991 and sought membership of Western institutions.
Germany: the chancellor Helmut Kohl pushed for rapid unity after the Wall fell; a currency union came into force on 1 July 1990, and the Two Plus Four Treaty let a united Germany remain in NATO.

Yugoslavia: after Tito's death in 1980 a federal presidency governed; from 1991 Serbia under Slobodan Milošević opposed the secession of Slovenia and Croatia, and the war in Bosnia (1992–95) was the most savage conflict in Europe since 1945.
The European Community recognised Slovenia and Croatia in January 1992, and the Baltic states were admitted to the United Nations in September 1991, as Western institutions began to expand eastwards.
Historians explain the collapse through economic failure, the loss of legitimacy, and the decision not to use force.
Achievements of Gorbachev: arms control, the withdrawal from Afghanistan, freedom of speech and the peaceful transfer of power across eastern Europe.
Failures of Gorbachev: a worsening economy, the rise of nationalism in the republics and the failure to reform the party's monopoly fast enough.
Some historians stress the structural weakness of the command economy and the cost of the arms race, which the West pressed on through defence spending.
Others stress the agency of opposition movements such as Solidarity and Charter 77, which kept reform alive through repression.
Contemporary Western opinion often credited Reagan's firm policy, while later historians give more weight to the Soviet system's internal crisis.
Monnet was a French planner and diplomat who designed the first European communities and is widely called a founding father of European integration.
Born in Cognac in 1888, he worked in the family brandy business and then in international finance and diplomacy, including as deputy secretary-general of the League of Nations from 1919 to 1923.
During the Second World War he coordinated Anglo-French supply and proposed a union between France and Britain in June 1940, which was rejected.
As head of the French planning commission from 1946 he produced the Monnet Plan for modernising French industry, which relied on state investment.
He drafted the Schuman Declaration of 9 May 1950, which proposed pooling French and West German coal and steel production under a joint authority.
He was the first president of the High Authority of the European Coal and Steel Community from 1952 to 1955, and in 1955 he founded the Action Committee for the United States of Europe.
Contemporaries in France were divided: supporters praised him as a builder of peace, while Gaullists opposed the supranational powers he wanted.
Historians present him as an enthusiast for supranationalism who designed a method of gradual integration, though some stress that his role was as a planner rather than a politician.
Delors was the French socialist who led the European Commission from 1985 and relaunched integration through the single market and monetary union.
Born in Paris in 1925, he worked in the French planning and social service systems, and he was French finance minister in the Mitterrand government from 1981 to 1984.
He became president of the European Commission in January 1985, a post he held until 1995, the longest tenure in the Commission's history at that time.
He drove the Single European Act of 1986, which set a deadline of 1992 for completing a single market without internal border controls.
He chaired the committee whose 1989 report set out a three-stage route to economic and monetary union, which became the basis of the Maastricht Treaty.
He was a participant in the Maastricht negotiations of 1991, which created the European Union and committed member states to a single currency.
Margaret Thatcher opposed his federalist ideas and his social policy, and she said the Commission was overreaching; supporters across the EEC credited him with reviving the Community.
Historians credit him with the relaunch of the 1980s, though they debate how far his federalist vision was shared by member states.
After 1945 Western Europeans sought unity to prevent a return of war, to contain Soviet power and to rebuild their economies.
Reasons for unity after 1945: the wish to end Franco-German rivalry, the Soviet threat and the need for economic recovery, helped by American support for integration through Marshall Aid.
The Council of Europe was founded in London on 5 May 1949 by ten states, with its seat at Strasbourg, and it was a forum for debate rather than a source of binding law.
Its consultative assembly in Strasbourg lacked the power to make laws, which disappointed federalists who had wanted a European parliament with real authority.
The European Convention on Human Rights, drafted within the Council of Europe, was opened for signature in 1950 and entered into force in 1953.
Winston Churchill called in a speech at Zurich in September 1946 for a kind of United States of Europe, built on reconciliation between France and Germany, though he expected Britain to stay outside.
The Hague Congress of May 1948 brought together several hundred European political figures, with Churchill presiding, and led to the creation of the Council of Europe the following year.
Federalists such as Altiero Spinelli and Paul-Henri Spaak wanted a political federation, while the British and Scandinavian governments favoured cooperation between states.
The Benelux customs union of Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg came into effect in 1948 and served as a model for later integration.
The first supranational community was created to pool the coal and steel industries of France and West Germany.
The Schuman Declaration of 9 May 1950 proposed a joint high authority for French and West German coal and steel, open to other European states.
The Treaty of Paris, signed on 18 April 1951 by France, West Germany, Italy and the Benelux countries, created the European Coal and Steel Community, which came into force in July 1952.
The ECSC's High Authority had powers that were supranational: it could set prices and quotas and impose fines on firms, without needing the approval of member governments.

Coal and steel were the raw materials of the wartime arms economies, and pooling them under a common authority made a new war between France and Germany harder to imagine; the Saar and the Ruhr had been sources of Franco-German friction.
The Schuman Plan's economic logic was that a common market in coal and steel would give each state access to more resources at lower cost.

Robert Schuman, the French foreign minister, announced the plan on 9 May 1950; Monnet and Schuman had agreed that a joint authority for coal and steel would make war between France and Germany materially impossible.
Konrad Adenauer welcomed the plan because it treated West Germany as an equal and ended the international control of the Ruhr; the British Labour government declined to take part.
The ECSC also had a Common Assembly, a Council of Ministers and a Court of Justice, which became the model for the later institutions.
The attempt to create a European army under supranational control failed, and it pushed integration towards economic rather than military union.
The European Defence Community was proposed in 1950 by the French prime minister René Pleven, as an answer to West German rearmament within a supranational army.
The treaty establishing the EDC was signed in May 1952, but the French National Assembly rejected it on 30 August 1954.
The rejection was driven by fears of German rearmament, Gaullist and communist opposition, and the view of some that national sovereignty over the army must be kept; Britain had refused to join.
After the EDC failed, West Germany joined NATO in 1955, and the Western European Union was created to include West Germany in defence arrangements.
The Treaties of Rome created a customs union and a common market, and the EEC became the core of European integration.
The Messina Conference of June 1955 relaunched the project, and the Spaak Report of 1956 proposed a common market and atomic energy community.
The Treaties of Rome were signed on 25 March 1957 by the six ECSC members and came into force on 1 January 1958.
The EEC aimed at a customs union, with internal tariffs removed and a common external tariff, and at free movement of goods, services, capital and workers.
Euratom was created by the second treaty to develop nuclear energy for civil use across the six states.
The Common Agricultural Policy began in 1962 and set common prices for farm products, and it quickly became the largest item of the EEC's budget.
The customs union was completed in July 1968, eighteen months ahead of the original timetable.
The European Free Trade Association, formed in 1960 by Britain, Austria, Denmark, Norway, Portugal, Sweden and Switzerland, was a looser alternative for states that rejected supranationalism.

The EEC's institutions were the Commission (which proposed legislation, led at first by Walter Hallstein), the Council of Ministers, the European Parliament (then an appointed assembly) and the Court of Justice; the three communities' executives were merged in 1967.
The first president of the Commission, Walter Hallstein of West Germany, served from 1958 to 1967 and was a leading federalist.
Britain applied to join in 1961 under Harold Macmillan after the success of the EEC, and Ireland applied in 1961 and 1967 alongside Britain, but both applications were halted by de Gaulle's vetoes.
Charles de Gaulle opposed supranational institutions and used vetoes and a boycott to block British membership and to assert national sovereignty.
De Gaulle vetoed British membership of the EEC on 14 January 1963 and again on 27 November 1967, on the grounds that Britain was too closely tied to the USA.
The empty chair crisis began in June 1965 when France withdrew its representatives from the Council of Ministers over the financing of the CAP and the powers of the Commission.
The Luxembourg Compromise of January 1966 gave each member state a veto over matters it regarded as vital national interests, which weakened majority voting.
De Gaulle's vision was a Europe of nations, cooperating on intergovernmental lines, which contrasted with the federalist and supranational model of Monnet.
The EEC grew from six to twelve members, and the 1980s relaunch aimed at completing the single market and creating monetary union.
Britain, Ireland and Denmark joined the EEC on 1 January 1973, and Greece joined in 1981.
Spain and Portugal joined on 1 January 1986, which brought the membership to twelve.
The European Monetary System was launched on 13 March 1979, and its Exchange Rate Mechanism linked member currencies within fixed bands.
Britain's budget rebate, agreed at Fontainebleau in June 1984, reduced its net contribution, and it eased the dispute over the budget that had dogged the Community.
The Single European Act, signed in February 1986 and in force from July 1987, extended qualified majority voting and set the goal of a single market by 1992.
The Maastricht Treaty, signed on 7 February 1992, created the European Union, set out a timetable for economic and monetary union and introduced European citizenship.

The Hague summit of December 1969 agreed to enlarge the Community and to work towards monetary union, and membership talks with Britain, Ireland, Denmark and Norway followed; Norway's voters rejected membership in 1972.
Ireland joined after a referendum in May 1972 in which about 83 percent voted in favour; Britain confirmed its membership in a referendum in June 1975.
The first direct elections to the European Parliament were held in June 1979.
The Delors Commission published a White Paper in 1985 listing nearly 300 measures to remove physical, technical and fiscal barriers, and in 1989 the Social Charter set out workers' rights.

Maastricht set the aim of a single currency by 1999 at the latest, set up a common foreign and security policy and cooperation on justice and home affairs, and allowed Britain to opt out of the single currency and the social chapter.
Historians and politicians disagree about whether integration was a steady advance or a series of compromises between federalists and nationalists.
Achievements: peace between France and Germany, the creation of a single market and the growth of membership from six to twelve.
Limits: the CAP's costs, the British budget dispute, de Gaulle's vetoes and the failure of the EDC, which showed that defence remained a national matter.
Federalists regarded the Maastricht Treaty as the beginning of a political union, while intergovernmentalists insisted that member states remained the decision-makers.
Later historians stress that the EEC's success rested on the compromises reached between national governments, not on the supranational method alone.

Effects of unity: trade between members grew rapidly, farmers had guaranteed prices under the CAP, poorer regions received money from the structural funds, and citizens gained rights to live and work across the Community.

Thatcher's Bruges speech of 1988 (see the notes on Thatcher) was the sharpest statement of the intergovernmental position, and she opposed Delors's drive towards a social dimension and a single currency.
Western Europe emerged from the war with damaged cities, disrupted trade and food shortages, which made reconstruction the first priority.
Much of the industrial capacity of Germany, France and Italy was damaged or destroyed, and transport networks, bridges and ports had to be rebuilt.
Coal shortages in the harsh winter of 1946–47 slowed factories across Western Europe, and rationing of food and fuel continued in several countries into the late 1940s.
Britain borrowed heavily from the USA after the war, including an Anglo-American loan of about 3.75 billion dollars agreed in 1945.
Western Europe had a large trade deficit with the USA, which meant that it could buy American goods only with dollars it did not have.
About 12 million German refugees and expellees arrived in West Germany by the 1950s; they added to housing shortages but also supplied labour for industry.
Britain remained dependent on dollars and devalued the pound from 4.03 dollars to 2.80 dollars in September 1949.
The Cold War shaped recovery: the Marshall Plan was designed to prevent economic collapse from strengthening communist parties, notably in France and Italy.
US aid under the Marshall Plan supplied dollars and goods, and it encouraged the Western European states to cooperate on trade and payments.
The European Recovery Programme ran from 1948 to 1952 and provided about 13 billion dollars of aid, mostly in the form of grants rather than loans.
Recipients had to draw up plans for recovery, and the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation, set up on 16 April 1948, coordinated the allocation of aid.
The OEEC later became the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in 1961, after the USA and Canada joined.
Marshall Aid paid for imports of raw materials and machinery, and some of its counterpart funds were used for investment in industry and housing.
The historian Alan Milward argued in The Reconstruction of Western Europe (1984) that Marshall Aid was a modest share of total investment, and that domestic policy did much of the work of recovery.
Sixteen European states received Marshall Aid; Britain, France and West Germany received the largest sums, and conditions encouraged states to remove trade barriers and to reduce inflation.
The European Payments Union of 1950 allowed Western European currencies to be settled through a clearing system and helped to revive trade between members.

Marshall Aid also gave the USA leverage to shape European politics: it supported the Christian Democratic and social democratic parties against the communists and promoted American-style productivity methods.
The international monetary and trading order was rebuilt through the Bretton Woods system and the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, which encouraged freer trade.
The Bretton Woods conference of July 1944 created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, and it fixed currencies to the US dollar, which was convertible into gold at 35 dollars an ounce.
The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade was signed at Geneva in October 1947 and came into force in 1948, providing a framework for reducing tariffs through successive rounds.
The Benelux customs union between Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg was agreed in 1944 and came into effect in 1948.
The European Coal and Steel Community of 1952, the EEC of 1958 and the European Free Trade Association of 1960 each advanced freer trade in different ways.
The fixed exchange rate system gave Western economies stable conditions for trade and investment until the strains of the 1960s undermined it.
The GATT rounds, including the Kennedy Round of 1964–67, reduced tariffs on industrial goods across the Western world.
The EEC removed internal tariffs on industrial goods in July 1968 and introduced the Common Agricultural Policy; EFTA's members similarly removed tariffs on industrial goods but not on farm produce.
By the end of 1958 the main Western European currencies had become convertible, ending the controls on trade payments that had survived from the war.
The economic growth of 1945–1973 was fastest in West Germany, France and Italy, and it was driven by reconstruction, planning and cheap energy.

West Germany's currency reform of 20 June 1948 and the abolition of most price controls, carried out by Ludwig Erhard (economics minister from 1949 to 1963), created the basis of the economic miracle (Wirtschaftswunder).
Erhard's social market economy combined free markets with social insurance and trade union rights, and it gave West Germany a stable framework.
In France the state planning system, begun under the Monnet Plan, directed investment into coal, electricity, steel and transport, and the period was later called the trente glorieuses.
Italy experienced rapid industrial growth in the 1950s and 1960s, and the north-west attracted migrants from the rural south, which strained housing and services.
Cheap oil from the Middle East fuelled industrial expansion in Western Europe, and its relative cheapness was a significant factor in the growth of the 1950s and 1960s.
Skilled labour, the adoption of American production methods and the reintegration of trade all helped sustain productivity growth.
West Germany's economy grew at more than 7 percent a year on average in the 1950s, and its unemployment fell to very low levels by 1960.
Italy's economic miracle, strongest between 1958 and 1963, was built on exports of cars (Fiat), appliances and textiles, but the south stayed poor and large numbers moved north or abroad.
France's planning was run by the Commissariat général du Plan through four-year plans that set targets for key industries; the French economy grew strongly through the 1950s and 1960s.
Western European economies recruited large numbers of workers from abroad to meet labour shortages, which changed the social make-up of the continent.

West Germany recruited guest workers, the Gastarbeiter, under agreements with Italy from 1955, Spain and Greece from 1960, Turkey from 1961 and Yugoslavia from 1968; recruitment was halted in 1973, by which time there were over two million foreign workers.
France drew workers from its former colonies in North Africa and from Portugal, and Belgium from Italy and Spain.
Britain admitted workers from the Commonwealth, and the arrival of the Empire Windrush at Tilbury on 22 June 1948 with migrants from the Caribbean marked a major stage in Commonwealth migration.
The British Nationality Act of 1948 gave Commonwealth citizens the right to enter and settle in Britain, and this right was later restricted in 1962 and 1968.
Immigration brought social tensions, and the Race Relations Act of 1965 was Britain's first law against racial discrimination in public places.
Many guest workers were expected to return home, but many stayed and their families joined them, which made Western Europe multicultural in the later decades.
France received over 800,000 settlers (pieds-noirs) from Algeria around its independence in 1962, and Algerian, Moroccan and Portuguese workers filled jobs in construction and car factories.
Britain's Commonwealth migrants, from the Caribbean, India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, worked in the NHS, transport and textile factories, and they faced discrimination in housing and employment.
The Netherlands received migrants from its former colonies of Indonesia and Surinam, and Italy and Spain exported workers to northern Europe.
The welfare state gave citizens protection against sickness, unemployment and old age, and it was an important part of the post-war settlement.
The Beveridge Report of December 1942 identified five giant evils: want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness, and proposed a system of national insurance from the cradle to the grave.
Britain's National Health Service was established on 5 July 1948 and provided free treatment at the point of use.
France's social security system, set up by ordinances of October 1945, combined health insurance, family allowances and pensions for workers.
The Scandinavian countries developed universal welfare systems, and Sweden's model combined social security with active labour market policies.
West Germany's welfare system was closely tied to the social market economy, and it provided compulsory social insurance funded by employers and employees.
Welfare spending rose steadily across Western Europe in the 1950s and 1960s, and it became a permanent feature of the political consensus.
Britain's Labour government of 1945–51 under Clement Attlee passed the National Insurance Act (1946), set up the NHS and nationalised coal, the railways and the Bank of England.
Education was expanded: the 1944 Education Act in Britain made secondary education free, and universities grew in the 1960s.
Christian Democratic governments in West Germany, Italy and Belgium also supported social insurance, which showed that the welfare state was favoured by parties of both left and right.
Examiners ask what helped and what hindered growth, so group the factors.

Helped: high investment in industry; the move of workers from farms into factories in Italy, France and Germany; the supply of labour from refugees and later guest workers; access to cheap oil; the catching up with American technology; and growing export markets.
Helped: governments accepted responsibility for full employment, using the ideas of John Maynard Keynes to manage demand, and political stability supported long-term investment.
Helped: the Korean War boom of 1950–53 raised demand for European exports of steel and machinery.
Hindered: war damage and the shortage of dollars in the late 1940s; the cost of rearmament and the Cold War; and weak productivity and frequent strikes in Britain.
Hindered: inflation and the pressure on currencies as wages rose in the late 1960s, and the strain of the Vietnam War on American finances, which weakened the dollar.
Britain grew more slowly than France, Italy and West Germany, with balance-of-payments crises that led governments to alternate between expansion and restraint, known as stop-go policies.
The boom of 1945–1973 is judged as the most prosperous period in Western Europe's modern history, but its causes and its end are debated.
Achievements: rising living standards, full employment in many countries, the spread of home ownership and a large expansion of education.
Limits: dependence on cheap oil, the inflationary pressures of the late 1960s and the strain on the dollar-based system, which collapsed in 1971.
The Bretton Woods system broke down after the US president Richard Nixon suspended the convertibility of the dollar into gold on 15 August 1971; by 1973 the major currencies were floating.
Historians disagree on how far Marshall Aid caused growth: some stress American aid and pressure for cooperation, while Milward and others stress domestic policy and economic structure.
Western Europe's growth rate between 1950 and 1973 was far higher than in any earlier period, but it slowed sharply after 1973 (see the notes on the Oil Crisis).
Contemporary opinion saw the boom as the result of good management; later historians stress that it was partly a catching-up with the American economy that could not continue indefinitely.
The oil crisis struck an economy that had grown rapidly for almost thirty years on cheap energy and stable exchange rates.
Western European oil consumption had risen sharply since the 1950s, and most of the imported oil came from the Middle East.
The Arab members of OPEC had long sought higher prices, and the Organisation of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries had been formed in 1968.
Inflation had begun to rise in the late 1960s, and the collapse of the Bretton Woods system in August 1971 ended fixed exchange rates.
The Yom Kippur War, which began on 6 October 1973 when Egypt and Syria attacked Israel, provided the occasion for the Arab producers to act.

Oil had become Western Europe's main energy source during the 1950s and 1960s, supplying around half or more of its energy by 1973, and the price had stayed low, at about three dollars a barrel in 1973.
The Arab–Israeli conflict was the trigger: the USA's decision to resupply Israel with arms during the war led the Arab states to use oil as a weapon.
The Netherlands was targeted because its government supported Israel and because Rotterdam was Europe's main oil port.
Arab oil producers used a supply embargo and a sharp price increase to pressure states that supported Israel.
On 16 October 1973 OPEC's Gulf members raised the posted price of oil by about 70 per cent, and in the following months prices roughly quadrupled.

On 17 October 1973 the Arab oil-producing states (OAPEC) announced cuts in output of 5 per cent a month until Israel withdrew from occupied territory, and an embargo on oil exports to the USA followed from 19–20 October and on the Netherlands from 21 October, as supporters of Israel.
The embargo was lifted in March 1974, but the new higher prices remained in place.
The Yom Kippur War ended with a ceasefire in late October 1973 (UN Security Council Resolution 338 of 22 October), after which Western governments reassessed their dependence on imported energy.
The oil shock brought fuel rationing, falling production and rising inflation, and it ended the long period of steady growth.
Several countries introduced measures to save fuel, including car-free Sundays in the Netherlands and West Germany in the winter of 1973–74.
Britain's government introduced a three-day working week for industry from January to March 1974, when a miners' dispute and power shortage had cut electricity supplies.
Industrial production fell, and unemployment rose from the low levels of the 1960s, with the sharpest increases in heavy industry.
Inflation rose sharply, producing stagflation, a combination of stagnation and rising prices that conventional Keynesian policies struggled to address.
The second oil shock of 1979, after the Iranian revolution, raised prices again and pushed many economies back into recession in the early 1980s.
Prices were raised again at the end of 1973: in December the OPEC states agreed to double the posted price, and by early 1974 it was about four times the pre-war level.
Western governments reduced speed limits, introduced fuel rationing in some countries, banned Sunday driving in West Germany and the Netherlands, and asked households to turn down heating.

The balance of payments of oil-importing states went into deficit, as they had to pay far more for imports, and the Arab producers gained huge revenues (petrodollars) that were recycled through Western banks.
Unemployment across the EEC rose from low levels in the early 1970s to above 10 percent by the mid-1980s, and Spain and Ireland suffered even higher rates.
The second shock, after the Iranian revolution of 1979, led to a doubling of oil prices between 1978 and 1980 and a second recession in 1980–82.
Governments abandoned the post-war commitment to full employment; their main aim became the defeat of inflation.
Governments responded by seeking new energy sources, and by restructuring industries that could no longer compete.
France announced a nuclear power programme in 1974, the Messmer Plan, which made nuclear electricity the core of its energy supply in the 1980s.
North Sea oil began to flow in the mid-1970s, and by 1980 Britain was self-sufficient in oil and Norway a major exporter, which cushioned both economies against the second oil shock.
Heavy industries such as shipbuilding, steel and coal declined sharply in Britain, and deindustrialisation changed the regional economies of the north and Scotland.
Energy conservation measures and the development of coal and nuclear power were promoted as ways to reduce dependence on imported oil.
The International Energy Agency was set up in 1974 under the OECD to coordinate oil stocks and policy among importing states.
France relied on nuclear power for about 70 percent of its electricity by the late 1980s, with plants built under the Messmer Plan.

West Germany's industry moved up-market into machinery and cars, while older industries such as coal, steel and shipbuilding were cut back across Europe; the EEC introduced steel quotas in 1980 under the Davignon Plan.
Thatcher led the Conservative Party from 1975 and was Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990, pursuing monetarist and free-market policies.
Born in Grantham in 1925, she studied chemistry at Oxford and trained as a barrister before entering parliament in 1959.
She was elected Conservative leader on 11 February 1975, defeating Edward Heath, and became Prime Minister on 4 May 1979.

Her government pursued monetarism, cut public spending, reduced the power of the trade unions through the Employment Acts of 1980 and 1982 and the Trade Union Act of 1984, and sold state assets including British Telecom.
She was a participant in the Falklands War, after Argentina invaded the islands on 2 April 1982, and the British victory on 14 June 1982 helped her re-election in 1983.
The miners' strike of March 1984 to March 1985 was a major confrontation with the National Union of Mineworkers, which ended with the miners' defeat.
Contemporaries were divided: supporters admired her resolve, while critics pointed to unemployment passing three million in 1982 and to deindustrialisation.
Historians debate whether her policies were a decisive break with the post-war settlement or the continuation of trends already under way.

She was Secretary of State for Education in Heath's government (1970–74), and her break with Heath came after his defeats in 1974, with Keith Joseph's policy ideas (the Centre for Policy Studies) behind monetarism.
She won the general elections of 1979, 1983 and 1987, becoming the longest-serving British prime minister of the twentieth century.
Her government allowed tenants to buy council houses (the right to buy of 1980), removed exchange controls in 1979 and deregulated the City in 1986.
Unemployment reached about three million in 1982, and the early 1980s recession hit manufacturing in the north, Scotland and Wales hardest, with riots in English cities in 1981.
Thatcher's foreign policy combined close links with the USA, a hard line on the EEC budget and a cautious approach to the Soviet Union.
Her relations with President Ronald Reagan were close, and the two leaders coordinated the Western response to Soviet policy in the early 1980s.
She negotiated the Fontainebleau rebate of June 1984, which reduced Britain's net contribution to the EEC budget.
In her Bruges speech of 20 September 1988 she criticised plans for a federal Europe while supporting a single market.
The Soviet press nicknamed her the Iron Lady in 1976, a name she later adopted with some pride.
She resigned as Prime Minister on 22 November 1990 after a challenge within her party over Europe and the poll tax, and was succeeded by John Major.

She approved the Single European Act in 1986 because it supported the single market, but opposed moves to economic and monetary union and the Social Charter, and Britain joined the ERM only in October 1990.
She signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement with Garret FitzGerald on 15 November 1985, giving the Irish government a consultative role in Northern Ireland.
She met Gorbachev in December 1984 before he took power and said he was someone she could do business with; she then helped to persuade Reagan that he was sincere.
She allowed American aircraft to use British bases in the 1986 raid on Libya, and backed the American deployment of cruise missiles at Greenham Common.
Her fall: Geoffrey Howe resigned in November 1990 over her European policy, Michael Heseltine challenged her, and she withdrew after the first ballot gave her too narrow a lead.
Examiners ask how lasting the impact was, so weigh the oil shock against other causes.
The crisis ended the long boom and exposed the dependence of Western prosperity on cheap energy, and it shifted political attention from growth to inflation and unemployment.
It strengthened the case for the EEC to act together, leading to the European Monetary System in 1979 (see the notes on European unity).

Contemporaries blamed the Arab embargo and OPEC; many economists later argued that inflation, the end of Bretton Woods and falling productivity were already weakening the boom, so the oil shock hastened rather than caused the end of the boom.
The embargo also gave oil-producing states a new role in world politics and led Western states to look for energy independence, through nuclear power, North Sea oil and conservation.
The strike was the most severe test of Thatcher's trade union policy.
The strike began in March 1984 when the National Coal Board under Ian MacGregor announced pit closures, and Arthur Scargill's National Union of Mineworkers called a strike without a national ballot.
The government had built up coal stocks and used the police; violent clashes occurred at Orgreave in June 1984.
The strike ended in March 1985 without a settlement, and the defeat weakened the union movement and speeded up the closure of coal mines.
The record of the Western economies after 1973 is judged on whether they restored growth and whether the costs of adjustment were fair.
Achievements: lower inflation by the mid-1980s, a more flexible labour market in Britain, and a deeper single market in the EEC after 1986.
Limits: high unemployment for much of the decade, the decline of older industries and the widening of regional inequality.
Supporters of Thatcher regard her as having reversed Britain's relative decline, while critics regard the decline of manufacturing as a heavy and lasting cost.
Historians point out that the oil shock was a cause of recession but not the sole cause, since inflation and industrial change were already under way.
Communist economies were run by central planning, in which the state set production targets and allocated resources, and this model was copied across eastern Europe.
Gosplan, the state planning committee, drew up five-year plans that set output targets for industry, agriculture and trade.
Priority was given to heavy industry, steel, coal, machinery and armaments, while consumer goods and housing were neglected.

Collectivisation of agriculture was carried through in the Soviet Union in the early 1930s, and was imposed on most eastern European farms after 1945, with the exception of Poland, where most farms stayed private.
Comecon, founded in January 1949, coordinated trade and planning among the Soviet bloc, and trade was largely conducted in non-convertible currencies at prices set by planners.
Stalin's five-year plans from 1928 built heavy industry and cities at great human cost, and collectivisation of farms in the early 1930s, together with the famine of 1932–33, killed millions.

In eastern Europe, industry, banks and large estates were nationalised in 1945–48, and Six-Year or Five-Year Plans on the Soviet pattern were introduced from 1949–51, with new steel towns such as Nowa Huta in Poland and Stalinstadt in East Germany.

Comecon was set up in response to the Marshall Plan; in practice it became a system of trade with the Soviet Union, which supplied cheap raw materials and energy and took manufactured goods, so the east European economies became dependent on Soviet supplies.
In 1949–53 eastern Europe's trade shifted from the West to the Soviet Union, and reparations and joint companies in Hungary, Romania and East Germany took resources for the Soviet economy.
Output was driven by pressing workers to exceed their norms, as in the Stakhanovite campaigns, and consumer goods were rationed in the early 1950s.
Central planning produced chronic shortages of goods, poor quality and slow adoption of new technology, which undermined the economies over time.
Planners set targets in gross output terms, which encouraged factories to produce heavy and low-quality goods rather than goods that consumers wanted.
Shortages of consumer goods, meat, housing and cars were common, and long queues and black markets were a permanent feature of daily life.
Innovation was slow because managers had little incentive to adopt new technology, and the state discouraged risk-taking.
The arms race and the cost of maintaining an army and military industries absorbed a large share of national output, especially in the Soviet Union.
Soviet agriculture remained unproductive, with a large share of the labour force employed on farms, and the Soviet Union imported grain from the 1960s onwards.
Prices were fixed by the state rather than by supply and demand, so shortages in shops coexisted with surpluses of unwanted goods in warehouses.
Housing was built in standard blocks and was often overcrowded; in East Germany the wait for a car such as the Trabant could be many years.
Environmental damage was severe, as industrial regions such as northern Bohemia, Upper Silesia and the Aral Sea basin were polluted by heavy industry and irrigation.

The economies relied on extensive growth, adding labour and raw materials, and could not move to intensive growth based on technology and productivity once the supply of new workers dried up in the 1970s.
Several reforms tried to introduce market elements or decentralisation, but most were partial and some were reversed.
Khrushchev's 1957 decentralisation of industry replaced ministries with regional economic councils, a reform that was later reversed.
Alexei Kosygin's reform of September 1965 gave enterprises more control over profits and pricing, but it did not end central control of investment.
Hungary's New Economic Mechanism of 1968 allowed limited market prices and private enterprise in services, and it became a model of partial reform.
Hungary's policy under János Kádár, later called goulash communism, tolerated small private plots and enterprises and gave citizens more consumer goods than in other bloc states.
Czechoslovakia's New Economic Model of the 1960s, developed by the economist Ota Šik, proposed market mechanisms that the 1968 invasion ended.
Khrushchev tried to lift the production of consumer goods and housing, launched a mass housebuilding programme, and promised to overtake the USA in per capita output, but the targets were not met.
The 1965 Kosygin reforms were abandoned within a few years because ministries and the party feared the loss of control, and the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 discouraged further experiment.

Yugoslavia, outside Comecon after 1948, developed a system of worker self-management and market socialism, and allowed its citizens to travel and work abroad; but it ran up heavy foreign debt and suffered high inflation in the 1980s.
Hungary's reforms gave managers more freedom and allowed a second economy of private work after hours, but the state kept control of the main industries and prices.
Under Leonid Brezhnev from 1964 to 1982 the Soviet economy grew more slowly, and the period became known as the era of stagnation.
Growth in the Soviet economy slowed in the 1970s, as the labour force grew more slowly and the rise in productivity fell.

The Soviet Union earned large hard currency revenues from oil and gas exports after the price rises of 1973 and 1979, which let the leadership buy Western grain and technology and postpone reform; when oil prices fell in the mid-1980s this support vanished.
The Soviet leadership avoided reform, and living standards for most people improved only slowly during the 1970s.

Under Brezhnev the Soviet Union reached rough nuclear parity with the USA and increased its military spending, which took a large share of national output at the cost of consumer goods and investment.
The war in Afghanistan from 1979 added to the burden, and the system of rewarding party loyalty rather than performance led to corruption and an ageing leadership.
Consumers experienced shortages of basic goods, and the black market, bribery and informal networks (blat) became part of ordinary life.
Poland's attempts to raise living standards by borrowing from the West ended in debt and repeated waves of protest.
Protests in Gdańsk and other Baltic ports in December 1970, against food price rises, led to the fall of Władysław Gomułka and his replacement by Edward Gierek.
Gierek borrowed heavily from Western banks to finance imports of machinery and consumer goods, which were intended to modernise industry and win public support.
The June 1976 price rises led to strikes and protests, and the government withdrew most of the increases within days.
By 1980 Poland's foreign debt had become unsustainable, and the strikes of that summer at the Gdańsk shipyard led to the founding of Solidarity.
Poland's Western debt rose to more than 20 billion dollars by 1980, and a large share of its export earnings went on servicing it.
Price rises announced on 1 July 1980 sparked strikes that spread to Gdańsk in August; the economy had shrunk and shops were bare of meat.

Gierek's policy of importing Western technology failed because the new factories produced goods that were not competitive in Western markets, and agricultural output suffered from a lack of investment.
Poland's economic crisis was a cause of Solidarity, and the economic collapse in the 1980s helped to bring the communists to the Round Table talks of 1989.
By the late 1980s the economic gap between the communist states and the West had widened, and the reform attempts came too late.
Mikhail Gorbachev's perestroika aimed to restructure the economy, but it coincided with falling oil prices in 1986, which cut the Soviet Union's hard currency earnings.
Romania under Nicolae Ceaușescu repaid its foreign debt in the late 1980s by cutting imports and imposing severe austerity, and the population suffered shortages of food, heating and electricity.
East Germany was the most productive economy of the bloc, but it too depended on West German credit and trade concessions by the late 1980s.
The end of the Soviet bloc's economic system left a legacy of obsolete industry, environmental damage and unemployment that the successor states had to address.

Gorbachev's economic reforms included the Law on State Enterprise (1987), which gave factories more freedom, and the 1988 law on cooperatives, which allowed private business; they weakened central control without creating a functioning market.
By 1989–90 the Soviet economy was suffering from shortages, a growing budget deficit, rationing in some cities and falling output.

The gap with the West was visible by 1989: East German and Czechoslovak citizens could see how much better West Germans and Austrians lived on television and through travel, and living standards in the Soviet Union lagged far behind.

East Germany's economy had been propped up by loans from West Germany, including a billion-mark credit in 1983, and the German monetary union of July 1990 exposed its industries to competition and led to mass closures.
The bloc was not uniform, and examiners reward comparison of different states.

Czechoslovakia had been the most industrialised state in the region before the war, and its living standards were the highest in the bloc in the 1950s, but it stagnated under rigid planning in the 1960s and was the home of Ota Šik's reform.
East Germany was the most advanced economy in the bloc and the showcase of socialism, but it lost skilled workers to the West until the Wall was built in 1961.

Bulgaria and Romania were still largely agricultural in 1945 and were industrialised rapidly, Romania developing heavy industry, oil and chemicals and pursuing an independent foreign policy under Ceaușescu.
Ceaușescu's Romania exported food and fuel to pay its debts, rationed food and electricity in the 1980s, and planned to demolish thousands of villages in his systematisation programme.

Hungary's partial reforms and Poland's private farming made those states more flexible than the Soviet Union, but their dependence on Western credit made them vulnerable when interest rates and prices rose around 1980.
Communist economies achieved rapid industrialisation and social welfare, but they failed to sustain growth or satisfy consumers.
Achievements: rapid industrialisation, near-universal literacy, free health care and education, and full employment, including high employment of women.
Limits: chronic shortages, low quality, poor housing, environmental damage and a standard of living that fell further behind the West.
Contemporary Western accounts often stressed the failure of the planned economy, while Soviet and bloc officials emphasised the achievements of industrialisation and social welfare.
Later historians stress both the system's real successes in mobilising resources and the structural limits that made it impossible to sustain growth without political reform.
Eastern Europe's communist states did expand education, cheap housing and health care, but their living standards fell behind West European levels by the 1970s.
The final judgement of historians is that the planned economy could build basic industry, but could not adapt to the information-based economies of the 1980s.
De Beauvoir was a French philosopher and writer whose 1949 study The Second Sex became a founding text of modern feminism.
Born in Paris in 1908, she taught philosophy and became the partner of Jean-Paul Sartre, with whom she shared a close intellectual life for decades.
The Second Sex was published in two volumes in 1949, and it argued that women were defined as the 'Other' by a male-centred society.
Her best-known line, from The Second Sex, is that one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman, a statement that separated biological sex from social gender.
She was a witness to the Second World War and the Occupation of Paris, and her later activism made her a participant in the feminist movement of the 1970s.
In April 1971 she signed the Manifesto of the 343, in which women declared that they had had abortions and called for their legalisation.
Contemporaries were divided: many male intellectuals and conservative commentators mocked the book, while younger women read it as a guide to their own position.
Historians now treat the book as a foundational text of second-wave feminism, though later critics questioned its assumptions about universal experience.
She passed the highly competitive agrégation in philosophy in 1929, where she came second to Sartre, and she was among the first women to teach philosophy in French lycées.
She argued in the book that women's inferior position was created by history, law, religion and education, not by biology, and that women should win economic independence.
The Catholic Church put The Second Sex on its Index of Forbidden Books in 1956, and some on the left attacked it too; it sold very widely and was translated into English in 1953.
In the 1970s she joined the Women's Liberation Movement in France, campaigned for the legalisation of abortion and became a leading voice of second-wave feminism; she died in 1986.
The years after 1945 saw marriage and childbirth rise, and a more domestic model of family life became the norm in many Western European countries.
The baby boom in Western Europe ran roughly from 1946 to the mid-1960s, and birth rates were higher than in the 1930s.
Marriage was earlier and more common than before the war, and the nuclear family of two parents and their children became the ideal.
Housing shortages after the war meant that many young couples lived with relatives, and public housing programmes were used to increase family accommodation.
The post-war family was supported by family allowances, which were extended in France in 1945–46 and paid in other countries through social insurance schemes.
The new emphasis on the housewife and mother reflected the wish to restore stability after the war, and conservative parties and churches promoted the family as the basis of society.

In West Germany the law until 1977 allowed a husband to decide whether his wife could take a job, and in France married women won the right to work and open a bank account without their husband's consent only in 1965.
Cinema, magazines and television presented the ideal of the happy housewife with labour-saving appliances.
Women's employment grew after the 1950s, and women campaigned for equal pay, legal rights and control over their bodies.
The number of married women in paid employment rose steadily from the 1950s, especially in service and clerical work.
Article 119 of the Treaty of Rome required equal pay for equal work between men and women, a provision that the European Court of Justice enforced in the Defrenne case of 1976.
The Equal Pay Act of 1970 in Britain required equal pay for men and women doing work of equal value, and it took full effect in 1975 alongside the Sex Discrimination Act.
The contraceptive pill was approved in the USA in 1960 and became widely used in Western Europe in the 1960s, giving women control over childbearing.
France legalised contraception with the Neuwirth Law of 1967, and the Veil Law of 17 January 1975 legalised abortion in its first ten weeks, sponsored by the health minister Simone Veil.
The Manifesto of the 343 in 1971 publicly called for abortion to be legalised, and it was followed by campaigns by groups such as Choisir.
Women's work was mostly in low-paid jobs such as teaching, nursing, secretarial work and factory assembly, and women were paid less than men and were barred from many professions.

Second-wave feminism arose in the 1960s, influenced by Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963), and it demanded equal pay, nurseries and reproductive freedom; the Mouvement de libération des femmes (MLF) was formed in France in 1970.
Britain's Abortion Act of 1967 legalised abortion on medical grounds, West Germany reformed its abortion law in 1974–76, and Italy legalised abortion in 1978.

The Catholic Church opposed contraception and abortion, and Pope Paul VI's encyclical Humanae Vitae (1968) reaffirmed the ban on artificial birth control (see the notes on the Second Vatican Council).
Divorce became easier in most Western European countries after 1969, and this changed the legal basis of marriage.
The Divorce Reform Act of 1969 in Britain allowed divorce on the grounds of irretrievable breakdown, taking effect in 1971.
West Germany introduced no-fault divorce in its reform of marriage law in 1977, which replaced the requirement to prove the other party's fault.
In Italy, a referendum of 12 May 1974 upheld the divorce law of 1970 against an attempt to repeal it.
Divorce rates rose across the region in the 1970s, and single-parent families became a growing category of households.
Sweden and Denmark had liberal divorce laws earlier; Italy legalised divorce in 1970 and Spain in 1981, while Ireland, whose constitution banned it, legalised divorce only after a referendum in 1995.
Family law reform in West Germany and in Italy (1975) replaced the idea of the husband as head of household with equal rights for spouses.
The rise in divorce and in working mothers led to debate about the future of the family, with conservatives blaming the changes on permissiveness.
Rising incomes in the 1950s and 1960s allowed families to buy consumer durables, cars and holidays, which transformed daily life.
Households acquired refrigerators, washing machines, televisions and cars, and the Volkswagen Beetle became one of the most common cars in West Germany.
Self-service supermarkets spread across Western Europe in the 1960s, and they changed how families shopped and the goods available to them.
Hire purchase and consumer credit made it possible for families to buy goods before they could afford them outright.
Advertising and television encouraged consumption, and critics such as Vance Packard in The Hidden Persuaders (1957) argued that advertising manipulated consumers.
Car ownership expanded sharply: in the 1950s the Fiat 500, the Citroën 2CV and the Mini made cars affordable for ordinary families.
Television spread rapidly in the 1950s and 1960s, becoming the centre of the home and the main form of evening leisure.

Critics included John Kenneth Galbraith, whose The Affluent Society (1958) argued that private affluence went with public squalor, and the French Situationists, whose Guy Debord wrote The Society of the Spectacle (1967).
Paid holidays and rising incomes created mass tourism, and the Mediterranean coast became a destination for northern Europeans.
Paid annual holidays became standard in Western Europe in the 1950s and 1960s, extending the time that workers could spend away from work.
Package holidays to Spain, Italy and the Greek islands grew rapidly in the 1960s and 1970s, and the Costa Brava became a symbol of the trend.
Car ownership made domestic holidays and weekend trips possible, and camping and caravanning became popular in Britain and Scandinavia.
Herbert Marcuse, in One-Dimensional Man (1964), argued that consumer society encouraged conformity and suppressed critical thought.
Working hours fell, with the five-day week and the forty-hour week spreading in the 1960s, and paid holidays were extended to three or four weeks.
Charter flights and package tours brought the Spanish Costa del Sol and the Balearic islands within reach of workers; Club Méditerranée, founded in 1950, offered all-inclusive holidays.
Leisure included spectator sport, cinema, television, record-buying and home improvement, which show the rise of mass leisure industries.
The communist states offered women employment and childcare but not the same consumer choice, and their feminist movements were limited.
In East Germany a far higher proportion of women went out to work than in West Germany, supported by state childcare and the expectation that women would work.
Communist states promoted equal rights in law, but domestic responsibilities for housework and childcare remained largely with women.
Consumer goods in the East were scarcer and of lower quality, so the consumer society was far less developed than in the West.

In the Soviet Union abortion was legalised again in 1955, women formed a large part of the workforce including doctors and engineers, and Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in 1963, but women still did most of the housework, the so-called double burden.
East Germany offered paid maternity leave, a baby year from 1976 and state nurseries, and its divorce rate was high.
East German holidays were organised by the trade union federation in union holiday homes and Baltic resorts, and Black Sea resorts served the Soviet bloc, while travel to the West was restricted.
East Germans watched West German television and were conscious of the gap in goods; in the East cars such as the Trabant and Wartburg required waiting lists of years.
Historians debate whether the changes of the period liberated women and families or extended consumer pressures into private life.
Achievements: legal equality in employment, access to contraception and abortion in many states, and more choice in marriage and divorce.
Limits: women still bore most domestic work, pay gaps persisted, and the consumer society tied family life to paid work and credit.
Contemporaries disagreed about the family: conservative churches and politicians defended the traditional family, while feminists demanded new rights.
Later historians see the 1960s and 1970s as a turning point, but they stress that the gains were uneven across social classes and between countries.
Solzhenitsyn was the Soviet novelist whose writing on the Gulag made the camp system known to the world and made him the most famous dissident in the Soviet Union.
Born in Kislovodsk in 1918, he served as an artillery officer in the Second World War and was arrested in 1945 for criticising Stalin in private letters.
He was sentenced to eight years in labour camps and then to internal exile, and his experience of the Gulag became the basis of his later writing.
One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich was published in the Soviet journal Novy Mir in 1962 with Khrushchev's approval, and it brought the camps into Soviet public discussion.
The Gulag Archipelago, published in Paris in 1973, documented the Soviet camp system through testimony and history, and it had a major impact in the West.

He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970, was expelled from the Soviet Union in February 1974, lived first in Switzerland and from 1976 in Vermont in the USA, and returned to Russia in 1994.
Contemporaries in the Soviet leadership treated him as a traitor, while many Western intellectuals admired him, though some later disliked his nationalist and religious views.
Historians regard his work as central to Western understanding of Soviet terror, although some question the reliability of his testimony and his later political stances.
He spent eight years in camps and three years in internal exile in Kazakhstan from 1953; he was cured of cancer in a Tashkent hospital in 1954, an episode behind his novel Cancer Ward.
After Khrushchev fell, the authorities tightened censorship; his novels The First Circle and Cancer Ward could be published only abroad (1968), and he was expelled from the Writers' Union in 1969.
The KGB seized a copy of The Gulag Archipelago manuscript in 1973, which led him to authorise publication in Paris; he was arrested on 12 February 1974 and flown the next day to West Germany.
His Harvard address in 1978 criticised Western materialism as well as communism; from exile in Vermont he continued to write The Red Wheel, a historical cycle on the Russian Revolution.
In Russia after 1994 his reputation was divided between admirers who saw him as the nation's conscience and critics who disliked his Russian nationalism and his religious conservatism.
Beauvoir's later work was not only a feminist treatise but also a set of novels and memoirs that criticised Western society and its values.
Her novel The Mandarins portrayed the Parisian intellectual left after the Second World War and won the Prix Goncourt in 1954.
Her memoirs, including Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter (1958), described her youth and her relationship with Jean-Paul Sartre.
She was a participant in the political debates of the 1960s and 1970s, supporting the left and speaking out for the rights of women and of prisoners.
Contemporaries praised her as a writer and public intellectual, while conservative critics attacked her for challenging traditional morality.
Historians now judge her as one of the most influential critics of the twentieth century, though her later political views are contested.
She joined Sartre in founding the review Les Temps modernes in 1945, which became the leading journal of left-wing intellectuals in France.

In 1960 she signed the Manifesto of the 121 supporting French conscripts who refused to fight in Algeria, and she campaigned against torture by the French army, championing the case of Djamila Boupacha in 1962.
Her essay on old age, La vieillesse (The Coming of Age, 1970), attacked the way society treated the elderly.
She and Sartre visited the Soviet Union, China and Cuba in the 1950s and 1960s, where she observed communism, and her views on it changed over time.

Her relationship with Sartre, which was a partnership by choice without marriage, was presented by admirers as a model of equality and by critics as a privilege of the elite; she wrote about his death in 1980 in Adieux.
Writers in the communist states could not publish freely, so they circulated their work in unofficial copies and published abroad.
Samizdat, meaning self-published, was the system by which typed and copied manuscripts were passed from hand to hand in the Soviet Union and Czechoslovakia.
Boris Pasternak's Doctor Zhivago was published in Italy in 1957, and he was pressured to decline the Nobel Prize in 1958.
Václav Havel, a Czech playwright, wrote The Power of the Powerless in 1978, arguing that ordinary people could resist by living within the truth.
Milan Kundera's novel The Joke (1967) and the Czech writers' congress of 1967 were part of the intellectual ferment that led to the Prague Spring.
Dissident writers were often expelled, imprisoned or forced into exile, and Solzhenitsyn's expulsion in 1974 was the most famous example.
Andrei Sakharov, the physicist and father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, became a human rights campaigner and was exiled to Gorky in 1980 until Gorbachev released him in 1986.

In 1966 the writers Andrei Sinyavsky and Yuli Daniel were sentenced to labour camps for publishing satires abroad, and in 1964 the poet Joseph Brodsky was tried for social parasitism; both cases drew international protest.
Havel was imprisoned for his part in Charter 77 and spent most of 1979–83 in jail, before he became president of Czechoslovakia in December 1989.
Polish writers also took part: Czesław Miłosz, who defected in 1951, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1980, the same year as Solidarity's rise.
Western radio stations such as Radio Free Europe and the BBC broadcast banned works back to the East, and the Helsinki Final Act of 1975 gave dissidents a standard of rights to appeal to.
Western writers criticised totalitarianism, conformity and the moral condition of their societies, and their work reached a wide public.
George Orwell's Animal Farm (1945) and Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) criticised Stalinism and the abuse of power, and both became standard texts in the Cold War.
Albert Camus's The Plague (1947) used an epidemic as an allegory for resistance to tyranny, and he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957.
Jean-Paul Sartre refused the Nobel Prize in 1964, and his plays and essays criticised bourgeois society and colonialism.
Günter Grass's The Tin Drum (1959) examined Germany's wartime past and the moral compromises of ordinary people, and he received the Nobel Prize in 1999.
Heinrich Böll's novels criticised the restoration of West German society after 1945, and he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1972.

Sartre's existentialism, expressed in Being and Nothingness (1943) and in his plays, argued that people are free and responsible for their choices, and it dominated French thought in the late 1940s and 1950s.
Camus broke with Sartre in 1952 over the question of communism and violence, and he died in a car crash in 1960.
In Britain, John Osborne's play Look Back in Anger (1956) and the writers known as the Angry Young Men attacked class and complacency in post-war society.
Aldous Huxley's Brave New World (1932) and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four were read in the 1950s as warnings against conformity and totalitarian control, whether communist or consumerist.
Religious observance fell in much of Western Europe from the 1960s, and the authority of the churches over public life declined.
Attendance at Mass and other religious services fell in most Western European countries from the 1960s, and the fall was sharpest among young people.
The Second Vatican Council's reforms and the controversy over contraception in Humanae Vitae (1968) created divisions within the Catholic Church.
Secularisation meant that the state, education and family life increasingly ran without reference to religious authority.

Muslim communities grew in Western Europe through migration from North Africa, Turkey and South Asia, and from the 1970s prayer rooms and mosques were set up in cities such as Paris, Cologne and Birmingham, adding a visible new religion to societies that were becoming more secular.
Church attendance fell sharply in Britain, the Netherlands, France and Scandinavia from the 1960s, while in Ireland, Poland, Spain and Italy religious practice remained high for longer.
In the Netherlands the proportion of Catholics attending Mass fell dramatically between the 1960s and 1980s, and many left the Church.
Causes of secularisation included rising affluence, education, the growth of television, urban life, the welfare state taking over church services and the questioning of authority in the 1960s.
The decline of clergy vocations was visible by the 1970s, when seminaries and religious orders in many countries recruited far fewer men and women.
Churches in communist states were persecuted or controlled, though some kept real influence.
The Catholic Church in Czechoslovakia was suppressed after 1948, and bishops were imprisoned, while the Church in Poland retained real independence and mass support.
The Evangelical Church in East Germany adopted a policy of coexistence with the state, while maintaining its own institutions and social work.
In Poland, the primate Cardinal Stefan Wyszyński was interned from 1953 to 1956, but the Church retained its influence, and its authority grew after the election of the Polish pope in 1978.
In Hungary, Cardinal Mindszenty was jailed in 1949, freed during the 1956 uprising, and spent the next 15 years in the American legation in Budapest.
The Russian Orthodox Church was permitted to operate under tight state control and with KGB infiltration, and thousands of churches were closed under Khrushchev's anti-religious campaign of 1959–64.
In East Germany, Protestant churches provided shelter for peace and environmental groups, and church-led prayers for peace in Leipzig in 1989 became the starting point for mass protests.
After 1945 Christians of different denominations cooperated more closely than at any time since the Reformation.

The World Council of Churches was founded at Amsterdam in August 1948 by Protestant, Anglican and Orthodox churches; the Roman Catholic Church did not join, and the Russian Orthodox Church joined in 1961.
The ecumenical community of Taizé in Burgundy, founded in 1940 by Brother Roger, drew young people from many countries in the 1960s and 1970s.
Ecumenism made progress after Vatican II: in January 1964 Pope Paul VI met Patriarch Athenagoras in Jerusalem, and in 1965 the mutual excommunications of 1054 were lifted.
The Anglican–Roman Catholic International Commission was established in 1969 to discuss differences between the churches.
Historians debate how far writers and religious movements shaped political change, and how far they reflected social trends.
Achievements: dissident writing kept alive the memory of Stalin's crimes, and it helped to create an intellectual opposition in the communist states.
Limits: the readership of samizdat was small, and most people in the communist states were not directly influenced by dissident writing.
Contemporaries in the West often praised dissident writers as heroes of freedom, while Soviet officials dismissed them as enemies of the state.
Later historians stress that secularisation in the West was a broad social trend, not the result of a single movement or event.
Pope John XXIII called the Council to renew the Catholic Church and bring it into closer contact with the modern world.
Angelo Roncalli, aged 76, was elected Pope John XXIII on 28 October 1958, and he was regarded as a caretaker pope when he was chosen.
He announced the Council on 25 January 1959, and he used the term aggiornamento, meaning updating, to describe its aim of renewal.
The Church faced declining practice in Western Europe, the spread of secularisation and the division between Catholics and other Christians.
The Council was intended to deal with the relationship between the Church and the modern world, the liturgy, and Christian unity.

Pius XII (pope 1939–58) had centralised authority in Rome, and by the 1950s the Church faced pressure from secularisation, the loss of the working class in industrial Europe and the demands of theologians for renewal.
John XXIII wanted a pastoral Council, to renew the Church's teaching and practice rather than to condemn errors.
He also hoped the Council would help the Church speak to ordinary people in a world of nuclear weapons, television and rapid social change, and bring non-Catholic Christians closer to Rome.
Preparations from 1960 were carried out by commissions dominated by Roman Curia officials, including Cardinal Ottaviani, who expected a short Council to approve prepared drafts.
The Council met in four sessions in Rome, and its work was carried on after John XXIII's death in June 1963 by Pope Paul VI.
The Council opened on 11 October 1962 in St Peter's Basilica, with about 2,500 bishops attending, along with observers from other Christian churches.
John XXIII died on 3 June 1963, and Cardinal Giovanni Battista Montini was elected Pope Paul VI on 21 June 1963.
Paul VI kept the Council open and oversaw its completion, and it closed on 8 December 1965.
Joseph Ratzinger, later Pope Benedict XVI, attended as a theological adviser, and the Council drew on the expertise of many theologians.

At the first session (October to December 1962) the bishops rejected the prepared drafts and elected their own commission members, led by progressive cardinals such as Suenens of Belgium, Frings of Germany and Léger of Canada; this gave the Council its own direction.
The second session (September to December 1963) debated the nature of the Church and collegiality, the idea that the bishops share authority with the pope.
The third session (autumn 1964) approved Lumen Gentium and the decree on ecumenism, though a conservative minority and last-minute papal changes caused tension in a week known as Black Week.
The fourth session (autumn 1965) approved the declaration on religious liberty, Nostra Aetate and Gaudium et Spes; Paul VI also set up the Synod of Bishops in 1965 to continue consultation.
Observers from Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant churches attended the sessions, and the proceedings were widely covered by the press, radio and television.
The Council issued four constitutions and several declarations and decrees, and the constitutions set out its main teaching.
Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963) reformed the liturgy and allowed the use of local languages in the Mass.
Lumen Gentium (1964) described the Church as the people of God, and it gave a larger role to the laity and to bishops collectively.
Dei Verbum (1965) addressed revelation and Scripture, and it encouraged the study of the Bible by Catholics.
Gaudium et Spes (1965) addressed the Church in the modern world, including economic life, marriage, peace and social justice.
Unitatis Redintegratio (1964) committed the Church to ecumenism, the search for unity with other Christian churches.
Nostra Aetate (1965) addressed non-Christian religions and rejected the charge of collective Jewish guilt for the death of Christ.
Dignitatis Humanae (1965) affirmed religious liberty, the right of people to follow their conscience in religion.
The Council changed Catholic worship and relations with other faiths, and these changes were the most visible results.

Changes to the Mass began in 1964, when local languages were allowed in parts of it, and the new Roman Missal of 1969–70 completed the reform, so that Mass was said in the vernacular and the priest faced the congregation.
Lay Catholics were encouraged to take a more active part in worship, reading the Scriptures and serving as ministers.
The Church began formal dialogue with other Christian churches, and observers from other churches attended the sessions.
Relations with Judaism changed, and Nostra Aetate became the basis for improved Catholic–Jewish dialogue.
Pope John Paul II visited the Great Synagogue of Rome on 13 April 1986, the first pope in modern times to enter a synagogue, and he called Jews the elder brothers of Catholics.
Priests and religious orders were asked to return to their founders' ideals and to adapt their dress and rules, and many nuns changed their habits.
In December 1965 Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople lifted the mutual excommunications of 1054 between the Catholic and Orthodox churches (see the notes on the ecumenical movement).

The Council also accepted the principle of religious liberty, that the state should not coerce people in matters of faith, which reversed the earlier teaching and ended the ideal of the Catholic confessional state.
The Council divided Catholics, and its reforms produced a traditionalist reaction as well as progressive demands for further change.

Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre, a French bishop who had led opposition at the Council, founded the Society of St Pius X in 1970, which rejected the Council's teaching on religious liberty and the new liturgy; he was excommunicated in 1988 after consecrating four bishops without papal approval.
Progressive Catholics argued that the Council had not gone far enough on the role of women, on collegiality and on sexual ethics.
Paul VI's encyclical Humanae Vitae of 25 July 1968 reaffirmed the ban on artificial contraception, and it was widely rejected by Catholics in the West.
Many Catholics in Western Europe continued to attend Mass less frequently after the 1960s, a trend that historians link to the wider secularisation of society.

A papal commission on birth control reported in 1966 with a majority favouring a relaxation of the ban after the introduction of the pill, so the encyclical's confirmation of the ban in 1968 came as a shock to many Catholics.
Many theologians and bishops' conferences in the Netherlands, Belgium, West Germany and elsewhere publicly voiced dissent, and in practice many Catholic couples used contraception.
Humanae Vitae is often seen as a turning point because it opened a gap between the Church's teaching and the practice of lay Catholics, and weakened the authority of the hierarchy.
The Dutch Church, which held a pastoral council in 1968–70, was seen as the most progressive in Europe, and Rome moved to restore control under Paul VI and John Paul II.
Karol Wojtyła, a Polish bishop who had taken part in the Council, became pope in 1978 and led the Church for almost three decades.
Born in Wadowice in 1920, Wojtyła was made a bishop in Kraków in 1958 and archbishop in 1964, and he took part in the Second Vatican Council, where he contributed to the drafting of Gaudium et Spes.
He was elected pope on 16 October 1978, and he was the first non-Italian pope since 1523.
He travelled widely as pope, and his visits to Poland in 1979 and later were occasions when the Church and the national identity of Poland were linked.
He was shot on 13 May 1981 in St Peter's Square by Mehmet Ali Ağca and visited his attacker in prison in December 1983.
He reaffirmed traditional Catholic teaching on contraception, abortion and the priesthood, which contemporary critics and supporters saw as a conservative turn after the Council.
Historians disagree about his legacy: supporters see him as a defender of human dignity, while critics argue that he resisted reform and handled abuse scandals badly.
Contemporaries in the communist states saw him as a challenge to their authority, and his support for Solidarity made him a political figure.
He travelled more than any previous pope, making over a hundred foreign journeys, and drew huge crowds in Poland, Latin America, Africa and Europe.

He visited Ireland from 29 September to 1 October 1979, the first visit by a pope, saying Mass before about a million people in the Phoenix Park, Dublin, and visiting Drogheda, Galway, Knock and Limerick; at Drogheda he appealed to paramilitaries to end violence in Northern Ireland.
