He opposed the ordination of women, liberation theology, and a change to the discipline of clerical celibacy, and under his authority the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, led by Cardinal Ratzinger from 1981, disciplined theologians.
He launched World Youth Days in the mid-1980s and promoted new movements such as Opus Dei and the Neocatechumenal Way, and he apologised for historical wrongs of Christians.
He met Gorbachev at the Vatican on 1 December 1989, a sign that the Church had outlasted the communist regimes; he died in April 2005.
The effects of the Council on practice are debated because it coincided with wider social change.

Influence on religious practice: Mass attendance fell steeply in the 1960s and 1970s in Western Europe, though the same decline occurred among Protestants who had no Council, which suggests social causes.
In Ireland practice stayed high into the 1980s, but the number of vocations and Mass attendance began to fall, and the authority of the Church was shaken later.
Vocations to the priesthood and religious life fell in the 1970s, as many priests and nuns left their orders in the years after the Council and fewer young people entered.
Weekly Mass attendance in Western Europe's Catholic countries fell: in France and the Netherlands it dropped by half or more by the 1980s, while Poland and Ireland remained exceptions.
The Council did lead to increased lay involvement, in parish councils, readers and Eucharistic ministers, and to a stronger Catholic interest in social justice and in peace.
Historians differ on whether Vatican II was a successful renewal or a cause of decline, and the judgement depends on which measure is used.
Achievements: the vernacular liturgy, the new relations with other faiths, and a more open style of Church leadership.
Limits: falling practice, declining vocations to the priesthood and the conflict between traditionalists and progressives that continued after 1965.
Contemporaries in the Church were divided, with some seeing the Council as a new beginning and others as a betrayal of tradition.
Later historians stress that the changes in religious practice were part of wider social trends, and that the Council's effects differed between countries.
Traditionalists blame the Council for decline; progressives argue that the Church failed to implement its reforms, especially on the role of women and collegiality.
Lennon was a member of The Beatles who became one of the most influential figures of 1960s youth culture and an advocate of peace.
Born in Liverpool on 9 October 1940, he formed the Quarrymen in 1957, which later developed into The Beatles with Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr.

The Beatles played long residencies in Hamburg from 1960 to 1962 and at the Cavern Club in Liverpool, and their first UK number one, From Me to You, followed in April 1963, with Please Please Me reaching the top of some charts in early 1963.
Their appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show on 9 February 1964 gave them a mass audience in the USA, and Beatlemania spread across Western Europe.
During the Amsterdam Hilton 'bed-in' of March 1969 with Yoko Ono he promoted peace, and his song Give Peace a Chance became an anthem of the anti-war movement.
His 1966 remark that the Beatles were more popular than Jesus provoked protests and record burnings in parts of the USA, and it showed the controversy his fame attracted.

Contemporaries saw him as a symbol of youthful rebellion; the American authorities tried to deport him in 1972 because of his anti-war activity, and he won the right to stay and was granted a green card in 1976.
Historians present him as a symbol of the 1960s counterculture, and his post-Beatles work, including Imagine (1971), is judged as both radical and commercially successful.
He was shot dead in New York on 8 December 1980, and his death was widely mourned across Europe and America.

The Beatles' manager from 1962, Brian Epstein, polished their image, and George Martin produced their records; their albums such as Rubber Soul (1965) and Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967) showed pop could be an art form.
Lennon and McCartney wrote most of the Beatles' songs, and the group broke up in 1970 after the death of Epstein in 1967 and disputes about business and music.
In June 1967 the Beatles performed All You Need Is Love on Our World, the first live global television broadcast by satellite, watched by hundreds of millions.

He returned his MBE in November 1969 in protest at British support for the US in Vietnam and the Nigerian civil war, and he and Yoko Ono ran peace campaigns including the War Is Over billboard campaign of December 1969.
His solo career produced the Plastic Ono Band records and Imagine (1971); after 1975 he spent five years as a househusband caring for his son Sean before the album Double Fantasy (1980).
Historians treat the Beatles as the first global pop stars and the model for later artists writing their own songs; critics note that Lennon's radicalism was sometimes self-contradictory.
After 1945 young people became a distinct market with their own spending, music and style, which reshaped popular culture.
The term teenager spread in the USA in the 1940s and 1950s, and by the 1950s young people had money to spend on records, clothes and cinema.
Rock 'n' roll arrived in Europe in the mid-1950s, with Bill Haley's Rock Around the Clock reaching the UK singles chart in 1955 and Elvis Presley's first hits in 1956.
Youth rebellion was partly driven by the expansion of secondary education, which kept young people in school longer and gave them a shared identity.
Teenage magazines, dances and radio stations such as Radio Luxembourg created a youth media; record sales increased with the cheap 45 rpm single.
Live Aid, organised by the Irish singer Bob Geldof and held at Wembley and Philadelphia on 13 July 1985, raised funds for famine in Ethiopia and was watched by a global television audience.
Dress and music were how young people marked themselves out from their elders.
The Mods and Rockers of Britain in the early 1960s, and the later punk subculture of 1976–77, were examples of youth styles that sparked public debate.

Teddy boys in Britain in the 1950s wore Edwardian-style jackets and became associated with delinquency; their critics saw rock 'n' roll as a threat, and the films Rebel Without a Cause and The Wild One (1953–55) fed that fear.

Fashion expressed the new youth market: Mary Quant popularised the miniskirt in London in the 1960s, Carnaby Street became a centre of fashion, and hippies in the late 1960s adopted long hair, flowers and communal living.
Jeans, which symbolised America, were worn by young people across Europe and highly valued in the East, where they were scarce.
Mods and Rockers clashed on the beaches of Brighton, Margate and Clacton at Easter 1964, and the press coverage created a moral panic about youth.

Punk arose in 1976–77 with the Sex Pistols and The Clash, expressing the anger of unemployed young people in the recession, and the Sex Pistols' God Save the Queen was released in the Silver Jubilee week of 1977.
Skinheads and later the new romantics, mostly in Britain, were other styles that fused fashion, music and class identity.
The student protests of 1968 in France and elsewhere combined political dissent with the cultural revolt of the youth movement.
Student protests began at Nanterre in March 1968 and moved to the Sorbonne in May 1968, and they spread into a general strike involving about ten million workers in France.
The 'Night of the Barricades' of 10–11 May 1968 saw fighting in the Latin Quarter of Paris, and the government of Charles de Gaulle faced a severe crisis.
Students in West Germany, led by figures such as Rudi Dutschke, protested against the Vietnam War and the legacy of the Nazi past.
The 1968 protests did not overthrow governments, but they changed attitudes to authority, sexuality and the role of universities.
The French protests began as a demand for university reform and a protest against restrictions at Nanterre, and widened into attacks on de Gaulle's government and on consumer society.
De Gaulle left France briefly on 29 May, then called an election in which his supporters won a large majority in June 1968, and he resigned in April 1969 after losing a referendum.
In Czechoslovakia, students supported the Prague Spring, and in Poland student protests in March 1968 were suppressed; unrest also hit Italy, Britain and Spain.
The 1968 movement influenced the women's, environmental and peace movements of the 1970s.
Sport became a field of prestige and competition, with national success and the Olympic Games used as displays of political systems.
The European Champion Clubs' Cup began in the 1955–56 season, and it became the leading club competition in Western Europe.
England won the World Cup on 30 July 1966 at Wembley, and the BBC's television coverage made the tournament a mass event across Europe.
The 1972 Munich Olympics were marred by the killing of eleven Israeli athletes and coaches by Palestinian militants on 5–6 September 1972.

The United States and some of its allies boycotted the Moscow Olympics of 1980 after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, and the Soviet Union and most of its allies boycotted the Los Angeles Olympics of 1984.
East Germany ran a state-sponsored doping programme in the 1970s and 1980s, which was exposed after 1990.

The Soviet Union entered the Olympic Games for the first time at Helsinki in 1952 and made the medal table a measure of the rival systems; East Germany, with a population of 17 million, finished near the top in the 1970s and 1980s.
At the 1956 Melbourne Olympics the Hungary–USSR water polo match, played soon after the Soviet invasion, was known as the blood in the water match.
West Germany's win in the 1954 World Cup final, the Miracle of Bern, against Hungary was a boost to national morale, and Real Madrid won the first five European Cups from 1956 to 1960.
Television transformed football and money flowed in through broadcasting rights, sponsorship and advertising, making stars such as Pelé, Johan Cruyff and George Best celebrities.
Television spread rapidly across Western Europe in the 1950s and 1960s, and it changed how people received news, entertainment and advertising.
The Eurovision Song Contest began in May 1956 at Lugano, and it became a shared event across Western Europe in the 1960s.
Commercial television began in Britain with ITV in September 1955, challenging the BBC's monopoly of public broadcasting.
Public broadcasting in Western Europe, including the BBC, RAI in Italy and ARD and ZDF in West Germany, was funded by licence fees and governed by public-service duties.
Pirate radio stations such as Radio Caroline, which began broadcasting in 1964, played pop music that the official BBC radio stations did not provide.
Television's spread changed advertising, politics and sport, and political leaders increasingly had to present themselves on screen.

Television spread from a few sets in 1950 to being owned by most households in Western Europe by the 1970s, and the Coronation of Elizabeth II in June 1953 persuaded many British families to buy sets.
The European Broadcasting Union's Eurovision network, founded in 1954, linked national broadcasters and carried the Eurovision Song Contest and live coverage of major sporting events across borders.

Commercial and public broadcasting differed: ITV and radio stations such as Radio Luxembourg depended on advertising, while the BBC, funded by the licence fee, was bound to inform, educate and entertain.

In Italy and France, state control of television was used by governments, and in the East television was used by the party for propaganda, though East Germans could often receive West German broadcasts.
Newspapers remained influential: the mass-circulation tabloids such as Bild in West Germany and the Daily Mirror in Britain reached millions of readers.
Young people in the East listened to Western music on Radio Luxembourg, Radio Free Europe and tapes copied by hand, and the authorities in the bloc tried to control rock music.
In Czechoslovakia, the arrest and trial of members of the rock band the Plastic People of the Universe in 1976 helped to inspire Charter 77.
In East Germany the state sponsored the Free German Youth, and a ban on Western beat music in 1965 was followed by a limited tolerance in the 1970s.
In the Soviet Union, the Komsomol organised youth, and the stilyagi of the 1950s were young people who copied Western fashions and jazz.
Historians debate whether youth culture and the mass media were a form of liberation or a commercial system that absorbed rebellion.
Achievements: youth culture broadened tastes, challenged the authority of schools and churches, and gave young people a voice in politics and art.
Limits: much youth culture was commercially packaged, and the record companies and advertisers shaped what young people bought.
Contemporaries saw youth culture as a moral danger, with newspapers and politicians warning about delinquency, while young people saw it as freedom.
Later historians see the period as a major turning point in the cultural life of Western Europe, but they stress that its effects varied by class, country and gender.
Scientific advances after 1945 transformed medicine, and the new drugs and vaccines changed the health of Europeans.
Penicillin, discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, was developed into a mass-produced drug during the Second World War by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford.
Antibiotics were used widely in the 1950s, which cut deaths from bacterial infections such as pneumonia and tuberculosis in Western Europe.
Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was announced on 12 April 1955, and Albert Sabin's oral vaccine was widely used from the early 1960s.
The oral contraceptive pill, approved in the USA in 1960, spread through Western Europe in the 1960s and changed reproductive choice (see the notes on women and the family).
The first successful kidney transplant between identical twins took place in Boston in 1954, and the first human heart transplant was performed by Christiaan Barnard in Cape Town on 3 December 1967.
Streptomycin, discovered in 1943 by Selman Waksman, was the first effective drug against tuberculosis, and TB deaths fell sharply in Europe in the 1950s.
Vaccination campaigns against diphtheria, tuberculosis (BCG), polio and measles reduced child deaths, and smallpox was declared eradicated worldwide by the World Health Organization in 1980.
The welfare state made new drugs and hospital treatment available to all, and life expectancy in Western Europe rose by over a decade between 1945 and 1990.
Surgery advanced with the heart pacemaker, kidney dialysis and hip replacements (developed by John Charnley in England in the 1960s), and the CT scanner developed by Godfrey Hounsfield in 1971.
The discovery of the structure of DNA opened the way to genetic engineering and new understanding of heredity.
James Watson and Francis Crick published the double-helix structure of DNA in April 1953, using X-ray crystallography data gathered by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins.
Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962, and Franklin, who had died in 1958, was not included.
In 1973 Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer demonstrated recombinant DNA techniques, which allowed genes to be moved between organisms.
The first in-vitro fertilisation baby, Louise Brown, was born in Oldham in England on 25 July 1978, after work by Robert Edwards and Patrick Steptoe.

Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photograph of DNA, Photo 51 (taken in 1952 at King's College London), gave key evidence for the helical structure, and Watson and Crick worked at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge.
The genetic code was cracked in the 1960s, and in 1977 Frederick Sanger at Cambridge developed a method of sequencing DNA.
Recombinant DNA techniques led to the first genetically engineered drugs, such as human insulin produced by bacteria in 1978, and to the founding of the biotechnology industry in the 1980s.
Advances in biology brought benefits and new moral questions.

The thalidomide scandal of 1961 showed the risks: the drug, sold in West Germany from 1957 as a sedative and for morning sickness, caused birth defects in thousands of children and led to stricter drug testing.
The ethics of IVF, embryo research and genetic engineering were debated; the Warnock Report in Britain in 1984 recommended regulation, and Pope John Paul II's Church opposed IVF.
DNA fingerprinting, developed by Alec Jeffreys at Leicester in 1984, was first used in a criminal case in Britain in 1986.
Debates about genetic engineering, embryo research and drug safety led governments to set up regulatory bodies and ethics committees in the 1980s.
Nuclear power was developed for both weapons and electricity, and in the 1950s and 1960s governments promoted it as a source of cheap energy.
The Soviet Union's Obninsk reactor, which began supplying electricity to the grid in June 1954, was the first nuclear power station connected to a public electricity network.
Calder Hall in Cumbria, England, opened in October 1956 and was the world's first nuclear power station to supply electricity on a commercial scale; it also produced plutonium for weapons.
France developed a national nuclear programme, and in 1974 the Messmer Plan committed the country to building a large number of reactors, which by the 1980s provided most of its electricity.
CERN, the European Organisation for Nuclear Research, was founded in Geneva in 1954 by twelve European states to promote cooperative research in physics.
Atoms for Peace, an address by US President Eisenhower to the UN in December 1953, promoted civil nuclear power and led to the International Atomic Energy Agency in 1957.
The Treaty of Rome of 1957 created Euratom to coordinate nuclear energy in the six EEC states.
The Windscale fire in Cumbria in October 1957 was Britain's worst nuclear accident and released radioactive iodine over the countryside.

After the oil crisis of 1973 many governments, including France, West Germany, Sweden and the USSR, expanded nuclear programmes, and nuclear power came to supply around three quarters of French electricity by the 1990s.
The USSR built reactors across the bloc, including the RBMK reactors at Chernobyl, and nuclear weapons stockpiles grew on both sides.
The growth of nuclear power produced a strong opposition movement, and serious accidents in 1979 and 1986 strengthened it.
Greenpeace was founded in 1971 in Vancouver, Canada, and it campaigned against nuclear testing and nuclear power at sea.
The accident at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania on 28 March 1979 was the most serious in the USA, and it halted new nuclear orders there for many years.
The explosion at the Chernobyl reactor in Soviet Ukraine on 26 April 1986 released radioactive material across Europe, and the nearby town of Pripyat was evacuated.
Chernobyl led to the creation of a 30-kilometre exclusion zone around the plant, and its effects on health and the environment were the subject of long disputes.
Anti-nuclear protests in West Germany, Britain and the Netherlands grew in the early 1980s, alongside protests against NATO missile deployments.
The Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) was founded in Britain in 1958 and organised marches to Aldermaston, using the peace symbol designed in 1958.
In Ireland a plan to build a nuclear plant at Carnsore Point, Co. Wexford, was dropped after large protests in 1978–79 and was never built.
Sweden held a referendum in 1980 on the future of nuclear power, and Austria's Zwentendorf plant, completed in 1978, never operated after a referendum rejected it.

Chernobyl's explosion followed a safety test and design flaws in the RBMK reactor; the Soviet authorities were slow to admit it, and Swedish monitors detected the radioactive cloud, which forced an announcement on 28 April.
many hundreds of thousands of people were eventually resettled from the affected areas.
Chernobyl led to greater international safety cooperation and strengthened the case for glasnost; in Western Europe it prompted a re-think in Italy, which voted to end nuclear power in 1987.
Computers moved from wartime code-breaking and large mainframes to personal machines in the 1980s, changing work and daily life.
Colossus, built at Bletchley Park in 1943–44 by Tommy Flowers' team, was used to break German teleprinter codes, and it was one of the first programmable electronic computers.
ENIAC, completed in the USA in 1945, was one of the first general-purpose electronic digital computers.
The transistor was invented at Bell Laboratories in the USA in December 1947, and it replaced vacuum tubes in computers.
The integrated circuit, or microchip, was developed by Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce around 1958 and 1959, and the Intel 4004 microprocessor followed in 1971.
IBM's System/360 mainframe, launched in 1964, set the standard for business computing in Europe and the USA.
The IBM Personal Computer, launched on 12 August 1981, and the Apple II of 1977 spread personal computing into offices and homes in the 1980s.
The ARPANET, a US network, was first connected in 1969, and it became the basis of the internet.
Alan Turing's theoretical work in the 1930s and wartime code-breaking laid the foundations of computing, and the Manchester Baby of 1948 was the first stored-program computer to run.
The first commercial computer for business use was LEO, built for the Lyons tea shops in Britain in 1951, and IBM dominated the market for mainframes.
Minicomputers and microprocessors from the 1970s made computing cheaper; personal computers such as the Sinclair ZX Spectrum (1982) and the Commodore 64 were bought for homes in Britain and Europe.
In France the Minitel online terminal was launched in 1982 and was given free to telephone subscribers.
Tim Berners-Lee, working at CERN, proposed the World Wide Web in 1989, and it was launched publicly in 1991.
Advances in science and computing changed working life and the balance between East and West, as technology became central to economic power.
Computers automated routine office and factory work, and they reduced demand for some clerical and manufacturing jobs in Western Europe.
Western export controls, coordinated through COCOM from 1949, restricted the sale of advanced computing technology to the Soviet bloc.
The Soviet bloc fell behind the West in computing and electronics, a gap that Soviet planners tried to close through copying and espionage.
Information technology became a key concept in the economy, and the pace of change in the 1980s prepared the ground for the global networks that followed.
Banks introduced cash machines from 1967, supermarkets adopted bar codes in the 1970s, and word processors and spreadsheets transformed office work in the 1980s.
Automation reduced employment in manufacturing, while service jobs in banking, insurance and administration grew, contributing to deindustrialisation.
By the 1980s Soviet leaders recognised that the Soviet Union lagged badly in computing and microelectronics, which was one of the reasons for the push for economic reform.
Europe lagged behind the USA and Japan in computing and electronics, and the EEC launched programmes such as ESPRIT in 1984 to support research.
Historians and contemporaries have judged these advances by the benefits they brought and the new dangers and inequalities they created.
Achievements: longer life expectancy, the control of infectious disease, cheap electricity from nuclear plants and the transformation of communication and work.
Limits: nuclear accidents, the risks of radioactive waste, the ethical questions raised by reproductive and genetic technology, and job losses from automation.
Contemporaries in the 1950s often celebrated science as the key to progress, while the anti-nuclear and environmental movements of the 1970s and 1980s challenged that view.
Later historians stress that the impact of these technologies depended on political decisions about how they were used, not only on their scientific potential.
The defeat of the European colonial powers by Japan weakened their claim to rule in Asia and gave nationalists new arguments.
Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and invaded British Malaya on 7–8 December 1941; Hong Kong surrendered on 25 December 1941.
Singapore, Britain's main base in the East, surrendered on 15 February 1942; about 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops became prisoners of war.
Japan overran Burma in 1942, closing the Burma Road that supplied China and threatening India's eastern frontier.
The Dutch East Indies fell to Japan in early 1942, ending Dutch rule there until the Japanese surrender in August 1945.
Japan moved troops into northern Indochina in 1940 and took full control from the French colonial administration on 9 March 1945.
Japanese propaganda promoted a ‘Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere’ and ‘Asia for the Asians’, which encouraged anti-colonial nationalists across the region.
About 2.5 million men served in the British Indian Army during the war, and the army expanded greatly as a result.

Subhas Chandra Bose, a former Congress president, raised the Indian National Army in 1942-43 from Indian prisoners captured at Singapore to fight alongside Japan; the British trials of INA officers at the Red Fort in Delhi in 1945-46 caused a public outcry and made it politically risky to punish them.
The Bengal famine of 1943, in which an estimated two to three million people died, damaged British prestige in India; wartime requisitioning and the loss of Burmese rice imports contributed to it.
The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, moved from petitioning to mass civil disobedience under Mohandas Gandhi.
Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and became the dominant Congress leader after 1920.
Satyagraha, meaning ‘truth-force’, was non-violent civil disobedience; Gandhi first used it in peasant campaigns at Champaran (1917) and Kheda (1918).
The Amritsar massacre of 13 April 1919 at Jallianwala Bagh, when British-Indian troops fired on a crowd, killed hundreds and turned many Indians against British rule.
The Non-Cooperation movement of 1920–22 urged boycotts of British goods, courts, schools and councils; Gandhi called it off after the Chauri Chaura incident of February 1922.
The Salt March of 12 March to 6 April 1930 covered about 240 miles to the coast at Dandi, where Gandhi made salt in defiance of the British salt monopoly.

The Government of India Act 1935 gave Indians self-government in the provinces; in the 1937 elections Congress won outright majorities in five of the eleven provinces and went on to form governments in most of them.
In October–November 1939 Congress ministers resigned in protest at the Viceroy declaring war on India's behalf without consulting Indian leaders.
On 8 August 1942 Congress passed the Quit India resolution demanding British withdrawal; Gandhi and most leaders were arrested, and widespread unrest followed until Gandhi's release in May 1944.

The Cripps Mission of March 1942 offered India dominion status after the war, with the right to secede; Congress rejected it because it allowed provinces to opt out and gave no immediate control of defence, and it was withdrawn.
Partition grew out of the Muslim League's campaign for separate Muslim states, which the Congress leadership would not accept for the whole of India.
The All-India Muslim League was founded at Dhaka in 1906 to protect Muslim political interests.
Muhammad Ali Jinnah, a barrister who had once been a Congress member, led the League from 1934 and was known as Quaid-i-Azam (great leader).
The Lahore Resolution of 23 March 1940 called for independent states in the Muslim-majority areas of the north-west and east of India.
Jinnah argued that Hindus and Muslims were two nations, and that Congress claimed to speak for all Indians while representing mainly Hindus.
In the 1945–46 elections the League won most of the seats reserved for Muslims in the central and provincial assemblies, which gave it a claim to speak for Muslim India.
Punjab and Bengal, each with a large Muslim population but a large non-Muslim minority, became the central problem in the partition settlement.

The name Pakistan was coined in 1933 by the student Choudhry Rahmat Ali; the League did poorly among Muslim voters in the 1937 elections but used the years of Congress rule to claim that Muslims could not be safe in a Hindu-majority state, and Jinnah called a Day of Deliverance on 22 December 1939 when the Congress ministries resigned.
Britain's exhausted post-war economy and Labour's commitment to independence set the timing of withdrawal.
Clement Attlee's Labour Party won a landslide in the general election of July 1945, and Attlee became prime minister on 26 July 1945.
Britain had spent heavily on the war; it borrowed about 3.75 billion dollars from the United States in 1945-46, and its debts and the cost of occupation left it unable to hold a large army in India.

In February 1946 ratings of the Royal Indian Navy mutinied at Bombay over pay and conditions; the mutiny was suppressed, but it showed that the armed forces could no longer be relied on to support British rule.
The Cabinet Mission of March–June 1946 proposed a loose federal India with groups of provinces; it failed to win agreement between Congress and the League.
The League called Direct Action Day for 16 August 1946; communal killings in Calcutta left thousands dead and many more injured.
On 20 February 1947 Attlee announced that British rule would end by June 1948 at the latest, and Lord Wavell was replaced as Viceroy by Lord Mountbatten.
Mountbatten's plan of 3 June 1947 accepted partition, and the date was brought forward to 15 August 1947 once the principal Indian leaders agreed.
The Simla Conference of June-July 1945 broke down when Jinnah insisted that only the League could name the Muslim members of the Viceroy's council.
After the Cabinet Mission failed, an interim government headed by Jawaharlal Nehru took office in September 1946 and the League joined it in October; the two parties still could not work together.
Lord Mountbatten arrived as Viceroy on 22 March 1947; he judged that a united India was no longer possible and pressed for a quick transfer of power.
Under the 3 June 1947 plan the assemblies of Punjab and Bengal voted on dividing their provinces, and a referendum in the North-West Frontier Province and Sylhet decided their future.
Independence on 15 August 1947 created two dominions, India and Pakistan, and divided the Punjab and Bengal.
The Indian Independence Act, passed by the British Parliament in July 1947, ended British rule and made India and Pakistan independent dominions.
Pakistan was formed in two parts, West Pakistan and East Bengal, separated by about 1,600 km of Indian territory.
Cyril Radcliffe, a barrister who had never visited India, drew the Punjab and Bengal boundaries; the Radcliffe Line was announced on 17 August 1947, two days after independence.
Millions crossed the new border as Hindus and Sikhs moved from West Pakistan into India and Muslims moved into Pakistan; estimates of those displaced range from about 10 to 15 million.
Communal violence in the Punjab and Bengal killed many people; estimates of the death toll range from about 200,000 to about 2 million.
The princely states, over 500 in number, had to join India or Pakistan; the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Maharaja of Kashmir were the most contested cases.
The Maharaja of Kashmir signed an Instrument of Accession to India on 26 October 1947, and fighting over Kashmir between India and Pakistan began that year.
Independence did not end the conflicts that partition created, and India chose to remain in the Commonwealth.
Gandhi had fasted in Calcutta and Delhi in 1947–48 to stop communal violence; he was shot dead in Delhi on 30 January 1948 by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist.
The first Indo-Pakistani war over Kashmir ended with a ceasefire from 1 January 1949, leaving a line that became a long-term division of the state.
Jinnah became Governor-General of Pakistan and died in September 1948.
The London Declaration of April 1949 allowed India to become a republic while remaining a member of the Commonwealth, with the King recognised as head of the association.
India became a republic on 26 January 1950, with Jawaharlal Nehru as prime minister.
Independent India followed non-alignment under Nehru and remained a major trading partner of Britain, with the sterling area linking the two economies.
India was the largest and most valuable of the British possessions; its loss ended the British Raj, which had ruled India directly since 1858.
Burma and Ceylon became independent in 1948, and the Gold Coast became independent as Ghana on 6 March 1957, the first British colony in tropical Africa to do so.
The partition of the Indian Army, the civil service and the railways between the two dominions had to be done in a few weeks, causing administrative strain.
For Britain, the loss of India reduced its role in Asia and made the Commonwealth its main continuing link with former colonies.
India's decision to remain in the Commonwealth as a republic established that membership did not depend on accepting the monarch as head of state.
The war with Japan had left the British Indian Army the largest volunteer force in history, but its loyalty could not be taken for granted after the INA trials and the 1946 naval mutiny.

Nationalist explanation: decades of Congress agitation, from non-cooperation to Quit India, made British rule impossible to maintain without a degree of repression the British public would not accept.

Economic explanation: By 1945 Britain owed India over one billion pounds in sterling balances for wartime supplies, which reversed the old financial relationship and reduced the economic value of the Raj.
Political explanation: Labour's 1945 government was committed to Indian self-rule, and Attlee argued that Britain could not hold India against the will of its people.

Security explanation: the INA trials and the 1946 naval mutiny led some British officials, including Viceroy Wavell, to doubt that the Indian Army and police could be relied on to suppress a mass rising.
Communal explanation: the failure of Congress and the League to agree, and the violence in Calcutta, Bihar and the Punjab, led Mountbatten to fear civil war if he delayed.
Mountbatten's critics argue that bringing the date forward by ten months left too little time to plan the boundary and policing; his defenders argue that delay would have meant more violence.
Gandhi was the leading figure of the Indian independence movement and the most influential Indian voice in the British withdrawal.
Born 2 October 1869 at Porbandar in Gujarat, he trained as a barrister in London and practised law in South Africa from 1893 to 1914.
In South Africa he led campaigns against discriminatory laws affecting Indians, and developed the method of non-violent resistance that he later called satyagraha.
After 1915 he built a mass movement among peasants and urban workers, wore simple dress and promoted hand-spinning (khadi) as a symbol of self-reliance.
At the London Round Table Conference of 1931 he was Congress's only representative; the talks failed over separate electorates for minorities, which B. R. Ambedkar demanded for Dalits.
He was a participant in every major Congress campaign and was imprisoned several times, including from August 1942 to May 1944.
Contemporaries saw him in very different ways: many Indians revered him as the Mahatma, British officials often treated him as an obstacle, and Jinnah accused him of speaking for Hindus.

Historians differ on his impact: Judith Brown and others stress his skill in turning Congress into a mass movement, while others argue that war exhaustion, the INA and naval unrest and Labour's policy did more to end the Raj; critics point to his limited success on caste and his failure to prevent partition, and B. R. Ambedkar was among his sharpest contemporary critics.
Gandhi's stated aims were swaraj (self-rule), Hindu-Muslim unity and the end of untouchability; in Hind Swaraj (1909) he rejected industrial civilisation, and he called the untouchables Harijans.

After Ambedkar won separate electorates for Dalits in the 1932 Communal Award, Gandhi fasted in Yerwada jail and the Poona Pact (September 1932) replaced them with reserved seats in general electorates.
In late 1946 he walked through villages in Noakhali in East Bengal to calm communal violence, and he was in Calcutta on 15 August 1947 fasting rather than celebrating independence.
Achievement: non-violent mass protest became the central method of Indian politics, and campaigns such as the Salt March drew in very large numbers of people.
Limit: the Gandhian campaigns did not secure a united India, and partition and the violence that followed were not prevented.
Achievement: the Quit India movement and the 1942 unrest showed the British that their authority could not be maintained by force alone.
Limit: the decision to accept partition was taken by the Congress and League leadership in June 1947, not by Gandhi alone, and Gandhi publicly opposed partition.
Achievement: the transfer of power ended British rule without a colonial war of the kind France fought in Indochina and Algeria.
Limit: British withdrawal was rushed in 1947, and the boundary settlement was made within weeks, which left the population to face the consequences.
Limit: the Gandhian method relied on the moral restraint of the British government and on disciplined followers, and it did not stop the communal killings that followed Direct Action Day in 1946.
Later view: many historians judge the speed of withdrawal and the Radcliffe boundary commission's rushed work as major contributors to the scale of the violence.
France ruled Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos as French Indochina; the Japanese occupation of 1940–45 weakened French authority and gave the nationalists their chance.
French Indochina was formed as a federation in 1887 from Tonkin, Annam, Cochinchina and Cambodia, and Laos was added in 1893.

The French ruled through a colonial administration headed by a governor-general and kept the Vietnamese emperor in place as a figurehead at Hue; Cochinchina was a direct colony and Tonkin and Annam were protectorates.
Japan moved troops into northern Indochina in 1940 under an arrangement with the Vichy French administration, and Japanese forces took full control on 9 March 1945.
The Viet Minh (League for the Independence of Vietnam) was founded in May 1941 under Ho Chi Minh, combining communists and non-communist nationalists.
A famine in northern Vietnam in 1944–45 killed many people; estimates range from several hundred thousand to about two million.
The Viet Minh seized power in Hanoi and other towns in August 1945, and Emperor Bảo Đại abdicated on 25 August 1945.
Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh fought the Japanese from the hills of northern Vietnam and received some American supplies and training from the OSS in 1945.
Ho Chi Minh proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in Hanoi on 2 September 1945, quoting the United States Declaration of Independence.
Chinese Nationalist forces occupied the north and British forces the south after the Japanese surrender, and British troops helped the French return to Saigon in September 1945.
Under the Franco-Vietnamese agreement of 6 March 1946, France recognised the Democratic Republic as a free state within the French Union, but left the question of Cochinchina unresolved.
The French Union was set up under the French constitution of 1946 as a federation of France, its overseas territories and associated states.
Fighting broke out in Hanoi on 19 December 1946, starting the First Indochina War between France and the Viet Minh.

Ho Chi Minh went to France for the Fontainebleau conference in mid-1946 and signed a temporary agreement in September, but the talks failed; a French naval bombardment of Haiphong in November 1946 killed many civilians and made war likely.
Ho Chi Minh wrote several appeals to President Truman in 1945-46 asking for American support, and received no reply.
The French tried to defeat the Viet Minh with a French-backed Vietnamese state, but the war ended in defeat at Dien Bien Phu.
France set up a State of Vietnam under Bảo Đại in 1949 as an alternative to the Democratic Republic, and it was recognised by Western states.
After the Chinese communist victory of 1949, China supplied the Viet Minh with weapons and military advisers from 1950, while the United States financed much of France's war effort.
The French commander Henri Navarre set out to force a decisive battle in 1953, and he fortified the valley at Dien Bien Phu in north-west Vietnam.
The siege of Dien Bien Phu ran from 13 March to 7 May 1954; the Viet Minh commander Vo Nguyen Giap used artillery and supply routes to overrun the French garrison.
The Geneva Conference of April–July 1954 produced the Geneva Accords, signed on 21 July 1954, which divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel pending elections in 1956.
The planned 1956 elections were never held, and Ngô Đình Diem became premier of the South in 1954 and president in 1955 with United States backing.

Laos and Cambodia gained independence from France in 1953; in Cambodia King Norodom Sihanouk's 'royal crusade' pressed France for independence, and in Laos the communist Pathet Lao, allied to the Viet Minh, held the north-east and fought the royal government after 1954.

Dien Bien Phu ended with more than 10,000 French Union troops captured; the news reached the Geneva Conference the day after the surrender, and the new French prime minister Pierre Mendes France had promised to reach a settlement within a month of taking office in June 1954.
France withdrew its forces from the south by 1956, and the United States replaced it as the main outside power in South Vietnam.
Ho Chi Minh's government in the north was recognised by China and the Soviet Union; his land reform of 1953-56 was violent and was followed by a public admission of errors.
The Japanese occupation ended Dutch control and allowed Indonesian nationalists to build organisations and armed forces.
The Japanese occupation of 1942-45 ended Dutch rule, drew heavily on Indonesian forced labourers known as romusha, and left Indonesians in senior positions that they had never held under the Dutch.
The Japanese trained Indonesian forces, such as the PETA volunteer army, and allowed nationalists such as Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta to speak publicly.
On 1 June 1945 Sukarno gave a speech setting out the Pancasila, five principles on which an independent Indonesia would be based.
Sukarno and Hatta proclaimed Indonesian independence in Jakarta on 17 August 1945, a few days after Japan announced its surrender.
Dutch forces returned with Allied support in late 1945; Indonesian and British troops fought in Surabaya in November 1945, and British forces withdrew in 1946.

The Linggadjati Agreement of 15 November 1946 recognised the Republic's authority over Java, Madura and Sumatra and provided for a United States of Indonesia in union with the Netherlands; the Dutch soon reinterpreted it.
The first Dutch ‘police action’ began in July 1947 and occupied much of the Indonesian-held territory in Java and Sumatra.

The UN Security Council called for a ceasefire in August 1947 and set up a Good Offices Committee; the Renville Agreement of January 1948 was negotiated aboard the US ship Renville and left Dutch forces holding large parts of Java and Sumatra.
The second police action of 19 December 1948 captured Yogyakarta, the Republic's capital at the time, and imprisoned Sukarno and Hatta; a government in exile on Sumatra continued the resistance.
United States pressure on the Netherlands, which included threats over Marshall Plan aid, helped bring the Dutch to the negotiating table.
The Round Table Conference at The Hague in 1949 led to the transfer of sovereignty on 27 December 1949 to the United States of Indonesia.
The Dutch kept West New Guinea until 1962, when it passed to a UN administration, and it was transferred to Indonesia on 1 May 1963.
Sukarno's government had suppressed a communist rising at Madiun in September 1948, which helped to win American sympathy for the Republic before the second action.
At The Hague Indonesia agreed to take over about 4.3 billion guilders of Dutch East Indies debt, and the Netherlands retained West New Guinea for later negotiation.
The Netherlands-Indonesian Union created in 1949 was a weak association; Indonesia abolished it unilaterally in 1954.
The Asian–African Conference at Bandung in April 1955 brought together 29 countries; it promoted non-alignment and anti-colonialism, and Sukarno was its most prominent host.
From 1957 Sukarno took over Dutch businesses in Indonesia, and the Dutch-owned enterprises were placed under Indonesian control.
Sukarno introduced ‘Guided Democracy’ by decree on 5 July 1959, returning to the 1945 constitution and ruling with a National Front and the army.
Konfrontasi (confrontation) from 1963 to 1966 was Indonesia's opposition to the new Federation of Malaysia, including armed raids into Malaysian Borneo.
A UN-supervised 1969 vote, the Act of Free Choice, confirmed Indonesian rule in West New Guinea, though it was held among about 1,000 chosen representatives and has been widely criticised.
Sukarno withdrew Indonesia from the United Nations in January 1965, and he moved towards closer relations with China.

After an attempted coup on 30 September 1965 in which six generals were killed, General Suharto took control of the army; anti-communist killings followed, with estimates ranging from about 500,000 to one million or more.

Sukarno was stripped of real power by the Supersemar order of 11 March 1966 and placed under house arrest; Suharto became acting president in 1967 and president in 1968, and Sukarno died in June 1970.
The first free national election, in September 1955, left four parties of similar size (PNI, Masjumi, Nahdlatul Ulama and the PKI), and unstable coalition cabinets followed.
Regional rebellions in 1957-58, the PRRI in Sumatra and Permesta in Sulawesi, protested against Java's domination and were put down by the army, strengthening the army's political role.

Sukarno had himself named president for life in 1963 and promoted 'Nasakom', the union of nationalism, religion and communism; the PKI, with about three million members by the mid-1960s, was the largest communist party outside the communist states, and the army distrusted it.
Economic decline in the early 1960s, with high inflation and heavy spending on Konfrontasi, weakened his position before 1965.
Ho Chi Minh led the Vietnamese independence movement from the 1920s and was the head of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam.

Born Nguyen Sinh Cung in 1890 in central Vietnam, he left Vietnam in 1911 and spent about thirty years abroad, including in France, Britain, the Soviet Union and China, using the name Nguyen Ai Quoc before adopting Ho Chi Minh in 1942.
In 1919 he presented a petition for Vietnamese rights to the Versailles peace conference, which was ignored by the Allied powers.
He joined the French Communist Party in 1920 and worked with the Communist International, and in 1930 he helped found the Indochinese Communist Party.
He was a participant in the 1945 August Revolution and proclaimed the Democratic Republic on 2 September 1945, and he led the government through the war against France.
Contemporaries in France and the United States saw him as a communist agitator; many Vietnamese nationalists saw him as the leader who had made independence possible.
He died in September 1969, before the end of the Vietnam War, and his government took control of the whole country in 1975.
Historians debate whether his nationalism or his communism was the stronger force in his politics, and they also debate the role of the Soviet Union and China in supporting him.
He returned to Vietnam in 1941 and founded the Viet Minh; he was held by the Chinese Nationalists in 1942-43, and he led the First Indochina War as president, with Vo Nguyen Giap commanding the army.
He was known as Uncle Ho; after the 1954 division he led North Vietnam, and in the north the Lao Dong (Workers') Party ran the state with Soviet and Chinese aid.
Sukarno was the first president of Indonesia and the central figure in the independence struggle against the Dutch.
Born 6 June 1901 in East Java, he trained as an engineer and founded the Indonesian Nationalist Party (PNI) in 1927.
The Dutch imprisoned him in 1929 and released him in 1931; they later exiled him to remote islands, where he remained until the Japanese occupation.
Under the Japanese occupation he worked with the Japanese administration and encouraged mass mobilisation, which some Dutch and later Indonesian critics saw as collaboration.
He was a participant in the proclamation of 17 August 1945 and became the first president of the Republic of Indonesia.

Contemporaries were divided: Indonesians called him Bung Karno (brother Karno) and the father of the nation, while Dutch officials treated him as a collaborator with Japan and the army and the Islamic parties came to see him as too close to the communists.

His later rule is judged harshly by many historians: Guided Democracy ended parliamentary government, and the economy and foreign policy of confrontation left Indonesia isolated by 1965; others credit him with giving a diverse archipelago a national language, Indonesian, and a unifying ideology in the Pancasila.
He was never a leader of the Indonesian Communist Party but worked closely with it in the early 1960s, which caused suspicion in the army.
He was a gifted orator who studied engineering at Bandung (graduating in 1926); his Pancasila speech of 1 June 1945 showed his aim of balancing nationalists, Muslims and communists in one state.
Achievement: Vietnam and Indonesia both defeated attempts by returning colonial powers to restore their old authority, Indonesia in 1949 and the Viet Minh in 1954.
Limit: Vietnam was divided in 1954, and the division became the basis of a larger war between the two Vietnamese states from the late 1950s.
Achievement: Indonesia gained sovereignty in 1949 after a diplomatic campaign that involved the UN and the United States, not only military action.
Limit: the Dutch police actions, the French war and the Geneva settlement all showed that European powers could resist independence for years.
Achievement: Sukarno's diplomacy at Bandung gave newly independent states a voice in world politics.
Limit: Guided Democracy and the economic decline of the 1960s ended in the 1965 coup, the killings that followed, and Suharto's rise to power.
Later view: Benedict Anderson argued that the Indonesian revolution of 1945 was driven by young pemuda activists, trained under the Japanese, as much as by leaders such as Sukarno and Hatta.
Limit: independence did not bring stable government, as Vietnam divided in 1954 and Indonesia moved from parliamentary democracy to authoritarian rule within a decade.
Britain's wartime promise of a Jewish national home and its Mandate for Palestine created the conflicting claims that later drove the withdrawal.
Zionism was a movement that sought a Jewish national homeland; Theodor Herzl led its political organisation from 1897, when the first Zionist Congress was held at Basel.
The Balfour Declaration of 2 November 1917 stated British support for ‘a national home for the Jewish people’ in Palestine, provided the rights of existing non-Jewish communities were not prejudiced.

Britain received the Mandate for Palestine from the League of Nations, which came into force in 1923; the Mandate also covered the territory east of the Jordan, which was separated as Transjordan in 1921.

Jewish immigration rose sharply in the 1930s, especially after the Nazis came to power in Germany in 1933, and the Jewish share of Palestine's population grew from about 11 per cent in 1922 to roughly 30 per cent by 1939.
The Arab Revolt of 1936–39 against Mandate rule and Jewish immigration was crushed by British forces, and the Peel Commission of 1937 proposed partitioning Palestine.

The British White Paper of 17 May 1939 limited Jewish immigration to 75,000 over five years, after which Arab consent would be needed, restricted Jewish land purchases and promised an independent Palestine within ten years; the Zionist movement rejected it.

The Peel Commission of 1937 proposed a small Jewish state, an Arab state joined to Transjordan and a British-held enclave around Jerusalem; Arab leaders rejected it and the British dropped it in 1938.
The Holocaust killed about six million Jews in Europe between 1941 and 1945, and it intensified the demand for a Jewish state and for the admission of Jewish refugees to Palestine.
The Haganah, founded in 1920, was the main Jewish defence force in Palestine, and it was linked to the Jewish Agency under the leadership of David Ben-Gurion.
The Irgun, formed in 1931 by Revisionist Zionists and led from 1943 by Menachem Begin, and the smaller Lehi (Stern Gang) carried out attacks on British targets.
The Irgun bombed the south wing of the King David Hotel in Jerusalem, the headquarters of the British administration, on 22 July 1946, killing 91 Arabs, Britons and Jews.

From October 1945 to mid-1946 the Haganah, Irgun and Lehi co-operated in a Jewish Resistance Movement, but in 1944-45 the Haganah had handed Irgun members to the British in the 'Saison'; the Irgun hanged two British sergeants in July 1947 in reprisal for the execution of its members.
Britain's policy of restricting refugee ships led to the Exodus of 1947, when about 4,500 Holocaust survivors were sent back to Europe, a scene that drew world attention.

The Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry recommended in April 1946 that 100,000 Jewish refugees be admitted to Palestine; Britain, with about 100,000 troops in the country, refused without Arab agreement.
Unable to reconcile Arab and Jewish claims, Britain handed the problem to the United Nations in 1947.
In February 1947 the British government announced that it would refer the Palestine question to the United Nations, and in September 1947 it said it would end the Mandate.

The UN Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP) recommended partition in 1947, and the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 181 on 29 November 1947, by 33 votes to 13 with 10 abstentions, to divide Palestine into an Arab state and a Jewish state, with Jerusalem under international control.
The partition plan gave the proposed Jewish state about 55 per cent of the territory, although the Jewish population was only about a third of the total.
The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab states rejected partition, and fighting between Arab and Jewish forces began in December 1947.
Britain refused to implement partition itself and announced that it would withdraw its forces by 15 May 1948, which left a gap in security control during the spring of 1948.
The Mandate expired on 14 May 1948, the same day that Israel was proclaimed, so British authority in Palestine ended as the Jewish state began.
Both the United States and the Soviet Union supported partition, an unusual agreement in the early Cold War; Britain abstained.
In the civil war that followed, Jewish forces under Plan Dalet seized Tiberias, Haifa and Jaffa in April-May 1948, and the Arab population of those cities fled in large numbers.
The declaration of Israel on 14 May 1948 led to war with the neighbouring Arab states and the flight of many Palestinian Arabs.
David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel in Tel Aviv on 14 May 1948 and became its first prime minister.
Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon sent armies into former Mandate territory on 15 May 1948, starting the first Arab–Israeli war.

The attack on Deir Yassin on 9 April 1948 by Irgun and Lehi fighters killed roughly 100 to 120 villagers, though early reports said 254; it was used in propaganda by both sides and fuelled panic among Arabs. Four days later Arab forces killed about 78 Jews in a medical convoy near Jerusalem.

About 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled from territory that became Israel, mostly to the West Bank, Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Jordan; UN General Assembly Resolution 194 of December 1948 said refugees who wished to return should be allowed to, a right Israel has not accepted.
The armistice agreements of 1949 left Israel with more territory than the UN plan had allotted it; Jordan held the West Bank and Egypt administered the Gaza Strip.
Jordan annexed the West Bank in 1950, a step recognised by only a few states, and the refugee question remained unresolved.

About 6,000 Israelis died in the war, roughly one per cent of the Jewish population; Israel's Law of Return of 1950 gave Jews the right to immigrate, and Jews also left or were pushed out of Arab states in the years after 1948.
The United States recognised Israel within minutes of the declaration and the Soviet Union recognised it three days later; Israel's declaration did not fix its borders.
On 23 July 1952 the Free Officers movement overthrew King Farouk of Egypt; Gamal Abdul Nasser emerged as the leading figure and became prime minister in 1954.
The Anglo-Egyptian Agreement of October 1954 provided for the withdrawal of British troops from the Suez Canal base, which was completed in June 1956.
The Baghdad Pact of 1955 linked Britain, Iraq, Turkey, Iran and Pakistan in a defensive alliance that Nasser saw as an attempt to isolate Egypt.
In 1955 Nasser bought arms from the Soviet bloc through Czechoslovakia, a deal that made Egypt a point of Cold War rivalry.
Nasser's Arab nationalism was opposed to Western alliances and to the state of Israel; he attended the Bandung Conference in April 1955 and supported anti-colonial movements.

Nasser was elected president of Egypt by referendum in June 1956, and on 19 July 1956 the United States, followed by Britain, withdrew its offer to fund the Aswan High Dam, after Egypt recognised communist China and bought Soviet-bloc arms.

Egypt barred Israeli ships from the Suez Canal and, from 1955, from the Straits of Tiran, and fedayeen raids from Gaza led to Israeli reprisals such as the Gaza raid of February 1955, which killed 38 and pushed Nasser to seek arms.
Nasser's nationalisation of the Suez Canal provoked an Anglo-French and Israeli invasion that ended in political defeat.

The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, was run by the Suez Canal Company; Britain had bought the Khedive's 44 per cent of its shares in 1875, and about two-thirds of Western Europe's oil imports passed through it in the 1950s.
On 26 July 1956 Nasser announced the nationalisation of the Suez Canal Company, promising that canal revenues would fund the Aswan High Dam.
Britain and France planned military action with Israel; the secret Protocol of Sèvres, signed on 24 October 1956, set out an Israeli attack on Sinai followed by an Anglo-French ultimatum.

Israeli forces invaded the Sinai Peninsula on 29 October 1956, and Britain and France issued an ultimatum to both sides on 30 October; the Anglo-French bombing of Egyptian airfields followed on 31 October.

British and French paratroopers landed at Port Said and Port Fuad on 5 November 1956 and seaborne landings followed on 6 November; the operation was halted and a ceasefire took effect at midnight on 6-7 November.
The United States under Eisenhower opposed the invasion; Britain faced a run on the pound, and the US refused support from the IMF until Britain agreed to withdraw.
The Soviet Union threatened rocket attacks on London and Paris in a letter of 5 November 1956, and it supported Egypt in the UN.

The UN created the United Nations Emergency Force (UNEF) in November 1956 on a proposal by the Canadian foreign minister Lester Pearson, commanded by the Canadian general E. L. M. Burns, to supervise the withdrawal and the Sinai frontier.
The Hungarian rising had been crushed by Soviet troops on 4 November, which weakened Britain's and France's complaint against Soviet behaviour and made Eisenhower angrier at his allies.
A British-French force had advanced about 23 miles south of Port Said by the time of the ceasefire.

Anthony Eden, ill and discredited, resigned as British prime minister on 9 January 1957 and Harold Macmillan succeeded him; the crisis had also shown that Britain could not act against American wishes.
Israel withdrew from Sinai and Gaza in early 1957, after the United States gave assurances about the Straits of Tiran and the UNEF presence.
Egypt had sunk about fifty ships in the canal; a UN clearance operation reopened it in April 1957, under Egyptian control, and Egypt seized British and French property.
Nasser's prestige in the Arab world increased sharply because he had defied Britain, France and Israel and kept control of the canal.
Britain and France lost their position as the main Western powers in the Middle East, and the United States took a larger role there.
The crisis showed the limits of Anglo-French power after 1945 and led the United States to announce the Eisenhower Doctrine in January 1957 to fill the gap in the Middle East.
The Hashemite monarchy in Iraq, Britain's closest Arab ally, was overthrown in 1958, and Iraq left the Baghdad Pact in 1959.
Ben-Gurion led the Jewish community in Palestine and was the first prime minister of Israel.
Born David Grün in 1886 in Płońsk in the Russian Empire, he emigrated to Ottoman Palestine in 1906 and worked as a labour activist.
He led the Jewish Agency's executive from 1935 and accepted the partition plan of 1947 as a first step towards a Jewish state.

As a participant he proclaimed Israel on 14 May 1948 and served as prime minister in 1948-54 and 1955-63, also holding the defence ministry; he resigned in 1953 and retired to the kibbutz of Sde Boker before returning.

He oversaw the creation of the Israel Defence Forces in May 1948, ordering the shelling of the Irgun ship Altalena in June 1948 to establish one army, and in October 1956 he attended the secret talks at Sèvres with Britain and France.
Arab opinion regarded him as the architect of a state that displaced Palestinians, while most Jews saw him as the founder of the state.
Historians of the 'new history' school such as Benny Morris argue that there was no overall expulsion plan in 1948 but that Ben-Gurion backed the expulsions from Lydda and Ramle in July 1948.
Nasser was the leader of Egypt from 1954 to 1970 and the most important figure of Arab nationalism in the Suez crisis.
Born 15 January 1918 in Alexandria, he trained as an army officer and was one of the Free Officers who overthrew King Farouk in 1952.
As prime minister from 1954 and president from 1956, he pursued land reform, industrialisation and the building of the Aswan High Dam.

He was a participant in the Suez Crisis, in which he nationalised the canal and, though his army was defeated in Sinai, survived the Anglo-French-Israeli attack with Egyptian control of the canal confirmed.
He formed the United Arab Republic with Syria in 1958, which lasted until 1961, and he supported anti-colonial movements in Algeria and elsewhere.
British ministers, including Eden, compared him with dictators of the 1930s, while Arab nationalists across the region saw him as a hero who had defied the West.
Historians credit him with land reform, the Aswan High Dam and Arab self-confidence, but criticise his one-party rule, the suppression of the Muslim Brotherhood and the military failure of 1967.
After 1956 he sent troops into the Yemeni civil war in 1962, which became a costly commitment, and in 1967 he blocked the Straits of Tiran; Egypt lost Sinai in the Six-Day War of June 1967.
He offered to resign after the 1967 defeat, withdrew his resignation after mass demonstrations, and died on 28 September 1970.
Achievement: Britain ended the Palestine Mandate and passed the question to the UN instead of fighting both communities, as the cost and the attacks on British forces had become too great.
Limit: the Mandate's conflicting promises to Arabs and Jews were not reconciled, and the 1948 war left a legacy of refugees and hostility.
Achievement: Israel overran Sinai in days and the Anglo-French force had advanced down the canal before the ceasefire, so the military operation was largely successful as far as it went.
Limit: the Suez operation failed politically; the ceasefire was forced by the United States, the Soviet threat and the UN, and the canal remained in Egyptian hands.

Contemporary view: Eden presented the action as police action to separate Israel and Egypt, while Labour leader Hugh Gaitskell and the junior minister Anthony Nutting, who resigned, condemned the secret collusion with Israel.

Later view: many historians treat Suez as the moment that exposed Britain's limits as a power; others argue that Britain's withdrawal from empire was already under way, and they debate how far Britain's Mandate policy, including the 1917 declaration and the 1939 White Paper, helped to create Middle East tensions.
From 1957 British and French policy in Africa shifted towards rapid independence, and Algeria became the hardest case.
Ghana (the former Gold Coast) became independent on 6 March 1957, the first sub-Saharan African colony to do so.
Guinea voted against joining the French Community in the referendum of September 1958 and became independent on 2 October 1958, the first French colony in Africa to leave the community.
Harold Macmillan told the South African Parliament in Cape Town on 3 February 1960 that a ‘wind of change’ was blowing through Africa.
Seventeen African states gained independence in 1960, a year that became known as the Year of Africa.

France's neighbours Tunisia and Morocco became independent in March 1956, and Britain chose negotiated transfers of power in most of its colonies, while France's policy in Algeria was contested by about a million settlers and an armed nationalist movement.
The Loi-cadre of June 1956, introduced by the minister Gaston Defferre, gave the African territories elected assemblies and governments with wider powers, as an early step towards self-government.

De Gaulle toured Africa in August 1958 and at Brazzaville on 24 August offered the territories a choice between the Community and independence; the Brazzaville Conference of 1944 had earlier promised reforms but ruled out self-government.

In 1960 the Community broke up in practice: most French West and Equatorial African territories, along with Madagascar, became independent by negotiation and signed co-operation accords with France on defence, currency and aid.
France conquered Algeria from 1830, and by the 1848 constitution Algeria was divided into three départements that were treated as part of metropolitan France.
The settler population, known as pieds-noirs, numbered about one million by 1954 out of about nine million inhabitants, and dominated the economy, land and local administration.

Most Muslim Algerians were subjects rather than full citizens; the Statute of 1947 created an Algerian Assembly with two colleges of equal size, one elected by about a million Europeans and one by about nine million Muslims, which favoured the settlers.
Messali Hadj's Movement for the Triumph of Democratic Liberties (MTLD), founded in 1946, campaigned for independence, and it split in 1954 between moderates and the armed nationalists.
The French government's policy was assimilation: the French state aimed to make Algerians French in language, law and culture, a goal few Muslim Algerians accepted in practice.

The Sétif and Guelma uprising of 8 May 1945 killed about a hundred Europeans and was met by French repression that killed many thousands of Algerians; official French figures say about 1,500 and Algerian nationalists claim 45,000, and historians generally accept a figure in between.
Muslim Algerians who wanted full French citizenship had to give up their Islamic personal status, a condition that few chose to meet before 1954.
The National Liberation Front (FLN) launched a rising on 1 November 1954 with attacks on police and military targets across Algeria.
The French government sent conscripts in large numbers, reaching about 400,000 troops at the peak, and the army was given wide powers to restore order in the cities and countryside.
The FLN held the Soummam Valley Congress in August 1956, which created its political leadership and confirmed the primacy of the armed struggle.
The Morice Line, a barrier of wire, mines and electrified fencing along the Tunisian frontier from 1957, was built to stop arms and fighters crossing the border.
The Battle of Algiers of 1957 saw French paratroopers under General Jacques Massu break the FLN's urban network in the city through arrests, interrogation and torture.
The use of torture by French forces was reported in Henri Alleg's book La Question, which was banned in France in 1958.
The FLN used terrorism against civilians, including bombings in Algiers, and it killed Algerians who opposed it; the French forces also killed civilians in reprisal operations.
The French army moved large numbers of rural Algerians, probably more than a million, into fenced regroupement camps from 1955 and especially after 1957, as part of its counter-insurgency strategy.
French military deaths numbered about 25,000; estimates of Algerian deaths range from about 300,000 to the Algerian official figure of 1.5 million, and historians still debate the figures.

Support for the FLN abroad grew: Tunisia and Morocco sheltered its fighters, Egypt supplied arms, and the French bombing of the Tunisian village of Sakiet in February 1958 damaged France's reputation with the US and UN.
A revolt by settlers and army officers in Algiers brought Charles de Gaulle back to power.
On 13 May 1958 settlers and army officers seized government buildings in Algiers and demanded that Algeria stay French, and they formed a Committee of Public Safety.
The Fourth Republic's government under Pierre Pflimlin lost the confidence of the army, President Coty asked de Gaulle to form a government, and the National Assembly invested him on 1 June 1958.
A new constitution was approved by referendum on 28 September 1958, establishing the Fifth Republic with a strong presidency.
The constitution set up the French Community, which gave the colonies internal self-government, but kept foreign affairs, defence and currency with France.
De Gaulle was elected president in December 1958 by an electoral college, and he took office in January 1959.
Between 1946 and 1958 the Fourth Republic had some two dozen governments, which made it hard to sustain a consistent policy on Algeria.

Speaking to the crowd in Algiers on 4 June 1958 de Gaulle said 'Je vous ai compris' (I have understood you), and at Mostaganem on 6 June he cried 'Vive l'Algérie française', which led the settlers to believe he would keep Algeria French.
On 16 September 1959 de Gaulle announced that Algerians would be offered self-determination, a choice between independence, integration with France and a form of association.
In January 1960 settler militants staged the Barricades Week in Algiers, a revolt that de Gaulle put down with the army.
The referendum of 8 January 1961 approved self-determination by about 75 per cent of votes cast overall, and by about 70 per cent in Algeria itself.
In April 1961 a group of generals who opposed Algerian independence seized Algiers in the Algiers putsch, which failed after four days when conscripts and the army stayed loyal to de Gaulle.
The Secret Army Organisation (OAS), formed in early 1961, carried out bombings and assassinations in Algeria and in France to stop independence, and it attacked de Gaulle himself.
In a speech of 4 November 1960 de Gaulle spoke of an 'Algérie algérienne' and the prospect of an Algerian Republic, and an earlier set of talks with the FLN at Melun in June 1960 broke down.
The Évian Accords were signed on 18 March 1962 after negotiations between the French government and the FLN, and a ceasefire took effect the next day.
The Accords guaranteed the rights of the French minority, gave France continued use of military bases including Mers-el-Kébir for a time, and provided for French access to Saharan oil and gas.
The Évian Accords were approved in a referendum in France on 8 April 1962 and in Algeria on 1 July 1962, with an overwhelming majority in favour.
Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962, and Ahmed Ben Bella, after a struggle with rival nationalist leaders in the summer of 1962, became prime minister in September 1962 and president in 1963.
The OAS was defeated in Algiers and in France, and its leaders were tried; General Salan, arrested in April 1962, received a life sentence, and a general amnesty in 1968 freed those still in prison.

The OAS ambush of de Gaulle's car at Petit-Clamart on 22 August 1962 failed, and its organiser Jean Bastien-Thiry was executed in March 1963, the last person executed by firing squad in France for a political offence.
On 26 March 1962 French troops fired on pro-French demonstrators in the rue d'Isly in Algiers, killing about 50 people, deepening the settlers' sense of betrayal.

After independence Ben Bella was overthrown by his defence minister Houari Boumediene in June 1965; Algeria nationalised French oil and gas holdings in 1971, and France handed over the naval base of Mers-el-Kébir in 1968.
About 800,000 settlers left Algeria in 1962, many within a few months and most for France, which had to absorb them into an already strained economy; nearly a million had gone by the mid-1960s.

The harkis were Algerians who had served as auxiliaries in the French forces; the French government gave orders to prevent their organised transfer, and while about 90,000 reached France with their families, tens of thousands were killed in reprisals, with estimates ranging widely from about 30,000 to 150,000.

Most harkis who reached France were placed in camps and forest hamlets; the question of recognition and compensation remained a political issue, and President Chirac paid national tribute to them in 2001 and President Macron asked their forgiveness in 2021.
The departure of the settlers ended the French presence in Algerian agriculture and administration, and many farms were taken over by the new state.
On 5 July 1962, the day of independence, violence against Europeans broke out in Oran, where hundreds were killed or went missing, and many settlers fled the city.
De Gaulle led the Free French in the Second World War and then ended the Algerian war as president of the Fifth Republic.
Born 22 November 1890 in Lille, he was a career army officer who became undersecretary for war in June 1940 and then, with his appeal of 18 June 1940 from London, leader of the Free French.
He headed the provisional government from 1944 to January 1946, resigned, founded the Rally of the French People (RPF) in 1947 and withdrew from politics in the 1950s, returning to power in 1958.
As a participant in the 1958 crisis he was welcomed by the settlers, who believed he would keep Algeria French, but his 1959 policy changed course.
Contemporaries split sharply: the settlers and the OAS saw him as a traitor, while many in France and Algeria saw him as the leader who ended a costly war.

Some historians argue that de Gaulle always intended to end French rule in Algeria and moved slowly to avoid civil war, while others argue that he drifted from integration towards independence as the war's costs, the army's attitude and international pressure became clear; he moved from 'Je vous ai compris' in 1958 to self-determination in 1959.
He resigned as president in April 1969 and died on 9 November 1970.

He used the Community and, after 1960, bilateral co-operation accords to keep French influence in sub-Saharan Africa, working through Jacques Foccart, his adviser on African affairs, and the Brazzaville Conference of 1944 that he had convened had promised only reform within the empire.
Achievement: de Gaulle ended a war that the Fourth Republic had failed to win, and he gave Algerians the right of self-determination.
Limit: the war cost many lives, caused the exodus of about a million people and divided the French army and political class.
Achievement: the Fifth Republic's constitution gave France a stable government that could take the decision to withdraw.

Limit: the French Community did not hold the colonies together, and most independent states of West and Equatorial Africa kept close ties with France through co-operation accords, with French troops stationed in several of them.

Explanations for withdrawal: the cost and unpopularity of the Algerian war, the independence of Tunisia and Morocco in 1956, UN General Assembly debates on Algeria from 1955, American pressure and the growth of African nationalist parties.
The British and French cases differed: Britain's transfers were mostly negotiated, while France fought a war in Algeria before accepting independence.
Later view: the war divided the army, the political class and French society, and many judge that de Gaulle's greatest achievement was to end it without a collapse of the Republic.
Contemporary view: settlers, the OAS and the generals of the 1961 putsch saw withdrawal as betrayal, while about 91 per cent of French voters approved the Évian Accords in April 1962.
Britain joined separate northern and southern territories into one colony in 1914, and independence in 1960 was given to a federation of three regions.
Lord Lugard amalgamated Northern and Southern Nigeria into one colony in 1914, and the colonial government ruled much of the north through existing emirs under the system of indirect rule.
Nigeria's three main groups were the Hausa-Fulani in the north, the Yoruba in the west and the Igbo in the east; the north was predominantly Muslim, and the south had large Christian populations.
The 1954 constitution created a federation of three regions, Northern, Western and Eastern, with Lagos as a federal territory.

Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960 as a member of the British Commonwealth, with Abubakar Tafawa Balewa as prime minister; the Queen remained head of state, represented by a governor-general, Nnamdi Azikiwe from November 1960.
The regions had their own parliaments and revenue, and the regional parties drew support on ethnic lines, which made federal politics tense.
Nigeria became a republic on 1 October 1963 with Azikiwe as president, and a fourth region, the Mid-West, was created in 1963.

In the 1959 federal elections the Northern People's Congress won the most seats and formed a coalition with Azikiwe's National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons, and its leader Abubakar Tafawa Balewa became federal prime minister.
Nigeria's oil came from Oloibiri, discovered by Shell-BP in 1956, and exports began in 1958; the oil lay in the Eastern Region, which became a source of dispute in 1967.
On 15 January 1966 a group of army officers led by Major Chukwuma Nzeogwu killed the federal prime minister and several regional leaders, and the coup was seen as dominated by Igbo officers.
General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi took power, but a counter-coup in July 1966 brought Lieutenant-Colonel Yakubu Gowon to power.
Anti-Igbo massacres in the north in 1966 killed many thousands of Igbo people, and large numbers fled to the east.
The eastern region declared itself the Republic of Biafra on 30 May 1967 under Colonel Odumegwu Ojukwu, and the federal government responded with a blockade.
