The Biafran War, from July 1967 to 15 January 1970, caused widespread famine in Biafra; estimates of the total death toll range from several hundred thousand to more than two million, most from starvation and disease.

Biafra was recognised by only Tanzania, Gabon, the Ivory Coast, Zambia and Haiti, while Britain and the Soviet Union supplied arms to the federal government; France and Portugal gave covert support to Biafra.

Gowon created twelve states on 27 May 1967, three days before Biafra's declaration, which broke up the Eastern Region and cut the Igbo off from most of the oil; an earlier attempt to settle the crisis, the Aburi meeting in Ghana in January 1967, had failed.
Gowon announced a policy of reconciliation, rehabilitation and reconstruction at the end of the war on 15 January 1970 and declared that there was no victor and no vanquished.
Many outside Nigeria were moved by images of starving Biafran children; the relief flights of Joint Church Aid, Irish missionaries among them, kept supplies reaching the enclave.
Belgium ran the Congo as a colony for profit, and the country had very few trained Congolese when independence came suddenly in 1960.

King Leopold II ruled the Congo Free State from 1885 as his personal possession, and forced rubber collection caused widespread abuses, exposed by Roger Casement and E. D. Morel, that led to international protest.
The Belgian government took over the colony in 1908, and it was ruled by a paternalistic administration that gave little political role to Congolese.
The colony's wealth lay in copper, cobalt, tin and diamonds, much of it extracted in Katanga by the Union Minière du Haut-Katanga, a Belgian company.
By 1960 only a handful of Congolese had a university degree, and the Force Publique, the colonial army, had no Congolese officers, with Belgians commanding all the ranks above sergeant.
Congolese political parties emerged in the late 1950s, including Patrice Lumumba's National Congolese Movement (MNC), which won the most seats in the 1960 elections.
Riots in Léopoldville in January 1959 shocked Belgian opinion, and King Baudouin soon promised independence at an unspecified date.
The Round Table in Brussels in January-February 1960 fixed independence for 30 June 1960, only about five months later.
Joseph Kasa-Vubu became head of state and Patrice Lumumba prime minister at independence on 30 June 1960.
At the independence ceremony King Baudouin praised Belgium's colonial work; Lumumba replied with a speech attacking the humiliations of colonial rule, which offended Belgian opinion.
Soldiers of the Force Publique mutinied against their Belgian officers on 5–6 July 1960, and attacks on Europeans led Belgium to send troops back to the Congo.
Katanga seceded on 11 July 1960 with Belgian backing, and South Kasai declared its own state in August 1960.
The UN Security Council authorised the UN operation in the Congo (ONUC) in July 1960; at its height it had about 20,000 troops, and it was the largest UN operation of its time.
Kasa-Vubu dismissed Lumumba on 5 September 1960 and Lumumba tried to dismiss Kasa-Vubu, which gave Mobutu his pretext to intervene.
Colonel Joseph Mobutu, army chief of staff, took power on 14 September 1960; Lumumba, who had appealed to the Soviet Union for help, was confined to his residence under UN guard.

Lumumba left his residence in late November 1960, was captured in December, and was flown to Katanga and murdered there on 17 January 1961 in the presence of Belgian officers; Belgium's parliament concluded in 2002 that it bore a moral responsibility.
Mobutu seized power in a second coup on 24 November 1965, with Kasa-Vubu deposed and the army in charge of the state.
The country was renamed Zaire in 1971, and Mobutu's regime promoted authenticité, which banned Christian first names and European dress for men in favour of the abacost.
In 1973 Zairianisation transferred foreign-owned plantations and businesses to Zairian owners, mostly Mobutu's associates, and the economy collapsed as the copper price fell in 1974-75.
The one-party state, the Popular Movement of the Revolution (MPR), was the only legal party, and political opposition was suppressed.
Mobutu was supported by the United States, Belgium and France as a barrier to communism in central Africa, and their military help defeated the Katangan exile invasions of Shaba in 1977 and 1978.
Mobutu announced the end of the one-party state in April 1990 under pressure from protests and from the end of Cold War support, though he stayed in power until 1997.
Tanganyika moved to independence without armed conflict under Julius Nyerere and then united with Zanzibar.
Tanganyika had been German East Africa until 1918, then a British mandate under the League of Nations and a UN trust territory after 1946.
Julius Nyerere founded the Tanganyika African National Union (TANU) in 1954 and led it to a majority in the 1960 elections.
Tanganyika became independent on 9 December 1961 with Nyerere as prime minister, and it became a republic with Nyerere as president in December 1962.
Zanzibar became independent in December 1963, but a revolution in January 1964 overthrew its Arab-led government, and the new regime was dominated by the Afro-Shirazi Party.
Tanganyika and Zanzibar united on 26 April 1964 to form the United Republic, renamed Tanzania in October 1964; Zanzibar kept its own government and president, Abeid Karume of the Afro-Shirazi Party.
Tanzania was a multi-ethnic state with more than a hundred ethnic groups and no dominant majority, and Nyerere made Swahili the national language and avoided ethnic parties.
In January 1964 the Tanganyika Rifles mutinied against British officers; Nyerere asked Britain for help and Royal Marines put down the mutiny, after which the army was rebuilt.
Nyerere broke off diplomatic relations with Britain in December 1965 over its failure to act against the white minority regime in Southern Rhodesia, though Tanzania stayed in the Commonwealth.
Portugal under the Estado Novo regime of António de Oliveira Salazar regarded Angola as an overseas province rather than a colony, and it refused to grant independence.

Armed attacks in Luanda on 4 February 1961 began the Angolan war of independence, followed by a rising in the north on 15 March 1961 in which many Europeans and Africans were killed and Portuguese reprisals were severe; the war lasted until 1974.

Three nationalist movements fought the Portuguese: the MPLA, led by Agostinho Neto, founded in 1956 and strongest among the Mbundu and in Luanda; the FNLA, led by Holden Roberto and based among the Bakongo in the north; and UNITA, founded in 1966, led by Jonas Savimbi and based among the Ovimbundu.
The Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 in Lisbon overthrew the Portuguese regime, and the new government agreed to grant independence to Angola.
The Alvor Agreement of January 1975 set up a transitional government in which the three movements shared power, but it broke down into fighting.

Angola became independent on 11 November 1975, with the MPLA under Neto holding Luanda; the civil war that followed between the MPLA and UNITA and the FNLA lasted until 2002, with Cuban troops and Soviet aid for the MPLA, and South African and American support for its opponents.
Most of the roughly 300,000 Portuguese settlers left Angola in 1975, taking skills and capital with them, and oil from Cabinda and diamonds became the main sources of revenue.
Nigeria kept the Queen as head of state until becoming a republic in 1963, and stayed in the Commonwealth, with British companies such as Shell-BP dominating the oil industry.

Belgium retained large economic interests in the Congo through companies such as the Union Minière, and Mobutu nationalised the Union Minière's Katanga assets in 1966-67 before reaching a settlement with it in 1969.
Portugal's refusal to decolonise until 1974 meant that Angola faced a long war, and Portugal's exit left Angola with few trained administrators.

Tanzania remained in the Commonwealth and received British aid, but Nyerere pursued non-alignment and criticised Western economic influence; Britain also supplied arms to the federal side in Nigeria's war.
France kept influence in its former West and Equatorial African colonies through co-operation accords, the franc zone and military agreements, an arrangement later called Françafrique.
Colonial rulers defined and fixed ethnic identities through census categories, languages and indirect rule, and the term tribalism was used by colonial officials to describe ethnic loyalty.

In Nigeria, the three main parties each drew their support from one region and one ethnic group, and the army's officer corps divided on regional lines, which contributed to the coups of 1966 and the massacres that followed.

In the Congo, the leading politicians drew their support from particular regions and ethnic communities, such as Lumumba's base in the east, Kasa-Vubu's Kongo base in the west and the Lunda of Katanga.
Katanga's secession was partly based on the claim that the Katangan people had a separate identity from the rest of the Congo, a claim that the national government rejected.
Tanzania's single language, Swahili, and the policy of building a national identity were among the factors that reduced ethnic conflict after independence.
Opportunity: independence gave Africans control of government, and Nyerere's Tanzania pursued national unity and African development without a civil war.
Problem: the Belgian Congo's rapid independence left the new state with almost no trained administrators or officers, and the army's mutiny and the secession of Katanga followed within weeks.
Opportunity: Nigeria's oil revenue, which grew rapidly after the 1973 oil price rise, gave the federal government resources for reconstruction after the Biafran War.
Problem: the Biafran War and the 1966 coups showed how the federal structure could fail to hold ethnic groups together.
Contemporary view: many African leaders saw independence as the end of colonial domination, while the former colonial powers often saw it as the start of a new relationship of trade and aid.
Later view: historians stress that colonial borders, ethnic policies and the Cold War constrained the new states, but they also stress African agency in shaping the outcomes.
Problem: Angola's long war of independence ended in civil war because the three movements had different ethnic bases and different foreign backers.
Katanga was the richest mining region of the Belgian Congo, and its mining economy was controlled by a Belgian company.
Katanga, later called Shaba, was the copper-mining heart of the Congo, and it also produced cobalt, zinc, and uranium that was used in the first atomic bombs.
The Union Minière du Haut-Katanga, a company with Belgian shareholders, ran the mines and gave Katanga a far higher revenue base than other provinces.
Katanga's administration and its mining towns, such as Élisabethville (now Lubumbashi), were dominated by Europeans, and Congolese workers lived in segregated housing.

The Conakat party, founded in 1958 by Moïse Tshombe, represented the Lunda and related peoples of southern Katanga and campaigned for regional autonomy, arguing that Katanga should keep its own revenue; Tshombe was connected by marriage to the Lunda royal family.

The rival Balubakat party, led by Jason Sendwe, drew support from the Baluba of northern Katanga and Baluba migrants in the mining towns, and the rivalry between the two parties became a regional and ethnic conflict.
Belgian mining interests and officials supported Conakat's autonomy campaign, which made Katanga's secession more likely once independence came.

In the provincial elections of May 1960 Conakat won the most seats in the provincial assembly, though not a clear majority, and Tshombe became president of the province with the support of independents; in the national elections Lumumba's allies took many of Katanga's seats.
Tshombe proclaimed the secession of Katanga from the Congo on 11 July 1960, just eleven days after independence, and declared the Katangan State.
The secession was supported by Belgian officers, advisers and paid foreign mercenaries, who trained and led the Katanga Gendarmerie.
Lumumba's government saw the secession as a threat to national unity, and it asked the United Nations for help in restoring the Congo's territory.
Tshombe argued that Katanga was a separate state with its own revenue and that a central government in Léopoldville was controlled by outsiders and Communists.

The Katanga secession was not recognised by any state, and Belgium sent troops back to the Congo on 10 July 1960 and gave the Katangan authorities military and technical help, with Belgian officers commanding its gendarmerie.

The UN Security Council called on Belgium to withdraw from Katanga on 9 August 1960 and UN troops entered the province on 12 August; Belgian regular troops left by September, but Belgian officers and technicians stayed on in the Katangan forces.

Patrice Lumumba, prime minister, asked the UN for help against Katanga but was dissatisfied that ONUC would not use force against Tshombe, and turned to the Soviet Union for aircraft and advisers in August 1960.
President Kasa-Vubu dismissed Lumumba on 5 September 1960, Lumumba declared Kasa-Vubu deposed, and Colonel Mobutu intervened on 14 September to neutralise both.
Lumumba, confined to his residence under UN guard, slipped away in late November 1960 and was arrested by Mobutu's troops in early December.
On 17 January 1961 he was flown to Katanga and shot, with Belgian officers present and Katangan leaders taking part; his death was announced on 13 February 1961.
The murder provoked Soviet and African protests, riots in several capitals, and the UN Security Council's Resolution 161 of February 1961, which authorised the use of force as a last resort.
Lumumba became a martyr of African nationalism; in Moscow the Friendship University was renamed after him in 1961.
The UN Security Council set up the ONUC operation in July 1960, and the UN declared that it would not intervene in internal disputes except to prevent civil war.

Security Council Resolution 161 of 21 February 1961 authorised the UN to use force as a last resort to prevent civil war and called for the withdrawal of foreign military personnel and mercenaries; Resolution 169 of 24 November 1961 explicitly authorised action against the Katangan secession and foreign mercenaries.

Irish troops, forming part of the UN force, suffered nine dead when a patrol was ambushed at Niemba on 8 November 1960 by Baluba tribesmen, and 155 Irish soldiers were besieged at Jadotville in September 1961.

At Jadotville, A Company of the 35th Battalion under Commandant Pat Quinlan was besieged by Katangan gendarmes and foreign mercenaries from 13 September 1961; with no relief, little water and low ammunition they surrendered on 17 September without an Irish death, and were held prisoner for about a month.

Conor Cruise O'Brien, an Irish diplomat serving as the UN representative in Katanga, pressed for a more forceful UN policy, and after Operation Rumpunch (28 August 1961) the UN launched Operation Morthor on 13 September 1961 to arrest the foreign officers and take control of Élisabethville, which failed.
In August 1960 Lumumba's government accepted Soviet transport aircraft and trucks, used in an offensive in South Kasai, which heightened Western concern about Cold War involvement in the Congo.
O'Brien later wrote of his Katanga experience in To Katanga and Back (1962); the UN's Congo operation killed about 250 personnel, among them 26 Irish soldiers.

At the UN General Assembly in 1960 Nikita Khrushchev criticised Hammarskjöld's handling of the Congo and demanded replacing the Secretary-General with a three-person executive (a troika), a proposal that the West and most members rejected.
Dag Hammarskjöld, the UN Secretary-General, died in an air crash near Ndola in Northern Rhodesia on 18 September 1961 while travelling to negotiate a ceasefire with Tshombe.

Several inquiries examined Hammarskjöld's death, including a UN inquiry and a Rhodesian one in 1962 that favoured pilot error; later UN-appointed panels in 2013 and 2017 concluded that an external attack was possible and urged further investigation.

Fighting between UN and Katangan forces in Élisabethville in December 1961 ended with the Kitona Declaration of 21 December, in which Tshombe appeared to accept Katanga's place in the Congo but he later repudiated it.
The UN's operations in Katanga were continued under U Thant, and in December 1962 the UN launched Operation Grand Slam against the Katangan forces.
Tshombe announced the end of the secession on 14 January 1963 at Kolwezi, UN troops entered Kolwezi a week later, and Tshombe left for exile in 1963.
The secession had lasted about two and a half years, and its end removed the largest threat to the central government's authority.
Tshombe became prime minister of the Congo in July 1964, a post he held until his dismissal by President Kasa-Vubu in October 1965.

The Simba rebellion of 1964, by supporters of Lumumba, spread through the east of the Congo; Stanleyville fell in August 1964 and the rebellion was crushed with Belgian paratroopers, American aircraft and mercenaries in 1964-65.

Mobutu, who had been army chief of staff since 1960, seized power on 24 November 1965, and Tshombe went into exile in Spain; Tshombe's plane was hijacked to Algeria in 1967 and he died in custody there in 1969.
The Katanga secession had shown the army's importance and the effect of foreign support, and Mobutu's coup used the army to end the factional fighting of the 1960s.

In 1977 and 1978 former Katangan gendarmes based in Angola invaded Shaba province; the 1977 invasion was repelled with Moroccan troops and French transport, and in 1978 French and Belgian paratroops retook Kolwezi.
The United States supported Mobutu's regime with military aid after 1965, which made the army a key instrument of Cold War policy in central Africa.
Mobutu rose from the army to become the dictator of the Congo, which he renamed Zaire, and ruled it until 1997.
Born Joseph-Désiré Mobutu on 14 October 1930 at Lisala in the Congo, he served in the Force Publique and then worked as a journalist before independence.

Chief of staff of the Congolese army from July 1960, he led the coup of 14 September 1960 that 'neutralised' both Lumumba and Kasa-Vubu; his troops arrested Lumumba in December 1960, and he returned power to Kasa-Vubu in February 1961.

As a participant in the Congo crisis he worked with the CIA station chief Larry Devlin and Belgian advisers, and the United States saw him as the best anti-communist leader; the Church Committee of the US Senate in 1975 later revealed CIA plans against Lumumba.

He seized power a second time on 24 November 1965, had four political figures hanged in public in June 1966, founded his Popular Movement of the Revolution (MPR) in 1967 and ruled as president under a one-party system.
Contemporaries in the West, including the United States and Belgium, regarded him as a bulwark against communism in central Africa; many Congolese saw him as a corrupt ruler who enriched his circle.

Historians describe his rule as personal dictatorship and kleptocracy: he drew on mineral revenues and Western aid, rewarded loyalists, kept the state weak and left the economy in ruin by the 1990s, while some stress that his control of the army and his Cold War value to Washington kept him in power so long.

He renamed the Congo Zaire in 1971 and took the name Mobutu Sese Seko in 1972; he nationalised the Union Minière's Katanga assets in 1966-67, launched the policy of authenticité, and was overthrown in May 1997 by Laurent-Désiré Kabila's forces, dying in exile in Morocco in September 1997.

Mobutu's rule lasted from 1965 to 1997, so only the period to 1990 belongs to this topic; in April 1990 he announced the end of the one-party state, after which his support from the West weakened with the end of the Cold War.
Nationally, the secession tested whether the Congo could survive as one state, and the central government's victory preserved its territory.
Internationally, the crisis was a Cold War contest in which the United States and the Soviet Union, and the former colonial power Belgium, each supported different sides.
The Katanga case set a precedent for the UN's involvement in internal conflicts and for its peacekeeping role, which became a standard tool of the organisation.
Mobutu nationalised the Union Minière's Katangan assets in 1966-67 and set up the state company Gécamines, so the province's mineral wealth became the central state's main source of revenue.

African states split: the Casablanca group, including Ghana, Guinea and Egypt, backed Lumumba and the central government, while the more moderate Monrovia group was less hostile to Tshombe and the Western powers; the crisis was one of the first tests of African unity before the OAU was founded in 1963.
The cost of the operation, about 400 million dollars, caused a UN financial crisis when the Soviet Union and France refused to pay towards it.
Cause: Katanga's mineral revenues gave its leaders a strong economic reason to keep control of their wealth, and Belgian companies and officials supported that aim.
Cause: Tshombe's Conakat party claimed that Katanga's peoples had a separate identity, and the fear of Lumumba's centralising government strengthened regional loyalties.
Result: the secession was defeated by the central government with UN help, but the crisis left the Congolese state dependent on foreign military support.
International involvement came from Belgian self-interest, Cold War rivalry and the UN's need to protect a new member state's territorial integrity.
Contemporary view: the Congolese government and many African states saw the secession as a neo-colonial plot, while Tshombe and his supporters saw it as a defence against centralised rule.

Later view: Ludo De Witte's book on Lumumba's murder prompted a Belgian parliamentary inquiry that reported in 2001 that Belgian ministers and officials bore moral responsibility for it, and historians stress the roles of Belgium and the mining company in sustaining Katanga.
Achievement: the central government's victory preserved the Congo's borders as they had been drawn at independence, in line with the African principle of accepting colonial frontiers.
Limit: the defeat of the secession did not end the instability in the Congo, and the Simba rebellion of 1964 showed how much of the country remained outside central control.

Contemporary view of the UN: the Soviet bloc and some African states accused the UN of failing to protect Lumumba and the central government, while Britain and France criticised it for acting against Katanga.
Colonial rule built economies around exporting raw materials to Europe, and these structures outlived independence.
Colonial economies were organised around cash crops and minerals: cocoa in the Gold Coast, groundnuts in Senegal, cotton in Uganda and copper in Katanga.
Railways and ports were built to carry exports to the coast, so most African transport networks linked interior mines and farms to ports rather than to each other.
Colonial powers controlled trade through their own companies and currencies, and African states inherited trading patterns that tied them to a few markets.

Development economists such as Raúl Prebisch and Hans Singer argued from 1950 that the terms of trade, the ratio of export prices to import prices, tend to move against primary producers, so African countries have to export more to buy the same manufactured goods; commodity prices fell sharply in the 1980s.
Dependence on one or two commodities made African economies vulnerable to price falls, as with copper prices in the 1970s and cocoa and coffee prices in the 1980s.
Colonial governments in the Belgian Congo and French West Africa required peasants to grow set quantities of cotton and other cash crops, which were bought at fixed low prices.

Multinational companies such as Unilever's United Africa Company, Shell-BP and the Union Minière kept control of trade, oil and mining after independence, which is why the topic is linked to the idea of a transnational economy.
The European Economic Community set up trade and aid agreements with former African colonies, which later became the Lomé Conventions.
The Treaty of Rome of 1957 associated the overseas territories of the EEC members, mostly in Africa, with the Community.

The Yaoundé Convention of 1963 (with a second in 1969) between the EEC and 18 associated African states gave their exports duty-free access to European markets in return for limited reciprocal opening of their own markets.

Lomé I was signed on 28 February 1975 in Lomé, Togo, between the EEC and 46 African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) states, after Britain's entry in 1973 brought in Commonwealth countries; the ACP group as an organisation was formed later that year.
Lomé I gave ACP exports largely duty-free access to the EEC without requiring reciprocal concessions, which was a new departure in trade relations.
STABEX was a fund set up under Lomé I to compensate ACP countries when earnings from specified agricultural exports fell below a set level.
Later Conventions were signed in 1979 (Lomé II), 1984 (Lomé III) and 1989 (Lomé IV), and they increasingly added conditions on human rights and governance.

Lomé I also included a Sugar Protocol, which guaranteed quotas for ACP sugar at European prices, and Lomé II (1979) added SYSMIN, a fund to help mineral exporters; the Conventions were replaced by the Cotonou Agreement in 2000.
The IMF and the World Bank were created at the Bretton Woods conference of 1944; the IMF lent to countries with balance-of-payments problems and the World Bank funded development projects.
Oil price rises in 1973 and 1979 raised import costs for oil-importing African states, and many governments borrowed heavily from banks and international lenders in the 1970s.
When interest rates rose in the early 1980s and commodity prices fell, African countries struggled to repay, and Mexico's default in 1982 marked the start of the wider debt crisis.

From the early 1980s the IMF and World Bank made new loans conditional on structural adjustment programmes: devaluation, cuts in public spending, removal of subsidies and the sale of state enterprises.

The World Bank's Berg Report of 1981 blamed African governments' own policies, such as overvalued currencies and state marketing boards, while critics argued that structural adjustment reduced spending on health and education; UNICEF's 1987 report 'Adjustment with a Human Face' made the case for protecting the poor.
Ghana under Jerry Rawlings adopted an IMF-backed recovery programme in 1983, which was widely cited as an early success even though it brought hardship.
Aid came in two forms: bilateral aid given government to government by a donor state, and multilateral aid channelled through bodies such as the World Bank and the UN.
Tied aid required recipients to spend the money on goods and services from the donor country, which increased its cost and reduced its value.
Many former colonies received aid from their former rulers, so aid often reinforced existing trade and political links rather than diversifying them.
Aid was criticised for supporting corrupt or authoritarian governments, such as Mobutu's Zaire, and for creating dependence on donors for budgets and food.
Some African governments tried to reduce dependence by promoting local industry and regional trade, but many national markets remained small and fragmented.
The United Nations set a target in 1970 that rich countries give 0.7 per cent of national income as aid; few donors met it.

Cold War rivalry shaped aid: China built the TAZARA railway linking Zambia to the Tanzanian port of Dar es Salaam between 1970 and 1975, and the Soviet Union and the United States each aided their allies.
Famines in the post-colonial period were caused by war, drought and state policy, and they drew international relief efforts.
During the Biafran War, blockade and fighting caused a famine in Biafra in 1968–70, and the images of starving children drew wide attention in Europe and North America.
Relief flights into Biafra ran at night from São Tomé to the Uli airstrip, and they were limited by the federal government's control of the airspace; in June 1969 a Red Cross aircraft was shot down.

A drought in the Sahel from the late 1960s to the mid-1970s caused a famine across Mali, Niger, Chad, Mauritania, Upper Volta (now Burkina Faso) and Senegal, with large loss of livestock; the Wollo famine of 1972-74 helped bring down Ethiopia's Emperor Haile Selassie in 1974.

The Ethiopian famine of 1983-85 killed hundreds of thousands, with estimates from about 300,000 to one million; drought combined with the Derg regime's policies and the wars in Eritrea and Tigray, and a BBC report by Michael Buerk in October 1984 brought it to Western attention.

The British singer Bob Geldof organised the Band Aid charity single 'Do They Know It's Christmas?', released in December 1984, and the Live Aid concerts in London and Philadelphia on 13 July 1985 raised about 150 million pounds for famine relief.
Famine relief was also criticised for distorting local markets and for prolonging wars when food aid went to armed groups.
The Ethiopian government's resettlement programme of 1984-86 moved about 600,000 people from the drought-hit north, and tens of thousands died during the moves.
Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) are non-state charities and campaigning bodies that deliver aid and work on development projects.
Oxfam was founded in Oxford in 1942 as the Oxford Committee for Famine Relief, and it later expanded into development work across Africa and Asia.
Concern was founded in Dublin in 1968 by John and Kay O'Loughlin Kennedy in response to the Biafran famine, and it became one of Ireland's main aid agencies.
Trócaire was founded in 1973 by the Catholic bishops of Ireland as the Irish Catholic development agency, and it works through local partners in Africa.
NGOs distinguish between emergency relief and long-term development, and many shifted in the 1980s towards community projects and advocacy.
Trócaire's annual Lenten campaign raised money and awareness in Irish parishes, and it became one of the best-known development campaigns in Ireland.
GOAL was founded in Dublin in 1977 by John O'Shea, and Médecins Sans Frontières was founded in France in 1971 by doctors who had worked in Biafra.
Julius Nyerere tried to build African socialism in Tanzania through state control and rural villages.
The Arusha Declaration of 5 February 1967 committed Tanzania to ujamaa (familyhood or African socialism), self-reliance and state control of the main means of production.
The government nationalised the banks and major industries and insurance companies in 1967, and it introduced a policy of ‘Education for Self-Reliance’ to shape schooling around rural work.
The ujamaa villages were voluntary cooperative settlements at first, but from 1973-74 the government moved millions of people into villages, often by force, in a policy called villagisation.

Villagisation disrupted farming, and food shortages followed; the oil price rise, drought and the cost of the war to overthrow Idi Amin of Uganda in 1978-79 added to the crisis, the government had to import food and the economy declined by the early 1980s.
Tanzania made important gains in health and literacy, with adult literacy rising to a high proportion of the population by the early 1980s.
Nyerere stepped down as president in 1985, and his successor Ali Hassan Mwinyi accepted an IMF programme in 1986 that reversed many of the socialist policies.

Nyerere, known as Mwalimu (teacher), died in 1999; supporters stress his gains in education, health and national unity and his refusal to rule by ethnic favour, while critics stress the collapse of farm output, the use of compulsion and the one-party state.
TANU's Mwongozo guidelines of 1971 required party members to work for their living and to avoid exploitation and privilege.
Universal primary education launched in 1974 aimed to put every child in school by 1977, and primary enrolment rose rapidly.
Development workers, including missionaries, volunteers and agency staff, carried out most of the day-to-day aid work in rural Africa from the 1960s.

Development workers came from churches, voluntary bodies such as Britain's Voluntary Service Overseas (1958), government programmes such as the American Peace Corps (1961), and NGOs such as Concern and Trócaire.
Their typical work included well-digging, agricultural advice, primary health care and vaccination, the supply of food in famines, and training of local staff.
Many arrived as young volunteers on short contracts, and they often lived in rural communities with limited access to medicine, transport and communications.

Their problems included poor roads and supplies, cultural misunderstandings with local communities, the risk of violence during civil wars, and the difficulty of keeping projects running after the donor left.
They were participants in the aid system but also witnesses to its results, and their reports were important sources for NGO campaigns in Europe and North America.
Contemporaries in Europe often saw development workers as humanitarian heroes, while African critics sometimes saw them as agents of dependence on foreign money.
Historians have criticised ‘top-down’ development projects of the 1960s and 1970s, and they have praised the shift in the 1980s towards projects planned with local people.

Irish missionary orders such as the Holy Ghost Fathers and the Medical Missionaries of Mary ran schools, hospitals and clinics in Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania and other countries, and the Irish government began an official aid programme in 1974.
Achievement: the Lomé Conventions gave ACP states preferential access to European markets and a stabilisation fund, which was a recognised innovation in trade policy.
Limit: despite these trade preferences, most ACP exports stayed concentrated on a few primary commodities, and commodity prices fell in the 1980s.

Achievement: international health campaigns achieved the global eradication of smallpox by 1977, the last natural case being in Somalia, and aid and NGO work improved access to water and primary schooling in many areas.
Limit: debt and structural adjustment left many governments with cuts in public services, and the famines of the 1970s and 1980s showed how fragile food supply remained.
Achievement: Tanzania's rise in literacy and primary education showed what a government with limited resources could achieve in social services.
Limit: villagisation and the collapse of agricultural output showed that state-directed development could cause serious hardship.

Later view: dependency writers such as Walter Rodney (How Europe Underdeveloped Africa, 1972) blamed colonial exploitation, while the World Bank's Berg Report of 1981 blamed domestic policies; most historians now combine colonial legacies, falling commodity prices, Cold War pressures and government choices.
Britain's post-war labour shortage and the Commonwealth citizenship laws brought large numbers of migrants from the Caribbean and South Asia.
The British Nationality Act of 1948 gave citizens of Commonwealth countries the right to enter and settle in Britain as British subjects.
The SS Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury on 22 June 1948 with about 1,000 passengers, most of them from Jamaica and other Caribbean islands, and it became a symbol of this migration.
Post-war labour shortages led Britain to recruit workers for the National Health Service, London Transport and the postal service, many of them from the Caribbean.
Migration from India and Pakistan grew in the 1950s, with many migrants from Punjab and Gujarat settling in Birmingham, Leicester, Bradford and London.

Migration peaked in 1961–62 as migrants rushed to enter before new restrictions took effect; the migrant population was concentrated in a few cities, especially London, the West Midlands and Yorkshire.
The Commonwealth citizenship status of most migrants meant they had the right to vote and to live in Britain, but they faced discrimination in housing and jobs.
Caribbean migrants met a colour bar in lodgings; in Notting Hill the landlord Peter Rachman became notorious for overcrowded, exploitative lettings to newcomers.
In August and September 1958 white youths attacked West Indian residents in the Notting Hill and Nottingham areas, in the worst racial violence in post-war Britain up to that time.

The disturbances were caused by overcrowded housing, competition for jobs and housing, and the activities of far-right groups in the area, such as Oswald Mosley's Union Movement and the White Defence League.
The Trinidadian journalist Claudia Jones organised an indoor carnival in London in January 1959, which became a precursor of the Notting Hill Carnival.
Kelso Cochrane, an Antiguan-born carpenter, was murdered in a racist attack in Notting Hill in May 1959, and his death increased pressure for a legal response.
The Commonwealth Immigrants Act of 1962 introduced employment vouchers, which restricted the entry of Commonwealth citizens without jobs in Britain.
In 1968 a new Commonwealth Immigrants Act was rushed through Parliament in a few days to limit the entry of Kenyan Asians holding British passports, who faced discrimination and expulsion in Kenya.

Enoch Powell, a Conservative MP, warned in a speech to a Conservative meeting in Birmingham on 20 April 1968, known as the 'rivers of blood' speech, that continued immigration would lead to violence, and Edward Heath dismissed him from the Shadow Cabinet; London dockers marched in his support.
The Immigration Act of 1971 introduced the concept of patriality, which gave the right of abode to those with a parent or grandparent born in Britain.

The National Front, founded in 1967, campaigned for an end to immigration, stood candidates in the general elections of 1974 and 1979 and never won a parliamentary seat; the Battle of Lewisham (August 1977) and the death of the teacher Blair Peach at an anti-NF protest in Southall in April 1979 marked its confrontations with opponents.
President Idi Amin gave Asians in Uganda 90 days to leave in August 1972; about 27,000 of them, many holding British passports, settled in Britain, helped by a government resettlement board.
The Anti-Nazi League and Rock Against Racism, founded in 1976-77, organised counter-campaigns against the National Front.
The Race Relations Act of 1965 made discrimination on grounds of colour, race or ethnic origin illegal in public places, and it created a Race Relations Board.
The Race Relations Act of 1968 extended the ban on discrimination to housing and employment, and it created the Community Relations Commission.
The Race Relations Act of 1976 extended the law to indirect discrimination and created the Commission for Racial Equality.
The laws were enforced through complaints and conciliation, and critics argued that their effectiveness was limited by the difficulty of proving discrimination in practice.
Home Secretary Roy Jenkins said in 1966 that integration should not mean assimilation but equal opportunity together with cultural diversity, which set the direction of British policy.
Police stop-and-search powers under the ‘sus’ laws (the Vagrancy Act of 1824) were used heavily against young black men, which many black residents saw as harassment.

The Brixton riots of 10-12 April 1981 followed Operation Swamp 81, in which police stopped and searched nearly a thousand people, mostly young black men, in a week; the riots caused widespread damage and injured hundreds.
Riots broke out in Toxteth in Liverpool and Moss Side in Manchester in July 1981, as well as in other cities; police used CS gas on the British mainland for the first time in Toxteth.

The Scarman Report of November 1981 identified racial disadvantage, unemployment and poor relations between police and the community as causes of the riots; it found no institutional racism in the police but accepted that individual officers had acted improperly.
The Scarman Report recommended more accountable policing and community consultation, and it led to the Police and Criminal Evidence Act of 1984; the 'sus' law had already been repealed in 1981.
By the 1980s Britain had large Caribbean, Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi communities whose culture changed British life in many areas.
Caribbean communities shaped British music, including reggae, ska and calypso, and Caribbean food and festivals became part of urban life.
Notting Hill Carnival began as a street festival in 1966 and became one of the largest street festivals in Europe.
Muslims from South Asia built mosques in the 1960s and 1970s, and Sikh and Hindu communities built gurdwaras and temples in Birmingham, Leicester and London.
Britain's policy of multiculturalism, supported by local councils and the Race Relations Acts, encouraged the recognition of distinct cultures within a common framework of laws.

The Rushdie affair of 1988-89 showed the tensions between religious identity and freedom of expression: copies of The Satanic Verses were burned in Bradford in January 1989, and Ayatollah Khomeini issued a fatwa against Salman Rushdie in February 1989.

Black and Asian candidates entered Parliament: Diane Abbott, Paul Boateng, Bernie Grant and Keith Vaz were elected in 1987, and the Rampton Report (1981) and the Swann Report (1985) argued for schools to recognise the needs of ethnic minority children.

Algerians held French nationality until Algerian independence in 1962, and they could move freely between Algeria and France, so Algerian labour migration to mainland France was not legally immigration before that date.
Post-war reconstruction created labour shortages, and migrants from Portugal, Spain, Italy, Morocco, Tunisia and West Africa filled jobs in factories, mines and construction.
Many migrants lived in bidonvilles, makeshift shanty settlements on the edges of French cities, such as Nanterre near Paris, where living conditions were poor.
Algerian migration continued after 1962, and it brought the Algerian war's legacy into French politics; the harkis who came to France faced hostility and poor housing.
In July 1974 the French government suspended labour immigration, and in 1976 it allowed family reunification for migrants who had been living in France.
Migrants from North and West Africa formed the second generation, the ‘beurs’, who grew up in the banlieues and by the 1980s were a focus of French debate about integration.
The Franco-Algerian accord of 27 December 1968 gave Algerian nationals preferential rights to enter and work in France.
The harkis and their families were housed in camps known as hameaux de forestage in France, and some camps were still in use in the mid-1970s.
The French government set up the National Immigration Office in 1945, and Sonacotra, founded in 1956, built hostels for Algerian workers.
On 17 October 1961 Paris police under Maurice Papon attacked a demonstration by Algerians against a curfew, killing dozens or more; the number remains disputed.
After 1977 the government offered payments to migrants who agreed to go home, with little effect.
The French model of integration was based on universal citizenship: all citizens were equal before the law, and the state did not recognise ethnic or religious communities as such.
Assimilation meant that migrants were expected to adopt the French language, values and civic practices, and to keep their ethnic identities in private.
The law on the separation of church and state of 1905 established laïcité, a principle of state secularism that shaped how public religious expression was regulated.
France did not collect statistics on ethnic origin, which meant that discrimination was harder to measure and debate than in Britain.
The Pleven law of 1972 was France's main anti-racist legislation, and it made incitement to racial hatred a criminal offence.
Similarity: both states restricted immigration in the 1970s, both had far-right parties that gained support by the late 1970s and 1980s, and both had racial violence in urban areas.

Difference: most migrants to Britain were Commonwealth citizens with a legal right of entry, while migrants to France came from southern Europe as well as North and West Africa, and North African migrants had a complex legal status.
Difference: Britain developed a policy of multiculturalism that recognised ethnic groups, while France used the assimilation model that recognised individuals as citizens.

Difference: the colonial histories differed, since Britain's migrants came largely from its former colonies in the Caribbean and South Asia, and France's came from its former North African and West African colonies.
Achievement: Britain's anti-discrimination laws gave migrants a legal basis for challenging discrimination in jobs, housing and public services.
Limit: the laws did not end disadvantage, and the 1981 riots showed that unemployment and police practices remained sources of conflict.
Achievement: France's universal citizenship gave second-generation migrants a legal claim to French nationality, and many took part fully in French public life.
Limit: the assimilation model made it difficult to recognise ethnic discrimination, and the headscarf question and the banlieues showed the tensions it created.
Contemporary view: many politicians in both countries saw migration mainly as an economic and security problem, while migrant communities often saw discrimination as the main issue.

Later view: scholars contrast Britain's race-relations model, which counted ethnic groups and tackled discrimination through the law, with France's republican model, which counted no one by origin; each has been criticised for failing to end disadvantage.
By the early 1980s the children of North African and West African migrants lived in the banlieues, where unemployment and policing were the main grievances.
The banlieues were the working-class suburbs and high-rise estates around French cities, many built in the 1960s to house migrant families and urban workers.
Les Minguettes, an estate in Vénissieux near Lyon, was one of the best-known banlieues, and it became the scene of unrest in 1981.
The second generation, known as ‘beurs’ (a verlan term for Arabs), had been born or raised in France and had French citizenship or a right to it.
Youth unemployment in the banlieues was far above the national average, and many young people were in low-skilled work or outside the labour market.
Relations between young people and the police were poor, and identity checks and stop-and-search practices were a frequent complaint in the banlieues.
The oil shock of 1973 ended the post-war economic boom, and migrant workers in the factories were among the first to lose their jobs.
Many banlieue families lived in HLM estates, public housing built from the 1950s and 1960s that had become rundown by the 1980s.
By the 1982 census about 800,000 Algerians lived in France, making them the largest foreign nationality, ahead of Portuguese and Moroccans.

In the summer of 1981 young men in the Minguettes estate stole and burned cars in what the press called 'rodéos' and clashed with police, in an episode that had no single cause and drew national television coverage.
The unrest spread to other banlieues in Lyon and elsewhere, and it drew national attention to the living conditions of second-generation migrants.
The Socialist government of François Mitterrand, elected in May 1981, responded with social programmes for the banlieues and promised reforms to immigration law.

The government created Priority Education Zones (ZEP) in schools in 1981 and the 'Banlieues 89' regeneration project in 1983, which were criticised as too limited to address the causes of disadvantage.
The Dubedout report of 1983 recommended local regeneration and greater involvement of residents in their neighbourhoods, and it led to local development programmes.
Mitterrand's government regularised the status of about 130,000 undocumented migrants in 1981-82, and a law of 1984 created a ten-year residence card.
Mitterrand had promised local voting rights for foreign residents and spoke of a 'right to be different', but the voting-rights promise was never carried out.

The March for Equality and against Racism, which the press called the Marche des Beurs, set out from Marseille on 15 October 1983 with about 30 people, after Toumi Djaïdja, a young man from the Minguettes, was shot and wounded by a police officer in June 1983; the priest Christian Delorme and the pastor Jean Costil helped organise it.

The march grew as it crossed France, reached Paris on 3 December 1983 with tens of thousands of supporters, and a delegation was received by President Mitterrand, who promised the ten-year residence card.
The march's demands included equal treatment in jobs, housing and policing, and the right of second-generation migrants to be treated as French citizens.
The march was organised with local associations and churches, and it showed that second-generation migrants could organise a national political campaign.
SOS Racisme was founded in Paris in 1984, launched in October, by young activists including Harlem Désir and Julien Dray, and it quickly grew into a national organisation with local branches.
Its slogan, ‘Touche pas à mon pote’ (Hands off my pal), was printed on badges worn widely by young people, and it expressed a message of solidarity across ethnic lines.
SOS Racisme was supported by the Socialist government and by celebrities and trade unions, and it organised concerts and campaigns against racism in schools and workplaces.
Critics on the left argued that SOS Racisme focused on individual racism and did not address the social causes of disadvantage in the banlieues.
A free concert of SOS Racisme in the Place de la Concorde on 15 June 1985 drew hundreds of thousands of young people.
The Left's critics, including some of the 1983 marchers, accused the Socialists of using SOS Racisme to take over the anti-racist movement.

The Front National (FN) was founded in October 1972 by Jean-Marie Le Pen, a former paratrooper who had served in Algeria, with the backing of far-right groups including Ordre Nouveau, and it drew on supporters of the French Algeria cause.
Its policies included the restriction of immigration, the expulsion of illegal migrants and the preference for French citizens in jobs and housing, known as ‘national preference’.

The FN's breakthrough came in the Dreux municipal by-election of September 1983, where its list led by Jean-Pierre Stirbois won about 17 per cent in the first round and then joined a right-wing list that took the town, ending the taboo against allying with the FN.
In the 1984 European elections the FN won about 11 per cent of the vote and sent 10 deputies to the European Parliament.
In the 1986 parliamentary elections, held under a proportional system, the FN won 35 seats in the National Assembly.
The FN's support was strongest in the south and east of France, in areas with high unemployment and large migrant communities, such as Marseille and Nice.

In the 1988 presidential election Jean-Marie Le Pen won about 14.4 per cent of the first-round vote, over four million votes, while under the return to two-round constituency voting the FN won only one seat in the 1988 parliamentary election.

Le Pen was elected as the youngest deputy in 1956 as a Poujadist, and in September 1987 he called the Nazi gas chambers a 'detail' of the history of the Second World War, a remark that brought him a conviction and wide condemnation.
The Chirac government of 1986–88, with Charles Pasqua as interior minister, passed laws that tightened immigration controls, permitted identity checks and made deportation easier.

In 1986 the Chirac government proposed ending the automatic acquisition of French nationality at 18 by young people born in France to foreign parents, who would have to make a formal declaration; after mass protests, including from SOS Racisme, it dropped the plan in 1987 and set up the Long commission, and the Méhaignerie law of 1993 later introduced the declaration.
The Pasqua law of September 1986 made expulsion of illegal immigrants easier and required visas for most foreigners, and in October 1986 a charter flight deported about 100 Malians.

The Socialist government returned to power in 1988 and the Joxe law of 1989 eased some of the 1986 restrictions; the Rocard government created the Haut Conseil à l'intégration in December 1989 and favoured the word integration over assimilation.
In December 1986 the death of a student, Malik Oussekine, beaten by riot police during protests in Paris, caused outrage and led Chirac to drop an education bill.
In October 1989 the head of a collège in Creil, north of Paris, excluded three Muslim girls for wearing headscarves in class, which became a national controversy.

The Minister of Education, Lionel Jospin, referred the question to the Conseil d'État, which ruled on 27 November 1989 that headscarves were allowed unless they were ostentatious or used for propaganda.

The affair showed the tension between laïcité and Muslim identity in schools; it was debated in the press and by politicians of all parties, and the Conseil d'État's approach lasted until the law of 2004 banned conspicuous religious symbols in state schools.
The Jospin circular of December 1989 told schools to accept headscarves unless they were ostentatious or used for proselytising.
Algerian-origin families formed the largest group among the second generation, and the Algerian war, which ended in 1962, shaped how many French people saw North African migrants.
Many Algerian migrants and their children were linked by family and history to the war, while the harkis and their families remained a sensitive issue in French politics.
The FN drew support from some former settlers and army veterans of the Algerian war, and its rhetoric echoed arguments about French identity from the colonial period.
The government's policies on immigration in the 1980s were shaped by the memory of decolonisation, including the Évian Accords and the departure of between 800,000 and a million settlers in 1962.
Pieds-noirs settled in large numbers in southern France, a region where the FN later won much of its support, though the party's voters were not drawn only from former settlers.
Under the 'double jus soli' rule of the nationality code, children born in France to parents born in Algeria before 1962 were French from birth, which was one target of the right's proposed reforms.
Like Britain, France had racial violence in urban areas in the early 1980s and a far-right party that gained votes from anti-immigration feelings.
Unlike Britain, France had no race relations act and did not record ethnic statistics, which made the measurement of discrimination more difficult.
France's assimilation model, which treated citizens as individuals, meant that anti-discrimination arguments were framed in terms of universal rights rather than ethnic groups.
Britain's Scarman Report of 1981 and the Race Relations Acts offered a framework for responding to racial disadvantage that France lacked in the 1980s.
Britain's Commonwealth migrants had the vote from arrival, whereas in France non-citizen residents did not, which made the unfulfilled promise of local voting rights a live grievance.

Both countries saw confrontations between police and young people in the early 1980s, but Britain answered with a public inquiry, the Scarman Report, while France's response was through urban regeneration programmes.
Achievement: the second generation organised national movements such as the 1983 march and SOS Racisme, and they gained a public voice.
Limit: the government's responses in the 1980s focused on policing and immigration control, and social disadvantage in the banlieues remained a source of unrest.
Achievement: the Conseil d'État's 1989 headscarf ruling set a legal framework for religious expression in schools that lasted until the 2004 law.
Limit: the FN's electoral success showed that anti-immigrant politics could gain mainstream attention, and mainstream parties adopted some of its themes.
Contemporary view: supporters of assimilation saw the banlieue unrest as a failure of integration, while activists saw it as the result of racism and social exclusion.
Later view: historians stress that the banlieues were shaped by housing policy, deindustrialisation and the colonial past, not by immigration alone.
Contemporary government view: Socialist ministers presented integration, rather than assimilation, as the aim in 1989, while Le Pen's supporters said immigration was a threat to French identity.
Colonial powers presented their rule as a civilising mission, and education was the main means of spreading European culture.
The French idea of a mission civilisatrice held that France had a duty to spread French language, law and values among its colonial subjects.
Most schools in British and Belgian Africa were run by Christian missions, which taught literacy, scripture and European history and often discouraged African languages and customs.

The French colonial system created a small educated elite trained in French and expected to adopt French culture, through schools such as the Lycée Faidherbe in Saint-Louis, Senegal, and the École William Ponty near Dakar, which trained future teachers and officials.
In British colonies, indirect rule and mission schools produced clerks, teachers and interpreters, and the education of girls lagged far behind that of boys.

Colonial curricula taught European rivers, kings and battles, and schoolbooks in French Africa began with 'our ancestors the Gauls'; African historical and literary traditions were largely absent from schools until after independence.
The Négritude movement was founded in Paris in the 1930s by the poet Léopold Sédar Senghor of Senegal, the Martinican poet Aimé Césaire and the Guianese poet Léon-Gontran Damas.
The journal L'Étudiant noir, founded in 1934, was one of the first publications to bring together students from Africa, the Caribbean and Guiana around the idea of a shared black identity.
Négritude celebrated African and black cultural values, and it challenged the assumption that European culture was superior to African culture.

Senghor became the first president of Senegal in 1960 and held office until 1980, and in 1983 he became the first African elected to the Académie française; he advocated African socialism and kept close ties with France.
Critics such as Wole Soyinka and the South African writer Es'kia Mphahlele argued that Négritude was too closely tied to European intellectual traditions and romanticised African culture.
Césaire's poem Cahier d'un retour au pays natal (1939) gave the word négritude its first literary use, and Senghor's poetry celebrated an African sensibility based on rhythm and emotion.
Christianity and Islam spread in Africa through different routes, and both were reshaped by African societies and by colonial rule.
Christian missions, Catholic and Protestant, were the main agents of Christian expansion in colonial Africa, and they built schools, hospitals and churches across the continent.

African Independent Churches broke away from the mission churches; the Kimbanguist Church, founded by Simon Kimbangu in the Belgian Congo after his preaching began in 1921, became one of the largest, and the Aladura churches grew in Yorubaland in Nigeria.

Islam had spread across West Africa through trade and Sufi brotherhoods, and the Mouride brotherhood in Senegal, founded by Amadou Bamba and linked with the groundnut economy, became a major political and economic force despite his exile by the French.
On the East African coast Islam had been established for centuries through trade, and it shaped Swahili language and culture.

In northern Nigeria, Lugard's indirect rule worked through the Muslim emirs and barred most Christian missions from the emirates, so western education spread much faster in the south than in the north.
Many Africans combined Christian or Islamic belief with older religious practices, and the relationship between religion and political authority varied widely.
The White Fathers, a Catholic missionary order founded in Algiers in 1868 by Cardinal Lavigerie, became prominent in East and Central Africa.
The Church Missionary Society, an Anglican mission founded in 1799, was active across West and East Africa.
The Sokoto Caliphate, founded after the jihad led by Usman dan Fodio from 1804, spread Islamic law across much of northern Nigeria.
Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a freed slave from Yorubaland, became the first African Anglican bishop in 1864, an early sign of African leadership in mission churches.
Irish missionaries such as the Holy Ghost Fathers and the Society of African Missions worked in Nigeria and other British colonies, running schools and hospitals.
The Grand Mosque of Paris was inaugurated in 1926 to honour the Muslim soldiers who died for France in the First World War and as a symbol of the French state's relationship with Islam in its empire.

Muslim migration to Britain and France from the 1950s and 1960s led to the building of mosques in British cities, including Birmingham, Bradford and London, and to the establishment of Islamic cultural centres.
Salman Rushdie's novel The Satanic Verses was published in September 1988, and many Muslims in Britain objected to its portrayal of the Prophet Muhammad.
In January 1989 Muslims in Bradford burned copies of the book in a public protest, which drew national attention to the question of blasphemy in Britain.
On 14 February 1989 the Iranian leader Ayatollah Khomeini issued a fatwa calling for Rushdie's death, which led to his going into hiding under British police protection.
The Rushdie affair raised questions about freedom of expression and religious identity in Britain, and it was debated alongside the headscarf question in France.

France had the largest Muslim population in Western Europe, estimated at between two and three million by the 1980s, mostly of Algerian, Moroccan and Tunisian origin, and Islam became France's second religion.
Britain's blasphemy law protected only the Christian faith, and the courts refused in 1991 to extend it to Islam, which Muslim campaigners cited after the Rushdie affair.
English spread across the world through the British Empire and the Commonwealth, and it became the official language of many former British colonies, including Nigeria and Kenya.
In Nigeria, English was the language of government, education and the courts, and it became a second language for many Nigerians alongside the major local languages.
Tanzania chose Swahili as its national language and language of instruction in primary schools, making it one of the few African states to adopt an indigenous language as its main national language.
After 1945 the spread of English was also driven by American economic and cultural power, through films, music, business and the new international organisations.
The use of English in African literature raised the question of whether colonial languages could carry African experience, and writers answered this question in different ways.
Pidgin English developed in West African trading ports and became a widely spoken lingua franca in Nigeria and Cameroon.
In India Hindi was declared the official language in 1950 but English remained an associate official language, and it was retained after anti-Hindi protests in Tamil Nadu in 1965.
France promoted its own language through La Francophonie, whose first institution, an agency for cultural and technical cooperation, was founded in 1970 by French-speaking states.
Achebe was the Nigerian novelist whose work changed how Africa was represented in world literature.
Born 16 November 1930 at Ogidi in eastern Nigeria, he studied at University College Ibadan and worked for the Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation before becoming a full-time writer.

Things Fall Apart, published in 1958 by Heinemann, portrayed an Igbo community before and during the arrival of British colonial rule through the story of Okonkwo; its title comes from a line in a poem by W. B. Yeats, and it became one of the most widely read African novels in English.
His later novels, including No Longer at Ease (1960), Arrow of God (1964) and A Man of the People (1966), examined corruption and the failures of the new independent states.
During the Biafran War he supported Biafra and travelled abroad as an advocate for its cause, and he wrote about the war in There Was a Country (2012).

Contemporaries praised his novels, while critics such as Obi Wali argued that African literature in European languages was a dead end; Achebe replied in his 1965 essay on the African writer and the English language that English could be remade to carry African experience.
In his 1975 lecture An Image of Africa he criticised Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness for portraying Africa as the opposite of Europe, and historians of literature still debate his argument.
He died in March 2013, and his work is now studied as a foundational text of post-colonial literature.
His novel Anthills of the Savannah (1987) was set in a fictional West African state and examined military rule and its corruption.
As the first editorial adviser of Heinemann's African Writers Series from 1962, he helped to publish many other African writers.
Gordimer was a South African novelist whose writing examined white and black lives under apartheid and the limits of liberal opposition.
Born 20 November 1923 at Springs near Johannesburg, she was a white South African who wrote in English and lived most of her life in Johannesburg.
Her early novels, including The Lying Days (1953) and A World of Strangers (1958), explored the social divisions of white and black South Africans.

The Conservationist (1974) shared the Booker Prize, A World of Strangers (1958) was banned in South Africa for twelve years, and Burger's Daughter (1979), about the child of a communist activist, was banned for a time.
July's People (1981) imagined a South African revolution in which a white family takes refuge with their black servant in a village, and it was widely read internationally.

Contemporaries in South Africa saw her as a critic of apartheid whose work was subject to censorship; she was a supporter of the African National Congress and helped Nelson Mandela with his speech for the Rivonia trial in 1964, while some black writers argued that white liberal writers were limited in their perspective.
She was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1991, gave a lecture called Writing and Being, remained an opponent of censorship after apartheid ended, and died in July 2014.
My Son's Story (1990) explored the politics of the apartheid years through a family's divided loyalties.

Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o wrote his early novels in English but was held without trial in 1977-78 after staging a play in Gikuyu, and afterwards wrote in Gikuyu; his book Decolonising the Mind (1986) argued that writing in colonial languages restricted African culture.
The Nigerian playwright and poet Wole Soyinka won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986, the first African to receive it; he had been detained in solitary confinement during the Nigerian civil war.
The African Writers Series, begun by Heinemann in 1962, made African novels widely available in schools and universities across the English-speaking world.
Post-colonial writers often explored the tension between traditional beliefs and the new Christian or Islamic faiths, and between village life and urban modernity.
Wole Soyinka's novel The Interpreters (1965) and Ngũgĩ's A Grain of Wheat (1967) examined the moral failures of the independence generation.

French-language writers included Cheikh Hamidou Kane, whose novel Ambiguous Adventure (1961) explored a Senegalese Muslim boy's education in France, and Mariama Bâ, whose So Long a Letter (1979) described the lives of Muslim women in Senegal.
Achievement: African writers and religious movements created new forms of cultural expression that combined African traditions with European and Islamic influences.
Limit: colonial education and missions had reduced the teaching of African languages, and many African states inherited a dependence on English or French for higher education.
Achievement: Tanzania's choice of Swahili showed that an African language could be used as the language of government and education.
Limit: the debate over writing in English or in local languages showed the continuing tension between cultural identity and the legacy of colonial education.
Contemporary view: colonial officials and missionaries often saw African culture as backward, while African nationalists argued for the revival of African traditions.

Later view: Achebe argued that English could be reshaped to carry African experience, while Ngũgĩ argued that using European languages cut African writers off from the peasants and workers who spoke African languages.
The Constitution divides power between the federal government and the states, and that division shaped the civil rights and social policy fights of the period.
Federalism: powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states under the Tenth Amendment, so states controlled schools, policing, voting rules and marriage law.
Before the 1960s most southern states enforced segregation by state law, and federal action against it was met with the argument that such matters belonged to the states.

In 1948 southern Democrats angry at Truman's civil rights programme left the party and formed the States' Rights Democratic Party (the Dixiecrats) with Strom Thurmond as candidate; it carried four Deep South states.
The Civil Rights Act 1957 was the first civil rights law since Reconstruction; it set up a Civil Rights Commission and gave federal authorities power to act over voting rights.
The Civil Rights Act 1964 rested on federal power to regulate interstate commerce, which allowed Congress to ban segregation in hotels, restaurants and other public places.

In September 1957 Governor Orval Faubus of Arkansas used the National Guard to stop nine black students entering Little Rock Central High School; Eisenhower sent federal troops, including the 101st Airborne Division, to enforce integration.
The Constitution gives Congress, the President and the Supreme Court separate powers, and each can limit the others.

The Constitution (1787) gives Congress the power to make laws, raise taxes and declare war; the President executes the laws, commands the armed forces and conducts foreign policy; the Supreme Court interprets the Constitution.
The President can veto bills, but Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds majority in both houses; the Senate must confirm senior appointments and ratify treaties by a two-thirds vote.
Congress passed the Taft-Hartley Act in 1947, restricting trade union activity such as the closed shop, and overrode Truman's veto in June 1947.
Republicans won control of both houses of Congress in the 1946 midterm elections (slogan: "Had enough?") for the first time since 1928, leaving Truman to govern with a hostile Congress until 1948.

Youngstown Sheet and Tube Co v Sawyer (June 1952): the Supreme Court ruled that Truman had exceeded his powers by seizing the steel mills during a strike in April 1952 without congressional authority.

The Warren Court (Chief Justice Earl Warren, appointed by Eisenhower in 1953) used judicial review to extend civil rights and liberties, e.g. Brown v. Board of Education (1954) and Miranda v. Arizona (1966) on the rights of arrested suspects.
The Twenty-Second Amendment, passed by Congress in March 1947 and ratified in 1951, limits a president to two elected terms, a direct response to Roosevelt winning four elections.
United States v Nixon (July 1974): the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that Nixon must hand over the White House tapes, and his resignation followed in August 1974.
Congress passed the War Powers Resolution over Nixon's veto in November 1973 to limit the President's power to commit troops without congressional approval.

The Boland Amendments (1982 to 1984) restricted US aid to the Contra rebels in Nicaragua; officials in the Reagan administration kept the Contras supplied in breach of them, the core of the Iran-Contra affair.
The President's staff and agencies grew steadily from the 1930s, so that more policy was shaped inside the White House and its agencies.
The Executive Office of the President was created in 1939 under Roosevelt, giving the President a personal staff separate from the government departments.

The National Security Act of July 1947, signed by Truman, created the National Security Council, the Central Intelligence Agency and the National Military Establishment, later renamed the Department of Defense.
The National Security Council gave the President a forum of advisers on foreign and defence policy, often bypassing the State Department and Congress.
The Council of Economic Advisers was created by the Employment Act of 1946, which committed the federal government to promote maximum employment, production and purchasing power.
Kennedy held live televised press conferences from January 1961, using the press conference as a direct channel to public opinion.
Arthur Schlesinger Jr. described the expanded executive in The Imperial Presidency (1973), a phrase that became the standard label for concern over presidential power after Watergate.
Roosevelt's coalition and the wartime economy shaped the politics that Truman inherited in 1945.
Roosevelt won four presidential elections (1932, 1936, 1940 and 1944) and served from March 1933 until his death.
The New Deal coalition combined urban workers, trade unions, Catholics and Jews, farmers, southern whites and black voters who moved to the Democrats from the 1930s.
Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945, and Harry Truman, vice president since January 1945, became president.
Truman had chaired a Senate committee (the Truman Committee, 1941 to 1944) that investigated waste and fraud in wartime production, which gave him a reputation for careful oversight.
Truman inherited a wave of strikes in 1945 and 1946 as the wartime economy was converted to peacetime production.
Truman's party was divided between northern liberals and conservative southern Democrats, who often voted with Republicans in Congress (the conservative coalition) to block reform.
Truman was a participant in the domestic politics of his presidency and a figure whose popularity swung widely. His foreign policy record is covered in the notes on US foreign policy.
Born in Lamar, Missouri, in 1884, he worked as a farmer, a haberdasher and a county court official before being elected to the Senate in 1934 and taking his seat in 1935.
He served as an artillery captain in France in the First World War and owed his early political career to the Kansas City Democratic machine of Tom Pendergast.
As vice president from January 1945 he was not told of the atomic bomb project until he became president, a fact that shaped his early reliance on advisers.
In September 1945 he sent Congress a 21-point programme of reforms that continued the New Deal, but reconversion, inflation and strikes blocked most of it.
His domestic programme, the Fair Deal, was outlined in January 1949 and included national health insurance, a wider Social Security system, a higher minimum wage and public housing.
Congress blocked national health insurance and most other Fair Deal proposals; the Housing Act of 1949 and a rise in the minimum wage were among the main successes.

His civil rights programme began with the report To Secure These Rights (October 1947) from the President's Committee on Civil Rights, and Executive Order 9981 (26 July 1948) ordered the desegregation of the armed forces.
His loyalty programme (Executive Order 9835, March 1947) required checks on federal employees for disloyalty, and it fed the wider Red Scare.
Contemporaries were often dismissive: the 1946 joke "To err is Truman" mocked his handling of strikes and prices, and his Gallup approval rating fell to about 22 per cent in early 1952.

In 1948 he won an upset victory over Thomas Dewey after a campaign attacking the Republican Congress; the Chicago Daily Tribune had printed the headline "Dewey Defeats Truman" before the result was known.

In 1948 the Democrats split three ways (Thurmond's Dixiecrats on the right, Henry Wallace's Progressives on the left), yet Truman won 303 electoral votes to Dewey's 189 after a cross-country whistle-stop train campaign.

By 1952 his popularity had fallen sharply because of the Korean War, rising prices and corruption scandals in several federal agencies, and he announced in March 1952 that he would not seek re-election.

Historians since the 1970s, and David McCullough's biography Truman (1992), have generally ranked him among the stronger presidents for his decisiveness and his civil rights initiatives, while judging his domestic record more limited than he hoped and his loyalty programme damaging to civil liberties.
Eisenhower, a Republican and former Allied commander in the Second World War, kept most New Deal programmes and called his approach Modern Republicanism.
Eisenhower extended Social Security to about 10 million more workers in 1954 and created the Department of Health, Education and Welfare in 1953, accepting the New Deal's main structures.
Eisenhower's Farewell Address (January 1961) warned against the "military-industrial complex" (see the notes on the economic boom).
The Federal-Aid Highway Act of June 1956 funded an Interstate Highway System of about 41,000 miles, the largest federal public works programme of the period.
Kennedy won the 1960 election narrowly over Richard Nixon, and his New Frontier, presented in his nomination speech of July 1960, promised a more active federal role at home and in space.
Kennedy's civil rights bill was sent to Congress in June 1963, and it was only passed after his assassination.
Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas on 22 November 1963; Lyndon Johnson was sworn in as president on Air Force One that afternoon.
Kennedy's tax cut was proposed in January 1963 and passed as the Revenue Act of February 1964 under Johnson, cutting the top income tax rate from 91 to 70 per cent.
Johnson's domestic programme was the largest federal social effort since the New Deal. His Vietnam policy is covered in the notes on the case study.
Johnson, Senate Majority Leader from 1955 to 1961, used his legislative skills (the persuasive "Johnson treatment") and the national mood after Kennedy's death to pass Kennedy's stalled bills.
The Civil Rights Act of 2 July 1964 banned segregation in public places and discrimination in employment on grounds of race, colour, religion, sex or national origin.
In a speech at the University of Michigan on 22 May 1964, Johnson set out the Great Society, a programme to end poverty and racial injustice.
The Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 launched the War on Poverty, which included Job Corps and community action programmes.
The Voting Rights Act of 6 August 1965 suspended literacy tests and sent federal examiners to register voters in areas where discrimination was proven.
Medicare for the elderly and Medicaid for the poor were signed into law on 30 July 1965.
