The Elementary and Secondary Education Act (April 1965) and the Higher Education Act (1965) provided federal aid to schools and colleges, and Head Start for poor pre-school children began in 1965.
In the 1964 election Johnson won about 61 per cent of the popular vote against Barry Goldwater, who carried only six states.
The Great Society also included the Immigration and Nationality Act (1965), which ended national-origin quotas, and the creation of the Department of Housing and Urban Development (1965).
The cost of the Vietnam War from 1965 drained money and attention from the Great Society, and Republican gains in the 1966 midterms slowed new legislation.
Richard Nixon won the 1968 election narrowly and was re-elected in 1972 by carrying 49 states.
Nixon's domestic record included the Environmental Protection Agency (1970), wage and price controls (August 1971) and the expansion of affirmative action in federal contracts.
Five men were arrested for burgling the Democratic National Committee headquarters in the Watergate complex on 17 June 1972, and the Washington Post's reporting kept the scandal in the news.
Nixon resigned on 9 August 1974; Gerald Ford, who had become vice president in December 1973 after Spiro Agnew resigned, pardoned him on 8 September 1974.
Ford's pardon of Nixon damaged his standing; he faced inflation and recession in 1974 to 1975 and lost narrowly to Carter in 1976.
Jimmy Carter, a Democrat from Georgia, won the 1976 election and negotiated the Panama Canal treaties of 1977, under which the canal passed to Panama at the end of 1999.
The Camp David Accords of September 1978, brokered by Carter, led to a peace treaty between Egypt and Israel signed in March 1979.

Carter created the Departments of Energy (1977) and Education (1979), but high inflation and the 1979 oil shock undermined him; his televised speech of July 1979 on a "crisis of confidence", nicknamed the malaise speech, was seen by critics as blaming the public.

The Iran hostage crisis held 52 American diplomats and citizens from 4 November 1979 to 20 January 1981, 444 days; an attempted rescue in April 1980 failed, and it was a major cause of Carter's defeat.
Ronald Reagan defeated Carter in 1980 and was re-elected in 1984, carrying 49 states against Walter Mondale.
In his first inaugural address (20 January 1981) Reagan said that "government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem".
The Economic Recovery Tax Act of August 1981 cut income tax rates by about 25 per cent over three years and lowered the top rate from 70 to 50 per cent.
Reagan's first term combined cuts to many domestic social programmes with a large rise in defence spending, a pattern known as Reaganomics.
When air traffic controllers in the PATCO union struck in August 1981, Reagan dismissed the strikers, signalling a hard line on public sector unions.
Iran-Contra was revealed in November 1986: the administration had sold arms to Iran and diverted the money to the Contra rebels in Nicaragua despite congressional restrictions.
The Tower Commission (February 1987) criticised Reagan's detached management style; National Security Adviser John Poindexter and his aide Oliver North were among those prosecuted.
Reagan's popularity survived the scandal and he left office in January 1989 with high approval ratings, earning the nickname "the Teflon president" because scandals did not stick to him.
Truman's Marshall Plan and NATO are usually seen as successes of US leadership; his failure to pass national health insurance and the unpopularity of the Korean War are the main criticisms.
Johnson's Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts are counted as major achievements, while his Vietnam policy is widely judged a failure.
Nixon's opening to China and his arms control agreements are credited as achievements, while Watergate and the secret bombing of Cambodia are judged serious failings.
Carter's Camp David Accords are judged a success, while the Iran hostage crisis and his 1980 defeat are the main charges against him.
Reagan's supporters credit his tax cuts and his role in ending the Cold War; critics point to the rising deficit, the 1981 to 1982 recession and Iran-Contra.
Public opinion polls made presidential popularity visible from the 1930s onwards, and the Watergate and Iran-Contra scandals led Congress to reassert its oversight of presidents.

Contemporary verdicts often differed from later ones: Truman left office in 1953 deeply unpopular, yet his reputation rose sharply in later historians' rankings, as did Eisenhower's, while Johnson's soared in 1964 and collapsed by 1968.
After 1945 the United States abandoned its pre-war isolation and committed itself to resisting Soviet expansion, a policy known as containment.
The United States emerged from the Second World War as the richest industrial power and, from 1945, the only country with atomic weapons.
The atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, on Truman's authority, and the Soviet Union tested its own bomb on 29 August 1949.
George Kennan, a diplomat in Moscow, sent his Long Telegram in February 1946 arguing that Soviet expansion could be checked by firm, long-term resistance rather than by negotiation.
Kennan's article The Sources of Soviet Conduct, published in Foreign Affairs in July 1947 under the signature X, gave containment its name.

The Truman Doctrine of 12 March 1947 asked Congress for about 400 million dollars in aid to Greece and Turkey, and it committed the United States to support free peoples resisting armed minorities or outside pressure.
The Communist seizure of power in Czechoslovakia in February 1948 convinced many in Washington and Western Europe that the Soviet threat was immediate.
Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949, and Republicans later used the question "Who lost China?" to attack Truman's Asia policy.
In April 1950 the National Security Council paper NSC-68 called for a large rise in defence spending to meet the Soviet threat, and it was adopted after the Korean War began.
Economic aid and a military alliance were the two pillars of containment in Western Europe.
George Marshall, the Secretary of State, proposed a European recovery programme in a speech at Harvard University on 5 June 1947.
The European Recovery Program, passed by Congress in April 1948, provided about 13 billion dollars of aid to Western European countries between 1948 and 1952.
The Soviet Union refused Marshall aid and pressured its satellite states in Eastern Europe to refuse it too, so the division of Europe became more fixed.

Most aid was given as grants of food, fuel and machinery rather than loans, and the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC) was set up in April 1948 to allocate it; Britain, France and West Germany were the largest recipients.
The North Atlantic Treaty was signed on 4 April 1949 by twelve countries, including the United States, Britain, France, Canada and Italy.
Article 5 of the NATO treaty stated that an armed attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all, the basis of collective defence.
Germany was divided: the Federal Republic of Germany was founded in May 1949 in the Western zones, and the German Democratic Republic followed in October 1949 in the Soviet zone.
Berlin, divided into four sectors, was the most dangerous point of Cold War contact in Europe.
The Soviet Union began blocking road, rail and canal access to West Berlin on 24 June 1948, aiming to force the Western powers out of the city.
The Western powers responded with an airlift that flew food, coal and other supplies into West Berlin; more than two million tons were carried before the blockade was lifted on 12 May 1949.
In November 1958 Khrushchev demanded that the Western powers withdraw from Berlin within six months, and the issue was debated at the Vienna summit with Kennedy in June 1961.
The Berlin Wall was built from 13 August 1961, closing the border between East and West Berlin and stopping the flow of East German refugees.
In October 1961 American and Soviet tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie, the crossing point for foreigners, in a tense standoff that ended without shots.
Well over two million East Germans had fled to the West between 1949 and 1961, most of them by crossing from East to West Berlin, which drained the East's skilled workforce.
Kennedy visited West Berlin on 26 June 1963 and declared in German "Ich bin ein Berliner" (I am a Berliner), a statement of solidarity that was widely praised in the West.
The Korean War was the first major armed conflict of the Cold War, fought under a United Nations flag.

Korea had been divided at the 38th parallel in 1945; the Republic of Korea in the South under Syngman Rhee and the Democratic People's Republic in the North under Kim Il Sung were both founded in 1948.

US troops had left South Korea in 1949, and Secretary of State Dean Acheson's speech of January 1950 left Korea outside the American defence perimeter in the Pacific, which communist leaders may have read as a green light.
North Korean forces invaded the South on 25 June 1950, and the UN Security Council, with the Soviet delegate absent, condemned the attack and then recommended that members help South Korea repel it.
Truman sent American forces without asking Congress for a declaration of war, and he described the operation as a police action.
General Douglas MacArthur led the UN forces; his landing at Inchon on 15 September 1950 cut North Korean supply lines and led to the recapture of Seoul on 28 September.
UN forces advanced north of the 38th parallel in October 1950, and Chinese forces entered the war in large numbers from late October and November 1950, driving them back.
Truman dismissed MacArthur on 11 April 1951 after the general publicly argued for attacking China, a decision that caused a major domestic row.
An armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953; the frontier stayed close to the 38th parallel, and no peace treaty was ever signed.
About 36,000 American servicemen died in the war, and US troops remained in South Korea after the armistice.
Cuba lay ninety miles from Florida, and the United States had long treated the island as within its sphere of influence.
Under the Platt Amendment of 1901 the United States had the right to intervene in Cuba, a clause repealed in 1934 but leaving a legacy of US economic dominance.
Fidel Castro's revolution took power on 1 January 1959 after Batista fled, and the new government nationalised US-owned sugar, oil and other property in 1960.

Eisenhower cut the Cuban sugar quota in July 1960, imposed a partial trade embargo in October 1960 and broke off diplomatic relations in January 1961; Cuba turned to the Soviet Union for trade and oil.
CIA-trained Cuban exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs on 17 April 1961; they were defeated within three days, a humiliation for Kennedy.
Operation Mongoose, a covert campaign against Castro's government, was authorised in November 1961.
Soviet medium-range missiles were shipped to Cuba from September 1962, and photographs taken by a US U-2 spy plane on 14 October 1962 revealed the launch sites; Kennedy was shown them on 16 October.
Khrushchev's motives for the missiles included defending Cuba from another invasion, answering US Jupiter missiles in Turkey and Italy, and offsetting Soviet weakness in long-range missiles.
Kennedy and his advisers (the Executive Committee, ExComm) rejected an air strike or invasion, and on 22 October he announced on television a naval quarantine (blockade) of Cuba.
On 24 October Soviet ships turned back from the quarantine line; on 27 October ("Black Saturday") a U-2 was shot down over Cuba, killing its pilot, Major Rudolf Anderson.
On 28 October 1962 Khrushchev agreed on Moscow radio to remove the missiles in return for a US pledge not to invade Cuba.
Kennedy also secretly agreed to withdraw US Jupiter missiles from Turkey within months, a deal kept private for years; a hotline between Washington and Moscow was installed in 1963.
US involvement in Vietnam grew out of the containment of communism in Asia. Johnson's escalation of 1964 to 1968 is covered in the case study on Johnson and Vietnam.
Vietnam was part of French Indochina; the Viet Minh under Ho Chi Minh fought the French, who were defeated at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954.
From 1950 Truman gave aid to the French war, and by 1954 the United States was paying about three quarters of its cost.
In April 1954 Eisenhower described the domino theory: if Vietnam fell to communism, the rest of Southeast Asia would follow, like a row of falling dominoes.
The Geneva Accords of July 1954 divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, with elections planned for 1956 that were never held.
The United States backed Ngo Dinh Diem in South Vietnam and joined the Southeast Asia Treaty Organisation (SEATO) in 1954.
Under Eisenhower the United States trained the South Vietnamese army with a military advisory group, and the first American advisers killed in the conflict died in 1959.
The National Liberation Front, known to the Americans as the Viet Cong, was formed in December 1960 to fight the government in the South.
Kennedy backed the Strategic Hamlet programme (1962), which moved peasants into fortified villages and was deeply resented.
In 1963 Diem's persecution of Buddhists provoked protests, including the self-immolation of the monk Thich Quang Duc in Saigon in June 1963.
Diem was overthrown and killed in a coup that US officials had tacitly encouraged, on 2 November 1963, after which the South suffered a series of unstable governments.
Kennedy increased US military advisers in South Vietnam to about 16,000 by late 1963.
The Nixon Doctrine, announced at Guam in July 1969, stated that Asian nations should take the main responsibility for their own defence, and US troop numbers began to fall.
Nixon's Vietnamisation handed the ground war to the South Vietnamese army while US troops were withdrawn, falling from about 540,000 in early 1969 to under 30,000 by late 1972.

In April 1970 Nixon sent US and South Vietnamese troops into Cambodia to attack communist bases, which sparked protests at home, including Kent State; secret bombing of Cambodia had begun in March 1969.

In 1971 South Vietnamese forces invaded Laos with US air support and were driven back; in 1972 Nixon answered North Vietnam's Easter Offensive by mining Haiphong harbour and the Linebacker bombing raids, and ordered the Christmas bombing of Hanoi in December 1972.
The Paris Peace Accords were signed on 27 January 1973, and the last US combat troops left Vietnam by late March 1973; the fall of Saigon in 1975 is outside this subsection.
Eisenhower's Secretary of State John Foster Dulles relied on massive retaliation (1954): the threat of nuclear attack to deter communist aggression, which was cheaper than large conventional forces.
Eisenhower is said to have signalled through intermediaries in 1953 that he might use nuclear weapons if the Korean talks failed, though historians dispute how far this forced the armistice.
Kennedy replaced massive retaliation with flexible response, building up conventional and special forces (such as the Green Berets) so the United States could fight limited wars.
After the missile crisis Kennedy and Khrushchev signed the Partial Test Ban Treaty (August 1963), banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space and under water.
Truman's domestic record is covered in the notes on US politics. This block covers his foreign policy and how he is judged.
At the Potsdam conference of July and August 1945 Truman met Stalin for the first time, and he authorised the atomic bombings shortly afterwards.
The Truman Doctrine speech to Congress (12 March 1947) set out the principle that the United States would support free peoples against communist pressure.
He recognised the new state of Israel on 14 May 1948, within minutes of its declaration of independence, against the advice of parts of his State Department.
He decided in June 1950 to send American forces to defend South Korea without a congressional vote, a decision that set the pattern for later presidential war-making.
He was a direct participant in every decision: he chose the airlift rather than an armed convoy to Berlin (1948) and accepted a limited war in Korea rather than MacArthur's wider war with China.
A sign on his desk read "The buck stops here", summing up his view that the President must take final responsibility.
Contemporaries were divided: Republicans attacked him over China and the spy scandals of the period, and by 1952 his popularity had fallen sharply.

Revisionist historians from the 1960s, such as William Appleman Williams, argued that US economic expansion and the atomic bomb helped cause the Cold War; post-revisionists such as John Lewis Gaddis stressed Stalin's own responsibility and argued that containment worked in Europe.
Success in Western Europe: the Marshall Plan, NATO and the Berlin airlift contained Soviet power in Europe and helped to create a prosperous Western alliance.
Failure in Asia: the Korean War ended in a stalemate after about three years, with heavy American losses and no victory.
Korea can also be judged a limited success: South Korea survived, and Truman kept the war from spreading to China or becoming nuclear.
The Cuban missile crisis avoided nuclear war, but the Bay of Pigs was a clear failure and the Soviet missiles were removed only in exchange for a secret US concession.
Vietnam showed the limits of containment: a commitment that began with advisers had escalated to over half a million troops by 1968.
Supporters argue that US commitments in Asia deterred further Soviet and Chinese expansion, while critics say they drew the United States into costly wars in places of little strategic importance.
Contemporaries and later historians differ over whether the Cold War could have been managed by diplomacy earlier, and the debate shapes judgements of Truman, Kennedy and Johnson.
Johnson became president in November 1963 with an American commitment in South Vietnam that had already grown from advisers into a costly war against the Viet Cong.

Lyndon Baines Johnson was born in 1908 near Stonewall, Texas, worked in the New Deal's National Youth Administration in Texas, entered the House in 1937 and won his Senate seat in 1948 by 87 votes, a result that earned him the nickname Landslide Lyndon.
He became Democratic leader in the Senate in 1953 and Majority Leader in 1955, and in 1960 he accepted the vice presidency under Kennedy after losing the nomination.

He was a master of Senate politics and persuasion, using personal pressure on colleagues (the Johnson treatment) to pass legislation, but he could not apply those methods to a war against an enemy who would not bargain on his terms.
He was vice president under Kennedy and sworn in as president on 22 November 1963, after Kennedy's assassination in Dallas.

Kennedy had committed the United States to the survival of South Vietnam but had avoided combat troops, and the South Vietnamese government was in disarray after Diem's overthrow and killing on 2 November 1963.

Within days of taking office Johnson told his ambassador in Saigon that he would not lose Vietnam, and National Security Action Memorandum 273 (26 November 1963) confirmed the policy of supporting South Vietnam.

Johnson kept Kennedy's advisers, including Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara, Secretary of State Dean Rusk and National Security Adviser McGeorge Bundy, so there was continuity of thinking about the war.

Johnson feared that losing Vietnam would repeat the political damage of the loss of China, when Truman's party had been attacked as soft on communism, and he feared a right-wing backlash that would wreck his domestic programme.
When Johnson took office there were about 16,000 American military advisers in South Vietnam, and the government of Diem had been overthrown in November 1963.
Johnson inherited a South Vietnamese government that was unstable and a war in which the Viet Cong controlled large parts of the countryside.
He was a firm anti-communist who was also aware of the domestic cost of war, and he believed that losing South Vietnam would damage US credibility worldwide.
The Gulf of Tonkin incidents gave Johnson congressional authority for a larger war, and the 1964 election confirmed his mandate.

On 2 August 1964 North Vietnamese torpedo boats attacked the US destroyer USS Maddox in the Gulf of Tonkin, which was on an intelligence-gathering patrol near the North Vietnamese coast, days after South Vietnamese commando raids on the coast (Operation 34A) that Hanoi linked to the patrol.

A second attack reported on 4 August 1964, on the Maddox and the destroyer USS Turner Joy, probably never happened: sonar and radar readings in bad weather were misread, and later documents showed that officials doubted the report even as it was used.
On the evening of 4 August 1964 Johnson announced retaliatory air strikes on North Vietnamese naval bases, which were carried out on 5 August.

The Tonkin Gulf Resolution, passed on 7 August 1964 by 416 votes to 0 in the House and 88 to 2 in the Senate, authorised the President to take all necessary measures to protect US forces and to prevent further aggression.
Critics later argued that the resolution was prepared before the incidents were fully understood, and Senator Wayne Morse and Senator Ernest Gruening voted against it.
In the 1964 election Johnson won about 61 per cent of the popular vote against Barry Goldwater, who had called for stronger action in Vietnam, and he presented himself as the candidate of restraint.
The campaign's restraint was a political strategy, and Johnson privately prepared for a larger war while publicly promising not to send American boys to fight an Asian war.
The decision to bomb North Vietnam and to commit ground combat forces in 1965 turned an advisers' war into an American war.
In February 1965 a Viet Cong attack on the American base at Pleiku killed eight Americans, and Johnson ordered reprisal raids (Flaming Dart) that led on to the sustained bombing.
Operation Rolling Thunder, a sustained bombing campaign against North Vietnam, began on 2 March 1965, and it continued in stages until 1968.
The first US Marine combat units landed at Da Nang on 8 March 1965, the first American ground combat troops in Vietnam.
General William Westmoreland, commander of US forces from June 1964, argued that a war of attrition with large forces would wear down the North Vietnamese.

On 28 July 1965 Johnson announced at a press conference that US forces in Vietnam would rise from 75,000 to 125,000 at once and that more would be sent as commanders requested, without asking Congress for a declaration of war or calling up the reserves.
US troop numbers reached about 184,000 by the end of 1965, about 385,000 by the end of 1966 and over 500,000 in 1968, peaking at about 540,000 in 1969 before falling.
Johnson's strategy was to hold the South while signalling willingness to negotiate, and his April 1965 Johns Hopkins speech offered unconditional talks and a development plan for the Mekong Delta.
North Vietnam refused to negotiate while the bombing continued, and the Viet Cong kept fighting in the South, supplied through the Ho Chi Minh Trail in Laos and Cambodia.

Johnson's advisers were not united: Under Secretary of State George Ball argued in memos in 1965 that the United States would be dragged into an unwinnable land war, but Johnson, McNamara, Rusk and Bundy chose escalation.
Johnson avoided a formal declaration of war and wanted to keep the escalation low-key in order not to endanger his Great Society legislation, which was passing through Congress in 1965.
Westmoreland's strategy was search and destroy: large units hunted communist forces in the countryside, using helicopters, artillery and air power, and success was measured by the body count.
The communists could choose when to fight, and they replaced losses from a large population and from supplies carried down the Ho Chi Minh Trail, so attrition did not break their will.
Heavy firepower, including napalm and the defoliant Agent Orange, killed large numbers of civilians and drove peasants into government-controlled camps or towards the Viet Cong.

The pacification of the countryside and the building of a stable South Vietnamese government lagged behind: the Saigon regime was led by generals, and Nguyen Van Thieu became president in 1967 after elections criticised as flawed.
In November 1967 Westmoreland told Washington that the end was in view, which set up the shock of Tet.
In March 1968 American soldiers killed several hundred unarmed villagers at My Lai, an atrocity covered up until it was exposed in 1969.
American casualties passed 30,000 dead by the end of 1968, and the draft, which took young men who lacked college deferments, spread the war's costs through American families.
Johnson's public statements on Vietnam were increasingly doubted, and his critics in Congress and the media challenged the war from 1966.
The term credibility gap was used by journalists from the mid-1960s to describe the difference between official statements on the war and the reality reported from Vietnam.
Senator J. William Fulbright, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, held televised hearings on Vietnam in early 1966 that questioned the war's basis.
Fulbright's book The Arrogance of Power (1966) argued that the United States was acting as a great power imposing its will on a small nation.
The teach-in movement began at the University of Michigan in March 1965, and student and church opposition grew steadily through 1966 and 1967.
Martin Luther King Jr. spoke against the war in his Beyond Vietnam speech at Riverside Church, New York, on 4 April 1967, linking the war to poverty and racism.
Muhammad Ali refused induction into the army on 28 April 1967, a decision that cost him his heavyweight title and was widely discussed in the press.
Johnson's critics said the war was consuming money and attention needed for the Great Society, while his supporters argued that withdrawal would damage America's position abroad.

Opposition spread beyond students: on 21 October 1967 about 50,000 people marched on the Pentagon, and in April 1965 the Students for a Democratic Society had led a march of about 20,000 in Washington.
Johnson tried to fund both the war and his domestic programme, and the cost of the war weakened his reform agenda.
Johnson tried to pay for the war and the Great Society together, a policy critics called guns and butter, and he delayed asking Congress for a tax increase until 1967.
Federal deficits grew and inflation rose after 1965, and Congress passed a 10 per cent income tax surtax in June 1968 to restrain spending.
Funding for the War on Poverty was cut or diverted as military spending grew, and many programmes were underfunded as they expanded.
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 were passed before the war's costs became acute, and they stand as Johnson's most secure achievements.
By 1967 the rising cost of the war and the urban riots had turned public opinion against new domestic spending, weakening the Great Society's momentum.
The Tet Offensive of January 1968 did not defeat the Americans militarily, but it shattered their optimism and ended Johnson's chance of re-election.
On 30 January 1968, during the Tet holiday, Viet Cong and North Vietnamese forces attacked more than a hundred towns and cities across South Vietnam, including Saigon and the city of Hue.

A Viet Cong squad broke into the grounds of the US embassy in Saigon and held out for about six hours before being killed, and television pictures of it shocked American opinion, even though the offensive was militarily a failure for the communists.
General Westmoreland had said that the enemy could no longer mount major offensives, and Tet was taken by many Americans as proof that official optimism was false.
Tet was a heavy military defeat for the communists, who lost many of their best Viet Cong fighters, but American commentators judged it by Westmoreland's earlier promises.
On 27 February 1968 the television newsman Walter Cronkite broadcast a report calling the war a stalemate, and his views were widely reported as a sign of changing opinion.

In February 1968 Westmoreland and the Joint Chiefs asked for about 206,000 more troops; Johnson's new Secretary of Defense Clark Clifford studied the request and advised against it, and a group of senior outside advisers known as the Wise Men told Johnson in March that the war could not be won at an acceptable cost.
Eugene McCarthy's strong showing in the New Hampshire primary in March 1968 and Robert Kennedy's entry into the race weakened Johnson's position within his own party.
On 31 March 1968 Johnson announced a partial halt to the bombing of North Vietnam above the 20th parallel, offered peace talks and declared that he would not seek re-election.
Peace talks began in Paris in May 1968, but the war continued, and the Republican Richard Nixon won the presidency in November 1968 after promising an honourable end to the war.

1968 turned into a year of crisis: Martin Luther King was assassinated on 4 April and Robert Kennedy on 5 June, and the Democratic convention in Chicago in August was marked by rioting between police and protesters, and Johnson's vice president Hubert Humphrey lost narrowly to Nixon.
Historians and contemporaries have offered several reasons why an enormous American military effort failed to defeat a determined enemy.
The war was a limited one: the US avoided invading North Vietnam, mining Haiphong harbour, or using nuclear weapons, and this limited the pressure on Hanoi.
North Vietnam and the Viet Cong could use bases in Laos and Cambodia that the US was reluctant to attack, so they could withdraw and rebuild.
The South Vietnamese government was weak and corrupt, and the Army of the Republic of Vietnam could not hold the territory cleared by American forces.
The strategy of attrition and the body count measure of success were criticised within the US army and in the press as misleading about the progress of the war.
Many historians argue that Johnson's gradual escalation, and his refusal to consider a clear withdrawal, kept options open while the costs and divisions at home grew.
Johnson played down the war in public to protect the Great Society, so he never explained clear aims to the public, and the later gap between his optimism and events hurt his standing.
Johnson was the president who made Vietnam an American war and also the president of the Great Society. He was a decision-maker at the centre of events rather than a witness.
His career: congressman 1937, senator 1949, Senate Majority Leader 1955 to 1961, vice president 1961 to 1963, president from 22 November 1963 until January 1969.
His domestic record was one of the greatest legislative achievements of any president: the Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965), Medicare, Medicaid and federal aid to education.
In Vietnam he took decisions in 1964 and 1965 to bomb North Vietnam and send combat troops, always in steps, and he hoped to avoid a wider war with China or the Soviet Union, as in Korea in 1950.

Contemporaries saw him as a forceful, domineering leader who was crude, devious and driven, and the credibility gap made many doubt his word; his supporters pointed to his achievements for the poor and for black Americans.
Protesters chanted at him outside the White House, and the demonstrations helped to persuade him not to stand again in 1968.

Historians in the 1970s, such as the journalist David Halberstam in The Best and the Brightest (1972), blamed the arrogance of the advisers he inherited; later historians, such as Robert Dallek and Fredrik Logevall, stress that he had alternatives in 1964 and 1965 and chose to escalate partly to protect his domestic reputation.
Johnson's reputation has risen since the 1990s for civil rights and fallen over Vietnam, so most historians now regard him as a tragic figure.
Examiners reward evaluation that weighs Johnson's domestic achievements against his failure in Vietnam, and contemporary against later judgements.
Success at home: the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act, Medicare and Medicaid are judged as major achievements of the twentieth century's social reform.
Failure abroad: the war ended without victory in 1973 and cost about 58,000 American lives, and it damaged the Great Society and the trust of the public in government.

Contemporaries were divided: in 1964 and 1965 most Americans admired him as a strong, effective leader, but the war cut his approval below 40 per cent by late 1967, and he was jeered by protesters chanting about how many children he had killed that day.
Later historians disagree about whether Johnson was trapped by the assumptions of the Cold War or whether he made avoidable choices on escalation.
The phrase credibility gap summed up the lasting problem of trust between a president and the public, a theme that shaped politics after Vietnam and Watergate.
Fear of communist subversion in the United States grew after 1945 and shaped the domestic limits within which foreign policy was made.

The House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) investigated alleged communist influence in Hollywood, and its hearings in October 1947 led to the Hollywood Ten, who refused to answer questions, being convicted of contempt of Congress in 1948; they served prison terms of up to a year from 1950 after losing their appeals.
The studios adopted the Waldorf Statement in November 1947, agreeing not to employ anyone who was a suspected communist, which created the Hollywood blacklist.

Alger Hiss, a former State Department official, was convicted of perjury in January 1950 after denying that he had passed State Department documents to Whittaker Chambers, a former communist courier who accused him in 1948; the case was highly publicised and Nixon's role in it made his name.
Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were arrested in 1950 for passing atomic secrets to the Soviet Union and were executed in June 1953.
The McCarran Internal Security Act of September 1950 required communist organisations to register with the government, and Congress overrode Truman's veto of it.
Truman's loyalty programme of 1947 and the subsequent investigations made many federal employees fear losing their jobs over any past political association.
The Smith Act trial of eleven Communist Party leaders in 1949 led to convictions that the Supreme Court upheld in Dennis v. United States (1951).
Klaus Fuchs, a British physicist who had worked on the Manhattan Project, confessed to passing secrets to the Soviets in January 1950, which strengthened fears of spies.
The Red Scare reached teachers, trade unionists and entertainers: loyalty oaths were widely imposed and many people lost jobs for refusing to name former associates.
McCarthy was a participant who used the Red Scare to build a national following. He was also a figure whose methods were judged harshly by contemporaries and later historians.
Joseph McCarthy was born in 1908 in Grand Chute, Wisconsin, served as a Marine in the Second World War, and was elected a Republican senator for Wisconsin in 1946.
In 1950 he was a little-known senator whose record was thin; Klaus Fuchs's arrest as an atomic spy in Britain, the Hiss conviction and the loss of China made the Wheeling speech a national sensation.
The Tydings Committee of the Senate investigated his claims in 1950 and called them a fraud and a hoax, but McCarthy's attacks helped to defeat Senator Millard Tydings in the November 1950 election.
His methods were guilt by association, unnamed lists, shifting numbers and personal smears, and the term McCarthyism was coined by the cartoonist Herblock in 1950.
He investigated the Voice of America and the overseas libraries of the State Department in 1953, and his aides Roy Cohn and G. David Schine toured Europe checking them.
Edward R. Murrow's television programme See It Now, broadcast on 9 March 1954, used McCarthy's own words and film to criticise him.
In a speech at Wheeling, West Virginia, on 9 February 1950 he claimed to hold a list of communists working in the State Department, and the number he gave changed in later accounts.
He chaired the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations from 1953, where he made accusations against officials of the State Department and, in 1954, turned his inquiries on the army.
The Army-McCarthy hearings in April to June 1954 were televised, and the lawyer Joseph Welch's question Have you no sense of decency, sir? became a turning point in public opinion against him.
The Senate voted 67 to 22 on 2 December 1954 to censure him for conduct unbecoming a senator, and his influence collapsed after that vote.
Eisenhower avoided naming McCarthy in public for most of 1953 and 1954, and the president's private disapproval was not made clear until later.

McCarthy died in May 1957 of illness made worse by alcoholism; historians still debate how many of his accusations were justified, as the Venona decrypts published in 1995 showed that some Soviet spies were indeed active in the government.
Contemporaries split along party lines, with many Republicans and conservatives supporting him, while many liberals and the press denounced his methods as reckless smears.

Historians since Richard Rovere (1959) have judged him a demagogue; Ellen Schrecker argues that McCarthyism was a wider system, backed by the FBI under J. Edgar Hoover, HUAC and both parties, which McCarthy exploited rather than created, and M. Stanton Evans (2007) offered a minority defence based on Venona.
The climate of suspicion affected what officials said and did about China, the Soviet Union and Asia.
The Republican charge that Truman and the State Department had lost China, after the communist victory in October 1949, was amplified by McCarthy's attacks on State Department officials.

The China expert Owen Lattimore was accused by McCarthy in 1950 of being a leading Soviet agent in the United States; he was never charged with espionage, and perjury charges against him were dropped in 1955.
The State Department's China specialists were moved from their posts or dismissed in the early 1950s, weakening the government's expert knowledge of Asia.
McCarthy's campaign made it politically risky for Democrats to show any willingness to negotiate with communist states, which constrained diplomacy in the Korean and Chinese crises.
Eisenhower's administration was accused of appeasing McCarthy, and his State Department adopted the loyalty security checks that McCarthy had demanded.
Soviet propaganda used images of racial violence and discrimination in the United States, including the Little Rock crisis of 1957, to argue that American democracy was a sham.
Opposition to the Vietnam War grew from a small minority in 1965 into a mass movement that affected the government's choices from 1968 onwards.
The first major teach-in against the war was held at the University of Michigan on 24 March 1965, and teach-ins spread to many campuses in the following weeks.
Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), founded in 1960 and famous for the Port Huron Statement of 1962, organised large anti-war marches and campus protests from 1965.
The first draft lottery, which selected men for call-up by birthdate, was held on 1 December 1969, and it made young men more aware of the war's impact on their lives.
A large march on the Pentagon on 21 October 1967 was recorded by Norman Mailer in The Armies of the Night, which won major literary prizes.
The Vietnam Moratorium demonstrations of 15 October and 15 November 1969 drew very large crowds, and Nixon responded with a speech on 3 November 1969 appealing to a silent majority.
On 4 May 1970, after the US invasion of Cambodia had been announced on 30 April, the Ohio National Guard shot protesters at Kent State University, killing four students.
The Pentagon Papers, a secret government study of the war's history, were published by the New York Times on 13 June 1971, and the Supreme Court upheld the paper's right to publish on 30 June 1971.
Draft resistance spread: many young men burned draft cards or fled to Canada, and the draft deferment for college students meant that poorer and black men were more likely to be sent to Vietnam.
Muhammad Ali refused induction on 28 April 1967 on religious grounds as a Muslim minister, which made the draft a matter of conscience for a mass audience.

The Democratic National Convention in Chicago in August 1968 saw police beat protesters outside the convention hall in front of television cameras, and demonstrators chanted that the whole world was watching.
The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution was repealed by Congress in January 1971.
Racial discrimination at home was a serious problem for US foreign policy, because it weakened America's claim to lead the free world.
The Brown v Board of Education ruling of 17 May 1954 was reported abroad as evidence that the United States was tackling discrimination, although desegregation was slow in the South.
The Little Rock crisis of 1957 was broadcast around the world, and US diplomats argued that it damaged the country's standing in newly independent Asian and African states.
President Truman's Executive Order 9981 of 1948 ordering the armed forces to desegregate was partly motivated by the need to answer communist criticism of US racism.
The Freedom Rides of 1961 and the Birmingham campaign of 1963 were covered in the international press and undermined the US claim to be a model of democracy.
Black Americans such as Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. linked racial injustice to US foreign policy, with King linking the cost of the war in Vietnam to the funds needed for the poor.
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 were framed in part as steps needed to maintain US credibility abroad during the Cold War.

The Soviet Union and later the Chinese broadcast stories of lynchings and segregation to the Third World, and the State Department filed briefs in Brown arguing that segregation was an embarrassment in the Cold War.
Eisenhower's administration replaced Truman's loyalty rules with its own security criteria, which kept the anti-communist climate in place.
Eisenhower signed Executive Order 10450 in April 1953, which set new security criteria for federal employment and superseded Truman's loyalty programme.
Under the new criteria many government employees were dismissed as security risks, and past membership in suspect organisations could count against a person as well as proven disloyalty.
Eisenhower's administration did not challenge McCarthy's investigations directly, and his public reticence allowed the charges to spread until the Army hearings of 1954.
Richard Nixon, Eisenhower's vice president, had built his national reputation on the Hiss investigation, which made anti-communism a bipartisan position in 1950s politics.
Opposition in Congress moved from criticism to legislative limits on the war from 1970, and it reduced the President's room for manoeuvre.
The McGovern-Hatfield amendment of 1970, which proposed a date for withdrawing all US troops, was defeated in the Senate, though it attracted substantial support.

The Cooper-Church amendment sought to bar funds for US operations in Cambodia after 30 June 1970; the Senate passed it but the House did not, and a weaker version banning US ground troops in Laos and Thailand became law in December 1970, one of the first formal limits on the war.
The Case-Church amendment, passed in June 1973 and accepted by Nixon in a compromise bill, cut off funds for US combat in Indochina from 15 August 1973.
Congressional opposition was strengthened by the Pentagon Papers and by testimony from veterans, and it made the war a matter of political argument within the government.
Examiners reward judgements that weigh the influence of domestic fears and protests on decisions against the other causes of US policy.

Supporters of McCarthyism argue that the fear of espionage was justified by real Soviet spy networks, such as those uncovered in the Venona decrypts, and that anti-communism kept the country vigilant.
Critics argue that McCarthy's methods damaged the civil liberties of innocent people and weakened expert advice on China, and that the State Department lost its best Asia analysts.
The anti-war movement helped to end the draft and to bring Johnson's withdrawal, but the war continued for four more years after his decision not to run in 1968.
Historians disagree about whether protests changed the outcome of the war or simply sharpened a decision that the government had already made.
The Red Scare was a long-lasting feature of US politics, and the constraints it placed on foreign policy were most severe in the early 1950s.
The United States withdrew from the Vietnam War through a negotiated settlement, a result that weakened the consensus in favour of containment.
The Paris Peace Accords were signed on 27 January 1973 by the United States, North Vietnam, South Vietnam and the Viet Cong, and they provided for the withdrawal of American forces.
The last US combat troops left Vietnam by late March 1973, and the release of American prisoners of war was completed in the same period.

Congress passed the War Powers Resolution over Nixon's veto on 7 November 1973, requiring the President to report to Congress and to withdraw forces within sixty days unless Congress approved their continued use.

From August 1973 the Case-Church amendment barred further US combat in Indochina, so when the North broke the Accords the United States could not intervene, and South Vietnam depended on its own forces and on aid from Congress.
The North Vietnamese offensive of 1975 overran South Vietnam, and the capture of Saigon on 30 April 1975 ended the war.
In April 1975 Congress refused Ford's request for emergency military aid for Saigon, a sign of how far the American consensus behind the war had collapsed.

Ford told a university audience on 23 April 1975 that the war was finished as far as America was concerned, and the last Americans and many South Vietnamese were airlifted from Saigon by helicopter (Operation Frequent Wind) on 29 and 30 April.
Cambodia fell to the Khmer Rouge on 17 April 1975, and Laos came under communist control later that year, so all three Indochinese states had communist governments by the end of 1975.
About 58,000 Americans had died in the war, and the defeat produced a lasting caution about overseas military commitments, sometimes called the Vietnam syndrome.
Détente was a policy of easing tensions with the Soviet Union and China through negotiation, based on a balance of power rather than on trust.
Henry Kissinger, as national security adviser and later Secretary of State, designed a policy of linkage that tied arms control to Soviet behaviour in other regions.
Nixon visited China from 21 to 28 February 1972, meeting Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai, and the Shanghai Communiqué set out a process to normalise relations.
Nixon visited Moscow in May 1972, when the first major arms control agreements were signed and trade agreements were discussed.

The Helsinki Final Act of August 1975, signed by thirty-five states including the United States and the Soviet Union, set out principles on borders and human rights, which the Soviet Union later failed to honour.
Critics of détente, including conservative Democrats such as Senator Henry Jackson, argued that the Soviet Union was gaining military strength while the United States made concessions.
The Jackson-Vanik Amendment of 1974 linked trade with the Soviet Union to freedom of emigration for Soviet Jews, and the Soviet Union rejected the link.
Détente faced strain in October 1973 when the Yom Kippur War in the Middle East led Nixon to put US forces on a nuclear alert (DEFCON 3) after Soviet threats of intervention.
Ford and Brezhnev reached a framework at Vladivostok in November 1974 for a second SALT agreement.
Soviet and Cuban support for the MPLA in Angola in 1975 and 1976 convinced critics that the Soviet Union was exploiting détente.
The Strategic Arms Limitation Talks aimed to limit the size of the nuclear arsenals of the superpowers, and produced two agreements of very different outcomes.
SALT I was signed in Moscow on 26 May 1972 and contained an Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty limiting missile defence systems, and an Interim Agreement limiting the number of strategic launchers.
The Interim Agreement froze the numbers of land-based ICBMs and submarine-launched missiles for five years, but it did not limit the number of warheads each missile carried.

SALT II was signed in Vienna on 18 June 1979 by Carter and Brezhnev, setting an equal ceiling of 2,400 strategic delivery vehicles for each side, to fall to 2,250, and limiting the number of multiple-warhead missiles.
The Senate did not ratify SALT II, and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 led Carter to withdraw it from Senate consideration in January 1980.
Both sides continued to build up their arsenals under SALT I and after SALT II collapsed, so that the agreements limited growth without reducing the number of warheads.
SALT I was negotiated by Nixon and Brezhnev with Kissinger as the key American negotiator, and the Senate approved the ABM Treaty by 88 votes to 2 in August 1972.
Critics of SALT II, led by Senator Henry Jackson, said it let the Soviet Union keep a lead in heavy land-based missiles, and the Committee on the Present Danger campaigned against it.
The Soviet Union and the United States both said they would observe SALT II's limits informally after 1980, and Reagan's government dropped that restraint in 1986.
Carter combined a human rights emphasis with a sharp hardening of policy after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.
Carter made human rights a central theme of US foreign policy from 1977, and he criticised Soviet treatment of dissidents such as Andrei Sakharov.
The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan on 24 to 25 December 1979 was condemned by Carter as an unacceptable threat to regional stability, and it ended the era of détente.

Carter announced a grain embargo against the Soviet Union in January 1980, proclaimed in his State of the Union speech that the United States would resist any attempt to gain control of the Persian Gulf (the Carter Doctrine), and led a boycott of the Moscow Olympics: the US Olympic Committee voted to stay away in April 1980, and dozens of other countries did too, though Britain, France and Ireland sent teams.
Carter's Iran policy, including the admission of the deposed Shah to the United States in October 1979, led to the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran on 4 November 1979.

The failed rescue attempt of April 1980 (Operation Eagle Claw) was abandoned after helicopters broke down, and a helicopter collided with a transport aircraft at a desert staging point, killing eight servicemen; it contributed to Carter's defeat in the 1980 election.
Carter also gave full diplomatic recognition to the People's Republic of China from 1 January 1979, building on Nixon's opening.
Reagan rejected the logic of mutual deterrence and pursued a large increase in military spending, combined with a missile defence programme.
Reagan described the Soviet Union as an evil empire in a speech to the National Association of Evangelicals on 8 March 1983.
He announced the Strategic Defense Initiative on 23 March 1983 in a television address, proposing space-based systems that could destroy incoming missiles.

The programme, nicknamed Star Wars by critics, drew scientists' doubts about feasibility and cost and was never deployed, but it alarmed Soviet leaders who feared an American technological lead they could not match.
Reagan's military budget rose sharply between 1981 and 1985, and the B-1 bomber, MX missile and Pershing II missiles in Western Europe were among the projects funded.
The Soviet Union's leadership changed rapidly from Brezhnev's death in November 1982 to Andropov, Chernenko and then Mikhail Gorbachev, who came to power in March 1985.
The meetings between Reagan and Gorbachev produced the first treaty to abolish a whole category of nuclear weapons, and the end of the Cold War followed.

Reagan and Gorbachev met at Geneva in November 1985, and at Reykjavik in October 1986, where they came close to agreeing deep cuts in nuclear weapons but the talks broke down when Gorbachev insisted that SDI be confined to the laboratory and Reagan refused.
The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty was signed in Washington on 8 December 1987 and eliminated all US and Soviet land-based missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometres.
Reagan spoke at the Berlin Wall on 12 June 1987, declaring Mr Gorbachev, tear down this wall.
Gorbachev's policies of glasnost and perestroika reduced Soviet control over Eastern Europe, and the Soviet Union did not intervene when communist governments fell in 1989.
The Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November 1989, and the collapse of communist regimes across Eastern Europe during 1989 ended the division that had defined the Cold War.
The Senate ratified the INF Treaty in May 1988, and Reagan visited Moscow for a fourth summit in May and June 1988; a Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan was completed in February 1989.
Reagan's successor George H. W. Bush met Gorbachev off Malta in December 1989, and the two leaders declared that the Cold War was ending.
Cold War competition extended into Central America, where revolutions and civil wars drew in US military and financial support.
The Sandinista National Liberation Front overthrew the Somoza dictatorship in Nicaragua in July 1979, and it established a government with close links to Cuba and the Soviet Union.
Carter's administration gave aid to the Sandinista government in its early years, but Reagan opposed it as a Soviet and Cuban foothold in the Americas and backed the Contra rebels against it.
The Contra war in Nicaragua was funded in part by secret arrangements that Congress had sought to prevent through the Boland Amendments of 1982 to 1984.
In El Salvador the government fought left-wing guerrillas from 1980, and the United States gave military aid to the government while criticising its record on human rights.
Carter's administration suspended aid to the Sandinistas in January 1981, and Reagan authorised covert support for the Contras in late 1981.

In El Salvador, the murder of Archbishop Oscar Romero in March 1980 and of four American churchwomen in December 1980 drew attention to death squads linked to the security forces, yet Reagan continued military aid.
Popular fear of nuclear war grew in the early 1980s, and the nuclear freeze movement pressed for limits on arms that Reagan's build-up had not satisfied.
The Nuclear Freeze campaign called for a bilateral freeze on the testing, production and deployment of nuclear weapons, and it gathered wide public support in 1982 and 1983.
A very large demonstration in New York's Central Park in June 1982 was among the largest peace rallies in the country's history.
The House of Representatives passed a non-binding freeze resolution in 1983, which showed how far the nuclear issue had moved into mainstream politics.

The television film The Day After, about a nuclear attack on Kansas, was seen by about 100 million Americans on 20 November 1983, and in January 1984 Reagan said that a nuclear war could not be won and must never be fought.
Massive protests in Western Europe, including at Greenham Common in Britain, opposed the deployment of American Pershing II and cruise missiles from late 1983.
Examiners reward judgements that weigh US policy against Soviet internal failure and the choices of Gorbachev.

Supporters of Reagan argue that his build-up and the Strategic Defense Initiative forced the Soviet Union into an arms race it could not afford, and that his firm stance created the conditions for Gorbachev's reforms.
Critics of Reagan argue that the Soviet economy was already failing before 1980 and that Gorbachev's reforms were the decisive cause of the change.
Détente and arms control under Nixon, Ford and Carter laid the foundations for the later treaties, and the INF Treaty built on the principle of verifiable limits established in the 1970s.
The failures of the period included the collapse of détente after 1979, the Iran hostage crisis and the costs of the Afghan war, which weakened US confidence before Reagan's arrival.

The Soviet Union faced economic stagnation, the costs of the Afghan war and falling oil revenues in the mid-1980s, and Reagan's own adviser Jack Matlock argued that Gorbachev's reforms drove the change, rather than American pressure.
Reagan's turn to negotiation after 1984, once he had rebuilt American strength, is credited by supporters as proof that strength led to a settlement.
The Second World War left the United States with the strongest industrial economy in the world, and wartime production and savings provided the platform for the postwar boom.
US factories produced vast quantities of aircraft, ships, tanks and munitions between 1941 and 1945, and the economy expanded rapidly, with unemployment falling to very low levels.
The United States produced roughly half of the world's manufactured goods in 1945, while its European and Japanese rivals had been devastated by the war.
Wartime wage and price controls, and the savings that Americans built up during the war, left households with large sums to spend once rationing and controls ended.
Wartime shortages of consumer goods gave way to a pent-up demand for cars, houses and household appliances after 1945.
The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, known as the GI Bill, paid tuition and living costs for veterans and offered government-guaranteed loans for homes and businesses.
The GI Bill's home loans helped to create a mass market for housing, which fed demand for consumer goods and for the construction industry.
The wartime government became the largest customer in the economy, and it built factories that private firms bought cheaply after 1945, in industries such as aluminium, synthetic rubber and aircraft.
The United States designed the postwar international monetary order, which made the dollar the central currency and financed recovery abroad.
The Bretton Woods conference of July 1944 in New Hampshire created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank to support exchange rates and reconstruction.
Under the Bretton Woods system the US dollar was convertible to gold at 35 dollars an ounce, and other currencies were pegged to the dollar.
The Marshall Plan of 1948 to 1952 gave about 13 billion dollars of US aid to Western Europe, much of it spent on American goods, which boosted US exports.

The dollar's role as the reserve currency, and the shortage of dollars in war-damaged Europe (the dollar gap), meant that Marshall aid and American loans were spent on US goods, and American companies could invest abroad cheaply.
The Korean War and NSC-68 raised the federal defence budget from about 14 billion dollars in 1950 to about 50 billion dollars by 1953, which fed the economy's growth.
The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1947 committed the United States and other states to reduce trade barriers, which suited the world's biggest exporter.
Government spending on infrastructure, defence and science drove growth in several key industries during the 1950s and 1960s.
The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 funded an Interstate Highway System of about 41,000 miles, which opened up suburban development and boosted car production and steel.
Federal defence spending remained high through the 1950s and 1960s and supplied a large market for aircraft, electronics and missile manufacturers.
The National Science Foundation was created in 1950 and federal research funding grew steadily, with universities acting as partners to government research.
The space programme, created after the launch of Sputnik in 1957 and the founding of NASA in 1958, employed thousands of engineers and contractors in the 1960s.
Federal support for education was expanded through the National Defense Education Act of 1958, which funded science and language teaching after Sputnik.
The Interstate programme was paid for by a Highway Trust Fund financed by a petrol tax, and it was justified partly on defence grounds, since Eisenhower had seen the German autobahns.
Defence research funded the development of jet aircraft, radar, nuclear power for submarines and later computers, which spread into civilian industry.
Defence spending created a network of contractors, military officers and politicians with shared interests, a development that Eisenhower warned of in 1961.

Eisenhower used the phrase military-industrial complex in his farewell address of 17 January 1961, warning of the acquisition of unwarranted influence by a combination of the armed forces and the defence industry.
Major defence contractors such as Lockheed, Boeing, General Dynamics and Douglas received large government contracts, and many companies depended on them for much of their revenue.
The warning came from a former general whose own administration had built up the nuclear arsenal and relied on it, a point critics raised about the speech.
Defence spending and the Cold War gave high-technology industries, including electronics and computing, a stable source of contracts that encouraged the growth of Silicon Valley.
C. Wright Mills's The Power Elite (1956) had argued that a small group of corporate, military and political leaders made the major decisions, an idea that Eisenhower's speech echoed in warning form.
The Organization Man is not a single person. It is the type of corporate employee that William H. Whyte described in his 1956 book, The Organization Man.
William H. Whyte, an editor at Fortune magazine, published The Organization Man in 1956 as a study of white-collar workers in large corporations and suburban communities.
Whyte argued that the corporate employee had accepted a social ethic that valued belonging, teamwork and conformity over individualism and personal conscience.
Whyte described a social ethic with three beliefs: that the group is the source of creativity, that belonging is a person's greatest need, and that science can be applied to achieve belonging.
He studied the suburb of Park Forest, Illinois, where young corporate families moved often and valued being sociable, and he criticised the personality tests that companies used in hiring.

The same worry about conformity appeared in David Riesman's The Lonely Crowd (1950), which described the other-directed person, and in C. Wright Mills's White Collar (1951), which described anxious salaried workers.

The Organization Man was a salaried manager or professional, often moving between cities and suburbs as the company required, whose career depended on loyalty to the corporation and on fitting in with its expectations.
Sloan Wilson's novel The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit (1955) portrayed a similar figure, a corporate executive torn between career success and family life.
Contemporaries praised the corporation for stability and rising living standards, but many critics saw the Organization Man as a threat to individual creativity and independence.
Historians have used the figure to explain the conformity of the 1950s, although later scholars have argued that the book overstated the conformity of American corporate life.
From the 1950s American companies expanded overseas, creating multinational corporations that linked the US economy to the rest of the world.
General Motors, IBM, Coca-Cola and the International Telephone and Telegraph Corporation (ITT) were among the American multinationals that established large overseas operations by the 1960s.
IBM's World Trade Corporation, created in 1949, managed the company's overseas operations, and by the 1960s a large share of IBM's revenue came from outside the United States.
Coca-Cola's bottling networks spread across Europe, Latin America and Asia from the 1950s, using local franchises to supply the local market.
US multinationals invested heavily in Western Europe after the Treaty of Rome of 1957 created the European Economic Community, which offered a large single market.
The expansion of the multinationals was supported by US foreign policy, which encouraged open trade and investment as part of containment.
Critics in Europe, such as the French writer Jean-Jacques Servan-Schreiber in The American Challenge (1967), argued that US companies were gaining control of key European industries.
General Motors owned Opel in Germany and Vauxhall in Britain, and Ford had large European subsidiaries, so American carmakers built and sold cars across Europe.
ITT under Harold Geneen became a conglomerate in the 1960s, buying firms in many industries and countries, and it later became notorious for its involvement in Chile.
The Fortune 500 list of the largest American industrial companies was first published in 1955, and it showed how far a few big firms dominated the economy.
Trade unions were strong in the core industries of the boom, and their agreements with large firms helped to share its gains.
Union membership reached a peak of roughly a third of non-farm workers in the mid-1950s, concentrated in steel, car manufacturing, mining and transport.
The United Auto Workers and General Motors signed a five-year contract in 1950, often called the Treaty of Detroit, which tied wage rises to productivity and provided pensions and health insurance.
Such agreements gave many manual workers rising real wages and benefits, and they became a model for other unions in the core industries.
The Taft-Hartley Act of 1947 restricted union tactics such as secondary boycotts, and it required union leaders to sign affidavits disavowing communism until 1959.
The merger of the American Federation of Labor and the Congress of Industrial Organizations in 1955 created a single labour federation led by George Meany.
Unions were weakest in the South and among service and farm workers, who were often excluded from the postwar bargain.
Government economists believed that spending and tax policy could sustain growth, and the 1964 tax cut was a major test of that belief.
John Maynard Keynes's ideas, that governments could manage demand through spending and taxation, were accepted by the economic advisers of Kennedy and Johnson.
Walter Heller, chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers under Kennedy, argued for a tax cut to stimulate demand and growth.
The Revenue Act of 1964 cut income tax rates across the board and reduced the top rate from 91 per cent to 70 per cent.
The tax cut was followed by strong economic growth through the mid-1960s, and it is often cited as a successful example of demand management before the costs of the Vietnam War appeared.
Critics such as Milton Friedman, a monetarist, argued that governments could not fine-tune the economy, a view that gained ground in the 1970s when demand management failed to cope with stagflation.
Examiners reward evaluation that weighs the scale of the boom against its dependence on US dominance and on defence spending.
Achievements: a sustained rise in living standards, widespread home ownership and a large middle class were features of the period from 1945 to 1968.
Limits: the boom depended partly on the temporary dominance of the US economy after 1945, which was bound to decline as Europe and Japan recovered.
Critics argue that the boom was financed by defence spending and by the large public investment that followed the war, rather than by the free market.
Some groups did not share fully in the boom, and black Americans and many southern workers faced discrimination in jobs, housing and access to the GI Bill benefits.
John Kenneth Galbraith's The Affluent Society (1958) argued that the boom created private wealth but left public services such as schools and parks neglected.
Michael Harrington's The Other America (1962) showed that tens of millions still lived in poverty despite the boom.
Spending on the Vietnam War and on the Great Society together pushed up federal deficits and inflation, creating the economic problems of the 1970s.
Federal spending on the Vietnam War rose sharply after 1965, and Johnson chose not to raise taxes to pay for it while also expanding domestic programmes.
Inflation rose from the mid-1960s as demand increased faster than supply, and consumer prices began to climb steadily in the late 1960s.
Congress passed a 10 per cent income tax surtax in June 1968 to restrain spending and reduce the deficit, but it did not stop inflation.
The federal budget deficit grew through the late 1960s and 1970s, and deficits became a persistent feature of US government finance.

The Vietnam War cost the federal government well over 100 billion dollars in total, and Johnson's Great Society programmes were added to this spending at a time when the economy was already near full employment.
Because spending rose faster than output, inflation, which had been about 1 per cent in 1964, passed 4 per cent in 1968.

Johnson asked Congress for a tax increase only in 1967, and Congress, led by the Ways and Means chairman Wilbur Mills, made agreement conditional on spending cuts, which delayed the surtax until 1968.

The balance of payments also worsened, as US military spending abroad and foreign investment sent dollars overseas faster than exports earned them, and foreign governments began to exchange dollars for gold.
The postwar monetary and energy order collapsed in the 1970s, leaving the US economy exposed to inflation and to rising oil prices.
On 15 August 1971 Nixon suspended the convertibility of the dollar into gold and imposed a temporary wage and price freeze, ending the Bretton Woods system.
The Smithsonian Agreement of December 1971 tried to fix exchange rates again, but it did not last, and currencies were allowed to float by 1973.
The Arab members of OPEC imposed an oil embargo on the United States in October 1973 after the Yom Kippur War, and oil prices roughly quadrupled.
Oil prices rose again after the Iranian Revolution of 1978 to 1979, causing a second shock that deepened inflation and recession.
Inflation reached above 13 per cent in 1980, and the combination of high inflation and stagnant growth became known as stagflation.
Nixon's measures of August 1971 also included a 10 per cent surcharge on imports, and 1971 was the first year since 1893 in which the United States imported more goods than it exported.
The oil embargo of 1973 to 1974 brought petrol queues at filling stations and rationing by odd and even number plates in some states, and it was lifted in March 1974.
The recession of 1973 to 1975 was the deepest since the 1930s, with unemployment reaching about 9 per cent in 1975.
Ford's Whip Inflation Now campaign of 1974 relied on voluntary measures and was widely mocked, and Carter's first attempts at stimulus did not stop inflation rising again in 1978 and 1979.
American manufacturing in steel and cars lost ground to Japanese and European rivals, and whole industrial regions suffered decline.
The steel industry lost ground to imports from Japan and Europe in the 1970s, and steel mills in the Midwest and northeast reduced production or closed.
The Youngstown Sheet and Tube mill in Ohio closed in September 1977, a closure that cost about 5,000 jobs and became a symbol of the wider loss of industrial jobs in the region.
Japanese car makers, including Toyota and Honda, exported smaller and more fuel-efficient cars to the United States, taking a growing share of the market from Detroit's manufacturers.
The Japanese car makers' gains led the Reagan administration to negotiate voluntary export restraints in 1981, limiting Japanese car imports.
The US trade balance moved into deficit in the 1970s, and the deficit with Japan grew steadily through the 1980s.
The Plaza Accord of September 1985, signed by the leading industrial countries, aimed to lower the dollar's value to restore the competitiveness of American exports.
Japan overtook the United States as the world's largest car producer in 1980, and the Chrysler Corporation was saved from bankruptcy in 1979 by federal loan guarantees of 1.5 billion dollars.

Foreign cars were attractive after the oil shocks because they were small and fuel-efficient, while Detroit built large cars, and imports captured about a quarter of the American car market by the early 1980s.
Rust belt cities such as Detroit, Cleveland and Youngstown lost population and tax revenue as factory jobs vanished, while the Sun Belt in the South and West gained.
The growth of service and high-technology jobs, in Silicon Valley and the defence industries of California, partly offset the losses in manufacturing.
Reagan's economic policy aimed to cut inflation and taxes, reduce regulation and rebuild defence, and it produced a severe recession before recovery.
Paul Volcker became chairman of the Federal Reserve in August 1979 and raised interest rates sharply to bring down inflation, which helped to cause the 1981 to 1982 recession.
The Economic Recovery Tax Act of August 1981 cut income tax rates by about 25 per cent over three years, reducing the top rate from 70 to 50 per cent.
The Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act of 1982 raised some taxes to reduce the deficit, which had grown as the tax cuts took effect.
Deregulation continued the trend begun under Carter, including the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 and the Staggers Rail Act of 1980, which reduced government control of transport prices.
Unemployment rose above 10 per cent in late 1982, the highest level since the Great Depression, before recovery began in 1983.
Economic growth returned strongly in the mid-1980s, and inflation fell sharply, though unemployment and the deficit remained issues for the rest of the decade.
Reaganomics rested on supply-side theory, associated with the economist Arthur Laffer, which said that lower tax rates would encourage work and investment and so raise growth.
The Tax Reform Act of 1986 cut the top income tax rate to 28 per cent while removing many deductions.

The Savings and Loan crisis followed deregulation of the thrifts in the early 1980s: hundreds of savings institutions failed, and the federal bailout of 1989 cost taxpayers tens of billions of dollars.
Federal spending on social programmes was cut in 1981 (food stamps and aid to families) while the Gramm-Rudman Act of 1985 tried to force deficit reduction by setting targets.
The combination of tax cuts and high defence spending produced large deficits, which were financed by borrowing from abroad.
Government spending on defence rose sharply under Reagan, and the federal budget deficit remained large in every year of his presidency.
The national debt nearly tripled during the 1980s, reaching almost 3 trillion dollars, and by the late 1980s the government's interest payments had become a major item in the budget.
In 1985 the United States became a net debtor nation, owing more to foreigners than it owned abroad, for the first time since the early twentieth century.
On 19 October 1987 the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by about 22 per cent in a single day, a crash that prompted the Federal Reserve to add liquidity to the banking system.
The rise in foreign borrowing and the strong dollar of the early 1980s drew in large amounts of foreign capital, which financed the deficits but hurt exporters.
The trade deficit reached about 150 billion dollars in 1987, and the Plaza Accord of 1985 and the Louvre Accord of 1987 were attempts to bring the dollar down in an orderly way.
The oil crises made energy a central economic issue, and government responses ranged from conservation measures to deregulation of prices.
Congress passed a national maximum speed limit of 55 miles per hour in January 1974 as a measure to reduce petrol consumption.
The Department of Energy was created in August 1977 under Carter, bringing together federal energy programmes that had been spread across several agencies.
The National Energy Act of 1978 encouraged conservation and phased in higher natural gas prices, and it was a compromise reached after long debate in Congress.
Domestic oil production remained below its peak, and the United States depended on imports from the Middle East and other producers for a growing share of its oil by the late 1970s.
Nixon's Project Independence (1973) aimed to end dependence on foreign oil by 1980, but American oil imports kept rising.
The rise in living standards that had marked the postwar boom slowed after the early 1970s, and the gains of the 1980s were unevenly shared.
Real average hourly earnings of production workers stagnated from the early 1970s, so that the growth in household incomes depended increasingly on more family members working.
The gap between high-income and low-income households widened during the 1980s, as the tax cuts of 1981 and 1986 favoured higher earners and wages for less-skilled workers fell in real terms.
The decline of manufacturing reduced the bargaining power of many manual workers, and the share of workers in unions, already falling since the 1950s, fell faster in the 1980s.
Women's entry into paid work (see the notes on affluence) raised household incomes, but the extra earnings often only offset the stagnation of male wages.
The poverty rate, which had fallen to about 11 per cent in 1973, rose to around 15 per cent in the early 1980s before easing.
Service jobs in retail and catering paid less than the factory jobs they replaced, and the minimum wage was not raised between 1981 and 1990.
Black unemployment was roughly double white unemployment throughout the period, and urban areas with lost industries suffered most.
Examiners reward judgements that weigh the recovery of the 1980s against the longer-term problems of deficit, trade and manufacturing.
Supporters of Reagan point to the recovery of growth after 1983, the fall of inflation and the expansion of employment in service industries.
Critics point to the rising national debt, the trade deficit and the loss of manufacturing jobs in steel and cars, which made the United States more dependent on foreign capital.
The 1970s were marked by stagflation and falling real incomes for many families, while the wealthy gained most from the tax cuts of the 1980s.
Historians disagree about whether the decline of manufacturing was an inevitable result of global change or a result of policy choices, such as the high dollar and the lack of industrial policy.
The long expansion from late 1982 lasted until 1990 and created about 18 million jobs, a record to set against the weaknesses.

Declinists such as Paul Kennedy, in The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers (1987), argued that the United States was suffering imperial overstretch, while optimists pointed to US leadership in computers, services and finance.
Rising birth rates after the Second World War, and migration to the suburbs and the Sun Belt, reshaped American society and its demand for goods and services.
The baby boom ran from about 1946 to 1964, with the birth rate peaking in 1957 at about 4.3 million births in a single year.
Families were larger and married earlier than in the 1930s, and the average age of marriage for women fell during the 1950s.
Population moved from the northeastern cities to the suburbs, and many urban areas lost white middle-class residents to the outer rings of the metropolitan regions.
