The Sun Belt, the states of the South and the Southwest from Florida to California, grew rapidly after 1945, helped by air conditioning and federal defence spending.
Between 1950 and 1970 the cities of the Northeast and Midwest lost population while the suburbs of the West and South expanded quickly.
Dr Benjamin Spock's The Common Sense Book of Baby and Child Care (1946) sold tens of millions of copies and shaped how the boom generation was raised.
The 1950 and 1960 censuses showed that the suburbs were the fastest-growing part of the country, and by 1960 more Americans lived in suburbs than in the central cities or on farms.

Black Americans continued the Great Migration from the South to northern and western cities such as Chicago, Detroit and Los Angeles, while white families moved out to the suburbs, a pattern called white flight.
California overtook New York as the most populous state in the early 1960s, a measure of the Sun Belt's growth.
The mass production of houses on new suburban estates, financed by federal mortgage guarantees, became the physical image of the American Dream in the 1950s.
William Levitt's firm built Levittown on Long Island, New York, beginning in 1947, with about 17,000 standardised houses on mass-produced lines.
Federal Housing Administration and Veterans Administration mortgage guarantees allowed buyers to borrow with little or no deposit on long repayment terms.
Most of the new suburban houses were sold to white families; restrictive covenants and lending practices kept black families out of many new estates.
The suburbs were built around the car, with new highways and shopping centres replacing the public transport and downtown retail of the older cities.
Television sets were in most American homes by 1960, and advertising on television promoted the goods that suburban households were expected to buy.

Levitt built houses on a production line, with teams specialising in each stage, and the first Levittown houses were small Cape Cod style homes sold for under 8,000 dollars with a washing machine and a television set included in some models.
The Levittown leases and covenants excluded black buyers, and an ordinary suburban estate was in effect closed to black families.
Nixon and Khrushchev's Kitchen Debate in Moscow in July 1959 was staged in a model American house, where Nixon argued that suburban abundance showed the superiority of capitalism.
Mass production, consumer credit and advertising made the purchase of goods a central part of American life and identity.
Diners Club, launched in 1950, was among the first charge cards in the United States, and BankAmericard, launched in 1958, became the forerunner of Visa.
Credit allowed families to buy cars, appliances and furniture on instalments, so that spending was no longer restricted to current income.
Advertising agencies used television, magazines and market research to create demand for new products, and brand loyalty became a central marketing aim.
The economist John Kenneth Galbraith described the affluent society in his 1958 book of that title, arguing that consumers were persuaded to want goods they did not need.
Shopping malls, supermarkets and department stores spread through the suburbs, and consumer goods such as dishwashers, freezers and automatic washing machines became common in middle-class homes.
Television, which was in about 9 per cent of homes in 1950 and about 87 per cent in 1960, brought advertising into the living room, and sponsors paid for programmes such as I Love Lucy.
Vance Packard's The Hidden Persuaders (1957) accused advertisers of using psychological methods to manipulate buyers.
Disneyland opened in California in July 1955, and the leisure industry of theme parks, motels and package holidays grew with the car.
Shorter working hours, paid vacations and rising incomes gave Americans more leisure, but work in large organisations increasingly shaped their identity.
The standard working week remained about forty hours, while paid holidays became more widespread in the 1950s and 1960s.
Leisure centred on television, the car, the family holiday, and home ownership, with the suburban backyard a key place of recreation.
The number of white-collar jobs in management, sales and services grew faster than manufacturing jobs from the 1950s onwards.
Corporate culture, with its emphasis on teamwork and loyalty, shaped the working lives of many middle-class men, as William H. Whyte's The Organization Man described.
Many men's working lives centred on the family breadwinner role, which the suburban culture of the 1950s celebrated.
The 1950s promoted domesticity for women, but rising employment and feminist protest challenged that ideal from the early 1960s.
Many women left war-time industrial jobs after 1945 and were encouraged to return to the home, a message promoted in magazines, films and advice literature.
From the 1950s women's share of the paid workforce rose steadily, as married women with children increasingly took jobs outside the home.
The contraceptive pill, Enovid, was approved by the Food and Drug Administration in May 1960, giving women greater control over the timing of births.
The Equal Pay Act of 10 June 1963 required equal pay for equal work between men and women in the same establishment.
Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination in employment on grounds of sex as well as race, colour, religion and national origin.
The Equal Credit Opportunity Act of 1974 made it illegal to refuse credit to a woman on the basis of her sex or marital status.
Divorce rates rose in the 1960s and 1970s, and the number of single-parent families grew, changing the ideal of the traditional nuclear family.
Women were about 30 per cent of the labour force in 1950 and about 38 per cent by 1970, but they were concentrated in clerical, teaching, nursing and sales jobs at lower pay.

The Supreme Court decision in Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) struck down a ban on contraception for married couples, and Roe v. Wade (22 January 1973) ruled that the Constitution protected a woman's decision to have an abortion, in the early stages of pregnancy.
Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 banned sex discrimination in federally funded education, opening college admissions and sport to women.
Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign, begun in 1972, mobilised conservative women who argued that the amendment threatened the family, and it helped to block ratification.
Friedan was a participant in the feminist movement and a critic of the domestic ideal.
Betty Friedan was born in 1921 in Peoria, Illinois, and studied psychology at Smith College before becoming a magazine writer and suburban housewife.
Her survey of former Smith College classmates about their lives in the 1950s formed the basis of her book The Feminine Mystique, published in 1963.

The Feminine Mystique argued that American women were trapped by a domestic ideal (the feminine mystique) that denied them fulfilment, and she described their condition as the problem that has no name.
The book sold very widely and is widely credited with helping to start the second wave of the American feminist movement.
In June 1966 Friedan was a founder of the National Organization for Women (NOW) and became its first president, aiming to secure equal rights for women in employment and law.
NOW pressed for the Equal Rights Amendment, which passed Congress in March 1972 but fell short of ratification by the 1982 deadline, with 35 of the 38 states needed.
Contemporaries were divided: supporters admired her as a campaigner for women's rights, while critics attacked her as too middle-class and too concerned with professional women.
Historians have generally judged her a central figure in the feminist movement, although later writers have criticised The Feminine Mystique for focusing on white, middle-class women.
Friedan organised the Women's Strike for Equality on 26 August 1970, the fiftieth anniversary of the Nineteenth Amendment, and helped to found the National Women's Political Caucus in 1971.
Younger radical feminists criticised her as too moderate, and she was also criticised for her early hostility towards lesbians in the movement.

Monroe's screen image represented ideals of female beauty and desirability in the 1950s, a role that critics and later historians have examined. Her career, death and legacy are covered in the notes on culture and the collapse of consensus.

Born Norma Jeane Mortenson in Los Angeles in 1926, she became Marilyn Monroe after a modelling career and a first contract with Twentieth Century-Fox in 1946, which was dropped and renewed in 1951 as her roles grew.
Her films, including Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953) and The Seven Year Itch (1955), presented an ideal of glamorous, sexually attractive womanhood that was widely copied in advertising.
Monroe's image was closely tied to the consumer culture of the 1950s, appearing in advertisements and magazines that sold products by associating them with her appeal.
Contemporaries admired her beauty and screen presence, but she was also criticised by the press for the way Hollywood marketed her as a sex symbol rather than as a serious actress.
Later feminist critics read her image as a product of a male-dominated film industry, which limited women's roles to decorative or passive parts.
Historians now treat her as a symbol of both the glamour and the constraints placed on women in the 1950s and early 1960s.

Monroe tried to take control of her career by founding Marilyn Monroe Productions in 1955 and by studying at the Actors Studio in New York, and she won acclaim for her comic role in Some Like It Hot (1959).
Her public image of a childlike, available blonde fitted the 1950s ideal of femininity that Friedan attacked, but Monroe herself fought Hollywood's control and the typecasting it imposed.
Examiners reward judgements that weigh the material gains of the period against the exclusion of many groups from the American Dream.
Achievements: home ownership, rising incomes and the spread of consumer goods gave many white middle-class families a standard of living that earlier generations had not known.
Limits: federal mortgage policy and private lending excluded most black families from the suburbs, so the Dream was unevenly shared by race.
Women's employment grew strongly, but women were often confined to lower-paid jobs and had limited access to credit until the 1974 Act.
Friedan's critique showed that many women felt the ideal of domestic contentment failed them, which later critics argued was a sign of the Dream's narrowness rather than its success.
Segregation was enforced by state law across the South and by custom in much of the North, and the courts were the first route to change.

Jim Crow in the South meant separate schools, buses, waiting rooms and water fountains, and black voters were kept off the rolls by poll taxes, literacy tests and intimidation by the Ku Klux Klan and local officials; in the North discrimination in housing and jobs was enforced by custom and by restrictive covenants.
Plessy v Ferguson (1896) upheld segregation under the doctrine of separate but equal facilities, which in practice meant inferior schools, transport and public services for black Americans.
The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) led the legal campaign against segregation through cases on education and voting in the 1930s and 1940s.
Brown v Board of Education, decided unanimously on 17 May 1954, ruled that segregated public schools were unconstitutional, and Brown II in 1955 ordered desegregation with all deliberate speed.
Southern states responded with the Southern Manifesto of March 1956, signed by most southern members of Congress, which pledged to resist desegregation by all lawful means.

In September 1957 nine black students entered Little Rock Central High School under the protection of federal troops, sent by Eisenhower after Governor Orval Faubus used the National Guard to block them.
The brutal murder of the fourteen-year-old Emmett Till in Mississippi in August 1955, and the acquittal of the white men accused of it, shocked black Americans and made him a symbol of the cause.

The Civil Rights Act of 1957, the first federal civil rights law since Reconstruction, set up a Civil Rights Commission and a Civil Rights Division in the Justice Department, but it did little for voting in practice.
From 1960 students and activists turned to non-violent direct action, which exposed segregation to national and international audiences.
Four students from North Carolina A and T College sat in at a Woolworth lunch counter in Greensboro on 1 February 1960, and sit-ins spread to more than fifty cities within months.
The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) was formed in April 1960 to coordinate student protest across the South.
The Freedom Rides of May 1961, organised by the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE), tested the desegregation of interstate bus terminals, and a bus was burned by a mob near Anniston, Alabama.

The Birmingham campaign of April and May 1963 was led by King and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, and the police commissioner Eugene Bull Connor used dogs and fire hoses against demonstrators.
Photographs and television footage of the Birmingham violence shocked national opinion and helped to build support for federal civil rights legislation.
The March on Washington on 28 August 1963 drew about a quarter of a million people, and King's I Have a Dream speech became the defining statement of the movement.
The Albany Movement in Georgia in 1961 to 1962, led by King, failed because the police chief avoided violence and arrested protesters quietly, a lesson that shaped the choice of Birmingham.
In Birmingham in May 1963 hundreds of schoolchildren marched and were arrested, the so-called Children's Crusade, and the city agreed to desegregate its shops in May after bombings and riots.
In June 1963 Governor George Wallace stood in the door at the University of Alabama to block black students, and the NAACP leader Medgar Evers was murdered in Mississippi.

President Kennedy called civil rights a moral issue in a television address on 11 June 1963 and sent a civil rights bill to Congress, and he supported the March on Washington despite fears of violence.
Johnson's administration secured the two main civil rights laws of the period, which used federal power to end legal segregation and to protect voting rights.
The Civil Rights Act of 2 July 1964 banned racial segregation in public accommodations such as hotels, restaurants and theatres, and it created federal power to end segregation in schools.
The Voting Rights Act of 6 August 1965 banned literacy tests and sent federal examiners to register black voters in areas with a record of discrimination.
The march from Selma to Montgomery in March 1965 followed the attack on marchers at the Edmund Pettus Bridge on 7 March 1965, known as Bloody Sunday.
Within a few years of the Voting Rights Act, the number of black registered voters in the South rose sharply, and black elected officials began to take office in the region.
The Civil Rights Act passed after a Senate filibuster by southern senators that lasted 54 days, ended in June 1964 by a vote for cloture.
The Act also created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and it allowed federal funds to be cut from segregated programmes.
Freedom Summer in Mississippi in 1964, when volunteers registered voters, saw the murder of three civil rights workers, Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner, in June 1964.

King led the Selma campaign in early 1965 to dramatise the denial of the vote in Alabama, and Johnson called for the Voting Rights Act in a speech to Congress on 15 March 1965 in which he used the movement's words We shall overcome.
King was a participant and leader of the civil rights movement. His role in the Montgomery bus boycott is covered in the notes on that case study.
Martin Luther King Jr. was born in Atlanta, Georgia, on 15 January 1929, the son of a Baptist minister, and he was ordained as a Baptist minister himself.
He earned a doctorate in theology at Boston University in 1955, and his study of Gandhi shaped his commitment to non-violent direct action.
He was a founder and first president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, formed in 1957 to coordinate church-based civil rights protest across the South.
His Letter from Birmingham Jail of April 1963 argued for civil disobedience against unjust laws, and it was written in response to white Alabama clergy who had called the protests untimely.
He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964, at the age of 35, the youngest recipient up to that time.
King campaigned in Chicago in 1966 against housing discrimination, a campaign that met fierce resistance from white residents and produced little formal change.
In 1967 he linked the civil rights struggle with poverty and the Vietnam War, and his Poor People's Campaign was planned to bring poor Americans of all races to Washington in 1968.
He was assassinated at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, Tennessee, on 4 April 1968; James Earl Ray later pleaded guilty to the murder.
Contemporaries were divided: many whites in the South opposed him, and militant activists such as Malcolm X and later Black Power leaders criticised him as too moderate.
The FBI conducted surveillance of King and attempted to discredit him through its COINTELPRO programme, a fact revealed after the 1970s.
Historians now regard him as the most important leader of the civil rights movement, and Congress established a national holiday in his honour, first observed in 1986.

King's philosophy of non-violence combined Christian teaching on love with Gandhi's methods, and he argued that the movement should win over white opinion by accepting suffering rather than returning violence.
His main successes were Montgomery (1955 to 1956), Birmingham (1963) and Selma (1965); the Albany Movement (1961 to 1962) and Chicago (1966) were his main setbacks.

In his last years he turned to economic issues and to criticism of the Vietnam War, which lost him the support of Johnson and of some civil rights leaders, and in Memphis he was supporting a strike by black sanitation workers when he was killed.
From 1965 frustration with slow progress produced a more radical black politics and a wave of violence in the cities.
Malcolm X, who had left the Nation of Islam in 1964, was assassinated in the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem on 21 February 1965.
The slogan Black Power, popularised by Stokely Carmichael in 1966, expressed a demand for black self-determination and community control.
The Watts riot in Los Angeles in August 1965 left about 34 people dead, and the Detroit riot of July 1967 caused more than forty deaths.
The Kerner Commission, appointed after the 1967 riots, reported in February 1968 that the United States was moving towards two societies, one black and one white, separate and unequal.
The Fair Housing Act of April 1968, passed days after King's death, banned discrimination in the sale and rental of most housing.

Malcolm X, a minister of the Nation of Islam, criticised integration and non-violence in the early 1960s, but after leaving the Nation and a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1964 he adopted a more inclusive position, and his Autobiography (1965) made him a hero to many young black people.

The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense was founded in Oakland, California, in October 1966 by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale, and it combined armed self-defence with community programmes such as free breakfasts for children.

The Watts riot began on 11 August 1965 after a police traffic stop, with the National Guard called in and large areas burned; Detroit in July 1967 required federal paratroops, and Newark that month had 26 deaths.
The Kerner Report blamed white racism, poverty and police behaviour for the riots, and Johnson did not act on its recommendations for more spending.
Poverty in the inner cities became a national concern in the 1960s, and Johnson's War on Poverty was the federal response.
Michael Harrington's The Other America (1962) estimated that tens of millions of Americans lived in poverty and were largely invisible to the affluent majority.
Johnson declared an unconditional War on Poverty in January 1964, and the Economic Opportunity Act of that year created the Job Corps and community action programmes.
The War on Poverty's programmes were underfunded relative to the war in Vietnam, and many were cut back as the 1960s ended.
Poverty rates among black Americans remained far higher than among whites through the 1960s and 1970s, reflecting unemployment, poor schooling and housing segregation.

The official poverty rate fell from about 22 per cent in 1959 to about 12 per cent in 1969, partly because of economic growth and partly because of Social Security and programmes such as food stamps and Medicaid.
Daniel Patrick Moynihan's report The Negro Family (1965) blamed family breakdown for black poverty and aroused controversy.

The Office of Economic Opportunity ran Head Start and the Community Action Programs, which required the maximum feasible participation of the poor and brought conflict with city governments, so mayors lobbied against them.
Rising crime and the drug trade were given political attention from the 1970s, and their effects fell heavily on poor black communities.
Richard Nixon declared drug abuse public enemy number one in 1971 and launched a war on drugs, funding enforcement and treatment.
Crack cocaine spread through poor urban neighbourhoods in the mid-1980s, producing a wave of violence and drug-related crime.
The Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986 set mandatory minimum sentences that treated one gram of crack the same as one hundred grams of powder cocaine, a disparity that fell heavily on black defendants.
Ronald Reagan's Just Say No campaign, launched in 1982 with his wife Nancy, promoted drug prevention and was linked to tougher enforcement policies.
Harold Washington became the first black mayor of Chicago in 1983, and Jesse Jackson ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1984 and 1988, reflecting new black political power.
By 1989 black Americans had gained political office and legal protection, but segregation in housing and schools, and high rates of poverty and imprisonment, remained major problems.
Crime and urban disorder were used by Nixon in 1968 and by later Republican candidates as a political issue under the slogan of law and order.
Heroin addiction was concentrated in inner cities such as Harlem in the 1960s, and heroin use among US soldiers in Vietnam drew public attention in 1971.
The prison population rose steeply in the 1980s, and black men were imprisoned at several times the rate of white men.

Affirmative action in college admissions was limited, but not ended, by the Supreme Court decision in Regents of the University of California v. Bakke in 1978, and the busing of children to achieve school integration provoked riots in Boston in 1974.
Examiners reward judgements that weigh the legal achievements of the movement against the persistence of inequality.
Achievements: the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act and the Fair Housing Act ended legal segregation and gave black Americans the vote on equal terms in practice.
Limits: economic inequality, residential segregation and the failure of schools in poor areas meant that legal equality did not bring equal opportunity.
Contemporary white opinion was divided, with many northern whites supporting civil rights laws but resisting busing and open housing in their own neighbourhoods.
Later historians differ: some see the period as a great success that was later undermined, while others argue that its gains were narrower and less lasting than they appeared.
Montgomery, Alabama, was the first capital of the Confederacy, and segregation on its buses was enforced by city ordinance and Alabama state law. Black passengers made up most of the riders.

Montgomery's city buses reserved the front rows for white passengers and the rear for black passengers, and the driver could move the dividing line backwards to make more room for white riders, forcing black passengers to stand or give up their seats.

Black passengers had to pay at the front and then get off and re-enter by the rear door, and drivers, who carried guns and had police powers, often insulted black riders or drove off before they re-boarded.

Black riders made up the large majority of bus passengers, so the segregation rules affected most of the city's black working population, many of them maids and labourers who rode to work in white homes and businesses.

The Supreme Court's Brown v Board of Education decision of May 1954 raised black expectations, and the Women's Political Council (WPC), led from 1950 by Jo Ann Robinson, wrote to Mayor W. A. Gayle in May 1954 warning that a boycott of the buses was possible.

Earlier challenges had failed: in March 1955 Claudette Colvin, a fifteen-year-old schoolgirl, was arrested for refusing to give up her seat, and in October 1955 Mary Louise Smith, aged eighteen, was arrested on the same charge.

Local leaders including E. D. Nixon decided not to make Colvin the test case, because of her youth and because she became pregnant, and they judged that a respectable adult would command more support.
Bus boycotts had been tried before, including in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, in 1953, which Montgomery's organisers knew of.
Alabama's white Citizens' Councils, which had grown across the South after Brown, were committed to resisting any change.
The arrest of Rosa Parks on 1 December 1955 gave the organisers the case they wanted, and a one-day protest turned into a boycott lasting 381 days.

Rosa Parks, a seamstress in a department store and the secretary of the Montgomery branch of the NAACP, was arrested on 1 December 1955 for refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger on a Cleveland Avenue bus when the driver, James Blake, demanded it.

Parks was no accidental protester: she had investigated cases of sexual violence against black women for the NAACP, and in the summer of 1955 she had attended a workshop on racial equality at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee.

E. D. Nixon, president of the Montgomery NAACP and a Pullman porters' union leader, bailed Parks out with the help of the white couple Clifford and Virginia Durr, and he persuaded her to let her case be used to challenge the law.
Parks was tried on 5 December 1955, found guilty of violating the segregation law and fined 10 dollars plus costs, and her lawyer Fred Gray appealed.
That night Jo Ann Robinson and the WPC, with students at Alabama State College, ran off tens of thousands of leaflets calling for a one-day boycott of the buses on Monday, 5 December 1955.
Black ministers announced the boycott from their pulpits on Sunday 4 December, and the leaflets were handed out through churches and schools.
The boycott was almost completely observed on 5 December; and that evening a mass meeting of about 5,000 people at the Holt Street Baptist Church voted to continue the boycott.

The demands were modest: courteous treatment by drivers, seating on a first-come, first-served basis with black passengers filling seats from the back and white from the front, and the hiring of black drivers on mainly black routes; they did not at first demand an end to segregation.
The city refused to negotiate on these terms, and the bus company and city commissioners hardened their stance, so the demand for desegregation grew as the boycott continued.
The Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA) co-ordinated the boycott, and its car pool and church networks kept about 40,000 black bus riders off the buses for more than a year.

The MIA was formed on the afternoon of 5 December 1955, and the Reverend Martin Luther King Jr., a 26-year-old pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church who had arrived in Montgomery in 1954 and had no record of conflict with the white authorities, was elected its president.
King's address at the Holt Street meeting combined a demand for justice with a commitment to non-violence and Christian love, and it launched him as the movement's voice.

Other leaders included Ralph Abernathy, E. D. Nixon, Jo Ann Robinson and the Reverend Uriah Fields, and the movement drew on the black churches, whose ministers were free from white employers' control.

A car pool, run by volunteers with several hundred cars and by black taxi drivers who charged the bus fare of ten cents, took passengers to work and school, with dispatch points at churches and a pick-up system organised by the MIA.
Churches raised money to buy station wagons for the car pool, and funds and support came from northern supporters, unions and churches across the country.
Thousands of people walked, and many black domestic workers continued to walk long distances to their jobs in white households, a mark of the protest's determination.
The boycott hit the bus company's income hard, and city centre shops lost custom from black shoppers, so the economic pressure on white Montgomery was real.

Bayard Rustin, a pacifist and experienced organiser, and Glenn Smiley of the Fellowship of Reconciliation came to Montgomery in February 1956 to advise King on non-violence, and the movement was told to stay disciplined in the face of attacks.
King later said that in January 1956, after threatening phone calls, he had prayed at his kitchen table and felt a sense of divine reassurance, which strengthened his resolve.
Montgomery's white authorities responded with police harassment, legal action and violence, while the black community also began a federal court challenge that settled the matter.

The city's leaders first tried to divide the boycotters: the mayor and city commissioners announced falsely that the boycott had been settled, and the police arrested drivers in the car pool for minor offences and told taxi drivers to charge a minimum fare.
King was arrested on 26 January 1956 for driving 30 miles an hour in a 25 mile zone, a minor charge that showed the police were watching the leaders.

On 30 January 1956 a bomb was thrown on the porch of King's house while his wife Coretta and baby daughter were inside, and nobody was hurt; an angry crowd gathered, but King urged them to go home and not to retaliate.

In February 1956 a grand jury indicted 89 leaders of the boycott, including about twenty-four ministers, under a 1921 Alabama law against boycotts; King was tried in March 1956 and convicted, fined 500 dollars, and the sentence was suspended pending appeal.
The indictments produced national press attention, and the images of ministers lining up to be booked turned the arrests into a symbol of dignity.

On 1 February 1956 the lawyer Fred Gray filed Browder v Gayle in the federal court on behalf of four black women, Aurelia Browder, Susie McDonald, Claudette Colvin and Mary Louise Smith, challenging the constitutionality of segregation on the buses.
Rosa Parks was not a party to Browder, because her case was still in the Alabama courts and it could have taken years.
On 5 June 1956 a three-judge federal court ruled by two votes to one that segregation on buses violated the Fourteenth Amendment, and the city and state appealed to the Supreme Court.

On 13 November 1956 the Supreme Court affirmed the decision, in a brief unsigned order that relied on Brown v Board of Education and later decisions, and denied the city's request for a rehearing on 17 December.

On the same day Montgomery's city lawyers won a state court injunction against the car pools as a public nuisance operating without a licence, and King was in court for that hearing when reporters brought news that the Supreme Court had upheld the ruling.
The formal Supreme Court order was served on Montgomery on 20 December 1956, and the MIA meeting voted to end the boycott on that day.
The boycott ended bus segregation in Montgomery, but violence and continuing segregation elsewhere limited what it changed.
The buses were desegregated on 21 December 1956, the 382nd day, when King and Ralph Abernathy rode a bus with white passengers, in front of a press corps.
The MIA issued rules telling its members to be courteous and not to retaliate, and to sit anywhere without boasting.

In the weeks that followed, snipers fired on buses, a black teenager was shot in the legs, and on 10 January 1957 bombs damaged four black churches and the homes of Robert Graetz and Ralph Abernathy; the city suspended bus service for a time.
Several white men were arrested for the bombings, but they received little punishment.
In January 1957 King and other ministers met in Atlanta to form a regional organisation, which became the Southern Christian Leadership Conference in August 1957, with King as president.
Segregation remained in Montgomery's schools, housing, restaurants and parks, and black voters were still largely excluded.
Parks lost her job and received threats, and she moved to Detroit with her family in 1957.
The boycott provoked a campaign of intimidation across Alabama and showed how far white authorities would go to protect segregation.
The home of Robert Graetz, a white Lutheran minister serving a black congregation who supported the boycott, was bombed in August 1956.

Autherine Lucy became the first black student admitted to the University of Alabama, in February 1956; she was suspended after white rioting, and was later expelled, showing that the state's resistance extended beyond the buses.
The state authorities banned the NAACP in Alabama in June 1956, which was designed to cut off the boycott's legal support; the ban was overturned by the Supreme Court in 1958.
The White Citizens' Councils and the Ku Klux Klan threatened leaders, and employers dismissed black workers who took part, while the city police harassed car pool drivers.
The Southern Manifesto of March 1956 showed that most Southern members of Congress backed resistance to desegregation.
The violence did not break the boycott, and the national press coverage of the bombings and arrests brought sympathy from northern opinion and brought the matter to the federal courts.
King was the leader of the boycott rather than its originator, and Montgomery made him a national figure. His overall career is covered in the notes on racial conflict and the civil rights movement.

King, born in 1929, the son of a prominent Atlanta pastor and holder of a Boston University doctorate, had been pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church for only a year when the boycott began, and he was chosen partly because he was new and had no enemies.

He was a participant who shaped the boycott's tone: he insisted on non-violence and on love for the opponent, based on Christian teaching and on Gandhi's methods, which he had studied as a student and which Rustin and Smiley helped him to apply during the boycott.
His arrest in January and February 1956, the bombing of his home on 30 January and his conviction in March made him a target and a symbol, and national magazines made him famous.
His memoir Stride Toward Freedom (1958) described the boycott and his thinking about non-violence.

Contemporaries in Montgomery's white leadership called him an outside agitator and tried to portray the boycott as run by communists; black contemporaries saw him as an inspired speaker, though some older leaders such as E. D. Nixon resented his rise.

Historians such as Taylor Branch (Parting the Waters, 1988) emphasise King's growth into a national leader through Montgomery, while Aldon Morris and others argue that the movement depended on local leaders and the church networks which existed before him, so that King was a product as well as a maker of the movement.
Historians see the Montgomery bus boycott as a model for the mass civil rights movement of the 1960s, though they disagree on how far it started the movement.
Non-violence was adopted as the movement's guiding principle, and the boycott brought together the Christian ideas of love and forgiveness with Gandhi's methods of mass non-violent resistance.
The boycott showed that black communities could organise sustained economic pressure on segregation, a method later used in Tallahassee (1956) and in sit-in campaigns.
It made the church the base of protest, and the MIA became a model for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference.
The role of women, including Rosa Parks, Jo Ann Robinson and the Women's Political Council, was crucial, though men such as King and Nixon were more often given public recognition.

Historians of Parks, such as Jeanne Theoharis in The Rebellious Life of Mrs Rosa Parks (2013), argue that the popular image of a tired seamstress who acted on impulse hides her long career as an activist.

The legal outcome, Browder v Gayle, rested on Brown, so some historians argue that the courts rather than the boycott ended bus segregation, while others argue that the boycott kept the case alive and made the ruling effective.
The boycott also gave the movement international publicity, which mattered in the Cold War, when the Soviet Union used American racism as propaganda.
Achievement: Montgomery ended bus segregation in the city and defeated white resistance after 381 days, showing that organised, disciplined protest could defeat segregation.
Achievement: it produced a national leader, King, a lasting organisation, the SCLC, and a method of non-violent mass action that was used in Birmingham and Selma.
Limit: the legal victory applied only to buses, and it did not change schools, housing, jobs or the voting restrictions across Alabama.
Limit: violence followed the victory, and white resistance across the South hardened after Brown and Montgomery, so change came slowly until the laws of 1964 and 1965.
Contemporary white opinion in Montgomery condemned the boycott and used intimidation, while black residents who had endured segregation for decades saw the victory as a long overdue success.

Later historians stress the importance of the organisation the boycott created, the leaders it produced and the example it set, and they debate whether it was the start of the civil rights movement or one phase of a longer struggle that began in the 1930s and 1940s.
The studio system dominated American film in the postwar years, and its films celebrated family, prosperity and patriotic values.

The studio system, in which major companies such as MGM, Warner Brothers and Paramount controlled production, distribution and cinema chains, was weakened by the Supreme Court's Paramount decree of 1948, which required the studios to sell their cinemas.

Frank Capra's It's a Wonderful Life (1946) portrayed small-town community and decency against greed; it did poorly on release but became a Christmas television favourite from the 1970s and a lasting image of the American Dream.
Hollywood films of the 1950s increasingly addressed family life, race and juvenile delinquency, while the Production Code continued to restrict the treatment of sex and crime.
Television drew audiences away from cinemas from the early 1950s, and the studios began to sell films to television and to produce television series.

The Best Years of Our Lives (1946) won seven Academy Awards and dealt with the return of veterans, and Hollywood also produced social-problem films on anti-Semitism and race, such as Gentleman's Agreement (1947) and Pinky (1949).

Cinema attendance, which had peaked at about 90 million a week in 1946, roughly halved by 1960 as television spread, so the studios turned to wide-screen CinemaScope (1953), colour and epics such as The Ten Commandments (1956) and Ben-Hur (1959).

Musicals such as Singin' in the Rain (1952) and family comedies promoted cheerful abundance, and the American Dream of home, family and consumption was the staple of studio films and of the new television comedies.

Westerns and science fiction carried Cold War messages: High Noon (1952) was read as an allegory of the blacklist, while Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956) was read as a fable of conformity or of communist infiltration.
The Production Code, enforced by the Hays Office, was weakened in the 1950s by films such as The Moon Is Blue (1953) and was replaced by a ratings system in November 1968.
The House Un-American Activities Committee's investigations of the film industry from 1947 created a blacklist that ended many careers.

HUAC opened hearings on communist influence in Hollywood in October 1947, and the Hollywood Ten, screenwriters and directors who refused to answer questions, were sentenced to prison for contempt of Congress in 1948.
The studios' Waldorf Statement of November 1947 committed them to dismiss suspected communists, and a blacklist operated for years afterwards.
Writers who could not work under their own names, such as Dalton Trumbo, continued to write scripts under pseudonyms or the names of friends.
Kirk Douglas and Otto Preminger broke the blacklist in 1960 by openly crediting Trumbo on Spartacus and Exodus, a sign that the industry's rules were changing.

Friendly witnesses before HUAC included the actor Ronald Reagan, then president of the Screen Actors Guild, and Walt Disney, and in 1952 the director Elia Kazan named former communist colleagues, a decision he defended in On the Waterfront (1954).
Hundreds of writers, actors and directors were blacklisted in the 1950s, and Charlie Chaplin left the United States in 1952 after his re-entry permit was withdrawn.
Anti-communist films such as I Was a Communist for the FBI (1951) were made by the studios to show their loyalty.
Monroe was a major film star and a public figure. Her role as an image of women is covered in the notes on the family and women.
Her screen career began with small roles in the late 1940s, and she gained wider fame in Asphalt Jungle (1950) and All About Eve (1950) before becoming a star in 1953.
Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953), How to Marry a Millionaire (1953) and The Seven Year Itch (1955) made her one of the most popular box office stars of the decade.
She studied at the Actors Studio in New York in the mid-1950s, and her marriage to the playwright Arthur Miller in 1956 brought her an association with serious drama.
Some Like It Hot (1959), directed by Billy Wilder, won critical praise and remains her most admired comedy.
Her difficulties with studio executives, including disputes over her contract and her choice of roles, were widely reported in the press.
She sang Happy Birthday, Mr President to John F. Kennedy at a Democratic Party fundraiser in Madison Square Garden on 19 May 1962.

She died at her home in Los Angeles on the night of 4 August 1962, found early the next morning, from an overdose of barbiturates; the death was ruled a probable suicide, and it remains a subject of debate.

Contemporaries judged her as a glamorous star whose personal life was a matter of public fascination, while later critics argued that her career showed how the studio system exploited women performers.
Her last completed film was The Misfits (1961), written by Miller, and in June 1962 Twentieth Century-Fox dismissed her from Something's Got to Give after repeated absences.
Her death at the age of 36 produced years of conspiracy theories, including claims of a link to the Kennedys, which are not supported by the official investigation.
Teenagers became a distinct consumer group in the 1950s, and new music and writing challenged the conformity of the era.
Rock and roll drew on black rhythm and blues and reached white teenagers through radio and records, with Elvis Presley's Heartbreak Hotel (1956) one of the first to become a national hit.
The actor James Dean, who starred in Rebel Without a Cause (1955) and died in a car crash in September 1955, became a symbol of teenage alienation, as did Marlon Brando in The Wild One (1953).
The Beat writers, including Jack Kerouac, whose On the Road appeared in 1957, and Allen Ginsberg, whose poem Howl was published in 1956, rejected the conventions of suburban life.

Bill Haley's Rock Around the Clock (1955) and Elvis's television appearances on the Ed Sullivan Show in 1956 and 1957 made rock and roll a national craze, and Dick Clark's American Bandstand, on the national network from 1957, made youth culture into a commercial market; older critics condemned the music as a threat to morals.
Mailer was a novelist, essayist and public figure whose writing and persona made him a central voice of the 1960s debate.
Norman Mailer's first novel, The Naked and the Dead (1948), drew on his service in the Pacific during the Second World War and became a best seller.
He was a co-founder of the Village Voice newspaper in New York in 1955, which was part of the counter-cultural press of the period.
His essay The White Negro (1957) argued that the hipster, who borrowed from black culture and lived for the moment, offered a model of rebellion against the conformity of postwar America.
The Armies of the Night (1968) described the anti-war march on the Pentagon in October 1967, and it won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award.

Mailer was arrested at the Pentagon march in October 1967, and he wrote about himself in the third person in the book; his public persona, including a campaign for mayor of New York in 1969, made him a celebrity as well as a literary authority.

Contemporaries were divided: admirers saw him as a serious critic of American culture, while critics attacked his self-promotion, his machismo, and his stabbing of his second wife Adele in 1960, for which he received a suspended sentence.
Historians today generally treat his non-fiction, especially The Armies of the Night, as an important account of the 1960s protest movement.
The White Negro was widely attacked for romanticising black life, and James Baldwin criticised Mailer for it.
In his later career Mailer wrote Miami and the Siege of Chicago (1968), The Fight (1975) about Ali and Foreman in Zaire, and The Executioner's Song (1979), which won the Pulitzer Prize for fiction.
Ali's career linked sport, religion and the anti-war movement, making him a symbol of black pride and political resistance.
Born Cassius Clay in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1942, he won the Olympic gold medal in the light-heavyweight division at Rome in 1960.
He won the world heavyweight title by beating Sonny Liston in Miami Beach on 25 February 1964, and announced his membership of the Nation of Islam and his new name, Muhammad Ali, in March 1964.

He had told reporters in 1966 that he had no quarrel with the Viet Cong; on 28 April 1967 he refused induction into the army in Houston as a Muslim minister and conscientious objector, and boxing authorities stripped him of his title and licence. In June 1967 he was convicted of draft evasion, sentenced to five years in prison and fined 10,000 dollars, but he stayed free on appeal.

The Supreme Court overturned the conviction on 28 June 1971 by 8 votes to 0 (Justice Marshall took no part), ruling that the government had not given a valid basis for rejecting his conscientious objector claim.

He was barred from boxing for over three years, returned to the ring in October 1970 and lost to Joe Frazier in the Fight of the Century at Madison Square Garden on 8 March 1971, before winning back the title by beating George Foreman in Kinshasa in October 1974.
Contemporaries were sharply divided, with many white Americans and sports writers condemning him, while many young black Americans and anti-war activists saw him as a principled leader.
His famous saying float like a butterfly, sting like a bee summed up his style, and he became one of the best known sportsmen in the world by the 1970s.

Ali beat Foreman in Kinshasa, Zaire, on 30 October 1974 in the Rumble in the Jungle, and he beat Joe Frazier in the Thrilla in Manila in 1975, before retiring in 1981 and living with Parkinson's disease.
He was Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. and rejected his birth name as a slave name; Elijah Muhammad, leader of the Nation of Islam, gave him the name Muhammad Ali.

Historians such as David Remnick (King of the World, 1998) treat Ali as a sportsman who became an international symbol of black pride and of resistance to the Vietnam War, and his reputation became widely admired from the 1970s.
The late 1960s counter-culture rejected the consumer and corporate values of the 1950s and linked personal liberation to political protest.
The Summer of Love of 1967 drew thousands of young people to the Haight-Ashbury district of San Francisco, where a counter-culture of music, drugs and communal living developed.
The Woodstock music festival, held near Bethel, New York, from 15 to 18 August 1969 attracted an estimated crowd of about 400,000 people and became a symbol of the generation.
The Stonewall riots in New York in June 1969 began the modern gay rights movement, after police raided a gay bar in Greenwich Village.
The Students for a Democratic Society and the Black Panther Party were among the political groups that drew on counter-cultural style and protest in the late 1960s.
Timothy Leary, a former Harvard psychologist, told young people in 1966 to turn on, tune in and drop out, and LSD was a central part of the hippie scene until it was banned in California in 1966.

Rock musicians such as Bob Dylan, Jimi Hendrix and the Beatles, whose Sgt Pepper album appeared in 1967, gave the movement its soundtrack, and the film Easy Rider (1969) put the counter-culture on screen.
The festival at Altamont Speedway in California in December 1969, where a man was killed by the Hells Angels during a Rolling Stones concert, was seen as the end of the dream of peace and love.
The Yippies, led by Abbie Hoffman and Jerry Rubin, mixed theatre and politics and took part in the protests at the Democratic Convention in Chicago in 1968.
Most young Americans were not hippies, and the counter-culture provoked a backlash among the silent majority that Nixon appealed to in 1968 and 1972.
The 1960s and 1970s saw minority groups assert their identities and demand equal rights, challenging the idea of a single American culture.
The Chicano movement, led in part by Cesar Chavez and the National Farm Workers Association, organised farm workers in California from the early 1960s.
The American Indian Movement was founded in Minneapolis in 1968 to campaign against discrimination and for treaty rights.
The women's liberation movement disrupted the Miss America pageant in Atlantic City in September 1968, protesting the way women were presented to the public.
The concept of consensus, which historians used to describe the 1950s, was challenged as Americans debated race, gender, sexuality and national identity in the 1960s and 1970s.
The National Farm Workers Association merged with another union to become the United Farm Workers in 1966, and the Delano grape strike and boycott from 1965 won national support for Chavez.
In November 1969 American Indian activists occupied Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay, an occupation that lasted until 1971, and AIM occupied Wounded Knee, South Dakota, in 1973.
The Immigration Act of 1965 and the Bilingual Education Act of 1968 encouraged a more diverse society and gave a legal basis to minority languages in schools.
The Stonewall riots of 28 June 1969 followed a police raid on the Stonewall Inn, and the Gay Liberation Front was founded shortly afterwards; marches commemorating Stonewall began in 1970.
Black Power, the Black Panther Party and the black arts movement asserted pride in African American culture, and the television series Roots (1977) drew about 100 million viewers.
Examiners reward judgements that test the idea of consensus against evidence of conflict within the postwar culture.
Supporters of the consensus view argue that most Americans shared a belief in prosperity, family and anti-communism in the 1950s, as shown by the popularity of the films and television of the period.
Critics of the consensus view argue that the 1950s were marked by conflict over race, sex and loyalty, and that the Red Scare shows the limits of the supposed consensus.
The 1960s counter-culture showed that a sizeable minority rejected the values of the 1950s, but the majority of Americans in 1968 still backed conventional candidates and the war.
Historians differ over whether the collapse of consensus was a sudden break in 1968 or a gradual shift that began with the civil rights movement in the 1950s.
Church membership and religious observance grew strongly in the 1950s, and the government began to express the nation's faith in public symbols.
Church membership rose sharply in the 1950s, with the proportion of Americans belonging to a church reaching a high point by the end of the decade.
Congress added the words under God to the Pledge of Allegiance in June 1954, and a bill of 1956 made In God We Trust the national motto.
Religion was seen by many commentators as a bulwark against communism, and presidents from Eisenhower onwards attended church and spoke of the nation's faith.
New churches were built in the suburbs in large numbers, and church groups and social clubs became central to suburban community life.

Black churches, such as the Baptist congregations of the South, provided the meeting places, leadership and fundraising networks on which the civil rights movement depended, as the Montgomery boycott showed.

Eisenhower said, in the early 1950s, that American government made no sense unless founded on a deeply felt religious faith, and he was baptised soon after taking office in 1953; his comment is often quoted as an example of the civil religion of the period.
Norman Vincent Peale's The Power of Positive Thinking (1952) was a best seller that mixed religion with self-help, and the rise of the megachurch and television ministry followed.
The Cold War gave religion a political role: communism was condemned as atheistic, and the national motto and Pledge changes were part of this.
Graham was a participant in the religious revival and a figure with close ties to the presidents. His relationship to the religious right is covered in the notes on the Moral Majority.
William Franklin Graham was born on 7 November 1918 near Charlotte, North Carolina, and trained as a Baptist minister at Wheaton College in Illinois.
His Los Angeles crusade of September and October 1949 was extended from three weeks to eight after Hearst newspapers reported it widely, and it made him a national figure.
He founded the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association in 1950 and began a radio programme, Hour of Decision, which later reached a worldwide audience.
He held a crusade at Madison Square Garden in New York in 1957, which ran for about sixteen weeks, and he later spoke at large stadium rallies across the world.
He co-founded the magazine Christianity Today in 1956 to provide a conservative evangelical voice alongside the mainstream press.
He became a regular adviser and visitor to presidents from Eisenhower to Nixon, and he preached at presidential events, which brought him close to the centre of political life.
Graham refused to hold segregated crusades from 1953, which was an early sign of his commitment to racial integration, though he was criticised for not supporting King's protests more openly.
Contemporaries were divided: admirers saw him as a unifying figure who spoke to millions, while liberal theologians and critics saw him as a tool of Cold War patriotism.

Historians have judged his influence on modern evangelicalism as very large, while noting that his closeness to presidents, and in particular to Nixon, compromised his independence; tapes released in 2002 caught him making anti-Semitic remarks to Nixon in 1972, for which he later apologised.

Graham's association with Truman began awkwardly in 1950, when he was criticised for revealing his talk with the president, but he became a friend and adviser of Eisenhower, and later of Nixon, whom he supported in 1960 and 1968.

Watergate damaged his standing, and Graham said afterwards that he had been used and that he would avoid partisan politics; he declined to join Falwell's Moral Majority in 1979 and warned against mixing religion with party politics.

He took his crusades abroad, to London in 1954, Moscow in 1982 and Eastern Europe in the 1980s, and he organised the Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization in 1974, which made him a leader of world evangelicalism.
He invited Martin Luther King to pray at his New York crusade of 1957, but he declined to endorse the mass protests of the early 1960s and urged patience.
The Catholic faith of John F. Kennedy became a political issue in 1960, and his response showed the place of religion in public life.
Catholics were a large minority in the United States, and the election of a Catholic president was a question that had been open since the nineteenth century.

Kennedy addressed the Greater Houston Ministerial Association on 12 September 1960, declaring that he believed in an America where the separation of church and state was absolute, and that his religion was his private affair, to quieten Protestant fears that he would take orders from the Pope.

The only Catholic to run for president before him, Al Smith in 1928, had been defeated amid anti-Catholic prejudice, and in 1960 some Protestant ministers, including Norman Vincent Peale, voiced doubts about a Catholic president.
Kennedy won narrowly in November 1960 with strong support from Catholic voters, becoming the first Catholic president, and his election weakened the old Protestant dominance of national politics.

Catholic life in the 1950s was strong, with parish schools, church building and a public figure in Bishop Fulton Sheen, whose television series Life Is Worth Living reached millions between 1952 and 1957.
Catholics and Jews, as well as Protestants, were seen as part of a common American religious tradition, a view popularised by Will Herberg's Protestant, Catholic, Jew (1955).
Conservative Protestant churches grew in influence and used television to reach millions of viewers from the 1960s onwards.
Fundamentalism rejected modernist interpretations of the Bible and held to the literal truth of scripture, a tradition traced to the early twentieth century and the 1925 Scopes trial.
The National Association of Evangelicals, founded in 1942, brought together a broader group of conservative churches that stressed personal conversion and evangelism.
Televangelists such as Jerry Falwell, Pat Robertson and Jim and Tammy Bakker built large audiences through religious broadcasts, using television to raise money and to influence politics.
The Bakker scandal of 1987, in which the PTL ministry was found to have misused funds, damaged the reputation of televangelism and led to Jim Bakker's imprisonment.
Televangelists reached audiences far larger than most local churches could, and their programmes often combined religious teaching with political messages.
The Supreme Court had ruled in 1962 in Engel v Vitale that state-sponsored prayer in public schools was unconstitutional, a decision that provoked strong protest from religious conservatives.
In Abington School District v Schempp (1963) the Supreme Court also ruled against compulsory Bible reading in public schools, and these decisions helped to mobilise conservative Christians.
Roe v. Wade (1973) and the pressure for the Equal Rights Amendment gave conservative Christians further issues, as did the campaign of the singer Anita Bryant against gay rights in Florida in 1977.

Jimmy Carter, a born-again Southern Baptist, was elected in 1976, and the press called 1976 the year of the evangelical, but many evangelicals turned against him by 1980 over abortion and the Equal Rights Amendment.
Pat Robertson founded the Christian Broadcasting Network, and its programme The 700 Club began in 1966; Falwell's Old Time Gospel Hour reached a national audience from the 1970s.
The scandals of Jim Bakker in 1987 and Jimmy Swaggart in 1988 damaged the image of televangelism.
From 1979 conservative Christians became an organised political force, closely associated with the Republican Party and Ronald Reagan.
The Moral Majority was founded in 1979 by Jerry Falwell and others, campaigning against abortion, pornography, the decline of the family and the secular influence in schools.
The Moral Majority mobilised conservative voters and churches before the 1980 election, and its support helped the Republican campaign of Ronald Reagan.
Its influence was greatest in the early 1980s, and it declined after its leaders were embarrassed by the scandals of the late 1980s and the failure of its political strategy.

Falwell, a Baptist pastor from Lynchburg, Virginia, founded the Moral Majority in 1979 with the encouragement of conservative organisers such as Paul Weyrich, and it used direct-mail lists to register voters.

In August 1980 Reagan told a conference of conservative Christians in Dallas that he knew they could not endorse him but that he endorsed them, and the Republican platform of 1980 opposed abortion and backed school prayer.

The movement's agenda included opposing abortion, the Equal Rights Amendment and gay rights, and supporting school prayer and a strong defence; it was seen by critics as a threat to the separation of church and state.

Falwell disbanded the Moral Majority in 1989, but its voters and organisers moved into groups such as Robertson's Christian Coalition (1989), and the religious right remained a lasting part of the Republican coalition.
Television became the main source of news and entertainment in most American homes, and it shaped politics, the Vietnam War and the Watergate crisis.
By 1960 most American homes had a television set, and network news programmes became the principal source of national news for millions of viewers.
The first televised presidential debate, between Kennedy and Nixon on 26 September 1960, was watched by a large audience and is widely credited with shaping the outcome of the election.
The quiz show scandals of 1958, in which contestants were given answers in advance, damaged public trust in television and led to new rules on rigging.
Walter Cronkite's broadcast of 27 February 1968, calling the war a stalemate, was among the reports that influenced public opinion on Vietnam.
The Washington Post's reporting of the Watergate burglary and its cover-up, led by Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, showed the power of the press to expose a presidency.
The Pentagon Papers and other press revelations about government deception strengthened the role of the press as a check on power.
The Public Broadcasting Act of 1967 created the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, which funded the public television network that began broadcasting in 1970.
Advertising expanded rapidly on television and in magazines, and the mass media turned consumer goods and celebrity into central features of public life.
CBS and NBC extended their evening news to thirty minutes in September 1963, and surveys showed that by the mid-1960s television overtook newspapers as the main source of news for most Americans.

Vietnam was called the first television war: the CBS reporter Morley Safer's film of Marines burning the village of Cam Ne in August 1965, the broadcast execution of a Viet Cong prisoner in Saigon during Tet in 1968 and the photograph of a child burned by napalm in 1972 were among the images that shaped opinion.
The Senate Watergate hearings of 1973 were televised live, and the revelation of the White House tapes made the media a central actor in the downfall of Nixon.
The FCC abolished the Fairness Doctrine in 1987, which helped talk radio and partisan broadcasting to grow, and cable television expanded with CNN (1980) and MTV (1981).
The number of students in colleges and universities grew sharply after 1945, supported by the GI Bill and later federal aid, and campuses became centres of protest.
The GI Bill allowed large numbers of veterans to attend college after 1945, and many of them were the first in their families to do so.
The number of college students rose from about 2.6 million in 1950 to more than 8 million by 1970, more than tripling in twenty years.
The California Master Plan for Higher Education of 1960 set out a three-tier system of universities, state colleges and community colleges that became a model for other states.
The Higher Education Act of 1965 provided federal scholarships and loans, and it extended federal support to students and institutions.
The Free Speech Movement at the University of California, Berkeley, began in September 1964 when students protested against restrictions on political activity on campus.
Mario Savio's speech of 2 December 1964 urged students to put their bodies upon the gears of the machine, and the sit-in in Sproul Hall that followed became the movement's best-known protest.
Campus protest spread to many universities through the anti-war movement, and the killings at Kent State University in May 1970 brought mass student strikes across the country.
The GI Bill sent about 2 million veterans to college, and the Sputnik shock led to the National Defense Education Act of 1958 and more federal funding for universities.
The University of California's president Clark Kerr described the huge research university as a multiversity, and Berkeley's size and impersonality were among the Free Speech Movement's grievances.
The Free Speech Movement's occupation of Sproul Hall ended in the arrest of about 800 students on 3 December 1964, and the university conceded to most of the movement's demands soon after.

Students occupied buildings at Columbia University in April 1968, and the shootings at Kent State and at Jackson State College, Mississippi, in May 1970 were followed by strikes at hundreds of campuses.
Examiners reward judgements that weigh the influence of religion, media and education against their limits and against the views of contemporaries and later historians.
Supporters of the religious revival argue that faith gave Americans a common identity against communism and a moral basis for civil rights, as Graham and King both claimed.
Critics argue that the religious right of the 1980s narrowed debate on social issues, and that televangelism encouraged dependence on wealthy donors.
Television made politics more visible and personal, which helped Kennedy and Reagan but also exposed governments to scrutiny over Vietnam and Watergate.
Mass higher education gave many more Americans social mobility, but it also produced campus unrest and debates about the role of universities in politics and society.
Nuclear weapons and the means of delivering them drove military technology after 1945, and the same research often fed the space and computing programmes.
The United States tested the first thermonuclear device, Ivy Mike, at Eniwetok Atoll in the Pacific on 1 November 1952, and the Soviet Union tested a thermonuclear device in August 1953.
Intercontinental ballistic missiles, first the Atlas in 1959 and then the Minuteman from 1962, gave the United States the ability to strike the Soviet Union within about thirty minutes.
Submarine-launched Polaris missiles, first deployed in 1960, gave the United States a second strike capability that could not easily be destroyed in a surprise attack.
The B-52 Stratofortress, a long-range jet bomber that entered service in 1955, carried nuclear weapons on strategic patrols during the Cold War.
Reconnaissance satellites, first successfully used in the Corona programme from 1960, allowed the United States to monitor Soviet missile sites without flying over Soviet territory.
Military research on computers, radar and jet propulsion created technologies that were later adopted in civil aviation and in commercial electronics.

The decision to build the hydrogen bomb in 1950 was opposed by scientists such as J. Robert Oppenheimer and supported by Edward Teller, and Truman approved it in January 1950 after the Soviet atomic test.
Warning of a missile gap in 1960, Kennedy's campaign argued that the Soviet Union was ahead in missiles; in fact the United States held a large lead, which later became clear from satellite pictures.
By the late 1960s the United States had about 1,000 Minuteman missiles, 41 Polaris submarines, and from 1970 multiple warheads (MIRVs) on single missiles, which made arms control more difficult.

Jet fighters and bombers, nuclear submarines (USS Nautilus, 1954) and guided missiles were funded by the Pentagon, and defence contracts supported the aerospace industry in California, Texas and Washington State.
Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative of 1983 sought a space-based missile shield, and it was not built, but its research funded lasers and sensors.
The satellite navigation system GPS began as a military programme with the first satellites launched in 1978.
The Soviet launch of Sputnik in 1957 began a competition in space that the United States came to see as a test of its technological and political strength.
The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, on 4 October 1957, and the American satellite Explorer 1 followed on 31 January 1958.

The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) was created in 1958 to direct the civil space programme, taking over work from the military and from the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics.

The Mercury programme of 1958 to 1963 sent the first American astronauts into space: Alan Shepard became the first American in space on a short suborbital flight on 5 May 1961, and John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth on 20 February 1962.
Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on 12 April 1961, a Soviet achievement that increased pressure on the United States to respond.
In a speech to Congress on 25 May 1961 President Kennedy committed the United States to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the end of the decade.
The Gemini programme of 1965 and 1966 tested the techniques of rendezvous and docking needed for a Moon landing, and it prepared the way for the Apollo missions.

Sputnik caused alarm in the United States about Soviet technology and education, and it led to the National Defense Education Act of 1958 and to the creation of NASA, which Eisenhower signed in July 1958.
The Soviet Union scored further firsts: the first woman in space (Valentina Tereshkova, 1963) and the first spacewalk by Alexei Leonov in March 1965.

Kennedy's Moon decision followed Gagarin and the Bay of Pigs, and he believed the Moon landing was a field in which the United States could win; at Rice University on 12 September 1962 he said the nation chose to go to the Moon, not because it was easy but because it was hard.
NASA chose lunar orbit rendezvous in 1962 as the method for the Moon landing, with a separate lunar module descending from the orbiting command module.
The Soviet Union's Moon rocket, the N1, failed in every test, and the Soviet crewed lunar programme was cancelled.
The Apollo programme was the largest peacetime technological effort the United States had undertaken, and its cost and organisation shaped the Moon landing.
The Apollo programme was managed by NASA with major contractors such as North American Aviation, Grumman, Boeing and IBM, and it employed hundreds of thousands of people across the country.
The Saturn V rocket, the most powerful rocket built until then, was used for the Moon missions and was developed under the direction of Wernher von Braun at the Marshall Space Flight Center.
The Apollo programme cost about 25 billion dollars in the money of its time, and NASA's budget peaked in 1965 and 1966 at about 4 to 5 per cent of federal spending.
The Apollo spacecraft had three parts: the command module, which carried the crew back to Earth, the service module, and the lunar module, which took two astronauts to the surface.
The Apollo 1 fire on 27 January 1967, during a test on the launch pad, killed the astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee and led to a redesign of the spacecraft.
Apollo 8 in December 1968 was the first crewed mission to orbit the Moon, with Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and William Anders, and it returned images of the Earth rising over the lunar horizon.
The Apollo 13 mission of April 1970 was crippled by an oxygen tank explosion, and the crew returned safely, an achievement that was widely praised as a triumph of engineering and teamwork.

NASA administrator James Webb, appointed by Kennedy in 1961, managed the political side and the vast contracting system, and Mission Control in Houston, Texas, directed flights from the Manned Spacecraft Center, opened in 1963.
The Saturn V stood about 110 metres tall, and its first stage burned fuel at a rate of about 13 tonnes a second; it flew thirteen times without a failure that lost a crew.

The Apollo Guidance Computer, developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, was one of the first to use integrated circuits, which made the programme a major customer for the new technology.

Apollo 7 (October 1968) tested the command module in Earth orbit, and Apollo 9 and Apollo 10 in 1969 tested the lunar module, the last mission flying to within about 15 kilometres of the Moon's surface.
Employment in the programme was concentrated in Florida, Texas, Alabama and California, which tied the Sun Belt's growth to federal spending.
Amitai Etzioni's The Moon-Doggle (1964) criticised the programme as a waste, and some in Congress argued that the money would be better spent on poverty.
Apollo 11 was launched from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, landed in the Sea of Tranquillity, and returned its crew to the Pacific.
The crew were Neil Armstrong, commander, Edwin Buzz Aldrin, lunar module pilot, and Michael Collins, command module pilot, who remained in orbit around the Moon.
Apollo 11 was launched on 16 July 1969 from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, and entered lunar orbit on 19 July 1969.
The lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquillity on 20 July 1969, and Armstrong stepped onto the surface several hours later.
Armstrong's first words on the Moon were one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind, and Aldrin joined him on the surface for about two and a half hours of activity.
The crew collected about 21 kilograms of lunar rock and soil, placed a plaque and a flag, and set up experiments that measured the Moon's seismic activity.
Apollo 11 splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on 24 July 1969, and the crew were recovered by the aircraft carrier USS Hornet.
The landing was broadcast live on television to an audience estimated at about 600 million people across the world, making it one of the most watched events in history.
The landing was risky: during the descent computer alarms sounded, and Armstrong took manual control to avoid a boulder field, landing Eagle with very little fuel left.

Armstrong's words as he stepped on to the surface at 10.56 pm Eastern time on 20 July were meant to be one small step for a man, and he said afterwards that he had intended the word a; Aldrin joined him, and the two spent about two and a half hours outside.

The crew left a plaque reading We came in peace for all mankind, and planted an American flag; they did not claim the Moon for the United States, as the 1967 Outer Space Treaty banned national claims.
Nixon spoke to the astronauts by telephone from the White House, and the crew spent 21 days in quarantine after their return in case of lunar germs.
The Soviet Union's Luna 15 probe crashed on the Moon on 21 July 1969 while trying to return samples, and Soviet media played down the Apollo achievement.
The mission came in the same year as the rise of the anti-war movement, and some commentators contrasted the technical triumph with the troubles at home.
The Moon landing ended the race to the Moon, but later missions and the space shuttle showed the limits of US ambitions in space.
The Apollo missions after 11 landed on the Moon in five further expeditions, the last being Apollo 17 in December 1972.
Public interest and political support for the Moon missions declined after 1969, and NASA's budget fell substantially in the early 1970s.
Skylab, the first American space station, was launched in May 1973, and the Apollo-Soyuz mission of July 1975 was the first joint US-Soviet space flight.
The Space Shuttle made its first flight on 12 April 1981, and it was intended to make space access routine and cheaper.

The Space Shuttle Challenger broke up 73 seconds after launch on 28 January 1986, killing all seven crew members, and the failure of the seals in the solid rocket boosters was identified as the cause.
Apollo 12 (November 1969) landed on the Moon after Apollo 11, and Apollo 13's near-disaster in April 1970 made the public aware of the risks.
Apollo 17 in December 1972 was the last crewed lunar mission, and no human has been beyond low Earth orbit since; budget cuts cancelled Apollo 18 to 20.
The Moon landing was a national and global event, a Cold War victory for the United States over the Soviet Union, and it was an image of American technology for the rest of the world.
The Challenger disaster killed the teacher Christa McAuliffe, and the Rogers Commission report of 1986 blamed the O-ring seals and failures in NASA's decision-making.
Computing developed from wartime machines into commercial and military systems, and the microprocessor made the personal computer possible.

ENIAC, completed in 1945 and publicly unveiled in February 1946 at the University of Pennsylvania, was one of the first general-purpose electronic computers, built to calculate artillery firing tables.
The transistor, invented at Bell Laboratories in 1947, replaced the vacuum tube and made computers smaller, faster and more reliable.
IBM's System/360 family of computers, launched in 1964, set a standard for compatible business computers and made IBM the dominant computer firm of the period.
The integrated circuit was developed independently by Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments in 1958 and Robert Noyce at Fairchild in 1959, placing many transistors on a single chip.
Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that the number of components on a chip doubled roughly every year, later revised to about two years, became a guide to the industry's growth.
Intel's 4004 microprocessor, released in 1971, put a complete central processing unit on a single chip.
The ARPANET, a Defense Department network, sent its first message between UCLA and the Stanford Research Institute on 29 October 1969.
Apple's Apple II (1977) and IBM's personal computer (1981) brought computing into homes and offices, and the Santa Clara Valley became known as Silicon Valley, the centre of the industry.
UNIVAC, the first commercial computer in the United States, was delivered in 1951, and it was used by CBS to predict the 1952 presidential election.
Defence money paid for much early computing: the SAGE air-defence system and the Pentagon's research agency ARPA, created in 1958 after Sputnik, funded the ARPANET.
Silicon Valley grew around Stanford University and firms such as Hewlett-Packard, Fairchild Semiconductor and Intel, which were helped by defence contracts and by university research.
Apple's Macintosh of 1984 popularised the graphical interface, and Microsoft supplied the operating system for the IBM PC, which made it the dominant software firm.
Space and military research produced satellites that transformed communications and weather forecasting, and their civilian uses became a justification for the programmes.
TIROS 1, launched on 1 April 1960, was the first successful weather satellite, and it sent back television images of cloud cover.
Telstar, launched on 10 July 1962, was the first active communications satellite to relay live television and telephone signals across the Atlantic.
The Communications Satellite Act of 1962 created the Communications Satellite Corporation, a private-public body that set up the Intelsat global satellite system.
Space technology also contributed to the miniaturisation of electronics, computer memory and materials, although the scale of these spin-offs has been debated by historians.
Examiners reward judgements that weigh the scientific and prestige gains of the programme against its costs and its link to the Cold War.
Supporters argue that the Moon landing was a triumph of American engineering and organisation, and that it inspired advances in computing, materials and medicine.
Critics argue that the programme was driven by Cold War competition rather than scientific need, and that the cost of Apollo could have funded other priorities.
Contemporaries celebrated the landing as a national and global achievement, while some on the left saw the cost as a diversion from poverty and urban problems.

Later historians have stressed that the space race helped to shape the technologies of computing and satellites, but that the lack of follow-up missions suggests the programme was a short burst of Cold War spending.
